Everything here is built on the same two skills: get the meat properly dry and properly salted, then cook it to a number instead of to a guess.

Reverse-Seared Ribeye with Herb Butter⏱ 1 hr 25 min🍽 2 servingsMedium▾

A thick ribeye brought up slowly in a low oven, then blasted in a screaming skillet for 60 seconds a side. You get wall-to-wall pink and a crust like a steakhouse, with almost no way to overshoot.

Date NightCast IronSteakhouse
Prep
15 min
Cook
1 hr
Total
1 hr 25 min
Serves
2 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the steaks

Herb butter and basting

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Pick the right thickness
    This method only works on steaks at least 1½ inches (4 cm) thick, so ask the butcher to cut them for you rather than buying two thin ones. A thin steak will race past medium-rare in the oven before you ever get to sear it. Look for ribeyes with fine white marbling threaded through the muscle, not just a fat cap on the edge, because that intramuscular fat is what bastes the meat from the inside.
  2. Dry brine the steaks
    Pat both steaks completely dry with paper towels, then season all over with the 2 tsp kosher salt, including the edges. Set them on a wire rack over a sheet pan and refrigerate uncovered for at least 45 minutes, or up to 24 hours if you are planning ahead. The salt first pulls moisture to the surface, then that seasoned liquid gets reabsorbed, and the surface dries out — which is exactly what you want for a crust.
  3. Make the herb butter
    Mash the softened butter with the minced garlic, parsley, and chopped thyme in a small bowl until it is evenly streaked green. Scrape it onto a piece of plastic wrap, roll it into a log about 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick, and chill it in the fridge while the steaks cook. Cold, firm butter melts slowly over hot meat instead of instantly turning to a greasy puddle.
  4. Set up a low oven
    Heat the oven to 250°F (120°C) with a rack in the middle. Leave the steaks on their wire rack over the sheet pan — elevating them lets hot air circulate underneath so they cook evenly instead of steaming on one side. Season them now with the black pepper; adding it before the low bake, rather than before a hard sear, keeps it from scorching and turning bitter.
  5. Slow-roast to 115°F
    Slide the pan into the oven and cook until the center of the thickest steak reads 115°F (46°C) on an instant-read thermometer, usually 40 to 55 minutes for 1½-inch steaks. Start checking at 35 minutes and probe from the side, aiming for the true center and avoiding bone or a fat seam. For medium instead of medium-rare, pull at 125°F (52°C); the searing step will add another 10 to 15°F (6 to 8°C).
  6. Rest while the pan heats
    Take the steaks out and let them sit on the counter while you heat the skillet, about 8 to 10 minutes. Pat the surfaces dry one more time with paper towels — the oven will have drawn out a little more moisture and any wetness costs you crust. This pause is not a real rest; it is just efficient use of the time it takes to get cast iron truly hot.
  7. Get the skillet ripping hot
    Set a 12-inch (30 cm) cast-iron skillet over high heat and let it preheat for a full 5 minutes, then add the tablespoon of neutral oil. You want the oil shimmering with the first wisps of smoke curling off it, around 450 to 500°F (230 to 260°C). Turn on the exhaust fan and open a window now, not after the smoke alarm has an opinion about it.
  8. Sear the first side
    Lay the steaks away from you into the pan and press down gently for the first 5 seconds so the whole surface makes contact. Do not touch them again for 45 to 60 seconds — it should roar with a loud, steady sizzle. If the pan is silent, it was not hot enough; if the oil is billowing black smoke, pull the pan off the burner for 20 seconds before continuing.
  9. Flip and sear the second side
    Flip with tongs and sear the second side for another 45 to 60 seconds. Then stand each steak on its fat edge, holding it upright with tongs for 20 to 30 seconds, until that strip of fat turns golden and renders. Rendered fat edge is the difference between a steak that tastes finished and one that leaves a waxy ribbon on your plate.
  10. Butter baste with aromatics
    Drop the heat to medium, add 2 tbsp of the herb butter and the 4 thyme sprigs, and tilt the pan so the butter pools at the low edge. Spoon that foaming butter over the steaks continuously for 45 to 60 seconds. The butter should be tan and nutty smelling, not dark brown and acrid — if it darkens fast, pull the pan off the heat and keep spooning.
  11. Check the final temperature
    Probe the center again: 128 to 130°F (53 to 54°C) means a perfect medium-rare after resting. If you are 5°F short, give the steaks another 20 seconds per side rather than leaving them sitting in the pan, where the bottom will overcook. Trust the thermometer over the clock every single time — thickness varies more than recipes admit.
  12. Rest, slice, and top
    Move the steaks to a warm plate or cutting board and rest for 8 to 10 minutes; because they came up slowly, they need far less resting than a hard-seared steak. Slice against the grain into ½-inch (1 cm) strips, or serve whole. Lay a ¼-inch coin of the cold herb butter on top of each steak and finish with the flaky salt just before it hits the table.
Know when it is done
This is a pull temperature: take the steaks out of the oven at 115°F (46°C). The sear plus carryover adds another 15 to 20°F (8 to 11°C), landing you at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium-rare. Medium is 140°F (60°C); past 150°F (66°C) a ribeye goes gray and dry.
Serve it with
Creamy mashed potatoes and a wedge salad, with a big Cabernet Sauvignon or a cold dark beer.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆The uncovered overnight dry brine is the single biggest upgrade here — 24 hours in the fridge on a rack gives you a noticeably better crust than 45 minutes.
  • ◆No cast iron? A heavy stainless steel skillet works. Nonstick does not — it cannot safely take the 450°F+ (230°C+) heat a real crust needs.
  • ◆Leftover herb butter keeps 2 weeks in the fridge or 3 months in the freezer; slice coins off the frozen log for vegetables, fish, or toast.
  • ◆If your kitchen fills with smoke, you can finish the sear on a grill or outdoor burner — the technique is identical, just hotter and better ventilated.
  • ◆Save the rendered beef fat left in the skillet, strain it into a jar, and use it to roast potatoes; it is the best fat in your kitchen.

Cast-Iron New York Strip with Garlic Butter⏱ 30 min🍽 2 servingsEasy▾

The 30-minute steak dinner worth knowing by heart. One pan, one flip, a shower of foaming garlic-thyme butter, and you are eating in less time than delivery takes.

Weeknight30 MinutesCast Iron
Prep
10 min
Cook
12 min
Total
30 min
Serves
2 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the steaks

Garlic butter baste

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Temper and dry the steaks
    Take the steaks out of the fridge 20 to 30 minutes before cooking and set them on a plate lined with paper towels. A steak straight from the fridge cooks unevenly, giving you a gray band around a cold center. While they sit, pat the surfaces bone dry — every drop of surface moisture has to boil off before browning can even start.
  2. Season generously
    Sprinkle the kosher salt and black pepper over both sides and the edges, holding your hand about 10 inches (25 cm) above so it lands evenly. It will look like more salt than you would put on anything else, and that is correct: a thick steak is mostly interior, and only the surface gets seasoned. Press the seasoning in gently with your palm so it sticks.
  3. Preheat the skillet properly
    Set a 10- or 12-inch (25 to 30 cm) cast-iron skillet over medium-high heat and leave it alone for 4 to 5 minutes. Test it by flicking in a few drops of water — they should skitter and evaporate in about 2 seconds. Cast iron heats slowly and unevenly at first, so this preheat is doing real work, not wasting your time.
  4. Add oil and lay in the steaks
    Pour in the tablespoon of oil and swirl to coat; it should shimmer and thin out within 15 seconds. Lay the steaks in the pan pointing away from you so any splatter goes toward the back, and leave 1 inch (2.5 cm) of space between them. Crowding drops the pan temperature and traps steam, which is how you end up with gray, sad steak.
  5. Sear the first side undisturbed
    Cook for 3½ to 4 minutes without moving, nudging, or peeking more than once. You are listening for a steady, aggressive sizzle — if it goes quiet the pan is too cool, and if the oil throws black smoke turn the burner down one notch. Lift a corner at 3 minutes: the crust should be deep brown and evenly colored, not spotty.
  6. Flip once and sear
    Flip with tongs, never a fork, and cook the second side for 3 minutes. Resist the urge to flip repeatedly; each flip resets the surface temperature and slows crust development on a pan this size. The second side always takes slightly less time because the pan and the meat are both hotter now.
  7. Render the fat cap
    Grab the steaks with tongs and stand them on their fat edge, leaning them against each other or the side of the pan. Hold for 30 to 45 seconds until the fat turns golden and translucent and you can smell it toasting. This step takes almost no time and completely changes how the strip eats — unrendered fat is chewy and cold-tasting.
  8. Butter baste with garlic and thyme
    Lower the heat to medium and add the butter, smashed garlic cloves, and thyme sprigs to the pan. Once the butter foams, tilt the skillet toward you and spoon it over the steaks nonstop for 60 to 90 seconds, aiming for the thickest part. The butter should smell nutty and look tan; if it turns dark brown and smells sharp, take the pan off the burner and keep basting off heat.
  9. Check with a thermometer
    Slide an instant-read thermometer into the side of a steak toward the center: 125°F (52°C) is your pull temperature for medium-rare, 135°F (57°C) for medium. If you are under, keep basting in 30-second bursts and re-check rather than searing harder. Carryover cooking will add 5 to 8°F (3 to 4°C) while the steak rests.
  10. Rest before you cut
    Move the steaks to a cutting board or warm plate and let them rest 8 minutes, loosely tented with foil if your kitchen is cold. Cutting immediately dumps the juices onto the board because the muscle fibers are still contracted and pressurized. Spoon the pan butter and softened garlic cloves over the top and finish with flaky salt.
  11. Slice against the grain
    Find the direction the muscle fibers run — on a strip they run the length of the steak — and cut across them at a slight angle into ½-inch (1 cm) slices. Cutting against the grain shortens those fibers so each bite is tender instead of stringy. Serve right away, and pour any board juices back over the slices.
Know when it is done
These are pull temperatures, not serving temperatures: pull at 125°F (52°C) for medium-rare or 135°F (57°C) for medium. Carryover cooking during the 8-minute rest adds 5 to 8°F (3 to 4°C), so they finish at 130 to 143°F (54 to 62°C).
Serve it with
Crispy roasted potatoes and blistered green beans, with a glass of Malbec.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆If your steaks are thicker than 1½ inches (4 cm), sear both sides then finish in a 400°F (205°C) oven for 4 to 6 minutes so the center catches up without burning the crust.
  • ◆Cook one steak at a time in a 10-inch skillet. Two crowded steaks steam; the first one stays perfectly warm resting while the second cooks.
  • ◆Do not throw away the garlic cloves — they turn sweet and jammy in the butter and are fantastic smashed onto bread.
  • ◆No fresh thyme? Rosemary works, or skip the herbs entirely; the garlic and butter carry the dish on their own.

Filet Mignon with Red Wine Pan Sauce⏱ 50 min🍽 2 servingsMedium▾

The most tender cut on the animal, seared hard and served under a glossy red wine sauce built from the browned bits in the pan. It looks like a special occasion and takes under an hour.

Date NightPan SauceSpecial Occasion
Prep
15 min
Cook
35 min
Total
50 min
Serves
2 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the steaks

Red wine pan sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Prep and tie the filets
    Take the filets out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead and pat them completely dry. If they look uneven or floppy, tie a loop of kitchen twine around the equator of each one so it holds a tall, round shape. A tied filet cooks evenly and gives you a taller cylinder with more surface area to brown.
  2. Season on all surfaces
    Season the filets with the kosher salt and black pepper on the top, the bottom, and all the way around the sides. Filet is lean and mild, so it needs more seasoning than a fatty cut like ribeye to taste like anything. Let them sit at room temperature while you mince the shallot and garlic and heat the oven.
  3. Heat the oven and the pan
    Set the oven to 400°F (205°C) with a rack in the center. Put a 10-inch (25 cm) oven-safe skillet — cast iron or heavy stainless — over medium-high heat for 4 minutes, then add the tablespoon of oil. When the oil shimmers and moves like water in the pan, you are ready.
  4. Sear the flat sides
    Lay the filets flat-side down and sear for 3 minutes without moving them, until a deep brown crust forms. Flip and sear the second flat side another 3 minutes. The pan should sizzle loudly and steadily the entire time; if the sound dies down, your heat is too low and you are stewing the meat.
  5. Roll the sides
    Using tongs, stand each filet on its edge and roll it slowly around the circumference, giving each section about 30 seconds, for 1½ to 2 minutes total. That band around the outside is a third of the steak's surface and skipping it leaves a pale, bland ring. Add the tablespoon of butter in the last 30 seconds and spoon it over the tops.
  6. Finish in the oven
    Transfer the whole skillet to the 400°F (205°C) oven and roast 5 to 8 minutes, depending on thickness. Start checking at 5 minutes with an instant-read thermometer pushed into the center from the side. Pull at 125°F (52°C) for medium-rare or 135°F (57°C) for medium; filet is so lean that even 10 extra degrees turns it chalky.
  7. Rest the steaks
    Move the filets to a plate, tent loosely with foil, and rest for 10 minutes while you build the sauce. Do not skip this — filet holds a lot of water in a tight muscle and cutting early will flood your board. Snip off the twine before serving if you tied them.
  8. Sweat the shallot
    Set the skillet back over medium heat, pouring off all but about 1 tablespoon of fat but leaving every brown speck stuck to the bottom. Add the minced shallot and cook 90 seconds until soft and translucent, then add the garlic and thyme for 30 seconds more. Keep it moving so the garlic perfumes the fat without burning and turning bitter.
  9. Deglaze with red wine
    Pour in the ¾ cup red wine and immediately scrape the bottom of the pan with a wooden spoon; those stuck-on brown bits, called fond, are the entire flavor of the sauce. Let it bubble and reduce by about half, 3 to 4 minutes, until it coats the back of the spoon thinly. If it smells sharply of alcohol, it needs another minute.
  10. Add stock and reduce
    Pour in the ¾ cup beef stock along with any juices that have collected under the resting steaks. Simmer briskly for 5 to 7 minutes until the liquid has reduced to about ⅓ cup and looks syrupy. Drag your spoon through it — the sauce should leave a clear path across the pan bottom for a full second.
  11. Mount with cold butter
    Take the pan off the heat and let it cool for 20 seconds, then whisk in the cold butter cubes one or two at a time until each melts before adding more. This is called mounting, and cold butter is essential — it emulsifies into a glossy sauce instead of separating into an oil slick. Taste and add the ¼ tsp salt, adjusting if your stock was already salty.
  12. Plate and serve
    Spoon 2 to 3 tablespoons of sauce onto each warm plate and set the filet on top rather than drowning it, so the crust stays crisp. Pour any remaining sauce into a small pitcher for the table. Serve immediately, while the sauce is still glossy and warm — it will tighten as it cools.
Know when it is done
Pull at 125°F (52°C) for medium-rare — that is a pull temperature, taken the moment the skillet leaves the oven. Carryover adds 5 to 10°F (3 to 6°C) over the 10-minute rest, so the center settles at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C). Medium is 140°F (60°C) and is as far as filet should ever go.
Serve it with
Roasted asparagus and a potato gratin, with the same red wine you used in the sauce.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Use a wine you would actually drink. Cooking wine is salted and harsh, and in a sauce reduced this far, every flaw gets concentrated.
  • ◆The pan sauce can be made up to 2 days ahead through the stock reduction; reheat gently and whisk in the cold butter right before serving.
  • ◆If the sauce breaks and looks oily, pull it off the heat and whisk in 1 tablespoon of cold stock or water to bring it back together.
  • ◆Filet has almost no fat, so it is the one steak worth wrapping in bacon if you like — secure it with the twine and render the bacon in the pan first.
  • ◆Do not use nonstick for this recipe. You need fond stuck to the pan, and nonstick is specifically designed to prevent it.

Steak au Poivre with Cognac Cream⏱ 55 min🍽 2 servingsMedium▾

A French bistro classic: steak pressed into cracked peppercorns and finished with a cognac cream sauce. The pepper crust goes floral and warm instead of harsh once it hits the hot pan.

Date NightFrenchPan Sauce
Prep
15 min
Cook
25 min
Total
55 min
Serves
2 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the steaks

Cognac cream sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Crack the peppercorns coarsely
    Put the whole peppercorns in a zip-top bag or on a cutting board and crush them with the bottom of a heavy skillet until they are cracked into rough halves and quarters. You want coarse, uneven pieces — not powder, which turns acrid and burns. If you use a grinder, set it to the coarsest possible setting and accept that hand-cracking is genuinely better here.
  2. Sift out the dust
    Shake the cracked pepper in a fine-mesh sieve over the sink for a few seconds to lose the finest powder. That dust is what makes a badly made au poivre taste harsh and dusty rather than warm and aromatic. What stays behind in the sieve is exactly what you want pressed into the meat.
  3. Salt and crust the steaks
    Pat the steaks completely dry and season both sides with the 1¼ tsp kosher salt. Spread the cracked pepper on a plate and press each steak firmly into it, coating both flat sides but leaving the edges mostly bare. Press hard with your palm so the pepper embeds and does not fall off in the pan.
  4. Let them sit 15 minutes
    Leave the crusted steaks on a rack at room temperature for 15 minutes before cooking. The salt begins to dissolve and draw into the meat, and the steaks lose the deep chill that causes uneven cooking. Meanwhile, mince the shallot and measure out the cognac, stock, and cream so everything is within arm's reach — this sauce moves fast.
  5. Heat the skillet
    Set a 10- or 12-inch (25 to 30 cm) heavy skillet over medium-high heat for 4 minutes, then add the oil. Wait for a shimmer with just the barest wisp of smoke, around 425°F (220°C). A stainless or cast-iron pan is required; you need the fond for the sauce.
  6. Sear the first side
    Lay the steaks in and cook undisturbed for 3½ to 4 minutes. You will smell the pepper toasting almost immediately, which is the whole point — heat mellows piperine into something floral. If the pepper starts smelling scorched rather than fragrant, lower the heat one notch.
  7. Flip and add butter
    Flip and cook the second side 3 to 4 minutes, adding the tablespoon of butter in the last minute and spooning the foam over the tops. Check the center with a thermometer: pull at 125°F (52°C) for medium-rare. For steaks thicker than 1½ inches, finish them in a 400°F (205°C) oven for 4 to 5 minutes instead of pushing the sear longer.
  8. Rest the steaks
    Move the steaks to a plate and tent loosely with foil while you make the sauce, about 8 minutes. Any juices that pool go straight into the sauce later, so keep the plate handy. Pour off all but about 1 tablespoon of fat from the pan but leave every browned speck.
  9. Cook the shallot and add cognac
    Lower the heat to medium, add the shallot, and cook 90 seconds until soft. Pull the pan off the burner completely, then pour in the ⅓ cup cognac — off-heat is how you avoid a flare-up, and no, you do not need to flambé anything. Return to the heat and simmer 2 to 3 minutes, scraping up the fond, until the liquid has reduced by about two-thirds.
  10. Build the cream sauce
    Add the ½ cup beef stock and simmer 2 minutes, then stir in the ¾ cup heavy cream and the 1 tsp Dijon. Let it bubble gently for 4 to 5 minutes until it thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon and a finger swiped through leaves a clean line. Stir in any resting juices from the steak plate, then season with the ¼ tsp kosher salt, tasting as you go — the stock and the peppercorn crust already bring salt, so add the last pinch only if it needs it.
  11. Serve immediately
    Spoon a generous puddle of sauce onto each warm plate, set the steak on top or slightly off center, and pour a little extra over one end so the pepper crust stays exposed. This sauce thickens noticeably as it cools, so plate the second it looks right. A few extra cracked peppercorns on top make it look like the bistro version.
Know when it is done
Pull the steaks at 125°F (52°C) for medium-rare, resting to 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C). The sauce should simmer gently around 190°F (88°C), never at a hard boil.
Serve it with
Thin French fries or buttered haricots verts, with a Côtes du Rhône.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆If cognac is not in the house, use brandy, bourbon, or even dry sherry. For an alcohol-free version, use ½ cup extra beef stock plus 1 tsp red wine vinegar for brightness.
  • ◆Always add the spirit off the heat and away from the flame. Alcohol vapor ignites easily, and this is the number one way people get scared out of making pan sauces.
  • ◆Crack the peppercorns up to a week ahead and keep them in a jar; it makes this a genuinely fast weeknight dish.
  • ◆Heavy cream is required — half-and-half and milk will break and curdle when reduced this hard.

Citrus-Marinated Carne Asada Skirt Steak⏱ 2 hr 40 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Skirt steak soaked in orange, lime, garlic, and cumin, then grilled fast over the hottest fire you can build. Charred edges, juicy middle, and it slices into the best taco filling there is.

GrillingMarinadeCrowd Pleaser
Prep
20 min
Cook
10 min
Total
2 hr 40 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the steak

Citrus marinade

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Buy outside skirt if you can
    Outside skirt is thicker, more tender, and more evenly shaped than inside skirt, which is the one most supermarkets sell. Either works, but inside skirt is thinner and needs about 30 seconds less per side. Ask the butcher to peel off the tough membrane if it is still attached; you can also pull it off yourself with a paper towel for grip.
  2. Whisk the marinade
    In a large bowl, whisk together the orange juice, lime juice, olive oil, garlic, cilantro, jalapeño, cumin, oregano, and 1 tsp salt. The oil will not fully emulsify and that is fine — just whisk it again before pouring. Taste it: it should be bright and aggressively garlicky, because most of that flavor stays behind in the bag.
  3. Marinate 2 to 8 hours
    Put the steak pieces in a large zip-top bag or a shallow dish, pour the marinade over, press out the air, and refrigerate for at least 2 hours and no more than 8. Citrus acid tenderizes at first and then starts to break the surface down into mush, so 8 hours is a real ceiling, not a suggestion. Flip the bag once halfway through so every surface gets contact.
  4. Build a screaming hot fire
    For charcoal, light a full chimney and dump the coals into one dense layer; for gas, run all burners on high with the lid closed for 12 to 15 minutes. You want a grate around 550 to 600°F (290 to 315°C) — you should only be able to hold your hand 5 inches above it for about 2 seconds. Skirt steak is thin, so heat is the only thing standing between you and a gray, boiled result.
  5. Dry the steak thoroughly
    Pull the steak out of the marinade and scrape off the clinging bits of garlic and cilantro, which will only burn on the grate. Then pat both sides very dry with paper towels — this is the step people skip and then wonder why they have no char. Discard the used marinade; it has held raw meat and is not safe to reuse as a sauce.
  6. Season and oil the grate
    Season the dried steak with the 1½ tsp kosher salt and 1 tsp black pepper right before it goes on — salting earlier would pull moisture back to the surface you just dried. Fold a paper towel into a pad, soak it with the 2 tsp neutral oil, and wipe the hot grate with it held in long tongs so the meat releases cleanly instead of tearing. Have your platter and tongs ready by the grill, because from here the cooking takes under 6 minutes.
  7. Grill the first side
    Lay the pieces directly over the coals and grill 2½ to 3 minutes without moving them. You want dark char across roughly 70 percent of the surface with the rest deep brown. Flare-ups will happen when fat drips; move the meat to a cooler patch for a few seconds rather than dousing the fire with water.
  8. Flip and finish
    Flip once and grill 2 to 3 minutes more. Check with an instant-read thermometer inserted sideways into the thickest piece: 125 to 130°F (52 to 54°C) is where skirt eats best. Past 140°F (60°C) the muscle fibers seize and skirt turns tough and dry very quickly, so pull early if you are unsure.
  9. Rest on a board
    Move everything to a cutting board and rest for 8 to 10 minutes, uncovered or very loosely tented. Foil wrapped tight will steam the char you just worked for. The juices redistribute in this window, and the internal temperature will drift up another 5°F (3°C).
  10. Find the grain and cut
    Skirt steak has very long, obvious muscle fibers running the length of the strip. First cut the steak crosswise into 3- to 4-inch (8 to 10 cm) sections, then slice each section thinly against those fibers at a slight angle. Cutting with the grain instead of against it is the single most common way people ruin an otherwise perfect skirt steak.
  11. Warm the tortillas and serve
    Lay the corn tortillas directly on the grill grate for 20 to 30 seconds a side until they puff slightly and smell toasty, then stack them in a clean towel so they steam themselves soft. Pile the sliced steak onto a platter and scatter over the ½ cup diced white onion and the ⅓ cup chopped cilantro, with the lime wedges around the edge. Serve immediately while the meat is hot and the tortillas are still pliable — a squeeze of lime right before eating is what ties the whole thing together.
Know when it is done
Pull skirt steak off the grill at 125 to 130°F (52 to 54°C) — a pull temperature, not a serving one. Carryover over the 8- to 10-minute rest adds about 5°F (3°C), finishing at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C). Do not take it past 140°F (60°C) or it will turn tough.
Serve it with
Charred scallions, refried beans, and a cold Mexican lager with lime.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆No grill? A cast-iron skillet or a ridged grill pan over high heat works, but open a window and run the fan — the smoke is real.
  • ◆Marinate in the morning for dinner that night. Anything longer than 8 hours and the citrus turns the surface pale and mealy.
  • ◆Flank steak is the best substitute; it is thicker, so grill it 4 to 5 minutes per side to the same 125 to 130°F (52 to 54°C).
  • ◆Leftovers make outstanding quesadillas and steak-and-egg breakfasts; slice only what you need and keep the rest in a whole piece so it stays juicy.
  • ◆Save a few tablespoons of the marinade in a separate container before it touches the meat, then brush it on after grilling for a fresh citrus hit.

A two-pound ribeye on a long rib bone, cooked low over indirect heat and then finished over the coals. It is a showpiece, and the reverse-sear method makes it far easier than it looks.

Finishing

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Dry brine the day before
    Pat the tomahawk dry, season it all over with the tablespoon of kosher salt, and set it on a rack over a sheet pan in the fridge, uncovered, for 12 to 24 hours. On a steak this thick, a long dry brine is the only way to get seasoning past the surface. The exterior will look dark and slightly leathery when it is ready, which is exactly right.
  2. Temper and season
    Pull the steak out 45 minutes before cooking and let it sit at room temperature; a 2½-inch steak straight from the fridge takes forever to come up and cooks unevenly. Season with the black pepper and garlic powder just before it goes on the grill. Do not add more salt — the dry brine has already handled that.
  3. Set up two heat zones
    For charcoal, bank a full chimney of lit coals against one side of the kettle, leaving the other half empty. For gas, light only the burners on one side and leave the rest off. Close the lid and let the grill stabilize at 250°F (120°C) on the cool side, adjusting the vents until the temperature holds steady for 5 minutes.
  4. Cook indirect, bone toward the fire
    Set the steak on the cool side with the exposed rib bone pointing toward the coals, since the bone can take direct heat and the meat cannot. Close the lid and leave it alone for 40 minutes before checking anything. Every time you lift the lid you lose 5 to 10 minutes of cooking time, so be patient.
  5. Probe toward 115°F
    Start checking at 40 minutes with an instant-read thermometer pushed into the thickest part of the eye, staying at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) away from the bone, which reads falsely cool. Continue until the center hits 115°F (46°C) for medium-rare, typically 50 to 75 minutes total. If your grill drifted hotter than 250°F, it will get there considerably faster — go by temperature, never by the clock.
  6. Rest while you build the sear fire
    Take the steak off and set it on a board while you open all the vents and, for charcoal, add half a chimney of fresh lit coals. You want the direct side blazing at 550°F or hotter (290°C+). This 10-minute pause is free — the steak's temperature evens out while the fire builds.
  7. Oil the steak, not the grate
    Brush the steak lightly on both sides with the 2 tsp of neutral oil and pat off any surface moisture that has beaded up. Oiling the meat instead of the grate puts the fat exactly where the browning happens and reduces flare-ups. Have long tongs and a heatproof glove ready, because you are about to stand over a very hot fire.
  8. Sear over direct heat
    Lay the steak directly over the coals and sear 60 to 90 seconds per side, moving it to a fresh hot spot if the flames get out of control. Flip it two or three times if needed to build even color without burning. You are chasing a deep mahogany crust with dark grill marks, not a black shell.
  9. Sear the fat cap
    Stand the steak on its fat edge using the bone as a handle and hold it there for 30 to 45 seconds until the fat is golden and bubbling. Expect flare-ups here and be ready to lift it away for a second. Rendering that thick ribeye fat cap is what makes the outer edge delicious instead of chewy.
  10. Check the final temperature
    Probe the center again: 130 to 132°F (54 to 56°C) is a finished medium-rare, and 138°F (59°C) is medium. If it is still under 125°F, move it back to the cool side with the lid closed for 3 to 5 minutes rather than searing longer and burning the crust. Remember the temperature will climb another 3 to 5°F (2 to 3°C) as it rests.
  11. Rest, butter, and hold
    Move the steak to a cutting board with a groove, smear the softened butter over the top, and lay the rosemary sprigs across it. Rest 12 to 15 minutes uncovered — a steak this big holds heat easily and will still be hot when you cut it. The butter will melt down into the crust and pick up the rosemary as it goes.
  12. Carve off the bone and slice
    Run a sharp knife along the rib bone to release the entire eye of the steak in one piece, then turn it and slice across the grain into ½-inch (1 cm) strips. Fan the slices back along the bone for presentation and pour the board juices over the top. Finish with the flaky salt right before serving — it should crunch.
Know when it is done
Pull off indirect heat at 115°F (46°C) — that is a pull temperature. The direct sear plus carryover through the 12- to 15-minute rest adds 15 to 20°F (8 to 11°C), landing at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium-rare. Keep the probe 1 inch away from the bone or it will read low.
Serve it with
Grilled asparagus and a loaf of garlic bread, with a bold Zinfandel or Syrah.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆This same reverse-sear works in the oven: 250°F (120°C) until 115°F (46°C) internal, then sear in a ripping-hot cast-iron skillet 90 seconds a side.
  • ◆One tomahawk feeds 2 hungry people or 3 normal ones — a lot of that dramatic weight is bone, so plan on 12 to 14 oz of actual meat per person.
  • ◆Buy a leave-in probe thermometer if you cook big cuts often; opening the grill to check costs you far more than the thermometer does.
  • ◆Do not trim the fat cap before cooking. Render it on the grill and trim any leftover heavy pieces after slicing.
  • ◆Reheat leftovers gently in a 250°F (120°C) oven to 110°F (43°C), then flash them in a hot pan — microwaving turns great steak into gray rubber.

Chicken Fried Steak with Cream Gravy⏱ 55 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Cube steak pounded thin, double-dredged in buttermilk and seasoned flour, and shallow-fried until the crust shatters. The black-pepper cream gravy is built right in the pan from the browned bits, so nothing good gets thrown away.

Comfort FoodCast IronSouthern
Prep
20 min
Cook
25 min
Total
55 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the steaks

Seasoned flour dredge

Buttermilk wash

Black pepper cream gravy

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Pound and season the steaks
    Lay the 4 cube steaks between two sheets of plastic wrap and pound them with the flat side of a mallet to an even ⅜ in (1 cm) — the butcher's tenderizer already did most of the work, so this is about evening out the thickness, not flattening them further. An even steak fries evenly; a lopsided one burns at the thin end while the thick end is still raw. Pat both sides completely dry with paper towels, then season directly with the 1 tsp kosher salt and 1 tsp black pepper. Seasoning the meat itself, not just the flour, is what keeps the inside from tasting bland under all that crust.
  2. Mix the seasoned flour
    In a wide shallow dish, whisk together the 2 cups (250 g) flour, paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, 1½ tsp salt, 1½ tsp black pepper, cayenne if using, and the 1 tsp baking powder. Whisk for a full 20 seconds so the spices are evenly dispersed — pockets of unmixed cayenne or salt will show up as hot or salty bites later. The baking powder is not a mistake: it puffs the coating very slightly as it hits the oil, which is what gives real chicken fried steak that craggy, shattering crust instead of a flat shell.
  3. Whisk the buttermilk wash
    In a second shallow dish, whisk the 1½ cups (360 ml) cold buttermilk with the 2 eggs and the 1 tbsp hot sauce until no streaks of yolk remain, about 30 seconds. Buttermilk is acidic and slightly thick, so it clings to the meat better than plain milk and its tang cuts the richness of the fried crust. The hot sauce adds almost no heat at this dilution — it is there for the vinegar, which brightens the whole plate. Set the two dishes side by side with an empty rack at the end so you have a clean assembly line.
  4. Double-dredge each steak
    Working one steak at a time, press it firmly into the flour and coat both sides, shake off the excess, then dip it fully into the buttermilk and let the drips fall off for 2 seconds. Return it to the flour and press hard this time, scooping flour over the top and packing it on with your palm. That second pass is the whole secret: flour-wet-flour builds a thick, textured layer that survives the fryer, while a single dredge slides off in the oil. Keep one hand for wet and one for dry or you will end up with breaded fingers and a lumpy dish of paste.
  5. Rest the breading 10 minutes
    Set the breaded steaks on a wire rack over a sheet pan and leave them at room temperature for 10 minutes before frying. During that rest the flour absorbs moisture from the buttermilk and turns from dusty powder into a glued-on coating. Skip it and a good third of your crust will float away in the oil the moment the steak goes in. Do not stack them or refrigerate them uncovered for hours — the coating turns gummy and the crust ends up dense.
  6. Heat the oil to 350°F
    Pour the 3 cups (720 ml) oil into a 12 in (30 cm) cast-iron skillet or heavy Dutch oven to a depth of about ¾ in (2 cm) and heat over medium-high until a thermometer reads 350°F (175°C), roughly 6 to 8 minutes. Test it with a pinch of the dredge flour: it should sizzle briskly and float, not sink quietly or burn black in 2 seconds. Below 325°F (163°C) the crust drinks oil and goes greasy; above 375°F (191°C) the outside browns long before the middle is safe. Keep the thermometer clipped on — this is the number you will be chasing all through the fry.
  7. Fry two steaks at a time
    Lower 2 steaks into the oil away from you and do not touch them for 3 minutes; the oil will drop to about 325°F (163°C), which is exactly right, so nudge the burner up to hold it there. You are listening for a steady vigorous sizzle — if it goes quiet, the oil is too cool, and if it screams and smokes, pull the pan off the heat for 30 seconds. Flip once with tongs and fry the second side 2 to 3 minutes more until both sides are deep golden brown. Crowding all 4 steaks in at once crashes the oil temperature and is the single most common way this dish goes soggy.
  8. Cook to 160°F in the center
    Before you pull a steak, slide an instant-read thermometer in from the side into the thickest part and confirm it reads 160°F (71°C). Cube steak has been run through a mechanical tenderizer, which pushes surface bacteria down into the interior, so it cannot be treated like an intact steak you sear rare. If it is browned outside but short of temperature, drop the oil to 325°F (163°C) and give it another minute or two per side. Total fry time is usually 5 to 6 minutes for a ⅜ in (1 cm) steak.
  9. Drain and hold warm
    Move the finished steaks to a clean wire rack set over a sheet pan and slide them into a 200°F (93°C) oven while you fry the second batch. A rack lets air circulate underneath so the bottom crust stays crisp; paper towels trap steam and turn that side soft within a minute. Season the steaks with a small pinch of salt the moment they come out of the oil, when the surface is still hot enough to grab it. Let the oil come back up to 350°F (175°C) before the next two go in.
  10. Build the roux from drippings
    Carefully pour off all but about ¼ cup (60 ml) of the oil, leaving every browned crumb stuck to the bottom of the skillet — that fond is the entire flavor of the gravy. Set the pan over medium heat, sprinkle in the ¼ cup (32 g) flour, and whisk constantly for 2 to 3 minutes until the paste smells nutty and turns the color of peanut butter. Cooking the roux this long removes the raw-flour taste that ruins so many homemade gravies. Scrape the bottom with the whisk as you go so the crumbs lift into the roux instead of scorching.
  11. Whisk in the milk slowly
    Pour in the first ½ cup (120 ml) of the warmed milk and whisk hard until the roux tightens into a smooth thick paste, then add the remaining 2½ cups (600 ml) in three additions, whisking smooth after each. Adding it all at once is how you get lumps — the flour needs to hydrate gradually. Bring it to a bare simmer over medium heat and cook 4 to 6 minutes, whisking often, until it coats the back of a spoon and holds a line when you drag a finger through it. It will thicken a little more off the heat, so stop just before it looks right.
  12. Season hard and serve
    Kill the heat and stir in the 1½ tsp coarse black pepper, ¾ tsp salt, and the 2 tbsp heavy cream if you are using it, then taste and keep adding pepper until you can clearly see and taste it — cream gravy is supposed to be aggressively peppery. If it has gone too thick, loosen it with milk 1 tbsp at a time. Ladle it generously over the steaks right at the table rather than in the kitchen, because the crust starts softening the second the gravy lands. Serve immediately, while the edges are still audibly crisp.
Know when it is done
Fry in oil held at 350°F (175°C), letting it settle to about 325°F (163°C) once the steaks go in. Cube steak is whole-muscle beef that has been mechanically tenderized, which drives surface bacteria into the interior, so it must be cooked through to an internal 160°F (71°C) — it cannot be served pink like an intact steak.
Serve it with
Mashed potatoes with more of the gravy, buttered green beans, and a glass of cold sweet tea or a crisp lager.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆If your market does not sell cube steak, buy a 1¼ lb (570 g) piece of top round or bottom round, slice it into 4 portions, and pound each one to ⅜ in (1 cm) with the spiked side of a mallet.
  • ◆Add 3 tbsp of the buttermilk wash into the seasoned flour and rub it through with your fingertips before dredging. Those shaggy clumps fry into the extra-craggy bits everyone fights over.
  • ◆Keep a clip-on thermometer in the oil the whole time and adjust the burner between batches. Frying by guesswork is the difference between a crisp crust and a greasy one.
  • ◆The gravy thickens as it sits and will be almost solid by the time you sit down. Keep the warm milk nearby and whisk in a splash right before serving.
  • ◆Breaded steaks can be dredged, racked, and refrigerated up to 2 hours ahead. Let them sit out for 15 minutes before frying so the cold does not crash your oil temperature.

Classic Sunday Pot Roast⏱ 4 hr 25 min🍽 6 servingsEasy▾

Chuck roast braised until a spoon goes through it, with carrots, potatoes, and gravy made right in the pot. It ties up an afternoon, but only about half an hour of that is actual work.

Comfort FoodSunday DinnerOne Pot
Prep
25 min
Cook
4 hr
Total
4 hr 25 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the roast

Vegetables

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Salt the roast early
    Pat the chuck roast completely dry and season it all over with the tablespoon of kosher salt and the black pepper. If you have time, do this the night before and leave it uncovered on a rack in the fridge; even 45 minutes on the counter helps. Chuck is a thick, dense cut and salt needs time to move past the surface.
  2. Heat the oven and the pot
    Set the oven to 325°F (165°C) with a rack in the lower third. Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a 6- to 7-quart Dutch oven over medium-high heat until it shimmers and just begins to smoke. A heavy pot with a tight lid is important here — thin pots scorch and loose lids let all your braising liquid escape.
  3. Sear all six sides
    Lower the roast into the pot and sear 4 to 5 minutes per side, including the ends, until every surface is deeply browned — 15 to 20 minutes total. Do not rush this; browning is where the deep, roasty flavor of pot roast actually comes from, and pale meat makes pale, thin gravy. If the pot starts smoking hard or the bits on the bottom look black rather than brown, drop the heat a notch.
  4. Brown the aromatics
    Move the roast to a plate and pour off all but about 2 tablespoons of fat. Add the onion wedges, celery, and smashed garlic and cook 5 to 6 minutes over medium heat, stirring and scraping, until the onions have soft brown edges. The vegetables will release moisture that helps lift the fond off the bottom of the pot.
  5. Cook the tomato paste
    Push the vegetables aside, add the tomato paste to the bare spot, and cook it for 90 seconds, stirring, until it darkens from bright red to brick. Raw tomato paste tastes tinny; cooked paste tastes deep and savory. Stir it through the vegetables once it has darkened.
  6. Deglaze with wine
    Pour in the cup of red wine and scrape the bottom of the pot hard with a wooden spoon until nothing is stuck. Let it bubble and reduce by half, about 4 minutes, so the raw alcohol edge cooks off. Everything you scrape up now becomes gravy later.
  7. Add broth and braise
    Return the roast and any accumulated juices to the pot, add the 3 cups beef broth, and tuck in the thyme sprigs and bay leaves. The liquid should come about two-thirds of the way up the roast, not cover it — pot roast is a braise, not a boil. Bring it to a bare simmer on the stove, then cover and move it to the oven.
  8. Cook low for 2½ hours
    Braise for 2½ hours, flipping the roast once at the halfway point so both halves spend time submerged. Keep the lid on the whole time otherwise; every peek drops the pot temperature. The kitchen will start smelling right after about an hour, which is a good sign but not a doneness cue.
  9. Add the root vegetables
    After 2½ hours, add the carrots and potatoes, nestling them into the liquid around the roast. Cover and return to the oven for 45 to 60 minutes more, until the vegetables are tender when pierced with a paring knife. Adding them late is the difference between vegetables with texture and vegetables that have dissolved into the sauce.
  10. Test for fork-tender
    The roast is done when a fork slides in and twists with almost no resistance and the internal temperature reads 200 to 205°F (93 to 96°C). This is far above any steak temperature and that is the point — at this heat the collagen has melted into gelatin. If it still fights the fork, give it another 30 minutes; undercooked chuck is tough, not rare.
  11. Rest and make the gravy
    Move the roast and vegetables to a platter and tent with foil. Skim the fat off the top of the braising liquid with a wide spoon, bring it to a simmer on the stove, and whisk in the flour-and-water slurry. Simmer 3 to 5 minutes until it thickens enough to coat a spoon, then taste and add the ½ tsp salt as needed.
  12. Pull apart and serve
    Pull the roast into large chunks with two forks, following the natural seams, and discard any big pockets of hard fat. Arrange the meat and vegetables on the platter, ladle the gravy generously over everything, and scatter the parsley on top. Serve straight from the platter with the rest of the gravy on the side.
Know when it is done
Braise at 325°F (165°C) until the roast reads 200 to 205°F (93 to 96°C) and shreds with a fork. Anything under 195°F (90°C) will still be tough.
Serve it with
Crusty bread for the gravy and a simple green salad, with a glass of Merlot.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Pot roast is better on day two. Cool it in its liquid, refrigerate overnight, lift off the solid fat cap, and reheat gently at 300°F (150°C) for 45 minutes.
  • ◆Chuck roast is the right cut — it has the connective tissue that melts into richness. Round or sirloin roasts will come out dry and stringy no matter how long you cook them.
  • ◆No wine? Use an extra cup of beef broth plus 1 tbsp balsamic vinegar or Worcestershire for depth.
  • ◆If it is tough after 3 hours, it is undercooked, not overcooked. Put the lid back on and keep going — chuck needs to pass 200°F (93°C) to give up.
  • ◆This works in a slow cooker too: sear on the stove first, then 8 hours on low, adding the potatoes and carrots in the last 2 hours.

Red Wine Braised Short Ribs⏱ 4 hr 15 min🍽 4 to 6 servingsMedium▾

Bone-in short ribs braised in a whole bottle of red until the meat slumps off the bone. The sauce reduces down into something dark and glossy that tastes like a restaurant made it.

Comfort FoodMake AheadBraise
Prep
30 min
Cook

Total
4 hr 15 min
Serves
4 to 6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the ribs

Braising liquid

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Salt the ribs ahead
    Pat the short ribs dry and season them all over with the tablespoon of kosher salt and the black pepper. Refrigerate uncovered on a rack for 8 to 24 hours if you can, or at minimum leave them at room temperature for 45 minutes. Short ribs are thick and heavily marbled, and early salting is what gets seasoning into the middle.
  2. Dredge lightly in flour
    Just before searing, roll each rib in the ¼ cup flour and shake off the excess so only a thin dusting remains. The flour helps build a deeper crust and slightly thickens the finished sauce. Do not do this ahead — sitting flour turns gummy and will not brown properly.
  3. Sear in batches
    Heat the oil in a 7-quart Dutch oven over medium-high until shimmering, then sear the ribs in two or three batches, 2 to 3 minutes per side, until every side is deep brown. Never crowd the pot; ribs packed together drop the temperature and steam instead of searing. Move each finished batch to a plate and expect the whole process to take 20 minutes.
  4. Heat the oven and cook the vegetables
    Set the oven to 325°F (165°C). Pour off all but 3 tablespoons of fat, add the onions, carrots, celery, and garlic to the pot, and cook over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes until softened and lightly browned at the edges. Scrape the bottom as they release moisture — the fond lifting off is exactly what you want.
  5. Darken the tomato paste
    Stir in the 3 tbsp tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes, spreading it across the bottom of the pot so it toasts. It should go from bright red to a deep brick color and smell sweet rather than raw. This small step adds a surprising amount of body to the finished sauce.
  6. Reduce the wine hard
    Pour in the entire bottle of red wine and bring it to a strong simmer, scraping the bottom clean. Reduce it by about half, 15 to 20 minutes — a full 750 ml takes real time to come down in a wide pot, so do not cut this short. You will know it is there when the harsh alcohol smell is gone and the liquid smells like fruit and wood. Skipping this reduction is the reason home braises sometimes taste sour and thin.
  7. Add the ribs and stock
    Return the ribs and any juices to the pot, bone-side up, and add the 3 cups beef stock and the tied herb bundle. The liquid should come about three-quarters of the way up the meat; add a splash more stock if needed but do not submerge them. Bring everything to a bare simmer on the stovetop.
  8. Braise covered for 2½ hours
    Cover with a tight lid and transfer to the 325°F (165°C) oven for 2½ to 3 hours. Check once at the 2-hour mark and add a little water if the level has dropped below halfway up the ribs. The liquid should be barely burbling when you peek, not boiling — if it is boiling, lower the oven by 25°F.
  9. Test for doneness
    The ribs are ready when the meat has pulled back from the bone by about ½ inch (1 cm) and a fork twists in it with no resistance, around 200 to 205°F (93 to 96°C) internal. If they are still firm, they need more time, not more heat. Fully done short ribs will almost slide off the bone when lifted with tongs.
  10. Rest and defat the sauce
    Carefully lift the ribs out onto a platter and tent with foil. Strain the braising liquid through a fine-mesh sieve into a wide saucepan, pressing gently on the vegetables to extract flavor, then discard the solids and herb bundle. Let it settle 5 minutes and skim the fat off the top with a wide spoon or a fat separator — there will be a lot.
  11. Reduce and finish the sauce
    Simmer the strained liquid over medium-high heat for 10 to 15 minutes until it has reduced to about 2 cups and coats the back of a spoon. Take it off the heat, whisk in the red wine vinegar and the cold butter until glossy, and taste for salt. The vinegar is not optional — it lifts a sauce this rich out of heaviness.
  12. Serve over something soft
    Spoon the ribs over creamy polenta, mashed potatoes, or buttered egg noodles and ladle the sauce generously over the top. Finish with the ½ tsp flaky salt and scatter over the 2 tbsp chopped parsley — after three hours of dark, wine-heavy braising, that green freshness is what keeps the plate from tasting one-note. Serve in shallow bowls so nobody loses any of the sauce.
Know when it is done
Braise at 325°F (165°C) until the meat reads 200 to 205°F (93 to 96°C) and a fork twists freely. Bring the finished sauce to a simmer of about 200°F (93°C) to reduce.
Serve it with
Creamy parmesan polenta and a glass of the same Cabernet you braised with.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make this a day ahead. Cool the ribs in their strained liquid, refrigerate overnight, lift off the solid fat cap, and reheat covered at 325°F (165°C) for 30 minutes — the flavor is noticeably better.
  • ◆Ask for English-cut short ribs, thick blocks with one bone each, not flanken-cut cross-sections, which are meant for grilling.
  • ◆Use a dry, full-bodied red you would drink. It reduces to a quarter of its volume, so anything unpleasant becomes four times as unpleasant.
  • ◆If the finished sauce tastes flat, it needs acid or salt, not more cooking. Add vinegar ½ teaspoon at a time until it snaps into focus.
  • ◆The strained braising vegetables can be blended with a ladle of sauce into a thick purée if you would rather not waste them.

Beef Stroganoff over Egg Noodles⏱ 55 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Quick-seared strips of sirloin in a sour cream and mushroom sauce, spooned over buttered egg noodles. The whole thing comes together in under an hour and tastes like it took all day.

WeeknightComfort FoodSkillet
Prep
20 min
Cook
35 min
Total
55 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the beef

Sauce

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Slice the beef properly
    Firm the beef in the freezer for 15 minutes, which makes thin slicing far easier, then cut it across the grain into strips about ¼ inch (6 mm) thick and 2 inches (5 cm) long. Cutting against the grain shortens the muscle fibers so quick-cooked beef stays tender. Pat the strips very dry and season with the 1 tsp salt and ½ tsp pepper.
  2. Get the pan very hot
    Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a large 12-inch (30 cm) skillet over high heat until it shimmers and just wisps smoke. A large pan matters here — you need surface area so the beef browns instead of steaming. Set a plate next to the stove because the beef comes out fast.
  3. Sear the beef in two batches
    Add half the beef in a single layer with space between the pieces and sear 45 to 60 seconds per side, just until browned. Do not cook it through; it will finish in the sauce at the end and overcooked sirloin turns to leather. Move it to the plate and repeat with the second batch, adding a little more oil if the pan is dry.
  4. Brown the mushrooms
    Lower the heat to medium-high, add 2 tbsp of the butter, and add the sliced mushrooms in as close to a single layer as you can. Let them sit undisturbed for 3 minutes so they brown, then stir and cook 5 to 6 minutes more until they have released their liquid and it has cooked away. Mushrooms that are pale and swimming will make a watery, gray sauce.
  5. Soften the onion and garlic
    Add the remaining 2 tbsp butter and the sliced onion and cook 5 to 6 minutes over medium heat until soft and golden at the edges. Stir in the minced garlic for the last 45 seconds, just until it smells sweet. Scrape the bottom of the pan as you go to lift up the browned beef fond.
  6. Boil the noodles
    Around now, bring 4 quarts (4 L) of water to a rolling boil in a large pot and add the 1 tbsp kosher salt — noodles seasoned in the water taste seasoned all the way through, and no amount of sauce fixes bland pasta. Cook the egg noodles according to the package, usually 7 to 9 minutes, then drain them and toss with the 2 tbsp butter so they do not clump. Timing the noodles to finish with the sauce keeps them from turning gluey while they wait in the colander.
  7. Make the roux
    Sprinkle the 3 tbsp flour over the mushrooms and onions and stir constantly for 90 seconds so the raw flour taste cooks out. The mixture will look dry and pasty and cling to the vegetables, which is exactly right. This is what will give the sauce its body.
  8. Add the stock gradually
    Pour in about a third of the beef stock and stir hard until it thickens into a smooth paste, then add the rest in two more additions, stirring between each. Adding liquid in stages is how you avoid lumps — dumping it all in at once almost guarantees them. Bring it to a gentle simmer and cook 4 to 5 minutes until it thickly coats a spoon.
  9. Season the sauce
    Stir in the Dijon mustard and Worcestershire sauce and taste. It should taste savory and slightly sharp; add the ½ tsp salt as needed, remembering that sour cream will mute it slightly. If the sauce is thicker than heavy cream, loosen it with a splash of stock.
  10. Temper in the sour cream
    Take the pan completely off the heat and let it cool for 60 seconds. Whisk a ladle of the hot sauce into the room-temperature sour cream in a small bowl, then stir that mixture back into the pan. Sour cream curdles above about 180°F (82°C), and tempering it like this is the only reliable way to keep the sauce smooth.
  11. Return the beef and warm through
    Add the seared beef and all its resting juices back to the pan and set it over low heat for 2 to 3 minutes, just until everything is hot. Do not let it boil again or the sour cream will break and the beef will toughen. The beef should be barely pink in the center when you serve it.
  12. Serve over the noodles
    Spoon the stroganoff over the buttered egg noodles in wide shallow bowls and scatter the dill or parsley on top. Serve immediately — the sauce is at its best right off the heat and will tighten as it sits. A crack of black pepper at the table finishes it.
Know when it is done
Keep the sauce below 180°F (82°C) once the sour cream goes in or it will curdle. The beef should reach 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) and no more.
Serve it with
A crisp cucumber and dill salad, with a dry Riesling or a light Pinot Noir.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Full-fat sour cream only. Low-fat and nonfat versions have less fat to stabilize them and will split the moment they meet the hot sauce.
  • ◆Take the sour cream out of the fridge when you start cooking. Cold dairy hitting a hot pan is the other main cause of a broken sauce.
  • ◆Ground beef makes a fine weeknight shortcut version: brown 1½ lb (680 g) all the way to 160°F (71°C) — ground beef has no safe medium-rare — then drain the fat and continue from the mushroom step.
  • ◆Leftovers reheat best on the stove over low heat with a splash of stock. Microwaving on high will break the sauce every time.
  • ◆A splash of brandy or dry sherry, about 3 tbsp, added to the mushrooms before the flour is a traditional and very good addition.

Salisbury Steak with Mushroom Gravy⏱ 1 hr🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Seasoned beef patties simmered in a deep onion-mushroom gravy. This is old-school American diner food done properly, and it is genuinely one of the best cheap dinners going.

WeeknightComfort FoodBudget
Prep
15 min
Cook
45 min
Total
1 hr
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the patties

Mushroom onion gravy

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Make a panade
    Stir the ½ cup panko and ⅓ cup milk together in a large bowl and let it sit for 5 minutes until the crumbs have drunk up all the liquid and swelled into a thick paste. This is called a panade: the starch traps moisture and physically gets between the meat proteins so they cannot squeeze into a tight, springy mass. It is the single reason a diner Salisbury steak stays tender even after ten minutes of simmering in gravy. Without it, you get a dense meatball with a bouncy, sausage-like bite.
  2. Mix the patty base
    Add the egg yolk, grated onion, ketchup, 2 tsp Worcestershire, 1¼ tsp salt, and ½ tsp pepper to the panade and whisk until smooth. Grating the onion instead of chopping it releases juice and eliminates raw crunchy bits in the finished patty. Having everything combined before the beef goes in means less handling of the meat.
  3. Combine gently
    Add the ground chuck and mix with your hands or a fork just until no dry streaks remain, about 30 seconds. Overworking ground beef develops the proteins and gives you a bouncy, sausage-like texture. Stop while the mixture still looks a little rough.
  4. Shape four ovals
    Divide the mixture into 4 equal portions, roughly 7 oz (200 g) each, and shape each into an oval about 5 inches long and ¾ inch (2 cm) thick. Press a shallow dimple into the center of each with your thumb so they do not dome up as they cook. Set them on a plate and chill for 10 minutes if your kitchen is warm.
  5. Sear the patties
    Heat the tablespoon of oil in a 12-inch (30 cm) skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering, then add the patties without crowding. Sear 3 to 4 minutes per side until a solid brown crust forms, flipping only once. They will not be cooked through and should not be — they finish in the gravy.
  6. Set the patties aside
    Move the seared patties to a plate and pour off all but about 1 tablespoon of fat, leaving the browned bits behind. Those bits are the flavor base of the gravy, so do not wipe the pan out. Lower the heat to medium.
  7. Brown the mushrooms
    Add the 3 tbsp butter and the sliced mushrooms and cook 6 to 7 minutes, stirring occasionally, until they have given up their water and started to brown. They will look sad and shrunken halfway through, which is normal — keep going until the pan is dry again. Browned mushrooms taste meaty, boiled ones taste like nothing.
  8. Soften the onions
    Add the sliced onion and cook 6 to 8 minutes more, scraping the fond off the bottom as the onions release moisture. You are looking for limp, golden onions with browned edges, not translucent ones. This is where a diner-style gravy gets its sweetness.
  9. Make the roux
    Sprinkle the 3 tbsp flour over the vegetables and stir constantly for 90 seconds, coating everything evenly. The mixture will look dry and clumpy, which is exactly what you want before liquid goes in. Cooking the flour now prevents the pasty raw-flour taste that ruins a lot of homemade gravy.
  10. Build the gravy
    Pour in the beef broth in three additions, stirring smooth after each one, then add the 1 tbsp Worcestershire and the Dijon. Bring it to a simmer and cook 3 to 4 minutes until it thickens to the consistency of heavy cream. Taste and add the ½ tsp salt if it needs it.
  11. Simmer the patties through
    Nestle the patties and any juices from the plate back into the gravy, spooning some over the tops. Cover and simmer gently on low for 10 to 12 minutes, flipping once at the halfway point. Ground beef must reach 160°F (71°C) in the center for safety — check with an instant-read thermometer rather than guessing.
  12. Rest briefly and serve
    Take the pan off the heat and let it sit 3 to 4 minutes so the gravy thickens slightly and the patties settle. Serve over mashed potatoes or buttered egg noodles with plenty of gravy spooned over the top. Scatter the 2 tbsp chopped parsley over everything — a brown plate of beef and gravy needs that bit of green far more than it needs another garnish, and the fresh, grassy note cuts the richness.
Know when it is done
Ground beef must reach 160°F (71°C) in the center — this is a food-safety temperature, not a preference. The gravy should simmer gently, around 190°F (88°C).
Serve it with
Buttery mashed potatoes and steamed peas, with a cold amber ale.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆80/20 ground chuck is the right choice. Leaner beef, 90/10 or above, makes dry, crumbly patties no matter how good your panade is.
  • ◆The patties can be shaped up to a day ahead and kept covered in the fridge, which actually helps them hold together in the pan.
  • ◆This freezes beautifully. Cool completely, freeze patties and gravy together in a container for up to 3 months, and reheat covered at 325°F (165°C).
  • ◆If the gravy gets too thick while simmering, thin it with a splash of broth; if it is thin, uncover and simmer 3 minutes longer.
  • ◆For a richer version, swap 1 cup of the beef broth for a dark beer or ½ cup dry red wine plus ½ cup broth.

Marinated London Broil⏱ 6 hr 45 min🍽 4 to 6 servingsEasy▾

A lean top round soaked overnight in soy, balsamic, and garlic, then broiled hard and sliced paper-thin. It feeds a crowd for very little money and makes outstanding sandwiches the next day.

BudgetMake AheadCrowd Pleaser
Prep
15 min
Cook
20 min
Total
6 hr 45 min
Serves
4 to 6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the beef

Marinade

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Understand the cut
    London broil is a cooking method, not a cut — most stores sell top round or sometimes flank under that name. It is very lean and has almost no marbling, which means two rules are absolute: do not cook past medium-rare, and slice it as thin as you possibly can. Everything else in this recipe exists to support those two rules.
  2. Score the surface
    Using a sharp knife, cut a shallow diamond crosshatch about ⅛ inch (3 mm) deep into both sides of the meat, spacing the cuts 1 inch (2.5 cm) apart. Scoring gives the marinade more surface to work on and helps the lean muscle stay flat under high heat instead of curling. Keep the cuts shallow so you do not create channels for juice to escape.
  3. Whisk the marinade
    In a bowl, whisk together the soy sauce, balsamic vinegar, olive oil, lemon juice, Worcestershire, honey, garlic, oregano, and 1 tsp pepper until the honey has dissolved. The soy provides salt, the acid tenderizes the surface, and the honey helps it brown under the broiler. Taste it — it should be salty and tangy, almost too strong on its own.
  4. Marinate 6 to 24 hours
    Put the beef in a zip-top bag, pour in the marinade, press out the air, and refrigerate for at least 6 hours and up to 24. Flip the bag two or three times so both sides get equal contact. This cut genuinely needs the full time — 30 minutes will do almost nothing to a piece of meat this dense.
  5. Bring it to room temperature
    Pull the beef out of the fridge 45 minutes before cooking and leave it in the marinade on the counter. A cold, dense roast under a broiler will burn on the outside before the center gets anywhere near done. Meanwhile, set an oven rack so the top of the meat will sit about 4 inches (10 cm) below the broiler element.
  6. Preheat the broiler fully
    Turn the broiler to high and let it preheat for a full 10 minutes with the pan you will use already inside. A screaming-hot pan means the underside starts browning immediately instead of steaming. Use a heavy sheet pan or a cast-iron skillet, never glass, which can shatter under a broiler.
  7. Dry and season the meat
    Lift the beef out of the marinade and pat it thoroughly dry with paper towels, wiping away any garlic bits that would burn. Season both sides with the 1 tsp kosher salt and 1 tsp black pepper. Discard the used marinade — it has held raw meat and should not be reused.
  8. Broil the first side
    Set the meat on the preheated pan and broil for 7 to 9 minutes without opening the door. You are looking for a dark, well-browned surface with some charred spots at the edges. If your broiler is weak or your rack sits lower than 4 inches, this may take 10 or 11 minutes; watch through the window rather than trusting the clock.
  9. Flip and finish
    Turn the meat with tongs and broil the second side 6 to 8 minutes more, then start checking the internal temperature at the thickest point. Pull it at 125 to 128°F (52 to 53°C) for medium-rare — a pull temperature, since carryover will carry it up during the rest. This cut has no fat to protect it, so 140°F (60°C) is already dry and 150°F (66°C) is beyond saving.
  10. Rest a full 10 minutes
    Move the beef to a cutting board and rest it for 10 minutes, tented loosely with foil. Lean meat holds its juices precariously, and cutting into it early will leave a puddle on the board and a dry steak on the plate. The temperature will drift up about 5°F (3°C) during the rest.
  11. Slice paper-thin against the grain
    Find the direction the muscle fibers run, then hold your knife at a 45-degree angle and slice across them as thinly as you can manage, ⅛ to ¼ inch (3 to 6 mm). Thin slicing across the grain is what turns an inexpensive, chewy cut into something tender. Thick slices of top round will feel like leather no matter how perfectly you cooked it.
  12. Dress with the board juices
    Tilt the cutting board and spoon the collected juices back over the sliced meat, which reseasons it and keeps the surface glossy. Serve immediately on a warm platter. If you want a sauce, a spoonful of chimichurri or a simple horseradish cream is perfect here.
Know when it is done
Pull at 125 to 128°F (52 to 53°C) for medium-rare — a pull temperature. Carryover adds about 5°F (3°C) over the 10-minute rest, finishing at 130 to 133°F (54 to 56°C). Lean top round is unpleasantly dry above 140°F (60°C).
Serve it with
Roasted potatoes and a sharp arugula salad, with a Chianti or a dry rosé.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆A sharp, long knife matters more here than in any other recipe in this chapter. A dull knife tears lean beef into shreds instead of slicing it.
  • ◆No broiler you trust? Grill it over high direct heat for the same times, or sear in a cast-iron skillet and finish in a 425°F (220°C) oven.
  • ◆Leftovers make the best steak sandwiches — pile the cold thin slices on a roll with horseradish mayo, arugula, and red onion.
  • ◆Do not marinate past 24 hours. The acid will start breaking down the surface into a soft, mushy layer that never browns properly.

Santa Maria Grilled Tri-Tip⏱ 2 hr 15 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Central California barbecue at its simplest: salt, pepper, garlic, and a hot fire. Tri-tip has a beefy, almost mineral flavor and slices into thin, juicy fans if you read the grain right.

GrillingBarbecueCrowd Pleaser
Prep
15 min
Cook
45 min
Total
2 hr 15 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the roast

Santa Maria rub

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Trim and inspect the roast
    Trim the fat cap down to about ¼ inch (6 mm) and remove any silverskin, which is the thin, shiny membrane that never renders and turns rubbery. Notice the shape: a tri-tip is a triangle with a thick end and a thin tail, which is why the tail always cooks faster. Pat it completely dry before seasoning.
  2. Mix the Santa Maria rub
    Stir together the kosher salt, black pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, crumbled rosemary, and cayenne in a small bowl. Traditional Santa Maria rub is nothing but salt, pepper, and garlic, and the rest here is a light modern touch. Coarse pepper is important — it forms a crust rather than dissolving in.
  3. Season and let it rest
    Coat the tri-tip on all sides with the rub, pressing it in firmly with your hands so it adheres. Let it sit on a rack at room temperature for 1 hour, or refrigerate uncovered for up to 24 hours for a deeper dry brine. You will see the surface go from dry to wet to tacky as the salt does its work — tacky is when it is ready.
  4. Build a two-zone fire
    For charcoal, bank a full chimney of lit coals to one side; for gas, light half the burners on high and leave the other half off. Close the lid and let the grill settle so the indirect side reads about 350°F (175°C). Red oak is the traditional Santa Maria wood, and a couple of chunks on the coals is a genuine upgrade if you can find it.
  5. Start on the cool side
    Brush the tri-tip with the 2 tsp oil and set it on the indirect side, fat cap up, with the thin tail pointed away from the fire. Close the lid and cook for 20 to 30 minutes without opening it. Keeping the thin end away from the heat is how you avoid a well-done tail attached to a rare center.
  6. Cook to 115°F
    Start checking at 20 minutes with an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part of the roast. Continue until it reads 115°F (46°C), which usually takes 25 to 35 minutes total at 350°F. Grill temperatures vary a lot, so the thermometer decides when to move on, not the clock.
  7. Sear over direct heat
    Move the roast directly over the coals and sear 2 to 3 minutes per side, rotating as needed to build an even dark crust. Expect flare-ups from the rendering fat cap — slide the meat to a cooler spot for a few seconds rather than fighting the flames. The rub will darken noticeably, which is exactly what you want.
  8. Check the final temperature
    Pull the tri-tip when the thickest part reads 130°F (54°C) for medium-rare or 138°F (59°C) for medium. Remember that the thin tail will already be 10 to 15 degrees hotter, which is convenient if you are feeding people who like different doneness. Anything past 145°F (63°C) makes this cut noticeably chewy.
  9. Rest 15 minutes
    Move the roast to a cutting board and rest it uncovered for 15 minutes. This is a big, dense piece of meat and needs the full time for the juices to settle back into the fibers. Do not tent it tightly with foil, which will steam the crust you just built.
  10. Find where the grain changes
    Look closely at the surface: a tri-tip has two muscle groups whose fibers run in different directions, meeting roughly at the middle of the triangle. Cut the roast in half along that line first, separating the two sections. This one step is what separates good tri-tip from tough tri-tip, and almost everybody gets it wrong the first time.
  11. Slice each half against its grain
    Turn each half so its fibers run left to right, then slice across them at a slight angle, about ¼ inch (6 mm) thick. You will notice the two halves need to be turned differently, which is the whole point of separating them. Fan the slices out on a warm platter and pour the board juices over the top.
  12. Serve family style
    Santa Maria style means the meat goes on the table on a big board and everyone builds their own plate, so put out whatever sides you have made — pinquito or pinto beans, grilled garlic bread, and a fresh salsa are the traditional three. Serve immediately while the slices are hot and the crust is still crisp. Any leftovers should be kept in a whole unsliced piece and cut to order, because sliced beef dries out in the fridge within a day.
Know when it is done
Move to the sear at 115°F (46°C), then pull off the grill at 130°F (54°C) for medium-rare — that is a pull temperature. Carryover adds 3 to 5°F (2 to 3°C) over the 15-minute rest, finishing at 133 to 135°F (56 to 57°C). Above 145°F (63°C) tri-tip gets tough.
Serve it with
Pinquito beans, grilled garlic bread, and a big Zinfandel.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆This works in the oven too: 350°F (175°C) until 115°F (46°C) internal, roughly 30 to 40 minutes, then sear in a screaming-hot cast-iron skillet for 90 seconds a side.
  • ◆Tri-tip is common in the western United States and harder to find elsewhere; ask the butcher for a bottom sirloin triangle roast and they will know what you mean.
  • ◆The dry rub can be mixed in a big batch and stored in a jar for 6 months — it is excellent on steaks, chicken, and potatoes.
  • ◆Do not slice the whole roast at once if you are not serving it all. Sliced beef dries out within minutes on a platter.
  • ◆If you cannot find red oak, a chunk of hickory or a couple of soaked oak chips in a foil packet will get you close.
