Coconut Shrimp with Sweet Chili Sauce⏱ 55 min (includes 15 min chill)🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Big shrimp in a crunchy coconut and panko jacket, fried golden and dunked in sweet chili sauce. They taste like a vacation and disappear faster than you can fry them.

AppetizerFriedCrowd Pleaser
Prep
25 min
Cook
15 min
Total
55 min (includes 15 min chill)
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the shrimp

Dipping sauce and serving

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Stir together the sauce
    Whisk the 1/2 cup sweet chili sauce, apricot preserves, 1 tbsp lime juice, and 1/4 tsp red pepper flakes in a small bowl until smooth, then stir in the cilantro. The preserves add body so the sauce clings to the shrimp instead of running off, and the lime keeps it from being cloying. Set it aside at room temperature — cold sauce dulls the flavor.
  2. Prep and dry the shrimp
    Peel the shrimp but leave the tail segment on, which gives you a handle for dipping and eating. Butterfly each one by cutting about halfway through along the back curve and pressing it open, which makes them lie flat and look twice as big. Blot them completely dry on paper towels — wet shrimp will not hold a breading.
  3. Set up three stations
    In the first shallow dish, whisk the 1/2 cup flour with the 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp black pepper, and cayenne. In the second, beat the 2 eggs with the 2 tbsp coconut milk until completely uniform. In the third, toss the 1 1/2 cups shredded coconut with the 1 cup panko — the panko is not traditional but it keeps the coconut from burning and adds real crunch.
  4. Bread with one wet hand
    Hold each shrimp by the tail, dredge in flour and shake off every bit of excess, dip in the egg and let it drip for 3 seconds, then press firmly into the coconut mixture on both sides. Use one hand for the dry dishes and one for the egg or you will end up with clubs of batter on your fingers. Set the breaded shrimp on a parchment-lined sheet pan without touching.
  5. Chill the breading
    Refrigerate the breaded shrimp uncovered for 15 minutes before frying, or up to 4 hours. This lets the flour hydrate and the coating set so it does not slide off in the oil. It is the same reason breaded cutlets rest before they cook.
  6. Heat the oil to temperature
    Pour the 6 cups oil into a heavy 4 qt (3.8 L) pot so it is about 2 in (5 cm) deep and no more than a third of the way up the sides. Clip on a thermometer and heat to 350°F (175°C) over medium-high, which takes about 10 minutes. This is a lower temperature than most frying because sweetened coconut contains sugar and will darken fast.
  7. Test with one shrimp
    Fry a single shrimp first and watch it: it should bubble vigorously the second it hits the oil and turn light gold in about 60 seconds. If it browns instantly, drop the heat; if it sits quietly and soaks, raise it. That one test shrimp saves the whole batch.
  8. Fry in small batches
    Lower 5 or 6 shrimp into the oil at a time, never crowding, and fry 2 to 3 minutes total, turning once with a spider strainer after about 90 seconds. They are done when the coconut is a warm golden brown and the shrimp have curled into a loose C. Let the oil come back up to 350°F (175°C) between batches, checking the thermometer each time.
  9. Drain on a rack
    Lift the shrimp onto a wire rack set over a sheet pan and season them with the reserved 1/2 tsp kosher salt right away, dividing it across the batches. Salt sticks to hot fried food and slides off cold, so this has to happen in the first few seconds. Paper towels trap steam under the shrimp and turn the bottom coating soggy within a minute. Keep finished batches warm in a 200°F (95°C) oven for up to 20 minutes.
  10. Check one for doneness
    Cut into the thickest shrimp of the first batch — it should be opaque white all the way through with no gray translucent center, which is 145°F (63°C). Large shrimp cook in under 3 minutes, so if the coating is dark before the inside is done, your oil is too hot. Adjust and keep going.
  11. Serve hot with the sauce
    Pile the shrimp on a platter with the dipping sauce in the middle and the lime wedges around the edge. These are best within ten minutes of leaving the oil, while the coconut still crackles. If they do soften, five minutes on a rack in a 400°F (205°C) oven brings them right back.
Know when it is done
Fry at 350°F (175°C); shrimp are done at 145°F (63°C) — opaque throughout and curled into a loose C.
Serve it with
A cold pilsner or a rum punch, with a crunchy cabbage and lime slaw.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Sweetened shredded coconut browns better and tastes more like the restaurant version. Unsweetened works and is less sweet, but watch it closely because it toasts faster.
  • ◆To bake instead of fry, arrange on a greased rack over a sheet pan, spray generously with oil, and bake at 425°F (220°C) for 12-14 minutes, flipping once. Less crisp but far less work.
  • ◆An air fryer at 400°F (205°C) for 8-10 minutes works well, but spray the coating with oil or the coconut stays chalky and pale.
  • ◆Bread the shrimp up to 4 hours ahead and keep them uncovered in the fridge on a sheet pan. Do not stack or cover them or the coating will go soft.
  • ◆Save 1/4 cup (60 ml) of the frying oil after it cools and strain it — it will taste faintly of coconut and is great for the next batch.

Charleston Shrimp and Grits⏱ 1 hr🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Slow-cooked cheesy grits under shrimp in a bacon and lemon pan gravy. This is Sunday morning food that is just as good at nine at night.

Comfort FoodSouthernBrunch
Prep
15 min
Cook
45 min
Total
1 hr
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the grits

For the shrimp

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Rinse and skim the grits
    Put the 1 cup of stone-ground grits in a bowl, cover with cold water, swish, and pour off the chaff and hulls that float to the top. Real stone-ground grits carry bits of the corn hull that can taste bitter and never soften. Drain them well in a fine sieve — this takes two minutes and improves the texture noticeably.
  2. Start the grits low and slow
    Bring the 2 cups water, 2 cups milk, and 1 1/2 tsp salt to a bare simmer in a heavy 3 qt (2.8 L) saucepan, then rain the grits in while whisking constantly. Whisking as they go in is what prevents lumps, which you cannot whisk out later. Once they start to thicken, drop the heat to the lowest setting your stove has.
  3. Cook and stir for 35 minutes
    Cover and cook the grits 30 to 40 minutes, stirring well with a wooden spoon every 5 minutes and scraping the bottom corners of the pan where they catch and scorch. They are done when each grain is fully tender with no chalky center and the mixture falls slowly from the spoon in a thick ribbon. If they get too thick before they are tender, whisk in hot water 1/4 cup (60 ml) at a time.
  4. Season the shrimp
    While the grits cook, pat the shrimp dry and toss with the 1 tsp kosher salt, 1/2 tsp pepper, and 1/2 tsp paprika. Let them sit at room temperature for 15 minutes so they cook evenly. Dry, seasoned shrimp will pick up color in the bacon fat instead of steaming.
  5. Render the bacon
    Cook the bacon pieces in a cold 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until crisp and deeply browned. Starting in a cold pan renders the fat slowly instead of seizing the meat, which gives you both crisper bacon and more fat to cook in. Lift the bacon to a paper towel and leave 3 tbsp of the fat in the pan.
  6. Sear the shrimp fast
    Raise the heat to medium-high and cook the shrimp in the bacon fat in a single layer for about 60 seconds a side, until pink at the edges but still slightly translucent in the center. Work in two batches if they do not fit with space between them. Move them to a plate immediately — they finish in the gravy and will turn rubbery if you cook them fully now.
  7. Build the gravy
    Lower the heat to medium, add the minced garlic to the pan, and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant but not brown. Sprinkle the 1 tbsp flour over the fat and cook, stirring, for 1 minute — you are making a small blond roux that will thicken the gravy and take away the raw flour taste. It should smell faintly like toast.
  8. Deglaze and simmer
    Pour in the 3/4 cup stock while whisking, scraping up every browned bit from the bottom of the pan. Simmer 2 to 3 minutes until it thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon and leaves a clear line when you draw a finger through it. If it gets too thick, loosen it with another splash of stock.
  9. Finish the grits with cheese
    Off the heat, beat the 4 tbsp butter into the finished grits until it disappears, then add the 1 cup grated cheddar in two handfuls, stirring until smooth, and season with the 1/4 tsp pepper. Grate the cheese yourself — pre-shredded is coated in starch that makes grits grainy. Taste for salt; grits need more than you expect.
  10. Bring the shrimp back
    Add the 2 tbsp lemon juice, the hot sauce, the shrimp with any juices on the plate, and most of the bacon to the gravy. Toss over medium heat for 1 to 2 minutes, just until the shrimp are opaque throughout at 145°F (63°C) and curled into a loose C. Taste the gravy and adjust the lemon and hot sauce.
  11. Serve in warm bowls
    Spoon a generous ladle of grits into each warm bowl and make a shallow well in the center with the back of the spoon. Pile the shrimp and gravy into the well and scatter the reserved bacon and the sliced scallions over the top. Serve immediately, because grits set up like concrete as they cool.
Know when it is done
Shrimp are done at 145°F (63°C) — opaque and loosely curled. Grits are ready when each grain is tender with no chalky center, about 35 minutes.
Serve it with
A cold beer or a Bloody Mary, with hot sauce on the table and nothing else required.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Instant or quick grits will work in a pinch, following their package timing, but stone-ground grits are the whole point of this dish. Anson Mills and Geechie Boy are worth ordering.
  • ◆Leftover grits set firm in the fridge. Cut them into squares and pan-fry in butter until crisp for one of the best breakfasts there is.
  • ◆If your grits go lumpy, an immersion blender for 10 seconds saves them. Do not overdo it or they turn gluey.
  • ◆Buy shell-on shrimp and simmer the shells in the 3/4 cup stock for 15 minutes, then strain. It costs you nothing and makes the gravy taste like a restaurant made it.
  • ◆The grits can be made up to 2 days ahead. Reheat over low heat with a splash of milk, whisking until they loosen back up.

San Francisco Cioppino⏱ 1 hr 30 min🍽 6 servingsAdvanced▾

A big red tomato and wine broth loaded with clams, mussels, shrimp, and fish, invented by Italian fishermen in North Beach. Serve it with bread and a stack of napkins.

Weekend ProjectCrowd PleaserOne Pot
Prep
30 min
Cook
1 hr
Total
1 hr 30 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

The broth

The seafood

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Purge and check the shellfish
    Soak the clams in 2 qt (1.9 L) of cold water stirred with the 2 tbsp kosher salt — roughly 1 tbsp (18 g) per quart, about as salty as seawater — for 20 to 30 minutes so they spit out their sand, then lift them out rather than pouring, leaving the grit behind. Scrub and debeard the mussels, and tap any gaping shell on the counter; if it does not slowly close within 30 seconds, throw it away. Discard anything cracked. Sandy cioppino is the classic failure of this dish.
  2. Make a quick shrimp stock
    If you bought shell-on shrimp, simmer the shells in the 3 cups of fish stock or clam juice for 15 minutes, then strain and discard the shells. This costs you nothing and adds a sweet shellfish depth that bottled clam juice alone does not have. Keep the stock warm on a back burner.
  3. Sweat the fennel and onion
    Heat the 1/4 cup olive oil in a 7 qt (6.6 L) Dutch oven over medium heat and add the sliced fennel, diced onion, and 2 tsp kosher salt. Cook 10 to 12 minutes, stirring often, until everything is completely soft and translucent with just a little golden color at the edges. Do not rush this on high heat — the sweetness that develops here is the backbone of the broth.
  4. Bloom the garlic and chile
    Add the minced garlic and 1 tsp red pepper flakes and cook 1 minute more, stirring constantly, until the garlic smells sweet and the chile perfumes the oil. Fat-soluble flavors need hot oil to release, which is why this happens before any liquid goes in. Watch it closely; garlic burns in seconds.
  5. Caramelize the tomato paste
    Stir in the 2 tbsp tomato paste and cook it for 2 to 3 minutes, smearing it against the bottom of the pot, until it darkens from bright red to a deep brick color. This step drives off the tinny raw taste and builds a savory backbone. It should smell rich and slightly sweet, not sharp.
  6. Deglaze with wine
    Pour in the 1 1/2 cups white wine and scrape the bottom of the pot hard with a wooden spoon to release everything stuck there. Boil for 4 to 5 minutes until reduced by about half and the harsh alcohol smell is gone. If you can still smell raw wine, keep going — this stew has nowhere to hide it.
  7. Simmer the broth
    Add the crushed tomatoes, the warm stock, bay leaves, oregano, and the saffron if using. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a gentle simmer with the lid ajar and cook 30 to 40 minutes, stirring occasionally. The broth should reduce slightly and taste round and unified rather than like tomatoes and wine sitting next to each other. Taste and adjust the salt now, because you cannot stir the pot much once the seafood is in.
  8. Get everything ready to go in
    Cut the fish into even 1 1/2 in (4 cm) chunks, pat the shrimp and scallops dry, and have all the shellfish within arm's reach of the stove. From this point the whole thing takes about 12 minutes and each item goes in on a timer. Set out warm bowls and grill your bread now.
  9. Clams first
    Bring the broth to a strong simmer, add the clams and the crab pieces if using, cover, and cook 5 minutes. Clams have the thickest shells and take the longest to open, which is why they lead. Do not stir the pot from here on — use the lid and the simmer to move the heat around.
  10. Then mussels and fish
    Add the mussels and the chunks of white fish, nestling the fish into the broth without stirring, cover, and cook 3 minutes. The fish is fragile and stirring will break it into shreds. You should see most of the mussel shells beginning to gap open.
  11. Shrimp and scallops last
    Scatter the shrimp and scallops over the top, cover, and cook 2 to 3 minutes more, until the shrimp are pink and curled and the scallops are just opaque. Everything in the pot should now be done at once. Discard any clams or mussels that are still tightly shut.
  12. Check and finish
    The fish should flake at 145°F (63°C) and the shrimp should be opaque at 145°F (63°C). Turn off the heat, stir in the 1/2 cup parsley and the basil as gently as you can, and taste one last time for salt and heat. A squeeze of lemon at the end lifts the whole pot.
  13. Serve in wide bowls
    Ladle into warm wide bowls, making sure everyone gets some of each kind of seafood and plenty of broth. Serve with grilled sourdough, lemon wedges, an empty bowl for shells, and a bib if you own one. This is a stew you eat with your hands and a spoon at the same time.
Know when it is done
Fish and shrimp are done at 145°F (63°C); clams and mussels are done when their shells open wide. Discard any shellfish that stays shut.
Serve it with
A bold Italian white or a light Sangiovese, with grilled sourdough and a green salad after.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆The tomato broth is the make-ahead half of this dish. Make it up to 3 days ahead or freeze it for 3 months, then reheat and add seafood the night you serve it.
  • ◆Use whatever is good and fresh at the counter. Squid, halibut cheeks, king crab legs, and rockfish all belong here; skip delicate flounder, which disintegrates.
  • ◆The order matters more than the exact species: thickest shells first, then fish, then shrimp and scallops last. That is the whole technique.
  • ◆If the broth tastes flat, it needs salt or acid before it needs anything else. Try 1/2 tsp of salt or a squeeze of lemon before reaching for more herbs.
  • ◆Grill the bread with olive oil and a raw garlic clove rubbed over the hot surface. It sounds fussy and takes 90 seconds.

Grilled Swordfish with Salmoriglio⏱ 45 min (includes 20 min marinade and 5 min rest)🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Meaty swordfish steaks over a hot grill, finished with the Sicilian lemon, oregano, and olive oil sauce called salmoriglio. It eats like a steak but cooks in ten minutes.

Grilling30 MinutesSummer
Prep
10 min
Cook
10 min
Total
45 min (includes 20 min marinade and 5 min rest)
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the fish

Salmoriglio sauce

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Pick good steaks
    Look for swordfish that is firm, moist, and pale ivory to pink with a tight, close grain and no gaps between the muscle layers. The dark bloodline running through one edge is normal but strong tasting, so trim it if you are sensitive to it. Steaks under 3/4 in (2 cm) thick dry out on a grill, so ask the counter to cut them a full inch.
  2. Marinate briefly
    Rub the steaks all over with the 3 tbsp olive oil, the smashed garlic, 1 tsp dried oregano, the lemon zest, 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt, and 3/4 tsp pepper, then let them sit at room temperature for 20 minutes. Twenty minutes is long enough for the salt to season the outer layer and for the chill to come off, which is what keeps the center from staying cold while the surface overcooks. Do not add lemon juice to the marinade and do not go past 30 minutes — acid starts to cure the surface of the fish and turns it opaque and mealy before it ever hits heat. The zest gives you the perfume of lemon without any of that risk.
  3. Whisk the salmoriglio
    In a bowl, whisk the 3 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tbsp warm water, grated garlic, 1/2 tsp salt, and 2 tsp oregano, then drizzle in the 1/3 cup olive oil while whisking until it thickens slightly and looks creamy. The warm water is the traditional trick that helps it emulsify. Stir in the parsley and red pepper flakes and let it sit 15 minutes for the oregano to soften.
  4. Get the grill hot and clean
    Heat a gas grill on high or build a charcoal fire for direct high heat, aiming for around 500°F (260°C) at the grate, and give it 10 to 15 minutes with the lid closed. Scrape the grates with a wire brush until they are shiny, then oil them by wiping with a tongs-held paper towel dipped in neutral oil. Clean and oiled grates are the only reason fish does not stick.
  5. Blot the fish before it goes on
    Wipe the excess marinade off the steaks with a paper towel, leaving them lightly oiled but not dripping. Excess oil causes flare-ups that char the outside and leave the middle raw. Discard the smashed garlic, which would burn on the grate.
  6. Lay the steaks down and leave them
    Set the steaks on the hottest part of the grate at a 45 degree angle to the bars and close the lid. Cook 4 to 5 minutes without touching them — you should hear a steady sizzle and see the edges turn opaque and creep upward. Moving the fish before a crust forms is what tears it apart.
  7. Flip once with confidence
    Slide a wide metal spatula fully under a steak and lift; if it resists, give it another 30 seconds and it will release. Flip and grill the second side 3 to 4 minutes. Swordfish is dense and forgiving compared to flaky fish, but it still only wants about 8 to 9 minutes total for a 1 in steak.
  8. Check the temperature early
    Slide an instant-read thermometer in from the side into the center. The FDA guideline for fully cooked fish is 145°F (63°C); many cooks pull swordfish at 130-135°F (54-57°C) for a moister, faintly pink center and let carryover do the rest. Swordfish is lean and dries out fast, so start checking at the 7 minute mark.
  9. Rest the steaks
    Move the steaks to a warm platter and let them rest 3 to 5 minutes, loosely tented if your kitchen is cold. Like beef, swordfish is muscular enough that resting lets the juices settle back through the meat instead of running out onto the plate. They will climb about 5°F (3°C) as they sit.
  10. Sauce at the table
    Whisk the salmoriglio once more to bring it back together and spoon it generously over the rested steaks. Do not sauce them before resting or the lemon will make the surface soggy. Any leftover sauce is excellent on grilled vegetables or bread.
  11. Serve with something charred
    While the fish rests, brush the zucchini planks with the 1 tbsp olive oil and lay them on the still-hot grate along with the 2 lemons, cut side down. Give them 2 to 3 minutes per side for the zucchini and 2 to 3 minutes total for the lemons, until both carry dark grill marks. Grilled lemon squeezed over the fish at the table is sweeter and rounder than raw, because the heat caramelizes some of its sugar and knocks the sharp edge off the acid. Serve everything family style on one big platter.
Know when it is done
Grill to 145°F (63°C) for the FDA fully-cooked guideline; pull at 130-135°F (54-57°C) for a moister, faintly pink center.
Serve it with
A chilled Sicilian white like Grillo, with grilled vegetables and roasted potatoes.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆No grill? A cast iron grill pan or a heavy skillet over medium-high heat gives you the same result. Preheat it for 5 minutes and use the same timing.
  • ◆Mahi mahi, tuna, halibut steaks, and thick salmon fillets all work with this method and this sauce.
  • ◆Salmoriglio keeps 3 days in the fridge, but the garlic gets sharper each day. Bring it back to room temperature and whisk before serving.
  • ◆If a steak has a tough band of skin around the outside, cut through it in two or three places so the steak does not curl on the grill.
  • ◆Swordfish is a high-mercury fish. It is worth knowing if you are pregnant or feeding small children, in which case cod or salmon is the better choice for this dish.

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

The base

The rice and seafood

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Bloom the saffron
    Warm the 5 cups of stock in a saucepan until steaming but not boiling, crumble the 1/2 tsp saffron threads between your fingers, and stir them in. Let it steep at least 10 minutes while you prep everything else, until the liquid glows deep orange-gold. Saffron needs warmth and time to release its color and its honeyed, hay-like aroma, and adding threads directly to the rice wastes most of it.
  2. Prep every ingredient first
    Dice the onion, slice the pepper, mince the garlic, grate the tomatoes, scrub the mussels, and cut the squid before you light a burner. Paella has no pauses once it starts, and you cannot stop to chop an onion halfway through. Set everything in bowls around the stove in the order you will use it.
  3. Pick the right pan
    Use a 15 in (38 cm) paella pan or the widest, shallowest skillet you own — the goal is rice no more than 1/2 in (1.3 cm) deep, which is what lets it cook without stirring. A deep Dutch oven will give you rice pudding, not paella. If your burner is smaller than the pan, plan to rotate it every few minutes so the whole base heats evenly.
  4. Sear the seafood and pull it out
    Heat the 1/4 cup olive oil over medium-high and sear the shrimp for 60 seconds a side and the squid for about 60 seconds total, just until they take on a little color. Move both to a plate — they are only 70 percent cooked and will finish on top of the rice at the end. Cooking them now leaves shellfish flavor in the oil that carries through the whole dish.
  5. Build the sofrito
    Lower the heat to medium, add the onion, bell pepper, and 2 tsp salt to the same pan, and cook 8 to 10 minutes until very soft and lightly golden. Add the garlic and cook 1 minute more. This slow-cooked vegetable base is called sofrito and it is where most of the flavor in a paella actually lives, so do not shortcut it.
  6. Add paprika and tomato
    Stir in the 2 tsp smoked paprika and cook for just 30 seconds — paprika scorches almost instantly and turns acrid. Immediately add the 1 1/2 cups grated tomato and cook 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the mixture darkens to brick red and the oil separates and pools at the edges. That separation is your signal the sofrito is finished.
  7. Toast the rice
    Add the 2 cups of rice and stir for 2 minutes so every grain is coated in the oil and sofrito. Toasting the exterior of the grain helps it stay separate and absorb liquid evenly instead of turning creamy. Spread the rice into a flat, even layer across the whole pan.
  8. Add the stock and stop stirring
    Pour in all 5 cups of the saffron stock, shake the pan gently to level the rice, and bring it to a strong boil. From this moment on, do not stir the rice again — stirring releases starch and makes risotto, and it destroys the crust you are building. Taste the broth now and add salt if it needs it; this is your last chance to season.
  9. Boil hard, then simmer
    Boil hard for 5 minutes, rotating the pan a quarter turn every minute or two if your burner is smaller than the pan. Then reduce to a steady medium-low simmer and cook 10 minutes more, uncovered. You should see the liquid level dropping to just below the surface of the rice.
  10. Add the shellfish
    Nestle the mussels or clams hinge-down into the rice so they will open upward and keep their juices, and scatter the peas over the top. Cook 5 minutes more, until the shells open wide. Any shell still shut at the end gets thrown out.
  11. Return the shrimp and squid
    Arrange the seared shrimp and squid over the surface of the rice and cook 3 to 5 minutes more, until the shrimp are opaque at 145°F (63°C) and the rice is tender with no chalky center. Taste a grain from the middle of the pan rather than the edge. If the rice is still hard and the pan is dry, add 1/4 cup (60 ml) of hot stock around the edges.
  12. Make the socarrat
    Turn the heat to high for 60 to 90 seconds and listen closely — you want a crackling, popping sound and the smell of toasting rice, but stop the second it smells sharp or burnt. This forms the socarrat, the caramelized crust of rice on the bottom of the pan that is the most prized part of the dish. Scrape gently with a spoon at the edge to check for a golden brown layer.
  13. Rest before serving
    Take the pan off the heat, cover it loosely with a clean kitchen towel or foil, and let it rest 10 minutes. The rice finishes absorbing the last of the liquid and firms up so it does not fall apart when you serve it. Skipping this rest is why home paella often tastes wet.
  14. Serve from the pan
    Uncover, scatter the 1/4 cup parsley and the 1/2 tsp flaky salt over the top, and tuck the lemon wedges around the edge. Bring the whole pan to the table and let everyone serve themselves straight from it, digging down for a piece of the crust. Traditionally people eat from the wedge of the pan directly in front of them.
Know when it is done
Shrimp are done at 145°F (63°C); mussels and clams are done when they open wide. The rice should be tender with no chalky center and a crisp golden socarrat underneath.
Serve it with
A cold Spanish rosado or dry cava, with an olive oil and sherry vinegar green salad.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Bomba rice can drink close to three times its volume in liquid without going mushy. The ratio here is 2 1/2 cups of stock per cup of rice, and the 1 1/2 cups of grated tomato in the sofrito makes up the rest. Arborio works but needs about 1/2 cup less stock and turns creamier.
  • ◆Do not use long-grain or basmati rice. It will not absorb the broth the same way and you will never get a socarrat.
  • ◆Homemade stock from shrimp shells simmered 20 minutes with an onion, a bay leaf, and 6 cups of water is a huge upgrade over bottled clam juice.
  • ◆If your stovetop cannot heat the whole pan evenly, finish the paella uncovered in a 400°F (205°C) oven for the last 10 minutes, then do the socarrat over a burner for 90 seconds.
  • ◆Leftovers reheat surprisingly well in a covered skillet with a splash of stock over low heat, or make excellent arancini-style rice cakes the next day.

Real chiles toasted on a dry pan, tortillas warmed one at a time, and pots that fill the whole apartment with the smell of orange peel and cumin — this is the chapter that turns a weeknight into a taco night and a free Saturday into something worth remembering.

Carne Asada Tacos with Salsa Verde⏱ 2 hr 45 min (includes 2 hr marinade)🍽 4 servings (about 12 tacos)Medium▾

Thin skirt steak marinated in citrus and garlic, charred hard and fast, then chopped small and piled into warm corn tortillas with a bright tomatillo salsa. This is the taco that makes people ask what you did differently.

GrillTaco NightCrowd Pleaser
Prep
25 min
Cook
20 min
Total
2 hr 45 min (includes 2 hr marinade)
Serves
4 servings (about 12 tacos)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the carne asada

Salsa verde

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Trim and portion the steak
    Skirt steak arrives as a long rope with a thin silvery membrane and pockets of hard fat, so shave those away with a paring knife — they never render and they turn chewy. Cut the 2 lb (900 g) piece crosswise into 3 or 4 lengths of about 8 in (20 cm) so each piece fits flat in your pan or on the grill. Short pieces are much easier to flip and, more importantly, easier to slice against the grain later. Pat everything dry with paper towels so the marinade clings instead of sliding off.
  2. Mix the marinade
    Whisk together the orange juice, lime juice, oil, garlic, jalapeno, cilantro, cumin, chili powder, oregano, 1 tbsp kosher salt and the black pepper in a bowl. Orange juice is not there for sweetness — its gentler acid tenderizes the meat without turning the surface chalky and mushy the way straight lime does over hours. Taste it: it should be aggressively salty and sour, because only a thin film of it ends up on the steak.
  3. Marinate 2 to 8 hours
    Put the steak in a zip-top bag or a shallow dish, pour the marinade over, and press out the air so the liquid touches every surface. Refrigerate for at least 2 hours and no more than 8 — past that window the citrus starts breaking the muscle fibers down into something soft and pasty. Turn the bag once halfway through if you think of it. This is the one step you cannot rush, so start it in the morning if dinner is at seven.
  4. Char the salsa vegetables
    Arrange the tomatillos, serranos, onion wedges and unpeeled garlic on a foil-lined sheet pan and slide it 4 in (10 cm) under a preheated broiler. Broil for 8 to 10 minutes, turning everything once, until the tomatillos slump and blister and go from bright green to a dull olive with blackened patches. That char is where the smoky depth comes from, so let them get genuinely spotted black, not just soft. Pull the garlic early if the skins are burning and squeeze the cloves out of their papers.
  5. Blend the salsa verde
    Scrape the vegetables and every drop of juice from the pan into a blender, add the cilantro, lime juice and 1 tsp salt, and pulse 8 to 10 times. You want a loose, slightly chunky salsa, not a smooth green milkshake — over-blending whips in air and turns it pale and foamy. Taste and add salt a pinch at a time until the flavor snaps into focus. It will taste sharper hot than cold, so let it cool for 10 minutes before you judge it.
  6. Take the steak out early
    Pull the steak from the fridge 30 minutes before cooking and let it sit on the counter. Lift each piece out of the marinade and scrape off the garlic and cilantro bits with the back of a knife — solids like these burn black and bitter over high heat. Then pat both sides thoroughly dry with paper towels. A wet steak steams and stays gray; a dry one browns in seconds.
  7. Get the fire screaming hot
    Build a hot charcoal fire or set a gas grill to high, or heat a 12 in (30 cm) cast iron skillet over high heat for 4 to 5 minutes indoors. You want it hot enough that a drop of water vanishes instantly with a hiss. Skirt steak is only about 1/2 in (1.3 cm) thick, so it needs a ferocious surface temperature to build a crust before the inside overcooks. If you are indoors, turn the vent on high and open a window now, not later.
  8. Sear hard and fast
    Lay the steak down and leave it completely alone for 3 to 4 minutes — it should sizzle loudly and steadily, not smoke black. Flip once and give it 2 to 3 minutes on the second side, until an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part reads 130°F (54°C) for medium-rare. Work in batches if the pieces are crowding each other, because crowding drops the pan temperature and you get gray meat. Skirt steak goes from perfect to leathery in about 90 seconds, so keep the thermometer in your hand.
  9. Rest the steak
    Move the steak to a cutting board and let it rest for 8 to 10 minutes, loosely tented with foil. During the rest the internal temperature coasts up to about 135°F (57°C) and the juices that were driven to the center redistribute through the meat. Cut into it too early and half of that liquid runs onto the board instead of staying in the taco. Use this time to warm the tortillas.
  10. Warm the tortillas
    Heat a dry comal or skillet over medium-high and toast each corn tortilla for 20 to 30 seconds per side, until it is pliable, smells toasty, and puffs slightly in spots. Stack the warm ones inside a clean kitchen towel so they steam each other soft. Cold tortillas crack and taste like cardboard, and this step takes four minutes. For street-style tacos, double up two tortillas per taco so nothing falls through.
  11. Chop against the grain
    Look for the long parallel muscle fibers running across each piece of skirt steak — they are easy to see on this cut. Slice across them into thin strips, then turn the strips and chop them into rough 1/2 in (1.3 cm) pieces. Cutting with the grain instead of across it is the single most common reason carne asada comes out tough. Pour any juices from the board back over the chopped meat.
  12. Build and eat immediately
    Pile a generous 1/4 cup of chopped steak into each warm tortilla, then top with diced white onion, chopped cilantro, and a big spoonful of salsa verde. Finish with a hard squeeze of lime right before it goes in your mouth — the acid wakes the whole thing up. Tacos wait for no one, so serve them straight off the board with the salsa bowl in the middle of the table.
Know when it is done
Pull skirt or flank steak at 130°F (54°C) for medium-rare; it coasts to about 135°F (57°C) as it rests. Past 145°F (63°C) these thin cuts turn tough and dry.
Serve it with
A cold Mexican lager with lime, or a salty Tommy's margarita, with charro beans and Mexican rice alongside.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Skirt steak beats flank here because its loose grain grabs marinade and it cooks in half the time. If you can only find flank, slice it thinner and expect an extra minute per side.
  • ◆The salsa verde keeps in the fridge for 5 days and only gets better on day two. Make a double batch and put it on eggs.
  • ◆No broiler? Char the tomatillos and chiles in a dry cast iron skillet over medium-high heat for 10 to 12 minutes, turning until blackened in patches. The result is slightly more toasty and less juicy, which is not a bad thing.
  • ◆If the salsa tastes harsh or metallic, it needs salt, not more lime. Tomatillos are acidic enough on their own.
  • ◆Corn tortillas from a Mexican market are worth the detour. Warm them on the comal the moment before serving, not ten minutes ahead.

Chicken Tinga Tostadas⏱ 1 hr 15 min🍽 4 servings (12 tostadas)Medium▾

Shredded chicken simmered in a smoky chipotle and tomato sauce until it soaks up every bit of it, spooned onto crisp tostadas with beans and crema. It is a weeknight dinner that tastes like it took all afternoon.

WeeknightMake AheadSmoky
Prep
20 min
Cook
55 min
Total
1 hr 15 min
Serves
4 servings (12 tostadas)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the chicken

Tinga sauce

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Poach the chicken
    Put the thighs, onion half, garlic cloves, bay leaf and 1 tbsp salt in a saucepan and add the 6 cups (1.4 L) water, which should cover everything by an inch. Bring it to a bare simmer over medium-high heat, then immediately drop it to low so the surface only shivers with a bubble every second or two. A hard boil squeezes the thighs tight and dry, while a gentle poach leaves them silky. Cook for 18 to 20 minutes, until an instant-read thermometer in the thickest thigh reads 165°F (74°C).
  2. Cool and shred
    Lift the chicken out with tongs onto a plate and let it sit for 10 minutes so it is cool enough to handle and the fibers relax. Save 1 cup (240 ml) of the poaching broth and strain the rest into a jar for another day — it is far better than anything from a box. Pull the meat apart with two forks or your fingers into rough shreds about the width of a pencil. Leave them a little chunky; wispy shreds disappear into the sauce instead of holding onto it.
  3. Blanch and peel the tomatoes
    Bring a small pot of water to a boil, cut a shallow X in the bottom of each Roma tomato, and drop them in for 45 to 60 seconds. Move them to a bowl of cold water and the skins will slip off with your thumb. Peeling matters here because tomato skins roll up into little leathery curls in a simmered sauce. If you would rather skip it, use one 28 oz (794 g) can of whole peeled tomatoes, drained, which is the equivalent of 1 1/2 lb of fresh.
  4. Blend the tomato base
    Put the peeled tomatoes, chipotles, adobo sauce, oregano and cumin in a blender and run it for 30 seconds until completely smooth. Start with 2 chipotles if you are heat-shy — you can always stir a third in later, but you cannot take it out. The blended sauce should be the color of brick and smell distinctly smoky, not just tomatoey. Set it right next to the stove.
  5. Sweat the onions properly
    Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium heat, add the sliced onion, and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes. You are after soft, sweet, translucent onions with just a few golden edges, not crunchy ones — this is where the sauce gets its backbone. Add the sliced garlic in the last minute so it perfumes the oil without burning. Burnt garlic turns the whole pan bitter and there is no fixing it.
  6. Fry the sauce
    Pour the blended tomato mixture into the hot skillet all at once — it should hiss and spit, so stand back. Cook it hard for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring often, until it darkens a shade, thickens noticeably, and a spoon dragged through the pan leaves a trail that holds for a second. Frying the puree cooks off the raw tomato edge and concentrates everything. Skipping this step is why homemade tinga sometimes tastes thin and sour.
  7. Simmer the chicken in the sauce
    Stir in the shredded chicken and the reserved 1 cup (240 ml) broth, then bring it back to a gentle simmer. Cook uncovered for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring now and then, until the liquid reduces and clings to the meat instead of pooling in the pan. The chicken should look glossy and coated, not soupy. Add the 1 tsp salt, taste, and adjust — poached chicken drinks up more salt than you expect.
  8. Warm the beans and tostadas
    Heat the refried beans in a small pan over low with a splash of water until they are spreadable and loose, about 5 minutes. Crisp the tostada shells in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 3 to 4 minutes if they came from a bag and taste stale. Warm shells and warm beans hold up much better under a wet topping. Have everything ready before you assemble, because tostadas soften fast.
  9. Build the tostadas
    Spread about 2 tbsp of refried beans on each tostada all the way to the edge — the beans are the glue that keeps the topping from sliding off. Pile on a generous 1/3 cup of the hot tinga, then add sliced avocado, a shower of queso fresco, and a drizzle of crema. Finish with a squeeze of lime. Assemble them one at a time as people eat, not in a big batch on a tray.
  10. Serve with the pot on the table
    Bring the skillet of tinga right to the table with a spoon in it and let everyone build their own. Leftover tinga is even better the next day once the smoke settles into the meat. It reheats in a covered pan over low with a splash of water, about 5 minutes. Anything left after that goes into quesadillas or over rice.
Know when it is done
Chicken is safely cooked at 165°F (74°C) checked in the thickest part of a thigh. It then simmers in the sauce, which will not dry it out because thighs hold moisture well.
Serve it with
Mexican rice and a cold agua fresca de jamaica, or a light lager if you want something with bubbles.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Chicken thighs are the right call here — breasts turn stringy after ten minutes of simmering in sauce. If you only have breasts, poach them to 165°F (74°C) and stir them in during the last 4 minutes.
  • ◆Freeze leftover chipotles in adobo in a small container in single-chile portions; a can goes bad long before you use it up.
  • ◆Tinga freezes beautifully for up to 3 months. Cool it completely, then freeze flat in a zip-top bag and thaw overnight in the fridge.
  • ◆If it comes out too spicy, stir in 2 tbsp of crema or a spoonful of the refried beans directly into the pan — the fat blunts the capsaicin.
  • ◆The same tinga makes excellent tacos, quesadillas or a topping for baked potatoes. Make a double batch on Sunday.

Michoacan-Style Pork Carnitas⏱ 3 hr 45 min (includes 10 min rest)🍽 6 to 8 servingsMedium▾

Pork shoulder simmered slow in its own fat with orange and cinnamon, then crisped under high heat until the edges shatter and the middle stays juicy. This is the one worth clearing an afternoon for.

Weekend ProjectCrowd PleaserTaco Night
Prep
20 min
Cook
3 hr 15 min
Total
3 hr 45 min (includes 10 min rest)
Serves
6 to 8 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the pork

The braise

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Cut the pork the right size
    Cut the shoulder into 2 in (5 cm) chunks and leave the fat cap on — do not trim it, because that fat is the entire point of carnitas. Pieces this size hold their shape through a long braise and still develop plenty of surface area for crisping later. Anything smaller falls into threads before the connective tissue melts. Pat the chunks dry so the seasoning sticks.
  2. Season and let it sit
    Toss the pork with the 1 tbsp kosher salt, black pepper, cumin and Mexican oregano until every piece is coated. Let it stand at room temperature for 15 minutes while you get everything else ready, which gives the salt time to start working into the surface. Mexican oregano is more citrusy and less minty than Mediterranean oregano and is worth seeking out. If you only have the Italian kind, use half as much.
  3. Melt the lard and start the braise
    Melt the 1/2 cup (110 g) lard in a large heavy Dutch oven over medium heat, then add the pork in a single layer or as close as you can get. Squeeze the orange halves over the pot and drop the spent shells in, then add the onion, garlic, bay leaves, cinnamon stick, milk and the 2 cups (475 ml) water. The liquid should come about halfway up the pork, not cover it — top up with a splash more water if your pot is wide and the pork looks stranded. This is a confit, not a stew — the pork mostly cooks in fat with just enough liquid to keep the bottom from scorching.
  4. Simmer low and slow
    Bring the pot to a simmer, then turn the heat to low so you see a lazy bubble breaking the surface every second or so. Cover partially with the lid set askew and cook for 2 hours to 2 hours 30 minutes, stirring gently every 30 minutes. Resist the urge to crank the heat: a hard boil tightens the muscle fibers and gives you dry, stringy pork instead of meltingly soft chunks. The kitchen will smell like orange peel and pork fat, which is exactly right.
  5. Check for doneness by feel
    The pork is ready when a piece offers no resistance to a fork and pulls apart into large shreds under gentle pressure, at an internal temperature of about 200°F (93°C). Do not rely on the clock alone, because a well-marbled shoulder can take 30 minutes longer than a lean one. If it still feels springy or tight, give it another 20 minutes and check again. Undercooked carnitas is the most common failure and it cannot be fixed at the crisping stage.
  6. Boil off the liquid
    Fish out and discard the onion, garlic, bay leaves, cinnamon stick and orange shells with tongs. Raise the heat to medium and let the remaining liquid bubble away for 10 to 15 minutes until only clear fat and a little browned sediment are left in the pot. You will hear the sound shift from a wet gurgle to a sharp sizzle — that is the water gone and the frying starting. From here on, the pork is essentially deep-frying in its own rendered fat.
  7. Rest before crisping
    Lift the chunks onto a rimmed sheet pan with a slotted spoon and let them rest for 10 minutes, which firms them up enough to handle. Pour 3 to 4 tbsp of the rendered fat from the pot over the pork and save the rest in a jar for beans or eggs. Gently press each chunk with the back of a spoon to flatten it slightly, exposing more surface. More surface means more crispy edges, which is the whole reason anyone loves carnitas.
  8. Crisp under the broiler
    Set an oven rack 6 in (15 cm) below the broiler element and turn the broiler to high. Broil the pork for 4 to 6 minutes, until the tops are deep brown and crackling at the edges. Watch it constantly — the line between crisp and burnt is about 45 seconds under a broiler. Alternatively, crisp the pork in batches in a hot cast iron skillet over medium-high heat for 3 to 4 minutes per side.
  9. Flip and finish
    Pull the pan out, turn the pieces with tongs, and broil for another 3 to 4 minutes so the second side browns too. You are aiming for roughly half crisp, golden-brown exterior and half soft, juicy interior, not uniformly crunchy pork. If some pieces are done before others, move them to the edges of the pan where the heat is less direct. Give it all a squeeze of lime while it is still on the hot pan.
  10. Chop and dress
    Roughly chop or pull the crisped pork on a board, keeping some big shaggy pieces for texture. Drizzle a few tablespoons of the hot rendered fat and pan juices back over the top and toss once — that is the seasoning. Taste and add a pinch of salt if it needs it. Serve straight from the board while everything is still crackling.
  11. Warm the tortillas and build
    Toast the corn tortillas on a dry comal or skillet over medium-high heat for 20 to 30 seconds per side, then stack them in a towel to stay soft. Fill each with about 1/3 cup of carnitas, then top with diced white onion, cilantro, salsa and a hard squeeze of lime. Two tortillas per taco is standard for anything this juicy. Put the bowls in the middle of the table and let everyone go.
Know when it is done
Braise the pork to about 200°F (93°C), far past the 145°F (63°C) plus a 3-minute rest that pork needs for safety, because that is where the collagen turns to gelatin and the meat shreds. Judge it by fork tenderness, not the clock.
Serve it with
A Mexican lager or a michelada, with refried beans and pickled red onions on the side.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Lard makes noticeably better carnitas than oil and is sold cheaply at any Mexican grocery. Strain and refrigerate what is left over — it keeps for months and makes the best refried beans you will ever eat.
  • ◆The milk is not optional folklore; its sugars and proteins help the pork brown and add a subtle richness. It will look curdled during the braise, which is normal and disappears when you boil the liquid off.
  • ◆You can braise the pork up to 3 days ahead and refrigerate it in its fat. Crisp it under the broiler straight from the fridge, adding 2 extra minutes.
  • ◆If your pork tastes flat after crisping, it needs salt and acid, in that order. A pinch of salt and a squeeze of lime fixes almost every batch.
  • ◆Leftovers make outstanding breakfast: crisp them again in a skillet and top with two fried eggs and salsa verde.

Baja Fish Tacos with Cabbage Slaw⏱ 45 min🍽 4 servings (12 tacos)Medium▾

Beer-battered white fish that stays shatteringly crisp under a pile of lime-cut cabbage and chipotle crema. It is the taco stand in Ensenada, made in your kitchen in under an hour.

FriedWeeknightTaco Night
Prep
25 min
Cook
20 min
Total
45 min
Serves
4 servings (12 tacos)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Fish and beer batter

Cabbage slaw

Chipotle crema

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Salt the cabbage first
    Toss the shredded cabbage and red onion with the 1 tsp salt and 2 tbsp lime juice in a bowl and let it sit for at least 20 minutes while you do everything else. The salt pulls water out of the cabbage so it stays crunchy instead of going limp on the taco, and the lime softens the raw bite of the onion. Squeeze the slaw gently with your hands before serving and pour off the liquid that collects. Stir in the cilantro at the last minute so it stays green.
  2. Make the chipotle crema
    Whisk the crema, mayonnaise, 2 tbsp lime juice, minced chipotle, adobo sauce and 1/2 tsp salt in a small bowl until smooth. It should be thin enough to drizzle from a spoon in a steady ribbon; add water 1 tsp at a time if it is too thick. Taste it and remember it will be competing with fried fish, so it needs to be assertively tangy and a little spicy. Refrigerate until serving.
  3. Cut and dry the fish
    Cut the cod, halibut or mahi mahi fillets into strips about 1 in (2.5 cm) wide and 4 in (10 cm) long, roughly the width of two fingers, so they cook through in the same time it takes the batter to brown. Blot every piece dry on paper towels and season them lightly with half of the 1 tsp of salt set aside for the fish, saving the rest for after they come out of the oil. Wet fish makes the batter slide right off in the oil. Keep the fish in the fridge until the oil is at temperature.
  4. Heat the oil to 375°F
    Pour the 8 cups (1.9 L) of oil into a heavy 5 to 6 qt Dutch oven, which gives you a depth of about 1 1/2 in (4 cm) — enough for the strips to float free without the pot being dangerously full — and clip a thermometer to the side. Heat over medium-high to 375°F (190°C), which usually takes 8 to 10 minutes. Starting high matters because adding cold fish drops the oil by 25 to 50 degrees, and you want to land near 350°F (175°C) while frying. Oil below 325°F (163°C) gives you greasy, pale batter every time.
  5. Mix the batter at the last second
    Whisk the 1 cup (120 g) flour, cornstarch, baking powder, the 1 tsp of batter salt, garlic powder and chili powder in a bowl, then pour in the cold beer and stir just until it comes together with a few small lumps left. Overmixing develops gluten and gives you a bready, tough coating instead of a crisp shell. The batter should be about the thickness of heavy cream and drip off a spoon in a slow ribbon. Mix it right before frying so the bubbles are still lively.
  6. Dredge, then batter
    Put the extra 1/2 cup (65 g) flour in a shallow dish and toss each fish strip in it, shaking off the excess. That dry layer gives the wet batter something to grip so it does not slip off in the fryer. Dip a floured strip into the batter, let the excess run off for a count of two, then lower it into the oil away from you. Do not batter the fish ahead of time; do it one piece at a time as you fry.
  7. Fry in small batches
    Fry 3 or 4 strips at a time for 3 to 4 minutes total, turning once, until the coating is deep golden and audibly crisp when tapped with tongs. Crowding the pot drops the oil temperature and the batter absorbs oil instead of crisping. Let the oil come back up to 375°F (190°C) between batches, which takes about a minute. The fish is done at an internal temperature of 145°F (63°C) and will flake easily.
  8. Drain on a rack, not paper
    Lift each piece onto a wire rack set over a sheet pan and sprinkle immediately with the remaining 1/2 tsp of fish salt while the surface is still glistening — salt only sticks to hot, oily batter. A rack lets air circulate underneath so the bottom stays crisp; paper towels trap steam and the coating goes soft in two minutes. If you are frying several batches, keep the finished fish in a 200°F (95°C) oven. Never stack fried fish on top of itself.
  9. Warm the tortillas
    Toast the corn tortillas on a dry skillet or comal over medium-high heat for 20 to 30 seconds a side, until they are soft, flexible and smell like toasted corn. Wrap them in a clean towel to hold the steam and keep them warm. Warm tortillas fold without cracking and taste dramatically better than microwaved ones. Get these ready while the last batch of fish fries.
  10. Build the tacos
    Lay one or two pieces of fish in each warm tortilla, then top with a small handful of drained slaw, a heavy drizzle of chipotle crema, and a sprinkle of cotija. Squeeze a lime wedge over the top just before eating. Build them one at a time and eat them standing at the counter if necessary — the batter is at its best for about 90 seconds. Put the extra crema on the table for dipping.
Know when it is done
Fish is cooked through at 145°F (63°C) and will flake with gentle pressure. Keep the frying oil between 350°F (175°C) and 375°F (190°C) throughout.
Serve it with
A cold Pacifico with lime, or a grapefruit paloma, with a pile of tortilla chips and salsa to start.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Cod is the classic choice and the most forgiving, but any firm white fish works. Avoid thin, delicate fillets like sole, which fall apart in the batter.
  • ◆The beer must be cold and carbonated. The bubbles are what make the coating light, so open it right before you mix.
  • ◆For a lighter version, skip the batter entirely: season the fish with chili powder and cumin and sear it in a hot skillet for 2 to 3 minutes per side to 145°F (63°C).
  • ◆Slaw and crema both hold in the fridge for 2 days, so you can prep them in the morning and only fry at dinner.
  • ◆Save the frying oil: cool it completely, strain it through a coffee filter, and it is good for two more fish fries.

Chiles Rellenos in Tomato Caldillo⏱ 1 hr 30 min (includes 15 min chill)🍽 3 to 4 servings (6 chiles)Advanced▾

Charred poblanos stuffed with melting cheese, wrapped in a cloud-light egg batter, fried golden and set in a simple tomato broth. It takes patience and it is absolutely worth it.

VegetarianWeekend ProjectFried
Prep
40 min
Cook
35 min
Total
1 hr 30 min (includes 15 min chill)
Serves
3 to 4 servings (6 chiles)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chiles and filling

Tomato caldillo

Egg batter and frying

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Char the poblanos
    Set the poblanos directly over a high gas flame, or on a sheet pan 4 in (10 cm) under a hot broiler, and turn them every 2 to 3 minutes with tongs. You want the skin blistered and blackened over roughly 80 percent of each chile, which takes 8 to 12 minutes total. Do not rush this by cranking the heat higher — you are trying to blister the skin without cooking the flesh to mush. The chiles should still feel firm when you pick them up.
  2. Steam and peel
    Pile the hot chiles into a bowl and cover it tightly with plastic wrap or a plate for 10 to 15 minutes so they steam in their own heat. The trapped moisture separates the skin from the flesh and it will slip off under your thumb. Peel them with your fingers, not under running water, which washes away the smoky flavor you just spent ten minutes building. A few stubborn black flecks left behind are fine and traditional.
  3. Open and seed carefully
    Lay each chile flat and cut a single 3 in (8 cm) slit down one side, stopping about 1/2 in (1.3 cm) from the stem and the tip. Reach in with a small spoon or your fingers and pull out the seed pod and any loose seeds, keeping the chile otherwise intact. This is the delicate part: a tear means cheese leaking into the oil later. Sprinkle the inside of each with a pinch of the 1/2 tsp salt.
  4. Stuff and secure
    Slide 2 oz (55 g) of cheese batons into each chile, filling it generously but not so full that the slit gapes open. Press the edges of the slit together and pin them closed with a toothpick woven through like a stitch. Set the stuffed chiles on a plate and refrigerate for 15 minutes so the cheese firms up. Cold cheese takes longer to melt and run, which buys you time in the fryer.
  5. Make the caldillo
    Blend the tomatoes, onion and garlic until smooth, about 30 seconds. Heat the 1 tbsp oil in a saucepan over medium-high, pour in the puree — it will hiss — and cook for 5 minutes, stirring, until it darkens slightly. Add the broth, oregano and 3/4 tsp salt and simmer for 10 minutes until it is the consistency of a thin soup that lightly coats a spoon. Taste and adjust the salt; keep it warm over low heat.
  6. Heat the frying oil
    Pour the 4 cups (950 ml) oil into a 10 in (25 cm) skillet or wide saucepan, which gives a depth of about 3/4 in (2 cm), and heat over medium to 350°F (175°C). That is shallow on purpose: chiles rellenos are basted with hot oil rather than submerged, so the puffed batter never gets pressed flat against the pan. Use a thermometer — this batter is unforgiving. Too cool and it soaks up oil and slides off; too hot and the outside browns before the cheese melts. While it heats, set a wire rack over a sheet pan next to the stove.
  7. Beat the whites to stiff peaks
    Beat the 4 egg whites in a clean, completely dry bowl with a mixer on medium-high for 3 to 4 minutes, until they hold a stiff peak that stands straight up when you lift the beater. Any speck of yolk or drop of water will keep them from whipping, so wipe the bowl and the beaters with the 1 tsp of white vinegar on a paper towel first, which strips out any invisible film of fat. Stiff peaks are what make the coating puff into a golden cloud. Underwhipped whites give you a flat, eggy pancake.
  8. Fold in the yolks
    Add the 2 tbsp flour and 1/2 tsp salt to the whites and fold twice, then add the yolks and fold gently with a spatula just until no streaks of yellow remain, about 10 strokes. Cut down through the middle, sweep along the bottom, and turn the mixture over rather than stirring in circles. Every extra stroke deflates the air you just whipped in. Use the batter within 5 minutes; it will not wait.
  9. Dust the chiles with flour
    Spread the 1/2 cup (65 g) flour on a plate and roll each stuffed chile in it, patting off all but a thin film. Dry flour is the bridge between the wet chile skin and the egg batter, and skipping it is the number one reason the coating slides off in the oil. Hold each chile by the stem when you dust it. Have them all floured and lined up before you start frying.
  10. Batter and fry
    Holding a chile by the stem, lower it into the egg batter and spoon batter over it until it is completely coated, then lay it gently into the 350°F (175°C) oil away from you. Fry 2 at a time for 2 to 3 minutes, spooning hot oil over the top with a spoon so the exposed side sets. Flip carefully with two spoons and fry another 2 minutes until deep golden all over. Crowding the pan makes them stick together and tear.
  11. Drain and rest
    Lift each chile onto the wire rack with a slotted spoon and let it drain for 2 minutes while you fry the rest. A rack keeps the bottom crisp; a paper towel steams it soft. Pull the toothpicks out now while you can still see them. Sprinkle with a small pinch of salt while they are hot.
  12. Serve in the caldillo
    Ladle about 1/2 cup of the warm tomato caldillo into each shallow bowl and set one or two chiles on top so the batter stays crisp above the sauce rather than drowning in it. Serve immediately — chiles rellenos are a dish you eat the minute they are done, not one you hold. Pass extra caldillo and the 8 warm corn tortillas at the table for mopping the bowl. Warn everyone that the cheese inside is molten hot.
Know when it is done
Keep the frying oil at 350°F (175°C) — the batter needs that exact window to puff and set. The chiles are ready when the cheese inside is fully molten, around 160°F (71°C) in the center.
Serve it with
Mexican rice and black beans, with a crisp lager or a glass of dry Mexican rosé.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Oaxaca cheese is the right one: it melts into stretchy strands rather than breaking into grease the way cheddar does. Low-moisture mozzarella is a decent substitute.
  • ◆You can char, peel and stuff the chiles up to a day ahead and keep them covered in the fridge. Only the batter and the frying have to happen at the last minute.
  • ◆If the batter slides off during frying, the chiles were wet or under-floured. Pat them dry before dusting and use a light but complete coat of flour.
  • ◆Poblanos vary in heat from mild to genuinely spicy and there is no way to tell from the outside. Taste a fleck of one after peeling so you know what you are serving.
  • ◆Traditional versions add shredded picadillo instead of cheese. If you have leftover carnitas or tinga, mix 1 cup of it with the cheese for a heartier chile.

Chicken Enchiladas Verdes⏱ 1 hr 25 min (includes 10 min rest)🍽 4 servings (12 enchiladas)Medium▾

Tomatillo salsa with real heat and real acid, poured over chicken-filled corn tortillas and baked until the cheese blisters. Tangy, green and much brighter than any red enchilada.

CasseroleMake AheadWeeknight
Prep
30 min
Cook
45 min
Total
1 hr 25 min (includes 10 min rest)
Serves
4 servings (12 enchiladas)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Salsa verde

Filling and assembly

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Char the tomatillos and chiles
    Spread the tomatillos, serranos, onion halves and unpeeled garlic on a foil-lined sheet pan and broil 4 in (10 cm) from the element for 8 to 10 minutes, turning once. The tomatillos should slump, blister and turn from bright green to olive with blackened patches. That char is the difference between a salsa that tastes flat and one that tastes like a taqueria. Pull the garlic as soon as its skin is browned and squeeze the soft cloves free.
  2. Blend the salsa
    Scrape everything, including all the juices on the pan, into a blender with the cilantro and blend until smooth, about 45 seconds. It will look pale and foamy right out of the blender, which is normal and disappears once it is cooked. Start with 2 serranos if you are cautious; tomatillo salsa hides its heat until the third bite. Do not add salt yet.
  3. Fry the salsa
    Heat the 1 tbsp oil in a large saucepan over medium-high until it shimmers, then pour in the blended salsa all at once and stand back from the spitting. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring often, until it darkens to a deeper green and thickens enough to coat a spoon. Frying the salsa is what turns a raw, sharp puree into a rounded sauce. Add the chicken broth and 1 1/2 tsp salt and simmer 5 more minutes.
  4. Season the chicken
    Toss the 3 cups shredded chicken with 1/2 cup of the warm salsa verde and the 1/2 tsp salt in a bowl. Moistening the filling now keeps it from drying out in the oven and means every bite has sauce in it, not just on it. Use thigh meat if you can — it stays juicy through baking where breast meat can go chalky. Taste it; the filling should be seasoned enough to eat on its own.
  5. Heat the oven
    Preheat the oven to 400°F (205°C) and set a rack in the middle. Spread 3/4 cup of the salsa verde across the bottom of a 9 x 13 in (23 x 33 cm) baking dish in a thin, even layer. That base layer keeps the tortillas from sticking and gluing themselves to the dish. Have the dish, the filling, the cheese and the salsa all lined up before you start rolling.
  6. Soften the tortillas in oil
    Heat the 1/4 cup (60 ml) oil in a small skillet over medium until it shimmers, then slip in one tortilla at a time for about 10 seconds per side. It should turn pliable and slightly puffy but never crisp. This quick fry is the traditional step everyone skips, and it is why restaurant enchiladas hold together while home versions dissolve into mush. Drain each tortilla on paper towels and stack them as you go.
  7. Dip and roll
    Dip a softened tortilla into the pot of warm salsa verde so both sides are lightly coated, then lay it on a plate. Spoon about 1/4 cup of chicken down the center, add a small pinch of cheese, and roll it up snugly. Place it seam side down in the baking dish and repeat, nestling each one against the last. Working assembly-line style keeps your hands from getting hopelessly sticky.
  8. Sauce and cheese
    Pour the remaining salsa verde evenly over the rolled enchiladas, making sure the ends are covered because exposed tortilla edges turn to leather in the oven. Scatter the shredded cheese over the top in an even layer. Do not drown them — you want the tops sitting just at the surface of the sauce, not submerged. A little sauce should pool at the sides.
  9. Bake until bubbling
    Bake uncovered for 18 to 22 minutes, until the sauce bubbles vigorously around the edges and the cheese is fully melted with a few golden-brown blisters. If the cheese has melted but not browned, run the dish under the broiler for 60 to 90 seconds, watching it constantly. The center of the dish should register 165°F (74°C) on a thermometer. The bubbling is your real cue, not the clock.
  10. Rest before serving
    Let the dish sit on the counter for 5 to 10 minutes before serving. Straight out of the oven the sauce is thin and the enchiladas will slide apart when you lift them; a short rest lets everything set enough to plate cleanly. It is also the difference between tasting your dinner and burning the roof of your mouth. Loosen the edges with a spatula while it rests.
  11. Finish with cold toppings
    Drizzle the crema over the hot enchiladas in thin lines, then scatter the queso fresco, thin-sliced white onion and cilantro across the top. Fan the avocado slices along one side. The cold, sharp toppings against the hot, tangy sauce are the whole point, so do not skip them. Serve with a lime wedge and plenty of napkins.
Know when it is done
Bake until the center of the dish reaches 165°F (74°C) and the sauce bubbles at the edges. Any pre-cooked chicken filling must be reheated to that same 165°F (74°C).
Serve it with
Black beans, Mexican rice and a cold michelada, or a bright Sauvignon Blanc if you want wine.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make the salsa verde up to 4 days ahead; it improves overnight. It also freezes for 3 months in a zip-top bag laid flat.
  • ◆Assemble the whole dish, cover, and refrigerate up to 24 hours before baking. Add 8 to 10 minutes to the bake time if it goes in cold.
  • ◆If your tomatillos are very tart, blend in 1/4 of a peeled avocado or 2 tbsp of crema to round the sauce out without dulling the flavor.
  • ◆Never use flour tortillas here. They turn gummy and pasty under sauce, and corn is what makes these taste right.
  • ◆A rotisserie chicken makes this a 45-minute weeknight dinner. One bird gives you almost exactly the 3 cups of meat you need.

Enchiladas Rojas with Guajillo Sauce⏱ 1 hr 25 min (includes 10 min rest)🍽 4 servings (12 enchiladas)Medium▾

A real red chile sauce built from toasted guajillos and anchos, not chili powder from a jar. Learn this sauce and you have unlocked half of Mexican cooking.

CasseroleChile SauceMake Ahead
Prep
30 min
Cook
45 min
Total
1 hr 25 min (includes 10 min rest)
Serves
4 servings (12 enchiladas)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Red chile sauce

Filling and assembly

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Clean the dried chiles
    Wipe each guajillo and ancho with a damp paper towel to remove dust, then snap off the stems and tear the chiles open along one side. Shake out and discard the seeds and pull away the pale veins inside, which carry bitterness more than heat. Guajillos are the tannic, bright, slightly fruity backbone; anchos are the sweet, raisiny, dark ones. Together they give you a sauce with both brightness and depth.
  2. Toast the chiles
    Heat a dry comal or heavy skillet over medium heat and press the opened chiles flat against the surface for 15 to 20 seconds per side. They should soften slightly, turn a shade lighter, and release a smell like sweet tobacco and dried fruit. Do not let them darken or smoke — a scorched chile turns the entire sauce acrid and bitter, and there is no way to rescue it. If you want real heat, toast the 2 chiles de arbol alongside them for 10 seconds a side only, since small thin chiles scorch in half the time. Work in batches so you can watch every piece.
  3. Rehydrate in hot water
    Put the toasted chiles in a bowl, pour the 3 cups (700 ml) of very hot water over them, and set a small plate on top to keep them submerged. Soak for 20 to 25 minutes until they are completely soft and floppy like wet leather. Taste the soaking water: if it is pleasantly fruity, save 1 cup for blending, and if it is bitter, dump it and use plain water instead. Old chiles that have gone brittle and gray will taste bitter no matter what you do.
  4. Blend the sauce smooth
    Put the drained chiles, onion, garlic, oregano, cumin, cinnamon, vinegar and 1 cup of the soaking liquid in a blender and run it on high for a full 90 seconds. It needs longer than you think — the skins are tough and a short blend leaves gritty flecks. The sauce should be the color of dark brick and completely smooth. Add up to 1/4 cup more liquid if the blender is struggling.
  5. Strain the sauce
    Pour the blended sauce through a fine-mesh sieve set over a bowl, pressing hard with a rubber spatula and scraping the underside of the sieve. You will leave behind a few tablespoons of tough skin, and what passes through will be silky. This one extra minute is the difference between a professional-tasting sauce and a slightly gritty one. Do not skip it, even with a high-powered blender.
  6. Fry the sauce
    Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a saucepan over medium-high until it shimmers, then pour in the strained sauce — it will hiss and spatter hard, so use a splatter screen. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring constantly, until it darkens, thickens, and smells toasted rather than raw. Frying the chile puree in fat blooms the fat-soluble flavors and is the single most important step in the recipe. Add the chicken broth and 1 1/2 tsp salt and simmer 8 minutes more.
  7. Taste and balance
    Taste the finished sauce and adjust: if it is flat, add salt; if it is harsh, add another 1/2 tsp of the vinegar; if it is bitter, stir in the 1 tsp of honey to pull it back. It should coat a spoon like heavy cream and taste deep, faintly sweet and gently earthy. Season the shredded chicken with 1/2 cup of it and toss to coat. Keep the rest warm over low heat.
  8. Preheat and prep the dish
    Heat the oven to 400°F (205°C) with a rack in the middle position. Ladle 3/4 cup of the red sauce over the bottom of a 9 x 13 in (23 x 33 cm) baking dish and spread it into an even film. That layer keeps the tortillas from cementing themselves to the dish. Line up the sauce, filling, cheese and dish so assembly goes quickly.
  9. Soften the tortillas
    Heat the 1/4 cup (60 ml) oil in a small skillet over medium and pass each tortilla through for about 10 seconds per side, until floppy and just barely puffed. This seals the tortilla so it absorbs sauce without disintegrating. Drain them on paper towels in a stack. If you skip this, you will be serving red chile soup with corn mush in it.
  10. Dip, fill and roll
    Dip each softened tortilla into the warm red sauce to coat both sides, then lay it flat and spoon about 1/4 cup of the seasoned chicken down the middle with a small pinch of cheese. Roll it up snugly and set it seam side down in the dish. Pack them side by side so they support each other and stay rolled. Twelve should fit in a single tight row.
  11. Top and bake
    Pour the remaining sauce evenly over the top, covering all the exposed tortilla ends, then scatter the shredded cheese across. Bake uncovered for 18 to 20 minutes, until the sauce bubbles at the edges and the cheese has melted with browned spots. The center should read 165°F (74°C). If you want more color, broil for 60 seconds at the end.
  12. Rest and garnish
    Let the dish rest for 8 minutes so the sauce thickens enough to hold the enchiladas together when you serve them. Drizzle with crema, then top with queso fresco, thin-sliced onion and cilantro. The cool creamy garnishes cut the deep, slightly bitter chile flavor and are not decoration. Serve with a wedge of lime and rice on the side.
Know when it is done
Bake until the center of the dish hits 165°F (74°C) and the sauce is bubbling. Toast the dried chiles only until fragrant, about 15 to 20 seconds per side — any smoke means bitterness.
Serve it with
Refried beans, Mexican rice, and a dark Negra Modelo or a glass of Garnacha.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Buy dried chiles that are still flexible and smell fragrant when you bend them. Brittle chiles that crack like a potato chip are old and will taste dusty and bitter.
  • ◆The red chile sauce is the workhorse of this chapter. Make a double batch and freeze half — it becomes the base for tamales, pozole and birria.
  • ◆If you toast a chile too far and it smells sharp and burnt, throw it out. One scorched chile will ruin an entire pot of sauce.
  • ◆Guajillo is mild, ancho is mild and sweet, and chiles de arbol are genuinely hot. Adjust heat with the arbols only, and start with one.
  • ◆Wear gloves or wash your hands thoroughly with soap after handling the soaked chiles, and keep your fingers away from your eyes for a while.
