Elote, Mexican Street Corn⏱ 25 min🍽 4 servings (4 ears)Easy▾

Charred corn slathered in a lime and crema dressing, rolled in salty cotija and dusted with chile. Fifteen minutes of work for the best thing on the grill.

GrillSide Dish30 Minutes
Prep
10 min
Cook
15 min
Total
25 min
Serves
4 servings (4 ears)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the corn

Crema dressing

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Pick and prep the corn
    Look for ears with tight green husks and moist, pale silk at the tip, which means they were picked recently. Pull the husks off and rub the remaining silk away with a dry paper towel, which grabs it better than your fingers do. Trim the stem end flat so the ear sits still on the grill. Pat each ear completely dry, because wet corn steams instead of charring.
  2. Mix the dressing
    Whisk the crema, mayonnaise, grated garlic, lime juice, lime zest and 1/4 tsp salt in a wide shallow bowl big enough to roll an ear of corn in. The mayonnaise is not a shortcut — its emulsified fat is what makes the coating cling to hot corn instead of sliding off. Taste it and add more lime if it feels heavy. Set it next to the grill along with the cotija on a second plate.
  3. Heat the grill hot
    Get a charcoal or gas grill to medium-high, around 450°F (230°C), with the grates scraped clean and lightly oiled. If you are indoors, heat a cast iron grill pan or a heavy skillet over medium-high for 4 minutes until a drop of water dances and vanishes. You need real heat to blister the kernels before the corn overcooks and goes chewy. Rub the ears with the 1 tbsp oil and the 1/2 tsp salt.
  4. Char the corn
    Lay the ears on the grill and cook for 10 to 12 minutes total, turning every 2 to 3 minutes with tongs. You are after individual kernels blackened in spots across roughly a quarter of the surface, with the rest deep yellow and glossy. Uniformly black corn is burnt and tastes like ash; uniformly yellow corn is boiled and boring. Listen for the occasional pop, which means the kernels are heating through.
  5. Check for doneness
    Corn carries no food-safety temperature, so judge it by texture: press a kernel with your thumbnail and it should give slightly and release a little milky juice rather than squirting thin water. The kernels should be plump and glossy and the cob too hot to hold bare-handed, roughly 150°F to 165°F (65°C to 74°C) if you push a thermometer into the center of a row. Fresh summer corn only needs to be warmed and charred, since it is perfectly good raw. Older supermarket corn wants the full 12 minutes to lose its starchy chew.
  6. Skewer them while hot
    Move the ears to a board and push a wooden skewer or a corn holder into the stem end of each one, using a folded towel to protect your hand. A handle is what makes elote street food rather than fork-and-knife food. Work fast, because the dressing clings best to corn that is still steaming. Do not let the corn sit and cool while you look for the cotija.
  7. Roll in the dressing
    Roll each hot ear through the crema mixture, using the back of a spoon to push the dressing into every gap between the kernel rows. You want a thin, even white coat over the whole ear, not thick globs on one side. The heat will loosen the dressing slightly, which is what helps it spread. Let the excess drip back into the bowl.
  8. Coat in cotija
    Immediately roll the dressed ear in the crumbled cotija spread on a plate, pressing gently so the cheese sticks in a heavy layer. Crumble the cotija finely first — big chunks fall off on the first bite and end up on the floor. Cotija is salty and dry, closer to a young Parmesan than to feta. If you cannot find it, Pecorino Romano grated fine is the best substitute.
  9. Dust and serve
    Dust each ear generously with chili powder or Tajin and the optional cayenne, then scatter the chopped cilantro over the top. Serve right away with lime wedges to squeeze over at the table, which brightens all that fat and salt. Elote is best within five minutes of coming off the grill. Put a stack of napkins out and warn people it is messy.
Know when it is done
Corn has no safety temperature — the cue is texture. Grill over a surface around 450°F (230°C) until the kernels are blistered in spots, plump, and release milky juice under a thumbnail, which lands around 150°F to 165°F (65°C to 74°C) inside.
Serve it with
Anything off the grill, especially carne asada, plus a cold Mexican lager or a watermelon agua fresca.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆No grill? Char the corn under a broiler 4 in (10 cm) from the element for 10 to 12 minutes, turning every 3 minutes, and you will get almost the same result.
  • ◆To turn this into esquites, cut the charred kernels off the cob and toss them with the dressing, cotija and chile in a bowl. Serve it warm with a spoon and it travels far better to a party.
  • ◆The dressing keeps for 5 days in the fridge and is excellent on grilled zucchini, sweet potatoes or a wedge of iceberg.
  • ◆Tajin brings lime and salt along with the chile, so if you use it, cut the added salt in the dressing to a pinch.
  • ◆Buy corn the same day you cook it. Sugars turn to starch fast, and day-old supermarket corn is noticeably less sweet.

Pozole Rojo with Pork and Hominy⏱ 3 hr 20 min🍽 6 to 8 servingsMedium▾

A deep red chile broth with tender pork and chewy hominy, finished at the table with cabbage, radish and lime. It is Mexico's great celebration soup and it feeds a crowd.

SoupWeekend ProjectMake Ahead
Prep
30 min
Cook
2 hr 50 min
Total
3 hr 20 min
Serves
6 to 8 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Pork and broth

Red chile paste

Hominy and finishing

Garnishes for the table

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Start the pork simmering
    Put the pork shoulder chunks, neck bones, onion halves, 8 garlic cloves, bay leaves, 1 tbsp oregano and 1 tbsp salt in a large stockpot and cover with the 14 cups (3.3 L) water. Bring it to a boil over high heat, then immediately drop the heat to low so it barely simmers. A rolling boil emulsifies the fat and turns the broth cloudy and greasy instead of clear and clean. You want a bubble breaking the surface every second or two, no more.
  2. Skim the foam
    For the first 15 minutes, gray foam will rise to the surface — skim it off with a wide spoon or a small ladle and discard it. That foam is coagulated protein and it makes the finished broth murky and slightly bitter if you stir it back in. Once the foam stops forming and the surface is clear, partially cover the pot. Let it simmer for 2 hours while you make the chile paste.
  3. Clean and toast the chiles
    Wipe the guajillos and anchos with a damp towel, snap off the stems, tear them open and shake out the seeds and pale veins. Press them flat on a dry comal or skillet over medium heat for 15 to 20 seconds per side, until they smell like sweet dried fruit and tobacco. The instant you see wisps of smoke or the color going dark, they are burnt and the whole pot will taste bitter. Toast the arbols for only 10 seconds; they scorch fast.
  4. Rehydrate the chiles
    Cover the toasted chiles with the 3 cups (700 ml) hot water in a bowl and weigh them down with a plate so they stay under. Soak for 20 to 25 minutes until they are completely limp and soft, like wet leather. Taste the soaking liquid — if it is fruity and pleasant, reserve 1 1/2 cups of it for blending; if it is bitter, discard it and use fresh water. The chiles should tear easily between your fingers when they are ready.
  5. Blend and strain the paste
    Blend the drained chiles with the 4 garlic cloves, quartered onion, cumin, 1 tsp oregano and 1 1/2 cups of soaking liquid on high for a full 90 seconds until absolutely smooth. Pour it through a fine-mesh sieve into a bowl, pressing hard with a spatula to force everything but the tough skins through. Straining is what separates a silky red broth from a gritty one. You should have about 2 1/2 cups of smooth red paste.
  6. Fry the chile paste
    Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a skillet over medium-high until it shimmers, then add the strained paste all at once — it will spit, so use a splatter guard. Fry for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring constantly, until the paste darkens noticeably and thickens to the texture of tomato paste. This step blooms the chiles' fat-soluble flavors and removes the raw, dusty taste. It should smell rich and toasted, never sharp.
  7. Check the pork
    After 2 hours, test a chunk of pork shoulder with a fork — it should yield with almost no pressure and shred at the edges, at an internal temperature around 195°F (91°C). If it is still firm, give it another 20 to 30 minutes and check again. Lift out the neck bones and discard them along with the onion halves and bay leaves. Skim the fat off the top of the broth with a ladle, saving 2 tbsp of it if you want extra richness.
  8. Marry the chile and the broth
    Stir the fried chile paste into the pot and watch the broth turn a deep, glowing brick red. Simmer uncovered for 20 minutes so the flavors knit together and the broth reduces slightly. Taste it now and start seasoning — this is a big pot and it will take more salt than you expect, probably another 1 to 2 tsp. It should taste rounded and savory with a slow chile warmth, not sharp.
  9. Add the hominy
    Drain and rinse the canned hominy well under cold water to wash off the tinny canning liquid, then stir it into the pot. Simmer for another 20 to 25 minutes so the kernels soften slightly and drink up the red broth. Properly cooked hominy is chewy and springy with a faint sweet corn flavor, never mushy. If the broth has reduced too far, add 1 cup of hot water.
  10. Shred the pork
    Lift the pork chunks out with a slotted spoon onto a board and pull them into large, rough shreds with two forks, discarding any hard lumps of fat. Return the shredded meat to the pot and let it warm through for 5 minutes. Shredding after cooking, rather than before, keeps the pieces juicy instead of letting them dry out in the broth. Taste one last time for salt.
  11. Set up the garnish table
    Put the shredded cabbage, sliced radishes, diced onion, cilantro, lime wedges, oregano and chile piquin in separate small bowls and set them all in the middle of the table. Pozole is only half made in the pot; the cold crunchy garnishes are what make it come alive. Everyone builds their own bowl, and there is no wrong combination. Warm the tostadas in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 3 minutes.
  12. Serve it very hot
    Ladle the pozole into wide bowls, making sure each one gets plenty of pork, hominy and broth. Encourage everyone to crush oregano between their palms over the bowl and squeeze in lime before the first bite. The soup should be steaming hot, because it cools fast once the cold cabbage goes in. Serve tostadas on the side for dipping and crumbling.
Know when it is done
Simmer the pork to about 195°F (91°C), far past the 145°F (63°C) plus 3-minute rest that pork needs for safety, so the collagen melts and the meat shreds. Serve the soup steaming at 165°F (74°C) or above.
Serve it with
Warm tostadas or a bolillo on the side, with a cold Mexican lager or a bright hibiscus agua fresca.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Pozole is famously better on day two. Make it a day ahead, chill it overnight, lift off the solid fat cap, and reheat gently — the chile flavor deepens noticeably.
  • ◆Dried hominy is traditional and better, but it needs an overnight soak and 2 to 3 hours of its own cooking. Canned hominy is a perfectly respectable shortcut and what most home cooks in Mexico use now.
  • ◆For pozole de pollo, swap in 3 lb (1.35 kg) of bone-in chicken thighs and cut the simmer to 45 minutes, pulling them at 175°F (79°C) for shreddable dark meat.
  • ◆If the broth tastes bitter, one of your chiles scorched during toasting. A teaspoon of honey and an extra pinch of salt will mask it, but next time pull the chiles the second they smell fragrant.
  • ◆Freeze leftovers without the garnishes in quart containers for up to 3 months. Add fresh cabbage and radish when you reheat.

Skillet Chicken Quesadillas⏱ 50 min🍽 4 servings (4 quesadillas)Easy▾

A crackling, blistered tortilla with a molten cheese seal and just enough seasoned chicken inside. Done right, a quesadilla is not lazy food at all.

WeeknightOne SkilletKid Friendly
Prep
15 min
Cook
35 min
Total
50 min
Serves
4 servings (4 quesadillas)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chicken filling

Assembly

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Shred your own cheese
    Buy Oaxaca or Monterey Jack in a block and shred it yourself on the large holes of a box grater. Pre-shredded cheese is dusted with potato starch and cellulose to keep it from clumping, and that coating makes it melt into a grainy, oily mess. Freshly shredded cheese melts into a smooth, stretchy sheet that glues the quesadilla shut. Keep it cold until the moment you build.
  2. Season the chicken
    Toss the diced chicken thighs with the cumin, chili powder, oregano, 1 tsp salt and pepper in a bowl until every piece is coated. Let it sit for 10 minutes while you slice the vegetables so the salt starts penetrating. Thighs are worth using over breast here because they stay juicy even after they go back into a hot skillet inside the quesadilla. Cut the pieces small so they lie flat and do not tear the tortilla.
  3. Cook the chicken hot
    Heat the 1 tbsp oil in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium-high until it shimmers, then add the chicken in a single layer and leave it undisturbed for 3 minutes. It should sizzle steadily and hard, not gently — that first contact is where the browning happens. Stir and cook 3 to 4 minutes more until the pieces are golden and register 165°F (74°C) on a thermometer. Scrape it all onto a plate.
  4. Soften the onion and poblano
    Add the sliced onion and poblano strips to the same pan with a pinch of salt and cook over medium-high for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring occasionally. You want them softened and streaked with brown at the edges, with the poblano just losing its raw grassiness. The browned bits left from the chicken will lift off the pan and season the vegetables. Return the chicken to the pan, add the lime juice, toss and turn off the heat.
  5. Drain the filling
    Tip the filling into a bowl and let it sit for a minute, then pour off any liquid that collects at the bottom. Wet filling is the number one cause of soggy quesadillas — the steam has nowhere to go and turns the tortilla limp. The filling should look glossy but not swimming. Stir the cilantro through it now.
  6. Build with cheese on both sides
    Lay a tortilla flat and scatter about 1/3 cup of shredded cheese over the entire surface, then spread a quarter of the chicken filling over one half only. Top the filling with another 1/3 cup of cheese and fold the bare half over. Cheese on both the bottom and the top of the filling is what welds the quesadilla into one piece instead of letting it fall open. Press the half-moon gently flat with your palm.
  7. Butter the outside
    Spread a thin film of the softened butter over the top surface of the folded quesadilla, using about 1/2 tbsp per side — 4 quesadillas buttered on both sides is where the 4 tbsp goes. Butter browns more evenly than oil and gives you that blistered, freckled crust with a nutty flavor. Do not use so much that it pools in the pan and fries the tortilla greasy. A thin swipe is all it takes.
  8. Griddle low and slow
    Wipe the skillet clean and set it over medium-low heat, then lay the quesadilla in butter side down and cook for 3 to 4 minutes. Medium-low is the key: the tortilla needs time for the cheese in the center to melt completely before the outside burns. It should hiss quietly, not crackle aggressively. Butter the exposed top side while the first side cooks. One skillet holds one quesadilla, so budget about 7 minutes each and hold the finished ones in a warm oven.
  9. Flip and finish
    Slide a wide spatula fully under the quesadilla and flip it in one confident motion, supporting the folded edge with your other hand. Cook the second side for 3 minutes until it is deep golden with dark blistered spots and the cheese is visibly molten at the seam. Press down gently with the spatula once to seal it. Cook the remaining quesadillas the same way.
  10. Rest, then cut
    Move each finished quesadilla to a cutting board and let it sit for 2 minutes before cutting. Molten cheese needs that moment to set up just slightly, or it all runs out the second the knife goes through. Cut each into 3 wedges with a large sharp knife or a pizza wheel, pressing straight down rather than sawing. Serve immediately with crema, salsa, avocado and lime.
Know when it is done
Cook the chicken to 165°F (74°C) before it goes into the quesadilla. Griddle over medium-low so the cheese fully melts, which takes 3 to 4 minutes per side.
Serve it with
Guacamole and chips, plus a lime agua fresca or an ice-cold Mexican lager.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆The Mexican street version uses corn tortillas folded around Oaxaca cheese and griddled dry. Try it once — it is a completely different and arguably better thing.
  • ◆Any leftover braise from this chapter turns this into a great quesadilla: carnitas, tinga or birria all work. Drain them well first.
  • ◆Keep finished quesadillas crisp in a 200°F (95°C) oven on a wire rack while you cook the rest. Never stack them, or the steam softens the crust.
  • ◆If cheese leaks and burns in the pan, wipe the skillet clean between quesadillas. Burnt cheese turns bitter and blackens the next one.
  • ◆For a make-ahead lunch, cook the filling up to 3 days in advance and refrigerate it. Assembly and griddling take under 10 minutes.

Loaded Sheet Pan Nachos⏱ 40 min🍽 6 servingsEasy▾

Layered so every single chip gets cheese, beef and beans, then baked until it all fuses together. The trick is building it in two layers instead of one big pile.

Game DaySheet PanCrowd Pleaser
Prep
20 min
Cook
20 min
Total
40 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Seasoned beef

For the pan

Cold toppings

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Heat the oven and pan
    Set the oven to 400°F (205°C) with a rack in the upper third and line a rimmed sheet pan, about 13 x 18 in (33 x 46 cm), with parchment or foil. The upper rack gets the cheese browning without overcooking the chips underneath. Have every topping prepped and within arm's reach before anything goes in the oven, because nachos go from perfect to sad in about four minutes. Shred your own cheese from a block for a smoother melt.
  2. Brown the beef properly
    Heat a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium-high and add the ground beef, breaking it into large chunks with a wooden spoon and then leaving it alone for 3 minutes. Letting it sit undisturbed builds a browned crust, which is where the flavor lives — constant stirring just steams gray meat. Add the onion and cook 4 minutes more, breaking the beef into smaller pieces. Stir in the garlic in the last 30 seconds.
  3. Season and reduce
    Sprinkle in the chili powder, cumin, oregano, smoked paprika and 1 tsp salt and stir for 30 seconds until fragrant, which toasts the spices in the hot fat. Add the 1/3 cup (80 ml) water and simmer for 2 to 3 minutes until the liquid has reduced to a glaze that clings to the meat. Ground beef must reach 160°F (71°C) to be safe, and this simmer takes it comfortably past that. The pan should look glossy, not soupy.
  4. Drain the fat
    Tilt the pan and spoon off all but about 1 tbsp of the rendered fat, or drain the meat in a sieve set over a bowl. Excess grease pools at the bottom of the sheet pan and turns the lower chips into a soggy raft. This is the step that separates good nachos from greasy ones. Taste the beef and adjust the salt now, while you still can.
  5. Drain the wet toppings too
    Tip the pico de gallo into a fine-mesh sieve and let it drain for 5 minutes, and shake the black beans and jalapenos dry. Water is the enemy of a crisp chip, and tomatoes hold a surprising amount of it. Set the drained toppings aside; the pico goes on cold at the end, never into the oven. Pat the beans dry with a paper towel if they still look wet.
  6. Lay the first layer
    Spread half the tortilla chips over the sheet pan in a single overlapping layer, edge to edge. Do not pile them into a mound — the whole point of a sheet pan is that every chip touches the heat. Choose thick, sturdy restaurant-style chips, since thin ones snap under a single spoonful of beef. A single flat layer is the foundation of the whole build.
  7. Build layer one
    Scatter half the beef, half the black beans, half the shredded cheddar and half the Monterey Jack over that first layer of chips, distributing them so no chip is left bare and none is buried. Layering matters more than quantity: two thin layers beat one thick pile every time. Cover the corners as generously as the middle, since those are the chips people fight over. Add half the pickled jalapenos.
  8. Build layer two
    Spread the remaining chips over the top, then repeat with the rest of the beef, beans, both cheeses and jalapenos. The second layer of cheese should be a little heavier than the first, because that top layer is what browns and blisters. Press the whole thing down gently with your palms so it holds together. Do not add anything fresh yet.
  9. Bake until it fuses
    Bake for 8 to 10 minutes, until the cheese is completely melted, bubbling at the edges, and just starting to brown in spots. Check at 8 minutes and pull it the moment the cheese stops looking wet and starts looking glossy. Overbaking dries the chips out and makes the cheese oily and separated. If you want more color, broil for exactly 60 seconds while watching it.
  10. Top cold and serve on the pan
    Pull the pan out and immediately scatter the drained pico de gallo, diced avocado, cilantro and scallions over the top, then drizzle the crema in thin zigzags from a spoon or a squeeze bottle. The contrast between the hot melted layer and the cold fresh toppings is what makes nachos good. Serve directly from the sheet pan with lime wedges. Eat within ten minutes, standing up, with your hands.
Know when it is done
Ground beef must reach 160°F (71°C) to be safe — check it in the pan before layering. Bake at 400°F (205°C) just until the cheese bubbles, 8 to 10 minutes.
Serve it with
A pitcher of margaritas or a cold lager, with extra guacamole and salsa on the side.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Two thin layers instead of one deep pile is the entire secret. Every chip gets a topping and nothing steams into mush at the bottom.
  • ◆Swap the ground beef for 2 cups of leftover carnitas, tinga or birria and these become genuinely special.
  • ◆Never bake the tomatoes, avocado or crema. Anything fresh goes on after the pan leaves the oven, or it turns hot and slimy.
  • ◆Cook the beef up to 3 days ahead and refrigerate it. Reheat it in a skillet before layering so it does not cool the cheese down.
  • ◆For vegetarian nachos, double the black beans and add 1 cup of roasted sweet potato cubes or sauteed poblano strips in place of the beef.

Red Chile Pork Tamales⏱ 4 hr 30 min (includes 15 min rest)🍽 Makes 24 tamalesAdvanced▾

Fluffy masa wrapped in corn husks around slow-braised pork in guajillo sauce, steamed until they slide clean out of the wrapper. Make them with someone you like, because it goes faster with two.

Weekend ProjectHolidayMake Ahead
Prep
45 min
Cook
3 hr 30 min
Total
4 hr 30 min (includes 15 min rest)
Serves
Makes 24 tamales
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Red chile pork filling

Masa

Wrapping and steaming

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Braise the pork
    Put the pork chunks, onion, garlic, bay leaves and 1 tbsp salt in a large pot with the 8 cups (1.9 L) water, bring to a boil, then lower to a bare simmer. Skim the gray foam off during the first 15 minutes so the broth stays clean. Simmer partially covered for 2 hours, until the pork shreds under fork pressure at about 195°F (91°C). Reserve every drop of the broth — you need 3 1/2 cups of it for the masa and another 1 1/2 cups for the chile sauce, and it is what makes homemade tamales taste like tamales.
  2. Soak the corn husks
    While the pork cooks, submerge the corn husks in the 12 cups (2.8 L) of hot water in a large bowl or clean sink, weighing them down with a plate. Soak for at least 30 minutes, until they are completely pliable and unfold without cracking. Rinse each one and rub off any grit or corn silk, then shake off the excess water. Tear 6 or 8 of the smaller husks lengthwise into thin strips to use as ties.
  3. Toast and rehydrate the chiles
    Press the stemmed, seeded guajillos and anchos flat on a dry comal over medium heat for 15 to 20 seconds per side, until they smell sweet and toasty. Pull them the instant they release their aroma; a chile that smokes has burned and will make the whole batch bitter. Cover them with 3 cups (700 ml) of hot water and soak 20 minutes until fully soft. Weigh them down with a plate so they stay submerged.
  4. Make the red chile sauce
    Blend the drained chiles with 1 1/2 cups of the pork broth, the cumin, oregano and vinegar for a full 90 seconds until perfectly smooth, then push it through a fine-mesh sieve to remove the skins. Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a skillet over medium-high and fry the strained sauce for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until it darkens and thickens. Frying is not optional — it turns raw chile puree into a deep, rounded sauce. Stir in the 1 tsp salt, taste, and add more until the sauce tastes seasoned on its own.
  5. Shred and sauce the pork
    Pull the cooled pork into rough shreds with two forks, discarding hard fat, and stir it into the red chile sauce in a bowl. You want the pork glossy and well coated but not swimming, so add sauce a ladle at a time until it looks right. Taste and season aggressively — the masa around it is mild, so the filling has to carry the flavor for both. Let it cool completely before assembling, or it will melt the masa.
  6. Whip the lard
    Beat the 1 1/3 cups (280 g) of room-temperature lard in a stand mixer with the paddle on medium-high for 4 to 5 minutes, until it is white, fluffy and roughly doubled in volume, like frosting. This is the step that decides whether your tamales are light or dense, so do not shorten it. Cold lard will not whip; leave it out for an hour first. Scrape the bowl down twice as you go.
  7. Build the masa
    In a separate bowl, whisk the masa harina, baking powder and 2 tsp salt together. Add this to the whipped lard in three additions, alternating with the 3 1/2 cups of warm pork broth, and beat on medium for 5 minutes after the last addition. The finished masa should look like thick, spreadable hummus and hold a soft peak on a spoon. Masa harina varies in how much it drinks, so start here and beat in more warm broth 2 tbsp at a time if it is stiff — you are aiming for the texture, not a number.
  8. Test the masa float
    Drop a 1/2 tsp ball of masa into a cup of cold water. If it floats within a few seconds, enough air has been beaten in and your tamales will be fluffy. If it sinks, keep beating for another 2 to 3 minutes and test again. This old kitchen test is the only reliable way to know before you have wrapped two dozen tamales.
  9. Spread the masa
    Lay a soaked husk flat with the wide end toward you and the smooth side up. Spread about 1/4 cup (60 g) of masa into a rectangle roughly 4 x 3 in (10 x 8 cm), leaving a 2 in (5 cm) border at the narrow end and about 1/2 in (1.3 cm) at the sides. Use the back of a spoon or an offset spatula and keep the layer about 1/4 in (6 mm) thick. Too thick and the tamale is stodgy; too thin and it tears.
  10. Fill and fold
    Spoon about 3 tbsp of the red chile pork down the center of the masa in a line, which is what divides 3 lb of braised shoulder evenly across 24 tamales. Fold one long side of the husk over so the masa wraps around the filling, then fold the other side over it like closing a book. Fold the narrow empty end up against the seam and tie it loosely with a strip of husk if you like. Loose is important — the masa expands as it steams and a tight tamale bursts.
  11. Load the steamer
    Set a steamer rack in a tall stockpot and add the 4 cups (950 ml) water, keeping the level below the rack. Stand the tamales upright with the folded end down and the open end up, packed snugly enough to support each other but not crushed. Tuck a few extra husks around and over the top, cover with the lid, and bring the water to a boil. If they will not stand, lay them flat with the seam side down in layers.
  12. Steam 75 to 90 minutes
    Steam over medium heat for 75 to 90 minutes, checking the water level every 30 minutes and adding boiling water down the side as needed. If the pot ever runs dry the tamales scorch and the whole batch is lost, so set a timer. The tamales are done when the masa pulls cleanly away from the husk and holds its shape rather than smearing. Test one at 75 minutes; if it sticks, give the batch another 15.
  13. Rest before eating
    Turn off the heat and let the tamales sit in the covered pot for 15 minutes before unwrapping. This rest lets the masa firm up, and a tamale opened straight off the steam will be gummy even when it is perfectly cooked. Serve them in their husks and let everyone unwrap their own. Pass any extra red chile sauce and the 1 cup of crema at the table.
Know when it is done
Braise the pork to about 195°F (91°C) so it shreds easily, far past the 145°F (63°C) plus 3-minute rest that pork needs for safety. The tamales are done when the masa peels cleanly from the husk after 75 to 90 minutes of steaming.
Serve it with
Champurrado or Mexican hot chocolate on a cold morning, or a cold lager and a bowl of pozole for a party.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Tamales are a group project. Set up an assembly line with one person spreading masa, one filling and one folding, and 24 tamales take 30 minutes instead of 90.
  • ◆Look for masa harina labeled for tamales, which is coarser than the kind for tortillas. Regular Maseca works, but the texture is a little finer than traditional.
  • ◆The float test is the real quality control. Under-whipped masa gives you dense, heavy tamales and no amount of extra steaming will fix it.
  • ◆Tamales freeze better than almost anything. Cool them completely, freeze in a bag for up to 6 months, and resteam from frozen for 20 to 25 minutes.
  • ◆Vegetarian version: fill with roasted poblano strips and Oaxaca cheese, and swap the lard for vegetable shortening plus vegetable broth.

Sizzling Skillet Steak Fajitas⏱ 1 hr 40 min (includes 1 hr marinade)🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Charred skirt steak and blistered peppers cooked in the same screaming-hot skillet, brought to the table still sizzling. The smell alone is worth the smoke alarm risk.

Cast IronDate NightCrowd Pleaser
Prep
20 min
Cook
20 min
Total
1 hr 40 min (includes 1 hr marinade)
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Steak and marinade

Peppers and onions

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Mix the marinade
    Whisk the 1/4 cup (60 ml) lime juice, 3 tbsp oil, garlic, Worcestershire, cumin, chili powder, oregano, 2 tsp salt and pepper in a bowl until it looks slightly creamy. The Worcestershire brings a savory, almost beefy depth that lime and spices alone cannot give you. Taste it and expect it to be sharp and salty, since only a coating stays on the meat. Reserve 2 tbsp of it in a separate cup for the vegetables later.
  2. Marinate one hour, not four
    Put the steak in a zip-top bag with the marinade, press out the air, and refrigerate for exactly 1 hour, or up to 2 at the outside. Lime juice is aggressive, and past a couple of hours it starts cooking the surface of the meat into something chalky and mealy. One hour is enough to season the outside and start tenderizing. Take the steak out 20 minutes before cooking so it is not fridge-cold.
  3. Cut the vegetables uniformly
    Slice the bell peppers, poblano and onion into strips about 1/2 in (1.3 cm) wide so they cook at the same rate. Thin slices go limp before they char and thick ones stay raw in the middle. Keep the onion in half-moons rather than rings so the pieces stay intact when you toss them. Have everything cut and within reach before the pan goes on, because this cooks fast.
  4. Heat the skillet hard
    Set a 12 in (30 cm) cast iron skillet over high heat for a full 5 minutes, until a drop of water evaporates on contact with a hiss. Cast iron is the right pan because it holds enough stored heat to keep searing when cold meat hits it. Turn on the vent hood, crack a window, and put a towel over the smoke detector if you have to. This is a genuinely smoky dish.
  5. Dry the steak
    Lift the steak out of the marinade and scrape off the garlic bits with the back of a knife, since they will scorch black in a pan this hot. Blot both sides thoroughly dry with paper towels. Any surface moisture has to boil away before browning can start, and in the 3 minutes that takes, the steak overcooks. A dry surface is the whole game with a thin cut.
  6. Sear the steak
    Lay the steak in the dry skillet — the oil clinging from the marinade is plenty — and sear undisturbed for 3 minutes. It should roar the moment it lands, not whisper; a quiet pan means it was not hot enough and the steak is stewing in its own juice. Flip once and cook 2 to 3 minutes more, then pull it the instant an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part reads 130°F (54°C), which is the pull temp for medium-rare, not the finished temp. Carryover heat carries it another 5 degrees while it rests, so 130°F off the heat lands at about 135°F (57°C) on the plate. Work in two batches if the pieces overlap, because crowding steams the meat gray.
  7. Rest the steak
    Move the steak to a cutting board and tent it loosely with foil for 10 minutes while you cook the vegetables. The internal temperature will drift up to about 135°F (57°C) and the juices will settle back into the fibers. Cutting into skirt steak straight off the heat costs you a puddle of juice on the board. Do not skip this, even though the pan is calling.
  8. Blister the vegetables
    Add the 2 tbsp oil to the same skillet, still over high heat, then dump in the onions and peppers with the 1 tsp salt. Spread them into a single layer and let them sit for 2 minutes without stirring so they char, then toss and repeat for 6 to 8 minutes total. You want blistered black edges with the centers still crisp-tender, not soft, wet stewed peppers. The browned steak fond on the pan bottom will lift into them.
  9. Deglaze with the reserved marinade
    Pour the reserved 2 tbsp of marinade and the 1 tbsp lime juice into the hot skillet and scrape the bottom hard with a wooden spoon for 30 seconds. Everything stuck to the pan will release and coat the vegetables in a glaze that tastes like the steak you just cooked. This is why you set that 2 tbsp aside in a separate cup before the raw beef ever went into the bag — marinade that has held raw meat is never safe to add at the end unless it is boiled hard for a full minute first. Let it bubble away to almost nothing, then turn off the heat.
  10. Warm the tortillas
    Toast the flour tortillas one at a time on a dry comal or in a skillet over medium-high for 20 to 30 seconds per side, until they puff slightly and show a few brown freckles. Stack them in a clean towel or a tortilla warmer so they steam soft. Warm tortillas fold without cracking and taste worlds better than cold ones. Do this while the steak rests.
  11. Slice against the grain
    Find the direction of the long muscle fibers in the skirt steak and slice straight across them at a slight angle, into strips about 1/4 in (6 mm) thick. Slicing with the grain leaves you chewing long tough strands, and this cut is completely unforgiving about it. Pour any juices from the board back over the sliced meat. Season with a final pinch of salt.
  12. Serve it sizzling
    Return the sliced steak to the hot skillet with the peppers and toss once, letting everything sizzle together for 30 seconds. Carry the skillet straight to the table on a trivet while it is still crackling and steaming. Serve with the warm tortillas, guacamole, crema, pico de gallo and lime wedges so everyone builds their own. The sizzle only lasts a minute, so have everyone seated.
Know when it is done
Pull skirt steak at 130°F (54°C) for medium-rare; it rises to about 135°F (57°C) while resting. If you swap in chicken, cook it fully to 165°F (74°C).
Serve it with
A frozen lime margarita or a cold Modelo, with Mexican rice and charro beans on the side.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Skirt steak is the traditional cut and the best one. Flank is a good substitute but slice it even thinner, and avoid stew meat or sirloin tips, which never get tender.
  • ◆Do not marinate longer than 2 hours. Long acidic marinades turn the outside of thin steak into a mealy gray band.
  • ◆For a real restaurant sizzle, preheat a second cast iron skillet or a fajita platter in a 450°F (230°C) oven and transfer everything onto it right before serving.
  • ◆Chicken fajitas work with the same marinade using 1 1/2 lb (680 g) of thighs, cooked to 165°F (74°C), about 5 to 6 minutes per side.
  • ◆If your kitchen cannot handle the smoke, cook this on a grill over direct high heat with a cast iron pan for the vegetables. Same times, no alarms.

Guacamole and Pico de Gallo⏱ 30 min (includes 10 min rest)🍽 6 servings (about 2 cups of each)Easy▾

Chunky guacamole made in a bowl with a fork and a pico that actually tastes of tomato, not water. Two five-ingredient recipes that everything else in this chapter leans on.

No Cook30 MinutesParty Food
Prep
20 min
Cook
0 min
Total
30 min (includes 10 min rest)
Serves
6 servings (about 2 cups of each)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Pico de gallo

Guacamole

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Seed the tomatoes
    Cut each Roma tomato in half lengthwise and scoop out the seeds and the watery gel with your thumb or a small spoon. That jelly is almost pure water, and leaving it in is exactly why homemade pico ends up sitting in a pink puddle. Dice the firm outer flesh into neat 1/4 in (6 mm) pieces. Roma tomatoes are the right choice because they are meaty and low in moisture.
  2. Tame the raw onion
    Dice the white onion small and even, then rinse it in a fine sieve under cold water for 20 seconds and shake it dry. Rinsing washes away the sulfur compounds that make raw onion taste harsh and linger on your breath, without touching the crunch or sweetness. This 20-second step makes a real difference in a raw salsa. Do the same for the onion going into the guacamole.
  3. Mix and rest the pico
    Combine the tomatoes, rinsed onion, minced serrano, cilantro, 2 tbsp lime juice and 3/4 tsp salt in a bowl and stir gently. Let it sit for 10 minutes so the salt draws out just enough juice to make a light dressing and the flavors get acquainted. Taste it after resting, not before — salt and lime read completely differently once everything has mingled. Drain off excess liquid if it looks watery.
  4. Judge the serrano heat
    Taste a tiny sliver of your serrano before adding it, because heat varies wildly from chile to chile even off the same plant. Scrape out the seeds and white veins for moderate heat, or leave some in if the chile is mild. Start with half and add the rest once you have tasted the finished bowl. It is the one thing here you cannot undo.
  5. Pick and open the avocados
    A ripe Hass avocado yields to gentle pressure near the stem and its little stem cap flicks off to reveal green, not brown. Halve each one around the pit, twist the halves apart, and strike the pit firmly with the heel of your knife to lift it out. Score the flesh in a crosshatch right in the skin and scoop it out with a spoon. Unripe avocados will never taste good, no matter what you add.
  6. Build the guacamole base
    Put the rinsed onion, minced serrano, cilantro and 1 tsp salt in the bowl first and mash them together with a fork or a molcajete before the avocado goes in. Grinding the aromatics with salt releases their oils and distributes them evenly instead of leaving pockets of raw onion. This is the traditional order and it makes a noticeably better guacamole. It takes 30 seconds.
  7. Mash it chunky
    Add the avocado and the 2 tbsp lime juice and mash with a fork just 8 to 10 times, leaving plenty of half-inch chunks intact. Guacamole should have texture you can feel — a food processor turns it into pale green baby food. The lime is doing two jobs here: seasoning and slowing the browning. Fold rather than stir once it starts coming together.
  8. Season at the end
    Taste the guacamole and adjust with salt a pinch at a time and lime a teaspoon at a time until it tastes bright rather than flat. Avocado is fatty and mild, so it swallows salt — most home cooks stop about half a teaspoon short. If it tastes dull, it needs salt; if it tastes heavy, it needs lime. Fold in 2 tbsp of the pico for extra brightness if you like.
  9. Keep it green
    If you are not serving right away, smooth the surface flat and press plastic wrap directly onto the guacamole so no air touches it, then refrigerate for up to 4 hours. Browning is oxidation, so contact with plastic works far better than the avocado-pit myth. Alternatively, pour a thin layer of cold water over the smoothed surface and pour it off before serving. Give it a stir and re-taste before it goes out.
  10. Serve both together
    Spoon the guacamole into a shallow bowl and the pico into another, and set them side by side with a big basket of tortilla chips. Sprinkle the guacamole with the optional cotija and set out lime wedges. Both should be made the day you serve them, and both are better at cool room temperature than straight from the fridge. Pull them out 15 minutes before eating.
Know when it is done
No cooking involved. The cue is texture: guacamole should stay chunky with visible half-inch pieces of avocado, and pico should be crisp and barely wet, never sitting in a pool of liquid.
Serve it with
Salty thick-cut tortilla chips and a cold beer, or as the cooling side to anything spicy in this chapter.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Ripen hard avocados in a paper bag with a banana for 1 to 2 days. Once ripe, refrigerating them buys you about 3 more days.
  • ◆Pico de gallo is best within 4 hours. After that the tomatoes weep and the cilantro darkens, so make it the same day.
  • ◆For a smokier guacamole, char the serrano and a couple of scallions over a flame until blistered before mincing them in.
  • ◆White onion is the right onion for both of these. Yellow is too sweet and red bleeds pink into the guacamole.
  • ◆Leftover pico is excellent stirred into scrambled eggs, spooned over grilled fish, or drained and used on the nachos in this chapter.

Queso Fundido with Chorizo⏱ 30 min🍽 4 to 6 servingsEasy▾

A skillet of melted Oaxaca cheese with spicy chorizo and blistered poblano, pulled apart with warm tortillas. It takes half an hour and disappears in ten minutes.

Appetizer30 MinutesCast Iron
Prep
10 min
Cook
20 min
Total
30 min
Serves
4 to 6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the skillet

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Heat the oven
    Set the oven to 425°F (220°C) with a rack in the upper third, and if you have a broiler you will want it ready too. A hot oven melts the cheese fast, which matters because slow melting gives the fat time to separate and pool. Have your tortillas, cilantro and salsa ready before the skillet goes in. Queso fundido waits for absolutely no one.
  2. Pull the cheese into strands
    Oaxaca cheese comes wound into a ball like a skein of yarn — unwind it and pull it into thin strands with your fingers rather than grating it. Pulled strands melt more evenly and give you the long stretchy pull this dish is famous for. Mix it with the shredded Monterey Jack, which is milder and helps keep the melt smooth. Never use pre-shredded bagged cheese here; the anti-caking starch turns the melt grainy.
  3. Brown the chorizo
    Squeeze the chorizo out of its casing into a cold 10 in (25 cm) cast iron skillet, set it over medium heat, and break it up with a wooden spoon. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until it is deeply browned in crumbles and the fat has run bright orange-red. Fresh Mexican chorizo is raw pork sausage and must reach 160°F (71°C), unlike cured Spanish chorizo. It should sizzle steadily, not scorch.
  4. Drain most of the fat
    Tip the skillet and spoon off all but about 1 tbsp of the rendered chorizo fat, or the finished queso will be a greasy orange slick. That single tablespoon is enough to cook the vegetables and season everything. Save the drained fat in a jar for frying eggs or potatoes, because it is delicious. Leave the browned crumbles in the pan.
  5. Cook the poblano and onion
    Add the poblano strips, sliced onion and 1/2 tsp salt to the skillet and cook over medium-high for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the vegetables are softened with charred edges. The poblano should lose its raw grassy taste and turn silky. Add the sliced garlic for the final 30 seconds only, since it burns fast in a hot pan. Scrape any brown bits off the bottom as you stir.
  6. Set aside the topping
    Scoop about two-thirds of the chorizo and vegetable mixture out of the skillet onto a plate, leaving the rest spread across the bottom. You will scatter the reserved portion over the melted cheese at the end so it does not sink and disappear. Layering it this way means every scoop gets both cheese and chorizo. Wipe the skillet rim clean so nothing burns in the oven.
  7. Add the cheese and liquid
    Pile the mixed cheeses over the chorizo in the skillet in an even mound and drizzle the 2 tbsp of lager or milk over the top. That small amount of liquid helps the cheese melt into a cohesive, saucy mass rather than breaking into strings and oil. Do not add more than 2 tbsp or the queso will be soupy. Press the cheese down gently so it sits level.
  8. Bake until molten
    Slide the skillet into the 425°F (220°C) oven and bake for 6 to 8 minutes, until the cheese is completely melted and bubbling at the edges. Start checking at 6 minutes: the moment it goes from a solid mound to a shimmering molten pool, it is done. Overbaking is the classic mistake here — the proteins tighten, the fat separates, and you get a rubbery raft floating in grease. If you want brown spots, broil for 45 to 60 seconds only.
  9. Warm the tortillas
    While the cheese bakes, toast the tortillas on a dry comal or skillet over medium-high heat for 20 to 30 seconds per side until soft and lightly freckled. Stack them inside a clean kitchen towel or a tortilla warmer to keep the steam in. You need them ready the second the skillet comes out. Cold tortillas will chill the queso on contact.
  10. Top and serve immediately
    Scatter the reserved chorizo and vegetables over the molten cheese, sprinkle the cilantro on top, and carry the skillet straight to the table on a trivet. Serve with the warm tortillas, salsa verde and lime wedges, and have everyone scoop and roll their own. Queso fundido stays perfect for about eight minutes and then begins to set, so this is not a dish to plate up quietly in the kitchen. Warn everyone that the handle is blistering hot.
Know when it is done
Fresh pork chorizo must reach 160°F (71°C) before the cheese goes in. Bake at 425°F (220°C) only until the cheese is molten and bubbling, 6 to 8 minutes, or it will break and turn greasy.
Serve it with
Cold Mexican lager or a michelada, served as the opener before carne asada or fajitas.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Oaxaca cheese is the correct cheese and it is worth a trip. Low-moisture whole-milk mozzarella is the closest substitute; avoid cheddar, which breaks and goes oily.
  • ◆If the queso sets before everyone is finished, put the skillet back in the oven for 2 to 3 minutes. It will re-melt once, though not twice.
  • ◆For a vegetarian version, skip the chorizo and use 8 oz (225 g) of sliced mushrooms browned hard in 2 tbsp of oil, plus an extra poblano.
  • ◆Fresh Mexican chorizo is raw and soft; Spanish chorizo is cured and firm. They are not interchangeable, and using the cured kind here leaves you with dry chips of sausage.
  • ◆Prep the chorizo and vegetables up to 2 days ahead. Reheat them in the skillet, add the cheese, and bake when your guests arrive.

Beef Birria Tacos with Consomé⏱ 4 hr 45 min (includes 15 min rest)🍽 6 servings (18 tacos)Advanced▾

Chile-braised beef shredded into cheese-crisped tortillas, dipped in the ruby red consomé it cooked in. It is a long afternoon and the best taco you will ever make at home.

Weekend ProjectTaco NightMake Ahead
Prep
30 min
Cook
4 hr
Total
4 hr 45 min (includes 15 min rest)
Serves
6 servings (18 tacos)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

The beef

Chile adobo

For the tacos

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Season the beef
    Pat the chuck chunks and short ribs completely dry and season them all over with the 1 tbsp salt and 1 tsp pepper. Let them sit at room temperature for 20 minutes so the salt begins to penetrate and the surface dries further. The short ribs are not optional filler — their bones and connective tissue are what give the consomé its body and glossy lip-sticking texture. Chuck alone makes a thinner broth.
  2. Sear in batches
    Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high until it just begins to shimmer, then sear the beef in two or three batches, 3 to 4 minutes per side. Each piece should be deeply browned and release from the pot on its own before you move it. Crowding drops the temperature and the meat steams gray, costing you the browned flavor that carries the whole braise. Set the seared beef aside on a plate.
  3. Toast the dried chiles
    Wipe out most of the fat, lower the heat to medium, and press the stemmed and seeded guajillos, anchos and arbols flat against the hot pot for 15 to 20 seconds per side. They should puff slightly, lighten in color, and smell like sweet dried fruit and tobacco. The second you see smoke or smell anything sharp, they have burned and the whole batch will taste bitter. Toast in batches so you can watch every chile.
  4. Rehydrate the chiles
    Move the toasted chiles to a bowl, pour the 3 cups (700 ml) of hot water over them, and hold them under with a small plate. Soak 20 to 25 minutes until they are completely soft and floppy. Taste the soaking liquid and reserve 1 1/2 cups if it is fruity, or discard it and use fresh water if it tastes bitter. Softened chiles blend smooth; stiff ones leave grit.
  5. Char the tomatoes and aromatics
    While the chiles soak, char the tomato halves, onion halves and garlic cloves in the same pot or a dry skillet over medium-high for 6 to 8 minutes, turning until blackened in spots. This char adds a smoky sweetness that raw vegetables cannot give you. The garlic will color fastest, so pull it after about 3 minutes. Let everything cool slightly before it goes into the blender.
  6. Blend the adobo
    Blend the drained chiles, charred tomatoes, onion, garlic, cinnamon stick, cloves, cumin, oregano, vinegar and 1 1/2 cups of soaking liquid on high for a full 2 minutes. Cinnamon and cloves are the signature of birria and they should be present but subtle, more warm than sweet. The adobo should be completely smooth and the color of dark garnet. Add a splash more liquid if the blender is laboring.
  7. Strain the adobo
    Push the blended adobo through a fine-mesh sieve into a bowl, pressing hard with a spatula and scraping the underside to get everything through. You will be left with a few tablespoons of tough chile skin and spice fragments to discard. A whole cinnamon stick will not fully break down, so this strain is what keeps the consomé silky rather than gritty. It takes two minutes and it matters.
  8. Fry the adobo, then braise
    Return the pot to medium-high, pour in the strained adobo, and fry it for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until it darkens and thickens like tomato paste. Add the beef broth, bay leaves and 2 tsp salt, then return the beef and any juices from the plate. Bring it to a simmer, cover, and either keep it at a bare simmer on the stove or slide it into a 325°F (163°C) oven. The liquid should just about cover the meat.
  9. Braise until it shreds
    Cook for 3 to 3 1/2 hours, checking at 3 hours, until the beef falls apart at the nudge of a fork and reads about 203°F (95°C) on a thermometer. Do not judge it by the clock alone — collagen breaks down on its own schedule, and a piece that is still tight needs another 30 minutes. The braise should bubble lazily, never boil. Underdone birria is stringy and tough, and the only cure is more time.
  10. Rest and skim the fat
    Turn off the heat and let the pot rest, uncovered, for 15 minutes so the fat rises and the meat relaxes. Skim the bright orange-red fat off the surface with a ladle and reserve every bit of it in a bowl — this is the birria fat you will dip the tortillas in, and it is the entire point of a quesabirria. You should end up with 1/2 to 3/4 cup. Do not throw it out.
  11. Shred the beef and finish the consomé
    Lift the beef out with a slotted spoon, pull the short rib meat off the bones, and shred everything into rough strands with two forks, discarding bones and hard fat. Taste the remaining broth — this is your consomé — and season it with salt until it is bright and savory, probably another 1 to 2 tsp. Moisten the shredded meat with about 1 cup of the consomé so it does not dry out. Ladle the rest into small bowls for dipping.
  12. Griddle the quesabirria tacos
    Heat a comal or large skillet over medium heat. Dip a tortilla into the reserved red fat so one side is coated, lay it fat side down on the griddle, and scatter about 3 tbsp of cheese over half of it. When the cheese melts, about 1 minute, add 1/4 cup of shredded beef, fold it over, and press gently with a spatula. Cook 1 to 2 minutes per side until the tortilla is crisp and lacquered deep red.
  13. Serve with consomé for dipping
    Stack three tacos per plate and top them with diced white onion and cilantro. Give each person a small bowl of hot consomé with a squeeze of lime and a pinch of onion and cilantro stirred in. The dipping is not a garnish, it is how the dish is eaten, so make sure everyone has enough. Serve immediately while the tortillas are still crackling.
Know when it is done
Braise the beef to about 203°F (95°C), far past the 145°F (63°C) safety minimum, so the collagen melts into gelatin and the meat shreds with a fork. Judge by fork tenderness first, temperature second.
Serve it with
A michelada or a cold Victoria, with the consomé itself as the first course.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Birria is dramatically better the next day. Braise it a day ahead, refrigerate overnight, lift off the solid fat cap to use for griddling, and reheat the meat gently in its consomé.
  • ◆Goat is the original meat for birria and lamb shoulder is a superb substitute. Both use the same adobo and the same timing.
  • ◆The reserved red fat is what makes a quesabirria taco. If you skim it away or throw it out, you get a regular taco and miss the point entirely.
  • ◆If your consomé tastes bitter, a chile scorched during toasting. Stir in 1 tsp of honey and a splash of vinegar to rebalance it, and be gentler with the comal next time.
  • ◆Freeze the shredded meat and consomé together in quart containers for up to 3 months. It reheats perfectly and turns a Tuesday into an event.

Crispy Chicken Parmesan⏱ 1 hr 5 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Thin cutlets fried until they shatter, a bright five-ingredient tomato sauce, and just enough mozzarella to melt into ropes. The trick is sauce and cheese only on top, so the crust never goes soggy.

Comfort FoodDate NightFried
Prep
25 min
Cook
40 min
Total
1 hr 5 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the cutlets

Quick tomato sauce

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Make the sauce first
    Warm the 2 tbsp olive oil and sliced garlic in a saucepan over medium-low heat for 2 to 3 minutes, until the garlic is pale gold and smells sweet but has no brown edges. Add the hand-crushed tomatoes, 3/4 tsp salt, and the red pepper flakes, then simmer uncovered over medium-low for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring now and then. It is ready when a spoon dragged through the pan leaves a track that fills in slowly. Stir in the basil leaves off the heat and set aside; making the sauce first means it is done before the fried cutlets have a chance to get cold.
  2. Cut the breasts into cutlets
    Lay a chicken breast flat and press one palm on top, then run a sharp knife horizontally through the middle to split it into two thin pieces. Repeat with the second breast so you have 4 cutlets. Thin cutlets cook through in the same few minutes it takes the crust to brown, which is the entire secret to chicken parm that is not dry in the middle.
  3. Pound them even
    Put each cutlet between two sheets of plastic wrap or in a zip-top bag and pound with a flat meat mallet, a small skillet, or a rolling pin until it is an even 1/4 in (6 mm) thick. Work from the center outward with firm taps rather than hard smacks, which tear the meat. Even thickness matters more than thinness — a cutlet that is thin at one end and fat at the other will always overcook somewhere. Season both sides with the 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp pepper.
  4. Set up three stations
    Line up three shallow dishes: flour in the first, the 3 eggs beaten with 1 tbsp water in the second, and the panko tossed with the 1/2 cup grated Parmigiano and 1 tsp oregano in the third. Keep one hand for dry and one hand for wet so your fingers do not turn into breaded clubs. Putting cheese directly into the crumbs means the crust itself tastes like Parmesan, not just the topping.
  5. Bread the cutlets
    Dredge a cutlet in flour and shake off every loose speck, dip it in egg and let the excess run off for 3 seconds, then press it firmly into the panko on both sides. Real pressure here is what makes the crust stick instead of sliding off in the pan. Set the breaded cutlets on a rack and let them rest 10 minutes if you have the time, which lets the coating hydrate and glue itself on.
  6. Heat the oil correctly
    Pour the 2 cups oil into a 12 in (30 cm) skillet — a pan that wide genuinely needs that much to sit 1/4 in (6 mm) deep — and heat over medium-high to 350°F (175°C). Without a thermometer, drop in a pinch of panko: it should sizzle steadily and float, not sit still and not crackle violently. Oil that is too cool soaks in and goes greasy; oil that is smoking burns the crumbs before the chicken is done. Let the oil cool completely before you strain it back into a jar; it is good for one or two more fries.
  7. Fry two at a time
    Lay 2 cutlets in the oil away from you and fry 3 to 4 minutes on the first side, until the edges you can see are deep golden. Flip once with tongs and fry 2 to 3 minutes more. Do not crowd the pan; four at once drops the oil temperature and you get pale, oily breading. Move the finished cutlets to a wire rack, never paper towels, so the underside stays crisp while the second batch fries.
  8. Check the temperature
    Slide an instant-read thermometer sideways into the thickest part of a cutlet — it must read 165°F (74°C) before the chicken is safe to eat. Pounded cutlets almost always get there during the fry, but if one reads low, put it back in the oil for another minute rather than hoping the broiler will catch it. Never rely on the color of the crust to tell you the chicken is cooked; panko goes golden long before a thick spot is done, and it can also brown while the very center is still cool.
  9. Sauce and cheese the tops only
    Heat the broiler with a rack 6 in (15 cm) below the element. Arrange the cutlets on a foil-lined sheet pan, spoon about 3 tbsp of sauce onto the center of each, and leave a wide border of bare crust all the way around. Divide the shredded mozzarella and 1/4 cup Parmigiano over the sauce. Sauce touching the crust is the number one reason chicken parm turns soggy, so resist the urge to drown it.
  10. Broil just until bubbling
    Broil for 2 to 4 minutes, watching the whole time, until the mozzarella is melted with a few brown blisters. Broilers vary wildly and cheese goes from perfect to burnt in about 30 seconds, so do not walk away or check your phone. Pull the pan the moment the cheese stops looking rubbery and starts to bubble at the edges.
  11. Rest, then serve
    Let the cutlets sit for 3 minutes so the molten cheese sets enough to slice without sliding off. Scatter the torn basil over the top and serve the remaining sauce warm in a bowl on the side for dipping or for a small pile of spaghetti. Serve immediately — chicken parm is at its best about four minutes out of the broiler and never really comes back.
Know when it is done
Chicken is safe and still juicy at 165°F (74°C) measured at the thickest point of the cutlet.
Serve it with
A simple arugula salad with lemon and a glass of Chianti Classico, with garlic bread for the extra sauce.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Bread the cutlets up to 6 hours ahead and keep them on a rack in the fridge, uncovered. The coating dries slightly and fries up even crisper.
  • ◆No San Marzano tomatoes? Any can of whole peeled tomatoes works better than pre-crushed, which is usually made from lower-grade fruit and tastes tinny.
  • ◆Fresh mozzarella in water releases too much liquid under a broiler and floods the crust. Use the firm low-moisture block and shred it yourself.
  • ◆If the breading slides off in the pan, the cutlets were wet or the flour layer was too thick. Pat them dry and tap off the flour like you mean it.
  • ◆Leftovers reheat well at 375°F (190°C) on a rack for 10 minutes. The microwave will turn that crust into a wet paper towel.

Chicken Piccata with Lemon and Capers⏱ 30 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Golden cutlets under a sharp, buttery lemon-caper pan sauce that comes together in the same skillet in about four minutes. This is the weeknight dinner that tastes like you tried much harder than you did.

30 MinutesWeeknightOne Pan
Prep
15 min
Cook
15 min
Total
30 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the chicken

Lemon caper pan sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Split and pound the breasts
    Press one hand flat on a chicken breast and slice it horizontally into two thin pieces, then repeat with the second breast for 4 cutlets total. Put each between plastic wrap and pound to an even 1/4 in (6 mm) with a mallet or small skillet. At that thickness the cutlets cook in about 6 minutes total, which is the whole point of piccata.
  2. Season and dredge
    Season the cutlets on both sides with the 1 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp pepper, then dredge each in the 1/2 cup flour and shake off the excess until you see only a thin, dusty film. Too much flour goes gummy in the sauce and tastes raw. Dredge right before cooking, because flour sitting on damp chicken turns into paste within a few minutes.
  3. Heat the skillet
    Set a 12 in (30 cm) stainless steel skillet over medium-high heat, add the 2 tbsp olive oil and 1 tbsp butter, and wait until the butter foam subsides and the fat shimmers. Skip nonstick if you can — the browned bits that stick to stainless steel are the backbone of the sauce. If the butter turns dark brown immediately, the pan is too hot; pull it off for 20 seconds.
  4. Brown the first two cutlets
    Lay 2 cutlets in the pan and cook 3 minutes without moving them, until the underside is golden and releases easily from the pan. Flip and cook 2 minutes more. They should sizzle steadily and confidently, not scream or smoke. Crowding the pan drops the heat and steams the chicken gray, so do not try to fit all four.
  5. Cook the second batch
    Move the first two cutlets to a plate and repeat with the remaining two, adding the extra 1 tsp oil if the pan looks dry. Check the thickest cutlet with an instant-read thermometer: 165°F (74°C) means done, and anything under that goes back in the pan for another minute. Tent the plate loosely with foil and let the chicken rest while you build the sauce — the juices that pool on that plate go into the sauce at the end, so do not tip them into the sink.
  6. Deglaze with wine
    Pour the 1/2 cup white wine into the hot skillet and scrape the bottom hard with a wooden spoon as it bubbles — every brown fleck is concentrated chicken flavor. Let the wine reduce over medium-high heat for about 2 minutes, until it has cooked down by half and no longer smells sharply of alcohol. This step is what separates a real pan sauce from lemon butter.
  7. Build the sauce body
    Add the 3/4 cup chicken stock, 3 tbsp lemon juice, and 3 tbsp capers, and simmer briskly for 3 to 4 minutes until the liquid reduces to about 2/3 cup and coats the back of a spoon lightly. Rinsing the capers first keeps the sauce from turning aggressively salty. Taste it now — it should be bracingly lemony, because the butter is about to soften all of that.
  8. Mount the butter off the heat
    Take the skillet completely off the burner, wait 15 seconds, then add the 4 tbsp cold butter one piece at a time, swirling the pan constantly until each piece disappears. Cold butter added off direct heat emulsifies into a glossy sauce; butter dumped into a boiling pan splits into greasy pools. The sauce should look silky and slightly thickened, like warm cream.
  9. Return the chicken
    Slide the cutlets and any juices from the plate back into the skillet and turn them once to coat, keeping the pan off the heat or on the lowest possible setting. Ninety seconds is plenty to warm them through. Boiling the chicken in the sauce now would both overcook it and break the emulsion you just made.
  10. Finish and serve
    Stir in the 3 tbsp chopped parsley, taste, and add a pinch more salt or a squeeze of lemon if it feels flat. Serve straight from the skillet or on a warm platter with the lemon rounds tucked around, spooning the sauce generously over each cutlet. Piccata sauce thickens as it cools, so get it to the table right away.
Know when it is done
Chicken cutlets are done at 165°F (74°C) at the thickest point; pull them from the pan the moment they get there.
Serve it with
Buttered angel hair or roasted asparagus, and the rest of the Pinot Grigio you cooked with.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆No wine in the house? Use an extra 1/2 cup (120 ml) stock plus 1 extra tsp lemon juice. The sauce will be a little less complex but still excellent.
  • ◆Bottled lemon juice tastes metallic here and there is nowhere to hide it. Squeeze real lemons — you need about a lemon and a half.
  • ◆Veal or pork cutlets pounded to the same 1/4 in (6 mm) work identically; pork should hit 145°F (63°C) with a 3 minute rest.
  • ◆If the sauce breaks and looks oily, pull it off the heat and whisk in 1 tbsp cold stock or an ice cube to bring it back together.

Chicken Marsala with Mushrooms⏱ 40 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Deeply browned mushrooms, sweet Marsala cooked down until it is almost syrupy, and cutlets that soak it all up. It is a thirty-five minute dinner that eats like a restaurant special.

Date NightOne PanWeeknight
Prep
15 min
Cook
25 min
Total
40 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the chicken

Mushroom Marsala sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Make even cutlets
    Slice each breast horizontally into two thin pieces, then pound them between plastic wrap to an even 1/3 in (8 mm). You want 4 cutlets of the same thickness so they all finish at the same moment. Season both sides with the 1 1/4 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp pepper.
  2. Dredge lightly
    Coat each cutlet in the 1/2 cup flour and tap off everything that is not clinging. The flour does two jobs: it browns fast for color, and the starch that sheds into the pan later helps thicken the Marsala sauce. A heavy, pasty coat will make the finished sauce cloudy and taste of raw flour.
  3. Sear the cutlets
    Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a 12 in (30 cm) stainless skillet over medium-high until it shimmers, then cook 2 cutlets at a time for 3 minutes on the first side and 2 on the second, until deeply golden. Work in two batches so the pan stays hot. Move them to a plate — they will finish cooking in the sauce, so a little pink in the very center is fine at this stage.
  4. Brown the mushrooms hard
    Add the remaining 1 tbsp oil and the 2 tbsp butter to the same pan, then add the sliced mushrooms in one layer and leave them alone for 3 full minutes. They will release water and look sad, then the water will boil off and they will start to brown. Keep cooking 5 to 6 minutes more, stirring occasionally, until they are genuinely dark brown at the edges. Undercooked, gray mushrooms are the most common thing wrong with homemade marsala.
  5. Add shallots and garlic
    Stir in the chopped shallots with a pinch of salt and cook 2 minutes until softened and translucent, then add the minced garlic and cook just 30 seconds more until fragrant. Garlic added earlier would burn against the hot mushrooms and turn bitter. The pan bottom should now be covered in brown glaze.
  6. Deglaze with Marsala
    Pour in the 3/4 cup Marsala and immediately scrape the bottom of the pan with a wooden spoon while it bubbles hard. Let it reduce over medium-high heat for 3 to 4 minutes, until the liquid is thick, glossy, and reduced by about half. This is the flavor engine of the dish — rushing it leaves a raw, boozy sweetness that no amount of cream will fix.
  7. Simmer with stock
    Add the 1 cup chicken stock and 1 tsp thyme leaves and simmer over medium heat for 5 to 6 minutes, until the sauce reduces by roughly a third and lightly coats a spoon. Scrape the pan again as it reduces. The sauce should smell nutty and winey rather than sharp.
  8. Add the cream
    Stir in the 1/3 cup heavy cream and let it bubble gently for 2 minutes to thicken slightly and turn the sauce a soft caramel color. Traditional Marsala is often made without cream, but a small amount rounds off the sweetness of the wine beautifully. Do not let it hit a rolling boil or it can separate.
  9. Return the chicken
    Nestle the cutlets and every drop of resting juice back into the pan, spoon sauce over them, and simmer gently for 3 to 4 minutes. Check the thickest cutlet with a thermometer: you are looking for 165°F (74°C). The cutlets will drink up sauce as they finish, which is exactly what you want.
  10. Finish with cold butter
    Pull the pan off the heat and swirl in the 3 tbsp cold butter, one piece at a time, until the sauce turns glossy and slightly thicker. Taste and adjust with salt and a few grinds of pepper. Scatter the 2 tbsp parsley over the top and serve immediately, with plenty of sauce spooned over each piece.
Know when it is done
Chicken is done at 165°F (74°C); simmer it in the sauce only until it reaches that, or it will go stringy.
Serve it with
Creamy polenta or mashed potatoes to catch the sauce, with a glass of Barbera or the dry Marsala itself.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Buy dry Marsala, not sweet, and never the salted cooking Marsala from the vinegar aisle. A drinkable bottle costs about ten dollars and lasts months.
  • ◆Mixing in 4 oz (115 g) of sliced shiitake or rehydrated porcini with the cremini gives the sauce far more depth for almost no extra work.
  • ◆Do not wash mushrooms under running water; wipe them with a damp towel so they brown instead of steaming.
  • ◆The sauce can be made through the cream step a day ahead and refrigerated. Reheat gently, then sear fresh cutlets and combine.
  • ◆If the sauce gets too thick while resting, loosen it with a splash of stock rather than water so you do not dilute the flavor.

Chicken Saltimbocca alla Romana⏱ 27 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Sage leaves pressed onto thin cutlets, wrapped in prosciutto, and crisped in butter until the ham goes crackly. The name means jump in the mouth, and after one bite you will understand why.

30 MinutesDate NightOne Pan
Prep
15 min

27 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the cutlets

Pan sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Make four thin cutlets
    Slice each breast horizontally into two pieces, then pound them between plastic wrap to a very even 1/4 in (6 mm). Saltimbocca lives or dies on thinness — the prosciutto needs to crisp in the same 3 minutes the chicken takes to cook. Pat the cutlets completely dry with paper towels.
  2. Season carefully
    Season the cutlets with only the 1/2 tsp kosher salt and all of the 3/4 tsp pepper. Prosciutto is already very salty and it will season the whole dish as it cooks, so this is one of the rare times you deliberately underseason the meat. Pepper, on the other hand, you want plenty of.
  3. Layer sage and prosciutto
    Lay 3 sage leaves down the length of each cutlet, then drape 2 slices of prosciutto over the top so they overlap slightly and cover the surface almost completely. Press the prosciutto down firmly with your palm — the moisture from the chicken makes it stick without any toothpicks. Do not wrap the prosciutto all the way around; leaving the bottom bare lets that side brown properly.
  4. Flour only the bare side
    Dust the naked chicken side of each cutlet lightly with the flour and shake off the excess, leaving the prosciutto side completely bare. The floured side browns evenly, and the unfloured ham side crisps directly against the metal. Handle them gently so the sage stays put.
  5. Heat the pan
    Set a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium-high heat, add the 2 tbsp olive oil and 2 tbsp butter, and swirl until the butter has foamed and the foam has just started to settle. The combination gives you the browning power of oil and the flavor of butter without the butter scorching. It should shimmer, not smoke.
  6. Cook prosciutto side down
    Lay 2 cutlets prosciutto side down in the pan and press them flat with a spatula for the first 20 seconds so the ham makes full contact. Cook 2 1/2 to 3 minutes without moving, until the prosciutto is deep bronze and crisp at the edges. Resist flipping early; that crackly ham surface is the entire dish.
  7. Flip and finish
    Turn the cutlets over and cook 2 minutes more on the floured side, until golden. Check the thickest one with an instant-read thermometer and pull only once it reads 165°F (74°C); if it is short, give it another 30 seconds and check again. Move them to a warm plate and cook the second pair the same way, adding the extra 1 tsp oil if the pan looks dry. Prosciutto leaves a lot of rendered fat behind, so you may not need any.
  8. Deglaze the pan
    Pour the 1/2 cup white wine into the empty skillet over medium-high heat and scrape up the browned bits with a wooden spoon. Let it bubble down for about 2 minutes, until reduced by half and no longer smelling boozy. There will be a lot of salty, sagey fond in that pan and you want all of it.
  9. Reduce with stock
    Add the 1/2 cup chicken stock and simmer 3 minutes until the liquid is reduced to roughly 1/3 cup and looks slightly syrupy. Taste it before adding any salt — prosciutto fond is salty enough that it usually needs none. This is a small, intense sauce, not a pool.
  10. Emulsify and serve
    Take the pan off the heat, swirl in the 3 tbsp cold butter piece by piece until glossy, then stir in the 1 tbsp lemon juice. Spoon the sauce around the cutlets rather than over them so the crisp prosciutto stays crisp. Finish with the flaky salt and serve right away, while the ham still crackles.
Know when it is done
Chicken is safe at 165°F (74°C) at the thickest point; thin cutlets get there in about 5 minutes total.
Serve it with
Sauteed spinach with garlic and a crisp Frascati or Vermentino.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Ask the deli to slice the prosciutto thin but not paper-thin, and to layer it between parchment. Slices that are too delicate tear when you lift them.
  • ◆Fresh sage only. Dried sage tastes dusty here and there are no other flavors to hide behind.
  • ◆Veal scaloppine is the Roman original if you can find it — cook it exactly the same way, about 90 seconds per side.
  • ◆Assemble the cutlets up to 4 hours ahead, cover, and refrigerate. Let them sit out 15 minutes before cooking so they cook evenly.
