Chicken Cacciatore with Peppers⏱ 1 hr 50 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Hunter's chicken — bone-in thighs braised with peppers, onions, wine, and tomatoes until the meat slides off the bone. It is a one-pot dinner that gets better the day after you make it.

One PotComfort FoodMake Ahead
Prep
20 min
Cook
1 hr 20 min
Total
1 hr 50 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the chicken

The braise

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Dry and season the thighs
    Pat the chicken thighs completely dry with paper towels, then season all over with the 2 tsp kosher salt and 1 tsp pepper. If you have 30 extra minutes, let them sit on a rack in the fridge uncovered — dry skin browns and wet skin steams. Take them out of the fridge about 20 minutes before cooking.
  2. Brown the skin properly
    Heat the 2 tbsp olive oil in a 12 in (30 cm) Dutch oven or deep skillet over medium-high until it shimmers, then lay in the thighs skin side down, 4 at a time. Cook 6 to 8 minutes without touching them, until the skin is deep golden brown and releases from the pan on its own. If the skin sticks, it is not ready to flip. Brown the second side for 3 minutes, then move all the thighs to a plate.
  3. Pour off excess fat
    Spoon off all but about 2 tbsp of the rendered fat, leaving every bit of the browned residue on the bottom of the pot. Chicken thighs give up a surprising amount of fat and leaving it all in makes a greasy braise. That brown layer on the pot is pure flavor and it goes into the sauce in two minutes.
  4. Soften the vegetables
    Add the sliced onion and both bell peppers with a pinch of salt and cook over medium heat for 7 to 8 minutes, stirring often, until they are limp and just beginning to color at the edges. The salt pulls water out of the vegetables, which loosens the fond so you can scrape it up. Do not rush this into a hard sear; you want them sweet and soft.
  5. Brown the mushrooms
    Add the quartered mushrooms and cook 5 minutes more over medium-high, stirring only occasionally so they get some real color. They will release liquid first and then start to brown once it evaporates. Stir in the sliced garlic and the 1/4 tsp red pepper flakes and cook 45 seconds until fragrant.
  6. Cook the tomato paste
    Push the vegetables to one side, add the 1 tbsp tomato paste to the bare spot, and fry it for 60 to 90 seconds, stirring, until it darkens from bright red to brick. Cooking the paste this way removes its tinny raw edge and builds a deep savory base. Then stir it through the vegetables.
  7. Deglaze with red wine
    Pour in the 3/4 cup red wine and scrape the bottom of the pot hard while it bubbles. Simmer 3 to 4 minutes until reduced by half and the sharp alcohol smell is gone. Under-reduced wine leaves the whole braise tasting thin and acidic, so let it cook down properly.
  8. Add tomatoes and herbs
    Stir in the hand-crushed tomatoes with their juice, the rosemary and thyme sprigs, and the bay leaf. Bring everything to a gentle simmer. Crushing whole tomatoes by hand gives you a rustic sauce with real texture instead of the uniform slurry you get from a can of crushed.
  9. Nestle the chicken back in
    Return the thighs and any juices to the pot skin side up, arranging them so the skin stays above the sauce line. Half-submerged chicken keeps its browned skin instead of turning to wet rubber. The liquid should come about two-thirds of the way up the thighs; add 1/4 cup water if it is much lower.
  10. Braise low and slow
    Cover with the lid slightly ajar and simmer over low heat for 35 to 40 minutes, adjusting so the surface barely blips rather than boils. Thighs are safe at 165°F (74°C) but they are genuinely tender closer to 185°F (85°C), when the connective tissue has melted. A hard boil will tighten the meat, so keep it lazy.
  11. Finish with olives
    Fish out the rosemary and thyme stems and the bay leaf, then stir the halved olives into the sauce around the chicken and simmer uncovered for 5 more minutes. Adding olives at the end keeps them bright and firm instead of leaching salt through the whole pot. Taste the sauce and adjust the salt now.
  12. Rest and serve
    Let the pot sit off the heat for 10 minutes so the sauce thickens slightly and the chicken reabsorbs its juices. Scatter the 3 tbsp parsley over everything just before serving. Bring it to the table in the pot with plenty of bread — this is a dish that wants to be eaten out of the middle.
Know when it is done
Thighs are safe at 165°F (74°C) but braise them to about 185°F (85°C) for meat that pulls off the bone.
Serve it with
Soft polenta or crusty bread, and a glass of the same Chianti that went into the pot.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Cacciatore is genuinely better on day two. Cool it, refrigerate, and reheat gently on the stove; crisp the skin under the broiler for 2 minutes if you want it back.
  • ◆Bone-in thighs are non-negotiable for flavor. Boneless thighs work in a pinch but cut the braise to 20 minutes and expect a thinner sauce.
  • ◆If your sauce is watery at the end, lift out the chicken and boil the sauce hard for 5 minutes to reduce before serving.
  • ◆A 2 in (5 cm) piece of Parmesan rind dropped in with the tomatoes adds savory depth for free. Remove it before serving.
  • ◆White wine and no peppers gives you the lighter Tuscan version; both are traditional depending on which part of Italy you ask.

Eggplant Parmigiana⏱ 2 hr 35 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Layers of silky roasted eggplant, long-simmered tomato, torn basil, and three cheeses that set into clean, tall squares. Made properly it tastes rich without ever being greasy.

VegetarianMake AheadComfort Food
Prep

Total
2 hr 35 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the eggplant

Tomato sauce

To assemble

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Slice and salt the eggplant
    Trim the eggplants and cut them lengthwise into 1/3 in (8 mm) planks — thinner slices collapse into mush and thicker ones stay spongy. Lay them on racks set over sheet pans and sprinkle both sides with the 1 tbsp kosher salt. Let them sweat for 30 minutes, until you see beads of moisture on the surface. Salting pulls out water so the finished dish is not soupy and seasons the eggplant from the inside.
  2. Start the sauce
    While the eggplant sweats, warm the 3 tbsp olive oil and sliced garlic in a large saucepan over medium-low for 3 minutes, until the garlic is fragrant and pale gold. Add both cans of hand-crushed tomatoes, 1 tsp salt, and the 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes. Bring to a simmer, then cook uncovered over low heat for 40 to 45 minutes.
  3. Reduce it properly
    Stir the sauce every 10 minutes and let it reduce until a spoon dragged across the bottom leaves a trail that closes slowly, roughly the texture of loose jam. You should end with about 5 cups. A thin, watery sauce is the single biggest cause of eggplant parm that slumps into a puddle on the plate. Stir in half the basil off the heat.
  4. Dry and oil the slices
    Press the eggplant slices firmly between paper towels or a clean kitchen towel to remove the surface water and most of the salt. Brush both sides lightly with the 1/3 cup olive oil — brushing uses a fraction of the oil that frying does, and eggplant will absorb every drop you give it. They should look glossy, not swimming.
  5. Roast until tender
    Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) and roast the slices on parchment-lined sheet pans for 20 to 25 minutes, flipping once halfway, until they are golden brown and completely floppy. Undercooked eggplant stays rubbery and bitter no matter how long the casserole bakes, so cook it all the way now. Let the slices cool for 10 minutes.
  6. Mix the ricotta
    Stir the 1 cup ricotta with the beaten egg and 1/2 cup (50 g) of the Parmigiano until smooth. The egg binds the ricotta so it sets into distinct creamy layers rather than running out when you cut a square. If your ricotta looked watery in the tub, drain it in a sieve for 30 minutes first.
  7. Lower the oven and build
    Reduce the oven to 375°F (190°C). Spread 1 cup of sauce across the bottom of a 9x13 in (23x33 cm) baking dish so nothing sticks. Lay down a snug single layer of eggplant, slightly overlapping, covering the whole surface. Gaps in the layers are where the finished dish falls apart.
  8. Layer it up
    Spread half the ricotta mixture over the eggplant, then a third of the remaining sauce, a third of the mozzarella, and a scattering of Parmigiano and torn basil. Repeat with a second layer of eggplant, the rest of the ricotta, more sauce, and more cheese. Finish with a third layer of eggplant, the last of the sauce, and all the remaining mozzarella and Parmigiano on top.
  9. Bake covered
    Cover the dish with foil tented so it does not touch the cheese, set it on a rimmed sheet pan to catch drips, and bake for 35 minutes. Covering it first heats everything through gently and lets the layers meld without the top browning too early. You should hear it bubbling when you pull it out.
  10. Uncover and brown
    Remove the foil and bake 20 to 25 minutes more, until the top is blistered and deep golden in spots and the sauce is bubbling around the edges. The center should register 165°F (74°C) on a thermometer, which tells you the whole casserole is hot through. If the top is pale, run it under the broiler for 90 seconds.
  11. Rest before cutting
    Let the dish rest on a rack for at least 25 minutes, and 40 is better. This is not optional — hot eggplant parm is molten and will slide apart the moment a knife touches it, while a rested one cuts into clean squares. Scatter the remaining fresh basil over the top just before serving.
Know when it is done
Bake until the center of the casserole reads 165°F (74°C) and the edges bubble; then rest 25 minutes before cutting.
Serve it with
A bitter green salad with lemon vinaigrette and a bottle of Aglianico or Nero d'Avola.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Modern eggplant is bred to be far less bitter, so the salting step is mostly about removing water. Do not skip it anyway — water is the enemy here.
  • ◆Assemble the whole dish a day ahead, refrigerate unbaked, and add 15 minutes to the covered bake time. It genuinely improves overnight.
  • ◆Roasting instead of frying uses about a quarter of the oil and makes a dish that is rich rather than heavy. Fried is traditional if you want it.
  • ◆Fresh mozzarella packed in water will flood the layers. Use the low-moisture block, or tear fresh mozzarella and drain it on towels for an hour first.
  • ◆Leftovers cut cleanly when cold. Reheat squares at 350°F (175°C) for 20 minutes rather than microwaving.

Sunday Gravy with Meatballs⏱ 4 hr 45 min🍽 8 servingsMedium▾

A big pot of tomato sauce simmered all afternoon with meatballs, sausage, and pork ribs until it turns dark and glossy. Start it after breakfast and let the smell take care of the rest of the day.

Weekend ProjectMake AheadComfort Food
Prep
45 min
Cook
4 hr
Total
4 hr 45 min
Serves
8 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the meatballs

For the gravy

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Make a panade
    Tear the bread into small pieces, cover it with the 3/4 cup milk in a bowl, and let it soak 10 minutes until completely soft. Mash it into a paste with a fork. This milk-and-bread paste is called a panade, and it is the reason great meatballs are tender — the starch traps moisture that would otherwise squeeze out as the meat proteins tighten.
  2. Mix the meatballs gently
    Add the ground beef, ground pork, beaten eggs, 3/4 cup Parmigiano, minced garlic, parsley, 2 tsp salt, and 1 tsp pepper to the panade. Mix with your hands just until you no longer see streaks of egg, about 30 seconds. Overmixing develops the proteins and gives you meatballs with the texture of a hot dog, so stop early.
  3. Roll and chill
    With wet hands, roll the mixture into 16 to 18 balls about 1 3/4 in (4.5 cm) across and 55 g each, roughly the size of a golf ball, setting them on a sheet pan. Wet hands stop the mixture sticking to you. Chill them for 20 minutes if you have time; cold meatballs hold their shape much better when they hit hot oil.
  4. Brown the meatballs
    Heat the 3 tbsp olive oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high and brown the meatballs in two or three batches, about 5 minutes each, turning to get color on several sides. They do not need to be cooked through — they will finish in the sauce for hours. Crowding the pot steams them gray, so give each batch room. Set them aside on a plate.
  5. Brown the pork and sausage
    In the same pot, brown the country-style ribs on all sides, about 8 minutes total, then set them aside and brown the sausage links for 5 minutes until well colored. Every one of these browning steps leaves fond on the bottom of the pot, and the layered fond from three different meats is what makes Sunday gravy taste different from ordinary marinara.
  6. Sweat the aromatics
    Pour off all but 3 tbsp of fat, then add the chopped onion with a pinch of salt and cook over medium heat 8 minutes until soft and translucent, scraping the bottom as the onion releases water. Add the sliced garlic and 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes and cook 1 minute more. Do not let the garlic brown or the whole pot will carry a bitter edge for hours.
  7. Caramelize the tomato paste
    Stir in the 1/4 cup tomato paste and cook it for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring constantly, until it darkens to a deep brick red and starts to stick to the pot. This step concentrates the tomato sugars and drives off the raw canned flavor. It smells noticeably sweeter and rounder when it is ready.
  8. Deglaze with wine
    Add the 1 cup red wine and scrape every bit of stuck-on fond loose with a wooden spoon while it bubbles. Simmer 4 to 5 minutes until the wine has reduced by about half and lost its sharp alcohol smell. The pot bottom should be clean and the liquid should look dark and glossy.
  9. Build the pot
    Add the three cans of hand-crushed tomatoes, the 2 cups water, 2 tsp salt, and the Parmesan rind, then return the ribs and sausage to the pot. Bring it up to a simmer, then drop the heat until the surface just barely blips once or twice a second. A rolling boil will scorch the bottom and turn the tomatoes bitter.
  10. Simmer, then add the meatballs
    Simmer partly covered for 2 hours, stirring every 30 minutes and scraping the bottom each time. Then gently lower the meatballs in, submerging them, and continue to simmer for 1 hour and 15 minutes more. Adding them partway through means they absorb sauce without falling apart over the full cooking time.
  11. Check the meats
    The pork ribs are ready when the meat pulls away from the bone with no resistance, around 195°F (91°C) internal, and both the sausages and the meatballs should read at least 160°F (71°C), the safe temperature for any ground meat — after an hour and a quarter submerged in simmering sauce they will be well past it, but check one anyway. Pull the ribs out, shred the meat off the bones, discard the bones and any cartilage, and stir the meat back in. Slice the sausages into thick coins and return them too.
  12. Finish and season
    Fish out the Parmesan rind, then tear the basil leaves in and stir. Taste carefully and adjust with salt — after four hours the sauce is concentrated, so add in small pinches. If it tastes sharp, stir the last 1 tbsp olive oil in off the heat; the fat coats your tongue and rounds the acidity off without making the sauce taste sweet.
  13. Serve in courses
    Traditionally the sauce goes on pasta first and the meats come out on a platter afterward as the second course. Spoon a ladle of gravy over each serving and put the platter of meatballs, sausage, and shredded pork in the middle of the table. Give everyone bread; there will be sauce left on every plate.
Know when it is done
Ground meat is safe at 160°F (71°C), but the ribs want 195°F (91°C) to shred; the meatballs finish far past safe during the long simmer.
Serve it with
Rigatoni or a big bowl of ziti, plenty of bread, and a jug of Sangiovese.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Sunday gravy freezes beautifully for 3 months. Freeze the sauce and meats together in quart containers, leaving an inch of headroom.
  • ◆Use 80/20 beef, not lean. Fat is what keeps the meatballs from turning into dry pellets over a long simmer.
  • ◆If you only have one afternoon and no ribs, the recipe still works with just meatballs and sausage. Cut the initial simmer to 1 hour.
  • ◆A scorched bottom ruins the whole pot and cannot be fixed. Set a timer to stir every 30 minutes and never let it boil.
  • ◆Bake the meatballs at 425°F (220°C) for 15 minutes instead of frying if you want a cleaner kitchen; you lose a little crust but save a lot of splatter.

1 Ingredients

Batch

For the shanks

The braise

Gremolata

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Tie the shanks
    Wrap a length of kitchen twine around the outside circumference of each shank and tie it snugly, like a belt. Veal shanks are ringed by a band of connective tissue that contracts as it cooks and will pull the whole shank apart into a loose mess. The twine keeps each one in a neat round for three hours. Pat them completely dry afterward.
  2. Season and flour
    Season the shanks all over with the 2 tsp kosher salt and 1 tsp pepper, then dredge them in the 1/2 cup flour and knock off the excess. The thin flour coat browns quickly and, over the long braise, thickens the sauce to exactly the right body. Only flour them right before they go in the pan, or the coating turns to glue.
  3. Sear hard
    Heat the 3 tbsp olive oil and 2 tbsp butter in a heavy Dutch oven over medium-high until the butter foam subsides. Brown the shanks 5 to 6 minutes per side, in two batches, until they are a deep even brown with no pale patches. This is the most important flavor step in the dish and it cannot be rushed. Set them on a plate; they will look almost cooked, but they are nowhere near done.
  4. Start the soffritto
    Lower the heat to medium and add the diced onion, carrot, and celery to the pot with a pinch of salt. Cook 10 to 12 minutes, stirring often, until everything is soft and the onion is translucent with just a little golden color. Dice them small and evenly so they melt into the sauce rather than showing up as chunks. Scrape the bottom as the vegetables give up their water.
  5. Add garlic and tomato paste
    Stir in the minced garlic and cook 45 seconds, then add the 2 tbsp tomato paste and cook 2 to 3 minutes more, stirring, until it darkens to brick red and coats the vegetables. Cooking the paste out removes its raw, tinny taste. The whole pot should smell sweet and deeply savory now.
  6. Deglaze with white wine
    Pour in the 1 1/2 cups white wine and scrape the bottom of the pot with a wooden spoon while it bubbles hard. Simmer 5 to 6 minutes until the wine has reduced by roughly half. White wine, not red, is the Milanese tradition — it keeps the sauce light enough that the veal still tastes like veal.
  7. Build the braising liquid
    Add the 2 cups stock, the hand-crushed tomatoes, the bay leaves, thyme sprigs, and lemon peel, and bring to a gentle simmer. Heat the oven to 325°F (165°C) while this comes up. Taste the liquid; it should be pleasantly seasoned but not salty, because it will reduce and concentrate over the next three hours.
  8. Return the shanks
    Nestle the shanks into the pot in a single layer, standing them so the marrow bones stay upright and the marrow does not slide out. The liquid should come about two-thirds of the way up the meat, not cover it — add a splash of stock if you are short. Spoon a little liquid over the exposed tops.
  9. Braise in the oven
    Cover with a tight lid and transfer to the 325°F (165°C) oven for 2 hours and 30 minutes to 3 hours. Check at the 2 hour mark: the liquid should be barely trembling, not bubbling. If it is boiling, drop the oven to 300°F (150°C), since a hard braise squeezes the meat fibers tight and makes veal stringy instead of silky.
  10. Test for doneness
    The shanks are ready when a fork slides into the meat with no resistance and the meat has pulled visibly away from the bone, around 200°F (93°C) internal. This is well past any food-safety threshold — collagen only melts into gelatin in that 190°F to 205°F (88°C to 96°C) window. If it is still tight, give it another 30 minutes and check again.
  11. Reduce the sauce
    Carefully lift the shanks onto a warm platter and snip off the twine. Fish out the bay leaves, thyme stems, and lemon peel, then simmer the sauce on the stovetop over medium-high for 8 to 10 minutes until it thickens enough to coat a spoon. Skim off any orange fat that rises. Taste and adjust the salt.
  12. Make the gremolata
    Chop the parsley, lemon zest, and garlic together on a board until they are fine and well mixed, then stir in the flaky salt. Making it at the last minute matters — the volatile oils in raw garlic and lemon zest fade within about 20 minutes. This raw, sharp mixture is what cuts through three hours of richness.
  13. Serve with a marrow spoon
    Spoon sauce over each shank, scatter the gremolata generously on top, and set the platter down with small spoons or the handle end of a teaspoon for digging out the marrow. Osso buco means bone with a hole, and that hole is the point. Serve immediately, while everything is hot enough that the marrow is soft.
Know when it is done
Braise to roughly 200°F (93°C) internal — fork-tender, far past the 145°F (63°C) safety point, which is where collagen turns to gelatin.
Serve it with
Risotto alla Milanese is the classic partner, with a Barolo or a good Nebbiolo.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Ask the butcher for center-cut hind shanks 1 1/2 in (4 cm) thick. Thin shanks dry out and end-cut shanks have almost no marrow.
  • ◆Osso buco is better made a day ahead. Cool it in its sauce, refrigerate, lift off the solid fat, and reheat at 325°F (165°C) for 40 minutes covered.
  • ◆Beef shanks are a third of the price and work with the same method, though they need about 30 extra minutes and taste heartier.
  • ◆Never let the braise boil. If you hear active bubbling through the lid, lower the oven 25 degrees — a trembling surface makes silky meat.
  • ◆Make the gremolata within 20 minutes of serving. Chopped ahead, it goes dull and slightly bitter.

Risotto alla Milanese⏱ 45 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Saffron-gold, loose enough to ripple across the plate, and finished with a shameless amount of butter and Parmigiano. Twenty minutes of stirring buys you the creamiest thing in this book.

Vegetarian OptionComfort FoodDate Night
Prep
10 min
Cook
35 min
Total
45 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the risotto

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Bloom the saffron
    Bring the 6 cups stock to a bare simmer in a saucepan, then ladle about 1/2 cup of it into a small bowl and crumble the saffron threads into it. Let the saffron steep for at least 10 minutes while you start cooking, until the liquid is a deep orange-red. Blooming pulls the color and flavor out of the threads; tossed in dry, saffron gives you pale, unevenly flavored rice.
  2. Keep the stock hot
    Leave the pot of stock on a back burner over low heat, at a temperature where you see steam and the occasional bubble but never a boil. Cold stock added to hot rice shocks the pan, stops the cooking, and adds ten minutes to your risotto. Set a ladle in the pot so it is always in reach.
  3. Sweat the onion
    Melt the 1 tbsp butter with the 1 tbsp olive oil in a wide heavy saucepan or 4 qt (3.8 L) Dutch oven over medium heat, then add the finely chopped onion and a pinch of salt. Cook 6 to 7 minutes, stirring, until the onion is completely soft and translucent with no color at all. Browned onion would muddy the clean saffron flavor, so keep the heat gentle.
  4. Toast the rice
    Add the 1 1/2 cups rice and stir constantly for 2 to 3 minutes, until the grains are coated in fat and the edges turn translucent while the centers stay chalky white. This step, called the tostatura, firms the outside of each grain so the risotto stays al dente instead of collapsing into porridge. The rice should smell faintly nutty and click against the spoon.
  5. Add the wine
    Pour in the 3/4 cup white wine and stir until it has almost completely evaporated, about 2 minutes. You will hear the sizzle change from a bubbling boil to a drier hiss when it is nearly gone. The wine adds acidity that keeps 4 tablespoons of butter and a cup of cheese from tasting heavy.
  6. Start ladling stock
    Add the saffron liquid and one ladle of hot stock, about 3/4 cup, and stir. Keep the heat at a steady medium so the pan is always at a lively simmer — too low and the starch never releases, too high and the outside of the grains blows out before the inside cooks. Stir often but you do not have to stir constantly.
  7. Repeat, ladle by ladle
    Each time the liquid reduces enough that dragging the spoon across the pan leaves a clear track for a second, add another ladle of stock and the 1 1/4 tsp salt in stages. Keep going for 16 to 18 minutes total. Adding stock gradually forces the grains to rub against each other, and that friction is what releases the starch that makes risotto creamy.
  8. Taste for al dente
    Starting at 16 minutes, bite a grain every couple of minutes. It should be tender all the way through with the faintest firm point at the very center, and absolutely no chalky white core. This usually lands between 17 and 20 minutes depending on your rice. You may not need all the stock, or you may need a splash of hot water.
  9. Get the texture right
    The finished risotto should be loose enough that it spreads slowly when you shake the pan — Italians call this all'onda, meaning wavy. If it is stiff, stir in another half ladle of stock. Remember it will tighten noticeably in the next two minutes and again on the plate, so err on the looser side.
  10. Mantecare off the heat
    Pull the pan off the burner, wait 30 seconds, then beat in the 3 tbsp cold cubed butter and the 1 cup Parmigiano vigorously with a wooden spoon for a full minute. This is the mantecatura, and beating hard is what emulsifies the fat into the starch and turns the whole pan glossy. Cold butter off the heat emulsifies; warm butter on the heat just makes it greasy. Stir in the marrow now if you are using it.
  11. Rest, then serve at once
    Cover the pan and let it sit for 2 minutes, then stir once more and check the salt and the 1/4 tsp pepper. Spoon into warm shallow bowls and tap the bottom of each bowl on the counter so the risotto settles into an even layer. Risotto waits for no one — serve within a minute or two, because it stiffens fast.
Know when it is done
No internal temperature here — go by the grain: tender through with the barest firm point at the center, and loose enough to ripple when you shake the pan.
Serve it with
The traditional partner for osso buco, or eat it alone with a glass of Franciacorta.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Carnaroli holds its shape better than Arborio and is much harder to overcook. If you can find it, buy it; it is the forgiving option.
  • ◆Never rinse risotto rice. The powdery surface starch is exactly what you are trying to release into the sauce.
  • ◆Saffron is expensive but you use only a pinch, and the cheap powdered stuff is often adulterated. Buy whole threads from a spice shop.
  • ◆Leftover risotto spread on a sheet pan and chilled overnight is the starting point for arancini, which is the best reason to make extra.
  • ◆If you must hold risotto, stop it 3 minutes early, spread it on a cold sheet pan, then finish with hot stock and butter just before serving.

Wild Mushroom Risotto⏱ 55 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Dried porcini soaked into a dark, savory broth, fresh mushrooms browned hard, and rice stirred until it turns to cream. This is the most flavor you can get out of five dollars of dried fungus.

Vegetarian OptionDate NightComfort Food
Prep
15 min
Cook
40 min
Total
55 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Mushrooms and broth

For the risotto

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Soak the porcini
    Put the 1 oz dried porcini in a heatproof bowl, pour the 2 cups boiling water over them, and press them under with a spoon. Let them soak 20 minutes until fully softened and the water is dark brown. That soaking liquid is the single most valuable ingredient in this recipe, so do not even think about pouring it down the drain.
  2. Strain and combine the broth
    Lift the porcini out with a slotted spoon, squeeze them gently over the bowl, and chop them coarsely. Pour the soaking liquid through a coffee filter or a sieve lined with a paper towel to catch the grit that always settles at the bottom. Combine the strained liquid with the 4 cups stock in a saucepan and keep it at a bare simmer on a back burner.
  3. Brown the fresh mushrooms
    Heat the 2 tbsp olive oil and 1 tbsp butter in a wide heavy pan over medium-high, add the sliced fresh mushrooms in as close to a single layer as you can, and leave them alone for 4 minutes. They will release water, look wet and gray, then start browning once the liquid cooks off. Continue 5 to 6 minutes more, stirring occasionally, until they are properly dark at the edges.
  4. Season and set aside
    Add the 1 tsp thyme and 3/4 tsp salt to the mushrooms and toss for 30 seconds. Season only after browning — salt added at the start draws water out and the mushrooms steam instead of searing. Scrape them onto a plate and reserve about a third for garnishing at the end.
  5. Sweat the onion
    In the same pan, melt the 2 tbsp butter over medium heat and cook the finely chopped onion with a pinch of salt for 6 to 7 minutes, until soft and translucent. Scrape the browned mushroom fond off the bottom as the onion releases moisture. Stir in the minced garlic and cook 45 seconds until fragrant.
  6. Toast the rice
    Add the 1 1/2 cups rice and stir constantly for 2 to 3 minutes until the grains look glossy and the outer edges turn translucent around a white center. You will hear them click against the pan and smell something like toasted popcorn. This toasting keeps the grains distinct instead of dissolving into paste.
  7. Deglaze with wine
    Pour in the 3/4 cup white wine and stir until the pan is nearly dry, about 2 minutes, and the sharp smell of alcohol has burned off. The sizzle will go from a wet bubble to a dry hiss when it is ready. Stir in the chopped rehydrated porcini now so they have time to give up their flavor to the rice.
  8. Ladle in the broth
    Add a ladle of the hot porcini broth, about 3/4 cup, and stir. Keep the pan at a steady, lively simmer and add another ladle each time the previous one has reduced enough to leave a clear track behind your spoon. Add the 1 tsp salt over the first few additions rather than all at once, since the broth is already savory.
  9. Keep going and taste
    Continue the ladle-stir-reduce cycle for 16 to 18 minutes, keeping the rice moving so the grains rub together and release starch. Start tasting at 16 minutes: the grain should be tender through with just a whisper of firmness at the core. If you run out of broth before it is done, use hot water rather than overcooking.
  10. Fold in the mushrooms
    Stir in two-thirds of the browned mushrooms and one more small ladle of broth, then cook 1 minute more. The risotto should be loose and wavy, spreading slowly when you shake the pan. Keep it slightly looser than you think you want; it thickens noticeably in the last two minutes.
  11. Mantecare
    Take the pan off the heat, wait half a minute, then beat in the 3 tbsp cold cubed butter and the 1 cup Parmigiano hard with a wooden spoon for a full minute. The whole pan should go glossy and creamy as the fat emulsifies into the starch. Season with the 1/2 tsp black pepper and check the salt.
  12. Serve immediately
    Spoon into warm shallow bowls, tap each bowl once on the counter so the risotto settles flat, and top with the reserved mushrooms, the chopped parsley, and a thin drizzle of good olive oil. Add a final shower of Parmigiano at the table. Risotto sets up as it cools, so this goes straight from pan to person.
Know when it is done
No internal temperature — judge by the grain, which should be tender with a faint firm center, and by the risotto rippling slowly when the pan is shaken.
Serve it with
A green salad with sharp vinaigrette and a glass of Barbaresco or an earthy Pinot Noir.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Never skip straining the porcini liquid. There is always sand in the bottom of that bowl and it will end up in every bite.
  • ◆A splash of dry Marsala or brandy added with the wine deepens the mushroom flavor noticeably for about a dollar.
  • ◆Use vegetable stock and skip nothing else to make this fully vegetarian; the porcini carry more than enough savoriness.
  • ◆Cook the mushrooms in two batches if your pan is under 12 in (30 cm). Piled-up mushrooms steam and stay pale and squeaky.
  • ◆Leftovers make excellent risotto cakes: chill overnight, form 3/4 in (2 cm) patties, and pan-fry in butter for 3 minutes a side.

Sicilian Arancini Rice Balls⏱ 3 hr🍽 Makes 12Advanced▾

Crisp golden spheres of saffron risotto hiding a molten center of ragu, peas, and mozzarella. They are a whole afternoon project and worth every minute of it.

Weekend ProjectFriedMake Ahead
Prep
45 min
Cook
45 min
Total
3 hr
Serves
Makes 12
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Saffron rice base

Ragu filling

Coating and frying

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Make the saffron rice
    Heat the 6 cups stock to a bare simmer and steep the saffron in a ladleful for 10 minutes. Melt the 3 tbsp butter in a wide pan, soften the chopped onion for 6 minutes, add the 2 cups Arborio and toast 2 minutes, then add the 1/2 cup wine and let it cook away. Ladle in the hot stock and saffron liquid a cup at a time, stirring, for 16 to 18 minutes until the rice is just tender. Two cups of rice drinks roughly three times its volume in liquid, so expect to use most but not quite all of the pot.
  2. Make it stiffer than risotto
    Cook this rice until it is noticeably drier than a risotto you would eat with a spoon — it should hold a mound rather than spread. Stir in the 1 1/2 tsp salt and the 1 cup Parmigiano off the heat. Loose rice will not hold a ball shape and the arancini will burst in the fryer, so err firm.
  3. Cool and bind the rice
    Spread the rice in a thin layer on a sheet pan and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, or overnight, until completely cold and firm. Once cold, mix in the 2 beaten eggs thoroughly with your hands. The egg is the glue that keeps the shell together in hot oil, and it must go into cold rice or it will scramble.
  4. Build the ragu
    Heat the 1 tbsp olive oil and brown the 8 oz ground beef over medium-high for 6 minutes, breaking it into small crumbles, then add the chopped onion and cook 5 minutes more. Stir in the 2 tbsp tomato paste and cook 2 minutes until it darkens to brick red. Deglaze with the 1/2 cup red wine and simmer until nearly dry.
  5. Finish the filling
    Add the 1 cup passata and 1 tsp salt and simmer over low heat for 20 to 25 minutes, until the mixture is thick enough that a spoon leaves a clean channel through it. Stir in the thawed peas in the last 2 minutes. Chill the ragu completely before filling — warm, loose filling turns your rice ball into a steam bomb.
  6. Shape the arancini
    With damp hands, scoop about 1/2 cup (115 g) of cold rice and flatten it into a disc in your palm about 5 in (13 cm) across. Press a shallow well into the center, keeping the rice an even 1/2 in (12 mm) thick all the way around so there are no thin spots to blow out in the oil. Keep a bowl of water nearby and re-wet your hands constantly, because dry hands will tear the rice. The batch should give you 12 discs with a little rice held back for patching.
  7. Fill and seal
    Spoon a generous 1 1/2 tbsp (about 30 g) of cold ragu into the well — that is the whole batch divided twelve ways — and press a cube of mozzarella into the middle of it. Fold the edges of the rice up and over the filling, then roll gently between your palms into a smooth ball or the traditional cone shape. Check carefully for cracks and patch them with a little extra rice — a single gap will leak cheese into the oil.
  8. Chill the shaped balls
    Set the finished arancini on a parchment-lined sheet pan and refrigerate for 30 minutes. Cold, firm balls hold together in the fryer and heat through more evenly. This is also the natural stopping point if you want to break the project across two days.
  9. Set up the breading
    Put the flour in one shallow dish, the 3 eggs beaten with 2 tbsp water in a second, and the breadcrumbs in a third. Roll each ball in flour, then egg, then press it firmly into the breadcrumbs, making sure every square inch is covered. Any bare spot is where the arancino will split open in the oil.
  10. Heat the oil to 350°F
    Pour the 8 cups oil into a heavy 4 qt (3.8 L) pot so it stands about 2 1/2 in (6 cm) deep and still comes no more than halfway up the sides, then heat it to 350°F (175°C) on a thermometer. Temperature control matters enormously here: below 325°F (163°C) they go greasy, and above 375°F (190°C) the crust burns before the center is hot. Have a slotted spider and a wire rack ready.
  11. Fry in small batches
    Lower 3 or 4 arancini into the oil with a spider and fry 5 to 6 minutes, turning once, until they are a deep even golden brown. Let the oil come back to 350°F (175°C) between batches; adding too many at once drops the temperature fast. Check one from the first batch with a thin probe: the center must reach 165°F (74°C), because the ball goes into the oil refrigerator-cold and the ragu inside is cooked ground beef being reheated. If the crust is dark but the center is short of temperature, finish the batch on a rack in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 5 minutes.
  12. Drain and rest
    Lift them onto a wire rack, never paper towels, and sprinkle immediately with the flaky sea salt while the surface is still oily enough to hold it. Let them rest 5 minutes before biting in; the mozzarella inside is well over 200°F (93°C) and will burn your mouth badly. Serve warm, with extra tomato sauce for dipping if you like.
Know when it is done
Fry at 350°F (175°C) until the center reads 165°F (74°C); the filling contains cooked ground beef, which is safe at 160°F (71°C).
Serve it with
Cold beer or a chilled glass of Grillo, with a bowl of marinara for dipping.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆This is a two-day recipe by design. Make the rice and ragu on day one, shape and fry on day two, and it stops being intimidating.
  • ◆Leftover Risotto alla Milanese from this chapter is the ideal starting rice. Chill it overnight and skip straight to the egg-binding step.
  • ◆Fine dry breadcrumbs, not panko, give the smooth crackly shell that arancini are supposed to have.
  • ◆Shaped, breaded arancini freeze well for 2 months. Fry from frozen at 325°F (163°C) for 7 to 8 minutes so the center catches up.
  • ◆If one bursts in the oil, take the whole batch out, strain the oil, and check the rest for cracks before continuing.

Neapolitan Pizza Margherita⏱ 30 hr🍽 Makes 4 pizzasAdvanced▾

A slow-fermented dough with a puffed, blistered rim, crushed San Marzano, torn mozzarella, and basil. Two days of waiting and ninety seconds of cooking, and it is the best pizza you will make at home.

Weekend ProjectBakingDate Night
Prep
40 min
Cook
25 min
Total
30 hr
Serves
Makes 4 pizzas
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

The dough

Sauce and toppings

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Dissolve salt and yeast
    Put the 325 g cool water in a large bowl and whisk in the 15 g salt until it dissolves, then whisk in the 1 g yeast. Neapolitan method dissolves the salt in the water first, so it never sits directly against the yeast in a concentrated pocket. Yes, that is a truly tiny amount of yeast — the long cold ferment does the work instead.
  2. Mix a shaggy dough
    Add the 500 g flour a third at a time, mixing with your hand or a wooden spoon until there is no dry flour left and you have a rough, sticky mass. Do not knead yet. Cover the bowl and let it rest 20 minutes, which lets the flour fully hydrate and makes the kneading dramatically easier.
  3. Knead until smooth
    Turn the dough onto an unfloured counter and knead for 10 to 12 minutes, using a bench scraper to fold it over on itself whenever it sticks. It will go from ragged and tacky to smooth and slightly springy. Test it by stretching a piece thin enough to see light through without tearing — that is the windowpane, and it means the gluten is developed.
  4. Bulk ferment at room temperature
    Shape the dough into a tight ball, put it in a lightly oiled container, cover, and leave at room temperature, around 70°F (21°C), for 2 hours. It will not double; you are just waking the yeast up. If your kitchen is much warmer than that, cut this to 90 minutes.
  5. Cold ferment overnight
    Move the covered container to the refrigerator for 20 to 24 hours. This slow cold fermentation is where all the flavor comes from — the dough develops complex, faintly sweet, slightly tangy notes that a same-day dough simply cannot have. It will rise slowly and look a little bubbly when you take it out.
  6. Divide and ball
    Turn the cold dough out and divide it into 4 equal pieces of about 210 g each, using a scale if you have one. Shape each into a tight ball by folding the edges into the center and then rolling it seam-side down under a cupped hand until the surface is taut. A tight skin is what makes the rim puff dramatically.
  7. Final proof
    Set the balls well apart in a covered container or on a floured tray under plastic and let them proof at room temperature for 4 to 6 hours, until they have visibly relaxed, spread slightly, and feel soft and pillowy when poked. An underproofed ball fights back when you stretch it and will not open properly. A gentle poke should leave a dent that fills in slowly.
  8. Preheat as hot as you can
    Put a pizza steel or stone on a rack about 6 in (15 cm) below the broiler and heat the oven to its maximum, usually 550°F (290°C), for a full hour. A steel or stone that has only been in for 20 minutes is not saturated with heat and will give you a pale, cracker-like base. Switch the broiler on 10 minutes before the first pizza goes in.
  9. Make the sauce
    Crush the canned tomatoes by hand or pass them through a food mill, then stir in the 1 1/2 tsp salt. Do not cook it and do not add garlic or herbs — the sauce cooks in 90 seconds on the pizza and stays bright and fresh that way. If it looks watery, drain off some of the thin juice.
  10. Open the dough by hand
    Flour a work surface, lay a ball down, and press from the center outward with your fingertips, leaving the outer 3/4 in (2 cm) completely untouched. Then lift the disc and let gravity stretch it as you rotate it over your knuckles until it is about 10 in (25 cm) across. Never use a rolling pin — it crushes the gas out of the rim and you lose the cornicione entirely.
  11. Top fast and lightly
    Slide the disc onto a semolina-dusted peel, spread about 1/3 cup of sauce in a spiral leaving the rim bare, scatter a quarter of the torn mozzarella, and drizzle with 1 tbsp of the olive oil. If you are using the Parmigiano, dust about 1 tbsp of it over the sauce before the mozzarella goes on — it is not strictly Neapolitan, but it adds a savory backbone in a home oven that cannot reach wood-fired heat. Work in under 60 seconds; dough sitting on a peel starts to stick almost immediately. Shake the peel gently to confirm it slides before you go anywhere near the oven.
  12. Bake under the broiler
    Slide the pizza onto the hot steel with a quick forward-and-back jerk and bake under the broiler for 4 to 6 minutes, until the rim is puffed with dark leopard spots and the cheese is bubbling. Turn the pizza halfway through with the peel for even color. Home ovens run cooler than a wood oven, so watch for color rather than the clock.
  13. Finish with basil
    Pull the pizza out, add 6 fresh basil leaves, and drizzle with another 1/2 tbsp of the olive oil. Basil added before baking turns black and bitter, which is why real pizzerias tuck it under the cheese or add it after. Cut and eat immediately, standing up, before making the next one.
Know when it is done
Bake at the oven's maximum, ideally 550°F (290°C) with the broiler on, until the rim is puffed and leopard-spotted, 4 to 6 minutes.
Serve it with
Cold Peroni or a light Aglianico, and nothing else on the table.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Weigh everything. Pizza dough is a percentage formula and cup measurements can be off by 15 percent, which is the difference between good and unworkable.
  • ◆A baking steel outperforms a stone by a wide margin because it transfers heat faster, which is exactly what a home oven lacks.
  • ◆The dough can hold in the fridge for up to 72 hours and gets more flavorful every day. Just pull it 5 to 6 hours before you want to bake.
  • ◆Drain torn fresh mozzarella on paper towels for 20 minutes. Undrained buffalo mozzarella will flood the center of the pizza.
  • ◆If the dough springs back and refuses to open, cover it and wait 15 minutes. Fighting it only tears it.

Sicilian Pan Pizza⏱ 5 hr 45 min🍽 Makes 8 squaresMedium▾

A thick, airy square with a fried-crisp bottom, cheese caramelized right into the edge of the pan, and sauce spooned over the top. Far more forgiving than round pizza and arguably more fun to eat.

BakingComfort FoodWeekend Project
Prep

5 hr 45 min
Serves
Makes 8 squares
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

The dough

Sauce

Toppings

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Mix a wet dough
    Stir the 400 g bread flour, 300 g lukewarm water, 9 g salt, and 3 g instant yeast together in a bowl with a spoon or your hand until no dry flour remains, about 1 minute. Add the 2 tbsp olive oil and squish it in. The dough will be very wet and sticky and that is correct — 75 percent hydration is what gives you the open, airy crumb.
  2. Rest, then fold
    Cover the bowl and let it sit 20 minutes, then do a set of stretch and folds: wet your hand, grab one side of the dough, stretch it up, and fold it over the center, rotating the bowl and repeating four times. Do three sets of folds spaced 20 minutes apart. Folding builds strength in a wet dough without any kneading.
  3. Bulk ferment
    Cover the bowl and leave it at room temperature, about 70°F (21°C), for 1 1/2 to 2 hours more — roughly 3 hours from mixing once you count the hour of folds — until the dough has doubled and the surface is dotted with bubbles. If your kitchen is cold this can take an hour longer, so judge by the look and not the clock. The dough should feel alive and jiggly when you shake the bowl.
  4. Oil the pan generously
    Pour the 3 tbsp olive oil into a 13x9 in (33x23 cm) metal baking pan or a quarter sheet pan and spread it up the sides with your fingers. That much oil sounds like a lot but it is the whole point — the dough essentially shallow-fries against the pan and comes out with a crisp, golden bottom crust.
  5. Transfer and let it relax
    Scrape the dough into the oiled pan, turn it once to coat both sides, and press it toward the corners with oiled fingertips. It will spring back and refuse to reach the edges, which is normal. Cover and wait 20 minutes, then press again; the gluten relaxes and it will go the rest of the way easily.
  6. Second proof in the pan
    Cover the pan loosely and let the dough proof for 1 1/2 to 2 hours, until it is visibly puffy, has filled the corners, and a light poke leaves a dent that springs back only halfway. Underproofed dough bakes dense and bready. This is the stage that decides whether your crumb is open or tight.
  7. Make the sauce
    While it proofs, warm the 2 tbsp olive oil with the minced garlic over medium-low for 2 minutes until fragrant but not colored. Add the crushed tomatoes, 1 tsp oregano, 3/4 tsp salt, red pepper flakes, and 1 tsp sugar, and simmer 20 minutes until thickened. Sicilian style spoons the sauce on top of the cheese, so it needs to be thick enough not to run.
  8. Preheat with a stone
    Heat the oven to 500°F (260°C) with a baking steel or stone on the lowest rack for at least 45 minutes. Setting the pan directly on preheated steel blasts the bottom crust with heat and is the difference between crisp and pale. If you have neither, use the lowest oven rack.
  9. Dimple and top
    Press your oiled fingertips into the proofed dough all over, going nearly to the bottom of the pan, to create dimples. Scatter the cubed mozzarella and shredded provolone evenly across the surface, pushing some cubes right up against the edges of the pan. Those edge cubes melt down the sides and fry into the caramelized cheese crust that makes this style famous.
  10. Add the sauce in stripes
    Spoon the sauce over the cheese in three or four thick stripes rather than spreading it everywhere. Leaving cheese exposed lets it brown and bubble, and stripes are the traditional look. Use about 1 1/2 cups of sauce and save the rest for dipping.
  11. Bake until deeply browned
    Set the pan on the hot steel and bake 18 to 22 minutes, until the cheese at the edges is dark brown and crackling and the top is bubbling. At 500°F (260°C) that is genuinely enough to cook a pan this thick through — push it to 25 minutes and the cheese crust crosses from caramelized into acrid. Do not pull it at the first sign of golden either; this style wants real color. Lift a corner with a spatula to check that the bottom is crisp and browned before you commit.
  12. Release and rest
    Run a thin metal spatula around the edges immediately to free the cheese crust, then slide the whole pizza out onto a wire rack within 2 minutes. Leaving it in the pan traps steam and softens that bottom crust you just worked for. Rest 5 minutes, scatter the Pecorino and basil, and cut into 8 squares.
Know when it is done
Bake at 500°F (260°C) for 18 to 22 minutes until the cheese edges are deep brown and the bottom crust is crisp and golden.
Serve it with
Cold lager and a big bowl of dressed greens to cut the richness.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆A dark metal or steel pan browns the bottom far better than glass or ceramic. Cast iron works beautifully too.
  • ◆The dough can bulk ferment in the refrigerator overnight instead. Bring it to room temperature for 2 hours before pressing it into the pan.
  • ◆Pepperoni cups nicely on this style; add it under the sauce stripes so the edges curl and crisp without burning.
  • ◆If the dough tears while you press it, stop and let it rest 15 more minutes. Torn gluten will not proof evenly.
  • ◆Leftovers reheat perfectly in a dry skillet over medium heat for 4 minutes with a lid on, which re-crisps the base.

Rosemary Sea Salt Focaccia⏱ 5 hr 30 min🍽 Makes 12 piecesEasy▾

A dimpled, olive-oil-soaked slab with a crackly bottom and a cloud-soft middle. It takes about fifteen minutes of actual work and makes the whole apartment smell incredible.

BakingVegetarianMake Ahead
Prep
20 min
Cook
25 min
Total
5 hr 30 min
Serves
Makes 12 pieces
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

The dough

Pan and topping

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Wake up the yeast
    Whisk the 5 g instant yeast and 1 tsp honey into the 400 g lukewarm water and let it sit 5 minutes until it looks slightly cloudy and smells faintly of bread. The water should feel like a warm bath, around 100°F (38°C) — anything above 120°F (49°C) starts killing yeast. Instant yeast does not strictly need proofing, but this tells you it is alive before you commit.
  2. Mix by hand
    Add the 500 g bread flour and 10 g fine sea salt to the water and stir with a sturdy spoon or your hand for about 90 seconds, until there are no dry patches and you have a shaggy, very wet dough. Then drizzle in the 3 tbsp olive oil and squish it through. There is no kneading in this recipe at all — time does the work.
  3. Do two sets of folds
    Cover the bowl and rest 30 minutes, then wet your hand, reach under one side of the dough, stretch it upward, and fold it over the middle; rotate the bowl and repeat four times. Rest 30 minutes and do one more set. These folds build the gluten structure that traps the big bubbles you want in focaccia.
  4. Bulk ferment until doubled
    Cover the bowl tightly and leave it at room temperature for 2 more hours, which puts you at about 3 hours of fermentation counting the hour you spent folding, until the dough has doubled in size and is full of visible bubbles across the surface. In a cool kitchen this may take an hour longer, so watch the dough and not the clock. It should look inflated and wobble when you nudge the bowl.
  5. Oil the pan properly
    Pour the 4 tbsp olive oil into a 13x9 in (33x23 cm) metal pan or a quarter sheet pan and use your fingers to coat the bottom and all four sides thoroughly. This is more oil than feels reasonable and it is doing something specific: the underside of the focaccia essentially fries in it and comes out golden and crisp.
  6. Transfer without deflating
    Slide an oiled hand or bowl scraper down the side of the bowl and gently ease the whole mass of dough into the pan in one piece. Handle it as if it were a sleeping cat — every big bubble you knock out is a hole you will not have in the finished bread. Turn it once so both sides are oiled.
  7. Coax it to the corners
    Press the dough outward toward the corners with flat, oiled fingers. It will pull back and stop short of the edges the first time, which is normal. Wait 15 minutes and press again, and by the second or third try it will reach all four corners with no fighting.
  8. Proof in the pan
    Cover the pan loosely and let the dough proof 45 minutes to 1 hour, until it is puffy and jiggly and has risen visibly up the sides. Poke it gently: the dent should fill back in slowly and only partway. Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C) about 30 minutes into this proof.
  9. Dimple with authority
    Drizzle the 2 tbsp of top olive oil over the surface, then press all ten fingertips straight down through the dough until you feel the pan bottom, working across the whole surface. Do not be gentle — real dimples are what hold the pools of oil that define focaccia. The dough will deflate slightly and then recover in the oven.
  10. Season the top
    Scatter the 2 tbsp chopped rosemary, 1 1/2 tsp flaky salt, and 1/4 tsp cracked pepper evenly across the surface, pushing a little rosemary into the dimples so it does not scorch. Rosemary sitting fully exposed on top of a 450°F (230°C) bake will blacken. Let the pan sit 10 more minutes while the oven finishes heating.
  11. Bake until deep gold
    Bake on a lower-middle rack for 22 to 27 minutes, rotating the pan halfway, until the top is deeply golden and the edges are dark and crisp. The internal temperature of a fully baked focaccia is 200°F to 205°F (93°C to 96°C) if you want to check. Pale focaccia tastes doughy, so push it further than you think.
  12. Get it out of the pan
    Run a spatula around the edges and slide the focaccia onto a wire rack within 2 minutes of leaving the oven. Steam trapped under the bread in a hot pan will turn that crisp bottom soggy in about five minutes. Cool at least 15 minutes before cutting into 12 squares.
Know when it is done
Bake at 450°F (230°C) until deep golden; the center of a finished loaf reads 200°F to 205°F (93°C to 96°C).
Serve it with
Good olive oil and balsamic for dipping, a plate of prosciutto, and a glass of something cold.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆For much better flavor, do the bulk ferment in the fridge overnight, up to 24 hours. Bring the dough to room temperature for an hour before panning it.
  • ◆Halved cherry tomatoes, thin lemon slices, or olives pressed into the dimples before baking all work; press them in deep so they do not burn.
  • ◆If your dough will not reach the corners, you are being too impatient. Rest 15 minutes and try again rather than forcing and tearing it.
  • ◆Weigh the flour if you possibly can. A cup of flour can vary by 20 g depending on how you scoop, and this dough is sensitive to it.
  • ◆Focaccia is best the day it is baked. Day-two slices come back to life in a 400°F (205°C) oven for 5 minutes, or split them for sandwiches.

Bruschetta al Pomodoro⏱ 28 min🍽 Makes 8 piecesEasy▾

Thick bread grilled until it is charred at the edges, rubbed with raw garlic, and piled with tomatoes that have been salted just long enough to taste like summer. Five ingredients, and every one of them has to be good.

30 MinutesVegetarianAppetizer

20 min

28 min
Serves
Makes 8 pieces
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Tomato topping

The bread

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Choose good tomatoes
    Use tomatoes that smell like tomatoes at the stem end and give slightly when you press them. Pale, hard, refrigerated supermarket tomatoes in February will make a sad bruschetta no matter how good your technique is. If good tomatoes are not available, use cherry or grape tomatoes, which are reliable year round.
  2. Cut and salt them
    Core the large tomatoes and cut them into 1/2 in (12 mm) dice, halve any cherry tomatoes, and put everything in a colander set over a bowl. Toss with the 3/4 tsp kosher salt and let them drain for 15 to 20 minutes. Salting draws out the watery juice that would otherwise turn your toast to mush, and it seasons the tomatoes all the way through.
  3. Save the tomato water
    You will end up with about 1/3 cup of pink tomato liquid in the bowl below. Do not throw it away — it is intensely flavorful. Either sip it, add it to a vinaigrette, or reduce it in a small pan for two minutes and spoon it over the finished bruschetta.
  4. Dress the tomatoes
    Move the drained tomatoes to a clean bowl and toss with the 3 tbsp olive oil, 1 tsp red wine vinegar, torn basil, and 1/4 tsp black pepper. Tear the basil with your hands rather than chopping it, since a knife bruises the leaves and turns the cut edges black. Let it sit at room temperature while you toast the bread.
  5. Cut the bread thick
    Slice the loaf into 8 pieces about 3/4 in (2 cm) thick, cutting on a slight angle if the loaf is narrow so you get more surface area. Thin slices go limp under wet tomatoes within a minute. You want slices sturdy enough to pick up with one hand.
  6. Brush with oil
    Brush both sides of each slice lightly with the 3 tbsp olive oil, using about half a teaspoon per side. The oil helps the surface toast rather than dry out, and it carries flavor into the crumb. Do not soak the bread; it should look lightly sheened, not saturated.
  7. Grill or broil the bread
    Cook the slices on a hot grill, in a ridged grill pan over medium-high, or under the broiler 6 in (15 cm) from the element. Give them 2 to 3 minutes per side, until you have dark char marks on the ridges and a crisp, dry surface. Bruschetta gets its name from bruscare, meaning to char, so a little real blackening is authentic and delicious.
  8. Rub with raw garlic
    While each slice is still hot, drag a cut half of garlic clove firmly across the rough, toasted surface. The bread acts like a grater and the garlic melts into it. One clove half will do about four slices; go lighter if you are garlic-shy, because raw garlic on hot bread is potent.
  9. Top just before serving
    Spoon the dressed tomatoes generously onto each slice, letting a little juice soak in but not pooling. Do this within a minute or two of eating — bruschetta assembled ahead of time becomes soggy bread with a salad on it. Set the toasts out and top them at the table if you are feeding a crowd.
  10. Finish and eat
    Drizzle the last 1 tbsp of good olive oil over the toasts, sprinkle the 1/2 tsp flaky sea salt on top, and add a few whole basil leaves for looks. Serve immediately, with a plate underneath because the juice will run. This is a dish that rewards eating standing in the kitchen.
Know when it is done
No internal temperature — toast the bread until the surface is dry, crisp, and charred in spots on the ridges, about 2 to 3 minutes per side.
Serve it with
A chilled glass of Vermentino or Prosecco, as the first thing you put on the table.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆The salting and draining step is what separates real bruschetta from soggy toast. Do not skip it even if the tomatoes look dry.
  • ◆Day-old bread is better than fresh here; it toasts drier and holds up longer under the topping.
  • ◆Use your best olive oil for the topping, since it is never heated and you taste it directly. Save the ordinary bottle for brushing the bread.
  • ◆The tomato mixture can be made up to 2 hours ahead and left at room temperature. Never refrigerate it, which kills tomato flavor and turns the texture mealy.
  • ◆A spoonful of the topping over burrata or grilled fish is a very good use of leftovers.

Caprese Salad with Torn Basil⏱ 45 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Tomato, mozzarella, basil, olive oil, salt — the whole dish is in choosing well and seasoning properly. When the tomatoes are right, nothing on the table beats it.

No CookSummerVegetarian
Prep
15 min
Cook
0 min
Total
45 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Bring everything to room temperature
    Take the tomatoes and mozzarella out of the refrigerator at least 30 minutes before you plan to eat, and an hour is better. Cold mutes flavor and firms up the fat in cheese, so a fridge-cold caprese tastes like almost nothing. Never store tomatoes in the fridge in the first place, since below 55°F (13°C) they lose their aroma permanently.
  2. Choose your tomatoes
    Look for tomatoes that feel heavy for their size, smell green and sweet at the stem, and yield slightly to a gentle squeeze. A mix of colors — red, yellow, and a dark heirloom — looks beautiful, but flavor beats color every time. If it is winter, use ripe cherry tomatoes instead and halve them.
  3. Drain the mozzarella
    Lift the mozzarella out of its liquid and set it on a double layer of paper towels for 10 minutes, turning once. Fresh mozzarella carries a lot of water, and undrained cheese will release a milky pool that dilutes the olive oil into a watery mess. Save the liquid to store any leftover cheese.
  4. Slice the tomatoes
    Core the tomatoes and cut them into slices about 1/3 in (8 mm) thick with a very sharp or serrated knife, using a gentle sawing motion so you do not crush them. Cut through the equator rather than pole to pole for the prettiest cross sections. Lay them on a plate as you go.
  5. Salt the tomatoes first
    Sprinkle the tomato slices with about half of the flaky salt and let them sit for 5 minutes. This small head start seasons the tomatoes properly and pulls a little juice to the surface, which then mixes with the olive oil into an instant dressing. Salting everything at the end leaves the tomato itself tasting flat.
  6. Slice the mozzarella
    Cut the drained mozzarella into slices roughly the same 1/3 in (8 mm) thickness as the tomatoes so every bite is balanced. Wipe the knife between cuts if the cheese drags. For buffalo mozzarella, tearing it into rough pieces by hand is more traditional and gives the oil more nooks to sit in.
  7. Arrange the plate
    Overlap the tomato and mozzarella slices in alternating rows or a spiral on a large platter, or simply pile them casually — both are correct. Do not build a tall tower; caprese should be shallow so the oil and juices pool where you can get at them with bread. Work on a flat platter rather than a bowl.
  8. Tear the basil
    Tear the basil leaves in half by hand and tuck them between the layers as well as scattering some on top. Torn basil releases its oils without the bruising and blackening you get from a knife blade. Add it at the very last moment, because basil wilts and darkens within a few minutes of being dressed.
  9. Dress and finish
    Drizzle the 1/4 cup olive oil over everything in a slow, generous stream, then finish with the remaining flaky salt and the 1/2 tsp cracked pepper. If you are using it, add only a few drops of aged balsamic — the thick sweet syrup, not the thin sharp supermarket kind, and never enough to hide the tomato. Serve within 10 minutes, with bread for the plate.
Know when it is done
No cooking involved — serve everything at room temperature, around 68°F to 72°F (20°C to 22°C), which is when tomatoes and mozzarella taste their best.
Serve it with
Crusty bread for mopping the plate and a cold glass of Falanghina or a dry rosato.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆This dish has nowhere to hide. Buy the best tomatoes, the best mozzarella, and the best olive oil you can, and make something else in January.
  • ◆Buffalo mozzarella is creamier and tangier; fior di latte is milder and firmer and slices more cleanly. Both are correct.
  • ◆Skip the balsamic entirely if your tomatoes are excellent. In Italy caprese usually gets nothing but oil and salt.
  • ◆Burrata instead of mozzarella turns this into a richer dish; tear it open at the table so the cream runs into the tomato juices.
  • ◆Assemble at the last minute. A caprese that has sat for 30 minutes is a puddle with cheese in it.

🍜Pasta & Noodles16 recipes▾

Almost every great pasta comes down to three habits: salt the water like you mean it, save a mug of that starchy water before you drain, and finish the noodles in the pan with the sauce instead of pouring sauce on top. Learn those three things here and the rest of the chapter cooks itself.

Spaghetti alla Carbonara⏱ 30 min🍽 4 servingsAdvanced▾

Eggs, cured pork, sharp sheep's cheese and black pepper turned into a glossy sauce with nothing but heat control and pasta water. There is no cream in it, and once you feel how the emulsion comes together you will never need a recipe again.

Date Night30 MinutesItalian
Prep
15 min
Cook
15 min
Total
30 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the pasta

For the sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Set everything out first
    Carbonara happens in about 90 seconds at the end, so nothing can be hunting for a grater at that point. Grate the 3 oz (85 g) Pecorino now, crack the eggs into a wide bowl, cut the guanciale, and set a heatproof mixing bowl and tongs by the stove. Take the eggs out of the fridge 20 minutes ahead if you can, because cold yolks hitting hot pasta seize much faster than room-temperature ones.
  2. Salt the water properly
    Bring 4 qt (3.8 L) of water to a rolling boil in a large pot and add 1 tbsp (18 g) fine sea salt — it should taste like a mild soup, not the sea, because Pecorino is already very salty. Under-salted water is the single most common reason homemade pasta tastes flat no matter how good the sauce is. Do not add oil to the water; it coats the noodles and stops sauce from clinging later.
  3. Render the guanciale slowly
    Put the guanciale into a cold 12 in (30 cm) skillet and set it over medium-low heat. Starting cold lets the fat melt out gradually instead of the meat searing shut and staying chewy. Cook for 8-10 minutes, stirring now and then, until the pieces are deep gold with a crisp edge and about 1/4 cup (60 ml) of clear fat has pooled in the pan. It should sizzle steadily and smell nutty, never smoke.
  4. Toast the pepper in the fat
    Turn the heat off, scoop the crisp guanciale onto a plate with a slotted spoon, and leave the fat in the pan. Stir 1 1/2 tsp (4 g) coarse black pepper into the warm fat and let it sit for 30 seconds — the residual heat blooms the oils in the pepper and makes it taste floral rather than dusty. Do not do this over a live flame or the pepper turns bitter in seconds.
  5. Build the egg and cheese paste
    In your mixing bowl, whisk the 4 yolks and 1 whole egg with the grated Pecorino and a good grind of pepper until you have a thick, sandy paste that barely moves — think wet cake batter. The whole egg gives the sauce enough body to coat, while the extra yolks give richness without any cream. If it looks like scrambled-egg liquid rather than paste, add another tablespoon of cheese.
  6. Cook the pasta just under al dente
    Drop the pasta into the boiling water and stir for the first 30 seconds so it does not clump. Cook it 1 minute less than the low end of the package time, usually 8-9 minutes for spaghetti, so it still has a firm white thread in the center when you bite it. It will finish cooking in the pan, and pasta that is already soft when it leaves the water turns to mush in the sauce.
  7. Save the pasta water
    About a minute before draining, dip a heatproof measuring cup into the pot and pull out 2 cups (480 ml) of the cloudy, starchy water. That starch is the emulsifier that binds fat and egg into a sauce — plain tap water will not do the same job. Set the cup right next to your bowl, because you will use it three separate times in the next two minutes.
  8. Temper the eggs
    Whisking the egg mixture constantly, drizzle in about 1/3 cup (80 ml) of the hot pasta water in a thin stream. The mixture will loosen from a paste into a pourable cream and warm up to roughly 120°F (49°C), which is the whole trick: you are raising the egg temperature gradually instead of shocking it. Skip this step and the eggs will scramble the instant they meet the pasta.
  9. Combine off the heat
    Drain the pasta, dump it straight into the skillet with the peppery fat, and toss hard for 20-30 seconds so every strand is coated and glossy. Now take the skillet completely off the burner, wait 20 seconds so the pan drops below a sizzle, then pour in the tempered egg mixture and toss continuously. The residual heat of the pasta and pan is more than enough to cook the sauce.
  10. Toss until it turns to silk
    Keep the pasta moving with tongs for 45-60 seconds, adding pasta water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time until the sauce clings and slides off a strand in a smooth sheet rather than pooling at the bottom. If it seizes or looks grainy, the pan was too hot — pull it off, add a splash of cool pasta water, and keep tossing to bring it back. Finished carbonara should look like melted vanilla ice cream, not scrambled eggs.
  11. Fold in the pork and serve
    Stir in most of the crisped guanciale, saving a spoonful for the top, then taste for salt — with Pecorino this salty you usually need none, but if your guanciale was mild stir in the 1/4 tsp kosher salt now. Serve straight from the pan into warm bowls, because carbonara stiffens fast as it cools. Finish each bowl with the reserved guanciale, a little more Pecorino, and a heavy crack of black pepper.
Know when it is done
The sauce should thicken at about 160°F (71°C) — hot enough to be safe and creamy, and well below the 180°F (82°C) where egg proteins clump and scramble.
Serve it with
A crisp Frascati or any dry Italian white, and a simple green salad with lemon to cut the richness.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Guanciale is cured pork jowl and it is worth seeking out; pancetta is the next best thing, and thick-cut bacon works but brings smoke that is not traditional.
  • ◆If the pan is even slightly too hot when the eggs go in, you get scrambled eggs. When in doubt, wait ten more seconds off the heat — the pasta holds plenty of heat.
  • ◆Warm your serving bowls with hot tap water and dry them. Cold bowls drop the sauce temperature fast and it goes from silky to pasty in under a minute.
  • ◆Carbonara does not reheat. If you must, add 2 tbsp (30 ml) water and warm it gently in a skillet while stirring, and accept that it will never be as good as it was at minute one.
  • ◆No Pecorino? Use half Parmigiano-Reggiano and half Pecorino for a mellower sauce, and add a pinch more salt since Parmigiano is less salty.

Cacio e Pepe⏱ 20 min🍽 2 servingsMedium▾

Three ingredients, no cream, no butter — just cheese, pepper and starchy water whipped into a sauce that clings to every strand. It is the best thing you can make from an almost empty fridge, and it teaches you more about pasta water than any other dish.

Weeknight20 MinutesPantry
Prep
8 min
Cook
12 min
Total
20 min
Serves
2 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Grate the cheese very fine
    Use the smallest holes on a box grater or a rasp grater so the Pecorino turns into a fluffy powder rather than shreds. Fine cheese melts into the water instantly; coarse shreds sink, clump, and turn into a stringy knot at the bottom of the pan. Grate all 4 oz (115 g) before you start cooking and keep it at room temperature.
  2. Crack the peppercorns yourself
    Put 2 tsp (5 g) whole peppercorns in a zip bag and crush them with the bottom of a heavy pan, or use the coarsest setting on a grinder. You want cracked, uneven pieces about the size of coarse sand, not fine dust. Pre-ground pepper has already lost the volatile oils that make this dish smell like a Roman trattoria.
  3. Use less water on purpose
    Bring just 2 qt (1.9 L) of water to a boil with 1 1/2 tsp (9 g) salt — about half what most people put on for a pot of pasta, and barely enough to cover 8 oz of spaghetti once it softens. Less water means the starch that leaches out of the noodles is far more concentrated, and that starch is the only thing standing between you and a broken, greasy sauce. Use a narrow saucepan rather than a stockpot so the strands stay submerged, and stir a little more often than usual since crowded pasta likes to stick. Salt lightly here because Pecorino brings a lot of salt of its own.
  4. Toast the pepper
    Set a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium heat, add the 1 tsp (5 ml) olive oil and the cracked pepper, and swirl for 45-60 seconds until it smells sharp and perfumed. It should sizzle faintly at the edges, never smoke. Toasting wakes up the piperine and gives the finished dish a warm heat instead of a dry scratch at the back of the throat.
  5. Cook the pasta short
    Add the pasta to the boiling water and stir well for the first 30 seconds. Cook it 2 minutes shy of the package time — around 7 minutes for dried spaghetti — so it is distinctly chewy. It finishes in the pan, and this shortfall is what lets the noodles absorb the peppery liquid instead of just sitting in it.
  6. Pull a full mug of pasta water
    Before draining, ladle out 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of the cloudy water — take it from deep in the pot, where the starch is thickest. It should look faintly milky, almost like watered-down skim milk; that is the visual cue that you have enough dissolved starch to build a sauce. Because you started with only 2 qt, this water is roughly twice as starchy as normal pasta water, which is exactly the point. Set it beside the stove, because you will use most of it in the next two minutes.
  7. Make the cheese slurry
    In a small bowl, whisk about half the grated Pecorino with 1/3 cup (80 ml) of the hot pasta water until you have a smooth, loose paste with no lumps, roughly the texture of pancake batter. This pre-melting step is the safety net that stops the cheese from hitting a hot pan and instantly balling up. If it looks stringy, whisk in another tablespoon of water.
  8. Move the pasta into the pan
    Lift the pasta directly from the pot into the skillet with tongs, letting the water that clings to it come along, and add another 1/2 cup (120 ml) of pasta water. Turn the heat to medium and toss constantly for about 1 minute as the liquid bubbles and reduces around the noodles. The pasta should finish cooking here, drinking in the pepper as it goes.
  9. Kill the heat, then add cheese
    Take the skillet fully off the burner and let it cool for about 20 seconds — you should be able to hold your hand an inch above it without flinching. Pour in the cheese slurry and toss hard and continuously, adding the remaining cheese in two handfuls. Direct heat above roughly 170°F (77°C) makes Pecorino split into rubber and oil, so the pan must be off the flame.
  10. Whip it into a sauce
    Keep tossing and stirring vigorously for 30-60 seconds, splashing in pasta water 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time until the sauce turns creamy and coats the strands with a visible sheen. If it clumps, add a little more hot water and keep working it — most broken cacio e pepe can be rescued with water and motion. Serve immediately in warmed bowls with extra pepper on top.
Know when it is done
Add the cheese only once the pan is off the heat and below about 170°F (77°C); above that Pecorino breaks into oily strings instead of melting into cream.
Serve it with
A cold, dry white like Vermentino, and nothing else on the table — this dish deserves to be the whole meal.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆The number one failure is heat. If you can hear an aggressive sizzle when the cheese goes in, it is too hot and it will seize.
  • ◆A splash of cold pasta water can shock a clumping sauce back together — keep 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the reserved water cooling on the counter as insurance.
  • ◆For a slightly more forgiving version, use 3 oz (85 g) Pecorino plus 1 oz (30 g) Parmigiano-Reggiano; the Parmigiano melts more smoothly.
  • ◆Tonnarelli or spaghetti alla chitarra are traditional because their rough square edges hold the sauce, but any bronze-die dried pasta works better than a slick supermarket brand.
  • ◆Cook this for two at most. Scaling past 1 lb (450 g) of pasta makes the emulsion much harder to control in a single pan.
