Spaghetti Aglio e Olio⏱ 25 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Garlic gently toasted in good olive oil, chili, parsley and a splash of pasta water — dinner from a bare pantry in twenty minutes. Make it once at midnight and it becomes a permanent part of your life.

WeeknightPantryVegetarian
Prep
10 min
Cook
15 min
Total
25 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Slice the garlic thin and even
    Trim the root end off each clove and slice lengthwise about 1/16 in (2 mm) thick — thin enough to see light through, but not paper-shaved. Even slices brown at the same rate, and uneven ones mean some pieces are still raw while others have gone bitter and black. A small paring knife gives you far more control here than a chef's knife.
  2. Get the water going
    Bring 4 qt (3.8 L) of water to a rolling boil and add 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt. This is the dish where properly salted water matters most, because there is no cheese, cream, or meat to carry seasoning. Taste it — it should taste distinctly seasoned, like a good broth.
  3. Start the garlic cold
    Pour the 1/2 cup (120 ml) olive oil into a cold 12 in (30 cm) skillet, add the sliced garlic, and only then turn the heat to medium-low. Starting in cold oil lets the garlic release its flavor slowly over 5-7 minutes instead of scorching in 30 seconds. You are looking for a lazy, steady bubbling around the slices, not a hard fry.
  4. Take it to pale gold, no further
    Stir occasionally and watch closely; pull the pan off the heat the moment the slices turn the color of light straw, around 6-8 minutes in. Garlic carries residual heat and keeps darkening in the oil after the burner is off, so stopping early is the right call. Burnt garlic is acrid and there is no fixing it — if it goes dark brown, wipe the pan and start over.
  5. Bloom the chili
    With the pan off the heat, stir in the 3/4 tsp red pepper flakes and let them sit in the warm oil for 30 seconds. The heat draws the capsaicin and the red color out into the oil, which is what turns this from spicy specks into a sauce with an even warm glow. Add more flakes now if you want a real kick.
  6. Cook the pasta al dente
    Drop the spaghetti into the boiling water, stir for the first 30 seconds, then cook 1 minute less than the package says — usually 8 minutes. Bite a strand: there should be a thin, firm white core. That last minute of cooking happens in the oil, where the noodle drinks up garlic instead of plain water.
  7. Reserve the starchy water
    Scoop out 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of pasta water before draining, using a heatproof mug or measuring cup dipped straight into the pot. In a dish that is essentially oil and water, this starch is the only thing that will hold the two together into a sauce instead of a slick. Reserve more than you think you need — the single most common mistake here is draining the pot and realizing the water is gone. Keep the cup hot right next to the stove so you are not adding cold liquid to a hot pan.
  8. Marry pasta and oil
    Return the skillet to medium heat, add the drained pasta along with 3/4 cup (180 ml) of the reserved water, and toss with tongs for 1-2 minutes. The liquid will bubble hard and start to thicken as the starch does its work. Keep the pasta moving so every strand passes through the oil.
  9. Emulsify and finish
    Toss vigorously, adding more pasta water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time until the sauce looks slightly cloudy and clings to the noodles rather than sliding to the bottom of the pan. Off the heat, stir in the parsley, the 1 tbsp (15 ml) lemon juice, and the Parmigiano if using. Taste and add a pinch more salt or chili.
  10. Serve right away
    Divide among four warmed bowls and finish each with a thin drizzle of the reserved 1 tbsp (15 ml) raw olive oil for aroma. This dish waits for no one — the emulsion tightens within a few minutes and the parsley loses its brightness. Eat it standing up in the kitchen if you have to.
Know when it is done
No internal temperature applies; the garlic is the gauge — pale straw gold and fragrant, pulled off the heat before it reaches brown. The oil should stay around 250-275°F (120-135°C), gently bubbling.
Serve it with
A cold glass of Falanghina or a light beer, with crusty bread to mop the garlicky oil from the bowl.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Use the best olive oil you own. With four ingredients, the oil is the flavor, and a peppery unfiltered extra-virgin makes a noticeable difference.
  • ◆For a version closer to what you get in Naples, toast 1/2 cup (25 g) panko in 1 tbsp oil until golden and scatter it over the top for crunch.
  • ◆Anchovies are not traditional but 3 fillets melted into the oil with the garlic add savory depth without tasting fishy.
  • ◆If your garlic browns too fast, your heat is too high. Medium-low is not a suggestion — the whole point is a slow infusion.

Tagliatelle with Ragu alla Bolognese⏱ 4 hr🍽 6 servingsAdvanced▾

The real thing from Emilia-Romagna: mostly meat, barely any tomato, finished with milk, and simmered for hours until it turns velvety and dark. It is a Sunday project that fills the apartment with the best smell there is.

Weekend ProjectSunday DinnerItalian
Prep
30 min
Cook
3 hr 30 min
Total
4 hr
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Soffritto

Meat

Liquids and seasoning

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Cut the soffritto very fine
    Dice the onion, carrot and celery into pieces no bigger than 1/8 in (3 mm) — smaller than feels necessary. Over three hours these vegetables should melt away completely and become invisible body in the sauce, not chunks you bite into. A food processor pulsed 8-10 times works, but drain off any liquid it releases so the soffritto can brown.
  2. Sweat the vegetables
    In a heavy 6-8 qt (6-8 L) Dutch oven, melt the 3 tbsp butter with the 2 tbsp olive oil over medium heat, then add the soffritto with a pinch of salt. Cook for 10-12 minutes, stirring often, until everything is soft and the onion is translucent and just starting to take on color at the edges. It should sigh and sizzle gently, never brown hard — you want sweetness, not roast.
  3. Render the pancetta
    Add the chopped pancetta and cook another 5 minutes until its fat has rendered out and the pieces are lightly golden. This is the savory backbone of the sauce and it needs its own moment before the ground meat arrives. The pan will look a little greasy and that is exactly right.
  4. Brown the meat in stages
    Raise the heat to medium-high and add the beef and pork in two batches, breaking each up with a wooden spoon and letting it sit undisturbed for 2-3 minutes before stirring. Season with the 1 1/2 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp pepper. Crowding all the meat in at once drops the pan temperature and it steams grey instead of browning, which costs you the deep flavor that makes this sauce taste like more than the sum of its parts.
  5. Deglaze with white wine
    Pour in the 1 cup (240 ml) white wine and scrape the bottom of the pot hard with a wooden spoon to lift every browned bit. Simmer for 4-6 minutes until the sharp alcohol smell is gone and the liquid has reduced by about half. White wine, not red, is traditional here — it keeps the sauce bright rather than heavy.
  6. Add the milk and let it disappear
    Pour in the 1 cup (240 ml) whole milk and lower the heat to medium. Simmer gently for 10-15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the milk is almost fully absorbed and the surface looks glossy. Milk tenderizes the meat proteins and rounds out the acidity of the wine and tomato — do not skip it, and do not panic if it looks curdled at first, because it smooths out as it cooks down.
  7. Build the tomato base
    Stir in the 3 tbsp tomato paste and cook for 2 minutes until it darkens from bright red to brick and smells sweet rather than tinny. Add the hand-crushed canned tomatoes with their juice, the 2 cups (480 ml) stock, and the nutmeg. Bolognese is a meat sauce with tomato in it, not a tomato sauce with meat — this restraint is what makes it taste different from what most people call bolognese.
  8. Simmer low for three hours
    Bring the pot to a bare simmer, then drop the heat as low as it will go, leaving the lid slightly ajar. You want one lazy bubble breaking the surface every couple of seconds, roughly 195°F (91°C). Cook for 2 1/2 to 3 hours, stirring every 20-30 minutes and adding 1/2 cup (120 ml) of stock or water any time the surface looks dry.
  9. Know when it is done
    The ragu is ready when the fat has separated into orange pools at the edges, the color has gone from red to a deep russet brown, and a spoon dragged across the bottom leaves a track that fills in slowly. The meat should feel soft enough to crush against the roof of your mouth. Taste and adjust salt now, because a long-simmered sauce needs more than you would expect.
  10. Boil the tagliatelle
    Bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt. Fresh tagliatelle needs only 2-3 minutes and floats when it is close; dried needs 1 minute less than the package time. Reserve 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of pasta water before you drain.
  11. Finish the pasta in the sauce
    Ladle about 3 cups (700 ml) of ragu into a wide skillet over medium heat, add the drained pasta and 1/2 cup (120 ml) pasta water, and toss for 1-2 minutes so the noodles absorb the sauce instead of wearing it. Kill the heat, add the 2 tbsp cold butter and the grated Parmigiano, and toss until glossy. Add more pasta water a splash at a time if it looks tight.
  12. Serve and stash the rest
    Serve in warm bowls with extra Parmigiano and no basil, no garlic bread, no fuss. You will have 2-3 cups of ragu left over, which is the whole point. It keeps 4 days in the fridge and 3 months frozen, and it is even better on day two.
Know when it is done
Ground beef and pork are safe at 160°F (71°C); a proper ragu holds near 195°F (91°C) for hours, so you are cooking well past safety and purely for texture.
Serve it with
A bottle of Sangiovese or Lambrusco, and a plain arugula salad with lemon and olive oil afterward.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make the ragu a day ahead. Overnight in the fridge the flavors settle and deepen, and you can lift off any excess fat from the top before reheating.
  • ◆Tagliatelle exists because flat, porous egg noodles hold a meat sauce. Spaghetti is genuinely the wrong shape here — it sheds the ragu into the bottom of the bowl.
  • ◆If the sauce tastes sharp or thin at the two-hour mark, it needs more time, not more salt. Long simmering is what converts acidity into sweetness.
  • ◆Freeze leftovers flat in 2-cup portions in zip bags. They thaw in 20 minutes in a bowl of warm water and turn a Tuesday into something good.
  • ◆No white wine? Use dry vermouth, or skip it and add 1 extra cup of stock plus 1 tsp red wine vinegar at the end for lift.

Fettuccine Alfredo from Scratch⏱ 25 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

The original Roman version: butter, real Parmigiano, and pasta water beaten into a sauce so rich it seems like there must be cream in it. There isn't, and that is exactly why it tastes so clean.

Date Night30 MinutesVegetarian
Prep
10 min
Cook
15 min
Total
25 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Bring the butter and cheese to room temperature
    Set the 6 tbsp (85 g) butter on the counter for 30 minutes and grate the Parmigiano just before cooking. Cold butter and cold cheese hitting hot pasta is the fastest route to a broken, greasy sauce. The butter should dent easily when you press it but still hold its shape.
  2. Grate the cheese to a powder
    Use a rasp grater, not the box grater's shredding holes — you want the Parmigiano to look like fine snow. Powdered cheese dissolves into the water and butter almost instantly, while shreds clump and string. This single detail is the difference between silk and glue.
  3. Warm the serving bowl
    Fill a large, wide serving bowl with hot tap water and let it sit while the pasta water heats, then dump it out and dry the bowl right before you use it. Traditional Alfredo is tossed in a warm bowl, not a hot pan, because direct flame is what causes the cheese to split. A warm bowl keeps everything fluid without cooking it.
  4. Salt the water lightly
    Bring 4 qt (3.8 L) of water to a boil and add just 1 tbsp (18 g) fine sea salt — less than usual, because 5 oz of Parmigiano brings plenty of salt. Give the water a taste; it should be mildly seasoned, not aggressive. Over-salting here makes the finished dish taste harsh.
  5. Cook the fettuccine
    Add the pasta and stir for the first 30 seconds so the strands do not fuse. Fresh fettuccine takes 2-3 minutes and is done when it floats and the edges look tender; dried takes about 1 minute less than the package time. It should still be firm because the tossing at the end finishes it.
  6. Reserve plenty of water
    Scoop out 2 cups (480 ml) of the starchy cooking water before draining. This sauce is built almost entirely on that water, so having too much is far better than running short. The water should look cloudy — if it looks clear, your ratio of water to pasta was too high.
  7. Start the emulsion in the bowl
    Put the softened butter in the warmed bowl with 1/2 cup (120 ml) of hot pasta water and whisk until the butter melts into a cloudy, unified liquid. You are building a butter-and-water emulsion first, before any cheese enters the picture. If it looks like melted butter floating on water, keep whisking — it will come together.
  8. Add the pasta hot
    Lift the fettuccine straight from the pot into the bowl with tongs, dripping wet, and toss immediately so every strand is coated in the buttery liquid. Work fast and keep the pasta moving; this is where the noodle's own surface starch joins the party. Add a splash more pasta water if it starts looking dry.
  9. Fold in the cheese in stages
    Add the Parmigiano in three handfuls, tossing hard with tongs after each one and adding 2-3 tbsp (30-45 ml) of pasta water between additions. Doing it gradually keeps the cheese suspended instead of dropping into a lump. After the last handful the sauce should turn pale ivory and start visibly clinging to the strands.
  10. Beat it until glossy
    Toss and lift the pasta for a full 60-90 seconds, which feels like a long time but is what whips the sauce into that famous glossy cream. Add pasta water 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time until the sauce ribbons off a strand rather than clinging in clumps. Season with the pepper and nutmeg if using, then serve immediately — Alfredo waits about four minutes before it stiffens.
Know when it is done
There is no internal temperature — the cue is visual. Keep the mixture below about 175°F (79°C) so the Parmigiano stays emulsified, and stop when the sauce coats a strand in a glossy, unbroken sheet.
Serve it with
A crisp Pinot Grigio or Chardonnay and a bitter salad of radicchio and endive to cut through all that butter.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Use real Parmigiano-Reggiano with the pin-dot lettering on the rind. Pre-grated cheese is coated with cellulose to prevent caking and it will refuse to emulsify.
  • ◆If the sauce breaks and turns oily, take it off any heat, add 1/4 cup (60 ml) hot pasta water, and beat hard with a whisk — most breaks come back.
  • ◆For an American-style Alfredo, warm 1 cup (240 ml) heavy cream with the butter and reduce by a third before adding cheese. It is far more forgiving and holds better for leftovers.
  • ◆Grilled chicken or seared shrimp turn this into a full meal; cook them separately and lay them on top so their juices do not thin the sauce.
  • ◆Never make Alfredo ahead. The emulsion is temporary by design and reheated Alfredo separates into butter and grit.

Baked Ziti with Sausage and Ricotta⏱ 1 hr 55 min (includes 15 min rest)🍽 8 servingsEasy▾

Layers of tubey pasta, quick sausage tomato sauce, dollops of ricotta and a lid of browned mozzarella. It is the easiest big-pan dinner in the book and it feeds a crowd or a whole week of lunches.

Family DinnerMake AheadComfort Food
Prep

Total
1 hr 55 min (includes 15 min rest)
Serves
8 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Sauce

Cheese and pasta

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Heat the oven and pan
    Set an oven rack in the upper third and heat the oven to 375°F (190°C), giving it a full 15 minutes to come up to temperature before anything goes in. Lightly oil a 9x13 in (23x33 cm) baking dish, getting into the corners so the edges release cleanly later. Putting the rack high means the cheese on top browns properly instead of just melting into a pale blanket, because the heating element radiates down onto it. Start the oven now and it will be ready by the time the sauce has simmered.
  2. Brown the sausage hard
    Heat the 2 tbsp olive oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high, add the sausage, and press it into a flat layer. Let it sit untouched for 4-5 minutes so a deep brown crust forms, then break it into rough 1/2 in (1 cm) chunks and cook 3 minutes more. Those browned bits are the difference between a sauce that tastes like tomatoes and one that tastes like dinner.
  3. Soften the aromatics
    Lower the heat to medium and add the chopped onion with a pinch of salt, cooking 5-6 minutes until soft and translucent. Stir in the garlic, oregano, and red pepper flakes and cook just 45 seconds, until the garlic smells sweet. Garlic burns in about a minute at this temperature, so keep it moving.
  4. Simmer the sauce
    Pour in the crushed tomatoes and tomato sauce, add the 1 1/2 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp pepper, and bring to a gentle bubble. Simmer uncovered for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens enough that a spoon leaves a brief trail. Stir in the torn basil at the very end so it stays fresh and green.
  5. Boil the pasta very short
    While the sauce simmers, bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt and cook the ziti for only 6-7 minutes — a full 3 minutes less than the package time. It will feel unpleasantly firm and that is correct. The pasta absorbs sauce and finishes cooking in the oven, and fully cooked pasta going into a baking dish comes out mushy every single time.
  6. Save pasta water and drain
    Reserve 1 cup (240 ml) of the starchy water before draining, then drain the ziti and immediately toss it with about 1 cup (240 ml) of the sauce so it does not stick together. That coating of sauce also seals the surface starch so the noodles stay distinct. Do not rinse the pasta — you would wash away the starch that helps everything bind.
  7. Mix the ricotta filling
    In a bowl, stir the 15 oz (425 g) ricotta with the egg, two-thirds of the grated Parmigiano and the parsley, then season with the 1/2 tsp kosher salt and 1/4 tsp black pepper reserved for the filling. Mix until it is smooth and uniform, but stop there — overworking ricotta thins it out. The egg is what sets the filling into creamy pockets instead of letting it go grainy and watery in the oven, so do not leave it out. If your ricotta looks wet or has whey pooled on top, drain it in a sieve for 10 minutes first.
  8. Combine pasta and sauce
    Add the remaining sauce and about 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the reserved pasta water to the pasta and fold until every tube is coated inside and out. It should look a little looser than you think it needs to be, since the pasta will keep drinking liquid in the oven. Fold in half the shredded mozzarella.
  9. Layer the dish
    Spread half the pasta in the baking dish, dollop the ricotta mixture over it in tablespoon-sized spoonfuls, then top with the remaining pasta. Dollops beat a smooth layer here because you get distinct creamy pockets rather than one dense stratum. Press the top down lightly so everything settles.
  10. Top and bake covered
    Scatter the remaining mozzarella and Parmigiano over the top, cover tightly with foil, and bake for 25 minutes. Covering traps steam so the pasta hydrates fully and the middle heats through before the top sets. Tent the foil slightly so it does not stick to the cheese.
  11. Uncover and brown
    Remove the foil and bake another 15-20 minutes until the cheese is bubbling across the whole surface with brown freckles at the edges and the center reaches 165°F (74°C) on an instant-read thermometer. If it is hot but pale, run it under the broiler for 2 minutes, watching constantly. Broilers go from golden to burnt in about 45 seconds.
  12. Rest before serving
    Let the dish sit on the counter for 10-15 minutes before cutting. The molten cheese and sauce need that time to set enough to hold a square shape on the plate. Cut into 8 pieces with a sharp knife and serve with extra Parmigiano.
Know when it is done
Bake until the center registers 165°F (74°C) on an instant-read thermometer and the sauce is bubbling at the edges; cooked sausage is safe at 160°F (71°C).
Serve it with
A simple Chianti and a Caesar or a big garlicky green salad — this dish needs something sharp beside it.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Assemble it up to 2 days ahead, cover, and refrigerate unbaked. Add 15 minutes to the covered bake time and start it straight from cold.
  • ◆To freeze, assemble in a foil pan, wrap in plastic then foil, and freeze up to 3 months. Bake from frozen at 375°F (190°C) covered for 75 minutes, then uncovered for 20.
  • ◆Shred your own mozzarella from a block. Pre-shredded is coated in starch and bakes up rubbery and oily.
  • ◆Ziti, penne rigate and rigatoni all work because their ridges and hollows trap sauce; smooth penne lisce slides right out of it.
  • ◆For a vegetarian version, swap the sausage for 1 lb (450 g) of cremini mushrooms browned hard in two batches, plus 1 tsp fennel seed for that sausage note.

Lasagna alla Bolognese⏱ 6 hr (includes 30 min rest)🍽 8 servingsAdvanced▾

The northern Italian original — slow ragu, silky bechamel, thin sheets of pasta, and Parmigiano instead of a pound of mozzarella. It takes an afternoon, and it is the single most impressive thing you can put on a table.

Weekend ProjectSpecial OccasionMake Ahead
Prep
45 min
Cook
4 hr 45 min
Total
6 hr (includes 30 min rest)
Serves
8 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Ragu

Besciamella

Assembly

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Start the ragu
    Melt the 3 tbsp butter with the 2 tbsp olive oil in a heavy 6 qt (6 L) Dutch oven over medium heat and cook the finely diced onion, carrot and celery for 10-12 minutes until soft and barely golden. Add the pancetta and cook 5 minutes more until its fat renders and the bits turn light gold. Take your time here; this base carries the whole dish.
  2. Brown the meat in batches
    Raise the heat to medium-high and add half the beef and pork, spreading it flat and letting it sit for 3 minutes before breaking it up. Repeat with the second batch and season with the 2 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp pepper. If you dump all 1 1/2 lb in at once the pot floods with liquid and the meat boils grey instead of browning.
  3. Wine, then milk, then tomato
    Add the 1 cup (240 ml) white wine and scrape the bottom clean, simmering 5 minutes until the raw alcohol smell disappears. Stir in the 1 cup (240 ml) milk and cook 12-15 minutes until it is nearly absorbed and the surface looks glossy. Then add the tomato paste, cook it 2 minutes until brick-colored, and add the crushed tomatoes and 2 cups (480 ml) stock.
  4. Simmer for three hours
    Drop the heat to the lowest setting, set the lid ajar, and let the ragu simmer at about 195°F (91°C) for 2 1/2 to 3 hours. Stir every half hour and add 1/2 cup (120 ml) water whenever it looks dry. It is finished when the color is deep russet, the fat has separated into orange pools, and the meat crushes easily against the side of the pot.
  5. Make the besciamella
    Melt the 4 tbsp (57 g) butter in a 3 qt (3 L) saucepan over medium heat, whisk in the 1/2 cup (60 g) flour, and cook 2 minutes until it smells faintly like toasted popcorn but is still pale. Equal weights of butter and flour is the ratio that actually sets — a besciamella built on less flour stays runny and your layers will slide apart when you cut the lasagna. Pour in the warm milk in three additions, whisking hard after each until completely smooth before the next goes in. Bring it to a bare simmer and cook 6-8 minutes until it thickly coats the back of a spoon, then season with the salt, nutmeg and white pepper.
  6. Keep the sauce from skinning
    Press a piece of plastic wrap directly onto the surface of the besciamella, touching the sauce all over. A skin forms within minutes on exposed hot dairy and it turns into rubbery flecks in the finished lasagna. It should be the consistency of thin pancake batter, loose enough to spread with the back of a spoon.
  7. Blanch the pasta sheets
    Bring 6 qt (5.7 L) of water to a boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt and set a bowl of ice water beside it. Boil fresh sheets 45-60 seconds or dried sheets 4 minutes, then transfer them to the ice water for 30 seconds and lay them flat on clean kitchen towels. Under-cooking here is deliberate; the sheets finish in the oven and over-boiled pasta tears the moment you touch it.
  8. Heat the oven and prep the pan
    Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C) with a rack in the middle and grease a 9x13 in (23x33 cm) baking dish with the 1 tbsp softened butter, working it up the sides as well as across the base. Spread a thin layer of besciamella over that, about 1/2 cup (120 ml), just enough to film the bottom. That slick of fat and sauce keeps the first pasta layer from gluing itself to the dish, which is what tears the bottom sheet when you try to serve. Do this before you start layering, because once your hands are covered in ragu you will not want to stop.
  9. Layer it properly
    Build six layers in this order every time: pasta, about 3/4 cup (180 ml) ragu spread thin, about 1/2 cup (120 ml) besciamella, then a generous scatter of Parmigiano. Trim the sheets to fit rather than overlapping them much, since doubled-up pasta stays gummy. Traditional bolognese lasagna is thin-layered and restrained, not overstuffed.
  10. Finish the top
    End with a layer of pasta, the last of the besciamella spread all the way to the corners, a heavy shower of Parmigiano, and the 2 tbsp of butter bits dotted over the surface. Those butter dots are what give the top its blistered golden lace. Make sure no pasta is left exposed or it will dry into shards.
  11. Bake covered, then uncovered
    Cover with foil tented so it does not touch the cheese and bake for 30 minutes, then remove the foil and bake 20-25 minutes more. It is ready when the top is deeply golden with crisp brown edges and the center reads 165°F (74°C) on an instant-read thermometer. You should see the sauce bubbling slowly around the perimeter.
  12. Rest a full thirty minutes
    Move the lasagna to a rack and leave it alone for 30 minutes — this is not optional. Straight out of the oven the layers are liquid and a slice will slump into a puddle, while a rested lasagna cuts into clean squares that hold their stripes. It will still be hot at the center after half an hour.
Know when it is done
Bake until the center hits 165°F (74°C); the ground meat in the ragu passed its 160°F (71°C) safe point hours earlier during the simmer.
Serve it with
A structured Sangiovese such as Chianti Classico, and only a bitter green salad afterward — nothing else can compete.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Split the work over two days: ragu and besciamella on Saturday, assemble and bake on Sunday. The ragu is genuinely better after a night in the fridge.
  • ◆Fresh spinach lasagna sheets are what they use in Bologna and they are worth buying if your grocery store carries them. Skip the no-boil sheets, which stay chalky under a thin-layered lasagna.
  • ◆If your besciamella goes lumpy, blitz it with an immersion blender for 15 seconds and it will come back perfectly smooth.
  • ◆No mozzarella belongs in a real lasagna bolognese. The stretchy cheese pull is an American addition and it makes the layers heavy and greasy.
  • ◆Baked and cooled lasagna cuts even more neatly cold. Refrigerate overnight, cut into squares, and reheat individual portions at 350°F (175°C) for 20 minutes.

Shrimp Scampi Linguine⏱ 30 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Garlic, white wine, butter and lemon reduced into a glossy pan sauce with plump shrimp folded through. It comes together faster than the pasta boils, which makes it the best last-minute impressive dinner there is.

Date Night30 MinutesSeafood
Prep
15 min
Cook
15 min
Total
30 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Dry and season the shrimp
    Pat the shrimp completely dry with paper towels and toss with 1 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp black pepper. Wet shrimp steam in the pan and turn out pale and rubbery instead of picking up color. Leave them on the counter while you get the water going so they lose their refrigerator chill.
  2. Start the pasta water
    Bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a rolling boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt. Time it so the pasta goes in right when you start cooking the shrimp — the whole dish takes about 12 minutes from that point. Have your reserved-water mug and a colander ready.
  3. Sear the shrimp fast
    Heat the 3 tbsp olive oil in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium-high until it shimmers, then lay the shrimp in a single layer without crowding, working in two batches if needed. Cook 60-75 seconds per side, just until the outsides turn opaque pink with a little browning and the centers are still slightly translucent. They will finish in the sauce, and shrimp go from tender to rubber in about 30 seconds of overcooking.
  4. Get the shrimp out
    Transfer the shrimp to a plate immediately — do not leave them in a hot pan while you do anything else. Residual pan heat keeps cooking them, and this pause is the main thing separating a good scampi from a chewy one. Pour any juices that collect on the plate back into the sauce later.
  5. Drop the pasta
    Add the linguine to the boiling water now and stir for the first 30 seconds. Cook it 2 minutes less than the package time, usually about 8 minutes, so it is firmly chewy. It will finish in the pan sauce, which is where it picks up all that garlic and wine.
  6. Soften the garlic gently
    Lower the skillet heat to medium, add the sliced garlic and 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes to the oil left in the pan, and cook 60-90 seconds, stirring constantly. Stop the moment the garlic turns pale gold and smells sweet. If the pan is still ripping hot from searing, pull it off the burner for 20 seconds first — garlic goes from fragrant to bitter faster than anything else in a kitchen.
  7. Reduce the wine
    Pour in the 3/4 cup (180 ml) white wine and scrape up any browned bits stuck to the pan. Simmer briskly for 3-4 minutes until the liquid has reduced by about half and the sharp alcohol edge is gone. What is left should smell rounded and slightly sweet, and coat the bottom of the pan in a shallow layer.
  8. Reserve the pasta water
    Scoop out 1 cup (240 ml) of the starchy pasta water before draining, dipping a heatproof mug straight into the pot. This is what will bind the butter into the wine so the sauce clings to the linguine instead of pooling at the bottom of the bowl. Starch molecules coat the fat droplets and hold them suspended in the liquid, which is the same trick behind every pan sauce in this chapter. Keep the mug hot right beside the pan, because cold water dropped into a butter sauce will break it.
  9. Mount the butter
    Turn the heat to low, add 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the pasta water, then drop in the cold butter one piece at a time, swirling the pan constantly so each piece melts before the next goes in. This gradual, low-heat swirl is what emulsifies butter into a creamy sauce rather than letting it separate into oil. Stir in the 3 tbsp lemon juice and the zest.
  10. Finish the pasta in the sauce
    Add the drained linguine directly to the skillet and toss with tongs over low heat for 1-2 minutes, adding pasta water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time until the sauce clings to the noodles. The pasta will absorb some of the liquid and thicken the whole thing as it does. Taste for salt and lemon now, before the shrimp go back in.
  11. Return the shrimp and serve
    Fold the shrimp and any collected juices back into the pan and toss for 30-45 seconds, just until they are heated through and opaque all the way to the center, 145°F (63°C). Kill the heat, add the parsley, and toss once more. Serve immediately in warm bowls with the lemon wedges alongside.
Know when it is done
Shrimp are done at 145°F (63°C) — opaque, pink, and curled into a loose C. A tight O shape means they are overcooked.
Serve it with
The rest of the white wine you cooked with, and grilled bread rubbed with a raw garlic clove.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Buy shrimp with the shells on if you can and simmer the shells in the wine for 5 minutes before straining — it doubles the depth of the sauce for almost no work.
  • ◆Do not substitute cooking wine. Use something you would actually drink, because the wine reduces down and its flaws concentrate along with its virtues.
  • ◆Cold butter added off high heat is the whole trick to a mounted butter sauce. Melted butter poured in will split into a greasy slick.
  • ◆Frozen shrimp are usually better than the thawed ones at the counter. Thaw them in a bowl of cold water for 15 minutes and dry them very well.
  • ◆This does not hold. Have everyone at the table before the shrimp go back in the pan.

Penne alla Vodka⏱ 45 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Tomato paste cooked down until it is sweet and brick-dark, loosened with vodka and cream into a blush sauce that clings to every ridge. The vodka is not for show — it pulls out flavors in the tomato that water and fat cannot reach.

WeeknightComfort FoodVegetarian
Prep
10 min
Cook
35 min
Total
45 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Sauce

Pasta and finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Soften the onion
    Heat the 2 tbsp olive oil and 2 tbsp butter in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet or wide saucepan over medium heat until the butter foams. Add the chopped onion with a pinch of salt and cook 6-8 minutes, stirring often, until it is completely soft and translucent with no crunch left. Onion that is still firm here stays firm in the finished sauce.
  2. Add garlic and chili
    Stir in the minced garlic and 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes and cook 45-60 seconds until fragrant. Keep it moving with a wooden spoon, because minced garlic has far more surface area than sliced and can go from raw to scorched in under a minute at this heat. The flakes need those few seconds in hot fat to release their color and warmth into the oil rather than sitting as dry specks in the finished sauce. The pan should smell sweet and sharp, not toasted — if you see any brown edges on the garlic, pull the pan off the burner and move straight to the tomato paste.
  3. Cook the tomato paste properly
    Add the 1/3 cup (90 g) tomato paste and stir it around the pan for 4-5 minutes over medium heat, spreading it thin against the bottom. It should darken from bright red to a deep brick color and start to stick and caramelize in patches. This step converts the raw, metallic taste of canned paste into something roasted and sweet, and it is the single biggest flavor step in the recipe.
  4. Deglaze with vodka
    Pour in the 1/3 cup (80 ml) vodka and stir hard, scraping the caramelized paste off the bottom of the pan. Let it bubble for 2-3 minutes until the harsh alcohol smell has burned off and the mixture has thickened back into a paste. Ethanol dissolves aroma compounds that are not water-soluble, which is exactly why this sauce tastes different from a plain tomato cream sauce.
  5. Add the tomatoes and simmer
    Stir in the crushed tomatoes, the 1 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp pepper, and bring to a gentle bubble. Simmer for 12-15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce has thickened and darkened and a spoon dragged through leaves a track. If it spits at you, lower the heat and set a lid ajar.
  6. Start the pasta
    While the sauce simmers, bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt and add the penne. Cook it 2 minutes shy of the package time — about 9 minutes for most brands — so it is firmly al dente. The ridges on penne rigate exist to grip this sauce, so use them if you can find them.
  7. Temper in the cream
    Lower the sauce to the barest simmer and stir in the 3/4 cup (180 ml) room-temperature heavy cream in a slow stream. Room-temperature cream blends smoothly, while cold cream poured into a hot acidic tomato sauce can curdle into little flecks. The sauce will turn a warm salmon pink almost instantly.
  8. Let the sauce come together
    Cook the sauce for 3-4 minutes more, barely bubbling, so the cream and tomato marry into one color and thicken slightly. Do not boil it hard once the cream is in, since a rolling boil can break dairy in an acidic sauce. Taste and adjust salt — vodka sauce usually wants more than you expect.
  9. Reserve water and drain
    Scoop out 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of pasta water, then drain the penne in a colander. Do not rinse it under the tap, however tempting — the starch on the surface is exactly what helps the sauce grip the ridges instead of sliding off into a puddle. Move fast and give the colander a shake, because penne left standing in a heap fuses together within a couple of minutes. Keep the reserved water hot next to the stove so you are always adding warm liquid to a warm pan.
  10. Finish the pasta in the sauce
    Add the drained penne to the skillet with 1/2 cup (120 ml) of pasta water and toss over medium heat for 2 minutes so the pasta absorbs sauce and the sauce tightens around it. Add more water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time until it looks glossy and slightly loose, since it will thicken as it sits. Off the heat, stir in the Parmigiano and torn basil, then serve immediately with more cheese on top.
Know when it is done
No internal temperature applies; keep the sauce at a bare simmer around 185°F (85°C) once the cream is in, and stop when a spoon dragged through the pan leaves a track that fills in slowly.
Serve it with
A chilled Rosato or a light Barbera, with garlic bread for the sauce left in the bowl.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Use a cheap vodka — this is one place where the expensive bottle is wasted, because you are boiling off the alcohol anyway.
  • ◆The sauce alone freezes beautifully for 3 months. Freeze it before adding the cream, then stir the cream in when you reheat.
  • ◆For the viral spicy pink sauce version, add 2 tbsp (30 g) of Calabrian chili paste with the tomato paste.
  • ◆If the sauce ever looks broken or oily, take it off the heat and whisk in 2 tbsp (30 ml) of hot pasta water — the starch pulls it back together.
  • ◆Adding 4 oz (115 g) of chopped pancetta rendered at the start turns this into a heartier weekend version worth knowing.

Pesto alla Genovese with Trofie⏱ 35 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Raw basil, pine nuts, garlic and two cheeses pounded into a bright green sauce that never sees a stove. In Liguria they cook potatoes and green beans right in the pasta water and toss it all together, and it makes the whole thing a meal.

SummerVegetarian30 Minutes
Prep
20 min
Cook
15 min
Total
35 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Pesto

Pasta and vegetables

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Wash and dry the basil gently
    Rinse the basil in cold water and dry it completely in a salad spinner or between towels, handling the leaves as little as possible. Bruised basil oxidizes and turns dark within minutes, and stray water droplets will make the pesto separate. Use only leaves — the stems are fibrous and bitter.
  2. Toast the pine nuts
    Put the 1/3 cup (45 g) pine nuts in a dry skillet over medium-low heat and shake constantly for 3-4 minutes until they are speckled gold and smell like popcorn. Tip them onto a plate immediately, because pine nuts carry enough oil to keep browning and burn in the residual heat of the pan. Let them cool completely before they go into the pesto.
  3. Start with garlic and salt
    If using a mortar, pound the halved garlic cloves with the 1/2 tsp coarse salt into a smooth paste — the salt crystals act as an abrasive that shreds the garlic. If using a food processor, pulse the garlic and salt with the pine nuts 8-10 times until finely chopped. Removing the pale green germ from the center of each clove keeps the pesto from turning acrid as it sits.
  4. Add the nuts and basil
    Add the cooled pine nuts and work them into a paste, then add the basil in three handfuls. In a mortar, use a grinding, circular motion against the wall rather than pounding straight down; in a processor, pulse in short bursts and scrape the sides between them. Long continuous blending heats the basil and turns it bitter and army-green.
  5. Stream in the oil
    With the processor running on low, or while stirring the mortar, pour in the 2/3 cup (160 ml) olive oil in a thin steady stream until the pesto is a loose, spoonable paste. A gentle mild oil is traditional here — a fiercely peppery Tuscan oil will bully the basil. Stop as soon as it comes together.
  6. Fold in the cheeses by hand
    Transfer the pesto to a bowl and stir in the Parmigiano and Pecorino with a spoon rather than the machine. Blade-blended cheese gets pasty and can turn gluey. Taste and add salt only if needed, remembering the pasta water will bring more.
  7. Boil the potatoes first
    Bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt and add the cubed potatoes. Boil for 5 minutes; they need a head start because they take longer than the pasta. The starch they release also makes the water even better for building the sauce later.
  8. Add pasta and green beans
    Add the pasta and the green beans to the same pot with the potatoes. Cook until the pasta is 1 minute shy of the package time — trofie takes 7-8 minutes, dried linguine about 9. Everything finishes together, which is the whole elegance of the Ligurian method.
  9. Loosen the pesto with pasta water
    Scoop 1 cup (240 ml) of the starchy water and whisk about 1/3 cup (80 ml) of it into the bowl of pesto until it loosens into a pourable sauce. Doing this in the bowl, off the heat, prevents the cheese from seizing and the basil from cooking. The pesto should thin to about the consistency of heavy cream.
  10. Toss everything off the heat
    Drain the pasta and vegetables and add them to the pesto bowl, then toss hard for 30-45 seconds, adding more pasta water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time until everything is evenly coated and glossy. Never return pesto to a hot burner — heat dulls the green to olive and kills the raw perfume that makes it worth making. Serve immediately with extra Parmigiano.
Know when it is done
No cooking temperature applies to the sauce — pesto must stay raw. Toss it off the heat and keep it under about 140°F (60°C) or the basil darkens and the cheese goes grainy.
Serve it with
A cold Ligurian Vermentino or Pigato, and a plate of sliced ripe tomatoes with salt.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Freeze pesto in an ice cube tray without the cheese, then bag the cubes. Stir in the grated cheese after thawing and it tastes almost freshly made for up to 3 months.
  • ◆To keep leftover pesto green in the fridge, press it into a jar and pour a 1/4 in (6 mm) layer of olive oil over the top to block air. It keeps 5 days.
  • ◆Walnuts stand in for pine nuts at a fraction of the price and are traditional in parts of Liguria. Use 1/2 cup (55 g) and toast them the same way.
  • ◆Blanching the basil for 10 seconds and shocking it in ice water locks in a brilliant green forever, at the cost of a little fresh aroma. Good trick when you want it to look perfect.
  • ◆Trofie and trenette are the classic shapes because their twists and edges catch the pesto, but any short twisted pasta like fusilli or casarecce works well.

Linguine alle Vongole⏱ 1 hr 35 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Clams steamed open in white wine and garlic, their briny juice reduced into a sauce that tastes like the sea in the best way. Nothing but pasta water and starch binds it, and it comes together in the time it takes to boil linguine.

Date NightSeafoodItalian
Prep
1 hr 15 min (includes 1 hr clam purge)
Cook
20 min
Total
1 hr 35 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Purge the clams
    Dissolve the 1/3 cup (80 g) kosher salt in 4 qt (3.8 L) of cold water — roughly the salinity of seawater — and submerge the clams for 1 hour in the refrigerator. Water any fresher than this kills them instead of relaxing them, which is why plain tap water is the classic mistake. Salt water at the right strength tricks them into breathing normally and spitting out the sand trapped inside, and you will see grit on the bottom of the bowl afterward. Lift the clams out with your hands rather than pouring, so the sand stays behind.
  2. Sort out the dead ones
    Scrub the shells under cold running water and inspect each clam. Any that are cracked, or that stay wide open after you tap them firmly on the counter, are dead and must go in the trash. A live clam clamps shut within about 10 seconds of being tapped — this check is not optional with shellfish.
  3. Get everything ready
    Slice the garlic, chop the parsley, and set the wine, oil and a lid for your skillet within arm's reach. Once the clams start opening, the window between perfect and rubbery is about 90 seconds. This dish rewards a fully prepped counter more than almost anything else in the chapter.
  4. Boil the water
    Bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a rolling boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt. Salt a little lighter than usual because the clam liquor is genuinely salty and will season the finished sauce all on its own — over-salt here and there is no way to walk it back. Do not start the pasta yet; the clams and the linguine need to go in at the same moment so they finish together. Get the pot to a full boil and then just hold it there while you work on the clams.
  5. Infuse the oil
    Heat the 1/3 cup (80 ml) olive oil in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet with a lid over medium heat, add the sliced garlic and 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes, and cook 2 minutes until the garlic is pale gold at the edges. Adjust the heat so the garlic barely bubbles rather than fries. Burnt garlic here poisons the whole delicate flavor of the clams.
  6. Steam the clams open
    Add the clams and the 3/4 cup (180 ml) white wine, raise the heat to medium-high, and clamp the lid on. Steam for 5-8 minutes, shaking the pan once or twice, until most shells have opened. Lift each clam out with tongs the moment it opens rather than waiting for the last stubborn one — clams left in the pan for an extra 3 minutes turn into pencil erasers.
  7. Cook the linguine
    Drop the linguine into the boiling water as soon as the clams go in the skillet. Cook 2 minutes less than the package time, about 8 minutes, so it is stiffly al dente. It has two more minutes of cooking to do in the clam broth.
  8. Reduce and strain the broth
    Discard any clams that stayed shut after 8 minutes of steaming. If the broth looks sandy, pour it through a fine sieve lined with a paper towel and return it to the pan, then simmer 2-3 minutes to reduce it slightly and concentrate the flavor. You should have roughly 1 cup (240 ml) of intensely savory liquid.
  9. Shell some of the clams
    Pull the meat out of about half the clams and leave the rest in their shells for looks. This way every forkful actually gets clam meat instead of you chasing shells around the bowl. Keep the shelled meat with the reserved whole clams under a plate so they stay warm.
  10. Finish the pasta in the broth
    Reserve 1 cup (240 ml) of pasta water, drain the linguine, and add it straight to the skillet of broth over medium heat. Toss constantly for 2 minutes, adding pasta water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time, until the liquid turns slightly creamy and clings to the strands. That cloudiness is the starch emulsifying the oil and clam juice into a real sauce.
  11. Bring the clams back and serve
    Turn off the heat, add all the clams and their meat, the parsley, lemon juice and black pepper, and toss for 30 seconds just to warm them through. Finish with a thin drizzle of raw olive oil for aroma. Serve immediately with an empty bowl on the table for shells, and no cheese — cheese on clams is a genuine offense in Italy.
Know when it is done
Clams are done the instant their shells open, around 145°F (63°C) internally. Discard any that refuse to open after 8 minutes of steaming.
Serve it with
The same crisp Vermentino you cooked with, and grilled bread for the broth at the bottom of the bowl.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Buy clams the day you cook them and keep them in the fridge in an open bowl covered with a damp towel, never sealed in a plastic bag or sitting in fresh water, which suffocates them.
  • ◆Manila clams are smaller, sweeter and open faster; littlenecks are meatier. Either works, but do not mix sizes in one pan since they open at different rates.
  • ◆If your clams still taste gritty, next time purge them for a full 2 hours and change the salt water once halfway through.
  • ◆Canned clams are a reasonable pantry backup: use two 6.5 oz (184 g) cans with their juice, add them at the very end, and simmer just 1 minute.
  • ◆Vongole in bianco is the version here. For rosso, add 1 cup (150 g) of halved cherry tomatoes with the wine and cook them down until they collapse.

Baked Mac and Cheese with Bechamel⏱ 1 hr 20 min (includes 10 min rest)🍽 8 servingsMedium▾

A real flour-and-butter bechamel means this sauce stays creamy in the oven instead of turning oily and grainy. Sharp cheddar for flavor, Gruyere for melt, and a buttered panko lid that shatters when your fork goes in.

Comfort FoodFamily DinnerMake Ahead
Prep
20 min
Cook
50 min
Total
1 hr 20 min (includes 10 min rest)
Serves
8 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Pasta

Bechamel and cheese

Crumb topping

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Shred your own cheese
    Grate all 16 oz (455 g) of cheddar and Gruyere from blocks on the large holes of a box grater and let it sit at room temperature while you work. Bagged shredded cheese is dusted with potato starch and cellulose to stop clumping, and that same coating stops it from melting smoothly into a sauce. Room-temperature cheese also melts without shocking the bechamel.
  2. Heat the oven
    Set a rack in the upper third of the oven and heat it to 375°F (190°C). Butter a 9x13 in (23x33 cm) baking dish or a 3 qt (3 L) casserole. The high rack position puts the crumb topping close to the heat so it browns while the inside stays creamy.
  3. Undercook the macaroni
    Boil 5 qt (4.7 L) of water with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt and cook the pasta for only 5-6 minutes, roughly 3 minutes shy of the package time. It should still be chalky in the center. It will absorb sauce and finish cooking in the oven, and fully cooked pasta here turns to mush.
  4. Drain but do not rinse
    Drain the pasta and toss it with 1 tbsp (14 g) of butter so it does not fuse into a block while you make the sauce. Skip rinsing — the starch clinging to the surface helps the cheese sauce grab hold. Spread it out in the colander so it stops cooking.
  5. Make the roux
    Melt the 5 tbsp (70 g) butter in a large saucepan over medium heat, then whisk in the 1/3 cup (42 g) flour and cook for 2 minutes, whisking constantly. It should bubble like wet sand and smell faintly nutty, but stay pale blond — this is a white roux and browning it would cost you thickening power. Two minutes is the minimum to cook out the raw flour taste.
  6. Build the bechamel
    Pour in the warm milk in three additions, whisking hard after each one until completely smooth before adding the next. Adding it all at once is how you get lumps, and warm milk incorporates far more easily than cold. Once all the milk is in, the mixture will look alarmingly thin, which is normal.
  7. Cook it to nappe
    Bring the sauce to a bare simmer over medium heat, whisking often, and cook 6-8 minutes until it thickly coats the back of a spoon and holds a clean line when you draw a finger through it. It should read about 185°F (85°C). Stir in the salt, mustard powder, onion powder, nutmeg and cayenne now, while it is still just sauce.
  8. Melt in the cheese off the heat
    Take the pan completely off the burner and wait 1 minute, then add the cheddar and Gruyere in four handfuls, whisking each one in fully before the next. Direct heat above roughly 175°F (79°C) makes cheese proteins tighten and squeeze out fat, which is exactly what a grainy, greasy mac and cheese looks like. Reserve 4 oz (115 g) of the cheddar for the top if you want extra pull.
  9. Combine and taste
    Fold the drained macaroni into the cheese sauce until every piece is coated. The mixture should look almost soupy — noticeably looser than you want the final dish — because the pasta will drink up a lot of it in the oven. Taste for salt now, since the topping will not fix an underseasoned base.
  10. Make the crumb topping
    Toss the 1 1/2 cups (75 g) panko with the 3 tbsp melted butter, the grated Parmigiano and the paprika until every crumb is lightly slicked. Buttered crumbs brown evenly and stay crisp; dry crumbs scorch in patches and taste like sawdust. Scatter them over the top in an even layer.
  11. Bake until bubbling and gold
    Bake for 25-30 minutes, until the topping is deep golden and the sauce is bubbling up around the edges and the center reads 165°F (74°C). If the crumbs brown before the center is hot, tent loosely with foil. Let it rest 10 minutes so the sauce sets enough to serve in scoops.
Know when it is done
Melt the cheese off the heat below about 175°F (79°C) so it does not break, and bake until the center of the dish reaches 165°F (74°C).
Serve it with
A cold hard cider or a hoppy pale ale, with something sharp on the side like quick-pickled onions or a vinegary slaw.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Never let cheese sauce boil after the cheese is in. If it looks broken, whisk in 2 tbsp (30 ml) of warm milk off the heat and it will usually come back together.
  • ◆Cheese blend matters more than any single cheese: sharp cheddar brings the flavor but melts stringy, while Gruyere, fontina, or young Gouda bring the silk. Aim for roughly 3 parts flavor cheese to 1 part melter.
  • ◆Assemble it up to 24 hours ahead without the crumbs, refrigerate, then add the topping and bake from cold for 40-45 minutes covered plus 15 uncovered.
  • ◆For a stovetop version, stop after folding the pasta into the sauce and serve immediately — it is looser, faster, and honestly just as good.
  • ◆A teaspoon of mustard powder is not there to taste like mustard. The acid sharpens the cheese and keeps the sauce from tasting flat and heavy.

Stuffed Shells with Ricotta and Spinach⏱ 1 hr 40 min (includes 10 min rest)🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Big pasta shells filled with herby ricotta and spinach, nestled into marinara and baked until the tops go golden. It is fussy in the nicest way, and it is the kind of thing you can build ahead and slide into the oven when people arrive.

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Shells and sauce

Ricotta filling

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Drain the ricotta
    If your ricotta looks wet or has liquid pooled on top, spoon it into a fine sieve set over a bowl and let it drain for 20 minutes. Excess whey turns the filling loose and it will weep out into the sauce during baking, leaving you with watery shells. Good drained ricotta should mound on a spoon and hold its shape.
  2. Squeeze the spinach bone dry
    Wrap the thawed spinach in a clean kitchen towel and wring it out over the sink with real force. You should get about 1/2 cup (120 ml) of green water out of a 10 oz package, and the spinach should end up as a dense, dry puck. Any water you leave behind ends up in the filling.
  3. Heat the oven
    Set a rack in the middle of the oven and heat it to 375°F (190°C). Spread the 1 tbsp olive oil and 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of the marinara across the bottom of a 9x13 in (23x33 cm) baking dish. That layer of sauce keeps the shells from sticking and gently steams them from below.
  4. Boil the shells carefully
    Bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt and add the shells, stirring gently so they do not nest inside each other. Cook 3 minutes less than the package time — usually about 8 minutes — so they are pliable but still firm. Overcooked shells tear the second you try to fill them.
  5. Cool the shells flat
    Drain the shells and lay them in a single layer on a lightly oiled sheet pan, open side up, and let them cool for 5-10 minutes until you can handle them. Piling them in a colander glues them together and you will rip half of them apart. Discard any that split during boiling — that is why you cooked extra.
  6. Mix the filling
    In a large bowl, stir the drained ricotta with the squeezed spinach, the beaten egg, three-quarters of the Parmigiano, half the mozzarella, the basil, parsley, garlic, 1 1/4 tsp salt, pepper and nutmeg. Mix until uniform but do not overwork it. The egg binds the filling so it sets into creamy pockets instead of running out into the sauce.
  7. Taste and adjust
    Taste the filling now — it is safe apart from the raw egg, so take a small spoonful and check the seasoning. Ricotta is bland and soaks up salt, so it usually needs more than seems right. It should taste slightly over-seasoned on its own, since the pasta and sauce will mute it.
  8. Fill the shells
    Spoon the filling into a zip-top bag, snip 3/4 in (2 cm) off one corner, and pipe about 3 tbsp (45 g) into each shell. That is the amount that fills a jumbo shell to the rim without bulging, and it works out so that 24 shells use the bowl of filling almost exactly — if you are running ahead or behind, adjust on the next few. A bag is dramatically faster and neater than a spoon, and it packs the filling in without splitting the pasta. Do not overstuff, or the filling pushes out and scorches on the pan as it heats and expands.
  9. Nestle them in the sauce
    Arrange the filled shells open side up in the sauced dish in neat rows, packed snugly against each other so they support one another. Twenty-four shells fit a 9x13 in dish almost exactly. Spoon the remaining 2 1/2 cups (600 ml) of marinara over and between them, leaving the very tops of the filling exposed.
  10. Top and bake covered
    Scatter the remaining mozzarella and Parmigiano over the top, then cover the dish tightly with foil, tenting it so it does not touch the cheese. Bake for 30 minutes covered — the trapped steam finishes cooking the pasta and heats the filling through without drying the exposed edges. You should hear it bubbling when you pull it out.
  11. Uncover and brown
    Remove the foil and bake another 15-20 minutes, until the cheese is melted with golden brown spots and the center of a middle shell reads 165°F (74°C) on an instant-read thermometer. That temperature also confirms the egg in the filling is fully cooked. If it is hot but pale, broil for 90 seconds while watching it constantly.
  12. Rest and serve
    Let the dish sit for 10 minutes before serving so the filling firms up and the sauce stops running. Serve 4 shells per person with a spoonful of sauce from the bottom of the pan. Finish with torn basil and more grated Parmigiano at the table.
Know when it is done
Bake until the center of a middle shell registers 165°F (74°C), which both heats the dish through and fully cooks the egg in the ricotta filling.
Serve it with
A medium-bodied Montepulciano d'Abruzzo and garlic bread, with a lemony arugula salad to finish.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Assemble the whole dish up to 2 days ahead and refrigerate covered. Bake straight from the fridge, adding 15 minutes to the covered time.
  • ◆To freeze, assemble in a foil pan and freeze unbaked up to 3 months. Bake from frozen, covered, at 375°F (190°C) for 70 minutes, then uncovered for 20.
  • ◆Fresh spinach works too: wilt 1 lb (450 g) in a dry pan, cool it, then chop and squeeze it as hard as you would the frozen kind.
  • ◆Ricotta quality is the whole dish. Look for one with a short ingredient list and no gums; supermarket ricotta with stabilizers stays chalky no matter what you do.
  • ◆For a meaty version, brown 8 oz (225 g) of Italian sausage and stir it into the marinara rather than the filling, so the ricotta stays light.

Pasta Primavera⏱ 50 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Spring vegetables cooked in stages so each one keeps its own texture, tossed with butter, Parmigiano and lemon into a light sauce built on pasta water. It is bright and green and does not feel like a compromise.

SpringVegetarianWeeknight
Prep
25 min
Cook
25 min
Total
50 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Vegetables

Pasta and sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Cut everything to the same size
    Prep all the vegetables before you turn on a burner and aim for pieces around 1 1/2 in (4 cm) or a comparable bite. Primavera falls apart when half the vegetables are baby-sized and half are chunks, because they cook at wildly different rates. Keep each type in its own pile since they go into the pan separately.
  2. Set up an ice bath
    Fill a large bowl with cold water and a few handfuls of ice and set it next to the stove. Blanched green vegetables keep cooking on their own heat and turn drab olive within a minute or two unless you stop them cold. This is the single step that keeps primavera looking like spring.
  3. Blanch the asparagus and snap peas
    Bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt. Drop in the asparagus for 90 seconds and the snap peas for 60 seconds — cook them separately so you can time each — then lift them out with a spider straight into the ice bath. They should be bright green and still audibly crisp when you bite one.
  4. Dry the blanched vegetables
    Scoop the chilled vegetables out of the ice bath after 2 minutes and spread them on a towel to drain. Wet vegetables will thin your sauce and stop the zucchini from browning later. Keep the blanching water boiling — you are cooking the pasta in it.
  5. Brown the zucchini
    Heat 2 tbsp of the olive oil in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium-high until it shimmers, then add the zucchini in a single layer with a pinch of salt. Cook 3-4 minutes without stirring much until the cut sides are golden, then flip and cook 1 minute more. Zucchini holds a lot of water, so crowding the pan turns it to mush — do it in two batches if you must.
  6. Cook the aromatics and tomatoes
    Move the zucchini to a plate, add the last 1 tbsp oil to the pan, and cook the sliced shallot for 2 minutes until soft. Add the garlic for 45 seconds, then the halved cherry tomatoes with 1/2 tsp salt and cook 3-4 minutes until they slump and release their juice. Press a few against the pan with a spoon to help them break down into the base of the sauce.
  7. Cook the pasta al dente
    Add the pasta to the still-boiling salted water — the same water you blanched the greens in, which is now faintly vegetal and all the better for it — and cook 1 minute less than the package time, about 9 minutes for farfalle. Stir for the first 30 seconds so the pieces do not stick to each other or to the bottom. Farfalle is worth watching because the pinched center stays firm longer than the wings, so bite the middle of one to judge it. It gets a final minute in the pan with the sauce, which is where it finishes.
  8. Reserve the water
    Scoop out 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of pasta water before draining, then drain the pasta without rinsing it. This water is doing double duty here: it thins the cream to a coating consistency and its starch binds the cold butter into a sauce that clings rather than pooling. Because you cooked vegetables in this pot too, it carries a little of their flavor as well. Keep it hot beside the pan, since cold liquid dropped into a butter emulsion will split it in seconds.
  9. Build the sauce
    Add the 1/3 cup (80 ml) cream and 1/2 cup (120 ml) pasta water to the tomato pan and bring it to a gentle simmer for 1-2 minutes. Turn the heat to low and swirl in the cold butter one piece at a time until the sauce looks glossy and slightly thickened. Cold butter added slowly over low heat emulsifies; melted butter dumped in splits.
  10. Bring everything together
    Add the drained pasta, the blanched asparagus and snap peas, the browned zucchini, and the thawed peas to the pan and toss over medium heat for 1-2 minutes. Add pasta water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time until everything is lightly coated and the sauce clings rather than pools. The vegetables only need to warm through, not cook further.
  11. Finish off the heat
    Take the pan off the burner, then add the Parmigiano, lemon juice and zest, basil, mint, and the remaining salt and pepper, tossing until the cheese melts into the sauce. Adding cheese off the heat keeps it creamy instead of stringy, and the lemon added last stays bright. Taste and adjust — this dish needs more salt and acid than you expect.
  12. Serve right away
    Divide among four warm bowls and top with a little extra Parmigiano and a few torn basil leaves. Primavera is best in the first five minutes, while the greens still snap and the sauce is loose. If it tightens up on the way to the table, loosen it with a splash of the reserved water.
Know when it is done
No internal temperature applies. The cue is the vegetables: bright green and crisp-tender, meaning a piece of asparagus bends slightly but snaps back rather than drooping. Keep the finished sauce below 175°F (79°C) so the cheese stays smooth.
Serve it with
A cold Sauvignon Blanc or a dry rose, and crusty bread with good butter.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Cook the vegetables in stages rather than dumping them all in at once. Staggering is the entire technique here and it is what separates this from a sad pile of steamed vegetables.
  • ◆Swap freely with the season: broccolini, green beans, leeks, fennel, or corn all work. Just keep the rule of blanching the green things and browning the watery things.
  • ◆For a dairy-free version, skip the cream and cheese and build the sauce with 1/4 cup (60 ml) olive oil, the lemon, and an extra 1/2 cup (120 ml) pasta water.
  • ◆Blanch the greens up to a day ahead and refrigerate them dry in a container. It cuts the active cooking down to about 15 minutes on a weeknight.
  • ◆A pinch of red pepper flakes with the garlic gives the whole dish a lift without making it spicy.

Cajun Chicken Pasta⏱ 40 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Blackened chicken sliced over penne in a peppery cream sauce built on the browned bits left in the pan. It is the dish that makes a Tuesday feel like a night out, and the whole thing is done in forty minutes.

WeeknightSpicyComfort Food
Prep
15 min
Cook
25 min
Total
40 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chicken and seasoning

Sauce and vegetables

Pasta

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Butterfly the chicken
    Lay each breast flat, rest your palm on top, and slice horizontally through the middle to make two thin cutlets about 1/2 in (1 cm) thick. Thin, even cutlets cook in 3-4 minutes a side and stay juicy, while a whole thick breast dries out at the edges before the center is safe. You should end up with 4 cutlets of roughly the same thickness.
  2. Season and rest
    Pat the cutlets very dry and rub them all over with 1 1/2 tbsp of the Cajun seasoning and the 1/2 tsp salt. Let them sit at room temperature for 10 minutes while you prep the vegetables — this takes the fridge chill off so they cook evenly. Dry surfaces are what let the spices form a dark crust instead of a paste.
  3. Get the pan hot
    Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a 12 in (30 cm) cast iron or heavy stainless skillet over medium-high for 2 minutes until the oil shimmers and moves like water. Cast iron holds heat well enough to blacken the spice crust properly. If it starts smoking hard, pull the pan off for 20 seconds — Cajun spice blends contain paprika and garlic powder that scorch bitter.
  4. Blacken the chicken
    Lay the cutlets in the pan without crowding, working in two batches if needed, and cook 3-4 minutes per side without moving them. You want a dark mahogany crust and, more importantly, an instant-read thermometer reading of 165°F (74°C) at the thickest point of every cutlet — poultry is not safe below that, and a 1/2 in cutlet carries over only a degree or two off the heat, so do not pull it early and hope. If a piece is browned but reads low, give it another 30-60 seconds a side rather than turning the heat up. Move them to a cutting board and let them rest 5 minutes so the juices redistribute instead of running out when you slice.
  5. Start the pasta
    Bring 5 qt (4.7 L) of water to a boil with 2 tbsp (30 g) kosher salt and add the 12 oz (340 g) of penne. Cook it 1 to 2 minutes less than the package time, usually about 9 minutes, so it is firmly al dente with a chalky center. Time it to come out while the chicken is resting, so nothing sits around going cold. It finishes in the cream sauce, where it will drink up a good part of the liquid and the Cajun seasoning along with it.
  6. Cook the peppers
    Lower the skillet to medium, add the 2 tbsp butter, and cook the sliced bell peppers and red onion for 5-6 minutes until they soften and pick up a few charred edges. Stir occasionally, scraping the fond from the chicken up as you go. You want them tender but with a little bite left, not limp.
  7. Add the garlic
    Stir in the minced garlic and the remaining 1/2 tbsp of Cajun seasoning and cook 45 seconds until it smells fragrant. Toasting the spice in fat blooms the paprika and dried herbs and rounds out their flavor. Do not let the garlic take on color.
  8. Deglaze the pan
    Pour in the 1/2 cup (120 ml) chicken stock and scrape the bottom of the skillet hard with a wooden spoon until every browned bit lifts. Those bits are pure concentrated chicken flavor and they are the entire reason this sauce tastes like more than cream. Simmer 2 minutes until reduced by about half.
  9. Build the cream sauce
    Add the 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) heavy cream and the halved cherry tomatoes, then bring to a gentle simmer and cook 4-5 minutes, stirring often. The sauce should reduce enough to coat the back of a spoon and hold a line when you swipe a finger through it. Keep it at a lazy bubble; a hard boil can break the cream.
  10. Reserve water and add the pasta
    Scoop out 1 cup (240 ml) of pasta water, drain the pasta, and add it straight to the skillet. Toss over medium heat for 1-2 minutes so the noodles absorb some sauce and thicken it. Add pasta water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time if it gets too tight.
  11. Finish with cheese off the heat
    Pull the pan off the burner, add the grated Parmigiano, and toss until it melts smoothly into the sauce. Cheese added to a simmering pan goes stringy and grainy, while cheese added to a pan off the heat turns silky. Taste for salt — Cajun blends vary enormously in how salty they are.
  12. Slice, top, and serve
    Slice the rested chicken against the grain into 1/2 in (1 cm) strips and lay them over the pasta rather than stirring them in, so the crust stays crisp. Scatter the sliced scallions over the top. Serve immediately with extra Parmigiano at the table.
Know when it is done
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) on an instant-read thermometer at the thickest part of the cutlet — check every piece, since thin cutlets vary and carryover in a 1/2 in cutlet is only a degree or two, not enough to close a gap. Rest the cooked cutlets 5 minutes before slicing so the juices redistribute.
Serve it with
A cold lager or a lightly oaked Chardonnay, with cornbread or a simple slaw on the side.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make your own Cajun blend: 2 tsp paprika, 1 tsp each garlic powder, onion powder and dried oregano, 1/2 tsp each cayenne, black pepper, thyme and salt. You control the heat and the salt.
  • ◆Chicken thighs are more forgiving than breasts and hard to dry out. Use 1 1/2 lb (680 g) boneless thighs and cook them to 175°F (79°C) for the best texture.
  • ◆Half-and-half will not hold up here. The acid from the tomatoes plus the reduction needs the fat in heavy cream or it will curdle.
  • ◆Let the chicken rest the full 5 minutes before slicing. Cut it straight out of the pan and you will lose a puddle of juice to the cutting board.
  • ◆Leftovers reheat surprisingly well in a skillet over low heat with a splash of milk or stock to loosen the sauce.

Brown Butter and Sage Ravioli⏱ 20 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Butter cooked until its milk solids toast to hazelnut brown, crisp sage leaves, a squeeze of lemon, and good ravioli. Four ingredients and fifteen minutes, and it tastes like something you would pay thirty dollars for.

20 MinutesDate NightVegetarian
Prep
5 min
Cook
15 min
Total
20 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Use a light-colored pan
    Choose a stainless steel or light-enameled 10-12 in (25-30 cm) skillet rather than dark nonstick or cast iron. Brown butter is judged entirely by color, and in a dark pan you cannot see the milk solids change until they have already burned. This one choice makes the difference between nutty and acrid.
  2. Get the water going first
    Bring 4 qt (3.8 L) of water to a gentle boil with 1 tbsp (18 g) fine sea salt. Do not let it hit a violent rolling boil — fresh ravioli are fragile and hard boiling tears them open, spilling the filling into the pot. You want a lively simmer with bubbles breaking steadily across the surface.
  3. Melt the butter
    Set the skillet over medium heat and add all 8 tbsp (113 g) of butter at once, swirling the pan as it melts. Cutting it into even pieces means it melts at the same rate rather than some browning before the rest has liquefied. Once melted it will foam up loudly as the water in the butter boils off.
  4. Cook through the foam
    Keep swirling the pan every 15-20 seconds and let the butter foam and crackle for 2-3 minutes. That noise is water evaporating, and when it goes quiet you are close to the browning stage. Do not walk away at any point during this step.
  5. Watch for the brown flecks
    After 4-6 minutes total the foam will subside, the butter will turn a clear amber, and specks of milk solid will appear on the bottom of the pan. Tilt the skillet and look: when those specks are the color of toasted hazelnuts and the whole kitchen smells nutty and sweet, you are done. Butter goes from perfect to burnt in about 20 seconds, so be ready to move.
  6. Fry the sage
    Drop the 20 sage leaves and the walnuts if using into the hot butter and let them sizzle for 30-45 seconds. The leaves will curl, go a shade darker, and turn crisp like potato chips. Fish them out with a slotted spoon onto a paper towel and sprinkle with a pinch of salt — they are the garnish and half the pleasure of the dish.
  7. Stop the butter cooking
    Immediately pull the skillet off the heat and set it on a cool burner or a folded towel. The pan holds enough heat to keep browning the butter well past where you want it. If it looks like it is racing ahead, drop in the reserved 1 tbsp (14 g) of cold butter to bring the temperature down fast.
  8. Cook the ravioli gently
    Slide the ravioli into the simmering water in batches so they are not crowded and stir once, very gently, with a slotted spoon. They are done 2-4 minutes after they float to the surface, when the pasta at the sealed edges is tender to the bite. Overcooked ravioli split and dump their filling, so start tasting early.
  9. Save some pasta water
    Scoop out 3/4 cup (180 ml) of the starchy water before you lift the ravioli out. Brown butter alone is pure fat and will slide right off the pasta — the starch in this water is what turns it into a sauce that clings. Keep it right beside the pan.
  10. Emulsify the sauce
    Return the skillet to low heat, add 1/3 cup (80 ml) of the pasta water, and swirl vigorously for about 30 seconds until the butter and water come together into a slightly thickened, cloudy sauce. Stir in the 2 tsp lemon juice and the nutmeg. The lemon cuts the richness and keeps the whole thing from feeling heavy.
  11. Coat and serve
    Lift the ravioli straight from the pot into the skillet with a slotted spoon and toss gently for 30 seconds, adding a splash more pasta water if the sauce looks tight. Spoon them onto warm plates, scatter the crisp sage and walnuts over the top, and finish with the Parmigiano, flaky salt and black pepper. Serve at once, while the sage is still crisp.
Know when it is done
Butter browns at about 250°F (120°C) once the water has cooked off; pull it the moment the milk solids turn hazelnut brown, because past roughly 300°F (150°C) they burn bitter within seconds.
Serve it with
A glass of Pinot Noir or a dry Riesling, with a bitter salad of radicchio and toasted hazelnuts.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Brown butter keeps for 2 weeks in the fridge and freezes for 3 months. Make a double batch and you are ten minutes from dinner any night.
  • ◆Butternut squash or mushroom ravioli are the classic partners, but a good cheese ravioli with the nutmeg and lemon is just as strong.
  • ◆If you burn the butter, throw it out and start over. Burnt milk solids taste bitter and there is no ingredient that hides it.
  • ◆Fresh sage is essential; dried sage turns to dust in hot butter and tastes musty. If you cannot find it, use 10 fresh thyme sprigs instead.
  • ◆Toasting the walnuts in the butter for the full 45 seconds does double duty — it crisps the nuts and leaves a faint toasted flavor behind in the sauce.

Diner-Style Double Smash Burgers⏱ 30 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Two paper-thin patties pressed hard onto a screaming skillet so nearly the whole surface turns to crust. It takes about ninety seconds a side and beats almost any burger you have paid for.

30 MinutesCast IronWeeknight

15 min

15 min
