Slow-Roasted Pulled Pork Sandwiches⏱ 18 hr 30 min🍽 8 servingsMedium▾

A whole pork shoulder rubbed the night before and roasted until it collapses, dressed with tangy vinegar sauce and piled onto a soft bun with slaw. Almost all of the eight hours is waiting.

Weekend ProjectMake AheadCrowd Pleaser
Prep
30 min
Cook
8 hr
Total
18 hr 30 min
Serves
8 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Pork and rub

Vinegar sauce

To build

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Rub the pork a day ahead
    Pat the shoulder dry, smear it all over with the 1 tbsp of yellow mustard, then mix the brown sugar, 2 tbsp salt, smoked paprika, black pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, mustard powder, and cayenne and press that rub into every surface. The mustard is a binder only — you will not taste it. Wrap and refrigerate overnight, which lets the salt penetrate deep into a very thick cut.
  2. Temper before roasting
    Take the pork out of the fridge 1 hour before cooking and set it fat side up on a rack in a roasting pan. A 6-pound roast straight from the fridge takes an extra hour just to shake off the chill. Do not trim the fat cap below about ¼ inch (6 mm), since it bastes the meat for the entire cook.
  3. Roast low and steady
    Roast at 275°F (135°C) with a rack in the lower third of the oven. Pour 1 cup (240 ml) of water into the pan below the rack to keep the drippings from scorching and to add humidity. Plan on roughly 1 hour 20 minutes per pound, which is a full 8 hours for a 6-pound shoulder, and treat that as an estimate rather than a promise — the thermometer decides when it is done, not the clock.
  4. Expect the stall
    Somewhere around 160°F (71°C) the internal temperature will stop climbing for an hour or more. This is the stall, caused by evaporative cooling from the surface, and it is completely normal. Do not raise the oven temperature in a panic; just wait it out or wrap the roast in foil to push through faster.
  5. Make the vinegar sauce
    While the pork cooks, whisk the cider vinegar, 2 tbsp brown sugar, ketchup, 1 tsp salt, red pepper flakes, and black pepper in a jar until the sugar dissolves. Let it sit at room temperature for at least an hour so the pepper flakes infuse. This thin Carolina-style sauce is a seasoning, not a glaze — it is there to cut the richness of the pork, not to coat it.
  6. Cook to 203°F
    The pork is ready when an instant-read thermometer slides into the thickest part with no resistance, right around 203°F (95°C). Whole pork is safe at 145°F (63°C), but shoulder needs to go this much higher for the collagen to melt into gelatin and the meat to pull apart. Start probing at the 6-hour mark and check in a few different spots.
  7. Rest it long
    Tent the roast loosely with foil and rest it for a full hour before touching it. This is the longest rest in this whole book and it is worth every minute; the gelatin and juices need time to settle back into the muscle. Pulling it hot means a puddle on the board and dry pork in the bun.
  8. Pull, do not shred to death
    Pull the bone straight out — it should slide free with almost no effort — then pull the meat apart with two forks or gloved hands into rough, irregular strands. Leave some pieces chunky rather than reducing everything to fluff, because texture variation is what makes it interesting. Discard any large pockets of unrendered fat but keep the darker bark bits mixed in.
  9. Dress the meat
    Pour about ¾ cup (180 ml) of the vinegar sauce over the pulled pork along with ½ cup (120 ml) of the defatted pan drippings and toss to combine. Taste and add more sauce a splash at a time until it tastes bright and seasoned rather than merely rich. Keep the remaining sauce on the table.
  10. Butter and toast the buns
    Spread the softened butter on the cut faces and toast them in a skillet over medium heat for about 60 seconds until golden. Soft potato buns are the correct choice — they compress around the filling instead of pushing it out the sides the way a crusty roll does. The toasted face is your only defense against the vinegar sauce.
  11. Build with slaw on top
    Lay pickle chips on the bottom bun, pile on about 5 oz (140 g) of pulled pork, then finish with a generous handful of well-drained slaw and the top bun. Slaw goes on top so its dressing does not soak down through the pork into the bread, and its cold crunch is a deliberate contrast to the soft, hot meat. Press gently and serve immediately.
Know when it is done
Whole pork is safe at 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest, but shoulder must reach about 203°F (95°C) for the connective tissue to break down and the meat to pull.
Serve it with
Baked beans, cornbread, and an ice-cold cider or a hoppy pale ale.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Pulled pork keeps 4 days refrigerated and 3 months frozen. Reheat it in a covered pan with a splash of cider vinegar and stock so it steams back to life instead of drying out.
  • ◆Drain your coleslaw in a sieve for 10 minutes before it goes on the sandwich. Undrained slaw is the fastest way to destroy a good bun.
  • ◆A slow cooker works if the oven is spoken for: 8 to 10 hours on low, then spread the pulled meat on a sheet pan and broil for 5 minutes to get some bark back.
  • ◆Save the defatted pan drippings. That cup of concentrated pork jus is the best thing you can add back to the meat and most people throw it away.
  • ◆Bone-in beats boneless every time. The bone conducts heat toward the center, adds gelatin, and gives you an unmistakable doneness test when it pulls clean.

Triple-Decker Turkey Club⏱ 33 min🍽 2 servingsEasy▾

Three slices of toast, two fillings, and four frilled picks holding the whole architectural achievement together. It is a diner classic because the layering genuinely works.

LunchDeli ClassicWeeknight
Prep
15 min
Cook
18 min
Total
33 min
Serves
2 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Bake the bacon flat
    Lay the bacon in a single layer on a foil-lined sheet pan, put it in a cold oven, and set the temperature to 400°F (205°C). Bake 16 to 20 minutes until deep brown and just barely flexible. Flat oven bacon is essential in a triple-decker, because curled slices create air gaps that make the tower unstable and impossible to cut cleanly.
  2. Salt and drain the tomato
    Lay all 8 tomato slices on paper towels, season with ¼ tsp of the flaky salt, and let them drain 10 minutes while the bacon cooks. Blot the tops before using. A club has two layers of filling and twice the opportunity to go soggy, so drying the tomato matters even more here than in a BLT.
  3. Crisp the lettuce
    Soak the lettuce leaves in ice water for 5 minutes, then dry them completely in a salad spinner or between towels. Tear or trim them so they sit within the footprint of the bread rather than hanging over the edges. Overhanging lettuce is what makes a club fall apart when you cut it.
  4. Toast all six slices
    Toast the bread until firm and evenly golden, about 3 minutes in a toaster. Every slice must be properly toasted, including the middle one, since that center slice is the structural beam holding two separate sandwiches together. A soft middle slice collapses under the weight and the whole thing slides sideways.
  5. Mayonnaise every inside face
    Spread mayonnaise on one face of the top and bottom slices and on both faces of the middle slice, using about 1 tbsp per surface and going right to the crust. That is four mayonnaised surfaces per sandwich and eight across the two, which is exactly what the ½ cup covers. Beyond flavor, the mayo is a fat barrier that keeps moisture from wicking into the toast, so a bare corner is a corner that goes soggy first.
  6. Build the bottom layer
    On the bottom slice, lay down lettuce first, then half the turkey folded into loose ruffles rather than laid flat, then 2 tomato slices seasoned with salt and pepper. Ruffling the turkey traps air and gives the sandwich height and a better bite than a compressed slab. Lettuce on the bottom keeps tomato juice off the toast.
  7. Add the middle slice
    Set the double-mayonnaised middle slice on top and press down gently to settle the first layer. Make sure it is aligned squarely with the bottom slice, because a crooked middle slice guarantees a leaning tower. This is the moment to check that nothing is hanging over the edges.
  8. Build the second layer
    On the middle slice, layer the bacon first, broken into halves and crosshatched to cover the surface evenly, then the remaining turkey, then the last 2 tomato slices and more lettuce. Putting bacon directly against the dry middle toast keeps the salty fat where it can season everything. Finish with the top slice, mayonnaise side down.
  9. Pin it before you cut
    Press the whole stack down firmly with your palm for 5 seconds, then push a sandwich pick vertically through the center of each of the four quadrants, about 1 inch (2.5 cm) in from each corner. The picks are not decoration; they are the only thing keeping a five-inch tall sandwich together while a knife goes through it. Push them all the way to the bottom slice.
  10. Cut into four triangles
    With a long serrated knife, cut the sandwich corner to corner in both directions to make 4 triangles, sawing gently rather than pressing down. Wipe the blade between the two cuts for clean edges. Serve immediately with chips and a pickle, arranging the triangles points up the way a diner would.
Know when it is done
Deli turkey is already cooked and served cold here; if you roast your own breast, cook it to 165°F (74°C) and chill it fully before slicing.
Serve it with
Kettle chips, a dill pickle spear, and iced tea or a crisp lager.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Roast your own turkey breast if you have the time, or ask the deli to slice it thick, about ⅛ inch (3 mm). Paper-thin deli turkey packs into a wet, flavorless mat.
  • ◆Add a thin layer of sliced avocado in the bottom layer for a California club, or swap the mayo for herbed mayonnaise with 1 tbsp of chopped tarragon.
  • ◆Bacon can be cooked 3 days ahead and recrisped for 4 minutes at 350°F (175°C), which turns this into a genuinely fast lunch.
  • ◆If the sandwich is too tall to bite, that is normal. Cutting into quarters rather than halves is exactly why the club is traditionally served in triangles.
  • ◆Use a bread with a tight crumb. Airy bakery bread compresses unevenly and the tower will lean before you get a knife into it.

Chicken rewards two habits above all else — dry the skin before it meets heat, and cook to 165°F (74°C) instead of to a guess — and once those are yours, everything in this chapter is just a variation on a bird you already know how to handle.

Buttermilk Fried Chicken⏱ 9 hr 30 min🍽 4 servingsAdvanced▾

A long soak in salted buttermilk seasons the meat all the way to the bone and keeps it juicy, and a shaggy double-dredge fries into shards of crust. This is a weekend project that people remember years later.

Weekend ProjectSouthernFried
Prep
25 min
Cook
35 min
Total
9 hr 30 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Buttermilk brine

Seasoned dredge

For frying

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Break down the bird
    Cut the chicken into 10 pieces: two drumsticks, two thighs, two wings, and two breasts each cut crosswise in half. Evenly sized pieces are the whole trick, because a huge breast half will still be raw when the crust on a wing has gone bitter and dark. If jointing a bird feels like too much tonight, buy 4 lb (1.8 kg) of mixed bone-in pieces and just cut the breasts in half yourself with a heavy knife.
  2. Mix the brine
    Whisk the buttermilk, 2 tbsp kosher salt, sugar, hot sauce, and black pepper in a large bowl for about 30 seconds, until the salt has fully dissolved and you cannot feel grains on the bottom. The salt is doing the real work, seasoning the meat deep inside, while the mild acidity of the buttermilk tenderizes the surface without turning it to mush. It should taste aggressively salty, close to seawater — that is correct.
  3. Brine 8 to 24 hours
    Slide the chicken pieces into the brine, press them under the surface, cover, and refrigerate for at least 8 hours and up to 24. Turn the bowl or bag once partway through so no piece sits above the liquid the whole time. Do not push past 24 hours: the acid eventually breaks down the outer half-inch of meat into a chalky, cottony texture that frying cannot fix.
  4. Whisk the dredge
    In a wide, shallow dish, whisk the flour, cornstarch, 1 tbsp kosher salt, black pepper, paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, cayenne, and baking powder until the color is completely uniform. The cornstarch keeps the crust from turning bready and the baking powder gives it a little lift so it fries lighter. Streaks of pale flour mean the seasoning is not distributed, so keep whisking for a full 30 seconds.
  5. Make the craggy bits
    Drizzle 3 tbsp (45 ml) of the buttermilk brine over the flour and rub it in with your fingertips until the mixture looks like coarse, pebbly wet sand. Those little clumps are exactly what fry into the shattering, shaggy edges that everyone picks at first. Skip this step and you get a smooth, tight coating that tastes fine but feels flat and sheds off in one sheet.
  6. Dredge and rest
    Lift each piece from the brine, let it drip for three or four seconds, then press it hard into the flour, packing the coating on with your palm and getting into every crease. Set the coated pieces on a wire rack and let them sit at room temperature for 20 minutes. During that rest the flour hydrates and glues itself to the skin, so the crust stays put in the oil instead of sliding off in the pot.
  7. Heat the oil to 325°F
    Pour 2 in (5 cm) of peanut oil into a large Dutch oven, never filling it more than halfway up the sides, and heat over medium-high to 325°F (163°C) on a clip-on thermometer. That depth gives the oil enough thermal mass that cold chicken will not crash the temperature. A pinch of the dredge dropped in should sizzle steadily and float within a second or two, not sink silently or spit violently.
  8. Fry the dark meat
    Lower in the thighs and drumsticks, no more than 4 pieces at a time, and expect the oil to drop 40 to 50°F (22 to 28°C) the moment they hit. Adjust the burner to hold it between 300 and 325°F (150 and 163°C) and fry for 12 to 15 minutes, turning once at the halfway mark. It should sizzle steadily and smell nutty, not smoke — if the oil smokes, pull the pot off the heat for a minute.
  9. Fry the white meat
    Move the finished dark meat to a clean wire rack, bring the oil back up to 325°F (163°C), and fry the breast halves and wings for 10 to 12 minutes. White meat has less fat and less collagen, so it cooks faster and dries out sooner — this is exactly why you fry it separately instead of dumping everything in at once. Turn each piece once so both sides take on the same deep amber color.
  10. Check the temperature
    Probe the thickest part of each piece with an instant-read thermometer, staying off the bone, and look for a minimum of 165°F (74°C) in the breast. Thighs and drumsticks are safe at 165°F (74°C) too but taste noticeably better at 175°F (79°C), where the connective tissue has melted. If the crust is already dark and the center reads low, finish those pieces on a rack in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 5 to 8 minutes.
  11. Drain on a rack
    Rest the fried pieces on a wire rack set over a sheet pan, never on paper towels, which trap steam and turn the bottom crust soggy within a minute. Leave at least an inch between pieces so air can move around them. Season each piece with a pinch of flaky sea salt while the surface is still glossy with hot oil, because that is when salt actually sticks.
  12. Rest and serve
    Let the chicken sit for 5 to 10 minutes before anyone touches it so the juices redistribute and the crust firms up into something that audibly cracks. Serve it warm rather than blazing hot, when the flavor of the meat has come forward. If you are frying in batches for a crowd, hold the finished pieces on their rack in a 200°F (95°C) oven for up to 30 minutes.
Know when it is done
Hold the oil between 300 and 325°F (150 and 163°C). Chicken is safe at 165°F (74°C); pull thighs and drumsticks nearer 175°F (79°C) so the connective tissue melts.
Serve it with
Cold lager or sweet tea, with buttermilk slaw, dill pickles, and a hot skillet of cornbread.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Peanut oil has a high smoke point and a clean flavor, but refined vegetable, canola, or 2 lb (900 g) of shortening all fry beautifully. Never use olive oil, which smokes and turns acrid well below frying temperature.
  • ◆Make ahead: the chicken can brine a full 24 hours, and fried chicken is genuinely excellent cold from the fridge the next day. To reheat it hot, set the pieces on a rack in a 375°F (190°C) oven for 12 to 15 minutes.
  • ◆No buttermilk? Whisk 4 cups (960 ml) whole milk with 4 tbsp (60 ml) lemon juice or white vinegar and let it sit 10 minutes until it thickens and curdles slightly.
  • ◆If the crust slides off in the pot, you either skipped the 20-minute rest after dredging or moved the pieces too soon after they went in. Leave them alone for the first 4 minutes of frying.
  • ◆Strain the cooled oil through a coffee filter into a jar and it will fry two or three more times before it starts to taste tired.

Roast Chicken with Shatteringly Crisp Skin⏱ 3 hr 15 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

A plain bird, salted a day ahead and roasted hot over onions and garlic, is still the best thing you can put on a table. The pan drippings become a two-minute sauce that makes it feel like a restaurant.

Sunday DinnerCast IronClassic
Prep
20 min
Cook
1 hr 10 min
Total
3 hr 15 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the chicken

Aromatics and pan

Two-minute pan sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Dry the bird completely
    Take the chicken out of its packaging, pull out any giblets, and pat it bone dry inside and out with paper towels — the cavity holds more water than you expect. Water on the skin has to boil off before browning can begin, and that steam is the single reason home roast chickens come out pale and rubbery. Spend a full minute on this and blot the wing pits and the crease where the thigh meets the body.
  2. Salt it a day ahead
    Stir the kosher salt with the baking powder, then rub the mixture over every surface of the skin and sprinkle about a teaspoon inside the cavity. Set the bird breast-up on a rack over a sheet pan and refrigerate uncovered for at least 45 minutes, or up to 24 hours if you can plan ahead. The cold dry air of the fridge dehydrates the skin while the salt seasons the meat, and the baking powder raises the skin's pH so it browns faster and blisters.
  3. Let it lose the chill
    Pull the chicken out of the refrigerator 45 minutes before it goes into the oven and leave it on the counter, still on its rack. A bird straight from the fridge at 38°F (3°C) needs so much extra oven time that the breast overcooks before the thighs catch up. The skin should feel dry and papery to the touch, almost like parchment — that is exactly what you want.
  4. Heat the oven to 425°F
    Set a rack in the lower third of the oven and heat it to 425°F (220°C), giving it a full 20 minutes after the indicator beeps so the walls and floor are genuinely saturated with heat. Most ovens lie by 15 to 25°F, so if you own an oven thermometer, now is when it earns its keep. A hot oven is what crisps the skin before the meat has time to dry out.
  5. Fill the cavity
    Squeeze one lemon half over the outside of the bird, then tuck both halves, the thyme sprigs, and one half of the garlic head into the cavity. These aromatics will not perfume the meat much, but they release steam that keeps the breast from drying and they scent the drippings, which is where you will actually taste them. Do not pack the cavity tight — hot air needs to circulate through it.
  6. Truss loosely
    Tie the ends of the drumsticks together with a 12 in (30 cm) length of kitchen twine and tuck the wing tips behind the shoulders. Trussing keeps the legs from splaying and burning while pulling them slightly closer to the body so they finish nearer to the same time as the breast. Keep the tie snug but not strangling, since a tightly trussed bird traps raw juices between the thigh and the body.
  7. Butter and pepper the skin
    Rub the softened butter over the breast, thighs, and drumsticks with your hands, then grind the black pepper over everything. Do not add more salt now — the bird has already been salted and this second coat would push it over the edge. The butter gives the skin fat to brown in and helps the pepper stick where it lands.
  8. Build the onion bed
    Toss the onion wedges and the remaining garlic half with the olive oil in a 12 in (30 cm) cast-iron skillet or a small roasting pan, then set the chicken breast-up right on top of them. The vegetables lift the bird off the pan floor so the bottom skin roasts instead of stewing, and they turn jammy and sweet in the drippings. Push any stray onion out from under the wings where it would otherwise scorch.
  9. Roast 50 to 70 minutes
    Slide the pan into the oven and leave the door shut for the first 40 minutes so the oven holds its heat. A 4 lb (1.8 kg) bird usually takes 50 to 60 minutes, a 4 1/2 lb (2 kg) bird closer to 70. Rotate the pan 180 degrees once at the halfway point, since every oven has a hot corner and this is the cheapest insurance against one side going darker than the other.
  10. Temp both the breast and thigh
    Slide an instant-read thermometer into the thickest part of the breast, angling in from the neck end and stopping short of the bone: you want 165°F (74°C). Then check the inner thigh, where you are looking for 175°F (79°C), because dark meat is safe at 165°F (74°C) but tastes tough until its collagen has melted. If the thigh lags, give it another 5 to 8 minutes and re-check rather than guessing.
  11. Rest for 15 minutes
    Move the chicken to a carving board and let it rest, uncovered, for a full 15 minutes while you make the sauce. Resting lets the muscle fibers relax and reabsorb their juices, so they end up in the meat instead of flooding the board. Do not tent it with foil — trapped steam will soften the skin you just spent an hour crisping.
  12. Make the pan sauce
    Set the skillet with its onions over medium-high heat, pour in the wine, and scrape up the browned bits with a wooden spoon as it bubbles down by half, about 2 minutes. Add the stock and simmer until the sauce coats the back of a spoon, roughly 4 minutes more, then kill the heat and swirl in the cold butter and lemon juice. Taste it and add a pinch of salt only if it needs it, since the drippings are already seasoned.
Know when it is done
Roast at 425°F (220°C) until the breast reads 165°F (74°C) and the inner thigh reads 175°F (79°C). Dark meat is safe at 165°F (74°C) but eats better a bit higher.
Serve it with
A crisp unoaked Chardonnay or a light Pinot Noir, with roast potatoes and a sharp green salad to cut the fat.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make ahead: salt the bird up to 24 hours in advance and leave it uncovered in the fridge. This is the single highest-impact thing you can do, and it costs you two minutes of work.
  • ◆If the skin is browning too fast at 30 minutes, lay a loose piece of foil over the breast only and remove it for the last 10 minutes.
  • ◆Save the carcass. Cover it with cold water, add an onion, a carrot, and a bay leaf, and simmer for 3 hours for stock that is worlds better than anything in a box.
  • ◆A convection or fan setting works well here: drop the temperature to 400°F (205°C) and start checking 10 minutes early.
  • ◆Carve the legs first by cutting through the skin between thigh and body and popping the joint back, then take the breasts off the bone in one piece and slice them crosswise.

Spatchcock Chicken with Lemon and Thyme⏱ 2 hr🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Cutting out the backbone and pressing the bird flat drops roasting time to 45 minutes and puts every inch of skin against the heat at once. It is the fastest route to a whole roast chicken on a weeknight.

WeeknightOne PanRoasting
Prep
20 min
Cook
45 min
Total
2 hr
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the chicken

Lemon thyme butter

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Get the right tool
    You need sturdy kitchen shears or poultry shears, not scissors and not a knife, because you are cutting through rib bones on both sides of the spine. Set the chicken breast-down on a cutting board with the tail end facing you and pat it dry so it does not slip. If you have no shears at all, ask the butcher to spatchcock the bird for you — it takes them 20 seconds.
  2. Cut out the backbone
    Starting at the tail, cut up along one side of the backbone, staying about 1/4 in (6 mm) off the spine, and work through the ribs with steady squeezes rather than sawing. Repeat on the other side and lift the backbone free. It will feel like it takes more force than seems right; that is normal, and the bones give in a series of small pops.
  3. Flatten the bird
    Flip the chicken breast-up, set the heel of your palm on the center of the breastbone, and press down hard until you hear a crack and the bird lies flat. That crack is the keel bone giving way, which is what lets the whole chicken sit in one even plane. Tuck the wing tips behind the shoulders so they do not char in the hot oven.
  4. Salt and air-dry
    Season both sides with the 2 1/2 tsp kosher salt and the black pepper, then set the bird skin-up on a rack over a sheet pan. Leave it uncovered in the refrigerator for 45 minutes while the oven heats, or up to 24 hours if you have the time. The skin should go from tacky to dry and papery, which is the state that crisps rather than steams.
  5. Make the compound butter
    Mash the softened butter with the lemon zest, chopped thyme, minced garlic, and red pepper flakes in a small bowl until it is evenly flecked. Keep it soft but not melted — melted butter runs straight off the bird instead of clinging. Taste a fleck: it should be bright and garlicky, since it will be diluted across a whole chicken.
  6. Butter under the skin
    Slide your fingers between the skin and the breast meat, working carefully from the neck end so you do not tear it, and push about two-thirds of the butter into that pocket. Massage it from the outside to spread it evenly over both breasts and into the thigh pockets. Rub the remaining butter and the olive oil over the outside of the skin. Butter under the skin bastes the leanest meat from the inside while the outside crisps.
  7. Heat the oven to 450°F
    Set a rack in the upper-middle position and heat the oven to 450°F (230°C) with a heavy rimmed sheet pan or a 12 in (30 cm) cast-iron skillet inside. Preheating the pan means the thighs start searing the second the bird lands, which is what keeps the underside from stewing. Give the oven a full 20 minutes at temperature before you commit the chicken.
  8. Lay the bird on the hot pan
    Scatter the lemon slices and thyme sprigs onto the hot pan, then set the chicken skin-up on top, pressing lightly so it lies flat. It should hiss loudly on contact — if it is silent, the pan was not hot enough and you should give it 5 more minutes next time. Arrange the legs so the thighs sit toward the outside edges of the pan, where the heat is strongest.
  9. Roast 40 to 50 minutes
    Roast without opening the door for the first 30 minutes, then rotate the pan 180 degrees and check the color. A 3 1/2 lb (1.6 kg) bird usually finishes around 40 minutes, a 4 lb (1.8 kg) bird closer to 50. The skin should be deep mahogany with a few blistered spots and the drippings should be sizzling, not smoking.
  10. Check the temperature
    Probe the thickest part of the breast for 165°F (74°C) and the inner thigh for 175°F (79°C), keeping the thermometer tip away from bone, which reads hot and will lie to you. Because the bird is flat, the two numbers arrive much closer together than in a traditional roast — that is the entire point of spatchcocking. If the breast is there and the thigh is not, give it 5 more minutes.
  11. Rest, then carve
    Move the chicken to a board and rest it uncovered for 10 minutes so the juices settle back into the muscle instead of running out at the first cut. Squeeze the roasted lemon slices over the top, drizzle on the fresh lemon juice and any pan drippings, and finish with flaky sea salt. Carve the legs off first, then run your knife down either side of the breastbone and slice the breasts crosswise.
Know when it is done
Roast at 450°F (230°C) until the breast reads 165°F (74°C) and the thigh reads 175°F (79°C). Never serve chicken below 165°F (74°C).
Serve it with
A cold, dry Riesling or Sauvignon Blanc, with roasted potatoes and blanched green beans tossed in the pan drippings.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Freeze the backbone with the giblets. Two of them plus an onion and a carrot make a quart of excellent stock in about 3 hours.
  • ◆Make ahead: spatchcock and salt the bird up to 24 hours in advance and leave it uncovered on a rack in the fridge. The skin gets dramatically crisper and dinner becomes a 50-minute affair.
  • ◆Roasting potatoes underneath works beautifully — toss 1 1/2 lb (680 g) of halved baby potatoes in oil and spread them on the hot pan before the chicken goes on so they cook in the drippings.
  • ◆If your smoke alarm is sensitive, put the pan on a rack in the upper-middle rather than the very top, and make sure there is no dry flour or crumbs on the pan.
  • ◆Leftover meat pulled off the bone keeps 4 days refrigerated and makes the best chicken salad you will have.

Cast-Iron Crispy-Skin Chicken Thighs⏱ 1 hr🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Skin-on thighs pressed into a hot cast-iron pan and left alone give you glass-crisp skin and meat that is nearly impossible to overcook. A short shopping list, one pan, and it looks like you tried much harder than you did.

One PanCast IronWeeknight
Prep
10 min
Cook
30 min
Total
1 hr
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chicken

Quick pan sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Dry the skin hard
    Pat each thigh completely dry with paper towels, pressing down on the skin side rather than wiping, and change towels when they get damp. Any moisture left on the surface has to boil off before browning starts, which is why so many home cooks end up with flabby skin. Trim off any overhanging flaps of skin or fat with kitchen shears so the thighs sit flat.
  2. Season and let it sit
    Season both sides with the kosher salt and black pepper, using slightly more on the skin side, then leave the thighs skin-up on a plate for 15 to 20 minutes while the oven heats. In that time the salt draws moisture to the surface, where it evaporates, leaving the skin drier than when you started. If you have longer, salt them and leave them uncovered in the fridge for up to 12 hours.
  3. Heat the oven to 400°F
    Set a rack in the middle of the oven and heat it to 400°F (205°C). You will start the thighs on the stovetop and finish them in the oven, which renders the skin properly on the burner and then cooks the meat through with gentle, even heat. Preheating now means there is no dead time later while the chicken sits waiting.
  4. Heat the skillet
    Set a 12 in (30 cm) cast-iron skillet over medium heat for 4 minutes, add the oil, and swirl it to coat. The pan is ready when the oil shimmers and moves like water but does not smoke. Cast iron heats unevenly at first, so those 4 minutes matter more than they seem to — a pan rushed to temperature will have a scorching center and cool edges.
  5. Lay the thighs skin-down
    Place the thighs skin-side down, laying them away from you so no oil splashes toward your hand, and leave at least 1/2 in (1 cm) between them. You should hear a steady, moderate sizzle — a violent crackle means the pan is too hot and the skin will scorch before the fat renders. Press each thigh down with a spatula for 10 seconds so the whole skin surface makes contact.
  6. Render without moving
    Cook skin-side down for 12 to 15 minutes over medium heat and resist every urge to peek or shuffle them. The fat under the skin needs that long to melt out and the skin needs the constant contact to turn from rubbery to crisp. If it starts to smoke or smell sharp, drop the heat to medium-low; if there is no sizzle at all, nudge it up.
  7. Check the color and flip
    Lift one thigh with tongs: the skin should be deep golden-brown, taut, and release from the pan on its own. If it sticks, it is not done rendering, so give it another 2 minutes and try again. Flip all the thighs skin-side up, tuck the smashed garlic and thyme sprigs into the fat around them, and get ready to move to the oven.
  8. Finish in the oven
    Slide the whole skillet onto the middle rack and roast for 10 to 12 minutes, until the meat is cooked through and the skin has set hard. Do not turn the thighs again — leaving the skin facing up keeps it out of the rendered fat where it would soften. Remember the handle will be blistering hot when it comes out, so drape a towel over it the moment it hits the stovetop.
  9. Temp and rest
    Probe the thickest part of a thigh next to but not touching the bone; 165°F (74°C) is the safe minimum, but thighs are far better at 175 to 185°F (79 to 85°C), where the collagen has fully melted. Move them to a plate, skin-up, and rest 5 minutes. Do not cover them, because trapped steam will undo the crisp skin in under a minute.
  10. Build the pan sauce
    Pour off all but about 1 tbsp of fat, return the skillet to medium heat, and add the stock, scraping up the browned bits with a wooden spoon. Simmer until it has reduced by half and coats a spoon, roughly 3 minutes, then take the pan off the heat and swirl in the cold butter and lemon juice until glossy. Spoon it around, never over, the thighs so the skin stays crisp.
Know when it is done
Safe at 165°F (74°C), but thighs are at their best between 175 and 185°F (79 and 85°C) once the collagen has broken down.
Serve it with
A glass of Beaujolais or a dry cider, with buttered rice or crusty bread to catch the pan sauce.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Bone-in thighs are far more forgiving than breasts because the extra fat and collagen keep them juicy even 20°F past done. This is the cut to practice on.
  • ◆A stainless-steel skillet works just as well as cast iron; a nonstick pan does not, because it cannot get hot enough to render skin properly.
  • ◆If your skin is sticking hard, the pan was not hot enough when the chicken went in. Give it a full 4 minutes to preheat next time and let the oil shimmer.
  • ◆Make ahead: salt the thighs and leave them uncovered on a rack in the fridge for up to 12 hours. The skin dries out and crisps noticeably better.
  • ◆Save the rendered chicken fat in a jar in the fridge for up to a month — it is the best thing you can roast potatoes in.

Lemon Herb Grilled Chicken⏱ 1 hr 5 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Boneless thighs in a bright lemon, garlic, and oregano marinade, grilled hot and fast until the edges char. It is the simplest good thing you can make outside, and it works just as well in a grill pan.

GrillSummerEasy
Prep
15 min
Cook
15 min
Total
1 hr 5 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chicken

Lemon herb marinade

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Even out the thighs
    Open each thigh flat on the board and trim away any thick pockets of fat or dangling bits with a paring knife. If one end is noticeably thicker than the other, press it down with your palm or give it two light taps with the flat of a knife. Pieces of even thickness hit 165°F (74°C) at the same moment, which is the difference between all-juicy and half-dry.
  2. Whisk the marinade
    In a bowl, whisk the olive oil, lemon juice, lemon zest, garlic, oregano, parsley, and honey until it turns cloudy and slightly thickened, about 20 seconds. The honey is not there to sweeten it but to help the surface caramelize on the grill and to soften the raw edge of the garlic. Taste it — it should be sharply lemony, because the chicken will mute it considerably.
  3. Marinate 30 minutes to 4 hours
    Season the thighs with the kosher salt and black pepper, then turn them in the marinade until every surface is coated and refrigerate for 30 minutes to 4 hours. Thirty minutes is genuinely enough for boneless thighs, since the surface is where the flavor lives. Do not go past 4 hours: the lemon juice will start to chemically cook the outside and give it a mealy, opaque texture.
  4. Set up a two-zone fire
    For charcoal, bank the coals to one side so half the grate is directly over fire and half is empty; for gas, set one or two burners to medium-high and leave the others off. That cool zone is your escape hatch if the outside browns before the inside is done. Let the grate preheat for 10 minutes with the lid closed until it is genuinely hot.
  5. Clean and oil the grate
    Scrub the hot grate with a wire brush, then fold a paper towel, soak it with about 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the neutral oil, grip it with tongs, and wipe the bars two or three times. Oiling a hot grate rather than a cold one is what actually stops sticking, because the oil polymerizes on contact. The grate should look slick and dark, not pooled with oil.
  6. Grill the first side
    Shake the excess marinade off each thigh so it does not flare, and lay the pieces over the hot zone with the smoother side down. Close the lid and grill undisturbed for 4 to 5 minutes, until you see clear grill marks and the edges have gone opaque. If flames leap up around the meat, move it to the cool side for 30 seconds and let them die down rather than spraying water.
  7. Flip once
    Turn each thigh with tongs and grill the second side for another 4 to 5 minutes with the lid closed. Flipping repeatedly cools the surface each time and prevents the char you are after, so resist the urge to fuss. The thighs will shrink and firm noticeably, and the marinade on the surface should be visibly caramelized and dark in spots.
  8. Check the temperature
    Slide an instant-read thermometer into the thickest part of a thigh from the side, going in about 1 in (2.5 cm). Chicken is safe at 165°F (74°C), and thighs are still juicy well past that, so 170 to 175°F (77 to 79°C) is a comfortable target here. If they are not there, move them to the cool side of the grill, close the lid, and give them 3 more minutes.
  9. Rest and dress
    Pile the thighs on a platter and rest them for 5 minutes so the juices redistribute instead of running out onto the cutting board. Squeeze one lemon wedge over the top, scatter the chopped parsley and flaky sea salt, and serve the remaining wedges alongside. That final hit of raw lemon after cooking is what makes the dish taste bright rather than merely grilled.
  10. Indoor version
    With no grill, heat a cast-iron grill pan over medium-high for 5 minutes, or use a heavy skillet, and brush either one with the remaining 1 tbsp (15 ml) of neutral oil. Cook the thighs 5 to 6 minutes per side, working in two batches so the pan does not crowd and steam. Open a window and turn on the fan, because the marinade will smoke a little as it caramelizes.
Know when it is done
Grill over medium-high until the thickest part reads at least 165°F (74°C); thighs stay juicy up to 175°F (79°C).
Serve it with
Chilled rosé or a cold Greek beer, with a tomato and cucumber salad and warm pita.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Boneless breasts work too, but pound them to an even 3/4 in (2 cm) first, grill 5 to 6 minutes per side, and pull them at exactly 165°F (74°C) — they have no fat to forgive you.
  • ◆Make ahead: the marinade keeps 5 days in the fridge and the chicken can sit in it for up to 4 hours. Any longer and the acid ruins the texture.
  • ◆Leftovers are excellent cold, sliced over a salad with feta and cucumber, or stuffed into warm pita with yogurt.
  • ◆Double the marinade and reserve half before the raw chicken touches it — that reserved half becomes a dressing you can spoon over the cooked meat.
  • ◆Dried oregano is genuinely fine here and in some ways more traditional; use one-third the volume of fresh.

Chicken Pot Pie with All-Butter Crust⏱ 4 hr 10 min🍽 6 servingsAdvanced▾

A proper velouté thick enough to hold a spoon upright, sweet vegetables, and a flaky all-butter lid that shatters when you cut it. This is a Sunday afternoon spent well, and it feeds six generously.

Serves

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

All-butter crust

Chicken and vegetables

Velouté

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Cut the butter into the flour
    Whisk the flour, salt, and sugar in a large bowl, then add the cold butter cubes and toss to coat. Work the butter in with your fingertips or a pastry cutter until the largest pieces are the size of almonds and the smallest are like coarse sand. Those almond-sized pieces are what steam into flaky layers in the oven, so stopping too early is far better than going too far.
  2. Bring the dough together
    Drizzle in 6 tbsp (90 ml) of ice water while tossing with a fork, then squeeze a handful: if it holds without crumbling, it is ready, and if not, add water 1 tbsp at a time. Do not knead it — you want a shaggy mass, not a smooth ball, because gluten development here means a tough, shrinking crust. Press it into a 1 in (2.5 cm) thick disc, wrap it, and chill for at least 1 hour.
  3. Brown the chicken
    Pat the chicken pieces dry, season with 1/2 tsp of the salt, and brown them in 1 tbsp of the butter in a large Dutch oven over medium-high heat for 5 to 6 minutes, working in two batches. You are after color on two sides, not cooked-through chicken, since it will finish in the oven. Set the browned pieces aside on a plate and keep every bit of fond stuck to the bottom of the pot.
  4. Sweat the vegetables
    Melt the remaining 3 tbsp butter over medium heat, add the onion, carrots, and celery, and cook for 8 minutes, stirring often, until the onion is translucent and the carrots have lost their raw snap. Scrape the bottom as you go so the fond dissolves into the vegetables rather than burning. Season with 1/2 tsp of the salt now so the vegetables draw out their own moisture.
  5. Cook the mushrooms dry
    Add the quartered mushrooms and cook for 6 to 8 minutes over medium-high heat until they have released their water and it has all evaporated. Do not rush this — mushrooms added wet will thin your sauce later and taste like nothing. You will know they are ready when the pot goes quiet and the mushrooms start to squeak and brown at the edges.
  6. Make the roux
    Sprinkle the 1/2 cup flour over the vegetables and stir constantly for 2 full minutes, until the flour coats everything and smells faintly like toast rather than raw paste. This is a blond roux, so you want no real color, just the raw edge cooked out. It will look dry and clumpy and that is exactly right at this stage.
  7. Build the sauce
    Pour in the warm stock about 1 cup at a time, whisking hard after each addition until completely smooth before adding more. Adding it all at once is how you get lumps that no amount of whisking will fix later. Once all the stock is in, add the milk and bring it to a gentle simmer, stirring, until it thickens enough to coat the back of a spoon, about 5 minutes.
  8. Season and finish the filling
    Stir in the Dijon, thyme, remaining 1/2 tsp salt, and the black pepper, then return the browned chicken with any juices on the plate and simmer for 4 minutes. Kill the heat and fold in the frozen peas, which will thaw in the residual warmth without turning grey. Taste and adjust: the filling should be a shade over-seasoned, since the crust brings none of its own salt.
  9. Cool the filling completely
    Spread the filling in a 9x13 in (23x33 cm) baking dish or a 10 in (25 cm) deep pie dish and let it cool for at least 30 minutes, or refrigerate it to speed things up. A hot filling melts the butter in your crust before it ever reaches the oven, and melted butter means a greasy, flat lid instead of a flaky one. It should be barely warm to the touch, not steaming.
  10. Roll the top crust
    On a lightly floured counter, roll the chilled dough into a rectangle or round about 1/8 in (3 mm) thick and 1 in (2.5 cm) larger than your dish on all sides. Work from the center outward, turning the dough a quarter turn between rolls so it does not stick. If it softens or gets sticky at any point, slide it onto a sheet pan and chill it for 10 minutes before continuing.
  11. Top and seal
    Drape the dough over the cooled filling, trim the overhang to about 1/2 in (1 cm), and tuck or crimp the edge against the rim of the dish. Sealing the edge keeps the filling from bubbling up over the crust and burning onto the sides. Chill the whole assembled pie for 15 minutes while the oven comes to temperature — cold pastry hitting a hot oven is what makes it puff.
  12. Wash and vent
    Brush the crust evenly with the egg wash, getting into the crimped edge, then cut four 2 in (5 cm) slits in the center with a sharp knife. The vents let steam escape so the crust crisps instead of steaming from below and going soggy. Skip the vents and the lid will dome up and then split somewhere you did not choose.
  13. Bake at 400°F
    Set the pie on a rimmed sheet pan to catch drips and bake at 400°F (205°C) on the lower-middle rack for 45 to 55 minutes. It is done when the crust is deep golden brown all over and you can see the filling bubbling thickly through the vents. If the edges darken early, cover just them with strips of foil for the last 15 minutes.
  14. Rest 15 minutes
    Let the pie sit for a full 15 minutes before you cut it, no matter how good it smells. The velouté needs that time to set up, and cutting early gives you a soupy plate instead of clean wedges. The center should read at least 165°F (74°C) on a thermometer, which it will comfortably exceed after that bake.
Know when it is done
Bake at 400°F (205°C) until the crust is deep golden and the filling reads at least 165°F (74°C) in the center.
Serve it with
A buttery Chardonnay or a pint of English bitter, with a sharply dressed green salad to cut the richness.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make ahead: the dough keeps 3 days refrigerated or 3 months frozen, and the filling keeps 3 days. Assemble the pie cold and bake it straight from the fridge, adding 5 to 10 minutes.
  • ◆Leftover roast chicken or a rotisserie bird is a legitimate shortcut — use 4 cups (about 550 g) of shredded meat and skip the browning step entirely.
  • ◆The most common failure is a soggy bottom-of-the-crust texture, which is why this version has a top crust only. If you want a double crust, blind-bake the bottom at 375°F (190°C) for 20 minutes first.
  • ◆Store-bought all-butter puff pastry makes a perfectly respectable lid on a weeknight. Bake at 400°F (205°C) and start checking at 35 minutes.
  • ◆If your filling seems thin after simmering, let it bubble 3 more minutes uncovered; if it is too thick, whisk in warm stock 2 tbsp at a time.

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chicken

Honey garlic sauce

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Dry and season the thighs
    Pat the chicken thighs completely dry with paper towels and season both sides with the kosher salt and black pepper. Dry meat browns; wet meat steams, and you cannot glaze a piece of chicken that never developed any color. Trim off large flaps of fat but leave the thighs whole so they stay juicy.
  2. Mix the sauce first
    Whisk the honey, soy sauce, minced garlic, rice vinegar, sesame oil, and red pepper flakes in a small bowl until the honey has dissolved into the liquid. Having this ready before you turn on the heat matters, because once the chicken is seared everything moves fast. In a separate small cup, stir the cornstarch into the cold water until there are no lumps and set it aside.
  3. Heat the pan properly
    Set a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium-high heat for 3 minutes, then add the oil and swirl. The oil should shimmer and thin out immediately but not send up wisps of smoke. A pan that is not fully preheated is the reason chicken sticks and tears when you try to flip it.
  4. Sear the first side
    Lay the thighs in the pan in a single layer with about 1/2 in (1 cm) of space around each one — six thighs just fit in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet — and then leave them alone for 5 to 6 minutes. Crowding drops the pan temperature and the thighs will release water and simmer instead of browning, so use two batches rather than squeezing them in. You want a deep golden crust and a steady, confident sizzle, not a smoky roar.
  5. Flip and finish the sear
    Turn each thigh with tongs and cook the second side for 4 to 5 minutes. The chicken should release easily now; if it grips the pan, give it another 30 seconds and it will let go on its own. Move the finished thighs to a plate — they will not be fully cooked yet, and that is intentional.
  6. Wipe and lower the heat
    Pour off all but about 1 tsp of fat and turn the heat down to medium-low, waiting a full minute for the pan to cool a little. Honey and garlic both burn fast, and adding them to a screaming pan gives you bitter, black flecks in 20 seconds. The pan should be hot enough to sizzle but not so hot that liquid vanishes on contact.
  7. Build the glaze
    Pour in the sauce and stir constantly, scraping up the browned bits from the searing, for about 1 minute until the garlic smells sweet and mellow rather than sharp. Bring it to a gentle bubble, then stir in the cornstarch slurry and keep stirring for 30 to 60 seconds as it thickens. It should go from watery to a syrup that coats the back of a spoon and holds a line when you drag a finger through it.
  8. Return the chicken
    Slide the thighs and any juices from the plate back into the pan and turn them in the glaze to coat, spooning sauce over the top. Simmer gently for 3 to 4 minutes, flipping once, until the chicken is cooked through and the glaze has tightened around it. If the sauce reduces too far and starts pulling away from the pan, splash in 2 tbsp (30 ml) of water.
  9. Check, rest, and garnish
    Probe the thickest thigh for at least 165°F (74°C) on an instant-read thermometer — thighs are still tender well past this, so 170°F (77°C) is fine. Take the pan off the heat and let it sit for 3 minutes so the glaze clings instead of running off. Scatter the sliced scallions and sesame seeds over the top and serve straight from the skillet.
Know when it is done
Cook to at least 165°F (74°C) at the thickest point; boneless thighs stay juicy up to about 175°F (79°C).
Serve it with
Steamed jasmine rice and quick-blanched broccoli, with a cold lager or an off-dry Riesling.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Chicken breasts work if that is what you have: pound them to an even 3/4 in (2 cm), sear 4 minutes per side, and pull them at exactly 165°F (74°C).
  • ◆Make ahead: the sauce can be whisked together and refrigerated for up to a week. Mix the cornstarch slurry fresh, since it settles into a solid brick.
  • ◆If the glaze turns bitter, the garlic scorched — the fix is to lower the heat and wait a minute before the sauce goes in, and to use minced rather than grated garlic.
  • ◆Serve it over rice and spoon the extra glaze on top; the sauce is salty and sweet enough to season the whole plate.
  • ◆Leftovers keep 4 days and reheat well in a covered pan over low heat with a splash of water to loosen the glaze.

Fried Chicken and Buttermilk Waffles⏱ 2 hr 25 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Crisp boneless thighs on a tangy, crisp-edged buttermilk waffle with hot honey poured over the top. The salty-sweet thing that sounds like a gimmick until you eat it and understand.

BrunchFriedComfort Food
Prep
30 min
Cook
40 min
Total
2 hr 25 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chicken and soak

Dredge and frying

Buttermilk waffles

Hot honey

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Soak the chicken
    Whisk the buttermilk, 1 tbsp kosher salt, hot sauce, and black pepper in a bowl until the salt dissolves, then add the thighs and press them under. Cover and refrigerate for at least 1 hour and up to 12. The salted buttermilk seasons the meat past the surface and keeps boneless thighs from drying out in the fryer.
  2. Mix the waffle dry ingredients
    Whisk the 2 cups flour, sugar, baking powder, baking soda, and 3/4 tsp salt in a large bowl for 20 seconds so the leaveners are evenly distributed. Clumps of baking soda leave metallic-tasting pockets, so break up anything you see. Set this aside while you deal with the chicken.
  3. Whisk the seasoned flour
    In a wide dish, whisk the 2 cups flour, cornstarch, 2 tsp salt, paprika, garlic powder, black pepper, and cayenne until the color is completely uniform. Spoon in 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the buttermilk soak and rub it through with your fingers until you see small pebbly clumps. Those clumps fry into the craggy texture that stands up under syrup instead of going limp.
  4. Dredge and rest
    Lift each thigh from the buttermilk, let it drip a few seconds, then press it firmly into the flour on both sides and set it on a wire rack. Let the coated pieces sit at room temperature for 15 minutes so the flour hydrates and bonds to the meat. Skipping this rest is why coatings slide off in the oil.
  5. Finish the waffle batter
    Whisk the buttermilk, egg yolks, and melted butter together, pour them into the dry ingredients, and stir just until no dry flour remains — lumps are fine and welcome. In a clean bowl, whip the egg whites to soft peaks, about 90 seconds by hand, and fold them in with a spatula in three additions. The whites are what give you a waffle that is crisp outside and airy inside rather than dense.
  6. Heat the oil
    Pour 2 in (5 cm) of oil into a large Dutch oven and heat over medium-high to 350°F (175°C) on a clip-on thermometer. Set a wire rack over a sheet pan next to the stove and heat the oven to 200°F (95°C) for holding. A pinch of dredge dropped in should sizzle briskly and rise within two seconds.
  7. Fry the chicken
    Fry the thighs 4 at a time for 6 to 8 minutes, turning once, keeping the oil between 325 and 350°F (163 and 175°C) by adjusting the burner. Boneless thighs cook much faster than bone-in pieces, so start checking at 6 minutes. They should be deep golden and the sizzle should stay steady rather than dying to a whisper, which means the oil has cooled too far.
  8. Check and hold
    Probe the thickest part of a thigh for at least 165°F (74°C); 170 to 175°F (77 to 79°C) is even better for thigh meat. Move the finished pieces to the wire rack, season with a pinch of salt, and slide the pan into the 200°F (95°C) oven. Never stack fried chicken on a plate or on paper towels, where trapped steam softens the crust in about a minute.
  9. Cook the waffles
    Heat your waffle iron to medium-high and brush both plates lightly with the extra 1 tbsp (14 g) of melted butter. Ladle in enough batter to cover about two-thirds of the grid, close the lid, and cook 4 to 5 minutes, until the steam coming out the sides slows to almost nothing. That steam signal is more reliable than any indicator light on the machine.
  10. Keep the waffles crisp
    Move each finished waffle directly to a rack in the 200°F (95°C) oven alongside the chicken rather than stacking them on a plate. Waffles stacked on top of one another go soft and floppy within 2 minutes from their own steam. They will hold, crisp, for up to 25 minutes this way.
  11. Make the hot honey
    Warm the honey, hot sauce, red pepper flakes, and butter in a small saucepan over low heat, whisking, for about 2 minutes until the butter has melted and everything is glossy and pourable. Do not let it boil, which drives off the honey's floral flavor and can make it bitter. Taste and add more hot sauce if you want it sharper.
  12. Build the plates
    Set a waffle on each plate, lean two thighs against it, and pour the warm hot honey generously over both. Serve immediately, while the chicken still crackles and the waffle is hot enough to melt a knob of butter. A few grinds of black pepper over the honey is not traditional but it is very good.
Know when it is done
Fry at 325 to 350°F (163 to 175°C) and cook the chicken to at least 165°F (74°C); thigh meat is best at 170 to 175°F (77 to 79°C).
Serve it with
Strong black coffee for brunch, or a cold pilsner and pickles if you are doing this for dinner.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make ahead: soak the chicken up to 12 hours in advance and whisk the waffle dry mix a day ahead. The batter itself should be made within 20 minutes of cooking, since the leavening starts working immediately.
  • ◆No waffle iron? Make thick buttermilk pancakes with the same batter, cooking 3 minutes per side on a buttered griddle over medium heat.
  • ◆Bone-in thighs give better flavor but need 12 to 15 minutes in the oil at 325°F (163°C) instead of 6 to 8. Adjust and temp carefully.
  • ◆The hot honey keeps 2 months in a jar at room temperature and is excellent on pizza, roasted carrots, and cornbread.
  • ◆If the coating gets soggy while you finish the waffles, put the chicken back in a 400°F (205°C) oven for 4 minutes on a rack to re-crisp it.

Everything roasts on one pan, but staggered so the potatoes get a head start and the broccoli never turns to mush. Twenty minutes of work and one pan to wash.

4 servings

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chicken

Vegetables

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Heat the oven and the pan
    Set a rack in the upper-middle position and heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) with a heavy rimmed sheet pan inside. A preheated pan means the potatoes start crisping on contact instead of slowly sweating in their own steam. Give the oven a full 20 minutes so the pan is genuinely hot, not just warm.
  2. Dry and season the chicken
    Pat the thighs completely dry with paper towels, then season all over with the 2 tsp kosher salt, black pepper, and paprika, working a little extra into the skin side. Rub the 1 tbsp olive oil over the skin so it browns evenly. Let them sit at room temperature while you prep the vegetables — about 15 minutes, which also takes the fridge chill off.
  3. Cut the vegetables to size
    Halve the baby potatoes so they all have a flat cut face, cut the onion into 8 wedges through the root so they hold together, and break the broccoli into florets no bigger than 2 in (5 cm). Uniform sizes are the whole game on a sheet pan, because a pan of mixed chunks means half of it burns and half stays raw. Keep the broccoli in a separate bowl for now.
  4. Toss potatoes and onion
    Toss the potatoes and onion wedges with 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the olive oil, 1 tsp of the kosher salt, and the black pepper until every surface is slick. Do not skimp on the oil, since dry vegetable surfaces on a hot pan scorch rather than caramelize. Add the smashed garlic cloves now so they soften and sweeten under the chicken.
  5. Start the potatoes alone
    Pull the hot pan out carefully, tip the potatoes cut-side down and the onion wedges onto it, and listen for a loud sizzle. Roast for 15 minutes on their own. Potatoes take considerably longer than chicken thighs, so this head start is what gets everything finishing at the same moment.
  6. Add the chicken
    Slide the pan out, push the vegetables toward the edges, and nestle the thighs skin-up in the middle in a single layer with space around each one. Do not let the thighs overlap the potatoes, or the skin underneath will steam and stay pale. Return the pan to the oven and roast for another 25 minutes, which together with the final stretch after the broccoli goes in gives bone-in thighs the 35 to 37 minutes they genuinely need at this temperature.
  7. Toss and add the broccoli
    While the chicken roasts, toss the broccoli florets with the remaining 1 tbsp (15 ml) olive oil and 1/2 tsp kosher salt. Broccoli needs only about 12 minutes at this temperature and turns grey and limp if it goes in earlier. Getting the timing staggered like this is the difference between a good sheet-pan dinner and a sad one.
  8. Finish everything together
    Scatter the broccoli into any gaps on the pan, keeping it in a single layer and out from under the chicken, and roast for a final 10 to 12 minutes. The florets should be tender at the stem with charred, almost blackened tips, which is where all the flavor lives. If the pan is genuinely full, put the broccoli on a second small pan on the rack below.
  9. Check the chicken
    Probe the thickest thigh next to the bone: 165°F (74°C) is the safe minimum, and 175°F (79°C) is where dark meat actually tastes best. The skin should be deep golden and taut. If the chicken is done but the potatoes need more color, move the thighs to a plate and give the pan 5 more minutes.
  10. Dress and serve
    Let the pan sit for 5 minutes, then squeeze the lemon juice over everything and scatter the parsley and flaky salt. That acid at the end wakes up 40 minutes of roasted, fatty flavors and keeps the plate from tasting heavy. Serve straight from the pan, spooning the garlicky drippings over the potatoes.
Know when it is done
Roast at 425°F (220°C) until the thighs read at least 165°F (74°C); dark meat is best pulled around 175°F (79°C).
Serve it with
A simple red like Côtes du Rhône, or sparkling water with lemon, and nothing else on the table.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Use a heavy aluminum half sheet pan, 18x13 in (46x33 cm). A flimsy pan warps in a hot oven and pools the oil in one corner.
  • ◆Crowding is the number one sheet-pan mistake. If everything does not fit in a single layer with breathing room, use two pans and rotate them halfway through.
  • ◆Swap the broccoli for Brussels sprouts (halved, added with the chicken), green beans (added in the last 12 minutes), or cauliflower florets (added with the chicken).
  • ◆Make ahead: cut the vegetables and season the chicken up to 24 hours in advance and keep them covered in the fridge. Let the chicken sit out 15 minutes before roasting.
  • ◆Chicken breasts can be used but add them for the last 20 minutes only and pull at exactly 165°F (74°C), or they will be dry by the time the potatoes are done.

Japanese Teriyaki Chicken Thighs⏱ 35 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Real teriyaki is four ingredients simmered down around the chicken until it lacquers, not a bottled sauce poured over the top. Skin-on thighs, a hot pan, and 35 minutes.

30 MinutesJapaneseWeeknight
Prep
15 min

Total
35 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chicken

Teriyaki sauce

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Prepare the thighs
    Pat the thighs dry and lay them skin-side down, then use the tip of a knife to score the meat side about 1/4 in (6 mm) deep in a few places. Scoring helps the thick and thin parts cook at the same rate and gives the sauce somewhere to grip. Season the meat side only with the kosher salt, since the sauce is already salty.
  2. Mix the sauce
    Whisk the soy sauce, mirin, sake, sugar, and grated ginger in a small bowl until the sugar has dissolved, about 30 seconds. Equal parts soy sauce and mirin are the backbone of a real teriyaki — soy for salt, mirin for gloss and gentle sweetness — with the sake for depth and the sugar to give the sauce enough body to lacquer. Having it mixed before you start cooking is essential, because the pan moves quickly once the chicken is seared. If you want it sweeter, add sugar a teaspoon at a time rather than more mirin, which would thin the sauce.
  3. Start the skin in a cool pan
    Put the thighs skin-side down in a cold 10 in (25 cm) nonstick or stainless skillet with the 1 tsp oil, then turn the heat to medium. Starting cold lets the fat under the skin render out slowly instead of seizing, which is what gives you crisp skin rather than a rubbery layer. You should hear the sizzle build gradually over the first 2 minutes.
  4. Render the skin
    Cook skin-side down for 8 to 10 minutes without moving the thighs, pressing them flat with a spatula for the first 30 seconds so the whole skin makes contact. Fat will pool in the pan and the skin will go from pale to deep golden and taut. If the sizzle turns violent or you smell scorching, drop the heat to medium-low.
  5. Pour off the fat
    Take the pan off the heat for a moment and tip the rendered fat into a heatproof cup, leaving just a thin film behind. There will be a surprising amount — 2 to 3 tbsp is normal for four thighs. Leaving it all in makes the finished sauce greasy and stops it from clinging to the chicken, because fat and the water-based sauce will not emulsify on their own here. Save the poured-off schmaltz in the fridge; it is superb for frying rice or eggs.
  6. Flip and brown
    Turn the thighs skin-side up and cook the meat side for 3 to 4 minutes over medium heat. You are not looking for deep color here, just enough to firm the surface and set the juices. The thighs will still be a little underdone in the center, which is exactly right before the sauce goes in.
  7. Add the sauce
    Pour the sauce into the pan around the chicken, not over the crisp skin, and let it come to a brisk simmer. It will bubble hard and smell sharply of soy for the first minute as the alcohol cooks off from the sake and mirin. Keep the heat at medium so it reduces steadily rather than scorching at the edges.
  8. Reduce to a lacquer
    Simmer for 4 to 6 minutes, tilting the pan and spooning the sauce over the thighs every 30 seconds or so. The sauce will go from thin and watery to a glossy syrup that clings to the spoon and leaves a clear trail when you drag a spatula across the pan. Watch it closely at the end — the last 30 seconds are when sugar turns from glaze to burnt.
  9. Check, slice, and serve
    Probe the thickest part of a thigh for at least 165°F (74°C); 170 to 175°F (77 to 79°C) is ideal for thighs. Move them to a board, rest for 3 minutes, then slice crosswise into 1/2 in (1 cm) strips and lay them over bowls of hot rice. Spoon the remaining pan sauce over the top and finish with scallions, sesame seeds, and a handful of shredded cabbage on the side.
Know when it is done
Cook thighs to at least 165°F (74°C); they eat best at 170 to 175°F (77 to 79°C) once the fat has rendered.
Serve it with
Hot short-grain rice, shredded cabbage with a squeeze of lemon, and cold barley tea or a light Japanese lager.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Mirin is not optional for real teriyaki — it is what gives the sauce its shine. If you truly cannot find it, use 3 tbsp (45 ml) dry sherry plus 1 tbsp (12 g) extra sugar.
  • ◆Boneless skin-on thighs are worth asking your butcher for. Boneless skinless works, but you lose the rendered fat and the crisp skin that make this dish.
  • ◆Make ahead: the sauce keeps 3 weeks in a jar in the fridge and is excellent on salmon, tofu, or grilled mushrooms.
  • ◆If your sauce breaks or turns grainy, it reduced too far. Whisk in 2 tbsp (30 ml) of water off the heat and it will come back together.
  • ◆Short-grain Japanese rice matters here — rinse it until the water runs clear, then cook with a 1:1.1 ratio of rice to water.

Crispy Orange Chicken⏱ 50 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Cornstarch-battered chicken fried until it crackles, then tossed at the last second in a sharp orange sauce built on real zest and juice. The trick is to sauce it in the final thirty seconds so it never goes soft.

Takeout at HomeFriedFamily Favorite
Prep
25 min
Cook
25 min
Total
50 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chicken and batter

Orange sauce

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Cut and season the chicken
    Trim the thighs and cut them into pieces about 1 in (2.5 cm) across, aiming for cubes rather than long strips so they fry evenly. Toss them with the kosher salt and let them sit 10 minutes. Thighs are the right cut here because they stay juicy through a hard fry, where breast meat turns dry and stringy in the same time.
  2. Make the wet batter
    Whisk the beaten egg and 1 tbsp soy sauce into the chicken with your hands or a spatula until every piece is slick and evenly coated. This thin egg layer is the glue the dry starch grabs onto, so do not skip it or thin it with water — a watery coating slides off in the oil and leaves you with bald, pale chicken. Let it sit for 5 minutes while you set up the dredge, which gives the soy a moment to season the meat. The bowl should look glossy with no dry patches and no puddle of liquid at the bottom.
  3. Set up the starch coating
    Whisk the 3/4 cup cornstarch with the 1/4 cup flour in a shallow bowl. Cornstarch is the key to a shell that stays crisp under sauce, and the small amount of flour gives it enough structure not to shatter into dust. Lift each piece of chicken out and press it into the mixture, then set it on a rack in a single layer.
  4. Build the sauce
    Combine the orange juice, zest, 1/4 cup soy sauce, sugar, rice vinegar, ginger, garlic, and red pepper flakes in a small saucepan and whisk to dissolve the sugar. Bring it to a simmer over medium heat and cook for 4 to 5 minutes to soften the raw bite of the garlic and ginger. It should smell distinctly of orange, not just sweet — if it does not, add another teaspoon of zest.
  5. Thicken the sauce
    Stir the cornstarch slurry to recombine it, then whisk it into the simmering sauce and cook for 45 to 60 seconds. It will turn from cloudy to glossy and thick enough to coat a spoon in a smooth sheet. Take it off the heat immediately, because overcooked cornstarch loses its thickening power and goes thin again.
  6. Heat the oil to 350°F
    Pour 2 in (5 cm) of oil into a Dutch oven or wok and heat over medium-high to 350°F (175°C) on a clip-on thermometer. Set a wire rack over a sheet pan next to the stove. A pinch of cornstarch dropped in should sizzle immediately and float, and the surface of the oil should look faintly shimmery, not smoking.
  7. Fry the first round
    Lower in about a third of the chicken piece by piece so they do not clump, and fry for 3 to 4 minutes until pale golden and firm. Keep the oil between 325 and 350°F (163 and 175°C) by adjusting the heat. Move the pieces to the rack and repeat with the remaining two batches, letting the oil come back to temperature between them.
  8. Fry the second round
    Bring the oil up to 375°F (190°C) and fry all the chicken again, in two batches, for 60 to 90 seconds until deep golden and audibly crisp. This double fry is what makes takeout-style chicken stay crunchy — the first fry cooks it through, the second drives off surface moisture and hardens the shell. Do not skip it.
  9. Check the temperature
    Probe one of the larger pieces for at least 165°F (74°C); after a double fry they will usually be at 175°F (79°C) or above, which is perfect for thigh meat. If any pieces feel soft or look pale, give them another 30 seconds in the oil. Drain everything on the wire rack, never on paper towels.
  10. Toss at the last second
    Warm the sauce briefly in a large bowl or wok, add all the fried chicken at once, and toss for no more than 30 seconds until every piece is coated. Move fast: cornstarch shells stay crisp for about a minute in sauce and then start to soften. If the sauce has stiffened up while sitting, loosen it with 1 tbsp (15 ml) of hot water first.
  11. Serve immediately
    Turn the chicken out over hot jasmine rice and scatter the scallions and sesame seeds over the top. This is a dish that is genuinely at its best in the first three minutes, so have everyone at the table before you toss. Any sauce left in the bowl should be spooned over the rice, not the chicken.
  12. Deal with leftovers
    If you know you will have leftovers, hold back some fried chicken unsauced and store the sauce separately in the fridge for up to 4 days. Re-crisp the plain chicken on a rack in a 400°F (205°C) oven for 6 to 8 minutes, then toss it with warmed sauce. Sauced chicken stored overnight turns soft and cannot be brought back.
Know when it is done
Fry at 350°F (175°C), then again at 375°F (190°C). Chicken must reach at least 165°F (74°C); thigh pieces land around 175°F (79°C).
Serve it with
Steamed jasmine rice and stir-fried snow peas, with jasmine tea or a cold, simple lager.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Fresh orange juice and real zest are what separate this from the cloying bottled version. Bottled juice tastes flat and needs an extra tablespoon of vinegar to compensate.
  • ◆The double fry is non-negotiable for crispness, but you can do the first fry up to 2 hours ahead and leave the chicken on a rack at room temperature.
  • ◆If you own a wok, use it. The sloped sides let you fry in less oil and toss the chicken in sauce in the same vessel.
  • ◆Strain and save the cooled frying oil in a jar; it will handle two or three more fries before it starts tasting used.
  • ◆For a lighter version, toss the coated chicken with 3 tbsp (45 ml) oil and roast at 450°F (230°C) for 20 minutes, turning once. It will not be as crisp but it is genuinely good.

Oven-Roasted Chicken Shawarma⏱ 5 hr 20 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Thighs marinated in warm spices and lemon, roasted hot until the edges char like meat off a spit. Piled into pita with garlicky yogurt, it is one of the best things you can make from a bag of thighs.

Middle EasternMake AheadCrowd Pleaser
Prep
20 min
Cook
35 min
Total
5 hr 20 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chicken and marinade

Garlic yogurt sauce

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Mix the spice blend
    Whisk the cumin, paprika, coriander, turmeric, cinnamon, allspice, cayenne, kosher salt, and black pepper together in a bowl and smell it. This warm, slightly sweet blend is the whole identity of shawarma, and the cinnamon and allspice in small amounts are what make it taste right rather than merely spicy. If your ground spices are more than a year old, replace them, because they lose almost everything after that.
  2. Build the marinade
    Whisk the olive oil, lemon juice, and minced garlic into the spices until you have a loose, brick-red paste. The oil carries the fat-soluble flavors into the meat and protects the spices from burning in a hot oven. It should be thick enough to cling to a spoon but pourable — add another tablespoon of oil if it is pasty.
  3. Marinate 4 to 24 hours
    Turn the chicken thighs in the marinade until they are completely coated, then cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours and up to 24. Four hours is the minimum for the spices to move past the surface; overnight is noticeably better. Turn the container once partway through so nothing sits dry at the top.
  4. Make the yogurt sauce
    Whisk the Greek yogurt, tahini, grated garlic, lemon juice, and salt until smooth, then thin it with the cold water until it pours slowly off a spoon. Grating the garlic rather than mincing it dissolves it completely so nobody gets a raw chunk. Make this at least 30 minutes ahead and refrigerate it so the garlic mellows and the flavors marry.
  5. Heat the oven very hot
    Set a rack in the upper-middle position and heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) with a heavy rimmed sheet pan inside. You need real heat to char the edges of the chicken the way a vertical spit does, and a preheated pan gives you a hard sear on the underside. Give it a full 20 minutes at temperature.
  6. Take the chill off
    Pull the chicken out of the fridge 20 minutes before roasting and let it come partway to room temperature on the counter. Ice-cold thighs need extra oven time, which means the surface dries out before the center is done. Do not rinse or wipe off the marinade — those clinging spices are what char into the good bits.
  7. Roast in a single layer
    Lay the thighs flat on the hot pan with at least 1/2 in (1 cm) between them and listen for an immediate sizzle. Roast for 20 minutes without turning. Crowding the pan makes them release liquid and boil in it, which is the difference between shawarma and grey stewed chicken — use two pans if you must.
  8. Broil for the char
    Switch the oven to broil on high, move the pan to about 6 in (15 cm) below the element, and broil for 3 to 5 minutes until the edges blacken in spots and the surface blisters. Stay at the oven door and watch it, because it goes from perfect to burnt in under a minute. That char is exactly what you are chasing.
  9. Check the temperature
    Probe the thickest thigh for at least 165°F (74°C); thighs are still tender at 175°F (79°C), so do not panic if you overshoot. If the chicken is not there yet, turn the broiler off, return the oven to 425°F (220°C), and give it 4 more minutes. Never judge doneness here by color alone, since the dark spice crust makes everything look further along than it is.
  10. Rest and slice thin
    Rest the thighs on a board for 5 minutes, then slice them across the grain into strips about 1/4 in (6 mm) wide. Thin slicing is what makes it read as shawarma rather than as roast chicken pieces. Pour any juices left on the board and pan back over the sliced meat.
  11. Build the sandwiches
    Warm the pitas directly over a gas flame or in a dry skillet for 20 seconds a side until they are pliable and blistered. Smear yogurt sauce down the middle, pile on the sliced chicken, then add tomato, red onion, cucumber, parsley, and pickles. Roll it tightly and wrap the bottom half in foil or parchment, which is the only thing standing between you and it falling apart.
Know when it is done
Roast at 425°F (220°C), then broil. Chicken must reach at least 165°F (74°C); thighs remain juicy up to 175°F (79°C).
Serve it with
Warm pita, pickled turnips, and a cold Lebanese lager or mint lemonade over crushed ice.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make ahead: the marinade and the yogurt sauce can both be made 3 days in advance, and the chicken can marinate a full 24 hours. This is a great dish to prep on Sunday for a Tuesday.
  • ◆No pita? Serve it over rice or a chopped salad with the yogurt sauce thinned into a dressing. It loses nothing.
  • ◆Bone-in, skin-on thighs are even better if you have the time — roast them at 425°F (220°C) for 35 to 40 minutes, then broil and pull the meat off.
  • ◆The most common mistake is a crowded pan. Chicken that touches releases steam and never chars, so give every thigh its own space.
  • ◆Leftover sliced shawarma keeps 4 days and reheats best in a dry hot skillet for 2 minutes, which brings back some of the crisp edges.
