Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Handle the chiles carefully
    Wear gloves to stem and halve the Scotch bonnets, and keep your hands away from your face for the rest of the evening. Two chiles gives real heat you can eat comfortably, four gives you the authentic Jamaican level that will make you sweat. Removing the seeds and white pith drops the heat by roughly half without losing the fruity, apricot-like flavor that makes Scotch bonnets irreplaceable here.
  2. Blend the jerk paste
    Put the chiles, scallions, garlic, ginger, allspice, thyme, brown sugar, soy sauce, lime juice, oil, nutmeg, cinnamon, and black pepper in a blender and blend to a thick, dark green-brown paste, about 45 seconds. Scrape the sides down once and blend again — you want it smooth enough to spread but not liquid. Allspice, called pimento in Jamaica, is the defining flavor, so measure it generously and do not substitute.
  3. Score and salt the chicken
    Cut the chicken into 8 pieces, then slash each piece two or three times through the skin down to the bone with a sharp knife. Season all over with the 1 tbsp kosher salt. Those cuts are not decorative: they let the paste reach the meat and they let heat penetrate faster, so the surface does not burn while the inside catches up.
  4. Marinate 12 to 24 hours
    Rub the paste into every piece with gloved hands, pushing it into the slashes and under the skin wherever it will go. Seal it in a bag or covered container and refrigerate for at least 12 hours and up to 24. Jerk is a rub-and-wait dish; anything under 12 hours tastes like spiced chicken rather than jerk.
  5. Set up indirect heat
    For charcoal, bank a chimney of lit coals to one side of the kettle and leave the other side empty; for gas, light the burners on one side only and keep the others off. Aim for a grill temperature of 325 to 350°F (163 to 175°C) with the lid on and the vents about half open. Jerk is traditionally cooked slowly over smoldering pimento wood, and this two-zone setup is the home approximation.
  6. Add the smoke
    Drain the soaked wood chips and scatter about half of them directly onto the coals, or seal them in a foil packet punched with holes and set it over a lit gas burner. Wait until you see thin blue-white smoke rather than thick white billows, which taste acrid. Oil the grate with a folded paper towel gripped in tongs just before the chicken goes on.
  7. Cook on the cool side
    Lay the chicken pieces skin-up on the indirect side, close the lid, and cook for 30 to 35 minutes without opening. Do not put it over direct flame yet — the sugar and soy in the paste will scorch black in under 5 minutes. Add the second half of the wood chips at the 15-minute mark.
  8. Check the progress
    After 30 minutes, lift the lid and look: the paste should have dried into a dark crust and the skin should be pulling back from the drumstick bones. Rotate the pieces so the ones nearest the fire move to the far edge, since even an indirect zone has a hot end. Close the lid and give it another 5 to 10 minutes if the pieces still feel soft.
  9. Finish over direct heat
    Move the pieces over the coals skin-side down for 2 to 3 minutes to char and crisp, turning once. Stay right there with tongs, because flare-ups happen fast when rendered fat hits fire and 30 seconds of inattention costs you a piece. If flames climb, move the chicken back to the cool side rather than dousing the fire.
  10. Check the temperature
    Probe the thickest part of each piece away from bone: the breast needs 165°F (74°C) and the thighs and drumsticks are better at 175°F (79°C). The dark crust makes everything look done long before it is, so the thermometer is doing all the real work here. Pull each piece as it hits its number rather than waiting for the whole batch.
  11. Rest and chop
    Rest the chicken on a board for 10 minutes so the juices settle back into the meat. Traditionally jerk is then chopped through the bone into rough chunks with a cleaver, which is worth doing if you have the right knife and a sturdy board. Squeeze lime wedges over everything just before serving. Put the prepared jerk or hot pepper sauce on the table in a small bowl rather than pouring it over the chicken, so everyone can set their own heat level.
  12. Oven method
    With no grill, roast the marinated pieces skin-up on a rack over a sheet pan at 375°F (190°C) for 35 to 40 minutes, then broil 4 in (10 cm) from the element for 3 to 4 minutes to char. You lose the smoke, so whisk the 1 tsp (3 g) of smoked paprika into the paste before marinating to compensate. Temp the same way: 165°F (74°C) minimum, 175°F (79°C) for dark meat.
Know when it is done
Cook over indirect heat at 325 to 350°F (163 to 175°C) until the breast reads 165°F (74°C) and dark meat reads 175°F (79°C).
Serve it with
Rice and peas, fried plantain, and a cold Red Stripe with a lime wedge.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make ahead: the jerk paste keeps 2 weeks in the fridge and 6 months frozen in an ice cube tray. It is excellent on pork shoulder, shrimp, and roasted sweet potatoes.
  • ◆Scotch bonnets are worth hunting down for their fruity aroma, but habaneros are a genuine one-for-one substitute. Jalapeños are not — you lose the whole character.
  • ◆Wear gloves and wash the blender immediately. Capsaicin oil lingers on plastic and will find your eyes hours later.
  • ◆If the heat is too much for the table, serve it with plenty of rice and peas and a bowl of coleslaw. Dairy and starch both blunt capsaicin far better than water.
  • ◆Pimento wood is traditional and available online; hickory or apple chips are a fine everyday stand-in.

Herb Roasted Turkey Breast⏱ 7 hr 10 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

All the good parts of Thanksgiving without wrestling a twenty-pound bird — a bone-in breast, herb butter under the skin, and two hours in the oven. It feeds six and slices beautifully.

HolidayRoastingFeeds a Crowd
Prep
20 min
Cook
1 hr 45 min
Total
7 hr 10 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Turkey

Herb butter

Pan and gravy

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Thaw completely
    A frozen 6 lb (2.7 kg) breast needs about 24 hours in the refrigerator to thaw, so plan a day ahead. Roasting a partially frozen breast guarantees a dry outer inch and an undercooked center. Press the thickest part with your thumb — it should give evenly with no hard core.
  2. Dry and salt the breast
    Pat the turkey bone dry with paper towels, then mix the kosher salt with the baking powder and rub it over all the skin and into the underside. Set it on a rack over a sheet pan and refrigerate uncovered for at least 4 hours, or up to 24 if you can. The baking powder raises the skin's pH so it browns faster, and the dry fridge air dehydrates the surface for crisper results.
  3. Make the herb butter
    Mash the softened butter with the sage, parsley, rosemary, thyme, garlic, and lemon zest until it is uniformly green-flecked. Keep it at room temperature so it is spreadable but not melted — melted butter will not stay where you put it. Taste a small amount; it should be assertively herbal, since it has a lot of mild meat to season.
  4. Butter under the skin
    Slide your fingers between the skin and the meat, starting at the wide end, and work carefully to loosen the whole surface without tearing it. Push about two-thirds of the herb butter into that pocket and press from the outside to spread it evenly over both lobes. Rub the remaining butter over the outside of the skin and grind the black pepper over the top.
  5. Come to room temperature
    Leave the buttered breast on the counter for 45 minutes before it goes in the oven. Turkey breast is a thick, dense piece of lean meat, and starting it cold means the outside overcooks by 20°F before the center reaches temperature. This one step meaningfully improves how juicy the finished slices are.
  6. Heat the oven to 425°F
    Set a rack in the lower-middle position and heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). You will start hot to set the skin and then drop the temperature, which gives you color without drying out the meat. Give the oven a full 20 minutes after it beeps so it is truly saturated with heat.
  7. Build the vegetable rack
    Scatter the onion rings and carrot pieces across the bottom of a roasting pan or a large oven-safe skillet, then set the turkey breast skin-up directly on top of them. The vegetables lift the meat so hot air circulates underneath and they keep the drippings from scorching on the bare pan. Pour 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the stock into the pan around them.
  8. Roast hot, then drop the heat
    Roast at 425°F (220°C) for 20 minutes to set and start browning the skin, then reduce the oven to 350°F (175°C) without opening the door. Continue roasting for 75 to 90 minutes more, depending on size — figure roughly 15 minutes per pound at the lower temperature, so about 75 minutes for a 5 lb (2.3 kg) breast and 90 for a 6 lb (2.7 kg) one. If the skin browns faster than you like, lay a loose sheet of foil over the top.
  9. Temp in the right place
    Slide an instant-read thermometer into the thickest part of the breast, parallel to the bone and not touching it, and look for 160°F (71°C) if you are resting it or a full 165°F (74°C) if you are not. Carryover cooking will add 5 to 10°F (3 to 6°C) during the rest, which is why pulling at 160°F (71°C) and resting is the reliable way to hit 165°F (74°C) without overshooting. Check in two places, since one lobe is often thicker.
  10. Rest 20 minutes
    Move the breast to a carving board and rest it for a full 20 minutes, loosely tented only if your kitchen is cold. A large piece of meat needs this long for the juices to redistribute, and cutting early will flood your board and leave the slices dry. Use the time to make the gravy.
  11. Make the pan gravy
    Set the roasting pan over medium heat, pull out the vegetables, and whisk the flour into the fat and drippings, cooking for 2 minutes until it smells toasty. Pour in the remaining 1 cup (240 ml) of stock in a slow stream while whisking hard, and simmer for 4 to 5 minutes until it coats a spoon. Take it off the heat, swirl in the cold butter, and taste before adding any salt — the drippings are already seasoned.
Know when it is done
Pull the breast at 160°F (71°C) and rest 20 minutes; carryover brings it to a safe 165°F (74°C). Never serve poultry below 165°F (74°C).
Serve it with
A dry Riesling or Pinot Noir, with mashed potatoes, buttered green beans, and plenty of the pan gravy.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make ahead: salt the breast up to 24 hours in advance and make the herb butter up to 3 days ahead. On the day, it is mostly hands-off oven time.
  • ◆A boneless rolled breast works too but cooks faster — start checking at 60 minutes total and pull at the same 160°F (71°C) before resting.
  • ◆Save the bone. Simmered with an onion and a bay leaf for 3 hours it makes stock that turns leftover turkey into an excellent soup.
  • ◆Leftover slices keep 4 days and are best reheated gently in a covered pan with a splash of stock, which keeps them from turning to sawdust.
  • ◆Dried herbs can stand in at one-third the volume, but fresh sage and rosemary really do make the difference here.

Chicken Cordon Bleu⏱ 2 hr 5 min🍽 4 servingsAdvanced▾

Pounded chicken breast rolled around ham and Gruyère, breaded, seared, and baked until the cheese pulls in strings when you cut it. Fussy in the best way, and genuinely impressive on a plate.

Date NightImpressiveMake Ahead
Prep
40 min
Cook
30 min
Total
2 hr 5 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chicken rolls

Breading

Dijon cream sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Butterfly the breasts
    Lay each breast flat and, holding your knife parallel to the board, slice horizontally through the thick side almost but not all the way through, then open it like a book. Work slowly and keep your guiding hand flat on top of the meat. If a breast has a tenderloin attached underneath, pull it off and save it for another use, since it will not roll cleanly.
  2. Pound them thin
    Place each butterflied breast between two sheets of plastic wrap and pound from the center outward with a mallet or a heavy pan until it is an even 1/4 in (6 mm) thick. Use glancing, spreading blows rather than straight-down smashes, which tear holes. Any hole in the meat is a hole the cheese will escape through, so patch tears by overlapping the edges.
  3. Season and spread
    Season both sides of each pounded breast with the kosher salt and black pepper, then spread a thin layer of the 2 tsp Dijon over the inside face. The mustard adds a sharp note that cuts the richness and it also helps the ham stick to the meat. Do not oversalt — the ham and Gruyère are both already salty.
  4. Layer the filling
    Lay 2 slices of ham on each breast, leaving a clear 1/2 in (1 cm) border on all sides, then set a baton of Gruyère along the short edge nearest you. That border is critical: filling that reaches the edge will push out and leak in the pan. Cut the cheese into batons rather than using slices so it sits in a compact log.
  5. Roll them tight
    Starting from the cheese end, roll each breast up as tightly as you can, tucking the sides inward as you go like a burrito. Wrap each roll snugly in plastic wrap, twisting the ends like a candy wrapper to compress it into a firm cylinder. Chill the wrapped rolls for at least 30 minutes so they hold their shape when they hit the breading station.
  6. Set up the breading
    Put the flour in one shallow dish, the beaten eggs in a second, and the panko tossed with the melted butter and 1/2 tsp salt in a third. Buttering the panko is what lets it brown deeply in the oven without needing a deep fry. Keep one hand for dry and one for wet so you do not end up with breaded fingers.
  7. Bread the rolls
    Unwrap a roll, dredge it in flour and tap off every bit of excess, dip it in the egg and let the drips fall away, then press it into the panko, packing crumbs on firmly all over. Set it seam-side down on a rack. Excess flour is the usual reason breading falls off in the pan, so be thorough about that tap.
  8. Chill again
    Refrigerate the breaded rolls uncovered on the rack for 15 to 20 minutes while the oven heats to 375°F (190°C). This second chill sets the coating so it stays on during searing and firms up the rolls so they hold their cylinder. It also gives the panko time to absorb a little moisture and adhere.
  9. Sear all sides
    Heat the 1/4 cup oil in a 12 in (30 cm) oven-safe skillet over medium heat until it shimmers, then add the rolls seam-side down and sear for about 2 minutes per side, turning to hit all four faces. It should sizzle steadily and the panko should turn deep golden; if it browns in under a minute, the pan is too hot. Use two spatulas or tongs and turn gently so the coating stays intact.
  10. Bake to temperature
    Transfer the skillet to the 375°F (190°C) oven and bake for 15 to 18 minutes. If your skillet is not oven-safe, move the rolls to a rack set over a sheet pan instead, which keeps the bottom from going soft. The rolls will firm up noticeably and you may see a little cheese bubbling at a seam, which is fine.
  11. Check the center
    Slide an instant-read thermometer into the thickest part of a roll, through the side and into the chicken rather than the cheese pocket, and look for 165°F (74°C). Chicken breast has no fat to protect it, so pull them the moment they arrive. Rest the rolls on a rack for 5 minutes before slicing so the molten cheese sets just enough to stay put.
  12. Make the Dijon cream
    Pour the oil out of the skillet, add the 1 tbsp butter, and cook the shallot over medium heat for 2 minutes until translucent. Pour in the wine, scrape the bottom, and reduce it by half, about 3 minutes, then add the cream, Dijon, thyme, and salt. Simmer for 3 to 4 minutes until it coats a spoon, and taste before adding more salt.
  13. Slice and serve
    Cut each roll crosswise on a slight diagonal into three or four thick slices and fan them on the plate so the ham and cheese spiral shows. Spoon the sauce onto the plate underneath rather than over the top, which keeps the panko crisp. Serve immediately, while the cheese still stretches.
Know when it is done
Bake at 375°F (190°C) until the chicken at the center of the roll reads 165°F (74°C) on an instant-read thermometer.
Serve it with
A dry white Burgundy or Alsatian Pinot Blanc, with buttered egg noodles and a bitter greens salad.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make ahead: assemble and bread the rolls up to 24 hours in advance and keep them uncovered on a rack in the fridge. Sear and bake straight from cold, adding 3 to 4 minutes in the oven.
  • ◆Gruyère is traditional and melts beautifully, but Emmental, Comté, or a good Swiss all work. Avoid pre-shredded cheese, which is coated in starch and melts gummy.
  • ◆The number one failure is cheese leaking out. The fixes are a clean 1/2 in border, a tight plastic-wrap roll, and a full 30-minute chill before breading.
  • ◆For a fully crisp shell, shallow-fry the rolls in 1/2 in (1 cm) of oil at 350°F (175°C) for 3 minutes per side and skip the searing step, then bake 12 minutes.
  • ◆These freeze well breaded but unbaked. Freeze on a tray, bag them, and bake from frozen at 375°F (190°C) for 35 to 40 minutes to 165°F (74°C).

Chicken Satay with Peanut Sauce⏱ 2 hr 40 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Turmeric and lemongrass marinated chicken threaded onto skewers, grilled hard and fast, and dunked in a peanut sauce with real body. Great as dinner, even better as something to hand people standing in a kitchen.

GrillParty FoodSoutheast Asian
Prep
25 min
Cook
15 min
Total
2 hr 40 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chicken and marinade

Peanut sauce

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Cut the chicken for skewers
    Slice the thighs with the grain into strips about 1 in (2.5 cm) wide and 4 in (10 cm) long so they can be threaded and will not fall apart. Cutting with the grain rather than across it gives strips that hold together on a skewer. Keep the thickness even at about 1/2 in (1 cm) so they grill in the same amount of time.
  2. Prep the lemongrass
    Trim the dry top and root end off the lemongrass stalk, peel away the tough outer layers, and mince only the pale, tender bottom 4 in (10 cm) as finely as you can. Lemongrass fibers stay woody no matter how long you cook them, so the fineness of the mince genuinely matters. If you cannot find fresh, use 1 tbsp of lemongrass paste or the zest of one lime.
  3. Mix the marinade
    Whisk the 1 cup coconut milk, fish sauce, brown sugar, lemongrass, garlic, ginger, turmeric, coriander, cumin, and kosher salt until the sugar dissolves and the mixture is a uniform bright yellow. Turmeric stains everything it touches, so keep it off wooden spoons and light countertops. It should smell fragrant and savory rather than sharply fishy — the fish sauce mellows completely once cooked.
  4. Marinate 2 to 12 hours
    Turn the chicken strips in the marinade until coated, cover, and refrigerate for at least 2 hours and up to 12. Coconut milk marinades are gentle and there is no acid to worry about, so a long soak here only helps. Give the container a shake once partway through.
  5. Soak the skewers
    Submerge the bamboo skewers in water for at least 30 minutes, weighing them down with a plate so they stay under. Dry bamboo catches fire over direct heat and you will end up with half a skewer and chicken in the coals. Metal skewers skip this step entirely and are worth buying if you do this often.
  6. Make the peanut sauce
    Warm the peanut butter, 1 cup coconut milk, fish sauce, lime juice, brown sugar, soy sauce, and red curry paste in a small saucepan over medium-low heat, whisking constantly for 4 to 5 minutes. It will look separated and grainy at first and then suddenly come together into a smooth, glossy sauce. Whisk in hot water 1 tbsp at a time until it pours slowly off the spoon like heavy cream.
  7. Taste and balance
    Taste the sauce and adjust it against four points: salty from the fish sauce, sour from the lime, sweet from the sugar, and hot from the curry paste. It should taste slightly too intense on its own, because it will be eaten in small amounts alongside mild chicken. Set it aside off the heat, where it will thicken as it cools — loosen it again with hot water before serving.
  8. Thread the skewers
    Weave each strip of chicken onto a skewer in a loose S-shape, pushing it down to leave about 2 in (5 cm) of bare skewer at the handle end. Do not pack the meat tight against itself, because the pressed surfaces will steam instead of char. One or two strips per skewer is right for 16 skewers.
  9. Get the grill hot
    Heat a charcoal grill until the coals are covered in white ash, or a gas grill to high, aiming for a hot direct zone around 450°F (230°C). Scrub the grate, then wipe it with a paper towel soaked in the 1 tbsp (15 ml) of neutral oil and held in tongs, doing this just before the skewers go on so the oil is still slick. If the exposed skewer ends worry you, lay a folded strip of foil along the edge of the grate and rest the handles on it.
  10. Grill hard and fast
    Lay the skewers over direct heat and grill for 3 to 4 minutes per side, turning once, until the edges char and the surface looks lacquered. The coconut milk and sugar in the marinade brown quickly, so stay at the grill and move any skewer that is coloring too fast to a cooler spot. Total time is only 6 to 8 minutes — this is not a walk-away dish.
  11. Check, then serve hot
    Probe the thickest piece on a skewer for at least 165°F (74°C); thigh meat this thin usually gets there right as the char develops. Pile the skewers on a platter, scatter the cilantro and chopped peanuts, and serve with the warm peanut sauce, lime wedges, and sliced cucumber alongside. The cucumber is not decoration — its coolness is what lets you keep eating.
Know when it is done
Grill over direct high heat until the chicken reaches at least 165°F (74°C) at the thickest point.
Serve it with
Jasmine rice or cucumber salad, with a cold Singha or an off-dry Riesling to handle the chili.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make ahead: the peanut sauce keeps 1 week refrigerated and the chicken can marinate up to 12 hours. Reheat the sauce gently with a splash of water, since it sets firm when cold.
  • ◆Use natural peanut butter with no added sugar or palm oil. The sweetened kind makes a cloying sauce you cannot balance back.
  • ◆Chicken breast works if you slice it thin and pull it at exactly 165°F (74°C), but thighs stay far juicier over high heat.
  • ◆No grill? Broil the skewers 4 in (10 cm) from the element for 4 minutes per side, or cook them in a hot cast-iron grill pan in two batches.
  • ◆Double the peanut sauce and keep the extra for noodles, roasted broccoli, or as a dressing thinned with lime juice and water.

This is the patient chapter — rubs that sit overnight, fires that hold steady, and meat that goes from tough to tender if you just let it. Learn the stall, learn when to wrap, and always let it rest.

Oven Baby Back Ribs, Grill Finished⏱ 3 hr 50 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

A low oven does the patient work, then five minutes over live fire sets the glaze. You get ribs that pull cleanly off the bone with a lacquered edge, and you never need a smoker.

BBQOvenWeekend
Prep
20 min
Cook
3 hr 20 min
Total
3 hr 50 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the ribs

Dry rub

Glaze

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Pull off the membrane
    Flip each rack bone side up and slide a butter knife under the thin shiny membrane at one end until you can lift a corner. Grab that corner with a paper towel for grip and peel the whole sheet off in one steady pull. If it tears, start again at the nearest bone. Left on, it turns papery and rubbery, blocks the rub, and never becomes tender.
  2. Mix and apply the rub
    Whisk the brown sugar, paprika, salt, pepper, garlic powder, onion powder, chili powder, and cayenne together until the color is completely uniform. Smear each rack with 1 tbsp of yellow mustard — at this amount you will not taste it, it just glues the rub down. Sprinkle the rub from about 12 inches (30 cm) above so it lands evenly, heavy on the meat side and light on the bone side. Let the racks sit 30 minutes at room temperature until the rub looks wet and dissolved rather than powdery.
  3. Set up a low oven
    Heat the oven to 275°F (135°C) with a rack in the middle position. Line a large rimmed sheet pan with foil and set a wire rack inside it so hot air can circulate underneath the ribs. Low and slow is not just a slogan: below about 300°F (150°C) the collagen has time to melt into gelatin before the lean meat between the bones dries out.
  4. Bake uncovered for two hours
    Lay the racks bone side down on the wire rack and bake uncovered for 2 hours. The surface will darken and dry into a tacky crust, which is the bark forming, and you want it set before you wrap anything. Somewhere in the second hour the internal temperature usually parks between 150 and 165°F (65 and 74°C) and simply stops climbing. That plateau is the stall: moisture evaporating off the surface cools the meat almost exactly as fast as the oven heats it.
  5. Wrap through the stall
    Tear two double-layer sheets of heavy foil about 24 inches (60 cm) long. Set each rack meat side down on a sheet, dot with 1 tbsp butter, splash 2 tbsp (30 ml) apple juice around it, and fold the foil into a tightly sealed packet. Wrapping stops evaporation, which breaks the stall — the temperature usually starts climbing again within 20 minutes. Meat side down means the top of the rack sits in the buttery liquid instead of above it.
  6. Braise inside the foil
    Return the packets to the sheet pan and bake another 1 hour to 1 hour 15 minutes. The ribs are steaming now rather than roasting, and that moist heat is what carries them from tough to tender quickly. Move the packets gently, because a torn seam dumps hot liquid onto the oven floor and costs you the steam you just built.
  7. Test for real doneness
    Open one packet carefully with your face turned away, since the trapped steam is scalding. Lift the rack in the middle with tongs: it should bow deeply and the surface should crack slightly, and a toothpick pushed between two bones should slide in with no resistance at all. In the meat between the bones you want 198 to 203°F (92 to 95°C). If it is still stiff, seal it back up and give it another 20 minutes.
  8. Warm the glaze
    While the ribs finish, whisk the barbecue sauce, cider vinegar, and honey together in a small saucepan over low heat for 3 to 4 minutes. The vinegar cuts the sweetness so the glaze tastes bright instead of like candy, and the honey helps it cling to the bark. Keep it just warm and pourable, because if it reduces too far it sets like glue the moment it hits the meat.
  9. Finish over high heat
    Heat a grill to medium-high, around 425°F (220°C), or move an oven rack to 6 inches (15 cm) below the broiler. Unwrap the racks, brush the meat side with a thin coat of glaze, and cook 4 to 6 minutes while watching constantly. Sugar goes from glossy to scorched in under a minute, so pull them the second the surface bubbles and darkens at the edges.
  10. Glaze a second time
    Brush on one more thin layer of glaze and give it 2 more minutes to set into a tacky lacquer. Two thin coats build a far better shine than one thick coat, which tends to slide off in sheets the moment you cut. Keep whatever glaze is left in the pan to pass at the table.
  11. Rest, then slice
    Move the racks to a cutting board and let them rest 10 minutes so the juices redistribute and the glaze firms up. Flip each rack bone side up, where you can see exactly where the bones run, which makes clean cuts easy. Slice between the bones with single long strokes of a sharp knife instead of sawing, and serve with the reserved glaze.
Know when it is done
Ribs are tender at 198 to 203°F (92 to 95°C) in the meat between the bones, but the bend test matters more than the number.
Serve it with
Vinegary coleslaw, buttered corn, and a cold lager or a glass of dry cider.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make-ahead: cook through the foil stage up to 2 days early, chill the sealed packets, then reheat at 300°F (150°C) for 30 minutes and glaze right before serving.
  • ◆Baby backs are leaner and faster than spare ribs. If you swap in a 3 lb (1.4 kg) St. Louis rack, add about 1 hour to the uncovered stage.
  • ◆Meat that literally falls off the bone is technically overcooked. If you want a little bite left, start checking at 45 minutes in the foil.
  • ◆No apple juice on hand? Use apple cider, cola, or plain water with a splash of cider vinegar — the point of the liquid is steam, not flavor.

Spritz and wrap

Glaze

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Trim to the St. Louis cut
    Lay a rack meat side down and find the line of cartilage-tipped rib ends running diagonally across one side. Cut straight across just outside that line with a sharp boning knife to remove the whole strip, then trim the flap of meat and the pointed skirt off the back. What is left is a neat rectangle that cooks evenly instead of a wedge with thin ends that scorch. Save the trimmings — they smoke in about 2 hours and are the cook's snack.
  2. Remove the membrane
    Slip a butter knife under the silverskin membrane at the wide end of the bone side and lift a corner free. Grip it with a paper towel and peel it off the whole rack in one motion. Spare ribs have a tougher membrane than baby backs, so work slowly and re-start at a bone if it shreds. Smoke and rub cannot get through it, and it cooks up like plastic.
  3. Season the night before
    Combine all the rub ingredients and break up any lumps of sugar with your fingers. Coat each rack with 1 tbsp mustard, then dust the rub on heavily from a foot above, about 3 tbsp per side. Refrigerate uncovered on a rack over a sheet pan for at least 4 hours and ideally overnight; the salt penetrates and the surface dries, which is what lets smoke stick and bark form.
  4. Build a clean fire
    Light your charcoal or set your pellet grill for a steady 250°F (120°C) measured at the grate, not the dome thermometer, which usually reads 25°F (14°C) high. On a kettle, bank the coals to one side and set a foil pan holding the 2 cups (480 ml) of water on the empty side. Wait until the smoke coming out of the vent is thin and blue rather than thick and white — white smoke is unburnt fuel and it makes ribs taste like an ashtray.
  5. Add the wood
    Bury two chunks of wood in the hot coals and hold the other two in reserve. Pork takes smoke best in the first 2 to 3 hours, when the surface is still cool and damp, so you do not need to add wood all day. Hickory is the classic for ribs, oak is milder, and cherry gives the best mahogany color. Adding wood after hour three mostly just adds bitterness.
  6. Smoke bare for three hours
    Set the ribs bone side down on the grate away from the fire and close the lid. Leave them completely alone for the first 90 minutes so the rub can set into a crust; poking or flipping early smears it off. Keep the vents adjusted to hold 250°F (120°C), making small changes and waiting 10 minutes to see the effect rather than chasing the needle.
  7. Spritz and watch the stall
    After 90 minutes, spray the racks lightly with the vinegar-and-water mix every 45 minutes, just enough to darken the surface without washing off rub. Around hour 3 the internal temperature will stall somewhere between 150 and 165°F (65 and 74°C) and refuse to move for an hour or more. Nothing is wrong: evaporating moisture is cooling the meat as fast as the fire heats it. This is exactly where impatient cooks crank the heat and ruin ribs.
  8. Wrap with butter and honey
    Lay each rack meat side down on two overlapping sheets of heavy foil, dot with 2 tbsp butter, sprinkle 2 tbsp brown sugar, and drizzle 2 tbsp honey over it. Spritz once more, then fold the foil into a tight packet with no gaps. This is the Texas crutch: sealing the meat stops evaporation, ends the stall, and steams the ribs tender in about half the time bare smoking would take.
  9. Cook wrapped for two hours
    Return the packets to the smoker meat side down and hold 250°F (120°C) for about 2 hours. Start checking at 90 minutes by pressing the packet — the racks should feel loose and floppy through the foil. When a toothpick pushed between the bones meets no resistance and the meat reads 198 to 203°F (92 to 95°C), they are ready to come out of the foil.
  10. Unwrap and set the bark
    Open the packets away from your face, pour the liquid into a bowl, and put the racks back on the grate bone side down. Give them 20 to 30 minutes uncovered so the softened bark firms back up and stops feeling wet. Skipping this step is why crutched ribs sometimes come out pot-roasty instead of barbecued.
  11. Glaze in thin coats
    Stir the barbecue sauce with the cider vinegar and 2 tbsp of the reserved foil liquid, then brush a thin coat over the meat side. Close the lid for 10 minutes to let it tighten, then brush on a second thin coat and give it another 10. Two light coats set into a glossy lacquer, while one heavy coat slides off and tastes raw.
  12. Rest before cutting
    Take the racks off and let them sit on a board for 15 minutes, loosely tented with foil. Rendered fat and gelatin are liquid at cooking temperature and need a few minutes to thicken back up inside the meat. Cut too soon and all of that runs onto the board instead of staying in the ribs.
  13. Slice and check your work
    Flip the racks bone side up and slice between the bones in single long strokes. A perfect rib holds together when you pick it up and takes a clean bite that leaves a crescent-shaped tooth mark in the meat. If the meat falls off before you get it to your mouth, pull the ribs 20 minutes earlier next time.
Know when it is done
Pull between 198 and 203°F (92 and 95°C) when a toothpick slides between the bones with no resistance; the stall sits at 150 to 165°F (65 to 74°C).
Serve it with
White bread, pickles, sliced raw onion, and a very cold pilsner.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆The dome thermometer on most grills reads high because it sits far from the meat. Clip a probe thermometer at grate level next to the ribs and trust that one.
  • ◆If the fire runs hot early, the ribs will be tough no matter how long you cook them. Open the lid for 2 minutes and close the bottom vent halfway rather than dumping water on the coals.
  • ◆Make-ahead: smoked ribs reheat beautifully. Wrap in foil with a splash of apple juice and warm at 275°F (135°C) for 30 minutes, then glaze fresh.
  • ◆Skip the wrap entirely for a firmer, chewier, more traditional Texas-style rib. Expect to add 1½ to 2 hours and to spritz more often.
  • ◆Turbinado sugar resists burning better than brown sugar over a long cook, which is why competition rubs use it.

Slow-Roasted Pulled Pork Shoulder⏱ 10 hr 25 min🍽 10 to 12 servingsMedium▾

One cheap, fatty cut and a very patient oven turn into enough pork for a crowd, with crackly bark edges mixed through the soft meat. It is nearly impossible to overcook, which makes it the friendliest big-batch meat there is.

BBQFeeds a CrowdWeekend
Prep
25 min
Cook
9 hr
Total
10 hr 25 min
Serves
10 to 12 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the pork

Rub

Carolina finishing sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Buy the right cut
    Ask for bone-in pork shoulder or Boston butt, not the leaner picnic shoulder and definitely not pork loin. The butt is laced with fat and connective tissue that melt into gelatin over a long cook, which is what makes pulled pork juicy. The blade bone should slide out clean at the end, and that is your best doneness signal.
  2. Trim and score the fat cap
    Trim the fat cap down to about ¼ inch (6 mm) thick, leaving enough to baste the meat but not so much that the rub never touches it. Score the remaining fat in a crosshatch about ½ inch (1 cm) apart, cutting into the fat but not the meat. Those cuts let fat render out and let rub get down into the surface.
  3. Rub it the night before
    Mix all the rub ingredients until evenly colored, smear the shoulder with the mustard, and pack the rub on every surface including the underside. Use all of it — an 8 lb (3.6 kg) roast can carry far more seasoning than you think, because only the outside gets any. Set it on a rack over a sheet pan and refrigerate uncovered 12 to 24 hours so the salt works its way in.
  4. Temper and heat the oven
    Take the pork out of the fridge 45 minutes before it goes in the oven so the surface is not ice cold. Heat the oven to 275°F (135°C) with a rack in the lower third. Pour the 2 cups (480 ml) of water into a roasting pan and set a rack in it, then put the pork on the rack fat side up. The water keeps drippings from scorching and adds a little humidity.
  5. Roast uncovered until the bark sets
    Roast uncovered for about 5 hours, until the outside is deep mahogany and dry to the touch. Do not baste, and do not open the door more than once an hour — every peek costs you 25 to 50°F (14 to 28°C) of oven recovery. By now the internal temperature is usually somewhere around 160°F (71°C).
  6. Recognize the stall
    Somewhere between 150 and 170°F (65 and 77°C) the temperature will stop rising and may even drop a degree, and it can sit there for 3 hours. This is the stall, and it is evaporative cooling — the meat is sweating and that sweat is refrigerating it. Nothing is broken, the oven is fine, and turning up the heat will only dry out the exterior.
  7. Wrap to power through
    Once the bark is dark and firm, pull the pan out and set the shoulder on two overlapping sheets of heavy foil. Pour the ½ cup (120 ml) cider vinegar around it and wrap tightly, sealing every seam so no steam escapes. Return it to the rack in the pan; wrapping ends the stall within about 30 minutes and typically saves you 2 hours.
  8. Cook to 203°F
    Continue roasting for roughly 3½ to 4 more hours, until the thickest part away from the bone reads 203°F (95°C). Start checking at 195°F (91°C) by pushing a probe or a skewer into several spots — it should slide in like the meat is room-temperature butter. Temperature is a guide here, but probe tenderness is the real test, and some shoulders need 207°F (97°C).
  9. Rest it properly
    Leave the pork wrapped, set it in a small cooler or an unheated oven, and rest it at least 1 hour and up to 3. This is not optional: at 203°F (95°C) the melted fat and gelatin are thin as water and will pour out if you open it now. A long rest lets them thicken and get reabsorbed, and the pork stays above 140°F (60°C) the whole time.
  10. Make the finishing sauce
    While the pork rests, whisk the cider vinegar, sugar, ketchup, red pepper flakes, salt, and black pepper in a jar until the sugar dissolves. Let it sit at room temperature for 30 minutes so the pepper flakes bloom. This thin Eastern Carolina sauce is not a glaze — it is seasoning for the pulled meat, and it wakes the richness right up.
  11. Pull the pork
    Unwrap over a bowl to catch every drop of juice, then twist the blade bone; it should pull free with no meat clinging to it. Shred with two forks or gloved hands into big, irregular strands rather than mush, and chop the darkest bark pieces so they distribute through the whole batch. Fish out and discard any thick pockets of unrendered fat.
  12. Season and serve
    Skim the fat off the reserved juices and pour about ½ cup (120 ml) of the defatted juice back over the meat, then add the finishing sauce a few tablespoons at a time, tasting as you go. It should taste bright and lightly salty, not soupy. Serve immediately on soft buns, or hold it covered in a 200°F (95°C) oven for up to an hour.
Know when it is done
Pull at 203°F (95°C) when a probe slides in with no resistance; the stall parks at 150 to 170°F (65 to 77°C) and is normal.
Serve it with
Soft potato buns, sharp coleslaw, dill pickles, and sweet tea or a light amber ale.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Plan on 1 to 1¼ hours per pound (about 2 to 2½ hours per kg) at 275°F (135°C), then add an hour of slack. Pork is done when it is done, and a stubborn stall can wreck a dinner schedule.
  • ◆Make-ahead: pulled pork is better the next day. Cool it in its own juices, refrigerate up to 4 days, and reheat covered at 300°F (150°C) with a splash of stock.
  • ◆Freeze leftovers in 2-cup portions with plenty of juice; they keep 3 months and thaw into tacos, nachos, or hash.
  • ◆For smoker instead of oven, run 250°F (120°C) with hickory or apple wood and follow the exact same wrap-and-rest timeline.
  • ◆If the bark goes soft under the foil, unwrap for the last 20 minutes of cooking and let the dry heat firm it back up.

Thick-Cut Pork Chops with Pan Sauce⏱ 30 min🍽 2 servingsMedium▾

Two big bone-in chops, a hot skillet, and a mustard-cider sauce built from the browned bits left behind. Thirty minutes start to finish and it eats like something you would order out.

30 MinutesCast IronDate Night
Prep
10 min

30 min
Serves
2 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the chops

Pan sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Buy chops thick enough
    Ask the butcher for rib chops cut 1½ inches (4 cm) thick, which usually means about 12 oz (340 g) each. A thin chop hits 145°F (63°C) before the outside has any color, so it is guaranteed to be either pale or dry. The bone insulates one side and adds flavor, and the fat cap along the edge bastes the meat as it renders.
  2. Salt and air-dry
    Pat both chops completely dry with paper towels and season all over with the kosher salt, including the fat edge. Set them on a rack and leave them uncovered at room temperature while you mince the shallot and heat the pan, about 10 minutes, or refrigerate them uncovered for up to 12 hours if you are working ahead. Salt draws moisture out and then the meat reabsorbs it seasoned, while the surface dries — dry surface is the whole secret to browning.
  3. Preheat the skillet properly
    Set a 12-inch (30 cm) cast-iron or stainless skillet over medium-high heat for a full 3 minutes before adding the oil. Add the tablespoon of oil and swirl; it should shimmer and thin out almost instantly and send up the faintest wisp of smoke. If it just sits there looking thick, the pan is not ready and the pork will stick.
  4. Season with pepper and sear
    Grind the black pepper over both sides now, right before cooking, so it toasts rather than burns. Lay the chops in the pan away from you and press down for 5 seconds so the full surface touches metal. It should sizzle steadily and loudly, not smoke violently — if it screams and smokes, drop the heat to medium.
  5. Build the first crust
    Leave the chops alone for 4 minutes without moving, poking, or peeking under them. Meat releases from the pan on its own when a crust has formed, so if it sticks when you nudge it, it needs another 30 seconds. Flip once and sear the second side for 3 minutes.
  6. Render the fat edge
    Stand the chops on their fat edge, leaning them against each other or holding them with tongs, for 60 to 90 seconds. The strip of fat should go from white and firm to golden and soft, and it will pour more fat into the pan for basting. Unrendered fat is chewy and unpleasant, and this one minute fixes it.
  7. Baste with butter and aromatics
    Lower the heat to medium, add the 2 tbsp butter, thyme sprigs, and smashed garlic, and tilt the pan so the butter pools at the near edge. Spoon the foaming butter over the chops continuously for 2 to 3 minutes. The butter should be foaming and smell nutty; if it turns dark brown and smells acrid, pull the pan off the heat for 20 seconds.
  8. Cook to 145°F and rest
    Check the center of the thickest part, away from the bone, and pull the chops onto a plate at 140°F (60°C) — carryover will carry them to the safe 145°F (63°C). Rest them at least 3 minutes, which is both a food-safety requirement for whole-muscle pork and what keeps the juice inside. Modern pork is safe and best at 145°F (63°C) with a faint blush of pink in the center.
  9. Start the sauce
    Pour off all but 1 tbsp of fat, return the pan to medium heat, and add the minced shallot with a pinch of the salt. Stir for 60 to 90 seconds until it is translucent and smells sweet, scraping constantly so it does not scorch in the residual heat. Discard the thyme and garlic if they look dark.
  10. Deglaze and finish
    Pour in the cider and scrape every browned bit off the bottom with a wooden spoon — that fond is the entire flavor of the sauce. Simmer until reduced by half, about 2 minutes, then add the stock and reduce again to about ⅓ cup (80 ml), 4 to 5 minutes. Whisk in the mustard and vinegar, take the pan off the heat, then swirl in the cold butter cubes one at a time until glossy. Pour any resting juices from the plate into the sauce, taste, and spoon it over the chops.
Know when it is done
Pull pork chops at 140°F (60°C) and rest 3 minutes to reach the safe serving temperature of 145°F (63°C).
Serve it with
Buttered mashed potatoes or soft polenta, a pile of sautéed greens, and the rest of the cider.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆If your chops are thinner than 1 inch (2.5 cm), skip the basting stage entirely — sear 2½ minutes per side and go straight to the sauce.
  • ◆Substitutions: dry white wine, apple cider, or even ¼ cup (60 ml) stock plus 1 tsp cider vinegar all work in place of hard cider.
  • ◆The butter must be cold and go in off the heat. Boiling it will break the sauce into a greasy pool instead of an emulsion.
  • ◆Make-ahead: salt the chops in the morning and leave them uncovered in the fridge; they will brown noticeably better at dinner.

Cider-Brined Grilled Pork Chops⏱ 2 hr 30 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

A two-hour salt-and-cider soak is the cheapest insurance there is against dry pork. The chops come off the grill juicy, faintly sweet, and seasoned all the way through.

GrillMake AheadEasy
Prep
15 min
Cook
15 min
Total
2 hr 30 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Brine

Chops and finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Dissolve the brine
    Bring the cider, salt, brown sugar, garlic, bay leaves, peppercorns, and thyme to a simmer in a saucepan over medium heat, stirring until the salt and sugar completely dissolve, about 3 minutes. You have to heat it or the salt sits in crystals at the bottom and never gets into the meat. Take it off the heat as soon as it is clear.
  2. Chill it fast
    Pour the hot brine into a large bowl, add the 2 cups (480 ml) cold water and all the ice, and stir until the ice mostly melts. The brine must be below 40°F (4°C) before the pork goes in — warm brine sits in the food-safety danger zone and starts to cook the outside of the chops. Feel the side of the bowl; it should be cold to the touch, not lukewarm.
  3. Brine the chops
    Submerge the chops in the cold brine, pressing them under with a small plate if they float, and refrigerate for 2 hours. Do not go past 4 hours: this brine is strong, and over-brined pork turns spongy and tastes like ham. Two hours is enough for salt to reach the center of a 1¼-inch (3 cm) chop.
  4. Dry them thoroughly
    Lift the chops out, rinse them briefly under cold water, and pat them absolutely dry with paper towels, pressing rather than wiping. Set them on a rack for 20 minutes at room temperature so the surface dries further. A wet chop steams on the grill and comes off gray; a dry one gets those brown grill marks in half the time.
  5. Set up two heat zones
    Heat a gas grill with one side on high and the other off, or bank lit charcoal to one side of a kettle. You want the hot side around 500°F (260°C) and the cool side around 300°F (150°C). Two zones let you sear hard and then move the chops out of the flames to finish, which is how you avoid a burnt outside and raw middle.
  6. Oil and pepper the chops
    Brush the chops with the neutral oil and grind the black pepper over both sides. Do not add any more salt — the brine already handled it, and salting again now makes them inedible. Scrape the grates clean with a wire brush and wipe them with an oiled paper towel held in tongs.
  7. Sear over direct heat
    Lay the chops over the hot side and grill 3 minutes without moving them, then rotate each 45 degrees and go 2 more minutes for crosshatch marks. Flip and repeat on the second side, about 3 minutes. If flames flare up from dripping fat, slide the chops to the cool side for 20 seconds instead of squirting water, which just kicks up ash.
  8. Finish over indirect heat
    Move all four chops to the cool side of the grill, close the lid, and cook 4 to 8 more minutes depending on thickness. This gentle heat brings the center up without adding any more char. Start checking early — the difference between juicy and dry pork is about 90 seconds.
  9. Pull at the right number
    Slide an instant-read thermometer into the side of a chop, aiming for the center and staying off the bone, and pull at 140°F (60°C). Carryover heat will take them to the safe 145°F (63°C) while they rest. A little pink in the center of a whole-muscle pork chop is correct and safe.
  10. Rest with butter
    Move the chops to a warm platter, smear the softened butter over the tops so it melts into the grooves, and tent loosely with foil for 5 minutes. Resting lets the juices that were driven to the center redistribute back out through the meat. Sprinkle with flaky salt and serve with lemon wedges to squeeze over.
Know when it is done
Pull at 140°F (60°C) and rest 3 to 5 minutes so the chops finish at the safe 145°F (63°C).
Serve it with
Grilled peaches or apple sauce, a shaved fennel salad, and a chilled off-dry Riesling.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Never brine pork that is already enhanced or injected — check the label for a saline solution percentage. It will come out far too salty.
  • ◆Make-ahead: mix and chill the brine up to 3 days early, then drop the chops in on the day. The chilled brine is the slow part.
  • ◆No grill? Sear in a cast-iron skillet over medium-high for 3 minutes a side, then finish in a 375°F (190°C) oven for 6 to 8 minutes.
  • ◆The same brine works on a 3 lb (1.4 kg) pork loin roast — just extend the soak to 6 hours and roast at 375°F (190°C) to 140°F (60°C).

Pork belly wrapped around a loin, packed with fennel, garlic, and rosemary, roasted until the skin shatters like glass. It takes two days of mostly waiting and it is the best thing you can put on a table.

ProjectFeeds a CrowdRoastWeekend
Prep

Cook

Total

Serves
10 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the pork

Herb paste

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Order the right pieces
    Ask your butcher for a squared-off, skin-on pork belly about 5 lb (2.3 kg) and a boneless loin that is no longer than the belly's short side. The loin should be roughly the same length as the belly is wide, so the roll comes out even. Ask them to score the skin in a crosshatch for you if they have a proper blade, since a dull home knife makes ragged cuts.
  2. Toast and grind the spices
    Toast the fennel seeds, peppercorns, and red pepper flakes in a dry skillet over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes, shaking constantly, until the fennel smells sweet and licorice-like. Tip them onto a plate immediately so they stop cooking. Grind them coarsely in a mortar or spice grinder; toasting first is what turns fennel from grassy to warm and is worth the three minutes.
  3. Make the herb paste
    Pound or pulse the garlic with 1 tbsp of the kosher salt into a rough paste, then work in the ground spices, rosemary, sage, lemon zest, and 3 tbsp olive oil. It should look like coarse green mud and smell strongly of fennel and lemon. The salt acts as an abrasive that breaks the garlic down properly instead of just chopping it.
  4. Score the skin
    Lay the belly skin side up and, using a very sharp utility knife or box cutter, score a crosshatch of lines about ¾ inch (2 cm) apart. Cut through the skin and just into the fat but never into the meat, or juice will bubble up and stop the skin from crisping. Working with the belly cold, straight from the fridge, makes this dramatically easier.
  5. Season the inside
    Flip the belly meat side up and rub 1 tbsp of the kosher salt evenly over the flesh, then spread all the herb paste across it, leaving a bare 1-inch (2.5 cm) border along the far long edge. Season the loin all over with the last 1 tbsp of the divided salt, which accounts for all 3 tbsp: one in the paste, one on the belly, one on the loin. That bare border is what lets the roll seal instead of squeezing paste out as you tie it.
  6. Roll and tie
    Lay the loin along the near long edge of the belly and roll it up tightly into a log, keeping the skin on the outside and the seam underneath. Tie with butcher's twine at 1½-inch (4 cm) intervals, starting at the middle and working outward, pulling each loop snug enough to compress the roll without cutting into it. A loose roll cooks unevenly and falls apart when you slice it.
  7. Dry the skin overnight
    Rub the skin all over with the extra 1 tbsp kosher salt, then set the tied roast on a rack over a sheet pan and refrigerate uncovered for 24 hours, and up to 48. This is the single most important step for crackling: the cold dry air of the fridge pulls water out of the skin so it can puff instead of steam. Do not cover it, and do not skip it.
  8. Temper and start low
    Take the porchetta out 1 hour before cooking and wipe the skin with a paper towel to remove any beaded moisture. Heat the oven to 300°F (150°C) with a rack in the lower third. Set the roast on a rack in a roasting pan, rub the skin with the 2 tbsp olive oil, and roast for about 2½ hours. The gentle heat renders the belly fat and cooks the loin without seizing it.
  9. Check the center
    Start checking at 2 hours by pushing a thermometer through the end of the roll into the loin at the center. You are looking for 140°F (60°C) in the loin at this stage, since the high-heat blast still to come will push it past the safe 145°F (63°C). The belly wrapped around it is far more forgiving and will be fine either way.
  10. Blast for crackling
    Crank the oven to 500°F (260°C) and roast 20 to 30 minutes more, turning the pan every 8 minutes so the skin browns evenly. The skin will bubble, blister, and go from leathery to hard and glassy — you can hear it crackle and pop. Watch it closely from minute 15, because it goes from mahogany to burnt very quickly. If patches stay soft, hit them directly under the broiler for 60 seconds.
  11. Rest for real
    Move the porchetta to a cutting board and rest it, uncovered, for 30 minutes. Do not tent it with foil, because trapped steam will soften the crackling you just spent half an hour building. Uncovered resting still lets the internal juices settle while the skin stays hard.
  12. Slice with a serrated knife
    Snip and remove all the twine, then cut with a serrated bread knife in a firm sawing motion — a smooth chef's knife slips off the skin and squashes the roll. Cut slices ½ to ¾ inch (1 to 2 cm) thick. Each one should show a spiral of belly around a pale loin center with a rim of shattered crackling.
  13. Serve and store
    Fan the slices on a warm platter and spoon a little of the rendered pan fat over them, or leave them plain if the crackling is at its best. Serve within 20 minutes while the skin is still crisp. Leftovers are extraordinary the next day, sliced thin on crusty bread with mustard and pickled onions.
Know when it is done
The loin center must reach 145°F (63°C); pull the low roast at 140°F (60°C) before the 500°F (260°C) crackling blast.
Serve it with
Roasted potatoes in the pork fat, bitter greens with lemon, and a bright Chianti or Barbera.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆The overnight uncovered chill is non-negotiable for crackling. If your skin comes out chewy, moisture is almost always the reason.
  • ◆Make-ahead: assemble and tie the roast up to 2 days early. It has to sit in the fridge anyway, so the work is genuinely front-loaded.
  • ◆No loin? A 7 lb (3.2 kg) belly rolled on its own makes a classic porchetta di Ariccia — cut the low-oven time to 2 hours.
  • ◆Save the rendered fat in a jar in the fridge for up to a month. Roasting potatoes in it is the best possible use of leftovers.
  • ◆Buy an extra foot of twine and practice the tie once on the untreated belly. It is much less stressful than learning while the paste slides everywhere.

Maple mustard glaze

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Remove the silverskin
    Slide a thin knife under the shiny silver membrane running along one side of each tenderloin, angle the blade slightly upward, and pull the membrane taut as you cut it away in strips. It will not render or soften, so anything you leave behind will make the meat curl and turn tight in the oven. Take your time; you should lose only a little meat.
  2. Season the pork
    Pat the tenderloins dry and season all over with the kosher salt, black pepper, and smoked paprika. Let them sit at room temperature for 15 minutes while you get everything else ready. Keep the seasoning modest — bacon brings plenty of salt of its own, and it is easy to overshoot here.
  3. Choose the right bacon
    Use regular-cut bacon, not thick-cut: thin slices render and crisp in the time it takes the pork to reach temperature, while thick slices stay flabby and raw-looking. Lay 6 slices side by side on a cutting board, slightly overlapping, in a sheet slightly longer than one tenderloin. Repeat for the second one.
  4. Wrap and secure
    Set a tenderloin across one end of the bacon sheet and roll it up so the slices spiral around it, tucking the thin tail end of the pork under itself so the roast is an even thickness. Finish with the bacon seam on the bottom, which keeps it from unraveling. Tie with butcher's twine at 2-inch (5 cm) intervals or secure with toothpicks if the bacon is loose.
  5. Mix the glaze
    Whisk the maple syrup, Dijon, cider vinegar, grated garlic, and salt in a small bowl until smooth and glossy. The vinegar and mustard keep it from being cloying, and the sugar in the syrup is what gives you the lacquered finish. Set it aside; do not brush it on yet, or it will burn during the sear.
  6. Heat the oven and pan
    Heat the oven to 400°F (205°C) with a rack in the middle. Set a large oven-safe skillet over medium-high heat for 2 minutes, then add the neutral oil and let it shimmer. A cast-iron or heavy stainless skillet means you can sear and roast in the same pan, which saves you a dish and keeps all the drippings.
  7. Sear the bacon crust
    Lay the tenderloins seam side down and sear, turning with tongs every 2 minutes, until the bacon is browned on all sides, about 8 minutes total. Start seam side down so the heat welds the bacon shut. It should sizzle steadily; if the bacon fat starts smoking hard, drop to medium heat and pour off some of the rendered fat.
  8. Roast and glaze
    Slide the skillet into the oven and roast for 10 minutes, then pull it out and brush half the glaze over both roasts. Return to the oven for 6 to 10 minutes more, brushing on the rest of the glaze for the last 4 minutes. Glazing late means the maple caramelizes instead of scorching black.
  9. Check temperature early
    Begin checking at the 14-minute mark by inserting a thermometer into the thickest part of one tenderloin, parallel to the length of the meat. Pull them out at 140°F (60°C) — carryover will take them to the safe 145°F (63°C). Tenderloin is very lean and there is a hard line between juicy and chalky, so check often rather than guessing.
  10. Rest and slice into medallions
    Move the roasts to a cutting board and rest 10 minutes, loosely tented, which also satisfies the required 3-minute rest for whole-muscle pork. Snip off the twine, then slice crosswise into medallions about ¾ inch (2 cm) thick. The centers should be pale pink and the juices clear. Spoon any pan glaze and resting juices over the top and serve.
Know when it is done
Pull at 140°F (60°C) and rest 10 minutes; whole-muscle pork is safe at 145°F (63°C) after a 3-minute rest.
Serve it with
Roasted brussels sprouts, a wild rice pilaf, and a light Pinot Noir.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Do not confuse pork tenderloin with pork loin. Tenderloin is a 1 lb (450 g) tapered muscle that cooks in 25 minutes; a loin roast is 3 to 4 lb (1.4 to 1.8 kg) and needs an hour or more.
  • ◆Make-ahead: wrap and tie the tenderloins up to a day ahead and keep them covered in the fridge. Take them out 20 minutes before searing.
  • ◆If the bacon is still soft when the pork reaches 140°F (60°C), do not keep roasting and overcook the meat. Move the skillet 6 inches (15 cm) under the broiler for 60 to 90 seconds instead — the fierce top heat crisps the bacon while the pork gains only a degree or two.
  • ◆Substitutions: honey works for maple, and whole-grain mustard gives a nice texture. Add 1 tsp chopped rosemary to the glaze if you have it.

Honey Glazed Spiral Ham⏱ 2 hr 30 min🍽 12 to 16 servingsEasy▾

The ham is already cooked, so your only two jobs are to warm it gently without drying it and to build a sticky, burnished glaze. It is the least stressful holiday centerpiece in this book.

HolidayFeeds a CrowdEasy
Prep
15 min
Cook
2 hr
Total
2 hr 30 min
Serves
12 to 16 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the ham

Honey glaze

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Understand what you bought
    Almost every ham at the supermarket is fully cooked and cured, so you are reheating, not cooking. Look for bone-in and, ideally, one labeled ham rather than ham with water added, which is wetter and less flavorful. Bone-in tastes better and gives you a bone worth saving for soup.
  2. Bring it toward room temperature
    Take the ham out of the fridge 1 hour before it goes in the oven and unwrap it, discarding any plastic disc covering the bone. A 9 lb (4 kg) ham straight from the fridge takes far longer to warm through, and every extra oven minute dries out the spiral-cut slices. Pat the surface dry with paper towels.
  3. Set up the pan
    Heat the oven to 325°F (165°C) with a rack in the lower third so the ham fits with headroom. Set the ham cut side down in a roasting pan and pour the water or cider into the bottom of the pan, not over the ham. That liquid steams gently and keeps the exposed slices from turning into jerky.
  4. Tent it tightly
    Cover the whole pan tightly with heavy foil, crimping it around the rim so steam cannot escape. If you like, stud the fat cap with the whole cloves in a diamond pattern first — they add a warm background note and look traditional. A tight seal is what makes the difference between a moist ham and a salty, dry one.
  5. Warm it low and slow
    Bake for about 1 hour 30 minutes, roughly 10 minutes per pound (22 minutes per kg). You are aiming for an internal temperature of 110 to 120°F (43 to 49°C) at this stage, not the final number. Going slowly means the middle warms before the outer slices overcook.
  6. Make the glaze
    While the ham warms, combine the honey, brown sugar, butter, Dijon, cider vinegar, cinnamon, ground cloves, and salt in a small saucepan over medium heat. Simmer for 4 to 5 minutes, whisking, until it thickens slightly and coats the back of a spoon. Do not let it boil hard or it will turn to candy in the pan and set solid.
  7. Uncover and start glazing
    Pull the pan out, remove the foil, and raise the oven to 400°F (205°C). Brush about a third of the glaze all over the ham, working some down between the spiral slices with a pastry brush or spoon. Getting glaze between the slices is what makes every piece taste glazed instead of only the outside ones.
  8. Build the layers
    Return the ham uncovered and bake 10 minutes, then brush on another third and bake 10 more. Repeat with the last of the glaze for a final 10 minutes, so you have three thin layers rather than one thick one. Watch closely in these last minutes, because honey and brown sugar go from burnished to burnt fast at 400°F (205°C).
  9. Check the final temperature
    Slide a thermometer into the thickest part, avoiding the bone, and look for 140°F (60°C) for a fully cooked ham. If it is not there yet, tent it back up and give it 15 more minutes. The USDA line for reheating a fully cooked ham is 140°F (60°C); for one labeled cook-before-eating, you need 145°F (63°C) plus a 3-minute rest.
  10. Rest, then carve
    Rest the ham for 15 minutes on a board, spooning some of the pan drippings and loose glaze over the top as it sits. Run a knife around the bone to free the pre-cut slices, then lift them off in sections and fan them on a warm platter. Pour the remaining pan glaze into a small pitcher to pass at the table.
Know when it is done
Reheat a fully cooked ham to 140°F (60°C); if the label says cook-before-eating, take it to 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest.
Serve it with
Scalloped potatoes, buttery green beans, and a sparkling wine or a crisp lager.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Save the bone. Simmered with split peas or white beans and a bay leaf, it makes a soup that is arguably better than the ham dinner itself.
  • ◆Make-ahead: the glaze keeps in the fridge for 2 weeks. Rewarm it gently and thin with 1 tbsp water if it has stiffened.
  • ◆If the glaze runs off instead of clinging, it needed another minute of simmering. Reduce it until it visibly coats a spoon before brushing.
  • ◆Leftovers keep 5 days refrigerated. Slice them thick for sandwiches and dice the scraps for omelets, fried rice, or potato hash.

Rack of Lamb with Herb Crust⏱ 1 hr🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Sear, paint with mustard, press on a garlicky herb crumb, and roast to a rosy medium-rare. It looks like a special occasion and takes an hour from fridge to table.

Date NightRoastSpecial Occasion
Prep
20 min
Cook
30 min
Total
1 hr
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the lamb

Herb crust

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Trim and temper
    If the racks are not already frenched, scrape the meat and membrane from the top 1½ inches (4 cm) of each bone with a small knife. Trim the fat cap on the meaty side down to about ¼ inch (6 mm), leaving enough to baste but not so much that the crust slides off. Let the racks sit at room temperature for 20 minutes while you heat the oven and mix the crust, so the centers are not fridge-cold and they cook evenly.
  2. Season and heat the oven
    Pat the racks completely dry and season all over with the kosher salt and black pepper. Heat the oven to 400°F (205°C) with a rack in the upper third. A hot oven and a short roast is right for lamb racks, which are small and lean and turn gray if you cook them gently for a long time.
  3. Mix the crust
    Toss the panko, parsley, rosemary, thyme, garlic, Parmesan, olive oil, salt, and pepper in a wide dish until every crumb is lightly coated and the mixture looks damp, like fresh sand. Squeeze a handful; it should just hold together. Dry crumbs will not brown properly and will fall off the moment you carve.
  4. Sear the fat side
    Heat the neutral oil in a large ovenproof skillet over medium-high until it shimmers, about 2 minutes. Lay the racks fat side down and sear 3 to 4 minutes without moving them, until deeply golden and much of the fat has rendered out. It should sizzle steadily, not smoke; lamb fat burns faster than beef fat.
  5. Brown the other sides
    Turn the racks onto the meaty ends and sear 1 minute per side, using tongs to hold them upright. Do not sear the bones themselves, which will just blacken and taste bitter. Move the racks to a foil-lined sheet pan, bones curving upward, and let them cool for 5 minutes.
  6. Paint with mustard
    Brush a thin, even layer of Dijon over the fat side and the two ends of each rack while they are still warm but not hot. The mustard is glue first and flavor second, so do not glob it on. Skipping this and pressing crumbs onto bare meat guarantees a crust that slides off in the oven.
  7. Press on the crust
    Press the crumb mixture firmly onto the mustard, packing it about ¼ inch (6 mm) thick over the fat side and the ends. Use the heel of your hand and really compact it — loose crumbs fall away, packed crumbs form a sheet. Leave the bones clean so they stay presentable.
  8. Roast to a pull temperature
    Roast for 15 to 20 minutes for medium-rare, depending on the size of the racks. Start checking at 12 minutes with a thermometer pushed into the center of the eye of meat, parallel to the bones and not touching them. Pull at 125°F (52°C) for medium-rare or 130°F (54°C) for medium; carryover adds another 5 to 8°F (3 to 4°C).
  9. Fix a pale crust
    If the lamb hits temperature before the crumbs are golden, that is normal and easily solved. Move the pan to 6 inches (15 cm) under the broiler for 60 to 90 seconds, watching it the entire time. Panko goes from blond to burnt in about 15 seconds, so do not walk away for any reason.
  10. Rest without foil
    Rest the racks on a board for 10 minutes, uncovered. Foil traps steam and would turn your crisp crust soggy, and the racks hold heat well enough on their own. Resting lets the juices, which the heat drove toward the center, spread back through the meat so they stay in the chops instead of on the board.
  11. Carve into chops
    Set a rack bone side down and slice straight down between the bones with a sharp knife, cutting single or double chops depending on how generous you want to be. Cut confidently in one motion so you do not saw the crust off. Arrange them crossed on a warm platter and sprinkle any fallen crumbs back over the top.
Know when it is done
Pull at 125°F (52°C) for medium-rare or 130°F (54°C) for medium; after resting they will read 130 to 138°F (54 to 59°C).
Serve it with
Potato gratin, blistered green beans, and a Bordeaux or a Rioja Reserva.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Buy the racks frenched if you can — it is fiddly work and butchers do it in seconds. American racks run about 1½ lb (700 g); smaller New Zealand racks need 4 to 5 fewer minutes.
  • ◆Make-ahead: sear and crust the racks up to 6 hours ahead, keep them refrigerated on the sheet pan, and add 3 to 4 minutes to the roast time.
  • ◆Wrap the exposed bones in a strip of foil if they darken too much for your liking. It is cosmetic, not functional.
  • ◆Substitutions: fresh breadcrumbs from stale bread work in place of panko but brown faster, so check at 10 minutes.
  • ◆Lamb fat tastes best hot. Serve on warmed plates, because it congeals and turns waxy on a cold one.

Red Wine Braised Lamb Shanks⏱ 4 hr🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Three hours in a low oven turns the toughest, cheapest piece of the lamb into something that collapses at the touch of a spoon. The braising liquid reduces into a glossy sauce that does half the work of dinner.

BraiseComfort FoodSunday Dinner
Prep
30 min
Cook
3 hr 30 min
Total
4 hr
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the shanks

Braise

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Season the shanks early
    Pat the shanks dry and season them all over with the kosher salt and pepper, ideally 4 hours ahead or even the night before. Salting early lets the seasoning get past the surface, which matters a lot on a piece of meat this thick. Take them out of the fridge 30 minutes before cooking.
  2. Heat the oven and pot
    Heat the oven to 325°F (165°C) with a rack low enough that a covered Dutch oven fits. Set a heavy 7-quart (6.6 L) Dutch oven over medium-high heat with the olive oil and let it get hot enough that the oil shimmers, about 3 minutes. The shanks need real space, so use the biggest pot you have.
  3. Dredge and sear
    Dust the shanks lightly with the flour, shaking off all the excess, then brown them two at a time so the pot is never crowded. Give each side 3 to 4 minutes until deeply browned, about 12 minutes per pair. It should sizzle hard and steadily; if you hear a dull hiss the pan is too cool and the meat will stew instead of brown.
  4. Build the vegetable base
    Set the browned shanks aside, pour off all but 2 tbsp of the fat, and add the onion, carrots, and celery with a generous pinch of salt. Cook over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes, scraping the bottom as the vegetables release their water and lift the fond. The onions should be soft and translucent with brown edges.
  5. Cook the tomato paste
    Push the vegetables to one side, add the tomato paste to the bare spot, and let it fry for 2 minutes, stirring, until it darkens from bright red to brick and smells sweet rather than tinny. This step is called pincage and it removes the raw metallic edge. Stir it through the vegetables along with the halved head of garlic, cut sides down.
  6. Deglaze with wine
    Pour in the red wine and scrape the bottom of the pot hard with a wooden spoon until nothing is stuck. Bring it to a boil and reduce by about half, 6 to 8 minutes, until it no longer smells sharply of alcohol. Reducing now concentrates the wine and prevents a harsh, boozy sauce three hours from now.
  7. Assemble the braise
    Add the stock, hand-crushed tomatoes with their juice, rosemary, thyme, and bay leaves, then nestle the shanks back in along with any juices from the plate. The liquid should come about two-thirds of the way up the shanks, not cover them — the exposed tops brown while the bottoms braise. Top up with a little water if you are short.
  8. Braise low and covered
    Bring everything to a bare simmer on the stove, then cover and move the pot to the oven. Cook for 2½ hours, turning the shanks once at the halfway point so the exposed side does not dry out. A gentle 325°F (165°C) oven surrounds the pot with even heat, which is far kinder than a stovetop burner hitting it from below.
  9. Check for fork tenderness
    After 2½ hours, test with a fork: it should slide into the thickest part with no resistance, and the meat should be visibly pulling back from the bone. Internally that is around 205°F (96°C), well past any food-safety concern and into the range where collagen has melted into gelatin. If it still grips the bone, cover and give it 30 more minutes.
  10. Reduce the sauce
    Lift the shanks onto a plate and tent them, then fish out the herb stems, bay leaves, and garlic halves, squeezing the soft garlic cloves back into the pot. Skim the fat off the surface with a wide spoon or a ladle. Simmer the liquid on the stove over medium-high for 10 to 15 minutes until it coats a spoon and has reduced by about a third.
  11. Return and glaze
    Slide the shanks back into the reduced sauce and spoon it over them repeatedly for 2 to 3 minutes so they take on a glossy coat. Taste the sauce now and add salt in small pinches until it tastes savory rather than flat. If it tastes too sharp, a teaspoon of honey rounds it out.
  12. Finish with gremolata
    Stir the parsley and lemon zest together and scatter it over the shanks just before serving, along with the flaky salt. Three hours of braising makes everything deep and rich, and this raw, bright hit at the end is what stops it from feeling heavy. Serve each shank in a wide bowl with plenty of sauce.
Know when it is done
Braise until fork-tender, roughly 205°F (96°C) internal, when the meat pulls away from the bone with no resistance.
Serve it with
Creamy polenta or mashed potatoes to catch the sauce, and a big Syrah or Cabernet.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make-ahead: braises are better on day two. Cool the shanks in their liquid, refrigerate up to 3 days, lift off the solidified fat cap, and reheat gently at 300°F (150°C) for 40 minutes.
  • ◆If your pot is too small to hold 4 shanks in one layer, use a roasting pan covered tightly with two layers of foil. Crowding is what causes gray, steamed meat.
  • ◆Do not cook with wine you would not drink, but do not use anything expensive either. A $12 dry red is exactly right.
  • ◆Veal shanks, beef short ribs, and oxtail all work in this braise with the same timing. Pork shanks need about 30 minutes less.

Lamb Chops with Mint Chimichurri⏱ 30 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Little rib chops cook in about four minutes total, and a sharp herb sauce cuts straight through the richness. This is the fastest impressive dinner in the whole chapter.

30 MinutesCast IronDate Night
Prep
15 min
