10 min
Total
30 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the chops

Mint chimichurri

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Make the chimichurri first
    Stir the shallot, garlic, red wine vinegar, kosher salt, and red pepper flakes together in a bowl and let them sit for 10 minutes. The acid takes the raw bite off the garlic and shallot and softens them, which is the difference between a balanced sauce and one that burns. This is also why you make it before you touch the lamb.
  2. Chop the herbs properly
    While the shallot mixture sits, chop the parsley and mint with a very sharp knife, using a rocking motion rather than crushing them, and do it right before you mix the sauce. A dull blade tears the leaves instead of cutting them, and mint bruises and darkens within minutes once its cells are torn, turning black and tasting flat. If you want to prep ahead, chop the parsley early and add the mint at the last moment.
  3. Finish the sauce
    Stir the chopped parsley, mint, and dried oregano into the soaked shallot and garlic, then pour in the olive oil and stir it through — do not blend it. A food processor turns chimichurri into a dull green purée, while hand-chopping keeps the herbs distinct and the texture loose. It should look like herbs suspended in oil, not a paste, and it should taste sharp and salty on its own, since the lamb is rich.
  4. Season the chops
    Pat the chops completely dry with paper towels and season both flat sides with the kosher salt and pepper. Leave them at room temperature for 15 minutes while the pan heats, which takes the fridge chill off and helps them cook evenly. Do not salt more than 20 minutes ahead unless you plan to salt them a full hour ahead — the in-between window leaves the surface wet.
  5. Get the skillet hot
    Set a 12-inch (30 cm) cast-iron skillet over medium-high heat for 3 full minutes, then add the neutral oil. The oil should shimmer and move like water when you tilt the pan, with the very first wisp of smoke. Turn on your exhaust fan now — these chops are fatty and the pan will smoke.
  6. Render the fat edge first
    Stand the chops on their fat edges in two batches, leaning them against each other or the pan wall, and cook 60 to 90 seconds per batch until that strip turns golden and gives up its fat. This is not optional with lamb: unrendered lamb fat is waxy and is the main reason people think they dislike lamb. The rendered fat then cooks the chops.
  7. Sear both flat sides
    Lay the chops flat in the pan in a single layer, six at a time in a 12-inch (30 cm) skillet, with space between them. Sear 2 minutes without moving, until a deep brown crust forms, then flip and go 1½ to 2 minutes more. Crowding the pan drops its temperature and steams the chops gray, so keep the second batch waiting rather than squeezing all twelve in at once. Hold the first batch on a warm plate while the second cooks; they will only lose a degree or two.
  8. Check the temperature
    Slide a thermometer horizontally into the side of a chop, into the eye of meat and away from the bone, and pull at 125°F (52°C) for medium-rare. Carryover will bring them to about 130°F (54°C). On chops this thin the whole cook is over in about 4 minutes, so start checking at 3.
  9. Rest and dress
    Pile the chops on a warm platter and rest 5 minutes, uncovered, so the juices settle without steaming the crust. Sprinkle with the flaky salt, then spoon the chimichurri generously over the top and pass more at the table. Serve on warmed plates, because lamb fat sets fast on a cold one.
Know when it is done
Pull lamb chops at 125°F (52°C) for medium-rare; after a 5-minute rest they land around 130°F (54°C).
Serve it with
Warm pita or crushed potatoes, a cucumber-tomato salad, and a glass of Malbec.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Chimichurri keeps 5 days in the fridge and gets better after a few hours, but the mint will darken. For a make-ahead version, mix everything except the mint and stir that in before serving.
  • ◆Rib chops are the elegant lollipop ones; loin chops look like tiny T-bones and are meatier and cheaper. Both work with the same timing.
  • ◆If your chops are 1½ inches (4 cm) thick, sear 2 minutes per side and then finish them in a 400°F (205°C) oven for 3 to 5 minutes.
  • ◆The same sauce is excellent on grilled steak, roast potatoes, or a bowl of white beans, so make a double batch.

Gyro-Style Lamb with Tzatziki⏱ 2 hr🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

A food-processor loaf of lamb and beef, baked, chilled, sliced paper-thin, and crisped in a pan — the honest home version of the vertical spit. Tucked into warm pita with tzatziki, it is exactly what you want it to be.

Make AheadFamily FavoriteGreek
Prep
25 min
Cook
1 hr 15 min
Total
2 hr
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Gyro loaf

Tzatziki

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Squeeze the onion dry
    Grate the onion on the large holes of a box grater, then wrap it in a clean kitchen towel and wring it out hard over the sink. You want at least ¼ cup (60 ml) of liquid out of it. Excess onion water makes the loaf steam and crumble instead of setting into a sliceable block, and this is the mistake that ruins most homemade gyro meat.
  2. Chill everything
    Put the ground lamb, ground beef, and the bowl of your food processor in the freezer for 15 minutes before you start. Cold fat stays in suspension when you process the meat, while warm fat smears and breaks, which gives you a greasy loaf. The mixture should never feel warm to the touch.
  3. Process to a paste
    Combine the chilled meats, squeezed onion, garlic, oregano, marjoram, rosemary, salt, and pepper in the food processor and run it for 60 to 90 seconds, scraping down twice. Keep going until it looks like a smooth, sticky pink paste rather than ground meat. That emulsified texture is what lets you slice it into thin sheets without it falling apart.
  4. Pack the loaf pan
    Heat the oven to 325°F (165°C). Press the mixture into an 8½ x 4½-inch (21 x 11 cm) loaf pan, pushing it firmly into the corners and slamming the pan on the counter three or four times to knock out air pockets. Smooth the top flat. Air pockets become holes and holes become crumbly slices.
  5. Bake in a water bath
    Set the loaf pan inside a larger roasting pan and pour boiling water into the outer pan until it comes halfway up the sides of the loaf pan. The water bath keeps the edges from overcooking while the dense center comes up to temperature. Bake for about 55 to 65 minutes.
  6. Make the tzatziki
    Grate the cucumber, salt it lightly, let it sit 10 minutes, then squeeze it dry in a towel just like the onion. Stir it into the yogurt with the grated garlic, lemon juice, olive oil, dill, and salt. Refrigerate at least 30 minutes so the garlic mellows and the flavors come together; it will taste harsh straight away and lovely after half an hour.
  7. Check for doneness
    The loaf is done at 165°F (74°C) in the center, measured with a thermometer pushed through the top into the middle. Ground meat needs a higher final temperature than whole cuts because bacteria get mixed throughout during grinding — 160°F (71°C) is the safety line and 165°F (74°C) gives the firm, sliceable texture you want here. It will have pulled away from the sides of the pan.
  8. Press and chill
    Pour off the rendered fat, cover the loaf with foil, set a second loaf pan on top, and weight it with two large cans for 20 minutes. Pressing compacts the loaf so it slices cleanly instead of shredding. For the best slices of all, chill the pressed loaf in the refrigerator for at least 2 hours or overnight.
  9. Slice it thin
    Turn the loaf out and cut it crosswise into slices as thin as you can manage, ideally under ⅛ inch (3 mm), using a long serrated or very sharp chef's knife. Cold loaf slices far better than warm loaf. Thin slices are the entire point — thick slabs eat like meatloaf, thin ones eat like gyro.
  10. Crisp the slices
    Heat the olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high and fry the slices in a single layer for 60 to 90 seconds per side. You want frizzled brown edges and a slight curl, which is what the outside of a spinning spit tastes like. Work in batches and do not crowd the pan, or they will steam instead of crisping.
  11. Warm the pita
    Brush the pitas lightly with the seasoned oil left in the skillet and warm them 30 seconds per side in that same pan, or directly over a gas flame for 15 seconds a side. A warm, pliable pita folds around the filling; a cold one cracks down the middle and dumps everything on your plate. Stack them in a towel to stay soft.
  12. Build the gyros
    Spread a generous spoonful of tzatziki down the center of each pita, then pile on the crisped lamb, tomato, red onion, and lettuce. Add another spoonful of tzatziki on top and fold the pita around it, wrapping the bottom half in foil or parchment to hold it together. Serve immediately while the meat is still hot and the pita soft.
Know when it is done
Cook the ground meat loaf to 165°F (74°C) in the center; the food-safety minimum for ground lamb and beef is 160°F (71°C).
Serve it with
Lemony roast potatoes or fries tucked right in the pita, and an ice-cold Greek lager.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make-ahead: bake, press, and chill the loaf up to 3 days ahead, or freeze it whole for 2 months. Slicing and crisping takes 10 minutes on the night.
  • ◆No food processor? Use the finest plate on a meat grinder twice, or knead the mixture hard by hand for a full 5 minutes until it turns tacky and sticks to your palm.
  • ◆All lamb makes a stronger, more traditional flavor; all beef makes it milder if lamb is not your thing. The 50/50 split is the crowd-pleaser.
  • ◆Squeeze the cucumber harder than feels necessary. Watery tzatziki slides straight out of the pita.
  • ◆Leftover crisped slices are excellent over a Greek salad or on rice with the tzatziki thinned into a dressing.

Central Texas Smoked Brisket⏱ 14 hr 45 min🍽 12 to 15 servingsAdvanced▾

Salt, coarse pepper, post oak smoke, and twelve unhurried hours. This is the big one — the cook that teaches you fire management, the stall, the wrap, and why the rest matters as much as the smoke.

BBQSmokerProjectWeekend
Prep
45 min
Cook
12 hr
Total
14 hr 45 min
Serves
12 to 15 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the brisket

Fire and wrap

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Choose the brisket
    Buy a whole packer, which is the flat and the point still joined, in the 12 to 14 lb (5.5 to 6.4 kg) range. Prime grade has more intramuscular fat and is far more forgiving than Choice for a first attempt. Pick one up by the middle: it should droop and bend easily, which means a thick, floppy flat rather than a thin, stiff one that will dry out.
  2. Trim the fat cap
    Work with the brisket cold and use a sharp, flexible boning knife. Trim the fat cap to an even ¼ inch (6 mm), cut away the hard, waxy deckle fat between the point and the flat, and round off every thin corner and edge so nothing sticks out to burn. Aim to remove about 2 lb (900 g) total. A well-trimmed brisket cooks evenly; a lumpy one cooks in patches.
  3. Season heavily
    Mix the black pepper, kosher salt, and optional garlic powder in a shaker — the classic Central Texas ratio is two parts pepper to one part salt. Rub the brisket with a thin film of mustard or water so the rub grips, then apply it from 12 inches (30 cm) up in even passes on every surface, including the sides. It should look like the meat has a coat on, not a dusting. Let it sit 1 hour at room temperature, or refrigerate overnight uncovered.
  4. Build and stabilize the fire
    Light your coals and bring the smoker to a steady 250°F (120°C) measured at grate level, then hold it there for a full 30 minutes before the meat goes on. Add two splits of post oak and wait for the smoke to turn thin and blue — thick white smoke is smoldering wood and it makes brisket taste bitter and sooty. Fire management is 80 percent of brisket, and stability beats any particular number.
  5. Put it on fat side up
    Set the brisket on the grate fat side up, with the thicker point end facing the fire and the thin flat end pointed away. The fat cap shields the meat from direct heat above, and the point can take more heat than the flat. Close the lid and leave it completely alone for 3 hours.
  6. Spritz and rotate
    After 3 hours, start spritzing lightly with water every hour, just enough to darken the surface without washing the rub off. Rotate the brisket 180 degrees each time so both ends see the same heat. Keep lid-opening to under 30 seconds; every peek costs you 15 to 20 minutes of recovery time.
  7. Understand the stall
    Somewhere between 150 and 170°F (65 and 77°C), usually around hour 6, the internal temperature will simply stop rising and can sit there for 4 hours or more. This is evaporative cooling: the brisket is sweating, and that evaporation refrigerates it as fast as the fire heats it. Do not raise the temperature and do not panic. Every good brisket goes through it.
  8. Judge the bark before wrapping
    Wait to wrap until the bark is dark mahogany and firm enough that dragging a fingernail across it does not smear the rub, typically at 165 to 175°F (74 to 79°C). Wrapping earlier will soften a bark that never fully set. Wrapping later, or never, gives you a firmer crust but adds hours and risks a dry flat.
  9. Wrap in butcher paper
    Lay out two overlapping arm-lengths of pink butcher paper, brush the paper with warmed beef tallow if you are using it, set the brisket in the middle fat side up, and roll it tight, tucking the sides in like a burrito. Paper is porous, so it stops most evaporation and breaks the stall while still letting the bark breathe — foil would end the stall faster but steams the bark soft. Return it to the smoker seam side down.
  10. Ride it out to probe tender
    Cook wrapped for another 3 to 5 hours. Start testing at 195°F (91°C) by sliding a thermometer probe or a skewer into the thickest part of the flat: it should go in and out with the resistance of warm butter, with no grabbing at all. Most briskets land between 200 and 205°F (93 and 96°C), but tenderness is the real test and the number is only a signpost.
  11. Vent, then rest long
    Take the wrapped brisket off and let it sit on the counter for 20 to 30 minutes until the internal temperature drops to about 170°F (77°C). Then put it, still wrapped, into a dry empty cooler lined with a towel and let it rest 2 to 4 hours. Venting first stops it from carrying over and overcooking in the cooler, and the long rest lets rendered fat and gelatin thicken and get reabsorbed. Slicing a hot brisket dumps all of that on the board.
  12. Separate the point from the flat
    Unwrap on a big board and find the thick line of fat that runs between the two muscles, then cut along it with a long knife to separate the point from the flat. The two muscles have grain running in different directions, so you cannot slice the whole thing one way and get it right. Save the point for burnt ends if you like.
  13. Slice against the grain
    Look at the flat and find the direction the muscle fibers run, then slice perpendicular to them in pieces about the thickness of a No. 2 pencil, ¼ inch (6 mm). Use a long slicing knife and pull it through in single strokes without sawing. Rotate the point 90 degrees from the flat and slice it thicker, about ½ inch (1 cm), since it is richer.
  14. Check your work and serve
    A good slice should hold together when you lift it by one end but pull apart with a gentle tug, and it should leave a glistening smear on the board. Look for a pink smoke ring about ¼ inch (6 mm) under the bark — it is a chemical reaction, not a flavor, but it tells you the fire ran clean. Serve immediately with white bread, pickles, and onion, and never with sauce until someone asks.
Know when it is done
Probe tender between 200 and 205°F (93 and 96°C); the stall sits at 150 to 170°F (65 to 77°C) and wrapping happens at 165 to 175°F (74 to 79°C).
Serve it with
White bread, dill pickles, raw white onion, and a very cold Shiner or Lone Star.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Budget 1 to 1½ hours per pound (2 to 3 hours per kg) at 250°F (120°C), then add 3 hours of slack. A brisket that finishes early can hold in a cooler for 4 hours; one that finishes late ruins dinner.
  • ◆Two thermometers, always: one clipped at grate level for the fire and one probe in the thickest part of the flat. Dome thermometers routinely read 25 to 50°F (14 to 28°C) off.
  • ◆Leftovers: slice only what you will eat and refrigerate the rest in whole chunks. Sliced brisket dries out in a day, while a chunk reheats beautifully wrapped in foil at 300°F (150°C).
  • ◆If the flat comes out dry but the point is good, you either trimmed too much fat or cooked past probe tender. Next time, start testing at 195°F (91°C).
  • ◆Save every scrap of trimmed fat, render it slowly in a low oven, and keep the tallow. It is what you brush on the butcher paper and it makes a real difference.

Kansas City Brisket Burnt Ends⏱ 7 hr 50 min🍽 8 servingsMedium▾

Cubes of the fatty brisket point, sauced and put back in the smoke until they tighten into sticky, candied bites. Barbecue people call them meat candy and they are not exaggerating.

BBQSmokerParty Food
Prep
20 min
Cook
7 hr 30 min
Total
7 hr 50 min
Serves
8 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the point

Sauce and finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Get the right cut
    Ask the butcher for the brisket point or deckle, which is the thick, fatty muscle that sits on top of the flat on a whole packer. If they only sell whole packers, buy one and separate the two muscles along the fat seam yourself. The point is far fattier than the flat, and that fat is exactly what renders into the sticky texture burnt ends need.
  2. Trim, but not too much
    Trim the outer fat cap down to about ¼ inch (6 mm) and cut away any hard, waxy fat, but leave the interior marbling alone. Square off thin edges so nothing hangs out to burn. Over-trimming is the classic mistake here: without internal fat you get dry brown cubes instead of glossy ones.
  3. Season the night before
    Mix the black pepper, salt, and garlic powder and set 1 tbsp aside for the sauce later. Coat the point with the mustard and press the rest of the rub on heavily from every angle, including the underside. Refrigerate uncovered on a rack for 8 to 24 hours; the salt penetrates and the surface dries so the bark can set.
  4. Set the smoker
    Bring your smoker to a steady 250°F (120°C) at grate level and add two wood chunks once the coals are ashed over. Wait for thin blue smoke before the meat goes on, since thick white smoke will make everything taste acrid. Fill a water pan if your cooker has one, which helps hold humidity and steadies the temperature.
  5. Smoke it whole
    Put the point on fat side up and smoke it whole for about 5 hours, spritzing lightly with water after the third hour. Do not cube it yet — cutting early exposes too much surface and dries the meat out. Add one more wood chunk at the 2-hour mark if the smoke has thinned out.
  6. Push through the stall
    The internal temperature will stall somewhere between 150 and 165°F (65 and 74°C), often for two hours. This is evaporative cooling and it is completely normal, so hold your fire steady rather than raising it. If you are pressed for time, wrap the point in butcher paper once the bark is dark and firm and it will push through in about half the time.
  7. Cook to 195°F
    Continue until the point reaches 195 to 200°F (91 to 93°C) and a probe slides into the thickest part with only slight resistance. You want it just short of fully tender, since it has another 90 minutes of cooking ahead of it in the sauce. Total time is usually 5 to 6 hours at 250°F (120°C).
  8. Rest, then cube
    Let the point rest 20 minutes on a board so it firms up enough to cut cleanly. Slice it into even 1½-inch (4 cm) cubes, which is big enough that they do not dry out and small enough that every cube gets sauce on all six sides. Even sizing matters more than exact size, because mixed sizes cook unevenly.
  9. Sauce and pan them
    Toss the cubes in a disposable foil pan with the barbecue sauce, brown sugar, honey, cider vinegar, and the reserved 1 tbsp of rub until every piece is coated. Dot the pats of butter over the top. Spread them into a single layer so they roast rather than stew in a pile.
  10. Finish uncovered
    Put the pan back in the 250°F (120°C) smoker, uncovered, for 60 to 90 minutes, stirring gently every 30 minutes. The sauce will reduce and cling, the edges will darken, and the cubes will go from wet to tacky. They are done when a cube lifted on a fork holds a glossy coat that does not run off.
  11. Taste and serve hot
    Pull one cube out and cut it in half: the inside should be juicy and the fat fully rendered with no chewy white streaks left. If it is still firm, give it another 20 minutes covered with foil. Serve them straight from the pan while they are hot, with toothpicks and plenty of napkins.
Know when it is done
Smoke the point to 195 to 200°F (91 to 93°C) before cubing, then finish in sauce until the fat is fully rendered.
Serve it with
Creamy potato salad, baked beans, white bread, and a cold bourbon and Coke.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make-ahead: smoke the point a day early, refrigerate it whole, then cube, sauce, and finish the next day. Cold meat cubes even more neatly.
  • ◆Poor man's burnt ends use a 4 lb (1.8 kg) chuck roast the exact same way and cost half as much. They are excellent, just a little less fatty.
  • ◆If the cubes come out dry, you trimmed too much fat or overcooked the point before cubing. Pull it at 195°F (91°C), not 205°F (96°C).
  • ◆Do not cover the pan during the finishing stage. Covering traps steam and gives you saucy stew meat instead of candied edges.

Char Siu Chinese Barbecue Pork⏱ 13 hr 15 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Strips of pork shoulder marinated overnight in hoisin, five-spice, and honey, then roasted until the edges char and the glaze turns to red lacquer. It is the sweet-savory pork that hangs in every Chinatown window.

Make AheadOvenTakeout at Home
Prep
20 min
Cook
45 min
Total
13 hr 15 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the pork

Marinade

Glaze

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Cut the pork into strips
    Trim the shoulder of any thick fat sheets but leave the marbling, then cut it with the grain into long strips about 2 inches (5 cm) wide and 1½ inches (4 cm) thick. Strips give you far more surface area than a roast, which is where the charred, caramelized edges come from. Uniform thickness matters more than uniform length so everything finishes together.
  2. Mix the marinade
    Whisk the hoisin, soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, oyster sauce, sugar, honey, garlic, five-spice, and white pepper in a bowl until smooth. If you are using red fermented bean curd, mash the cubes with the brine first until they dissolve — this is what gives authentic char siu its reddish color and savory funk, not food coloring. Taste it: it should be aggressively sweet and salty, since it has to season the whole strip.
  3. Reserve and marinate
    Set aside ¼ cup (60 ml) of the marinade in a covered container in the fridge for the glaze later. Put the pork strips in a zip-top bag with the rest, press out the air, and massage it until every surface is coated. Refrigerate at least 12 hours and up to 24, turning the bag once or twice.
  4. Bring the pork to room temperature
    Take the bag out 45 minutes before roasting so the strips are not fridge-cold going into a hot oven. Cold meat browns unevenly and takes longer, which risks drying out the thinner ends. Meanwhile, take the reserved marinade out too.
  5. Set up the pan
    Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) with a rack in the upper third. Line a rimmed sheet pan with foil, pour in the 1 cup (240 ml) of water, and set a wire rack over it. The water catches the sugary drips and keeps them from burning into acrid smoke, which is the single most common char siu problem at home.
  6. Roast the first side
    Shake the excess marinade off each strip and lay them on the rack with at least 1 inch (2.5 cm) between them. Roast for 15 minutes, until the surface is dry to the touch and starting to darken at the corners. Space matters — strips that touch will steam instead of roasting.
  7. Boil the reserved marinade
    While the pork roasts, pour the reserved ¼ cup (60 ml) of marinade into a small saucepan and boil it hard for a full 2 minutes. It touched raw pork, so it must be boiled before it goes anywhere near cooked meat. Take 2 tbsp of it, whisk in the 3 tbsp honey and 1 tbsp hot water, and you have your glaze.
  8. Flip and roast again
    Turn each strip over with tongs and roast 15 minutes more. The pork should be firming up and the edges going deep brown-red. If the water in the pan has evaporated, add another ½ cup (120 ml) so the drippings never scorch.
  9. Glaze in layers
    Brush the strips with a thin coat of glaze and roast 5 minutes, then flip, glaze the other side, and roast 5 minutes more. Repeat once more if you want a heavier lacquer, watching closely because honey burns quickly at 425°F (220°C). Thin repeated coats build a glossy shell; one thick coat just slides off.
  10. Check the temperature
    Push a thermometer into the thickest strip. Char siu is taken further than a pork chop on purpose, to 160°F (71°C), because shoulder has enough fat and collagen that the extra heat makes it tender rather than dry. Whole-muscle pork is safe at 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest, so anything from there up is fine — 160°F (71°C) is simply where the texture is best.
  11. Char the edges
    Move the pan 6 inches (15 cm) under the broiler for 1 to 2 minutes per side, watching it every second. You are after blackened tips and blistered edges, which is where the name char siu comes from. There is a 20-second window between beautifully charred and burnt, so do not answer your phone.
  12. Rest and slice
    Rest the strips on a board for 10 minutes so the juices settle and the glaze sets into a tacky shell. Slice across the grain about ¼ inch (6 mm) thick; each slice should have a dark ring and a rosy interior. Brush the slices with any leftover glaze and serve warm over rice or in steamed buns.
Know when it is done
Roast to 160°F (71°C) for the best texture on pork shoulder; the food-safety minimum for whole-muscle pork is 145°F (63°C) plus a 3-minute rest.
Serve it with
Steamed jasmine rice, blanched gai lan with oyster sauce, and jasmine tea or a cold pilsner.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Pork shoulder is the right cut — it has the fat to stay juicy through a hot roast. Tenderloin makes a dry, disappointing char siu no matter how carefully you cook it.
  • ◆Maltose is the traditional glaze sugar and gives an unmistakable sheen. It is rock-hard in the jar, so warm the jar in hot water for 5 minutes before you try to scoop it.
  • ◆Make-ahead: char siu keeps 4 days refrigerated and freezes for 2 months. Slice cold, then warm it in a hot pan for 60 seconds a side.
  • ◆Leftovers are the whole point for a lot of people. Dice them into fried rice, tuck them into steamed bao, or lay slices over a bowl of wonton noodle soup.
  • ◆Red fermented bean curd is worth seeking out at an Asian grocery, but the recipe is still excellent without it — just expect a browner, less crimson color.

Italian Sausage and Peppers⏱ 40 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

One skillet, forty easy minutes, and the smell that takes over a street fair. Brown the sausages, soften the peppers in their fat, and let a splash of wine pull it all together.

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Do not prick the sausages
    Leave the links whole and resist the urge to poke holes in them, which is a myth that only lets fat and juice escape. Pat them dry with a paper towel so they brown rather than steam. If the links are very thick, more than 1¼ inches (3 cm), leave them whole anyway and just plan on a couple of extra minutes.
  2. Brown the sausages
    Heat 1 tbsp of the olive oil in a 12-inch (30 cm) skillet over medium heat until it shimmers, then add the links in a single layer. Cook 8 to 10 minutes total, turning every 2 minutes, until they are browned on all sides but still slightly underdone in the middle. Medium heat, not high, is the key here — high heat splits the casings and pushes all the fat out at once.
  3. Set them aside
    Move the browned sausages to a plate; they will finish cooking in the peppers later. Leave every drop of rendered fat in the pan, because that seasoned fat is what the vegetables cook in and it carries all the fennel and garlic flavor from the sausage. Add the second tablespoon of oil only if the pan looks dry.
  4. Cook the onions first
    Add the sliced onion with the ¾ tsp salt and cook over medium-high heat for 4 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the edges start to brown and the slices soften. Salting now pulls water out and speeds up the browning. Scrape the bottom as you go to lift the browned sausage bits.
  5. Add the peppers
    Add the sliced bell peppers and cook 5 to 6 minutes more, stirring every minute or so. You want them softened and blistered in spots but still holding their shape, not collapsed into mush. If the pan looks crowded, that is fine — they will shrink by nearly half as they cook.
  6. Bloom the aromatics
    Push the vegetables to the edges of the pan, add the sliced garlic, oregano, red pepper flakes, and black pepper to the center, and stir them in the hot fat for 45 seconds until fragrant. Garlic burns in about 90 seconds at this heat, so keep it moving and do not let it go past pale gold. Then stir everything together.
  7. Cook the tomato paste
    Clear another small space, add the tomato paste, and let it fry for 90 seconds, stirring, until it darkens from bright red to brick. This drives off the raw canned flavor and deepens the whole dish. Stir it through the vegetables so they take on a rusty coating.
  8. Deglaze and finish the sausages
    Pour in the wine and scrape the bottom of the pan clean with a wooden spoon while it bubbles. Nestle the sausages back in with any juices from the plate, turn the heat to medium-low, cover, and simmer 6 to 8 minutes. The steam finishes cooking the sausages through while the peppers turn silky.
  9. Check and serve
    Cut into the thickest sausage or probe it: fresh pork sausage needs 160°F (71°C) in the center and should show no pink. Taste the peppers and add salt in pinches until they taste bright rather than flat, then scatter the basil over the top. Pile everything into warm split rolls, or serve it over polenta with the pan juices spooned on.
Know when it is done
Fresh pork sausage is done at 160°F (71°C) in the center, with no pink remaining.
Serve it with
Crusty rolls or soft polenta, a simple green salad, and a glass of Chianti or a cold Peroni.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Mix sweet and hot links — three of each — so everyone at the table gets what they want without you making two pans.
  • ◆Make-ahead: the whole dish reheats well and is arguably better the next day. Keep the rolls separate and warm them fresh.
  • ◆For a saucier version, add a 14 oz (400 g) can of crushed tomatoes with the wine and simmer 15 minutes instead of 8.
  • ◆Leftovers make a great baked ziti: slice the sausages into coins, toss with the peppers and a pound of cooked pasta, top with mozzarella, and bake at 375°F (190°C) for 20 minutes.

These are the plates you would pay real money for in a room with cloth napkins — lacquered duck skin, scallops on a cloud of cauliflower, a Wellington that gets a gasp when you slice it. None of it is magic; it is a handful of careful steps done in the right order, and you can absolutely do this.

Crispy Duck Breast with Cherry Gastrique⏱ 1 hr 15 min🍽 2 servingsMedium▾

Skin rendered until it shatters like glass, meat the color of a rose, and a sweet-sour cherry sauce that cuts straight through the richness. This is the dish that makes people ask where you learned to cook.

Date NightRestaurant at HomeCast Iron
Prep
15 min
Cook
30 min
Total
1 hr 15 min
Serves
2 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the duck

Cherry gastrique

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Trim and score the skin
    Pat the duck breasts completely dry and trim any flaps of skin or fat that hang past the meat. With a sharp knife held at a shallow angle, cut a crosshatch through the skin and fat about 1/4 in (6 mm) apart, stopping before you reach the red meat — if you see meat in the cuts you have gone too deep and juice will leak out and steam the skin. Those channels give the fat a road to escape by, which is the whole secret to crisp duck.
  2. Salt and rest the duck
    Season both sides with the 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp pepper, then set the breasts skin side up on a rack over a plate. Refrigerate uncovered for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours. Cold dry air pulls water out of the skin, and dry skin browns while wet skin steams. If you are short on time, even 30 minutes makes a visible difference.
  3. Start in a cold pan
    Lay the duck skin side down in a dry, cold 10 in (25 cm) stainless or cast iron skillet — no oil, no preheating. Then turn the burner to medium-low. Starting cold lets the fat melt slowly and evenly instead of seizing the skin shut, and it is the single most common thing home cooks get wrong with duck.
  4. Render low and slow
    Let the duck sit undisturbed for 12 to 15 minutes over medium-low heat. You want a lazy, steady bubbling sound, never a violent sizzle or any smoke — if it gets loud, drop the heat. Every 4 to 5 minutes, carefully pour the rendered fat into a heatproof jar so the skin is frying in a thin film, not swimming in a deep pool. You should end up with 1/4 to 1/3 cup of gorgeous duck fat; save it for potatoes.
  5. Check the skin, then flip
    Lift a breast with tongs and look: the skin should be evenly deep golden brown, thin, and stiff, and the fat layer beneath it should have shrunk to almost nothing. If it is still pale or soft in the middle, give it another 3 to 4 minutes. When it looks right, flip the breasts over and add the thyme sprigs to the pan.
  6. Finish on the flesh side
    Cook flesh side down for just 2 to 4 minutes over medium heat, spooning a little of the hot fat over the top as it goes. Check the thickest part with an instant-read thermometer and pull the duck at 130°F (54°C) for a rosy medium-rare. Duck breast is whole-muscle red meat and is traditionally served pink, exactly like a steak, but know the rule you are working around: the USDA guideline for all poultry is 165°F (74°C), so cook it there if you want the full guideline. Past about 150°F (66°C) it turns dry and livery.
  7. Rest the duck
    Move the breasts to a cutting board, skin side up, and rest them 8 to 10 minutes. The internal temperature will coast up to about 135°F (57°C) and the juices will settle back into the fibers instead of running out on your board. Never tent duck with foil — trapped steam will soften the crackling skin you just spent 15 minutes building.
  8. Make the caramel
    Wipe out a small saucepan, add the 1/3 cup sugar in an even layer, and set it over medium heat. Do not stir; just swirl the pan occasionally as the edges melt and the sugar turns from clear to straw to a deep amber, which takes about 4 to 6 minutes. Amber is where the flavor is, but it goes to burnt fast, so pull it the moment it smells like toasted caramel rather than coffee.
  9. Deglaze with vinegar
    Stand back and pour in the 1/3 cup red wine vinegar all at once — it will hiss violently and throw off sharp-smelling steam, and the caramel will seize into a hard lump. That is completely normal. Keep it over medium heat and stir for 1 to 2 minutes until the lump dissolves back into a smooth syrup. This sweet-sour base is what gastrique means.
  10. Build and reduce the sauce
    Add the 1/4 cup port and 1/2 cup stock and simmer briskly for 6 to 8 minutes, until the sauce has reduced by about half and coats the back of a spoon. Drag your finger through it — the line should hold for a second before closing. Stir in the cherries and simmer 3 more minutes, just until they soften but still hold their shape.
  11. Mount with butter
    Take the pan off the heat, add the 1 tbsp cold butter, and swirl the pan until it disappears into the sauce and gives it a glossy sheen. Season with the 1/4 tsp salt and taste: it should hit sweet, then sour, then savory, in that order. If it is too sharp add a pinch of sugar; too sweet, a few drops more vinegar.
  12. Slice and plate
    Slice each breast against the grain into 1/4 in (6 mm) planks, cutting straight down through the skin with a sharp knife so the crust does not tear. Spoon a shallow pool of gastrique slightly off-center on two warm plates, then fan the duck slices over the sauce with the crisp skin facing up and visible. Scatter the cherries around, add the 1/2 tsp flaky sea salt on the meat, and serve at once. Never pour sauce over the skin — that is how you undo all of it.
Know when it is done
Pull the duck at 130°F (54°C) for medium-rare; it will rest up to about 135°F (57°C). Duck breast is whole-muscle meat and is traditionally served pink like steak, but the USDA guideline for all poultry is 165°F (74°C) — cook it to that if you want the full guideline or are serving anyone pregnant, very young, elderly, or immunocompromised.
Serve it with
A cool glass of Pinot Noir and a pile of duck-fat roasted potatoes or a bitter greens salad.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Save the rendered duck fat in a jar in the fridge for up to 3 months. Roast potatoes in it at 425°F (220°C) and you will understand why cooks hoard the stuff.
  • ◆Frozen cherries work beautifully here and need no thawing — just add them straight to the reducing sauce and give them an extra minute.
  • ◆The gastrique can be made up to 5 days ahead through the reduction step. Rewarm it gently, then add the cherries and butter fresh so the sauce stays glossy.
  • ◆If your skin is browning fast but still thick and soft underneath, your heat is too high. Move the pan off the burner for a minute and go back at a lower setting; rendering is a patience game.
  • ◆No port on hand? Use dry red wine plus 1 tsp sugar, or even a splash of balsamic vinegar cut with water.

Seared Scallops with Cauliflower Puree⏱ 45 min🍽 2 servingsMedium▾

Silky white puree, deeply caramelized scallops, and a nutty brown butter poured over at the table. It looks like a tasting menu course and takes about forty-five minutes.

Date NightRestaurant at HomeUnder an Hour
Prep
15 min
Cook
30 min
Total
45 min
Serves
2 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Cauliflower puree

For the scallops

Hazelnut brown butter

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Cook cauliflower in milk
    Put the cauliflower florets in a 3 qt (3 L) saucepan with the 1 1/2 cups milk, the 2 tbsp butter, and the 3/4 tsp salt. Bring to a bare simmer over medium heat and cook 14 to 18 minutes, stirring now and then so the milk does not scorch on the bottom. The cauliflower is ready when a knife slides through a floret with zero resistance — undercooked cauliflower will never blend smooth, no matter how long you run the blender.
  2. Blend the puree silky
    Drain the cauliflower, saving the milk. Blend the florets with the 1/4 cup warm cream and about 1/3 cup (80 ml) of the reserved milk on high for a full 60 to 90 seconds. Add more milk a tablespoon at a time until it moves like thick pancake batter and falls off the spatula in a ribbon. Season with the white pepper and more salt to taste, then keep it warm in the covered pot over the lowest heat.
  3. Pull the side muscle
    Look along the side of each scallop for a small rectangular tab of firmer, slightly fibrous flesh. Pinch it and peel it away with your fingers; it takes two seconds each and needs no knife. That tab is the muscle the scallop used to clamp its shell shut, and it turns rubbery and stringy when cooked, so removing it is the difference between silky and chewy. Discard the tabs, or freeze them for a seafood stock.
  4. Dry the scallops hard
    Lay the scallops on a doubled paper towel, press another towel firmly on top, and leave them uncovered for 10 minutes. Change the towel once if it soaks through. Surface water has to boil away before browning can even begin, so every drop you blot now is a second of real searing you get back later. They should feel dry and slightly tacky.
  5. Season at the last second
    Season the scallops with the 3/4 tsp kosher salt and 1/4 tsp pepper right before they go in the pan, not a minute earlier. Salt draws moisture back to the surface within about 60 seconds, which quietly undoes all your blotting. Set the seasoned scallops in a row next to the stove so you can load the pan quickly.
  6. Get the pan properly hot
    Heat a 12 in (30 cm) stainless or cast iron skillet over medium-high for 2 to 3 minutes, then add the 1 tbsp oil and swirl to coat. The oil should shimmer and run thin like water with the very first wisp of smoke. If it is billowing smoke, pull the pan off the burner for 30 seconds — scorched fat tastes acrid. Skip nonstick here; it does not hold enough heat to build a crust.
  7. Sear and do not touch
    Lay the scallops in one at a time, working clockwise so you know which went in first, leaving 1 in (2.5 cm) between them. Do not move, poke, or peek for 2 to 3 full minutes — you want a steady aggressive sizzle, not a quiet hiss. When the bottom edge has gone deep amber, each scallop will release from the pan on its own. If it sticks, it is not ready.
  8. Flip and finish
    Turn each scallop with a thin spatula and cook just 60 to 90 seconds on the second side, which is only there to set the interior. Press the side gently: it should feel like the fleshy pad below your thumb, with a little give. Pull them at 125 to 130°F (52 to 54°C) in the center for a sweet, barely translucent middle. Firm and springy means overcooked.
  9. Brown the butter
    Move the scallops to a warm plate, seared side up, and turn the heat to medium. Add the 4 tbsp butter to the same pan and swirl constantly as it melts, foams, and quiets down. In 2 to 3 minutes the milk solids on the bottom will turn hazelnut brown and it will smell toasty and sweet. Brown butter goes from perfect to burnt in about 20 seconds, so trust your nose over your eyes.
  10. Finish the butter off heat
    Pull the pan off the burner and stir in the hazelnuts, the 1 tbsp lemon juice, and the chives. The lemon will hiss and instantly cut the richness, and the residual heat is enough to warm the nuts and wilt the chives without scorching either. Taking the pan off the heat also stops the butter cooking any further, which matters because it is already sitting right at the edge of too dark. Taste and add a pinch of salt if it needs it.
  11. Plate it like a restaurant
    Spoon a generous pool of warm puree into the center of each warm plate and drag the back of the spoon through it to make a wide comma-shaped swoosh. Arrange 5 or 6 scallops along the puree, seared side up, spaced evenly so each one is visible. Spoon the hazelnut brown butter over and around them, finish with the 1/2 tsp flaky salt on the scallops only, and serve immediately while the crust is still crisp.
Know when it is done
Pull the scallops at 125 to 130°F (52 to 54°C) for a sweet, just-set center. The FDA guideline for fully cooked shellfish is 145°F (63°C), which will be noticeably firmer.
Serve it with
A cold, mineral white like Sancerre or Chablis, with a thin slice of grilled sourdough to chase the brown butter.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Buy dry-packed scallops. Wet-packed ones sit in a phosphate solution, leak liquid the moment they hit the pan, and will never brown properly.
  • ◆The puree can be made 3 days ahead and refrigerated. Rewarm it gently with a splash of milk, whisking, and it comes right back to silky.
  • ◆If your puree is grainy, it is either undercooked cauliflower or an underworked blender. Give it another 60 seconds on high before you add more liquid.
  • ◆Sear in two batches rather than crowding a small pan. Two great batches beat one steamed one, and the second batch benefits from a hotter pan.
  • ◆Toast the hazelnuts at 350°F (175°C) for 8 to 10 minutes and rub off the skins in a towel — it takes ten minutes and doubles their flavor.

Filet Mignon with Bordelaise Sauce⏱ 1 hr 45 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Thick, tender filets with a dark crust, sitting in a glossy red wine sauce that took an hour of quiet reducing and tastes like a hundred dollars. This is the classic French steakhouse plate, done properly at home.

Date NightRestaurant at HomeCast Iron
Prep
15 min
Cook
45 min
Total
1 hr 45 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the steaks

Bordelaise sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Salt the steaks early
    Pat the filets bone dry and season all over, including the sides, with the 2 tsp kosher salt and 1 tsp pepper. Set them on a rack over a sheet pan and refrigerate uncovered for at least 45 minutes and up to 24 hours. The salt first pulls moisture out, then the meat reabsorbs it seasoned all the way through, and the surface dries so it can brown. Take them out 30 minutes before cooking so the centers are not ice cold.
  2. Sweat the shallots
    Melt the 2 tbsp butter in a 2 qt (2 L) saucepan over medium-low heat and add the minced shallots with a pinch of salt. Cook gently for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until they are soft and translucent but not browned. Browned shallots turn the sauce bitter and cloudy, so keep the heat modest and stop the moment they go glassy.
  3. Reduce the wine to almost nothing
    Stir in the 1 tsp tomato paste and cook 30 seconds until it darkens, then pour in the 1 1/2 cups red wine and add the thyme, bay leaf, and crushed peppercorns. Simmer briskly over medium heat for 12 to 15 minutes until only about 1/4 cup (60 ml) of syrupy liquid remains. This step burns off the raw alcohol and concentrates the wine into something deep and sweet rather than sharp.
  4. Add stock and reduce again
    Pour in the 1 1/2 cups veal or beef stock and simmer over medium-low for 20 to 25 minutes, until the sauce has reduced to about 3/4 cup (180 ml) and coats the back of a spoon. Drag your finger through the coating: the line should hold for a beat before closing. Strain through a fine sieve into a small clean pot, pressing on the solids, and set it aside off the heat.
  5. Heat the pan properly
    Set a 12 in (30 cm) cast iron skillet over medium-high heat for 4 to 5 minutes, until a drop of water skitters and vanishes instantly. Preheat the oven to 400°F (205°C) at the same time. Add the 1 tbsp oil and swirl — it should shimmer with the first thread of smoke. A properly hot pan is what gives you crust in 3 minutes instead of gray meat in 8.
  6. Sear the flat sides
    Lay the filets in the pan without crowding, leaving at least 1 1/2 in (4 cm) between them, and press each one down for the first few seconds so the whole face makes contact. Sear 2 1/2 to 3 minutes without moving them; you want a loud steady roar, not smoke pouring off. Flip and sear the second side another 2 1/2 minutes, until both faces are deep brown all the way to the edges.
  7. Roll the edges
    Filets are tall, so use tongs to stand each one on its rounded side and roll it around the pan for 30 to 45 seconds per section until the whole perimeter is browned. Untouched sides are pale and taste boiled next to the seared faces. Work quickly here so the centers do not run away from you.
  8. Baste with butter and herbs
    Drop in the 2 tbsp butter, the thyme sprigs, and the smashed garlic and let the butter foam. Tilt the pan toward you and spoon the foaming butter over the steaks continuously for about 60 seconds. The butter should be sputtering and smell nutty and herbal — if it is smoking black, the heat is too high, so pull the pan off for a moment.
  9. Finish in the oven
    Slide the whole skillet into the 400°F (205°C) oven and roast 4 to 7 minutes depending on thickness. Start checking at 4 minutes with an instant-read thermometer pushed into the center from the side. Pull the steaks at 125°F (52°C) for medium-rare or 133°F (56°C) for medium — these are pull temperatures, not final ones.
  10. Rest the steaks
    Move the filets to a warm plate or board and let them rest for 8 to 10 minutes, loosely tented if your kitchen is cold. They will carry over about 5 to 8°F (3 to 4°C), landing at a final 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium-rare. Cutting early dumps the juices onto the board and leaves the meat dry, so this wait genuinely matters.
  11. Mount the sauce with cold butter
    Warm the strained sauce over low heat until it steams but does not boil, then take it off the burner and whisk in the 3 tbsp cold butter one cube at a time. Each cube should melt into a glossy emulsion before the next one goes in; if you rush it or let it boil, the sauce will break and look oily. Season with the 1/2 tsp salt and taste for balance.
  12. Plate and pour
    Spoon 2 to 3 tablespoons of bordelaise slightly off-center onto each warm plate and set a rested filet on top so the sauce frames it rather than drowning it. Add a small pile of something creamy at the two o'clock position — potato puree or spinach — and keep one third of the plate empty so the food has room to breathe. Finish with the 1/2 tsp flaky sea salt on the meat and serve immediately with the rest of the sauce in a small pitcher.
Know when it is done
Pull filets at 125°F (52°C) for medium-rare or 133°F (56°C) for medium; after a 10 minute rest they finish at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) and 138 to 140°F (59 to 60°C) respectively.
Serve it with
The same red you reduced into the sauce, plus potato puree and a handful of buttered haricots verts.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆The sauce is better made a day ahead. Reduce and strain it, refrigerate, then rewarm and mount with cold butter right before serving — never reheat a mounted sauce, it will break.
  • ◆Use a wine you would happily drink. Cooking does not fix a bad bottle, it concentrates it, and cooking wine from the supermarket is salted and harsh.
  • ◆If you cannot find veal stock, reduce 3 cups (720 ml) of good beef stock down to 1 1/2 cups first — the extra body is what makes a bordelaise cling.
  • ◆Traditional bordelaise finishes with poached beef marrow. If you can get a marrow bone, poach 2 oz (55 g) of diced marrow in the sauce for 2 minutes at the end.
  • ◆A broken sauce can often be saved: whisk 1 tbsp (15 ml) of hot water into it off the heat, drop by drop, to bring the emulsion back together.

Butter-Poached Lobster Tails⏱ 35 min🍽 2 servingsEasy▾

Lobster gently cooked in a warm bath of emulsified butter comes out sweeter and more tender than boiling could ever manage. No sous vide machine, no immersion circulator, just a small pot and a thermometer.

Date NightRestaurant at HomeUnder an Hour
Prep
15 min
Cook
20 min
Total
35 min
Serves
2 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the lobster

Beurre monte poaching butter

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Blanch to release the shells
    Bring a large pot of water with the 2 tbsp kosher salt to a rolling boil, then drop the tails in for exactly 60 to 90 seconds. This is not cooking them, it is loosening the meat from the shell so it slides out whole. Pull them immediately into a bowl of ice water and leave them 2 minutes to stop the cooking cold. Skip this step and you will end up shredding the meat trying to pry it free.
  2. Remove the meat whole
    Set a cooled tail on the cutting board and snip down both sides of the soft underside shell with kitchen shears. Peel back the flap and lift the meat out in one piece, using your thumb to work it loose from the wide end. Pull out the dark digestive vein along the back with the tip of a knife, then pat the meat completely dry and season it with the 1/2 tsp kosher salt.
  3. Set up the butter bath
    Pour the 3 tbsp water into a small deep saucepan, 1 1/2 to 2 qt (1.5 to 2 L), and bring it to a simmer over medium heat. The pot needs to be small and deep so the butter is deep enough to actually submerge the lobster — a wide skillet will spread it too thin. Have a clip-on or instant-read thermometer ready, because temperature control is the entire technique here.
  4. Build the beurre monte
    Turn the heat to low and whisk in the cold butter one or two pieces at a time, adding the next only after the last has melted and the mixture looks like glossy cream. Never let it boil — above about 190°F (88°C) the emulsion breaks and separates into oil and milky solids. Keep whisking steadily and you will end up with roughly 2 cups of thick, opaque, sauce-like butter, not a clear puddle of grease.
  5. Hold the temperature
    Add the smashed garlic, the tarragon, and the 1/2 tsp salt, then adjust the burner to hold the butter between 160 and 180°F (71 and 82°C). On most home stoves that means the lowest setting, with the pot pulled halfway off the burner whenever it climbs. Check the thermometer every couple of minutes; this range is warm enough to cook lobster gently but cool enough that the proteins never seize and toughen.
  6. Poach the tails
    Slip the lobster meat into the butter, making sure each piece is fully submerged, and poach for 6 to 8 minutes depending on thickness. Turn the pieces once halfway through with a spoon. The meat will go from translucent to opaque ivory and firm up slightly, and it should stay glossy and plump rather than shrinking and curling tight.
  7. Check for doneness
    Push an instant-read thermometer into the thickest part of a tail; you are looking for 135 to 140°F (57 to 60°C). At that point the meat is just set, sweet, and yielding — the FDA guideline for fully cooked shellfish is 145°F (63°C), which is firmer. If your thermometer will not read a piece that thin, press it: it should feel like a ripe plum, springy but not hard.
  8. Rest in the butter
    Take the pot off the heat and let the lobster sit in the warm butter for 2 to 3 minutes while you get the plates ready. It will hold at serving temperature without overcooking as long as the butter stays under 150°F (66°C). Stir the 1 tsp lemon juice into the butter now, off the heat, so the acid brightens it without threatening the emulsion.
  9. Spoon out the sauce
    Ladle about 1/3 cup (80 ml) of the poaching butter into a small warm bowl and whisk in a teaspoon of the lobster juices that have settled at the bottom of the pot. That is your sauce and it is already finished — do not try to reduce it or heat it further, because boiling will split the emulsion you just spent ten minutes building. Keep the bowl somewhere warm, near the stove or on the back of the range, so it stays pourable. Strain and save the rest of the butter.
  10. Slice and plate
    Cut each tail on a slight bias into 4 or 5 thick medallions, or leave them whole if you want the shape to show. Fan the medallions in a slight arc across the upper half of two warm plates, overlapping them like fallen dominoes so every cut face catches the light. Spoon the warm butter sauce over the meat, add a few torn tarragon leaves and a lemon wedge at the edge, and serve right away.
Know when it is done
Hold the butter at 160 to 180°F (71 to 82°C) and pull the lobster at 135 to 140°F (57 to 60°C) for tender, just-set meat; the FDA guideline for fully cooked shellfish is 145°F (63°C).
Serve it with
A buttery Chardonnay or a glass of Champagne, with asparagus and a lemon wedge on the side.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Strain and refrigerate the leftover butter — it keeps for 2 weeks and is spectacular tossed with pasta, brushed on corn, or used to poach fish or shrimp another night.
  • ◆Cold-water tails (Maine, Canadian) are sweeter and firmer than warm-water ones, which can be mushy. Look for tails whose shell is hard and whose meat is white, not gray.
  • ◆If your butter breaks and turns oily, take it off the heat, add 1 tbsp (15 ml) cold water, and whisk hard — it will usually pull back together.
  • ◆You can poach in a smaller amount of butter by using a narrow pot and turning the pieces every 90 seconds, but keep at least enough to half-cover them.
  • ◆The same beurre monte poaches shrimp in 3 minutes and thick fish fillets in 10 to 12 — this technique is worth learning for more than lobster.

Pistachio-Crusted Rack of Lamb⏱ 1 hr 25 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

A frenched rack roasted rosy pink under a green, garlicky pistachio crust, carved into chops at the table. It is the most impressive thing you can put on a plate for the least amount of actual work.

Special OccasionRestaurant at HomeOven Roast
Prep
20 min
Cook
30 min
Total
1 hr 25 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the lamb

Pistachio crust

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Trim and temper the racks
    Take the lamb out of the fridge 45 minutes before cooking so the center is not refrigerator-cold when it hits the heat. Trim the fat cap down to about 1/8 in (3 mm) — a thick cap will not render in the short roasting time and turns waxy. Scrape any meat scraps off the exposed rib bones so they roast clean and white instead of burning black.
  2. Season and preheat
    Pat the racks dry and season them all over with the 2 tsp kosher salt and 1 tsp pepper, pressing it into the surface. Preheat the oven to 400°F (205°C) with a rack in the center position. Line a sheet pan with foil and set a wire rack on it, which lets hot air circulate underneath so the bottom does not steam.
  3. Sear the fat cap first
    Heat the 1 tbsp oil in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium-high until it shimmers. Lay the racks fat side down and sear 3 to 4 minutes without moving them, until the fat is deep golden and has rendered some of itself into the pan. You should hear a firm steady sizzle; adjust the heat down if the fat starts smoking or spitting hard.
  4. Sear the remaining sides
    Turn each rack onto its meaty side and sear another 2 minutes, then briefly stand it on each end for about 30 seconds. Use tongs and be patient — every browned surface is flavor you cannot get later, since the crust will insulate the meat once it goes on. Move the racks to a plate and let them cool for 5 minutes so the mustard will actually stick.
  5. Mix the crust
    In a bowl, combine the chopped pistachios, panko, parsley, grated garlic, lemon zest, and 1/2 tsp salt, then drizzle in the 2 tbsp melted butter and toss with a fork. The mixture should look like damp green sand that just barely clumps when you squeeze it. Chop the pistachios by hand rather than in a food processor, which turns them to paste and makes a heavy, pasty crust.
  6. Paint and press
    Brush the 2 tbsp Dijon in a thin even layer over the fat cap and meaty sides of each rack, avoiding the bones. The mustard is glue and seasoning at once, and its sharpness disappears in the oven. Press the pistachio mixture firmly onto the mustard with your palm, packing it into an even 1/4 in (6 mm) layer — press hard, or it will slide off when you carve.
  7. Roast to temperature
    Set the racks crust side up on the wire rack, interlocking the bones if they fit better that way, and roast at 400°F (205°C) for 15 to 22 minutes. Start checking early with an instant-read thermometer pushed into the thickest part of the loin from the end, avoiding bone. Pull at 125°F (52°C) for medium-rare or 133°F (56°C) for medium.
  8. Watch the crust
    If the crust is browning faster than the meat is cooking, lay a loose piece of foil over the top for the last few minutes. The crust is done when it is toasty gold and smells like buttered nuts, which usually lines up almost exactly with medium-rare. Burnt pistachios taste bitter, so foil early rather than late.
  9. Rest, crust side up
    Move the racks to a cutting board, crust side up, and rest them 10 minutes. The temperature will climb about 8°F (4°C) to a final 133 to 135°F (56 to 57°C) for medium-rare, and the juices will redistribute instead of flooding the board. Do not cover them tightly — steam will turn your crisp crust to mush.
  10. Carve into chops
    Set the rack bones-up on the board and slice straight down between the bones with a sharp knife, using the bones as your guide. For thick chops cut every two bones; for a more elegant plate cut single chops. Cut with confidence in one long stroke rather than sawing, so the crust stays on the meat.
  11. Plate and serve
    Stand 3 or 4 chops on a warm plate leaning against each other with the bones crossing upward, so the pink centers face out and the crust catches the light. Add a swipe of something green or creamy behind them — pea puree, whipped potato, or minted yogurt — and spoon a little of the pan juice around the base, never over the crust. Scatter a few chopped pistachios and torn parsley on the plate and serve at once.
Know when it is done
Pull the lamb at 125°F (52°C) for medium-rare or 133°F (56°C) for medium; after a 10 minute rest it lands at 133 to 135°F (56 to 57°C) or 140°F (60°C).
Serve it with
A medium-bodied red like Rioja or Cotes du Rhone, with roasted new potatoes and buttered spring peas.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Ask the butcher to french the racks for you and to remove the chine bone, which makes carving between the ribs effortless.
  • ◆The crust mixture can be made 3 days ahead and refrigerated in a sealed container, or frozen for a month. Bring it to room temperature before pressing it on.
  • ◆If the crust slides off during roasting, the meat was too hot or too wet when you applied the mustard. Cool the seared racks 5 full minutes and blot them before painting.
  • ◆Almonds, walnuts, or hazelnuts all work in place of pistachios; keep the same volume and the same butter-to-crumb ratio.
  • ◆One rack feeds two generously. If you are cooking a single rack, everything stays the same but check the temperature 3 to 4 minutes earlier.

Mushroom-Crusted Halibut with Lemon Butter⏱ 45 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Thick halibut fillets under a savory lid of mushroom duxelles, roasted just until the flesh flakes into big pearly petals. The mushrooms keep the fish from drying out, which is the trick with lean white fish.

Weeknight ElegantRestaurant at HomeUnder an Hour
Prep
20 min
Cook
25 min
Total
45 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the fish

Mushroom crust

Lemon butter

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Chop the mushrooms fine
    Chop the cremini as finely as you can by hand, or pulse them in a food processor in two batches, 8 to 10 short pulses each. You want pieces the size of coarse couscous, not a puree — over-processed mushrooms release water and turn to sludge. Uniform small pieces are what let the crust hold together in a neat layer.
  2. Cook the duxelles dry
    Melt the 2 tbsp butter with the 1 tbsp olive oil in a 10 in (25 cm) skillet over medium heat and add the shallot with a pinch of salt, cooking 2 minutes until soft. Add the mushrooms and the 1/2 tsp salt and cook 10 to 12 minutes, stirring often. They will first release a pool of liquid, then the pan will go quiet and the mushrooms will darken and start to squeak against the pan — that dry stage is exactly what you want.
  3. Deglaze and finish the crust
    Pour in the 2 tbsp sherry and scrape the browned bits off the bottom, cooking 1 minute until the pan is dry again. Stir in the thyme, then take the pan off the heat and fold in the panko and Parmesan. Spread the mixture on a plate to cool for 10 minutes; warm duxelles will start cooking the fish before it goes in the oven.
  4. Preheat and prep the pan
    Preheat the oven to 400°F (205°C) with a rack in the upper third, and give it a full 15 minutes to actually come up to temperature. Line a sheet pan with parchment and brush it lightly with about 1/2 tsp of the oil so the fillets lift off cleanly later. Having the oven fully up to temperature matters for thick fish, because a slow oven overcooks the outside while it waits for the center. The upper-third rack also puts the crust nearer the top element so it toasts while the fish cooks.
  5. Dry and season the halibut
    Blot the fillets thoroughly with paper towels on every surface, including the sides. Season with the 1 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp pepper about 5 minutes before cooking. Halibut is very lean, so a dry, well-seasoned surface and a short cooking time are your only defenses against dry fish.
  6. Sear the presentation side
    Heat the remaining 1 tbsp oil in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium-high until it shimmers, then lay the fillets in what was the skin side down and sear 2 to 3 minutes without moving them. You are only browning one face for flavor and structure, not cooking them through. When the edges turn opaque about 1/4 in (6 mm) up the side, lift them off with a fish spatula, seared side up, onto the parchment.
  7. Cap each fillet
    Divide the cooled duxelles among the four fillets and press it into an even layer about 1/3 in (8 mm) thick, covering only the top and stopping at the edges. Press firmly with the back of a spoon or your fingers so it holds together as one lid. The crust acts like a blanket, shielding the delicate flesh from direct oven heat.
  8. Roast until just done
    Roast at 400°F (205°C) for 8 to 12 minutes depending on thickness — figure roughly 8 minutes per inch of thickness. Start checking at 8 minutes with an instant-read thermometer in the thickest part. Pull the fish at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for moist, large-flaked halibut; the USDA guideline for fully cooked fish is 145°F (63°C), which will be firmer and drier.
  9. Confirm with the flake test
    If you have no thermometer, slide a paring knife into the thickest part and twist gently: the flesh should separate into big opaque petals with just a whisper of translucence at the very center. It will finish cooking on the plate. Fish that flakes into small dry shards has already gone too far.
  10. Make the lemon butter
    While the fish roasts, melt the 4 tbsp butter in a small saucepan over medium heat until it foams and just begins to smell nutty, about 2 minutes. Pull it off the heat and whisk in the 2 tbsp lemon juice, the zest, and the chives — it will sputter briefly. Do not let it boil after the lemon goes in or it will separate.
  11. Rest briefly and plate
    Let the fillets sit on the pan for 2 minutes so the crust firms up and stops steaming. Slide a wide spatula fully under each one and set it slightly off-center on a warm plate with the crust facing up and level. Spoon the lemon butter in a ring around the fish rather than over the crust, so the crust stays crisp, then finish with the 1/4 tsp flaky salt and a few extra chives.
Know when it is done
Pull halibut at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for moist, large flakes; the USDA guideline for fully cooked fish is 145°F (63°C).
Serve it with
A crisp white like Albarino or dry Riesling, with buttered new potatoes and blistered green beans.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆The duxelles can be made up to 4 days ahead and refrigerated, or frozen for 2 months. It is also the base for Beef Wellington, so make a double batch while you are at it.
  • ◆Cod, black bass, or thick sea bass fillets all work here. Adjust the roasting time by thickness, not by weight — about 8 minutes per inch.
  • ◆Frozen halibut is fine if it was flash-frozen at sea; thaw it overnight in the fridge on a rack, then blot it very well since it releases extra water.
  • ◆If the crust is sliding off, the duxelles was still too wet. Cook it until the pan goes completely silent and no liquid pools when you push the mushrooms aside.
  • ◆Watery mushrooms are usually crowded mushrooms. Use a wide skillet so the moisture has room to evaporate rather than pooling.

Roast Beef Tenderloin with Truffle Butter⏱ 2 hr 45 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

A center-cut tenderloin roasted whole, sliced into thick rosy medallions, and finished with truffle butter melting down the sides. Almost no technique, enormous payoff — it is the easiest showstopper in the book.

Special OccasionOven RoastMake Ahead
Prep
15 min
Cook
30 min
Total
2 hr 45 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the roast

Truffle butter

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Tie and salt the roast
    If the butcher has not tied it, loop kitchen twine around the tenderloin every 1 1/2 in (4 cm) so it holds a compact cylinder and cooks evenly. Season it all over with the 2 1/2 tsp kosher salt and 1 1/2 tsp pepper, pressing the pepper in. Set it on a rack over a sheet pan and refrigerate uncovered for at least 1 hour and up to 24 hours.
  2. Make the truffle butter
    Mash the softened 6 tbsp butter with the truffle, minced shallot, chives, 1/2 tsp salt, and 1/4 tsp pepper until fully combined. Scrape it onto plastic wrap or parchment, roll it into a log about 1 1/2 in (4 cm) thick, twist the ends, and chill at least 30 minutes until firm. Making it ahead lets the shallot mellow and the truffle perfume the whole thing.
  3. Bring the meat to temper
    Take the tenderloin out of the fridge 45 minutes before cooking and pat it dry again with paper towels, since the surface will have wept a little while the salt worked. A roast that starts at 55°F (13°C) instead of 38°F (3°C) cooks far more evenly from edge to center and leaves a much thinner gray band under the crust. Preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C) with a rack in the middle. Leave the truffle butter in the fridge until the very last moment — it needs to be firm enough to slice into coins.
  4. Sear all four sides
    Heat the 1 tbsp oil in a 12 in (30 cm) oven-safe skillet over medium-high until it shimmers and just begins to smoke. Lay the tenderloin in and sear 2 minutes per side, rolling it a quarter turn each time, for 8 to 10 minutes total. Do not rush this — you want a continuous dark brown crust all the way around, and it should roar steadily rather than smoke violently.
  5. Roast to temperature
    Scatter the thyme sprigs over the meat and slide the whole skillet into the 425°F (220°C) oven. Roast 18 to 25 minutes for a 2 lb (900 g) center cut, starting to check at 18 minutes — thickness drives the timing far more than weight, so a short fat roast takes longer than a long slim one. Push an instant-read thermometer in through the end of the roast so the tip lands dead center rather than in the hotter outer inch. Check in two spots if the log is at all uneven.
  6. Know your pull temperature
    Pull the roast at 120 to 122°F (49 to 50°C) for rare, 125 to 128°F (52 to 53°C) for medium-rare, or 135°F (57°C) for medium. A whole roast carries over more than a single steak — expect a rise of 8 to 10°F (4 to 5°C) as it rests. Tenderloin is extremely lean, so a few minutes past your target is the difference between luxurious and disappointing.
  7. Rest it properly
    Move the tenderloin to a cutting board and rest it for 15 minutes, tented loosely with foil. This is not optional on a roast this size; slicing early will pour a puddle of pink juice onto the board and take it straight out of the meat. The center will finish at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium-rare.
  8. Slice thick medallions
    Snip off and discard the twine, then slice the roast crosswise into medallions about 3/4 to 1 in (2 to 2.5 cm) thick, using a long sharp knife in smooth pulling strokes rather than pressing straight down. Thin slices go cold and dry within a minute of hitting the plate, which is exactly why steakhouses cut tenderloin thick. You should get 8 to 10 pieces from a 2 lb (900 g) roast. Wipe the blade between cuts so every face shows clean and rosy.
  9. Top with the butter
    Cut the chilled truffle butter into 1/4 in (6 mm) coins and lay one on each medallion while the meat is still hot. It will slump and melt within 20 seconds, running down the sides and mixing with the juices to make an instant sauce. The heat is what releases the truffle aroma, so do this at the last possible moment.
  10. Plate and serve
    Overlap two or three medallions in a gentle arc across the middle of each warm plate, cut faces angled toward the person eating so all that pink shows. Spoon the melted butter and any board juices back over the meat, then add a small mound of potato puree or roasted mushrooms at the top edge. Finish with the 1/2 tsp flaky sea salt and a few chives, and serve immediately with the extra butter on the table.
Know when it is done
Pull at 125 to 128°F (52 to 53°C) for medium-rare; after 15 minutes of rest it settles at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C). Whole roasts carry over 8 to 10°F (4 to 5°C).
Serve it with
A big Cabernet or Bordeaux, with creamed spinach and a pile of roasted mushrooms.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Truffle butter keeps 2 weeks in the fridge and 3 months in the freezer. Slice coins straight off the frozen log for steaks, eggs, or pasta any night of the week.
  • ◆Real truffle paste beats truffle oil, which is usually synthetic. If you use oil, use it sparingly — half a tablespoon can be plenty, and too much tastes like perfume.
  • ◆For a 3 to 4 lb (1.4 to 1.8 kg) whole tenderloin, tuck the thin tail end under and tie it, then roast 30 to 40 minutes and start checking at 28.
  • ◆Leftovers make the best steak sandwiches of your life. Slice them cold and thin on good bread with horseradish cream and arugula.
  • ◆No oven-safe skillet? Sear in any pan and transfer the roast to a rack set over a sheet pan for the oven; you will lose a little pan juice but nothing else.
