Risotto with Seared Prawns⏱ 1 hr 5 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Creamy saffron-tinged risotto built on a quick stock made from the prawn shells, with the prawns seared separately so they stay snappy. It is twenty minutes of stirring that pays you back completely.

Date NightOne PotRestaurant at Home
Prep
15 min
Cook
50 min
Total
1 hr 5 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Prawns and stock

For the risotto

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Peel and save the shells
    Peel the prawns, leaving the tails on if you like the look, and set the meat on a paper towel in the fridge. Put every shell and head in a bowl — they are the whole reason this risotto will taste like the sea instead of like rice. Devein the prawns by running a knife shallowly down the back and lifting out the dark line.
  2. Build a quick prawn stock
    Warm 1 tbsp of the olive oil in a saucepan over medium-high and cook the shells for 3 to 4 minutes, pressing them with a spoon until they turn bright coral and smell sweet and toasty. Pour in the 5 cups stock, bring to a simmer, and cook uncovered for 15 minutes. Strain out the shells, return the stock to the pot, add the saffron, and hold it at a bare simmer — cold stock added to hot rice stalls the cooking and makes risotto gluey.
  3. Sweat the aromatics
    In a wide 4 qt (4 L) heavy pot or deep skillet, heat the 2 tbsp olive oil and 2 tbsp butter over medium heat. Add the minced shallot and onion with a pinch of salt and cook 5 to 6 minutes, stirring, until completely soft and translucent with no color at all. Browned onion makes a sweet, muddy risotto; you want them to disappear into the background.
  4. Toast the rice
    Add the 1 1/2 cups rice and stir constantly for 2 to 3 minutes over medium heat. The grains should turn glassy at the edges with an opaque white dot at the center, and the pot will smell faintly like popcorn. This toasting step firms the outside of each grain so it releases starch slowly instead of collapsing into porridge.
  5. Deglaze with wine
    Pour in the 1/2 cup white wine and stir until it has almost completely evaporated, about 2 minutes. You should hear the sizzle change from a wet gurgle to a dry hiss, and the sharp alcohol smell should be gone. Do not skip the wine — its acidity is what keeps a rich risotto from tasting flat.
  6. Add stock a ladle at a time
    Add about 3/4 cup (180 ml) of the hot saffron stock and stir steadily but not frantically until the rice is nearly dry and a spoon dragged across the bottom leaves a trail that slowly closes. Repeat, ladle by ladle, keeping the pot at a lively simmer where the surface bubbles gently all over. Adding stock gradually is what coaxes the starch out and builds the creaminess without any cream.
  7. Taste for the right bite
    After 16 to 18 minutes and roughly 4 1/2 cups (1 L) of stock, start tasting a grain every minute or two. It should be tender all the way through with the faintest firm core — creamy, never crunchy and never mushy. Season with about 1/2 tsp salt, remembering the prawns and any cheese will add more.
  8. Sear the prawns
    While the last of the stock goes in, heat the 1 tbsp butter in a 10 in (25 cm) skillet over medium-high. Pat the prawns dry, season with the 3/4 tsp salt and the pepper flakes, and lay them in a single layer with the sliced garlic. Sear 60 to 90 seconds per side, until they are opaque, pink, and curled into a loose C — a tight O means they are overcooked.
  9. Finish with the mantecatura
    Take the risotto off the heat, add the 3 tbsp cold butter and the lemon zest, and beat it in vigorously with a wooden spoon for 30 to 45 seconds. This is the mantecatura, and the vigorous beating plus cold butter is what makes risotto glossy and wavy rather than stiff. Italians traditionally skip cheese with seafood, but a small handful of Parmesan is your call.
  10. Check the consistency
    Loosen the risotto with a final splash of hot stock until it is all onda, on the wave — spoon some onto a plate and it should slowly spread into a soft pool on its own in about 3 seconds. If it holds a mound, add more stock; if it runs like soup, stir over low heat for 30 seconds. Risotto keeps tightening as it sits, so err on the loose side.
  11. Plate and serve immediately
    Spoon the risotto into the center of warm shallow bowls and tap the base of each bowl once against your palm so it settles into an even circle. Arrange 4 or 5 prawns on top in a small pile or fanned in a line, drizzle the garlicky pan butter over them, and scatter the parsley and a little more lemon zest. Serve right now — risotto waits for absolutely no one.
Know when it is done
Prawns are done the moment they turn opaque and form a loose C, about 120 to 125°F (49 to 52°C); the FDA guideline for fully cooked shrimp is 145°F (63°C). The rice should be tender with a faint firm center.
Serve it with
A crisp Italian white like Vermentino or Soave, with a simple lemony arugula salad after.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Carnaroli is worth seeking out over Arborio. It holds its bite longer and is far more forgiving if you get distracted for a minute.
  • ◆The prawn stock can be made a day ahead and refrigerated, or frozen for 3 months. It is also the best base you will ever have for seafood pasta.
  • ◆Never rinse risotto rice. The surface starch is exactly the thing you are trying to release, and washing it away guarantees a thin, sad result.
  • ◆Bloom the saffron in a few tablespoons of hot stock for 5 minutes before adding it if you want a deeper color and a more even perfume.
  • ◆Leftover risotto becomes arancini: chill it solid, roll it into balls around a cube of mozzarella, bread them, and fry at 350°F (175°C) for 3 to 4 minutes.

Crispy Pork Belly with Apple Puree⏱ 15 hr 55 min🍽 4 servingsAdvanced▾

Meltingly soft pork under a sheet of crackling that shatters when your knife hits it, with a sharp green apple puree to cut through all that fat. It takes two days, and almost all of it is waiting.

Weekend ProjectRestaurant at HomeMake Ahead
Prep
25 min
Cook
3 hr 15 min
Total
15 hr 55 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the pork belly

Apple puree

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Score the skin
    Pat the belly dry and set it skin side up. With a very sharp knife or a clean box cutter, score the skin in parallel lines about 1/2 in (12 mm) apart, cutting through the skin and into the fat but stopping well short of the meat. If you cut into the meat, juices will bubble up during roasting and ruin the crackling. Chilling the belly for 30 minutes first makes the skin firmer and much easier to score cleanly.
  2. Cure it overnight
    Mix the 2 tbsp (28 g) kosher salt, 1 tsp sugar, fennel seeds, and 1/2 tsp pepper, then rub about two thirds of it into the meat side and the ends. Rub the remaining third onto the skin, working it into the score lines. Set the belly skin side up on a rack over a sheet pan and refrigerate uncovered for 12 to 24 hours. The salt seasons the meat and the dry fridge air dehydrates the skin, which is the single biggest factor in whether you get crackling or leather.
  3. Dry the skin again
    The next day the skin should feel dry, taut, and slightly leathery to the touch. Wipe any beaded moisture and excess salt off the skin with a paper towel, then brush the skin with the 1 tsp white vinegar and blot it dry once more. The vinegar helps break down surface proteins so the skin puffs and blisters more evenly.
  4. Set up the low roast
    Preheat the oven to 300°F (150°C) with a rack in the lower middle. Set the belly skin side up on a rack over a foil-lined sheet pan so the rendering fat drips away rather than frying the underside. If the belly is uneven, prop the thin end on a crumpled ball of foil so the skin surface sits level — flat skin crisps evenly, tilted skin burns on the high side.
  5. Roast low and slow
    Roast at 300°F (150°C) for 2 1/2 hours. The meat should feel yielding when you press it and a skewer should slide into the center with almost no resistance, which means the collagen has turned to gelatin. Check the internal temperature: you are aiming for 190 to 200°F (88 to 93°C), well past the 145°F (63°C) food-safety minimum for pork, because tenderness in a fatty cut comes from time and heat, not just safety.
  6. Rest and dry before the blast
    Take the pan out and let the belly sit at room temperature for 20 minutes. Blot the skin thoroughly with paper towels — there will be rendered fat sitting in the score lines and it must go. This pause also lets the meat relax so the crackling stage does not squeeze juice out through the skin.
  7. Blast for crackling
    Crank the oven to 475°F (245°C) and return the belly, skin side up, for 20 to 30 minutes. Watch it closely from minute 15: the skin will bubble, puff, and turn deep amber, and it will crackle audibly. Rotate the pan halfway through, and if one corner is racing ahead, shield it with a small piece of foil.
  8. Make the apple puree
    While the pork roasts, melt the 2 tbsp butter in a saucepan over medium heat, add the chopped apples, 1 tbsp sugar, 1/4 cup water, and 1/4 tsp salt, and cover. Cook 12 to 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the apples completely collapse when pressed with a spoon. Blend until glass smooth, then stir in the 2 tbsp cider vinegar off the heat — the acid is what keeps the puree tasting bright against all that pork fat.
  9. Rest the pork
    Move the belly to a cutting board, skin side up, and rest it for 15 minutes uncovered. Never tent pork belly with foil; the trapped steam will soften crackling that took two days to earn. If the skin has any soft patches, you can hit them directly with a kitchen torch or slide the belly back under the broiler for 60 seconds.
  10. Build a quick pan sauce
    Pour off all but 1 tbsp of fat from the sheet pan, set it over a burner on medium heat, and add the 1/2 cup chicken stock. Scrape up every browned bit with a wooden spoon — that fond is concentrated pork flavor and it is essentially the whole sauce. Simmer 2 to 3 minutes until it has reduced by about half and looks lightly syrupy on the spoon. Take it off the heat, swirl in the 1 tbsp cold butter until glossy, and taste; it should be savory and sharp enough to stand up next to all that fat.
  11. Cut with the right knife
    Flip the belly skin side up and cut it with a heavy serrated bread knife, using a firm sawing stroke to get through the crackling before you press down through the meat. A chef knife will crush the layers and shatter the skin sideways. Cut into 4 thick rectangles or 8 batons, following your score lines.
  12. Plate the pork
    Spoon a wide swoosh of apple puree across each warm plate and set the pork on top, skin side up and clearly proud of the sauce so it stays crisp. Spoon a little pan sauce around the base but never over the crackling, then finish with the 1/2 tsp flaky salt on the skin and a few watercress leaves leaning against the pork for height. Serve immediately, while the skin is still loud.
Know when it is done
Cook the belly to 190 to 200°F (88 to 93°C) so the fat and collagen fully render — far past the 145°F (63°C) plus 3 minute rest minimum for whole cuts of pork, which applies to lean cuts like loin.
Serve it with
An off-dry Riesling or hard cider, with a sharp shaved fennel and apple salad to keep things lively.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Ask the butcher for a center-cut, evenly thick slab with the skin on. An uneven belly cooks unevenly, and no technique fixes that.
  • ◆For an even more restaurant look, press the cooked belly: after the low roast, cool it, sandwich it between two sheet pans with cans on top, chill overnight, then cut squares and crisp them skin down in a hot pan.
  • ◆Both the apple puree and the low-roasted belly can be done 2 days ahead. Do the 475°F (245°C) crackling blast right before serving; reheated crackling is never the same.
  • ◆If the skin stays chewy instead of puffing, it was still damp. Next time cure a full 24 hours and blot the skin twice before the high-heat stage.
  • ◆Pour the rendered fat through a sieve into a jar. Pork fat keeps 3 months in the fridge and makes the best roast potatoes and refried beans you will ever eat.

Duck Confit with Crackling Skin⏱ 27 hr 20 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Duck legs cured in salt and herbs, then cooked slowly submerged in their own fat until the meat gives way at the touch of a fork. Crisp the skin at the last minute and it is one of the great dishes of southwest France.

Weekend ProjectMake AheadFrench Classic
Prep
20 min
Cook
3 hr
Total
27 hr 20 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

The cure

For cooking and serving

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Trim the legs
    Pat the duck legs dry and trim off any loose flaps of skin and fat that hang past the meat, saving them in a bowl. Leave the skin covering the leg itself completely intact, since it is what protects the meat and later becomes the crisp part. Those trimmings can be rendered in a low pan for 30 minutes to give you extra duck fat for free.
  2. Mix and apply the cure
    Combine the 3 tbsp (42 g) kosher salt, 1 tsp sugar, cracked peppercorns, torn bay leaves, and the leaves stripped from 6 thyme sprigs, then rub the mixture evenly over every surface of the legs. Tuck the smashed garlic underneath and around them in a dish or zip-top bag. Do not overdo the salt or add more than the recipe says — with only 24 hours the cure penetrates deeply and extra salt makes the duck inedible.
  3. Cure for 24 hours
    Cover and refrigerate for 24 hours, turning the legs once at about the halfway point so both sides sit in the brine that forms. Liquid will pool in the dish as the salt draws water out of the meat, which is exactly right — that is what firms the texture and seasons it to the bone. Curing longer than 36 hours starts to make the duck too salty and too firm, so keep an eye on the clock. If you need to work further ahead, cure for the 24 hours and then cook, rather than leaving the legs sitting in salt.
  4. Rinse and dry thoroughly
    Rinse the legs well under cold running water to wash off every trace of the salt cure, including from the crevices around the joint. Pat them absolutely dry with paper towels, then leave them uncovered on a rack for 20 minutes to air-dry. Any surface water will spit and sputter in the hot fat and can make it bubble over.
  5. Set up the confit
    Preheat the oven to 225°F (107°C). Warm the duck fat in a saucepan until just melted and pourable, then arrange the legs snugly skin side down in a Dutch oven or deep baking dish where they fit in one layer without much extra room. Pour the melted fat over until the legs are completely submerged, adding a little more fat or oil if any part of the meat is poking out.
  6. Cook it low and long
    Add the 2 remaining thyme sprigs, cover, and cook in the 225°F (107°C) oven for 2 1/2 to 3 hours. Check at the 30 minute mark: the fat should be barely moving, with a lazy bubble rising every few seconds. If it is simmering actively, drop the oven 25 degrees — confit is poaching, not frying, and a real simmer will make the meat stringy.
  7. Test for doneness
    The duck is ready when a thin knife or skewer slides into the thickest part of the thigh with no resistance and the meat has pulled back about 1/2 in (12 mm) from the end of the drumstick bone. Internally that lands around 195 to 205°F (90 to 96°C), well past the 165°F (74°C) safety minimum for poultry, because the point here is dissolving collagen. If it still grips the skewer, give it another 30 minutes.
  8. Cool and store in the fat
    Let the legs cool in the fat for at least 1 hour. You can serve them the same day, but confit genuinely improves after 3 to 7 days: transfer the legs to a container, strain the fat over them until fully covered, and refrigerate. Sealed under fat this way, they keep for a month and the texture and flavor deepen the whole time.
  9. Bring them out to crisp
    Scrape most of the solidified fat off the legs and let them sit at room temperature for 20 minutes, or gently warm the container in a low oven until the fat melts enough to lift them out cleanly. Blot the skin dry with paper towels. Wet skin will not crisp, and warm legs are far less likely to tear apart when you handle them.
  10. Crisp the skin in a skillet
    Heat a dry 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium heat and lay the legs skin side down with nothing added — there is plenty of fat clinging to them already. Press them flat with a spatula for the first 20 seconds and cook 6 to 10 minutes without moving them. Listen for a steady moderate sizzle and lift a corner at 6 minutes; you want deep mahogany and rigid, not scorched.
  11. Warm through and dress the greens
    Flip the legs and cook 2 to 3 minutes on the meat side just to heat them through, or finish them in a 400°F (205°C) oven for 5 minutes if your skillet is crowded. Meanwhile toss the frisee with the 1 tbsp red wine vinegar, 1 tbsp of the warm duck fat from the pan, and a pinch of salt. The sharp greens exist to cut the richness, so do not skip them.
  12. Plate and serve
    Set each leg skin side up on a warm plate, angled with the drumstick bone pointing to the upper right so the shape reads clearly. Pile a small handful of dressed frisee against the thigh rather than under it, so the skin never touches anything wet. Finish with the 1/2 tsp flaky salt directly on the skin and serve immediately — confit skin softens within a few minutes of leaving the pan.
Know when it is done
Cook the legs to 195 to 205°F (90 to 96°C) so the connective tissue melts; poultry is safe at 165°F (74°C), but confit needs the higher temperature for that fall-apart texture.
Serve it with
A rustic red from southwest France like Cahors or Madiran, with garlicky sauteed potatoes and bitter greens.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Duck fat is reusable. Strain it after each confit, discard the meat juices that settle at the bottom, and it will serve you for several rounds and a year of potatoes.
  • ◆If you cannot source enough duck fat, a mix of duck fat and mild olive oil or even all lard works fine. The fat is a cooking medium, not a flavoring.
  • ◆Confit legs are the best make-ahead main there is. Cure and cook them a week ahead, keep them submerged in the fridge, and dinner is a ten minute skillet job.
  • ◆Shred any leftover confit meat and fold it into white bean cassoulet, hash, or a tart with caramelized onions — it is far too good to waste.
  • ◆If the meat comes out too salty, you cured too long or used table salt instead of kosher. Table salt is nearly twice as dense by volume, so always weigh it if you substitute.

Coq au Vin⏱ 6 hr 15 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Chicken braised slowly in a whole bottle of red wine with bacon, mushrooms, and pearl onions until the sauce turns dark and velvety. It is the Sunday dish that made French home cooking famous, and it is better the next day.

Weekend ProjectOne PotFrench Classic
Prep
30 min
Cook
1 hr 45 min
Total
6 hr 15 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chicken and marinade

The braise

Garnish and finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Marinate in the wine
    Put the chicken pieces in a large nonreactive bowl with the quartered onion, carrots, smashed garlic, and bouquet garni, then pour the entire bottle of wine over the top. Cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours and ideally overnight. The wine seasons the meat all the way to the bone and gives the finished sauce its depth — a rushed coq au vin always tastes thinner.
  2. Separate and dry everything
    Strain the marinade into a bowl, reserving the wine, and pick out the vegetables and bouquet garni into a separate pile. Lay the chicken on a rack and pat every piece completely dry with paper towels, then let it sit 15 minutes. Wine-soaked chicken will steam rather than brown, and the browning is where half the flavor of this dish comes from.
  3. Render the lardons
    Cook the bacon lardons in a cold 6 qt (6 L) Dutch oven over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until they are golden and crisp at the edges but still tender in the middle. Lift them out with a slotted spoon and set them aside, leaving the fat in the pot. Starting cold coaxes the fat out gradually instead of scorching the outside.
  4. Brown the chicken hard
    Season the chicken with the 2 tsp salt and 1 tsp pepper and dust it lightly with the 3 tbsp flour, shaking off the excess. Brown the pieces skin side down in the bacon fat over medium-high heat, in two batches so nothing touches, for 5 to 6 minutes per side. You want a genuine deep brown, not tan — this is where the sauce gets its color and body. Set the browned chicken aside.
  5. Cook the vegetables and tomato paste
    Pour off all but 2 tbsp of fat, add the reserved marinade vegetables, and cook over medium heat for 6 to 8 minutes until they take on some color. Stir in the 2 tbsp tomato paste and cook 1 minute more until it darkens from red to brick and smells sweet rather than raw. Cooking out the tomato paste removes its tinny edge.
  6. Flame the cognac
    Pull the pot off the burner, pour in the 1/4 cup cognac, and either light it carefully with a long match and let the flames burn out, or simply simmer it for 60 to 90 seconds until the sharp alcohol smell fades. Keep a lid within reach and your face well back if you flame it. Either method works; you only need the alcohol gone.
  7. Reduce the wine
    Pour in the reserved wine, bring it to a boil, and cook uncovered for 8 to 10 minutes until it has reduced by about a third. This concentrates the wine and, more importantly, cooks off the raw harshness that makes an under-reduced braise taste sour rather than deep. Skim off any purple foam that rises to the surface with a spoon, since it carries the bitterest of the tannins. Before you go on, it should smell like warm wine and dark fruit, not alcohol.
  8. Braise low and covered
    Preheat the oven to 325°F (165°C). Return the chicken to the pot along with any juices, add the 2 cups chicken stock so the liquid comes about three quarters of the way up the pieces, and tuck in the bouquet garni. Bring it to a bare simmer on the stove, cover, and braise in the oven for 60 to 75 minutes.
  9. Glaze the pearl onions
    While the pot is in the oven, melt 1 tbsp of the butter in a skillet over medium heat, add the pearl onions and a pinch of salt with 1/4 cup (60 ml) water, cover, and cook 8 minutes. Uncover and cook another 4 to 5 minutes, shaking the pan, until the water is gone and the onions are golden and just tender. Cooking them separately keeps them whole and sweet instead of dissolving into the braise.
  10. Brown the mushrooms
    In the same skillet, melt another 1 tbsp butter over medium-high, add the mushrooms in a single layer, and leave them undisturbed for 3 minutes before stirring. Cook 6 to 8 minutes total until deeply browned and squeaky-dry, seasoning with a pinch of salt only at the end. Salting early pulls out water and you will end up steaming them gray.
  11. Check the chicken and strain
    The chicken is ready when the meat pulls back from the drumstick bone and a thermometer in the thickest thigh reads 175 to 185°F (79 to 85°C) — well above the 165°F (74°C) safety minimum, because dark meat needs the extra heat to become tender. Lift the chicken out to a plate, strain the sauce through a sieve into a clean saucepan, and discard the spent vegetables and bouquet garni. Skim the fat off the top with a wide spoon.
  12. Thicken with beurre manie
    Mash the remaining 1 tbsp butter with the 2 tbsp flour into a smooth paste. Bring the strained sauce to a simmer and whisk in the paste in small pieces, then simmer 4 to 5 minutes until the sauce coats the back of a spoon and holds a clean line when you drag a finger through it. Return the chicken, lardons, onions, and mushrooms to the sauce and simmer gently 5 minutes to bring everything together. Taste and add the 1/2 tsp salt.
  13. Serve it family style
    Spoon a bed of buttered egg noodles or potato puree into wide warm bowls and set two pieces of chicken on top, then ladle the sauce over so the garnish lands visibly around the meat. Arrange a few glazed onions, mushrooms, and lardons on top rather than letting them sink, and scatter the parsley last for a flash of green against the dark sauce. Bring the pot to the table so people can go back for more.
Know when it is done
Braise the dark meat to 175 to 185°F (79 to 85°C) for tenderness; the food-safety minimum for all poultry is 165°F (74°C).
Serve it with
The same Burgundy or Pinot Noir you cooked with, plus buttered egg noodles and a crusty baguette.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Coq au vin is genuinely better on day two. Cool it, refrigerate overnight, lift off the solid fat cap, and rewarm gently on the stove.
  • ◆Use thighs and drumsticks only. Breast meat dries out long before dark meat becomes tender, and traditional coq au vin used an old rooster for exactly this reason.
  • ◆Do not use so-called cooking wine. Whatever red you would pour into a glass is what belongs in the pot, since an hour of simmering concentrates every flaw.
  • ◆Frozen peeled pearl onions save you twenty minutes of fiddly work and taste no different once glazed.
  • ◆If the sauce is thin at the end, simply simmer it uncovered for another 5 to 10 minutes before adding the beurre manie. Reduction always beats extra flour.

Bouillabaisse with Saffron Rouille⏱ 1 hr 35 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

The great fisherman stew of Marseille: a saffron and fennel broth perfumed with orange and anise, loaded with fish and shellfish, and served with garlicky rouille on toast. It smells like a harbor town from the moment the fennel hits the pot.

Weekend ProjectOne PotFrench Classic
Prep
30 min
Cook
1 hr 5 min
Total
1 hr 35 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

The broth

The seafood

Saffron rouille

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Sweat the aromatics slowly
    Warm the 1/4 cup olive oil in an 8 qt (8 L) pot over medium-low heat and add the sliced fennel, onion, and leek with 1 tsp of the salt. Cook 12 to 15 minutes, stirring often, until everything is completely soft and sweet but has taken on no color at all. This slow sweat builds the sweet vegetal base that saffron needs to sit on; rushing it with high heat gives you a harsh, oniony broth.
  2. Bloom the garlic and spices
    Add the sliced garlic, the 1 tsp fennel seeds, the bay leaf, and the orange zest strips and cook 2 minutes until fragrant. Crumble in the 1/2 tsp saffron and stir it through the hot oil for 30 seconds — the heat and fat release far more color and aroma than dropping it into liquid would. The pot should smell like licorice and warm honey at this point.
  3. Add tomatoes and reduce
    Stir in the canned tomatoes with their juice and cook 8 to 10 minutes over medium heat, mashing them against the side of the pot with a spoon. Cook until the mixture thickens and the liquid mostly disappears, leaving a jammy base. This concentration step is what keeps the finished broth from tasting watery and thin.
  4. Build and simmer the broth
    Pour in the 4 cups fish stock and 2 cups clam juice, add the remaining 1 tsp salt, and bring it to a simmer. Cook uncovered at a gentle bubble for 25 to 30 minutes to marry the flavors and reduce slightly. Taste it — it should already be delicious on its own, well-salted and clearly saffrony, because the seafood will only add to it, not fix it.
  5. Make the rouille base
    In a medium bowl, whisk the egg yolk with the grated garlic, the soaked saffron and its liquid, the 1/4 tsp cayenne, and the 1/2 tsp salt until smooth and slightly thickened. Set the bowl on a damp folded towel so it cannot spin while you whisk. Room temperature yolk emulsifies far more reliably than a cold one.
  6. Emulsify the rouille
    Add the 1/2 cup olive oil drop by drop at first, whisking constantly, until the mixture visibly thickens and turns pale gold, then pour the rest in a very thin steady stream. If it looks like it is separating, stop adding oil and whisk hard until it comes back together. Finish with the 1 tbsp lemon juice; the rouille should be thick enough to hold a soft peak on the whisk.
  7. Toast the bread
    Arrange the baguette slices on a sheet pan and toast at 375°F (190°C) for 8 to 10 minutes, flipping once, until dry and crisp all the way through. Rub one side of each hot toast with the cut garlic clove, which melts into the rough surface. These need to be genuinely crisp so they hold up when they hit the broth.
  8. Strain or leave it rustic
    For a refined restaurant broth, pass the soup through a food mill or press it through a coarse sieve, pushing hard on the solids, and return the liquid to the pot. For a rustic Marseille version, leave the vegetables in. Either way, stir in the 1/4 cup Pernod now and simmer 2 minutes so the alcohol cooks off but the anise perfume stays.
  9. Cook the fish first
    Season the fish chunks with the 1 tsp salt. Bring the broth to a bare simmer — never a rolling boil, which shreds delicate fish and turns shrimp to rubber — and slide in the thickest pieces first so everything finishes at the same moment. Poach 4 minutes, then add the shrimp and the mussels, cover, and cook 3 to 4 minutes more. Keep the lid on for the mussels, because the trapped steam is what forces the shells open.
  10. Judge the seafood by sight
    The mussels are done the moment they open wide; discard any that stay firmly shut after 5 minutes. The shrimp should be opaque and curled into a loose C, and the fish should flake into big petals when nudged with a spoon at around 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C), with 145°F (63°C) being the USDA guideline for fully cooked fish and shellfish. Everything cooks in under 8 minutes, so stand at the pot.
  11. Finish and taste
    Take the pot off the heat immediately and taste the broth one last time, adding salt or a squeeze of lemon if it tastes flat. Seafood releases its own salty liquid as it cooks, so the seasoning always shifts at the end. Stir a spoonful of the hot broth into the rouille to loosen it into a pourable sauce if you like.
  12. Serve the traditional way
    Ladle broth into wide warm bowls first, then arrange the seafood on top so the mussels, shrimp, and fish are all visible rather than buried, with the mussel shells angled upward. Spread a thick spoonful of rouille on each toast, top with a pinch of Gruyere, and float two on each bowl. Scatter the parsley and reserved fennel fronds over everything and put the extra rouille on the table.
Know when it is done
Poach the broth at a bare simmer, around 190°F (88°C). Fish is done at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for large moist flakes; 145°F (63°C) is the USDA guideline for fully cooked fish and shellfish, and mussels are done when they open. The rouille is built on a raw egg yolk, so use a pasteurized egg if you are serving anyone pregnant, very young, elderly, or immunocompromised.
Serve it with
A chilled rose from Provence or a dry white like Picpoul, with plenty of bread for the broth.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Use at least two kinds of fish and buy whatever is freshest rather than chasing a list. Firm fish that holds its shape matters far more than the specific species.
  • ◆The broth can be made through the simmering step up to 3 days ahead or frozen for 3 months. Cook the seafood only in the last 8 minutes before serving.
  • ◆Never boil the pot once the seafood is in. A hard boil turns fish to cotton and shrimp to rubber within a minute.
  • ◆If your rouille breaks, start a fresh yolk in a clean bowl and whisk the broken mixture into it drop by drop; it will come back every time.
  • ◆Ask the fish counter for the bones and heads from whatever they filleted that morning. Simmered 25 minutes with an onion, they make a fish stock no carton can touch.

Steak Diane with Cognac Pan Sauce⏱ 30 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

The old tableside classic: quick-seared medallions in a creamy mustard and cognac sauce built in the same pan in about four minutes. It is the fastest genuinely fancy dinner you will ever make.

Date Night30 MinutesRestaurant at Home
Prep
10 min
Cook
20 min
Total
30 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the steaks

Diane sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Flatten the medallions
    Set each medallion between two sheets of plastic wrap and pound it gently with the flat side of a mallet or a heavy pan until it is an even 3/4 in (2 cm) thick. You are evening them out, not flattening them to paper — uniform thickness is what lets all four finish at the same moment. Pat them dry afterward, since pounding pushes moisture to the surface.
  2. Season and prep everything first
    Season the steaks all over with the 1 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tsp pepper. This sauce comes together in about four minutes, so mince the shallot and garlic, slice the mushrooms, and measure the cognac, Dijon, Worcestershire, stock, and cream into small bowls before you turn on the heat. Cooking this dish while still chopping is how it goes wrong.
  3. Heat the pan properly
    Set a 12 in (30 cm) stainless steel skillet over medium-high heat for 2 to 3 minutes, then add the 1 tbsp oil and the 1 tbsp butter. When the butter foam subsides and the fat shimmers, you are ready. Use stainless rather than nonstick here, because the browned bits stuck to the pan are literally the sauce.
  4. Sear the first side
    Lay the medallions in the pan with at least 1 in (2.5 cm) between them and do not touch them for 2 minutes. You want a loud, confident sizzle and a rising smell of browning meat, not smoke — crowding drops the pan temperature and the steaks will steam gray instead of browning. If your pan is not big enough for all four with space, cook them in two batches and leave the fond in the pan between them. Resist lifting them to peek, because the crust is still knitting itself to the meat.
  5. Flip and pull early
    Turn the steaks and cook 1 1/2 to 2 minutes on the second side, then check with an instant-read thermometer. Pull them at 120 to 125°F (49 to 52°C) for medium-rare, remembering they will keep cooking and will also go back into hot sauce at the end. Move them to a warm plate and tent loosely.
  6. Brown the mushrooms
    Add the 2 tbsp butter to the same pan over medium-high and tip in the mushrooms in one layer. Leave them alone for 2 full minutes to take color, then stir and cook 3 to 4 minutes more until browned and the pan is dry again. Salt them only at the end, since salting early draws out water and steams them gray.
  7. Soften the aromatics
    Add the minced shallot and garlic to the mushrooms and cook 1 to 2 minutes, stirring constantly, until fragrant and softened but not browned. Garlic burns in about 45 seconds at this heat and turns the whole sauce acrid, so keep everything moving and drop the heat to medium the moment you can smell it. The shallot should go from sharp to sweet in about the same time. If the browned bits on the bottom start darkening fast, move straight on to the cognac.
  8. Deglaze with cognac
    Pull the pan off the burner and pour in the 1/4 cup cognac, then scrape the bottom hard with a wooden spoon to lift every browned bit. If you want the traditional flame, tilt the pan away from you and touch a long match to the edge, then let it burn out on its own — or simply return the pan to the heat and simmer 60 to 90 seconds until the raw alcohol smell is gone. Keep a lid nearby and your face well back if you flame it.
  9. Build the sauce
    Whisk in the 1 tbsp Dijon and 1 tbsp Worcestershire, then pour in the 3/4 cup beef stock and simmer briskly for 3 to 4 minutes until reduced by about half. Add the 1/2 cup heavy cream and simmer another 2 to 3 minutes until the sauce coats the back of a spoon. Drag your finger through it — the line should hold for a beat.
  10. Return the steaks and finish
    Slide the steaks and every drop of their resting juices back into the pan and turn them once to coat, warming them for 30 to 60 seconds. That is enough to bring them to a final 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium-rare. Take the pan off the heat and stir in the 1 tsp lemon juice and half the chives, then taste and adjust the salt.
  11. Plate it warm
    Set one medallion slightly off-center on each warm plate and spoon the sauce over the top so the mushrooms land visibly on and around the meat. Add a small pile of buttered green beans or a spoonful of potato puree at the upper edge and leave a clean crescent of plate showing. Finish with the remaining chives across the sauce and serve immediately, while the cream is still glossy.
Know when it is done
Pull the steaks at 120 to 125°F (49 to 52°C); after returning them to the hot sauce they finish at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium-rare.
Serve it with
A glass of Malbec or Cotes du Rhone, with green beans and a crusty loaf for the sauce.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Sirloin or New York strip, sliced and pounded, works beautifully and costs a third of tenderloin. Just keep the thickness at 3/4 in (2 cm).
  • ◆No cognac? Use brandy, dry sherry, or Madeira. In a pinch, add 2 tbsp (30 ml) more beef stock plus 1 tsp (5 ml) sherry vinegar for the same lift.
  • ◆Do not flame in a pan with a nonstick coating or under a low range hood, and never pour alcohol from the bottle straight into a hot pan. Measuring it into a cup first is the whole safety rule.
  • ◆If the sauce breaks or looks oily, whisk in 1 tbsp (15 ml) of cold stock off the heat to pull it back together.
  • ◆The mushroom and shallot base can be cooked an hour ahead and left in the pan. Sear the steaks fresh and finish the sauce in three minutes.

Chicken Ballotine with Mushroom Duxelles⏱ 2 hr 20 min🍽 4 servingsAdvanced▾

Boned chicken legs rolled around mushroom duxelles and spinach, poached gently, then seared until the skin is lacquered brown. Slice it and you get a perfect spiral — this is the trick that makes chefs look like magicians.

Special OccasionMake AheadFrench Classic
Prep
40 min
Cook
1 hr
Total
2 hr 20 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the chicken

Duxelles filling

Pan sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Bone out the legs
    Lay a leg skin side down and find the thigh bone with your fingertip, then cut along its length with a small sharp knife and scrape the meat away from it on all sides. Work down to the joint, then follow the drumstick bone the same way, keeping your blade against the bone so you never pierce the skin. Twist and pull both bones free, snip the tendons, and repeat with the rest. Save the bones for stock, and go slowly — a torn skin will not hold a roll.
  2. Flatten and even the meat
    Open each boned leg flat, skin side down, and make shallow cuts through the thickest parts of the thigh meat so you can fold the flaps outward. You are trying to create a roughly even rectangle about 1/2 in (12 mm) thick. Season the meat side, not the skin, with the 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt and the 1 tsp pepper.
  3. Cook the duxelles dry
    Melt the 2 tbsp butter in a 10 in (25 cm) skillet over medium heat, add the shallot with a pinch of salt, and cook 2 minutes until soft. Add the mushrooms, the 1/2 tsp salt, and the 1/4 tsp pepper and cook 10 to 12 minutes, stirring often. The mushrooms will release liquid, then the pan will go quiet and dry — that dry stage is essential, because a wet filling will steam the roll from the inside and leak everywhere.
  4. Finish the filling
    Add the 2 tbsp sherry and the thyme and cook 1 minute until the pan is dry again. Stir in the spinach a handful at a time and cook just until it wilts, about 2 minutes, then tip everything into a sieve and press firmly with a spoon to squeeze out every drop of liquid. Spread it on a plate and chill 15 minutes; a cold filling is far easier to roll.
  5. Roll the ballotines
    Lay a large sheet of plastic wrap on the counter and set a boned leg on it, skin side down. Spoon a quarter of the duxelles in a line along the long edge nearest you, leaving a 1 in (2.5 cm) border, then roll the chicken away from you into a tight cylinder with the skin ending up on the outside. Do not overfill; a heaped filling will burst out the ends.
  6. Wrap tight and twist
    Roll the cylinder up in the plastic wrap, then twist both ends in opposite directions like a candy wrapper, tightening as you go until the roll is firm and evenly cylindrical with no air pockets. Tie the twisted ends in a knot or with butcher twine. Wrap each ballotine in a second layer of plastic for insurance, then chill them for 30 minutes to set the shape.
  7. Set up the poach
    Fill a wide pot with enough water to cover the rolls and bring it to 170°F (77°C), which looks like faint wisps of steam and tiny bubbles clinging to the bottom, never a real simmer. Use a thermometer and adjust the burner to hold that temperature. Boiling water would burst the plastic and squeeze the juices out of the meat.
  8. Poach gently
    Slide the wrapped ballotines in, weigh them down with a small plate if they float, and poach for 30 to 35 minutes. Check the internal temperature by pushing a thin thermometer probe through the plastic into the center of a roll: you need 165°F (74°C) for chicken, no exceptions. If they are not there yet, give them another 5 minutes and check again.
  9. Rest, then unwrap and dry
    Lift the rolls out and rest them in their wrapping for 10 minutes so the filling sets and they stop leaking the moment you cut the plastic. Snip the twisted ends, unwrap carefully over the sink — there will be a surprising amount of hot juice — and pat the skin completely dry with paper towels. Any moisture left on that skin is the difference between browned and blotchy, so blot a second time if the towel comes away damp. The rolls should feel firm and hold their cylinder on their own.
  10. Sear the skin
    Heat the 1 tbsp oil in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium-high until shimmering, add the 2 tbsp butter, and lay the rolls in seam side down. Sear 6 to 8 minutes total, rolling them a quarter turn every 90 seconds with tongs so the entire surface goes deep golden. Spoon the foaming butter over as you go, and drop the heat if the butter starts smoking black.
  11. Make the pan sauce
    Move the ballotines to a warm board. Pour off the excess fat, add the 2 tbsp white wine to the pan, and scrape up the browned bits, then add the 1 cup chicken stock and the thyme sprig. Simmer 5 to 6 minutes until reduced to about 1/3 cup (80 ml) and slightly syrupy. Off the heat, whisk in the 2 tbsp cold butter one piece at a time until glossy, then add the lemon juice and 1/4 tsp salt.
  12. Slice into rounds
    Let the rolls sit 3 more minutes, then slice each one crosswise into 3 or 4 thick rounds with a very sharp knife, wiping the blade between cuts. Cut confidently in a single pulling stroke; sawing will drag the filling and smear the spiral. Discard the two ragged end pieces or eat them standing at the counter, as is tradition.
  13. Plate the spirals
    Fan three rounds across each warm plate slightly overlapping, cut face up so the mushroom spiral faces the person eating. Spoon the pan sauce in a ring around the base rather than over the crisp skin, then add a small mound of potato puree or wilted greens behind the slices for height. Finish with a few thyme leaves and the 1/2 tsp flaky sea salt on the cut surfaces.
Know when it is done
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) in the center of the roll, measured with an instant-read thermometer. Poach the water at a steady 170°F (77°C), never a boil.
Serve it with
A white Burgundy or oaked Chardonnay, with potato puree and buttered greens.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Ask the butcher to bone the leg quarters for you and to leave the skin fully intact. It costs nothing and saves the hardest twenty minutes of this recipe.
  • ◆If you would rather not poach in plastic, roll the ballotines in a double layer of buttered parchment then heavy foil, twisting the ends the same way, and poach or roast at 375°F (190°C) for 30 minutes to the same 165°F (74°C).
  • ◆These can be poached, chilled, and refrigerated up to 2 days ahead. Sear them straight from the fridge, adding 2 minutes to the pan time, and they are actually easier to slice cold-set.
  • ◆The duxelles is worth doubling. It freezes for 2 months and turns up again in beef Wellington, on toast, or folded into an omelet.
  • ◆If a roll splits during searing, do not panic. Roll it seam side down, finish it, and slice from the good end — the spiral will still read beautifully on the plate.

Lobster Thermidor with Gruyere Glaze⏱ 1 hr🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Lobster meat folded into a brandy and mustard cream sauce, piled back into the shells, and glazed under the broiler until it bubbles and browns. It is pure 1890s Paris and it never stopped being spectacular.

Special OccasionRestaurant at HomeFrench Classic
Prep
25 min
Cook
35 min
Total
1 hr
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the lobster

Thermidor sauce

The glaze

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Boil the lobsters
    Bring a large pot of water with the 1/4 cup kosher salt and the lemon halves to a hard rolling boil. Lower the lobsters in headfirst, cover, and cook 7 to 8 minutes for a 1 1/2 lb (680 g) lobster, or 5 minutes for tails alone. You are slightly undercooking them on purpose, because they will cook again under the broiler. Reserve 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the cooking water and pull the lobsters into an ice bath for 3 minutes.
  2. Split and clean the shells
    Set a cooled lobster belly down and drive a heavy knife straight down through the head, then cut the length of the body to split it in two neat halves. Lift out the meat from the tail, pull the claw and knuckle meat free by cracking the shells with the back of the knife, and remove the dark vein and the feathery gills. Rinse the empty half-shells, dry them, and set them on a sheet pan — these are your serving dishes.
  3. Cut the meat
    Chop all the lobster meat into generous 3/4 in (2 cm) pieces and season with the 1/2 tsp salt. Keep the pieces chunky; anything smaller disappears into the sauce and you lose the whole point of eating lobster. Leave the claw meat in whole pieces if you can, since it is the sweetest part and it looks best sitting proud on top. Refrigerate the meat while you build the sauce so it stays cold and firm and does not quietly overcook in its own residual heat.
  4. Sweat shallots and mushrooms
    Melt the 3 tbsp butter in a 10 in (25 cm) skillet over medium heat and cook the shallots for 3 minutes until soft and translucent. Add the diced mushrooms and cook 6 to 8 minutes, until they release their liquid and the pan goes dry again. Getting the pan dry now is what keeps the finished sauce thick instead of soupy.
  5. Make the roux
    Sprinkle the 2 tbsp flour over the vegetables and stir constantly for 90 seconds to 2 minutes. The mixture will look like wet sand and should smell faintly nutty and biscuity rather than raw and pasty — that smell is your signal the starch has cooked out. Do not let it take on color; you want a blond roux so the finished sauce stays pale and elegant instead of beige. Keep the heat at medium and work the spoon into the corners of the pan.
  6. Deglaze with brandy and wine
    Take the pan off the heat, add the 3 tbsp brandy, and return it to medium heat for 60 seconds until the sharp alcohol smell has burned off. Pour in the 1/2 cup white wine and whisk hard to work out any lumps, simmering 2 minutes until it thickens. Adding the liquid in stages and whisking is the difference between silk and paste.
  7. Build and reduce the cream sauce
    Whisk in the 1/2 cup reserved lobster liquid, then the 1 cup heavy cream, and simmer gently over medium-low for 8 to 10 minutes. The sauce should reduce until it heavily coats the back of a spoon and holds a clean line when you drag a finger through it. Stir in the 2 tsp Dijon, the tarragon, and the pinch of cayenne, then taste and season.
  8. Temper the yolk
    Whisk the egg yolk in a small bowl, then slowly drizzle in about 1/3 cup (80 ml) of the hot sauce while whisking constantly to warm it gently. Pour that mixture back into the pan off the heat and stir it through. Adding a cold yolk straight to a hot pan would scramble it instantly; the yolk is what gives thermidor its glossy richness and helps it glaze.
  9. Fold in the lobster
    Fold the chilled lobster meat into the warm sauce off the heat, turning gently until every piece is coated. Do not cook it further at this stage — the residual heat plus the broiler is all it needs, and lobster goes from tender to rubbery in about a minute of extra cooking. The sauce should be thick enough to cling to each piece rather than slide off and pool. Taste one last time for salt, cayenne, and acidity before it goes into the shells.
  10. Fill the shells
    Pile the mixture generously into the four cleaned half-shells, mounding it slightly above the rim so it looks abundant rather than skimpy. If your shells are cracked or you are using tails only, small gratin dishes work just as well. Set them on a sheet pan, snugging crumpled foil around the bases so they sit level and nothing spills.
  11. Glaze under the broiler
    Toss the Gruyere and Parmesan together and scatter it evenly over the tops, then drizzle with the 1 tbsp melted butter. Broil 6 in (15 cm) from a high element for 3 to 4 minutes, watching the entire time and rotating the pan once. Pull them the moment the surface is bubbling and blistered deep golden brown — thirty extra seconds turns the cheese bitter and the lobster tough.
  12. Plate and serve
    Set one filled shell on each warm plate at a slight diagonal, propped against a small mound of rice pilaf or a crumpled band of foil so it does not roll. Scatter the parsley across the bubbling top and add a lemon wedge at the edge of the plate. Serve immediately with small forks, while the cheese is still molten and the sauce is at a gentle simmer inside the shell.
Know when it is done
Boil 1 1/2 lb (680 g) lobsters 7 to 8 minutes to about 135°F (57°C) in the tail, then finish under the broiler; the FDA guideline for fully cooked shellfish is 145°F (63°C). Overcooked lobster turns rubbery fast.
Serve it with
Champagne or a rich white Burgundy, with a simple green salad in a sharp vinaigrette.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆If handling live lobsters is not for you, buy cooked lobster meat or frozen tails. Use 1 1/4 lb (570 g) of picked meat and skip straight to the sauce.
  • ◆The sauce can be made a day ahead through the cream reduction step, refrigerated, and rewarmed gently. Add the tempered yolk and the lobster only right before broiling.
  • ◆Do not let the sauce boil after the egg yolk goes in. It will split and turn grainy, and there is no fixing it.
  • ◆Save the shells and bodies in the freezer. Simmered with aromatics for 40 minutes they make a lobster stock that upgrades every seafood dish you cook for the next three months.
  • ◆No broiler? Bake at 450°F (230°C) for 8 to 10 minutes on a high rack. You will get slightly less blistering but the same glorious result.

Classic Beef Wellington⏱ 3 hr 30 min🍽 6 servingsAdvanced▾

Tenderloin wrapped in mushroom duxelles and prosciutto, sealed in golden puff pastry, and cut open at the table to a perfect rosy center. It is a project, but every single step is simple, and nothing you cook will get a bigger reaction.

Weekend ProjectSpecial OccasionMake Ahead
Prep
45 min
Cook
1 hr 10 min
Total
3 hr 30 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the beef

Mushroom duxelles

Pastry and assembly

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Shape and salt the beef
    Trim the tenderloin of silverskin and fold the thin tail end under, tying the whole log with kitchen twine every 1 1/2 in (4 cm) so it holds an even cylinder. Season all over with the 2 tsp salt and 1 tsp pepper and let it sit at room temperature for 30 minutes. An even thickness is not a detail here — it is the only way the whole roast reaches the same temperature at the same time.
  2. Sear the log hard
    Heat the 1 tbsp oil in a 12 in (30 cm) skillet over high heat until it just begins to smoke, then sear the tenderloin 60 to 90 seconds per side, rolling it a quarter turn at a time, including the ends. You want a uniform dark brown crust in about 5 minutes total. Go fast and hot — this is for flavor only, and slow searing will cook the outer inch gray.
  3. Chill the seared beef
    Snip off the twine, brush the hot beef all over with the 2 tbsp Dijon while the surface is still warm so it clings, and set it on a rack. Refrigerate uncovered for at least 20 minutes, or until completely cold. Wrapping warm beef in pastry is the classic way to end up with a soggy bottom and an overcooked roast.
  4. Make the duxelles
    Pulse the mushrooms and shallots in a food processor in three batches, 10 short pulses each, until they are the texture of coarse couscous. Melt the 3 tbsp butter in a wide 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium-high, add the mixture with the 1 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp pepper, and cook 20 to 25 minutes, stirring often. It will release an alarming amount of liquid, then slowly darken and dry — do not stop until the pan is completely dry and the mixture holds its shape when you push it aside.
  5. Deglaze and cool the duxelles
    Add the thyme leaves and the 1/4 cup sherry and cook 2 to 3 minutes more until the pan is dry again. Spread the duxelles thin on a sheet pan and refrigerate until completely cold, about 20 minutes. Any moisture or warmth left in it will steam the pastry from the inside, which is the number one reason Wellingtons fail.
  6. Build the prosciutto layer
    Lay a large sheet of plastic wrap on the counter and arrange the prosciutto slices in a slightly overlapping rectangle big enough to wrap the beef completely, about 12 by 10 in (30 by 25 cm). Spread the cold duxelles over the prosciutto in an even 1/4 in (6 mm) layer, leaving a 1 in (2.5 cm) border along the far edge. The prosciutto is a waterproof jacket that keeps mushroom moisture away from the pastry.
  7. Roll the first parcel
    Set the chilled beef along the near edge and use the plastic wrap to roll it up tightly, pulling the wrap taut as you go so there are no air pockets. Twist the ends like a candy wrapper and tighten until the parcel is a firm, even cylinder. Refrigerate for at least 30 minutes; this chill is what makes the log hold its shape when the pastry goes on.
  8. Roll out the pastry
    On a lightly floured surface, roll the cold puff pastry into a rectangle roughly 14 by 12 in (35 by 30 cm) and about 1/8 in (4 mm) thick — that is as far as 1 lb (450 g) of pastry will stretch and still cover the log, and anything thicker will not bake through underneath. Keep the pastry cold and work quickly, sliding it back into the fridge for 10 minutes if it starts to feel greasy or soft. Warm puff pastry loses its layers and bakes flat instead of rising.
  9. Wrap in pastry
    Unwrap the beef parcel and set it on the near third of the pastry. Brush the exposed pastry with egg wash, then roll the beef up snugly, pressing out air as you go, and trim the overlap so the seam is a single layer rather than a thick doubled slab. Press the seam closed, tuck and trim the ends like a present, and set the Wellington seam side down on a parchment-lined sheet pan.
  10. Chill, score, and glaze
    Brush the whole surface with egg wash and refrigerate uncovered for 30 minutes to firm the pastry — do not skip this. Brush with a second coat of egg wash, then score a shallow crosshatch or chevron pattern across the top with the back of a paring knife, cutting no deeper than 1/16 in (2 mm) so you do not pierce it. Sprinkle with the 1/2 tsp flaky salt.
  11. Bake hot
    Preheat the oven to 425°F (220°C) with a rack in the lower middle and a baking steel or heavy sheet pan preheating on it if you have one. Set the Wellington directly on the hot surface and bake 35 to 45 minutes. The pastry should be deep golden brown and firm all over, and the bottom should sound hollow when you tap it.
  12. Check the temperature
    Start checking at 30 minutes with an instant-read thermometer pushed through the end of the log into the center of the beef. Pull the Wellington at 120 to 125°F (49 to 52°C) for medium-rare or 130°F (54°C) for medium. If the pastry is browning too fast before the beef is ready, tent it loosely with foil for the last stretch.
  13. Rest a full fifteen minutes
    Move the Wellington to a cutting board and rest it 15 minutes, uncovered so the crust stays crisp. The center will climb to a final 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium-rare, and the juices will settle so they do not flood out and dissolve the pastry the moment you cut. This is the hardest fifteen minutes in cooking and it is not optional.
  14. Slice and plate
    Using a long serrated knife in gentle sawing strokes, trim off the two end pieces and then cut the log into 1 1/2 in (4 cm) thick slices — thick slices hold together, thin ones collapse. Set one slice slightly off-center on each warm plate, cut face angled toward the guest so the pink center and the dark mushroom ring are the first thing they see. Add a little pile of buttered greens or roasted carrots behind it, and pass any sauce separately at the table rather than pooling it against the pastry, which would soften the crust within a minute. Carry the whole Wellington to the table before you slice it, because half the pleasure is the reveal.
Know when it is done
Pull the Wellington at 120 to 125°F (49 to 52°C) for medium-rare or 130°F (54°C) for medium; after a 15 minute rest it settles at 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) or 140°F (60°C).
Serve it with
A serious Bordeaux or Barolo, with red wine sauce, buttered greens, and roasted carrots.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Everything except the baking can be done a day ahead. Assemble the pastry-wrapped Wellington, wrap it well, refrigerate overnight, and add 5 minutes to the bake time.
  • ◆A crepe layer between the prosciutto and the pastry is the old-school insurance against a soggy bottom. Two thin unsweetened crepes laid over the duxelles will absorb any stray moisture.
  • ◆Use all-butter puff pastry. Shortening-based pastry will not puff the same way and tastes waxy against the beef.
  • ◆If your duxelles still looks glossy or wet after 20 minutes, keep cooking. Dry duxelles is the single most important variable in this dish.
  • ◆Serve it with a simple red wine sauce: reduce 2 cups (480 ml) red wine with a shallot to 1/4 cup, add 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) beef stock, reduce by half, and mount with 2 tbsp (28 g) cold butter.

This is the chapter that replaces the takeout menu — get your knife work done before the pan gets hot, learn to velvet meat with a spoonful of cornstarch, and let the wok get hotter than feels sensible.

Beef and Broccoli⏱ 40 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Tender slices of beef in a glossy oyster sauce with broccoli that still has snap. The whole trick is velveting the meat, and once you know it you will never order this out again.

Takeout at HomeWokWeeknight
Prep
25 min
Cook
15 min
Total
40 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the velveted beef

Stir-fry sauce

For the wok

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Firm the beef in the freezer
    Lay the flank steak on a plate and freeze it for 15 to 20 minutes, until the outside is firm but the center still gives when you press it. Cold meat holds still under the knife, and that is the only reliable way to get thin, even slices. A soft room-temperature steak squashes and tears instead of slicing cleanly.
  2. Slice against the grain
    Find the long parallel muscle fibers running down the steak and cut straight across them, never with them, holding the knife at a slight 45 degree angle. Aim for slices about 1/4 in (6 mm) thick and no longer than 2 in (5 cm) so they cook in seconds. Cutting across the grain shortens those fibers, which is the difference between tender beef and stringy beef. If a slice comes out thick, lay it flat and press it once with your palm.
  3. Velvet the beef
    In a medium bowl, toss the beef with the 1 tbsp Shaoxing wine, 1 tbsp soy sauce, 1/2 tsp baking soda and 1 tbsp cornstarch until every piece is slick and evenly coated. Add the 1 tbsp neutral oil last and toss again so the slices do not glue into a single lump in the wok. Let it sit at room temperature for 20 to 30 minutes. The baking soda raises the surface pH so the proteins cannot clench up, and the cornstarch forms a thin gel that shields the meat from the pan. This is velveting, and it is the single reason takeout beef is softer than yours.
  4. Whisk the stir-fry sauce
    In a small bowl or a liquid measuring cup, whisk together the 1/2 cup broth, 3 tbsp oyster sauce, 1 tbsp soy sauce, 2 tsp sesame oil, 2 tsp sugar, 1 tbsp cornstarch and 1/4 tsp white pepper until no lumps remain. Set it right next to the stove and plan to whisk it once more before it goes in, because cornstarch settles to the bottom within a couple of minutes. Once the wok is hot there is no time to go measuring anything.
  5. Cut the broccoli evenly
    Cut the crowns into florets about 1 1/2 in (4 cm) across, each with a short piece of stem so they stand up in the pan. Peel the thick main stalk with a vegetable peeler and slice it into 1/4 in (6 mm) coins, because it is the sweetest part and most people throw it in the bin. Even sizing matters far more than pretty shapes, since mismatched florets mean some are mush while others are still raw.
  6. Set out your mise en place
    Line up four small bowls beside the stove: the beef, the broccoli, the garlic and ginger together, and the sauce. Put the serving platter and a spider or slotted spoon within arm's reach, and start the rice now if it is not already done. A stir-fry takes about eight minutes from first sizzle to plate and there is no pause button, so anything not chopped by this point will not make it into dinner. Cooks call this setup mise en place, and it is honestly ninety percent of the job.
  7. Steam the broccoli first
    Heat 1 tbsp of the oil in a 14 in (36 cm) carbon steel wok or a large heavy skillet over high heat, add the broccoli, and toss for 1 minute until the edges start to blister. Pour in the 1/3 cup water, cover immediately, and steam for 2 minutes. Uncover and check: the broccoli should be vivid green and a knife tip should slide into a stem with slight resistance, and the water should be gone. Tip it onto a plate and wipe the wok dry with a paper towel.
  8. Get the wok properly hot
    Return the dry wok to high heat for 1 to 2 minutes, until a drop of water flicked in vanishes instantly with a hiss. Add 1 tbsp of oil and swirl it up the sides so it coats the sloped walls, not just the bottom. It should shimmer, thin out, and send up the faintest wisp of smoke. That thin film on very hot metal is what gives you wok hei, the light smoky flavor real takeout has. If your burner is weak, use a heavy cast iron skillet instead, because it stores more heat than a thin wok.
  9. Sear the beef in two batches
    Lay half the beef in a single layer and do not touch it for 45 to 60 seconds; it should sizzle hard and steadily, not smoke black. Toss and cook another 30 to 45 seconds, until the outside is browned and the centers are just barely pink. Scrape it onto a plate, add the last 1 tbsp oil, and repeat with the second half. Crowding the pan drops the temperature and the beef will boil gray in its own juices instead of browning, which is the most common stir-fry mistake there is.
  10. Bloom the aromatics
    Turn the heat down to medium-high, add the minced garlic and ginger to the empty wok, and stir constantly for 20 to 30 seconds. They should smell sweet and sharp and turn pale gold, no darker than that. Garlic goes from fragrant to bitter in about fifteen seconds at this temperature, so keep it moving and have the sauce ready in your other hand.
  11. Bring it all together
    Whisk the sauce one more time and pour it into the wok all at once, scraping up the browned bits stuck to the bottom. Let it bubble hard for 45 to 60 seconds until it turns glossy and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. Return the beef, the broccoli and any juices from the plate, then toss for 30 to 45 seconds so everything is lacquered. If the sauce tightens too much, loosen it with a tablespoon of water at a time.
  12. Serve it right away
    Slide everything onto a warm platter or straight over the hot jasmine rice and eat immediately, while the broccoli still has snap. Stir-fries go soft and the sauce turns gluey if they sit around, so call everyone to the table before you start cooking, not after. Leftovers keep 3 days in the fridge and reheat best in a hot dry skillet rather than the microwave.
Know when it is done
Beef is safe at 145°F (63°C), but slices this thin blow past that in seconds, so go by looks: pull them when the outside is browned and the center has just lost its pink. Broccoli is done when it is bright green and a knife tip meets slight resistance in the stem, not olive green and floppy.
Serve it with
Steamed jasmine rice and a cold lager, or an off-dry Riesling that can stand up to the oyster sauce.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Flank, skirt, top sirloin and flat iron all work here. Avoid stew beef or chuck, which need hours of moist heat rather than ninety seconds of high heat.
  • ◆No Shaoxing wine? Dry sherry is the closest substitute. Skip it entirely rather than reaching for cooking sherry, which is salted and tastes harsh.
  • ◆Do not leave the baking soda on the beef longer than 30 minutes or the texture turns spongy and can pick up a faint soapy taste. If you get distracted, rinse the slices and pat them dry.
  • ◆Make-ahead: slice and velvet the beef and mix the sauce up to 24 hours in advance, both covered in the fridge. Let the beef sit out 20 minutes before it hits the wok so it does not chill the pan.
  • ◆For a vegetarian version, use 14 oz (400 g) extra-firm tofu, pressed and cubed, and swap the oyster sauce for vegetarian mushroom stir-fry sauce.

Kung Pao Chicken⏱ 40 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

The real Sichuan version: numbing peppercorns, toasted dried chiles, black vinegar and peanuts, with almost no sauce clinging to anything. It is sharper and more interesting than the gloopy takeout kind.

SpicyWokSichuan
Prep
25 min
Cook
15 min
Total
40 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the velveted chicken

Kung pao sauce

For the wok

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Cut the chicken evenly
    Trim any big pads of fat from the thighs and cut the meat into cubes about 3/4 in (2 cm) on a side, roughly the size of the peanuts they will share the plate with. Thighs are the right choice here because they stay juicy through high heat, while breast dries out in the time it takes to brown. Even cubes mean everything finishes at the same moment instead of some pieces burning while others are raw.
  2. Velvet the chicken
    Toss the chicken with the 1 tbsp Shaoxing wine, 1 tbsp soy sauce and 1 tbsp cornstarch until each cube is coated in a slippery film, then stir in the 1 tsp oil. Let it rest 20 minutes at room temperature while you prep everything else. The cornstarch sets into a thin protective jacket in the hot pan, sealing juices in and giving the sauce something to cling to. Skip this and the chicken will be noticeably drier and the sauce will pool at the bottom of the bowl.
  3. Mix the sauce
    Whisk the 3 tbsp black vinegar, 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp Shaoxing wine, 2 tbsp brown sugar, 1 tsp cornstarch, 3 tbsp broth and 1 tsp sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth. Chinkiang vinegar is the soul of kung pao, malty and slightly sweet like a Chinese balsamic, so seek it out rather than substituting white vinegar. Taste it now: it should read sour first, then sweet, then salty. Set it beside the stove.
  4. Prep the chiles and peppercorns
    Snip the dried chiles in half with scissors and shake out most of the seeds, since the seeds carry harsh heat without much flavor. Measure the 1 tsp Sichuan peppercorns into the same little bowl. Sichuan peppercorns are not spicy at all; they deliver a tingly, citrusy numbness called ma that is the whole point of this dish. If yours smell dusty rather than lemony, they are old and worth replacing.
  5. Lay out your mise en place
    Arrange small bowls next to the burner: chicken, chile and peppercorn mix, garlic and ginger, scallion whites, scallion greens, peanuts, and the sauce. This dish cooks in under six minutes and the aromatics burn in seconds, so there is no time to be rummaging in a drawer mid-cook. Set a warm serving platter out too. Having everything within arm's reach is what separates a clean stir-fry from a smoky, panicked one.
  6. Sear the chicken in batches
    Heat a 14 in (36 cm) wok or heavy skillet over high heat for 2 minutes, add 1 tbsp of the oil, and swirl until it shimmers with the first wisp of smoke. Add half the chicken in one layer and leave it alone for 90 seconds so a golden crust forms, then toss for another minute. Scrape it out and repeat with 1 more tbsp of oil and the rest of the chicken. It should sizzle steadily and loudly the whole time; if the sound drops to a mutter, your pan lost its heat and the chicken is stewing.
  7. Toast the chiles and peppercorns
    Lower the heat to medium, add the last 1 tbsp oil, then the chiles and Sichuan peppercorns, and stir for 20 to 30 seconds. You want the chiles to darken a shade and smell toasty and sweet, not acrid. Burnt chiles will make the entire wok taste bitter and there is no rescuing it, so if they go black, wash the pan and start this step again. Crack a window before you begin, because the fumes are genuinely eye-watering.
  8. Add garlic, ginger and scallion whites
    Toss in the sliced garlic, minced ginger and scallion whites and stir constantly for 30 seconds. They should turn fragrant and just barely golden at the edges. Keeping the heat at medium here is deliberate: the aromatics need to bloom in the oil, not scorch on it, and the residual heat in the pan is already doing plenty of work.
  9. Return the chicken and sauce
    Turn the heat back to high, return the chicken and all its juices, and pour in the whisked sauce. Stir and toss for 45 to 60 seconds, until the sauce reduces to a glaze that just coats each piece and you can see clean streaks on the bottom of the pan when you drag your spatula. Kung pao is not a saucy dish; the coating should be thin and shiny, not a puddle.
  10. Finish with peanuts and greens
    Kill the heat, add the 1/2 cup peanuts and the scallion greens, and toss twice. Adding the peanuts at the very last second is what keeps them crunchy, because even one minute in the sauce turns them soft. Check the biggest cube of chicken with an instant-read thermometer; it should read 165°F (74°C).
  11. Serve hot with rice
    Spoon it onto the warm platter and serve immediately with the hot jasmine rice. Warn everyone about the whole chiles and peppercorns, which are there for flavor and are not meant to be eaten by the mouthful. The numbing tingle builds over the first few bites, which is exactly right.
Know when it is done
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) at the center of the largest cube, with no pink and clear juices. At 3/4 in (2 cm) the pieces get there after roughly 4 minutes of total wok time, so check rather than guessing.
Serve it with
Plain jasmine rice to soak up the tingle, plus a cold pilsner or jasmine tea to reset your palate.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Chinkiang black vinegar keeps for years and costs a few dollars at any Asian market. If you truly cannot find it, use 2 tbsp balsamic plus 1 tbsp rice vinegar, which gets you close.
  • ◆Control the heat with the number of chiles, not by removing the Sichuan peppercorns. The chiles bring the burn; the peppercorns bring the tingle, and losing the tingle loses the dish.
  • ◆Make-ahead: velvet the chicken and mix the sauce up to a day ahead. Chop the aromatics the morning of and keep them in covered bowls in the fridge.
  • ◆Roast raw peanuts yourself at 350°F (175°C) for 10 to 12 minutes if you want the best texture. Cocktail peanuts work fine but rinse and dry them first if they are heavily salted.
  • ◆If the finished dish tastes flat, it almost always needs another splash of black vinegar rather than more salt.
