General Tso's Chicken⏱ 50 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Craggy, double-fried chicken in a sweet-tart chile glaze that stays crisp all the way to the table. It is a project, but it is the single most requested thing on any takeout menu for a reason.

Takeout at HomeDeep FriedCrowd Pleaser
Prep
30 min
Cook
20 min
Total
50 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chicken and marinade

Coating and frying

General Tso sauce

Aromatics and finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Marinate the chicken
    Toss the chicken pieces with the egg white, 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp Shaoxing wine and 1/2 tsp white pepper until the mixture looks foamy and clings to the meat. Let it sit 20 minutes at room temperature or up to 4 hours in the fridge. The egg white does two jobs: it seasons the meat and it glues the dry coating on so the crust does not slide off in the oil.
  2. Mix the dry coating
    In a wide shallow bowl, whisk together the 3/4 cup cornstarch, 1/4 cup flour and 1/2 tsp baking powder. Cornstarch fries up glassy and crisp where flour alone goes soft, and the baking powder puffs the coating into those craggy ridges that hold sauce. Whisk it well so the baking powder is evenly distributed rather than sitting in one bitter pocket.
  3. Whisk the sauce
    Combine the 1/4 cup broth, 3 tbsp soy sauce, 3 tbsp rice vinegar, 3 tbsp sugar, 1 tbsp hoisin, 1 tbsp cornstarch and 1 tsp sesame oil in a small bowl and whisk until no lumps remain. Taste it: it should be aggressively sweet and sour, because it will be coating a lot of plain fried chicken. Set it next to the stove along with the chiles, garlic, ginger and scallions.
  4. Heat the frying oil
    Pour the 6 cups oil into a heavy 5 qt (4.7 L) Dutch oven; it should come no more than a third of the way up the sides. Clip on a thermometer and bring it to 350°F (175°C) over medium-high heat, which takes about 10 minutes. Have a wire rack set over a sheet pan ready beside the pot. Never fill the pot more than a third, because the oil bubbles up violently the moment wet chicken hits it.
  5. Dredge the chicken
    Lift the chicken out of the marinade a few pieces at a time, letting the excess drip off, then drop them into the cornstarch mixture. Toss and press so every surface is packed with coating, then shake off the loose powder. Work in small handfuls and lay the coated pieces on a plate in a single layer. Dredging everything at once means the first pieces go gummy while you finish the last.
  6. Fry the first round
    Lower 8 to 10 pieces into the oil with tongs, one at a time, and fry for 4 minutes, stirring once at the halfway mark so they do not fuse. They should be pale gold and cooked through, not deeply browned; this first fry is about cooking the meat and setting the crust. Push an instant-read thermometer into the thickest piece of the first batch to confirm it reads 165°F (74°C), and if it is short, give that batch another 30 to 60 seconds and use that as your timing for the rest. Lift them to the rack and let the oil climb back to 350°F (175°C) before the next batch, which takes about a minute.
  7. Rest, then fry again
    Once every piece has had its first fry, raise the oil to 375°F (190°C) and let the chicken rest on the rack for at least 5 minutes. Fry each batch a second time for 60 to 90 seconds, until deep golden and audibly crisp when you tap a piece with tongs. The rest lets interior steam escape, and the hotter second fry drives off the last surface moisture, which is why double-fried chicken stays crunchy under sauce.
  8. Drain and season
    Return the chicken to the rack, not to paper towels, so air circulates underneath and the bottoms do not steam soft. Season with a small pinch of salt while it is still glistening. Keep it uncovered and near the stove; you have about ten minutes of peak crunch to work with, so make the sauce now.
  9. Toast the chiles and aromatics
    Set a large skillet or wok over medium heat, add the 2 tbsp neutral oil, then the halved dried chiles, and stir for 30 seconds until they darken slightly and smell toasty. Add the garlic and ginger and stir 30 seconds more, until fragrant and pale gold. Do not walk away here; garlic scorches in about fifteen seconds at this heat and burnt garlic will ruin the sauce.
  10. Reduce the sauce
    Whisk the sauce once more and pour it in all at once. Turn the heat to medium-high and let it bubble for 60 to 90 seconds, stirring, until it thickens to the consistency of warm honey and coats the back of a spoon in a sheet. If it goes past that and turns tacky, whisk in a tablespoon of water to bring it back.
  11. Toss and serve immediately
    Kill the heat, add all the fried chicken at once, and toss for no more than 20 to 30 seconds, just until every piece is glazed. The longer the chicken sits in sauce the softer it gets, so this is a fast, decisive move. Scatter the scallions and 1 tsp sesame seeds over the top and take it straight to the table with the hot rice.
  12. Deal with the oil
    Let the frying oil cool completely in the pot, which takes a couple of hours, then strain it through a coffee filter or fine mesh sieve into a jar. Stored in a cool dark cupboard it is good for three or four more fries. Never pour hot oil down the drain, and never leave a hot pot unattended on the stove.
Know when it is done
Fry at 350°F (175°C) for the first round and 375°F (190°C) for the second. Chicken is safe at 165°F (74°C); thigh pieces this size reach it during the first 4-minute fry, so the second fry is purely for crunch.
Serve it with
Steamed jasmine rice, a plate of garlicky bok choy, and something cold and simple like a lager or an iced oolong.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Thighs beat breast here by a mile. They hold up to two rounds of frying without drying out, and the darker meat stands up to a sauce this sweet.
  • ◆No thermometer? Drop in a pinch of the coating: at 350°F (175°C) it sizzles steadily and floats within two seconds. If it browns instantly the oil is too hot.
  • ◆Make-ahead: fry the chicken through the first fry up to 3 hours in advance and leave it on the rack at room temperature. Do the second fry and the saucing right before serving.
  • ◆For a lighter version, toss the coated chicken with 3 tbsp oil and air-fry at 400°F (205°C) for 14 to 16 minutes, shaking twice. It will not be quite as craggy but it is genuinely good.
  • ◆The sauce is easy to scale down if you like less glaze. Halve it and toss with a lighter hand for a drier, more restaurant-style plate.

Chicken and Shrimp Pad Thai⏱ 1 hr 15 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Sweet, sour and salty in equal measure, with tamarind doing the heavy lifting and a squeeze of lime at the end. Get the noodles soaked properly and the rest is a five minute sprint.

ThaiNoodlesDate Night
Prep
30 min
Cook
15 min
Total
1 hr 15 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Noodles and protein

Pad thai sauce

For the wok

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Soak the noodles cold
    Put the dried rice noodles in a large bowl, cover them with room-temperature water by 2 in (5 cm), and leave them for 45 to 60 minutes while you prep everything else. They should turn pliable and white but still snap when you bend one, roughly like al dente pasta. Boiling them is the number one pad thai mistake: they keep cooking in the wok and you end up with porridge. Drain them well and toss with 1 tsp of the oil so they do not clump.
  2. Make the sauce
    In a small saucepan over low heat, warm the 3 tbsp fish sauce, 3 tbsp palm sugar, 3 tbsp tamarind concentrate and 2 tbsp water, stirring until the sugar fully dissolves, about 2 minutes. Take it off the heat and taste it on a spoon. It should hit sour first, then sweet, then salty, and it should taste slightly too strong on its own because it will season a pound of noodles. Adjust with a little more tamarind for sourness or sugar for balance.
  3. Prep the protein
    Pat the chicken and shrimp dry with paper towels and keep them in separate bowls, because they go into the pan at different times. Surface water turns to steam and stops browning cold. Devein the shrimp if the shop has not, and leave the tails on or off as you prefer, though tails off is easier to eat with noodles.
  4. Set the table before you cook
    Line up bowls of noodles, chicken, shrimp, beaten eggs, garlic, preserved radish, 2 cups of the bean sprouts, scallions, and the sauce in the order you will use them. Put the peanuts, lime wedges, chile flakes, cilantro and remaining 1 cup sprouts on the table already. From the moment the pan gets hot, this dish takes about six minutes and never pauses, so everything must be within arm's reach.
  5. Sear the chicken
    Heat a 14 in (36 cm) wok or your largest skillet over high heat for 2 minutes, add 1 tbsp oil, and swirl. Add the chicken in one layer and cook without stirring for 90 seconds, then toss for another minute until browned and cooked through to 165°F (74°C). Scrape it into a bowl. It should sizzle hard the whole time; a quiet pan means the heat is too low.
  6. Cook the shrimp fast
    Add 1 tbsp oil and lay the shrimp in a single layer. Cook 60 to 90 seconds per side, just until they turn opaque pink all the way through and curl into a loose C, which is 145°F (63°C) on an instant-read thermometer pushed through the thickest part sideways. Move them to the bowl with the chicken. A shrimp that has curled into a tight O is already overcooked and will be rubbery, so pull them a moment before you think you should, remembering they get another minute of heat when everything comes back to the pan.
  7. Scramble the eggs
    Add the last 1 tbsp oil, then the garlic and preserved radish, and stir for 15 seconds until fragrant. Pour in the beaten eggs and let them sit undisturbed for 20 seconds until the bottom sets, then scramble them into large soft curds. Do not cook them dry; they will finish in the residual heat with the noodles.
  8. Add the noodles and sauce
    Tip in the drained noodles and pour the sauce over them, then toss constantly with tongs for 2 to 3 minutes. The noodles will drink the sauce, soften, and turn a glossy brown-orange. If they still feel stiff, splash in 2 tbsp of water at a time and keep tossing; the residual starch plus water is what finishes cooking them without turning them to mush.
  9. Return everything and finish
    Add the chicken, shrimp, scallions and 2 cups bean sprouts and toss for 60 to 90 seconds, until the sprouts are barely wilted and everything is evenly coated. The sprouts should still have crunch, since their whole job is textural contrast. Taste a noodle and adjust with a splash more sauce or fish sauce if it needs it.
  10. Plate and garnish
    Divide among four warm plates and top each with a generous spoonful of chopped peanuts, a scattering of cilantro and a pinch of chile flakes. Tuck a lime wedge and a small pile of the reserved raw bean sprouts alongside each portion. In Thailand these condiments arrive on the table so each person tunes their own plate, and that is genuinely how it tastes best.
  11. Squeeze and eat immediately
    Squeeze the lime over the noodles right before the first bite, not in the wok, because the fresh acidity fades fast once it hits heat. Pad thai has a short window where the noodles are chewy and the peanuts are crunchy, maybe five minutes. Serve it the second it hits the plate and do not make anyone wait.
Know when it is done
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) and shrimp 145°F (63°C), which for shrimp means opaque pink flesh curled into a loose C shape. Noodles are done when they are chewy and springy rather than soft, so bite one before you plate.
Serve it with
Thai iced tea or a very cold light lager, with extra lime wedges and chile flakes on the table.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Tamarind concentrate and tamarind paste are not the same. Concentrate is dark, thick and ready to use; if you only have block tamarind pulp, soak 2 tbsp in 1/4 cup hot water, mash and strain.
  • ◆Cook no more than two portions at a time in a home pan. Doubling the batch drops the temperature and you will steam the noodles rather than fry them.
  • ◆Make-ahead: the sauce keeps 2 weeks refrigerated and the noodles can be soaked and drained up to 4 hours in advance if you toss them with a little oil.
  • ◆Ketchup and sriracha are not pad thai. If the color looks pale, that is normal; tamarind gives a muted brown-orange, not the neon red of bad restaurant versions.
  • ◆For a vegetarian version, use 14 oz (400 g) pressed extra-firm tofu, swap the fish sauce for light soy sauce plus 1 tsp mushroom seasoning, and add extra sprouts.

Thai Drunken Noodles with Chicken⏱ 40 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Wide rice noodles charred in a screaming hot pan with garlic, bird chiles and a mountain of holy basil. Pad kee mao is loud, spicy food that comes together in about ten minutes.

ThaiSpicy30 Minutes
Prep
25 min
Cook
15 min
Total
40 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Noodles and chicken

Drunken noodle sauce

For the wok

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Loosen the noodles
    If you bought fresh wide rice noodles they will arrive as a cold solid brick. Microwave the unopened package for 60 to 90 seconds or steam it for 3 minutes, then gently peel the sheets apart into 1 in (2.5 cm) wide ribbons with your fingers. Cold noodles shatter into fragments when you try to separate them, so warming them first is not optional. If you are using dried noodles, soak them in room-temperature water for 45 minutes, then drain.
  2. Coat the chicken
    Toss the sliced chicken with the 1 tbsp cornstarch and 1 tbsp soy sauce until every piece is slick and there is no dry powder left. Let it sit 15 minutes at room temperature while you chop everything else. The cornstarch is a light velvet that keeps the thin slices juicy through very high heat and helps the sauce grip the meat later.
  3. Mix the sauce
    Stir together the 3 tbsp oyster sauce, 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp dark soy sauce, 1 tbsp fish sauce, 2 tsp sugar and 2 tbsp water in a small bowl. Dark soy sauce is thicker, sweeter and mostly there for color, and it is what gives drunken noodles their deep mahogany look. Set the bowl right next to the burner.
  4. Prep the aromatics and basil
    Roughly chop the garlic rather than mincing it, so the pieces survive the heat and stay sweet instead of burning to dust. Slice the chiles thin, seeds and all, and start with four if you are unsure. Pick the basil leaves off the stems and keep them in a big bowl; two cups looks absurd but it wilts down to almost nothing. Holy basil tastes peppery and clove-like, while Italian basil is sweeter but works fine.
  5. Get everything within reach
    Line up the noodles, chicken, garlic and chiles, onion and bell pepper, sauce, and basil in cooking order beside the stove, plus a warm serving platter. This whole dish takes about seven minutes and the noodles need constant attention once they hit the pan. There is no stopping to slice an onion halfway through, and a burnt clove of garlic can flavor the entire wok.
  6. Heat the pan until it smokes
    Set a 14 in (36 cm) carbon steel wok or your heaviest skillet over the highest heat you have for 2 to 3 minutes, until a bead of water flicked in disappears on contact. Add 1 tbsp of the oil and swirl it up the sides; it should shimmer and send up a thin wisp of smoke. Drunken noodles depend on real char, so if you have an outdoor burner or a gas hob, use it and open a window.
  7. Sear the chicken
    Add the chicken in a single layer and leave it completely alone for 90 seconds so it browns, then toss for another 60 seconds until cooked through to 165°F (74°C) on an instant-read thermometer, with no pink left in the thickest slice. It should sizzle violently and steadily. Scrape it out onto a plate. Cook in two batches if your pan is smaller than 12 in (30 cm), because crowding turns searing into steaming, and steamed chicken will not reach a safe temperature nearly as fast as you expect.
  8. Fry the aromatics and vegetables
    Add 1 tbsp oil, then the garlic and chiles, and stir for 15 to 20 seconds until fragrant and just barely golden. Add the onion and bell pepper and stir-fry for 90 seconds; they should soften slightly at the edges but stay crunchy in the middle. Vegetables in this dish are meant to be crisp, not stewed, so resist the urge to keep going.
  9. Char the noodles
    Push everything to one side, add the last 1 tbsp oil to the empty half, and lay the noodles in a flat layer. Let them sit untouched for 45 to 60 seconds so the bottoms blister and pick up brown spots, then fold everything together gently. Toss with a spatula rather than tongs and use a folding motion, because wide rice noodles tear easily once they are hot.
  10. Add the sauce and chicken
    Pour the sauce around the edge of the pan rather than into the middle, so it hits hot metal and caramelizes on the way in. Return the chicken and any juices and fold everything for 60 to 90 seconds until the noodles are evenly dark and glossy. If the pan looks dry, add a tablespoon of water; if it looks wet, let it cook 30 seconds longer.
  11. Fold in the basil and serve
    Kill the heat, dump in all 2 cups of basil, and fold two or three times until the leaves just collapse. The residual heat is enough, and cooking basil any longer turns it black and bitter. Pile it onto the warm platter, serve with lime wedges, and eat immediately while the charred edges are still crisp.
Know when it is done
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C), which thin slices hit after about 2 1/2 minutes in a properly hot pan. The noodles are right when the edges are charred and chewy and the whole pan smells faintly smoky rather than steamy.
Serve it with
An ice-cold lager and a plate of cucumber slices to cool your mouth between bites.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Fresh wide rice noodles are worth the trip to an Asian market and are usually in a refrigerated case. Never refrigerate them at home before use; the cold makes them brittle and they will shatter.
  • ◆Thai holy basil is the traditional leaf and tastes peppery with a hint of clove. Thai sweet basil is the next best, and Italian basil is a fine last resort.
  • ◆If your stove is weak, cook in two half batches. One crowded pan of noodles will steam and go gummy, and you cannot get char back once you have lost it.
  • ◆Make-ahead: mix the sauce and slice everything up to a day ahead. The cooking itself is too fast and too texture-dependent to do in advance.
  • ◆Four bird chiles is genuinely spicy and six is fiery. For a milder version use one chile plus 1/2 tsp red pepper flakes so you keep the flavor without the burn.

Chicken Fried Rice⏱ 25 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

The whole secret is cold day-old rice and a pan that is far hotter than feels reasonable. Twenty-five minutes from fridge to table, and it is better than any container you have paid for.

Weeknight30 MinutesLeftovers
Prep
15 min
Cook
10 min
Total
25 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Rice and chicken

Seasoning

For the wok

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Understand the day-old rice
    Fried rice needs rice that was cooked at least 12 hours ago and chilled uncovered or loosely covered in the fridge. As cooked rice cools, the starch retrogrades and the grains firm up and dry out, so they fry into separate fluffy kernels instead of collapsing into paste. Fresh hot rice is full of surface moisture and will steam itself into a sticky lump no matter how hot your pan is. If you must use same-day rice, spread it on a sheet pan and chill it uncovered for 45 minutes.
  2. Break up the cold rice
    Tip the rice into a wide bowl and work through it with wet fingers or a fork, crushing every clump until the grains are loose and individual. Cold rice compacts into a solid brick in the container, and any clump that goes into the pan intact will still be a clump on your plate. This takes two minutes and it is the difference between good fried rice and a rice cake.
  3. Coat the chicken
    Toss the chicken pieces with the 1 tbsp soy sauce and 2 tsp cornstarch until slick and evenly coated, then let them sit 10 minutes. This light velvet keeps the small pieces from drying out in a very hot pan and gives them a slightly glossy surface. Cut the pieces small, about 1/2 in (1 cm), so they cook through in the same time everything else needs.
  4. Mix the seasoning
    Stir the 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp oyster sauce, 1 tsp sesame oil, 1/2 tsp white pepper and 1/2 tsp salt together in a small bowl. Mixing the liquids in advance means you add them in one quick pour instead of shaking bottles over a smoking pan. White pepper is the flavor most people cannot place in restaurant fried rice, so do not leave it out.
  5. Line up your mise en place
    Put the rice, chicken, eggs, peas and carrots, garlic, scallion whites, scallion greens and the seasoning bowl in a row next to the stove. The entire cook is under eight minutes and every step runs into the next. Once the pan is hot you will not have a free hand or a spare thirty seconds to go looking for anything.
  6. Scramble the eggs first
    Heat a 14 in (36 cm) wok or large nonstick skillet over medium-high, add 1 tbsp of the oil, and pour in the beaten eggs. Let them set for 20 seconds, then scramble into large soft curds and slide them onto a plate while they still look slightly underdone. They will finish cooking later in the residual heat, and eggs that are fully cooked now will be rubbery by the time you eat.
  7. Sear the chicken
    Add 1 tbsp oil, turn the heat to high, and spread the chicken in a single layer. Leave it undisturbed for 90 seconds so it browns, then toss for 60 to 90 seconds more until cooked through to 165°F (74°C). Move it to the plate with the eggs. The pan should sizzle sharply the whole time, not hiss quietly.
  8. Bloom the garlic and scallion whites
    Add the last 1 tbsp oil to the empty pan along with the garlic and scallion whites, and stir for 20 to 30 seconds. They should smell sweet and turn barely golden. This is a fast window because garlic burns in about fifteen seconds over high heat, so have the rice ready to go in immediately.
  9. Fry the rice hard
    Add all the rice at once and press it into a flat layer with your spatula. Let it sit for 45 seconds to toast against the metal, then toss and press again, repeating for about 3 minutes total. You are listening for a dry crackling sound like light rain, which means moisture is leaving and the grains are frying rather than steaming. Individual grains should start dancing and separating in the pan.
  10. Season and combine
    Pour the seasoning mixture around the edge of the pan rather than into the middle, so it hits hot metal and caramelizes on contact. Toss hard for 60 seconds until the color is even and no wet patches remain. Add the peas and carrots and toss another 30 seconds just to heat them through.
  11. Fold in the eggs and finish
    Return the chicken and eggs, breaking the egg curds into smaller pieces with the edge of your spatula as you fold. Toss for 30 to 45 seconds until everything is hot and evenly distributed. Kill the heat, scatter the scallion greens over the top, and taste for salt. Serve straight from the pan while the bottom grains are still crisp.
Know when it is done
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) at the center of the largest piece. Leftover rice needs to be reheated to at least 165°F (74°C) too, which in a hot wok means the grains are steaming and too hot to hold in your fingers.
Serve it with
A fried egg on top with a runny yolk, a dash of chile oil, and hot jasmine tea.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Cool leftover rice within one hour of cooking and refrigerate it. Rice left at room temperature for hours can grow Bacillus cereus, which reheating will not fix, so this is a real food safety rule and not fussiness.
  • ◆Long-grain jasmine is ideal because it dries out well. Short-grain sushi rice is too sticky and basmati is fine but tastes noticeably different.
  • ◆The classic upgrade is 4 oz (115 g) diced Chinese barbecue pork or leftover roast chicken instead of raw chicken. Add it with the peas so it just warms through.
  • ◆Make-ahead: cook the rice up to 3 days in advance. Fried rice is one of the few dishes where planning ahead makes the result genuinely better.
  • ◆If your pan is smaller than 12 in (30 cm), cook the rice in two batches. Overloading it drops the heat and you will get steamed rice with soy sauce on it.

Korean Beef Bulgogi⏱ 1 hr🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Paper-thin ribeye in a sweet-savory pear and soy marinade, seared until the edges caramelize. Wrap it in lettuce with rice and a smear of ssamjang and you will understand why Koreans eat it at every celebration.

KoreanGrillCrowd Pleaser
Prep
20 min
Cook
10 min
Total
1 hr
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Beef

Bulgogi marinade

To cook and serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Slice the beef paper thin
    Freeze the ribeye for 30 to 45 minutes until firm at the edges but not solid, then slice it across the grain as thinly as you can manage, ideally 1/8 in (3 mm). If that sounds like a fight, ask the butcher for beef sliced for bulgogi or shabu shabu, or buy a frozen pre-sliced pack from a Korean market. Thin slices are the entire point: they take on marinade fast and cook in about ninety seconds.
  2. Grate the pear
    Peel and grate the Asian pear on the large holes of a box grater, juice and all, straight into a large bowl. Asian pear contains enzymes that gently break down muscle protein, which is the traditional Korean tenderizer and adds a clean floral sweetness. A ripe Bosc pear or 1/4 cup unsweetened applesauce will stand in, but not a hard supermarket Bartlett.
  3. Mix the marinade
    Add the 1/4 cup soy sauce, 2 tbsp sesame oil, 2 tbsp brown sugar, 1 tbsp mirin, minced garlic, grated ginger, sliced onion and 1/2 tsp black pepper to the pear and whisk until the sugar dissolves. Taste it: it should be salty and sweet in near equal measure with a strong garlic backbone. This is a marinade, so it should taste a shade too intense on its own.
  4. Marinate the beef
    Add the sliced beef and use your hands to separate every slice and coat it, since stacked slices marinate unevenly. Cover and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 8 hours. Going much past that makes the surface mushy from the pear enzymes, so overnight is not better here. Pull it out 20 minutes before cooking so it is not fridge-cold going into the pan.
  5. Set up before you cook
    Wash and dry the lettuce leaves, cut the scallions, and get the rice steaming so it is ready when the beef is. Set a warm platter beside the stove along with tongs. Bulgogi cooks in batches of about ninety seconds each, so there is no time to be assembling side dishes once the pan is hot.
  6. Drain the beef
    Lift the beef out of the marinade with tongs and let the excess drip off, leaving most of the liquid behind in the bowl. Do not dump the whole bowl into the pan. Excess marinade floods the pan, drops the temperature, and boils the beef gray instead of letting it caramelize, which is the single most common bulgogi mistake.
  7. Heat the pan properly
    Set a 12 in (30 cm) cast iron skillet or grill pan over high heat for 3 minutes, until it is genuinely hot and a drop of water skitters and evaporates in a second or two. Add 1 tbsp of the oil and swirl. You want an aggressive sizzle the instant the meat lands, because the sugars in the marinade need high heat to caramelize before the thin beef overcooks.
  8. Sear in batches
    Lay one-third of the beef in a single layer with a little space between the slices and cook without touching for 60 seconds. Flip and cook 30 to 45 seconds more, until the edges are deeply browned and slightly charred; whole-muscle beef is safe at 145°F (63°C) and slices this thin blow past that in well under a minute, so the caramelized edge is your real cue. Move it to the platter and repeat with the remaining beef, adding the last 1 tbsp oil partway through. Crowding the pan is what turns bulgogi into a puddle of gray beef soup.
  9. Finish with scallions
    On the last batch, toss the scallion pieces into the pan for the final 30 seconds so they wilt and pick up some of the caramelized fond. Scrape everything, including the browned bits, onto the platter. Those crusty bits stuck to the pan are the best flavor in the whole dish.
  10. Rest and season
    Let the beef sit for 2 to 3 minutes on the platter so the juices redistribute, then scatter the 1 tbsp sesame seeds over the top. Taste a slice; if it needs anything it will be a small pinch of salt, though the marinade usually has it covered. It should taste sweet, savory and faintly smoky all at once.
  11. Serve as ssam
    Bring the platter to the table with the hot rice and the lettuce leaves. The Korean way is ssam: lay a leaf in your palm, add a spoonful of rice, a few slices of beef, a dab of ssamjang or gochujang, then fold it into a parcel and eat it in one bite. Kimchi, pickled radish and a bowl of soup round it out if you want the full spread.
Know when it is done
Beef is safe at 145°F (63°C), but slices this thin race past it in under a minute, so cook by sight: pull them the moment the edges caramelize and the surface loses its raw red. Anything beyond about 90 seconds per batch turns leathery.
Serve it with
Short-grain rice, kimchi, and a cold Korean lager or a chilled soju with soda.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Ribeye is traditional because the fat marbling melts and bastes the meat in seconds. Sirloin, top round and even chuck eye all work if sliced thin enough.
  • ◆No Asian pear? Use 1/4 cup unsweetened applesauce or half a ripe kiwi, but with kiwi cut the marinating time to 20 minutes because it tenderizes very aggressively.
  • ◆Make-ahead: the marinated beef freezes beautifully. Portion it flat in zip bags, freeze up to 3 months, and thaw overnight in the fridge so it marinates as it defrosts.
  • ◆Cook this on a grill or an outdoor burner if you can. Bulgogi puts out real smoke, and the extra char is exactly what you want.
  • ◆Leftovers make an excellent bibimbap or a bulgogi sandwich on a soft roll with mayo and quick-pickled cucumber.

Japchae Korean Glass Noodles⏱ 55 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Bouncy sweet potato noodles tossed with sesame, beef and a rainbow of vegetables cooked one at a time. It takes patience and it is worth every minute, warm or at room temperature.

KoreanPotluckMake Ahead
Prep
30 min
Cook
25 min
Total
55 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Noodles

Beef and marinade

Vegetables

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Marinate the beef
    Toss the beef strips with the 1 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tsp sesame oil, 1 tsp sugar and minced garlic, then set aside for 20 minutes while you prep the vegetables. The sugar helps the beef brown quickly and the sesame oil carries the flavor everywhere. Cut the strips no thicker than 1/4 in (6 mm) so they cook in about two minutes.
  2. Prep every vegetable first
    Slice the onion thin, cut the carrot into matchsticks about the size of the noodles, slice the mushrooms 1/4 in (6 mm) thick, and wash the spinach. Japchae is cooked component by component, so having each one in its own bowl before you turn on a burner keeps the whole process calm. Match the vegetable shapes to the noodle shape; long thin strands tangle together properly, while chunks fall to the bottom of the bowl.
  3. Blanch and squeeze the spinach
    Bring a medium pot of salted water to a boil, drop in the spinach for 30 seconds, then scoop it into a bowl of ice water. Once cool, gather it into a ball and squeeze out as much water as you physically can, then chop it roughly and season with 1/4 tsp of the salt and the 1 tsp toasted sesame oil set aside for the spinach. Wet spinach will dilute the sauce and make the noodles slippery, so squeeze harder than feels polite. Keep that pot of water boiling for the noodles.
  4. Cook the noodles precisely
    Boil the dangmyeon for 6 to 7 minutes, stirring often, until they are translucent and springy with no chalky white core. Taste one at 6 minutes; they should be chewy and bouncy, never soft. Drain and rinse briefly under cold water to stop the cooking, then cut through the pile two or three times with kitchen shears so they are manageable with chopsticks.
  5. Season the noodles while hot
    Return the drained noodles to the warm pot and toss immediately with the 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp sesame oil and 1 tbsp sugar. Hot noodles absorb seasoning the way a sponge does; cold ones just get coated on the outside. They should turn glossy and light amber. Set them aside, uncovered, so they do not steam themselves sticky.
  6. Cook the onion
    Heat 1 tsp of the neutral oil in a large skillet over medium-high heat, add the onion and a pinch of the salt, and cook for 2 to 3 minutes until softened and translucent at the edges. Tip it into the noodle bowl. Cooking each vegetable separately sounds fussy, but it is the entire technique: every ingredient needs a different amount of time, and cooking them together means mushy carrots and raw mushrooms.
  7. Cook the carrots
    Add another 1 tsp oil and the carrot matchsticks with a pinch of the salt, and stir-fry over medium-high for 2 minutes until they brighten to a vivid orange and just start to bend. They should still have a little snap when you bite one, because they will soften further sitting in the warm noodles and they are the only crunchy thing left in the finished bowl. Two minutes really is the whole window here; carrots cut this fine go from crisp to limp in another sixty seconds. Add them to the bowl with the onions.
  8. Cook the mushrooms
    Add 1 tbsp oil, then the shiitakes and a pinch of salt, and cook for 3 to 4 minutes without stirring much, until they release their water, it evaporates, and the edges brown. Mushrooms need a hot dry pan and patience; stirring constantly makes them steam in their own liquid and stay pale and squeaky. Add them to the bowl.
  9. Sear the beef
    Turn the heat to high, add the last of the oil, and spread the marinated beef in a single layer so every strip touches the pan. Cook 60 seconds without moving it, then toss for another 60 to 90 seconds until browned and cooked through; whole-muscle beef is safe at 145°F (63°C) and strips this thin sail past it in about two minutes, so brown edges and no red center are your cue. The sugar in the marinade browns fast, so keep it moving once you start tossing or it will scorch rather than caramelize. Scrape the beef and any pan juices into the bowl with everything else, because those juices are seasoning for the noodles.
  10. Toss it all together
    Add the noodles, spinach, the 1 tbsp sesame oil, 2 tbsp sesame seeds, sliced scallions and 1/2 tsp black pepper to the big bowl. Toss with clean hands or two large spoons for a full minute, lifting from the bottom, until the color is uniform amber-brown and no clumps of plain noodles remain. Hands genuinely work better than tongs here because you can feel the clumps.
  11. Taste and adjust
    Try a strand with a bit of everything on it. It should be sweet, savory and unmistakably sesame, with the noodles seasoned all the way through rather than just on the surface. Add soy sauce a teaspoon at a time if it is flat, or a pinch of sugar if it tastes sharp. Japchae is one of those dishes where the final seasoning check really matters.
  12. Serve warm or cool
    Pile it into a wide shallow bowl and serve warm, at room temperature, or cold from the fridge, all of which are traditional. Korean home cooks often make it hours ahead for parties, and it holds up better than almost any other noodle dish. It keeps 4 days refrigerated; loosen it with a splash of water and a few drops of sesame oil before reheating.
Know when it is done
Beef strips are safe at 145°F (63°C) and get there in roughly 2 minutes over high heat; pull them when browned outside and just cooked through. The noodles are ready when they are fully translucent with no white core and spring back against your teeth.
Serve it with
Serve alongside bulgogi or grilled fish with a side of kimchi, or eat it on its own with a cold barley tea.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Sweet potato starch noodles are not the same as mung bean vermicelli or rice vermicelli. Look for dangmyeon, which are thick, grayish and translucent when cooked, and do not substitute.
  • ◆Do not overcook the noodles. Six minutes is usually right and eight will leave you with mush; they keep softening as they sit in the seasoning.
  • ◆Make-ahead: japchae is genuinely better an hour after it is made, once the noodles have absorbed everything. It is the ideal potluck dish for exactly that reason.
  • ◆For a vegetarian version, skip the beef and add 8 oz (225 g) more mushrooms plus a thin egg omelet sliced into ribbons. Nobody will miss it.
  • ◆If the noodles clump in the fridge, run them briefly under warm water and toss with a teaspoon of sesame oil to bring them back.

Chicken Katsu with Tonkatsu Sauce⏱ 35 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Panko-crusted chicken cutlets fried until they shatter, sliced into strips and served with a tangy brown sauce you stir together in one bowl. It is the easiest way to make someone very happy on a Tuesday.

JapaneseWeeknightCrowd Pleaser
Prep
20 min
Cook
15 min
Total
35 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chicken

Breading and frying

Tonkatsu sauce

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Butterfly and pound the chicken
    Lay each breast flat and slice it horizontally almost all the way through, then open it like a book. Cover with plastic wrap and pound with a mallet or the flat of a heavy pan until it is an even 1/2 in (1 cm) thick all over. Even thickness is the whole ballgame: a cutlet that is thick at one end will either be raw in the middle or burnt at the thin edge.
  2. Season and rest
    Season both sides of each cutlet with the 1 1/2 tsp kosher salt and 1/2 tsp pepper and let them sit for 10 minutes at room temperature. The salt has time to penetrate rather than just sitting on the surface, and the chicken takes the chill off so it cooks evenly. Pat the surface dry with a paper towel right before breading.
  3. Stir the tonkatsu sauce
    Whisk the 1/2 cup ketchup, 3 tbsp Worcestershire, 2 tbsp oyster sauce, 1 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp sugar and 1 tsp Dijon in a bowl until smooth. Taste it: it should be tangy, sweet and deeply savory, somewhere between barbecue sauce and steak sauce. Refrigerate it while you cook, and know that it keeps for a month in a jar.
  4. Set up the breading station
    Put the flour in one shallow dish, the beaten eggs in a second, and the panko in a third, arranged left to right in that order. Season the flour with a pinch of salt. Designate one hand for dry and one for wet, which sounds fussy until you realize the alternative is breading your own fingers into clubs.
  5. Shred the cabbage now
    Slice the cabbage as thinly as you can, ideally on a mandoline, and drop it into a bowl of ice water for 10 minutes to crisp up. Drain and spin or pat it very dry. That mound of raw cabbage next to katsu is not garnish; the cold crunch cuts through the fried richness and it is genuinely part of the dish.
  6. Bread the cutlets
    Dredge a cutlet in flour and shake off all the excess, dip it in the egg and let it drip for a second, then press it firmly into the panko on both sides. Press hard enough that the crumbs stay put but do not crush them flat. Lay the breaded cutlets on a rack and let them sit 10 minutes so the coating hydrates and sets, which stops it sliding off in the oil.
  7. Heat the oil to 340°F
    Pour the 4 cups oil into a 12 in (30 cm) heavy skillet or Dutch oven, which gives you a depth of about 3/4 in (2 cm), and heat over medium-high to 340 to 350°F (170 to 175°C). Test it by dropping in a few panko crumbs: they should sizzle steadily and turn golden in about 15 seconds. Too hot and the crust browns before the chicken cooks; too cool and the coating drinks oil and goes greasy.
  8. Fry two at a time
    Slide two cutlets in away from you and fry for 3 to 4 minutes on the first side, until deep golden. Flip once with tongs and fry 2 to 3 minutes more. Do not crowd the pan or flip repeatedly; each flip knocks crumbs loose and drops the oil temperature. The sizzle should stay lively and steady the whole time, not fade to a whisper.
  9. Check the temperature
    Pull a cutlet and push an instant-read thermometer into the thickest part; it must read 165°F (74°C). At 1/2 in (1 cm) thick that usually lands right around 6 minutes of total frying. If it is under, return it to the oil for another minute rather than guessing.
  10. Drain on a rack
    Transfer the finished cutlets to a wire rack set over a sheet pan, never onto paper towels. A rack lets air circulate so the underside stays crisp, while paper towels trap steam and turn the bottom crust soggy within a minute. Sprinkle with a small pinch of salt while they are still hot and let the oil come back to temperature before the next pair.
  11. Slice and plate
    Let each cutlet rest 2 minutes, then slice crosswise into 3/4 in (2 cm) strips with a sharp knife, keeping the strips together so the cutlet holds its shape as you move it. Slicing before serving is the katsu way and it makes the whole thing eatable with chopsticks. Fan a cutlet on each plate with a mound of cold cabbage, a scoop of hot rice and a lemon wedge.
  12. Sauce at the table
    Pour a puddle of tonkatsu sauce beside the chicken or spoon it over the top just before eating, never earlier. Sauce sitting on panko softens it within a couple of minutes, and the contrast between the crunchy crust and the tangy sauce is the entire pleasure of the dish. Squeeze the lemon over the cabbage.
Know when it is done
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) at the thickest point, which takes about 6 minutes of total frying for a 1/2 in (1 cm) cutlet. Keep the oil between 340 and 350°F (170 to 175°C) so the panko browns at the same rate the chicken cooks.
Serve it with
Short-grain rice, a mound of icy shredded cabbage, and a cold Japanese lager or barley tea.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Panko is not optional. Regular breadcrumbs are dense and go soft, while panko flakes are large, airy and stay crisp much longer.
  • ◆Boneless pork loin chops pounded to the same thickness make classic tonkatsu. Cook them to 145°F (63°C) with a 3 minute rest instead of 165°F.
  • ◆Make-ahead: bread the cutlets up to 4 hours in advance and keep them on a rack in the fridge, uncovered. The drier surface actually fries up crisper.
  • ◆For katsu curry, serve the sliced cutlet over rice with Japanese curry sauce instead of tonkatsu sauce. It is one of the best comfort meals there is.
  • ◆Air fryer version: spray the breaded cutlets generously with oil and cook at 400°F (205°C) for 12 to 14 minutes, flipping once. Less shattering, still very good.

Pork and Cabbage Gyoza⏱ 1 hr 40 min🍽 Makes about 50 gyozaAdvanced▾

Juicy pork dumplings with lacy crisp bottoms and tender pleated tops, fried and steamed in the same pan. Make a big batch, freeze most of them, and you have dinner on standby forever.

JapaneseFreezer FriendlyWeekend Project
Prep
1 hr 15 min
Cook
25 min
Total
1 hr 40 min
Serves
Makes about 50 gyoza
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Filling

Wrappers and sealing

To cook

Dipping sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Salt and drain the cabbage
    Chop the napa cabbage as finely as you can, toss it with the 1 tsp kosher salt in a colander, and let it sit for 20 minutes. Then gather it in a clean kitchen towel and wring it out hard over the sink; you should squeeze out something like 1/2 cup of water. Cabbage is over 90 percent water, and any of it left behind will burst your dumplings open in the pan or turn the filling into slop.
  2. Mix the filling in one direction
    Combine the pork, squeezed cabbage, scallions, ginger, garlic, 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp sesame oil, 1 tbsp Shaoxing wine, 1 tsp sugar and 1/4 tsp white pepper in a bowl. Stir vigorously with chopsticks or a spatula in one direction only for 2 to 3 minutes, until the mixture turns sticky and tacky and starts to hold its shape. Mixing in a single direction aligns the meat proteins into a springy paste that stays juicy instead of crumbling.
  3. Test-fry a spoonful
    Take a teaspoon of the filling, flatten it into a small patty, and cook it in a skillet for 90 seconds per side until cooked through to 160°F (71°C). Taste it and adjust the whole batch with more salt, soy sauce or white pepper as needed. Nobody wants to discover a bland filling after folding fifty dumplings, and this thirty second test saves the entire batch.
  4. Chill the filling
    Cover the bowl and refrigerate the filling for at least 20 minutes while you set up. Cold fat is firm fat, which means the filling holds together as you fold and does not smear all over the wrappers. It also gives the seasonings time to distribute through the meat.
  5. Set up your folding station
    Lay out the stack of wrappers under a barely damp towel, the bowl of filling with a small spoon, the little bowl of water for sealing, and a parchment-lined sheet pan dusted with the 2 tbsp cornstarch. The cornstarch is what stops the wet dumpling bottoms from gluing themselves to the parchment while you fold the rest, so be generous rather than tidy about it. Work with five or six wrappers at a time and keep the rest covered, because exposed wrappers dry out in about two minutes and then crack instead of sealing. Set yourself up sitting down if you can, since fifty dumplings is a solid half hour of folding.
  6. Fill and pleat
    Hold a wrapper in your cupped palm, place a rounded teaspoon of filling in the center, and dip a fingertip in water to wet the top half of the rim. Fold it into a half-moon and pinch the center closed. Then make three or four small pleats along one side only, pressing each pleat against the flat back edge to seal. The pleats are what curve the dumpling into a crescent so it sits flat and stands upright in the pan.
  7. Seal and inspect
    Run your fingers along the seam of each finished dumpling and press firmly to make sure there are no gaps, then set it on the sheet pan with the flat bottom down and a little space around it. Overfilled dumplings burst while cooking, so if the wrapper is straining, use less filling. A rounded teaspoon really is the right amount even though it looks stingy at first.
  8. Freeze what you will not eat
    The quantities below cook two pans, about 26 dumplings, which feeds four people generously; freeze the rest on the sheet pan for 2 hours until solid, then transfer them to a zip bag. If you want to cook all fifty in one go, scale up to 1 tbsp of oil and 1/3 cup of the flour slurry for each additional pan. Frozen dumplings keep 3 months and go straight from freezer to pan with no thawing, just an extra 2 minutes of steaming. Never stack raw dumplings on top of each other, frozen or not, because they weld together and tear apart when you pry them loose.
  9. Mix the dipping sauce
    Stir the 1/4 cup soy sauce, 3 tbsp rice vinegar, 1 tsp chile oil and 1 tsp sesame oil together and divide it into small bowls. Gyoza sauce should lean sharply vinegary, since its job is to cut through rich pork. Set it on the table now so nothing waits once the dumplings come out.
  10. Arrange them in the pan
    Heat 1 tbsp of the oil in a 10 in (25 cm) nonstick skillet over medium heat until it shimmers, then arrange 12 to 14 dumplings flat side down in a tight spiral or rows, just touching. Fry undisturbed for 2 to 3 minutes, until the bottoms are deep golden brown. Lift one with a spatula to check rather than moving them all around.
  11. Steam with the flour slurry
    Whisk the flour-water slurry and pour about 1/3 cup (80 ml) into the pan, standing back because it will spit violently. Cover immediately and steam for 5 to 6 minutes for fresh dumplings or 7 to 8 for frozen, until the water is nearly gone and the wrappers look translucent. The flour in the water sets into a thin lacy sheet that fries crisp, which is the famous gyoza skirt.
  12. Crisp the skirt
    Uncover and let the pan cook 2 to 3 minutes more over medium heat, until every drop of liquid has evaporated and you hear the sizzle change from a wet spatter to a dry crackle. The skirt will turn golden and lift away from the pan on its own when it is ready. Do not rush this or the lace will tear and stick.
  13. Check and turn out
    Push a thermometer into the filling of one dumpling; ground pork must read 160°F (71°C). Slide a thin spatula under the whole sheet, then invert a plate over the pan and flip the dumplings out crisp side up in one piece. Serve immediately with the dipping sauce, and start the next batch while everyone eats.
Know when it is done
The ground pork filling must reach 160°F (71°C) at the center; check one dumpling with an instant-read thermometer before serving the batch. The wrappers are done when the tops are translucent and springy rather than chalky white, and the bottoms are deep mahogany.
Serve it with
A cold Japanese lager, a bowl of miso soup, and a sharp vinegary dipping sauce with extra chile oil.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Ground pork with real fat content matters. Lean pork makes dry, crumbly filling, so if your butcher only has lean, add 2 tbsp of finely chopped pork fat or a splash of neutral oil.
  • ◆Wrappers dry out fast. Keep the stack under a damp towel, and if one cracks while folding, patch it with a dab of water and press firmly rather than starting over.
  • ◆Make-ahead: this is the ultimate freezer recipe. Fold a double batch, freeze flat, and cook them straight from frozen with an extra 2 minutes under the lid.
  • ◆Use a nonstick pan for your first few batches. Stainless and cast iron both work but the skirt is much more likely to weld itself to the surface.
  • ◆Shrimp and chive is the other classic filling: swap in 1 lb (450 g) chopped shrimp and 1 cup minced garlic chives, keeping the rest of the seasoning the same.

Thai Green Curry with Chicken⏱ 35 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Coconut milk cracked in the pan with green curry paste until the oil separates, then simmered with chicken and basil. One pot, about half an hour, and it tastes like a restaurant.

ThaiOne PotWeeknight
Prep
10 min
Cook
25 min
Total
35 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Curry base

Seasoning

Vegetables and finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Do not shake the coconut milk
    Open both cans without shaking or stirring them and spoon the thick white cream off the top of one can into a wide pot or deep skillet, about 1/2 cup (120 ml). Full-fat coconut milk separates in the can into thick cream on top and thin water below, and that cream is the fat you are about to cook the paste in. Light coconut milk cannot do this, which is why every good Thai curry recipe insists on full fat.
  2. Crack the coconut cream
    Set the pot over medium heat and simmer the coconut cream for 3 to 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it thickens, sputters, and you can see clear oil pooling at the edges. This is called cracking the cream and it is the step nearly everyone skips. Frying the paste in coconut oil rather than boiling it in coconut water is what makes the difference between a flat curry and a fragrant one.
  3. Fry the curry paste
    Add 3 tbsp of the green curry paste and mash it into the hot cream with the back of your spoon, then fry for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring constantly. It should darken slightly, thicken into a glossy paste, and smell so strongly of lemongrass, galangal and chile that it makes your eyes water a bit. If it starts to catch on the bottom, lower the heat rather than adding liquid.
  4. Taste for heat
    Dip a spoon in and taste a tiny amount. Curry paste brands vary enormously in heat, so if yours is mild, add the last 1 tbsp now and fry it another minute. It should taste aggressively spicy at this stage, because two cans of coconut milk are about to mellow it substantially.
  5. Coat the chicken
    Add the sliced chicken and stir for 2 minutes so every piece is coated in the fried paste and the surfaces turn opaque. You are not browning it, just sealing the paste onto the meat so the flavor goes into the chicken instead of only floating in the sauce. Slicing the thighs 1/2 in (1 cm) thick keeps them juicy through the simmer.
  6. Add the rest of the coconut milk
    Pour in the remaining coconut milk from both cans, scraping the pot to loosen anything stuck. Bring it to a gentle simmer with small bubbles breaking the surface, never a hard rolling boil. Boiling coconut milk hard makes it split into grainy curds and an oil slick, and you cannot bring it back once that happens.
  7. Simmer with aromatics
    Add the torn makrut lime leaves, 2 tbsp fish sauce and 1 tbsp palm sugar, and simmer gently for 8 minutes. Tear the lime leaves rather than chopping them, so they release oil but are easy to spot and set aside on the plate. The sauce should reduce slightly and take on a pale sage green color.
  8. Cook the vegetables in order
    Add the eggplant first and simmer 4 minutes, then the bamboo shoots and bell pepper for a final 3 minutes. Eggplant needs the longest and turns creamy; the pepper should stay slightly crisp. Adding everything at once means either raw eggplant or dissolved pepper, so stagger them.
  9. Check the chicken and season
    Cut into the thickest piece of chicken or check with a thermometer; it must read 165°F (74°C) with no pink. Now taste the sauce properly. It should hit salty, sweet, spicy and a little sour all at once, so adjust with fish sauce for salt, palm sugar for balance, or a pinch of kosher salt.
  10. Finish with basil and lime
    Turn off the heat, stir in the 1 cup Thai basil and 1 tbsp lime juice, and let it sit 2 minutes so the leaves wilt in the residual heat. Adding the lime off the heat keeps its brightness, which simmering would cook straight out. Ladle over hot jasmine rice in shallow bowls and serve while the basil is still vivid green.
Know when it is done
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C). Keep the curry at a gentle simmer around 190°F (88°C) with small lazy bubbles, because a hard boil splits coconut milk into grainy curds and floating oil.
Serve it with
Jasmine rice, a cold Singha or a slightly sweet Riesling, and cucumber slices to cool the heat.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Maesri and Mae Ploy are the two paste brands worth seeking out, and both come in small cans for a couple of dollars. They are far more aromatic than the jarred supermarket versions.
  • ◆Full-fat coconut milk only. Light coconut milk will not crack, will not thicken, and produces a thin watery curry no matter how long you simmer it.
  • ◆Make-ahead: green curry is better on day two once the flavors settle. Reheat gently over low heat and add the basil and lime fresh each time.
  • ◆Swap the chicken for 1 1/2 lb (680 g) of shrimp added in the last 3 minutes, or 14 oz (400 g) of pressed tofu plus extra vegetables for a vegetarian pot.
  • ◆If the curry tastes flat, it almost always needs fish sauce rather than salt, and if it tastes harsh, a teaspoon more palm sugar will round it out.

Butter Chicken Murgh Makhani⏱ 2 hr 5 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Yogurt-marinated chicken charred under the broiler, then folded into a silky tomato and cream sauce finished with crushed fenugreek. It is rich, gentle and almost impossible to stop eating.

IndianComfort FoodMake Ahead
Prep
20 min
Cook
45 min
Total
2 hr 5 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chicken and marinade

Makhani sauce

To finish and serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Marinate the chicken
    Whisk the 1/2 cup yogurt, 1 tbsp lemon juice, 1 tbsp ginger, 4 minced garlic cloves, 2 tsp garam masala, 1 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp Kashmiri chile powder and 1 1/2 tsp salt in a large bowl, then fold in the chicken. Cover and refrigerate for at least 1 hour and up to 12. The lactic acid in yogurt tenderizes gently without turning the meat mushy the way a straight lemon marinade would, and it clings to the chicken so the spices actually stick.
  2. Start the sauce base
    Melt 2 tbsp of the butter in a heavy 5 qt (4.7 L) pot over medium heat, add the chopped onion and a pinch of salt, and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring often. You want the onion soft, translucent and just beginning to turn golden at the edges, not browned and crisp. This slow start builds the sweet foundation that makes butter chicken taste rounded rather than sharp.
  3. Bloom the aromatics and spices
    Add the 1 tbsp ginger and 4 minced garlic cloves and cook 90 seconds until fragrant, then stir in the 1 tsp Kashmiri chile powder and 2 tsp garam masala and cook 30 seconds more. Ground spices need fat and heat to release their oils, which is called blooming and takes well under a minute. Stir constantly here, because ground spices scorch and turn bitter almost instantly on a hot pot bottom.
  4. Add the tomatoes and simmer
    Pour in the can of whole tomatoes with their juice, crushing each one in your hand as it goes in, then add the 1 tsp sugar and 1 tsp salt. Simmer uncovered over medium-low for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce darkens to brick red and thickens noticeably. Whole canned tomatoes are consistently better than crushed or diced, which are firmed up with calcium chloride and never break down properly.
  5. Heat the broiler
    While the sauce simmers, set an oven rack about 6 in (15 cm) from the broiler element and turn the broiler to high. Line a sheet pan with foil and set a wire rack on top, then brush the rack with the 2 tbsp oil. The rack lets the marinade drip away so the chicken chars instead of poaching in its own liquid.
  6. Broil the chicken
    Shake the excess marinade off each piece and arrange the chicken on the rack with space between the pieces. Broil for 7 to 9 minutes, until the tops are charred in spots and blistered. This is standing in for a tandoor, and those blackened edges are a real flavor component, not an accident, so let them get properly dark.
  7. Flip and finish the chicken
    Turn each piece and broil another 5 to 6 minutes, then check the thickest piece with a thermometer; it must read 165°F (74°C). Pull the pan and let the chicken rest while you finish the sauce. Do not worry if it looks slightly dry, because it will spend the next ten minutes soaking in cream and butter.
  8. Blend the sauce smooth
    Take the tomato sauce off the heat and blend it with an immersion blender right in the pot, or in a countertop blender in two batches, until completely silky. Vent the blender lid and cover it with a towel, since hot liquid expands violently and will blow the lid off. Butter chicken should be smooth as velvet with no visible onion, which is what separates it from a rustic curry.
  9. Enrich with butter and cream
    Return the blended sauce to low heat, whisk in the remaining 2 tbsp butter one piece at a time, then stir in the 3/4 cup heavy cream. Keep the heat low and never let it boil, because dairy this rich will break into grainy specks and an oil slick. The sauce should turn from brick red to a warm terracotta orange.
  10. Add the fenugreek
    Crush the 1 tsp dried fenugreek leaves between your palms directly over the pot, which wakes up the aromatic oils. Kasoori methi is the maple-and-celery-like note you cannot identify in restaurant butter chicken, and there is no real substitute. Stir it in and simmer gently for 2 minutes.
  11. Fold in the chicken
    Add the broiled chicken and any juices from the sheet pan and simmer gently for 5 minutes so the pieces absorb the sauce and everything comes together. Taste and adjust with salt, a pinch of sugar if the tomatoes are sharp, or a splash of cream if it is too intense. The sauce should coat a spoon thickly but still pour.
  12. Rest, garnish and serve
    Take the pot off the heat and let it stand 5 minutes, which lets the sauce settle and thicken slightly. Scatter the chopped cilantro over the top and serve with warm naan or basmati rice. It reheats beautifully over low heat for 4 days, and honestly tastes even better the next day.
Know when it is done
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) at the thickest point after broiling, with charred blistered edges. Keep the finished sauce below a simmer, roughly 180°F (82°C), because boiling cream and butter will split the sauce into grainy curds.
Serve it with
Warm garlic naan for scooping, basmati rice, and a mango lassi or an off-dry Gewurztraminer.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Kashmiri chile powder brings deep red color with mild heat. If you only have cayenne, use 1/4 tsp cayenne plus 3/4 tsp sweet paprika to get the color without setting anyone on fire.
  • ◆Thighs, not breasts. Breast meat dries out under a broiler and in a long simmer, while thighs stay tender and forgiving.
  • ◆Make-ahead: the sauce can be made and blended up to 3 days ahead or frozen for 3 months. Broil the chicken fresh and combine the two just before serving.
  • ◆No broiler? Sear the marinated chicken in batches in a screaming hot cast iron skillet for 3 minutes per side. You want char, however you get it.
  • ◆Kasoori methi is sold at any Indian grocer and keeps for a year. It is the one ingredient here you should not skip, because it is the flavor people cannot name.

Chicken Tikka Masala⏱ 5 hr 20 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Charred spiced chicken in a warm, creamy tomato gravy with real backbone from toasted whole spices. Marinate it in the morning and dinner practically makes itself.

IndianMake AheadComfort Food
Prep
25 min
Cook
55 min
Total
5 hr 20 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Tikka marinade

Masala sauce

To finish and serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Build the marinade
    Whisk the 1 cup yogurt, 2 tbsp lemon juice, 2 tbsp ginger, 6 minced garlic cloves, 2 tsp cumin, 2 tsp paprika, 1 tsp turmeric, 1 tsp cayenne and 2 tsp salt in a large bowl until it is a uniform rust-orange paste. Use whole-milk yogurt, because low-fat versions are thin and watery and will slide off the chicken instead of clinging. It should be thick enough to coat a spoon heavily.
  2. Marinate for hours
    Add the chicken pieces and turn them until each one is thickly coated, then cover and refrigerate for at least 4 hours and ideally overnight. Yogurt tenderizes gently and slowly, so long marinating actually improves the texture rather than turning the surface to mush. Cutting the thighs into large 2 in (5 cm) pieces means they can char hard on the outside while staying juicy inside.
  3. Start the onions
    Heat the 3 tbsp ghee in a heavy 5 qt (4.7 L) pot over medium heat and add the diced onion with a pinch of salt. Cook for 10 to 12 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes, until deeply softened and golden brown at the edges. This is longer than you think it needs and it is the flavor foundation of the entire dish, so do not cut it short at five minutes.
  4. Bloom the ground spices
    Add the 2 tbsp ginger and 6 minced garlic cloves and cook 90 seconds, then add the 2 tsp coriander, 2 tsp cumin, 1 tbsp paprika and 2 tsp garam masala and stir constantly for 45 seconds. The pot will smell suddenly enormous and the spices will darken a shade. Ground spices burn in well under a minute at this heat, so have the tomatoes open and ready to go in.
  5. Add tomatoes and simmer
    Pour in the can of crushed tomatoes and the 1 1/2 tsp salt, scraping the bottom to lift every bit of stuck spice. Bring it to a simmer, then lower the heat and cook uncovered for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally. The sauce should darken from bright red to brick and thicken enough that a spoon dragged through leaves a trail for a second.
  6. Preheat the broiler
    Position an oven rack 6 in (15 cm) below the broiler element and heat the broiler to high for 5 minutes. Line a sheet pan with foil and fit a wire rack inside it. The rack matters: it lets the marinade drip away so the chicken blisters and chars rather than sitting in a puddle and steaming.
  7. Broil the chicken hard
    Shake the excess marinade off each piece and lay them out with at least 1/2 in (1 cm) of space between them. Broil for 8 to 10 minutes without opening the door, until the tops are blackened in spots. Those charred edges are the tikka part of tikka masala and they carry a smokiness the sauce cannot produce on its own, so be brave and let them go dark.
  8. Flip and check
    Turn each piece with tongs and broil for another 5 to 7 minutes. Check the largest piece with an instant-read thermometer; it must reach 165°F (74°C). Set the pan aside and do not discard the juices that collect in the foil, because they are pure concentrated flavor.
  9. Blend or leave rustic
    For a restaurant-smooth gravy, blend the tomato sauce with an immersion blender until silky, about 30 seconds. For a homestyle texture, leave it chunky with visible onion. Either is legitimate; blended sauces coat the chicken more evenly while rustic ones have more bite. If you use a countertop blender, vent the lid and work in batches, because hot liquid expands and can blow the top off.
  10. Add the cream
    Lower the heat and stir in the 1 cup heavy cream and 1 tbsp butter, whisking until the sauce turns a soft coral orange. Keep it below a simmer from here on, around 180°F (82°C), because boiling will curdle the cream into grainy flecks. Taste it now, before the chicken goes in, and correct the salt.
  11. Combine and simmer gently
    Add the broiled chicken along with every drop of juice from the sheet pan and simmer very gently for 8 to 10 minutes, uncovered. The chicken releases some of its marinade flavor into the gravy while it soaks the sauce up in return, and this exchange is what makes the finished dish taste unified rather than like two separate things. Stir a couple of times so nothing catches on the bottom.
  12. Finish and rest
    Stir in the 1 tsp lemon juice and half the cilantro, then take the pot off the heat and let it sit 10 minutes. That rest lets the sauce thicken and the flavors settle, and tikka masala genuinely improves in those ten minutes. Scatter the remaining cilantro over the top and serve over hot basmati rice with naan alongside.
Know when it is done
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) at the center of the largest piece, with blackened blistered edges from the broiler. Hold the finished sauce below a simmer, around 180°F (82°C), so the cream stays smooth instead of curdling.
Serve it with
Basmati rice, garlic naan, and a cold IPA or a chilled off-dry Riesling.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Marinate overnight if you possibly can. Four hours works, but twelve gives noticeably more tender, more deeply seasoned chicken.
  • ◆No broiler? Grill the chicken over high heat for 4 minutes per side, or sear it in a smoking hot cast iron skillet. The char is not optional flavor.
  • ◆Make-ahead: the sauce keeps 4 days refrigerated and freezes for 3 months without the cream. Add the cream when you reheat so it never gets boiled twice.
  • ◆Cayenne is the heat dial. One teaspoon is medium-warm; use 1/2 tsp for mild or 2 tsp if you want it to bite back.
  • ◆Skewer the marinated chicken and cook it over charcoal if you have a grill going. That is closest to a real tandoor and the difference is obvious.

1 Ingredients

Batch

Bones and meat

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Parboil the bones
    Put the bones and oxtail in a large stockpot, cover with cold water, and bring to a hard boil over high heat for 10 minutes. Gray foam and scum will rise to the top in alarming quantity. This step exists purely to purge blood and impurities, and it is the difference between a crystal clear pho broth and a cloudy murky one.
  2. Scrub the bones clean
    Dump the whole pot into the sink through a colander and rinse each bone under running water, scrubbing off any dark bits clinging to the surface. Scrub the pot itself clean too, because the residue sticks to the sides. Do not skip the scrubbing; leftover scum will cloud the broth all over again.
  3. Char the onions and ginger
    Set the onion halves and ginger cut side down directly on a gas burner over high flame, or under a broiler 4 in (10 cm) from the element, and cook 8 to 12 minutes until blackened in patches and soft. Turn them so several sides char. This charring is not optional decoration; it caramelizes sugars and adds the smoky sweetness that makes pho taste like pho. Rinse off any loose ash and set aside.
  4. Toast the spices
    Toast the 6 star anise, cinnamon stick, 6 cloves, 1 tbsp coriander seeds, 1 tsp fennel seeds and 3 black cardamom pods in a dry skillet over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking often, until intensely fragrant. Watch closely because they go from toasty to burnt fast, and burnt star anise will make six quarts of broth taste like ash. Tie them into a spice bag or a square of cheesecloth so you can fish them out later.
  5. Start the long simmer
    Return the scrubbed bones to the clean pot, add the 6 qt cold water, and bring it up to a bare simmer over medium heat, which takes about 30 minutes. Add the charred onion and ginger and the spice bag. Starting from cold water lets the proteins release slowly and rise as a raft you can skim, rather than clouding the broth all at once.
  6. Hold a bare simmer and skim
    Adjust the heat until you see only occasional lazy bubbles breaking the surface, roughly 195 to 205°F (90 to 96°C), and never let it reach a rolling boil. Skim the surface every 20 minutes for the first hour, then every 45 minutes after. A boiling pot emulsifies fat into the liquid and turns it permanently cloudy and greasy, and no amount of straining later will fix it.
  7. Add and remove the brisket
    Slide the brisket into the pot after the first hour of simmering and cook it for 90 minutes to 2 hours, until a fork slides in with little resistance. Pull it out, plunge it into a bowl of ice water for 10 minutes to stop the cooking and keep it from graying, then wrap and refrigerate. Cooling it firm makes it far easier to slice thin later.
  8. Simmer, then season
    Let the broth continue at that bare simmer for a total of 5 to 6 hours, topping up with hot water if the level drops below the bones. In the last hour, add the 3 tbsp fish sauce, the 1 oz rock sugar and 2 tsp salt. Seasoning late means you are salting a broth that has already reduced, so you do not overshoot and end up with something inedible.
  9. Strain and defat
    Pull out the bones and spice bag, then strain the broth through a fine mesh sieve lined with cheesecloth into a clean pot. Let it settle 10 minutes and skim the fat off the top with a wide spoon, or chill it and lift the solid cap off. Taste it now: it should be aromatic, savory and slightly sweet, and you should want to drink it plain from a mug.
  10. Slice the raw beef paper thin
    Freeze the eye of round for 30 minutes until firm, then slice it across the grain as thinly as you possibly can, ideally under 1/8 in (3 mm) so it is nearly translucent. Lay the slices flat on a plate and refrigerate until the moment you serve. Thin enough and the boiling broth cooks them through in seconds right in the bowl.
  11. Cook the noodles to order
    Bring a separate large pot of water to a boil and cook the rice noodles for 6 to 8 minutes according to the package, then drain. Cook them just before serving and portion them straight into bowls, because noodles that sit around clump into a solid mass. Never cook noodles in your broth; the starch they release will cloud six hours of careful work in about two minutes.
  12. Slice the brisket
    Take the chilled brisket out and slice it across the grain about 1/8 in (3 mm) thick, using your longest, sharpest knife in long drawing strokes rather than sawing. Cold meat slices cleanly where warm meat shreds and tears, which is the whole reason you chilled it hours ago. Look for the direction the fibers run and cut straight across them; brisket cut with the grain is stringy no matter how long it simmered. Arrange the slices with the raw eye of round on a platter along with everything else you need for assembly.
  13. Assemble the bowls
    Bring the strained broth back to a hard rolling boil, which is the one time boiling is correct. Divide the hot noodles among six large bowls, top each with sliced brisket and a layer of raw eye of round, then ladle 2 cups of furiously boiling broth over the top. The raw slices should go from red to gray-brown within about 20 seconds. If you would rather not serve barely-cooked beef, blanch the slices in the boiling broth for 30 seconds first so they reach 145°F (63°C).
  14. Garnish at the table
    Put the bean sprouts, Thai basil, lime wedges, sliced scallions, jalapenos and cilantro on a platter in the middle of the table so everyone builds their own bowl. Add herbs a few at a time as you eat rather than all at once, so they stay fresh and fragrant instead of wilting into the broth. Hoisin and sriracha belong in a small side dish for dipping the meat, not squeezed into the broth, though nobody will stop you.
Know when it is done
Hold the broth at 195 to 205°F (90 to 96°C) throughout the simmer, never a rolling boil. Brisket is tender around 195°F (91°C) internal, and the raw eye of round slices should be blanched to 145°F (63°C) if you want them fully cooked rather than just flashed in boiling broth.
Serve it with
A cup of the plain broth on the side, Vietnamese iced coffee afterward, and plenty of lime and herbs on the table.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆The parboil-and-scrub step is what separates homemade pho from restaurant pho. It takes fifteen minutes and it is the single highest-value thing you can do for clarity.
  • ◆Make-ahead: the broth is the whole project and it keeps 5 days refrigerated or 3 months frozen. Freeze it in quart containers and a bowl of pho is twenty minutes away any weeknight.
  • ◆Yellow rock sugar has a cleaner, less cloying sweetness than granulated. If you cannot find it, use 1 tbsp of granulated sugar instead.
  • ◆Ask the butcher for a mix of marrow bones and knuckle bones. Marrow gives richness and knuckles give collagen and body, and you want both.
  • ◆If your broth still comes out cloudy, the culprit is almost always heat. Keep it at a lazy bare simmer where a bubble breaks every second or two, not a bubbling boil.
