Mongolian Beef with Scallions⏱ 30 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Crisp cornstarch-coated beef in a dark, glossy soy and brown sugar glaze with a pile of scallions. Thirty minutes start to finish and it disappears faster than that.

Takeout at Home30 MinutesWeeknight
Prep
15 min
Cook
15 min
Total
30 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Beef

Sauce

To cook and serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Slice the flank steak
    Chill the flank steak in the freezer for 15 minutes so it firms up, then find the grain and cut straight across it into slices about 1/4 in (6 mm) thick. Angle your knife at roughly 45 degrees to get wider slices that hold more coating. Cutting against the grain shortens the muscle fibers, and with a lean cut like flank that is the only thing standing between tender and chewy.
  2. Dry the beef thoroughly
    Blot the slices with paper towels until they no longer feel wet, then season with the 1/2 tsp salt. Cornstarch will not adhere to a damp surface; it turns into a slimy paste that slides off in the oil. Two minutes of blotting here saves the entire texture of the dish.
  3. Coat in cornstarch
    Toss the beef with the 1/2 cup cornstarch in a large bowl until every slice is chalky white with no bare spots, then shake off the excess in a colander. A thin even coat fries into a crisp shell that grabs the sauce; a thick clumpy one goes gummy. Let the coated beef rest 10 minutes so the starch hydrates slightly and clings better.
  4. Mix the sauce
    Stir the 1/2 cup soy sauce, 1/2 cup water, 2/3 cup dark brown sugar, 1 tbsp ginger, 5 minced garlic cloves and 1/4 tsp red pepper flakes together in a bowl until the sugar mostly dissolves. It will look alarmingly sweet, and that is correct, since it reduces down to a balanced glaze. Low-sodium soy sauce matters here because you are reducing a half cup of it and regular soy would end up brutally salty.
  5. Set up your station
    Put the coated beef, sauce bowl, scallions and a wire rack set over a sheet pan all within arm's reach of the stove, along with a heatproof bowl for the used frying oil. Start the rice now if you have not, because it needs at least 15 minutes and this dish will not wait for it. From the moment the oil is hot this dish moves quickly and you will be using tongs with both hands. Keep a lid nearby too: it is the fastest way to smother a pan of oil if it ever gets away from you.
  6. Heat the frying oil
    Pour the 1 1/2 cups oil into a 12 in (30 cm) skillet or wok and heat over medium-high until it shimmers and a pinch of cornstarch dropped in sizzles immediately, about 350°F (175°C). This is shallow frying, not deep frying, so the oil only needs to come about 1/4 in (6 mm) up the pan, which is what that much oil gives you in a pan this wide. If the oil is not hot enough the coating absorbs it and turns greasy instead of crisping, so use a thermometer if you have one rather than guessing at the shimmer.
  7. Fry the beef in batches
    Lay a third of the slices in the oil in a single layer with space between them and fry for 60 to 90 seconds per side, until the edges are golden and the coating is set. Move them to the wire rack and repeat with the remaining beef. Crowding drops the oil temperature and the slices will stick together into a single mass, so three small batches beat one big one every time.
  8. Pour off the oil
    Carefully pour the frying oil into a heatproof bowl, leaving any browned bits behind, and wipe the pan with a paper towel if there is burnt cornstarch stuck to it. Return the pan to the heat with 1 tbsp of fresh oil. Cooking the sauce in old frying oil makes it heavy and greasy.
  9. Reduce the sauce
    Pour the sauce into the hot pan and bring it to a boil over medium-high heat, then let it bubble for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until it reduces by about a third and turns syrupy. Drag a spatula through it: the sauce should hold a clear line on the pan bottom for a second before flowing back. Watch it closely at the end, because sugar syrups go from perfect to burnt in under thirty seconds.
  10. Toss the beef in the glaze
    Add all the fried beef back to the pan and toss for 30 to 45 seconds, just until every slice is coated in dark shiny glaze. Do not linger here; the longer the crisp coating sits in liquid, the softer it gets, and thirty seconds past the mark is the difference between crunchy and soggy. The beef should look lacquered, not swimming, and there should be very little loose sauce pooling in the pan. If there is a puddle, lift the beef out with tongs and reduce the sauce another minute before tossing it back in.
  11. Finish with scallions and serve
    Add the scallions, toss twice, and kill the heat so they stay bright green with a little crunch. Scatter the 1 tsp sesame seeds over the top and serve immediately over hot jasmine rice with the pan sauce spooned around. Mongolian beef is at its best in the first five minutes, so get it to the table straight from the stove.
Know when it is done
Beef is safe at 145°F (63°C), and slices this thin get there within about 90 seconds per side in 350°F (175°C) oil. Go by the coating: pull the slices when the crust is golden and set, because overcooked flank turns tough no matter how it is sauced.
Serve it with
Steamed jasmine rice, quick-blanched broccoli, and a cold lager to cut the sweetness.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Flank is traditional, but skirt steak, sirloin or flat iron all work well. Any lean cut sliced thin against the grain is fine.
  • ◆Use low-sodium soy sauce. This sauce reduces significantly and regular soy sauce will make the finished dish nearly inedible.
  • ◆The sauce is very sweet by design. If you prefer it more savory, cut the brown sugar to 1/2 cup and add 1 tbsp of rice vinegar at the end.
  • ◆Make-ahead: slice and coat the beef up to 2 hours ahead and keep it on a rack in the fridge. Mix the sauce up to 3 days ahead.
  • ◆Broccoli or snow peas make this a full meal. Blanch 8 oz (225 g) for 2 minutes and toss them in with the scallions.

Beef Bibimbap with Crispy Rice⏱ 1 hr 15 min🍽 4 servingsAdvanced▾

A bowl of seasoned vegetables, marinated beef and a fried egg over rice that crackles against a hot pan. You stir it all together with gochujang and it becomes something entirely new.

KoreanWeekend ProjectMake Ahead
Prep
45 min
Cook
30 min
Total
1 hr 15 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Beef and marinade

Namul vegetables

Bibimbap sauce

Rice and eggs

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Marinate the beef
    Toss the sliced beef with the 2 tbsp soy sauce, 1 tbsp sesame oil, 1 tbsp brown sugar, 3 minced garlic cloves and 1/2 tsp black pepper, then refrigerate for 30 minutes while you prepare everything else. Slicing the beef at 1/8 in (3 mm) means it takes on the marinade quickly and cooks in about two minutes. If the meat is hard to slice, freeze it for 20 minutes first.
  2. Understand namul
    Each vegetable in bibimbap is cooked and seasoned separately, which is the technique called namul. Set out five small bowls, one per vegetable, and keep them separate all the way to the table. It sounds like extra work but it is the entire point: every component tastes distinctly of itself, and stirring them together at the last second is what makes the bowl interesting rather than muddy.
  3. Blanch and season the spinach
    Boil a medium pot of salted water, drop in the spinach for 30 seconds, then transfer it to ice water. Squeeze it into a tight ball and wring out every bit of water you can, then chop it and toss with 1/2 tsp sesame oil, a pinch of the salt and a third of the minced garlic. Wet spinach will leak into the rice and make the bottom soggy, so squeeze it harder than seems reasonable.
  4. Blanch the bean sprouts
    Using the same pot of boiling water, cook the mung bean sprouts for 2 minutes, then drain and rinse under cold water. Squeeze them gently and toss with 1/2 tsp sesame oil, a pinch of salt and another third of the garlic. They should stay crunchy, since raw sprouts taste grassy but overcooked ones go limp and sad.
  5. Saute the carrots
    Heat 1 tsp of the sesame oil in a skillet over medium-high, add the carrot matchsticks and a pinch of salt, and cook for 2 minutes until they turn bright orange and just start to soften. Tip them into their bowl. Cook the vegetables in order from lightest to darkest so you do not have to wash the pan between each one.
  6. Saute the zucchini
    Add another 1 tsp sesame oil, then the zucchini matchsticks and a pinch of salt, and cook 2 minutes until barely tender and still bright green. Zucchini is mostly water and will turn to mush in another minute, so pull it early. Salt it lightly, because it releases water as it sits.
  7. Brown the mushrooms
    Add 1 tbsp sesame oil, then the sliced shiitakes and a pinch of salt, and cook 4 to 5 minutes without stirring much, until they release their liquid, it cooks off, and the edges brown. Stir in the last of the garlic for the final 30 seconds. Mushrooms need a hot pan and patience; constant stirring keeps them pale and squeaky.
  8. Cook the beef
    Wipe the skillet, turn the heat to high, and spread the marinated beef in a single layer. Cook 60 seconds without touching it, then toss for 60 to 90 seconds more until browned and just cooked through. Beef is safe at 145°F (63°C) and slices this thin race past it, so pull them the moment the edges caramelize.
  9. Mix the gochujang sauce
    Whisk the 3 tbsp gochujang, 1 tbsp sesame oil, 1 tbsp water, 1 tbsp sugar, 1 tbsp rice vinegar and the grated garlic clove until smooth and pourable. Taste it: it should be spicy, sweet and tangy in about equal measure. This sauce is what unifies the whole bowl, so make more than you think you need and put extra on the table.
  10. Crisp the rice
    Heat 1/2 tbsp of sesame oil in a small nonstick or cast iron skillet over medium heat, add 1 cup of the hot rice, and press it into an even layer. Cook undisturbed for 4 to 5 minutes until you hear a steady crackling and the bottom is golden and crisp. Slide it into a warmed bowl crust side down and repeat for each serving. If you own a stone dolsot, oil it and heat it to about 400°F (205°C) instead, then press the rice in.
  11. Fry the eggs sunny side up
    Heat the 1 tbsp neutral oil in a nonstick skillet over medium heat and crack in the eggs. Cook 2 to 3 minutes until the whites are fully set and opaque but the yolks are still liquid, spooning a little hot oil over the whites to help them along. The runny yolk becomes part of the sauce when you stir the bowl, which is exactly the point.
  12. Arrange the bowls
    Over each bowl of crisped rice, arrange the seasoned vegetables and beef in separate wedges around the edge like spokes on a wheel, keeping the colors next to each other for contrast. Set a fried egg in the center. Take a moment with this, because the arrangement is genuinely part of the dish and it only stays pretty for about a minute.
  13. Garnish and serve hot
    Scatter the 2 tbsp sesame seeds and the nori strips over the top and bring the bowls to the table with the gochujang sauce alongside. Serve immediately while the bottom rice is still crackling. Bibimbap loses its magic if it sits, so this is a dish you plate and carry straight out.
  14. Stir it all together
    At the table, everyone adds a heaping spoonful of gochujang sauce and stirs the whole bowl vigorously with a spoon until the yolk, sauce, rice and vegetables are completely combined. Bibimbap literally means mixed rice, and the mixing is not optional. Scrape the crispy rice up from the bottom as you go so those toasted bits get distributed through every bite.
Know when it is done
Beef slices are safe at 145°F (63°C) and reach it in about 2 minutes over high heat; pull them the moment the edges caramelize. Fried eggs with fully set whites and runny yolks sit around 145°F (63°C), so use pasteurized eggs or cook them through to 160°F (71°C) if anyone at the table should avoid soft yolks.
Serve it with
A small bowl of kimchi, a cold Korean lager or barley tea, and extra gochujang sauce on the table.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Cook every vegetable separately even though it feels excessive. Together they steam into a single flavor, and the whole appeal of bibimbap is that each bite is slightly different.
  • ◆Make-ahead: all the namul vegetables can be made up to 3 days in advance and kept in separate containers. Then a bowl of bibimbap is a 15 minute dinner.
  • ◆For a runny yolk with less risk, use pasteurized eggs, or cook the eggs to 160°F (71°C) with a set yolk if anyone eating is pregnant, elderly or immunocompromised.
  • ◆A stone dolsot bowl gives you the best crust, but a small cast iron skillet or a nonstick pan gets you eighty percent of the way there.
  • ◆Leftover bulgogi, roast chicken or a can of drained tuna all work in place of the marinated beef. Bibimbap started as a way to use up side dishes.

This is the chapter for cold nights and slow Sundays — the pots that fill the apartment with smell for three hours and then feed you twice, because almost every one of these tastes better the next day.

Texas Red Chili con Carne⏱ 4 hr🍽 6 servingsAdvanced▾

No beans, no tomatoes, no filler — just cubes of beef chuck simmered until they collapse in a sauce built from whole dried chiles you toast and blend yourself. It tastes like nothing that comes out of a spice packet.

Weekend ProjectDutch OvenMake Ahead
Prep
30 min
Cook
3 hr 15 min
Total
4 hr
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chile paste

The chili

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Open and clean the chiles
    Tear the stem end off each of the 6 anchos, 4 guajillos, and the 2 chiles de arbol if you want real heat, split each one open along one side, and shake out the seeds and any pale veins. The seeds carry bitterness rather than useful flavor, and the veins are where most of the raw burn hides, so removing them lets you control the heat with the arbols instead. Work over a plate or a sheet pan because dried chiles shed like autumn leaves. Wash your hands afterward and keep them away from your eyes for the next hour.
  2. Toast the chiles
    Set a dry 12 in (30 cm) skillet over medium heat and press the chiles flat against it, 20 to 30 seconds per side. They should puff slightly, turn a shade lighter, and smell like raisins and cocoa. The instant you smell anything sharp or acrid, they have gone too far — burnt chile makes the entire pot bitter and there is no fixing it, so pull them early rather than late.
  3. Steep and blend the paste
    Put the toasted chiles and the 4 garlic cloves in a bowl, pour over the 3 cups (720 ml) boiling water, and press a small plate on top to keep them submerged for 20 minutes until fully soft and floppy. Transfer everything, soaking liquid included, to a blender with the 1 tbsp vinegar and blend on high for a full 2 minutes. You want it as smooth as tomato sauce; if your blender leaves flecks, push it through a fine mesh sieve with a ladle. This deep red puree is the entire backbone of the dish.
  4. Cut and salt the beef
    Trim the big knobs of hard fat off the chuck but leave the thin marbling and connective tissue — that collagen melts into gelatin and gives the chili its body. Cut the meat into 3/4 in (2 cm) cubes, which stay distinct after three hours instead of shredding into mush. Toss with 2 tsp of the kosher salt and let it sit for 15 minutes while you heat the pot. Then pat the surface dry with paper towels, because wet meat steams and never browns.
  5. Brown the beef in batches
    Heat the 2 tbsp tallow in a 6 qt (5.7 L) Dutch oven over medium-high until it shimmers and a test cube sizzles hard on contact. Add about a third of the beef in a single layer with space between the cubes and do not touch it for 3 minutes. Crowding the pan drops the temperature and traps steam, which is the single most common reason chili tastes flat. Brown each batch on two sides only, 5 to 6 minutes total, and move it to a bowl.
  6. Read the fond
    Look at the bottom of the pot: those dark brown stuck-on patches are fond, the browned proteins and sugars that carry most of the meaty flavor in this recipe. It should be the color of strong coffee, not black. If any spot looks genuinely burnt, lower the heat and add a splash of broth right now to lift it before it scorches further. Everything from here on is about dissolving that fond into the sauce.
  7. Cook the onion
    Drop the heat to medium, add the diced onion and the remaining 1/2 tsp salt, and cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring and scraping constantly. The water the onions release does the work for you — it loosens the fond and turns the whole pot mahogany. Cook until the onions are soft and translucent with browned edges, not raw and crunchy.
  8. Bloom the spices
    Add the 1 tbsp cumin and 2 tsp Mexican oregano and stir for 45 to 60 seconds, until they smell warm and toasty. Ground spices are fat soluble, so this brief fry in the hot beef fat pulls out flavor that would stay locked up if you just dumped them into liquid. Do not walk away — ground cumin scorches in under two minutes.
  9. Build the pot
    Pour in the chile puree and the 2 cups (480 ml) beef broth, add the brown sugar, and return the beef with every drop of juice from the bowl. Scrape the bottom of the pot hard with a wooden spoon until it is completely clean and the liquid is uniformly dark red. The liquid should just barely cover the meat; add a splash more broth if it does not. Bring it to a simmer, then immediately turn it down.
  10. Simmer low and slow
    Adjust the heat until you see a lazy bubble breaking the surface every second or two — around 200°F (93°C), never a rolling boil. Cover with the lid slightly ajar and cook for 2 1/2 to 3 hours, stirring every 30 minutes and scraping the bottom so nothing catches. A hard boil squeezes the muscle fibers tight and makes the beef stringy; a bare simmer melts the collagen and leaves the cubes silky. Add broth 1/2 cup (120 ml) at a time if it ever looks dry.
  11. Test the beef
    Fish out a cube and press it against the side of the pot with the back of a spoon. It should crush with light pressure and feel tender all the way through, which usually happens between 2 1/2 and 3 hours. If it still springs back or feels tight, it is not done — undercooked chuck is tough, and the only cure is more time. Keep simmering and check again in 20 minutes.
  12. Thicken with masa harina
    Whisk the 2 tbsp masa harina with 1/4 cup (60 ml) water in a small bowl until smooth with no lumps, then stir it into the pot. Simmer uncovered for 10 more minutes so the corn cooks out and stops tasting raw. Masa is the traditional Texas thickener and it adds a faint toasted tortilla flavor that cornstarch cannot. The chili should coat a spoon and hold a line when you drag your finger through it.
  13. Balance and rest
    Taste and adjust: add salt in 1/4 tsp increments if it tastes muted, or a teaspoon of vinegar if it tastes heavy and flat. Let the pot sit off the heat for 15 minutes before serving so the fat rises and can be skimmed with a spoon. Serve in warm bowls with diced white onion, cilantro, a lime wedge, and cheese on top. It is genuinely better on day two, so make extra.
Know when it is done
Beef chuck is safe at 145°F (63°C), but it only becomes tender around 200-205°F (93-96°C) internal, when the collagen has melted. Hold the pot at a bare simmer near 200°F (93°C) and judge by feel: a cube should crush against the side of the pot with light pressure.
Serve it with
Cold Mexican lager with lime, or an unoaked red like Zinfandel, plus a stack of warm corn tortillas or a wedge of skillet cornbread.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Anchos bring raisiny sweetness and guajillos bring bright tang — that combination is why the sauce tastes layered. If you can only find one, use 8 anchos and add an extra teaspoon of vinegar at the end.
  • ◆Make it two days ahead. Cool it uncovered for 30 minutes, refrigerate, then lift the solid fat cap off the top before reheating gently over medium-low.
  • ◆Real Texas red never sees beans or tomatoes, but if you want to stretch it, serve it over pinto beans or rice instead of stirring them in.
  • ◆If the finished chili tastes bitter, one of the chiles scorched during toasting. A tablespoon of brown sugar and a splash of vinegar will mask a little of it, but the real fix is toasting more gently next time.
  • ◆Freeze in 2 cup (480 ml) portions for up to 3 months. Thaw overnight in the fridge and reheat with a splash of broth to loosen it.

Classic Beef Chili with Beans⏱ 2 hr 30 min🍽 8 servingsMedium▾

The chili everyone actually wants at a football game — thick, deeply savory, loaded with beans, and built on browned beef and toasted spices instead of a seasoning packet. One pot, two hours, feeds a crowd.

Crowd PleaserOne PotMake Ahead
Prep
20 min
Cook
1 hr 55 min
Total
2 hr 30 min
Serves
8 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the chili

Liquid and beans

Toppings

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Brown the beef in two batches
    Heat the 1 tbsp oil in a 6 qt (5.7 L) Dutch oven over medium-high until it shimmers. Add half the ground beef, press it into a flat layer, sprinkle with 1/2 tsp of the salt, and leave it completely alone for 4 minutes. You are looking for a genuine brown crust on one side before you break it up, which is where most of the flavor in this pot comes from. Break it into chunks, cook 2 minutes more, and move it to a bowl. Repeat with the second half of the beef and another 1/2 tsp of the salt, which leaves you 1 tsp of the 2 tsp for the vegetables.
  2. Drain but keep the fat
    Tip the pot and spoon out all but about 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the rendered fat. That remaining fat carries fat-soluble flavor from the spices you are about to add, so do not drain it bone dry. Look at the bottom of the pot — the sticky brown patches are fond, and they are pure concentrated beef flavor waiting to be dissolved.
  3. Build fond with the vegetables
    Lower the heat to medium and add the onion, bell pepper, and remaining 1 tsp salt. Cook 7 to 9 minutes, stirring and scraping the bottom, until the onions are translucent and the pot bottom has gone from crusty to clean. The moisture from the vegetables is doing the deglazing for you; every brown streak you scrape up is flavor moving from the pan into the chili. Add the garlic and jalapeno and cook 1 minute more.
  4. Toast the tomato paste
    Push the vegetables to the side, add the 3 tbsp tomato paste to the bare spot, and let it fry undisturbed for 90 seconds. It will darken from bright red to brick and smell sweeter and less tinny. This step cooks off the raw canned edge and builds the savory depth that separates good chili from watery chili. Stir it into the vegetables once it darkens.
  5. Bloom the spices
    Add the chili powder, cumin, smoked paprika, oregano, and cinnamon and stir constantly for 45 to 60 seconds. The pot will look almost dry and the kitchen will smell dramatically stronger — that is the fat pulling flavor compounds out of the ground spices. Do not let it go past a minute or the chili powder will turn bitter.
  6. Deglaze and combine
    Pour in the 2 cups (480 ml) beef broth and scrape the bottom of the pot hard with a wooden spoon until nothing is stuck. Add the crushed tomatoes, Worcestershire, cocoa powder, and the browned beef with all its juices. The cocoa will not make it taste like chocolate; it adds a bitter-dark backbone the way it does in mole. Stir everything together and bring it up to a simmer.
  7. Simmer partly covered
    Set the lid slightly ajar and adjust the heat until the surface bubbles lazily every second or so, around 200°F (93°C). Cook for 1 hour, stirring every 20 minutes and scraping the bottom so the tomato does not scorch. A hard boil will make the beef grainy and the chili will taste harsh, so keep it gentle. The color should deepen from bright red to brick brown.
  8. Add the beans
    Stir in the drained kidney and pinto beans and simmer uncovered for 25 to 30 more minutes. Adding them late keeps them intact instead of blowing apart into paste, and the uncovered simmer lets the chili reduce and thicken. It is ready when a spoon dragged across the bottom leaves a trail that fills in slowly.
  9. Balance the seasoning
    Turn off the heat and stir in the 2 tsp cider vinegar, then taste. Acid is what makes a long-simmered pot taste bright instead of muddy, so do not skip it. If it tastes sharp or too acidic, add the 1 tbsp brown sugar; if it tastes flat, add salt 1/4 tsp at a time until the flavors snap into focus.
  10. Rest and serve
    Let the pot sit off the heat for 15 minutes so it thickens and the flavors settle, then skim any orange fat pooled on top. Ladle into warm bowls and top with grated cheddar, sour cream, scallions, and a squeeze of lime. Put the toppings on the table so everyone can build their own.
Know when it is done
Ground beef must reach 160°F (71°C) to be safe, which it passes easily during browning and the long simmer. Keep the pot at a bare simmer around 200°F (93°C) — hotter than that and the meat turns grainy.
Serve it with
Cold amber ale or a big Zinfandel, with buttered cornbread or a bag of Fritos for scooping.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Grate the cheddar off a block yourself. Pre-shredded cheese is coated in cellulose and starch, so it sits in clumps on the chili instead of melting into it.
  • ◆Chili is better on day two, full stop. Cool it, refrigerate overnight, and reheat over medium-low with a splash of broth — the spices soften and marry.
  • ◆For a thicker pot without more simmering, mash about 1/2 cup (90 g) of the beans against the side with a fork before stirring them in.
  • ◆Swap the ground beef for 2 lb (900 g) of ground turkey if you want it leaner, but add 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil since there is no rendered fat to carry the spices.
  • ◆Freezes beautifully for 3 months. Freeze it flat in a zip bag so it thaws in 20 minutes in a bowl of cold water.

White Chicken Chili⏱ 1 hr 20 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Creamy without being heavy, green and bright from poblanos and lime, thickened by mashed white beans instead of flour. It comes together in about an hour and it is the one people always ask for the recipe to.

WeeknightOne PotCreamy
Prep
20 min
Cook
1 hr
Total
1 hr 20 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the chili

Liquid and finish

Toppings

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Season and sear the chicken
    Pat the thighs dry and season all over with 1 1/2 tsp of the kosher salt. Heat the 1 tbsp oil in a 5 to 6 qt (4.7 to 5.7 L) Dutch oven over medium-high until it shimmers, then lay in the thighs without crowding, working in two batches if needed. Sear 4 minutes per side until golden — you are not cooking them through, just building browned flavor and fond in the pot. Move them to a plate; they will finish in the broth.
  2. Soften the poblanos
    Lower the heat to medium and add the diced poblanos and onion with the remaining 1/2 tsp salt. Cook 8 to 10 minutes, stirring often, until the peppers have lost their raw grassy edge and the onions are translucent with golden edges. Scrape the browned chicken bits off the bottom as the vegetables release moisture. Poblanos are mild and smoky rather than hot, and they are what makes this taste like chili instead of chicken soup.
  3. Add garlic and jalapeno
    Stir in the 5 minced garlic cloves and the minced jalapeno and cook for 60 to 90 seconds, just until fragrant. Garlic burns fast at this heat and turns acrid, so keep it moving and do not let it brown past pale gold. Going in now rather than with the onions matters — garlic has almost no water and would scorch long before the poblanos softened. If the pot looks dry, add a tablespoon of oil so the garlic fries rather than sticks.
  4. Bloom the spices
    Add the cumin, coriander, oregano, and cloves and stir constantly for 45 seconds. The residual fat in the pot pulls the flavor out of the ground spices, which is why this smells five times stronger than it did straight from the jar. The clove sounds odd but it gives white chili the warm background note that makes it taste finished.
  5. Mash some of the beans
    Put 1 can worth of the drained beans in a bowl with 1 cup (240 ml) of the chicken broth and mash them to a rough paste with a fork or potato masher. This is your thickener — bean starch gives a creamy body without any flour or cornstarch, and it will not break when reheated. Leave the other two cans whole for texture.
  6. Build the pot
    Pour the remaining 3 cups (720 ml) broth into the pot and scrape the bottom completely clean. Add the mashed bean mixture, the whole beans, and the can of green chiles, then return the seared chicken with any juices from the plate. Bring it to a gentle simmer, lower the heat, and cover partially.
  7. Simmer until the chicken is done
    Simmer for 20 to 25 minutes at a lazy bubble, stirring occasionally so the beans do not catch on the bottom. Check the thickest thigh with an instant-read thermometer — chicken is safe and, more importantly, shreddable at 165°F (74°C), and thighs stay juicy even up to 185°F (85°C). Do not let it boil hard or the beans will break down into mush.
  8. Shred the chicken
    Lift the thighs onto a cutting board and shred them with two forks into bite-sized pieces, discarding any large lumps of fat. Return the meat and any collected juices to the pot. Shredding rather than cubing gives every spoonful chicken instead of leaving it hiding in chunks.
  9. Temper in the dairy
    Turn the heat to low. Ladle about 1 cup (240 ml) of the hot broth into a bowl with the cubed cream cheese and sour cream and whisk until smooth, then stir that mixture back into the pot. Adding cold dairy straight into a hot pot makes it curdle into grainy specks; warming it first with a little broth prevents that. Never let the pot boil again after this point.
  10. Finish and serve
    Stir in the cilantro and the 2 tbsp lime juice off the heat, then taste and add salt 1/4 tsp at a time until it tastes bright rather than dull. Let it sit 5 minutes to thicken. Serve in warm bowls topped with Monterey Jack, avocado, crushed tortilla chips, and an extra lime wedge on the side.
Know when it is done
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part of the thigh, checked with an instant-read thermometer. Once the dairy goes in, hold the pot below 190°F (88°C) so it never boils and separates.
Serve it with
A crisp Sauvignon Blanc or a Mexican lager with lime, and warm flour tortillas for wiping the bowl.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Chicken thighs are the right call here — breasts go dry and stringy over a 25 minute simmer, while thighs stay tender well past 165°F (74°C).
  • ◆No poblanos at the store? Use 2 diced green bell peppers plus an extra can of green chiles for that mild roasted flavor.
  • ◆This is the one chili that does not love the freezer, because the dairy can separate. Make the base through the shredding step and freeze that, then add the cream cheese and sour cream fresh when you reheat.
  • ◆If it ends up thinner than you want, mash more beans against the side of the pot with a spoon rather than adding cornstarch.
  • ◆Leftovers thicken hard in the fridge overnight. Loosen with 1/4 cup (60 ml) broth per bowl and reheat over medium-low, never boiling.

French Onion Soup⏱ 2 hr 5 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Three pounds of onions cooked down for a full hour into something jammy and sweet, floated with a toasted baguette raft and broiled under a blanket of Gruyere. There is no shortcut, and it is worth every minute.

Date NightClassic FrenchCheesy
Prep
20 min
Cook
1 hr 45 min
Total
2 hr 5 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

The onions

The soup

The cheese toast

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Slice the onions correctly
    Trim the root and top, halve each onion through the root, peel, then lay it flat and slice pole to pole into 1/8 in (3 mm) strips, following the natural lines. Slicing with the grain this way keeps the strands intact through an hour of cooking instead of dissolving into fluff. You will have a mountain of onions — about 12 cups — and it will look like far too much. It cooks down to roughly 2 cups, so trust it.
  2. Start them hot and covered
    Melt the 4 tbsp butter with the 1 tbsp olive oil in a wide 6 qt (5.7 L) Dutch oven over medium-high heat, add all the onions and the 1 1/2 tsp salt, and stir to coat. Cover and cook for 15 minutes, stirring twice. The salt pulls water out and the lid traps steam, which collapses the pile down to a manageable level and softens every strand before browning starts.
  3. Uncover and settle in
    Take the lid off, stir in the 1/2 tsp sugar, and drop the heat to medium-low. From here you need 45 to 60 minutes of actual caramelization, stirring every 5 minutes. Anyone who tells you onions caramelize in 10 minutes is describing onions that are merely soft and a little brown — real caramelization takes an hour, and there is no way around it.
  4. Watch the color stages
    The onions will move through clear stages: pale and wet at 20 minutes, golden and shrinking at 35 minutes, honey-colored and jammy at 45 minutes, and finally deep russet brown at 55 to 60 minutes. Listen as much as you look — a steady quiet sizzle is right, while sharp crackling or any wisp of smoke means the heat is too high. If they are browning unevenly, your burner has hot spots; stir more often and rotate the pot.
  5. Deglaze with water, again and again
    Every 10 minutes or so, a brown glaze will build on the bottom of the pot — that is fond, caramelized onion sugar, and it is the flavor you are actually after. Splash in 1/4 cup (60 ml) of the water and scrape it up with a wooden spoon until the bottom is clean and the onions absorb the color. Repeat this three or four times over the hour, using up the full 1 cup (240 ml) of water. Each round makes the onions a shade darker and the finished soup deeper.
  6. Deglaze with sherry
    When the onions are uniformly deep brown and jammy, pour in the 1/2 cup (120 ml) sherry and scrape one final time. Let it bubble hard for 2 to 3 minutes until the raw alcohol smell burns off and the liquid has mostly reduced. Sherry is traditional and its nuttiness suits caramelized onions better than wine, but a dry white works if that is what you have.
  7. Add stock and simmer
    Pour in the 8 cups (1.9 L) beef stock, add the thyme bundle and 2 bay leaves, and bring to a simmer. Cook uncovered at a gentle bubble for 30 minutes so the broth reduces slightly and picks up the onion sweetness. Skim any foam that gathers at the edges. This is also when a weak store-bought stock reveals itself, so taste and simmer 10 minutes longer if it seems thin.
  8. Season the finished soup
    Fish out the thyme bundle and bay leaves. Stir in the 1 tsp sherry vinegar and 1/2 tsp black pepper, then taste and add salt 1/4 tsp at a time. The vinegar is small but crucial — it cuts the heavy sweetness and makes the soup taste like broth rather than syrup. It should taste rich, savory, and just barely sweet.
  9. Toast the bread
    Heat the oven to 400°F (205°C), brush both sides of the baguette slices with the 1 tbsp olive oil, and bake on a sheet pan for 8 to 10 minutes, flipping once, until dry and crisp all the way through. Soft bread turns to sludge the second it hits the soup, so it needs to be crouton-dry, not just warm. Day-old bread works better than fresh for exactly this reason.
  10. Fill and top the bowls
    Set four broiler-safe crocks or oven-safe bowls on a sheet pan and ladle the hot soup in, leaving 1 in (2.5 cm) of headroom. Float two toasts on each, edges touching so they form a raft, then pile the grated Gruyere and Parmigiano over the top and out to the rim of the bowl. Cheese that touches the rim melts onto the edge and gives you that crown of browned cheese to pull at.
  11. Broil until bubbling
    Set an oven rack 6 in (15 cm) below the broiler element, turn the broiler to high — around 500°F (260°C) at the element — and broil the bowls for 3 to 5 minutes. Do not walk away — cheese goes from bubbling to burnt in under 30 seconds. You want the surface molten with dark blistered spots. Let the crocks rest 5 minutes before serving; the soup underneath is well over 200°F (93°C) and will scald a mouth.
Know when it is done
The onions are done when they are uniformly deep russet brown and jammy after 45-60 minutes, not merely golden. Broil at 500°F (260°C) for 3-5 minutes and serve the soup hot at 190-200°F (88-93°C), resting 5 minutes so no one burns their mouth.
Serve it with
A glass of dry sherry or a light Beaujolais, with a simple green salad in mustard vinaigrette to cut the richness.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Use a wide pot, not a tall narrow one. More surface area means faster evaporation and better browning, which can cut 15 minutes off the caramelizing.
  • ◆The onions can be caramelized up to 5 days ahead and refrigerated, or frozen for 3 months. That turns this into a 40 minute weeknight soup.
  • ◆Beef stock quality decides this soup. If yours is thin, simmer it with 1 lb (450 g) of roasted beef bones for an hour first, or use a good demi-glace concentrate.
  • ◆No broiler-safe bowls? Broil the cheese-topped toasts on a sheet pan until molten, then slide one onto each filled bowl at the table.
  • ◆Gruyere is the classic for its nutty melt, but a mix of Comte and a little Emmental is excellent. Avoid pre-shredded blends — the anti-caking starch makes the top grainy.

Velvety, deeply tomato, and on the table in about forty minutes from a couple of cans you already have. This is the version that makes a grilled cheese feel like a real dinner.

4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Choose canned over fresh
    Unless it is peak August, canned whole peeled tomatoes will beat fresh ones every time because they are picked ripe and packed immediately. Buy whole peeled rather than pre-crushed — crushed tomatoes often include puree and citric acid that taste tinny. Open both cans and have them ready by the stove.
  2. Sweat the onion
    Melt the 3 tbsp butter with the 1 tbsp olive oil in a 4 qt (3.8 L) saucepan over medium heat, then add the sliced onion and 1/2 tsp of the salt. Cook 6 to 7 minutes, stirring often, until soft and translucent with just a hint of gold at the edges. You do not want deep browning here; this soup should taste clean and tomato-forward, not caramelized.
  3. Add garlic and pepper flakes
    Stir in the sliced garlic and 1/4 tsp red pepper flakes and cook for 60 seconds, until the garlic smells sweet and looks barely blond. Sliced garlic in butter is fragile, so keep the spoon moving. Burnt garlic will haunt the entire pot with a bitter edge you cannot blend out.
  4. Toast the tomato paste
    Add the 2 tbsp tomato paste and stir it around the bottom of the pan for 90 seconds until it darkens from bright red to brick and starts sticking. This concentrates the glutamates and gives the soup a savory backbone that canned tomatoes alone cannot deliver. If it sticks hard, that fond is exactly what you want — the tomatoes will lift it in a moment.
  5. Crush and add the tomatoes
    Pour in both cans with their juice, then crush the tomatoes against the side of the pot with a wooden spoon or squeeze them through your fingers as they go in. Add the 2 cups (480 ml) broth and the remaining 1 tsp salt, and scrape the bottom clean. Breaking them up now gives the blender less work and means a smoother finish.
  6. Simmer to concentrate
    Bring to a boil, then reduce to a steady simmer and cook uncovered for 15 minutes, stirring occasionally. The soup will reduce slightly, darken, and lose its raw canned smell. Do not skip this window — a 5 minute simmer tastes like warm tomato sauce, while 15 minutes tastes like soup.
  7. Blend safely
    Turn off the heat and add the basil leaves. Blend with an immersion blender right in the pot for 1 to 2 minutes until completely smooth. If using a countertop blender, fill it no more than halfway, remove the center cap, and cover the hole with a folded towel — hot liquid expands violently and will blow the lid off an overfilled blender. Blend in batches and return everything to the pot.
  8. Finish with cream
    Set the pot over low heat and stir in the 1/2 cup (120 ml) heavy cream and 1/2 tsp black pepper. Warm it through to about 180°F (82°C) but do not let it boil, since boiling dairy in an acidic soup can make it look curdled. The color should shift from deep red to a soft brick orange.
  9. Taste and balance
    Taste it. If it is sharp or metallic, stir in the 1 tsp sugar to balance the acidity, and add salt 1/4 tsp at a time until the tomato flavor jumps forward. Serve in warm bowls with torn basil on top and a thread of olive oil. A grilled cheese cut into fingers for dipping is not optional in this house.
Know when it is done
Simmer the tomato base at a steady bubble around 205°F (96°C) for the full 15 minutes, then hold it below 190°F (88°C) after the cream goes in so the dairy never boils and breaks.
Serve it with
A sharp cheddar grilled cheese cut into dipping fingers, and a glass of Chianti or just very cold milk.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆For a silkier restaurant texture, pass the blended soup through a fine mesh sieve before adding the cream. It takes 3 minutes and removes every last bit of skin and seed.
  • ◆Out of heavy cream? Swap in 1/2 cup (120 ml) full-fat coconut milk or 3 tbsp (42 g) more butter whisked in off the heat.
  • ◆A pinch of baking soda, about 1/8 tsp, neutralizes acidity if the tomatoes are especially sharp. Add it before the cream and expect it to foam for a few seconds.
  • ◆Freeze the soup before the cream goes in, up to 3 months. Cream can separate on thawing, so stir it in fresh when you reheat.
  • ◆Roasting the drained tomatoes on a sheet pan at 425°F (220°C) for 25 minutes first adds a smoky depth worth the extra time on a lazy Sunday.

Chicken Noodle Soup from Scratch⏱ 3 hr 10 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

You poach a whole chicken to build the stock, then use that same golden broth for the soup — it is a completely different animal from anything out of a carton. This is the pot you make for someone who feels lousy.

From ScratchComfort FoodSunday Cooking
Prep
25 min
Cook
2 hr 45 min
Total
3 hr 10 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

The stock

The soup

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Start the chicken in cold water
    Put the whole chicken breast-side up in a tall 10 to 12 qt (9.5 to 11 L) stockpot and add enough cold water to cover it by 1 in (2.5 cm), about 14 cups (3.3 L). Starting cold matters: as the water heats slowly, proteins leach out and coagulate into foam you can skim, which is how you get a clear broth instead of a cloudy one. Set it over medium heat and let it come up gradually, about 20 minutes.
  2. Skim the foam
    As the water approaches a simmer, gray-brown foam will rise and gather at the surface. Skim it off with a shallow spoon or small strainer every few minutes for the first 10 minutes until only clear liquid and a little fat remain. That foam is coagulated protein and it tastes dull and muddies the broth if you stir it back in. This is the single step that separates homemade stock from tasting like dishwater.
  3. Add aromatics and hold a bare simmer
    Add the halved onion, carrot and celery chunks, parsley stems, 2 bay leaves, 1 tsp peppercorns, and 1 tbsp kosher salt. Adjust the heat so you see a bubble break the surface only every second or two — about 185°F (85°C). A rolling boil emulsifies the fat into the water and turns the stock cloudy and greasy, so keep it lazy. Cook uncovered for 1 hour.
  4. Pull the chicken
    After an hour, check the thickest part of the thigh with an instant-read thermometer; it must read at least 165°F (74°C), and 175°F (79°C) is even better for dark meat. Lift the whole bird out with tongs and a big spoon into a bowl and let it cool for 20 minutes until you can handle it. Leaving it in longer only dries the meat out — the bones will keep giving to the stock without it.
  5. Keep the bones simmering
    Return the carcass, wing tips, and any skin to the pot after you strip the meat and simmer for another 45 minutes. This is where the collagen becomes gelatin, which is what gives good chicken soup that faintly sticky, lip-coating body. Top up with hot water if the level drops below the bones.
  6. Strip and shred the meat
    Pull all the meat off the bird and shred it into bite-sized pieces with your fingers, discarding skin, cartilage, and bones. You should end up with roughly 4 cups (about 1 1/2 lb / 680 g) of meat. Cover it and set it aside at room temperature if you are finishing within the hour, or refrigerate it.
  7. Strain and defat the stock
    Pour the finished stock through a fine mesh strainer set over a large bowl and discard the solids — the spent vegetables have given everything they have. Let it settle 10 minutes, then skim the golden fat off the top with a ladle, reserving 2 tbsp (30 ml) if you want to cook the vegetables in it. You should have about 10 cups (2.4 L) of clear amber stock.
  8. Cook the fresh vegetables
    Wipe out the pot, melt the 2 tbsp butter or reserved chicken fat over medium heat, and add the diced onion, sliced carrots, celery, and 1 1/2 tsp salt. Cook 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the onion is translucent and the carrots have started to soften at the edges. Using a second round of fresh vegetables is the trick — the ones from the stock are exhausted and mushy, while these stay sweet and have bite.
  9. Bring the soup together
    Pour the strained stock back into the pot and bring it to a gentle simmer. Cook 12 to 15 minutes, until the carrots are tender when pierced with a knife but not falling apart. Taste the broth now and salt it properly — it should taste seasoned on its own, because the noodles will dilute it.
  10. Cook the noodles separately
    Boil the 8 oz (225 g) egg noodles in a separate pot of salted water for 1 minute less than the package says, then drain. Cooking them in the soup releases starch that clouds the broth, and any leftovers turn into a pot of bloated noodle paste overnight. Divide the noodles among the bowls instead of dumping them in the pot.
  11. Finish and serve
    Return the shredded chicken to the simmering broth just to heat through, about 3 minutes, then turn off the heat and stir in the dill, parsley, and 1 tbsp lemon juice. The lemon is what makes the broth taste alive rather than heavy. Ladle the hot soup over the noodles in each bowl and serve immediately with extra black pepper.
Know when it is done
The chicken is safe at 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part of the thigh, though dark meat is more tender pulled at 175°F (79°C). Hold the stock at a bare simmer of 180-190°F (82-88°C) the entire time — a rolling boil makes it cloudy.
Serve it with
Buttered saltines or thick sourdough toast, with a squeeze of extra lemon and hot tea alongside.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make the stock a day ahead. Chilled overnight, the fat solidifies into a cap you can lift off in one piece, and good stock will set to a soft jelly — that wobble means gelatin and it is exactly what you want.
  • ◆Never boil stock hard. A rolling boil breaks fat into tiny droplets suspended in the liquid, and no amount of skimming will make it clear again.
  • ◆Store noodles and broth separately in the fridge for up to 4 days, or freeze the finished chicken-and-broth base for 3 months and cook fresh noodles at serving.
  • ◆Add a Parmesan rind to the stock pot for extra savory depth, or a 2 in (5 cm) piece of ginger and a few smashed garlic cloves if you are making it for someone with a cold.
  • ◆Substitute 3 lb (1.4 kg) of bone-in chicken thighs for the whole bird if that is what you have — the stock will be even richer, just pull them at 40 minutes.

Sunday Beef Stew with Red Wine⏱ 4 hr 25 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Chuck browned hard, red wine reduced down over the fond, and three hours in a low oven until the beef gives way to a spoon. The gravy is glossy and dark and tastes like it took all weekend, which it sort of did.

Weekend ProjectDutch OvenMake Ahead
Prep
30 min
Cook
3 hr 40 min
Total
4 hr 25 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

The beef

The braise

The vegetables and finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Cut and dry the beef
    Buy a whole chuck roast rather than pre-cut stew meat, which is usually trim from random muscles that cook at different rates. Cut it into generous 2 in (5 cm) cubes, leaving the interior fat and silvery connective tissue in place since that melts into gelatin over three hours. Pat every surface bone dry with paper towels — a wet cube will steam instead of brown, and browning is where the color and depth come from.
  2. Season and flour
    Toss the cubes with the 2 1/2 tsp salt and 1 tsp pepper, let them sit 15 minutes, then dust with the 1/3 cup flour and toss until every piece wears a thin coat. Shake off the excess in a colander; clumps of raw flour turn gluey. The flour browns alongside the meat and thickens the gravy later so you never need a slurry at the end.
  3. Render the bacon
    Heat 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the oil in a 7 qt (6.6 L) Dutch oven over medium heat and cook the bacon for 7 to 9 minutes until crisp and the fat has rendered. Scoop the bacon out with a slotted spoon and set it aside, leaving the fat behind. That smoky fat is the browning medium for the beef and the first layer of flavor in the pot.
  4. Brown the beef in three batches
    Raise the heat to medium-high, add another 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil, and lay in a third of the beef with at least an inch between cubes. Do not move them for 3 minutes, then turn and brown a second side, 6 to 7 minutes per batch. The pan should sizzle steadily and aggressively but never smoke heavily; if it smokes, pull it off the heat for 30 seconds. Crowding the pot is the number one stew mistake — the meat gives up water, the temperature crashes, and you end up with gray boiled cubes.
  5. Look at the fond
    After the last batch, the bottom of the pot should be covered in dark brown stuck-on glaze. That is fond: browned proteins and caramelized sugars, and it holds most of the flavor you just created. It should be deep coffee brown, not black — if any patch has turned black and smells acrid, splash in 1/4 cup (60 ml) broth immediately and scrape it loose before it burns further.
  6. Cook the onions into the fond
    Lower the heat to medium, add the remaining 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil and the chopped onions with a pinch of salt, and cook 8 to 10 minutes. As the onions release water, use a wooden spoon to scrape the fond off the bottom — it will dissolve into the onions and turn them deep brown. Add the garlic and cook 1 minute more until fragrant.
  7. Toast the tomato paste
    Stir in the 3 tbsp tomato paste and cook it for 2 minutes, spreading it against the bottom of the pot with your spoon so as much of it as possible touches hot metal. It should darken from bright red to brick and smell sweet and concentrated rather than raw and tinny. This adds glutamates for savoriness and gives the finished gravy its deep color. Untoasted paste stays sour and sharp even after three hours in the oven, so the two minutes here are not optional.
  8. Reduce the wine
    Pour in the 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) red wine, raise the heat, and scrape the pot bottom completely clean. Boil for 5 to 7 minutes until the liquid has reduced by about half and no longer smells sharply of alcohol. Skipping this reduction leaves a raw boozy edge that three hours in the oven will not fully cook out. Use a wine you would actually drink; cooking wine is salted and harsh.
  9. Assemble and get it into the oven
    Heat the oven to 325°F (165°C). Return the beef and bacon with any juices, then add the 4 cups (960 ml) broth, 2 tbsp Worcestershire, thyme sprigs, and bay leaves. The liquid should come about three-quarters of the way up the meat, not drown it. Bring to a simmer on the stove, cover, and slide it onto the middle rack.
  10. Braise for two hours
    Cook covered for 2 hours, checking once at the hour mark to confirm the liquid is barely trembling rather than boiling. Oven heat surrounds the pot evenly, which is why braises come out more tender in the oven than on a burner that scorches the bottom. If it is bubbling hard, drop the oven to 300°F (150°C).
  11. Add the root vegetables
    Stir in the potatoes, carrots, and pearl onions, pushing them under the liquid. Cover and return to the oven for 45 to 55 minutes more, until the vegetables are tender to a knife tip and the beef crushes easily against the side of the pot. Adding them at the start would turn them to mush over three hours, which is why the vegetables in most stews taste like nothing.
  12. Finish and rest
    Pull the pot out, remove the thyme stems and bay leaves, and skim the fat pooled on the surface with a wide spoon. Stir in the peas and let them warm through for 3 minutes off the heat, then add the 2 tsp red wine vinegar and the parsley. The vinegar wakes everything up after three hours of long cooking. Let the stew rest 15 minutes before serving so it thickens and stops scalding.
Know when it is done
Braise at an oven temperature of 325°F (165°C) so the pot stays at a bare simmer. Beef chuck is safe at 145°F (63°C) but only becomes fork-tender near 200-205°F (93-96°C) internal, when the collagen has fully melted.
Serve it with
The rest of the bottle of red, with crusty bread or buttered egg noodles to catch the gravy.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Chuck is the only cut for this. Round and sirloin are too lean and go dry and chalky no matter how long you braise them.
  • ◆Made a day ahead, this is measurably better. Cool, refrigerate overnight, lift off the fat cap, and reheat covered at 325°F (165°C) for 40 minutes.
  • ◆If the gravy is thinner than you like at the end, ladle out 1 cup (240 ml), whisk in 1 tbsp (8 g) cornstarch until smooth, and stir it back in over a simmer for 3 minutes.
  • ◆No wine? Replace it with an extra 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) beef broth plus 1 tbsp (15 ml) balsamic vinegar so you keep the acidity that balances the richness.
  • ◆Brown mushrooms are a great addition — sear 8 oz (225 g) of quartered cremini separately in butter and stir them in with the peas so they keep their texture.

Chicken and Dumplings⏱ 1 hr 45 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

A creamy chicken stew with fluffy buttermilk dumplings steamed right on top, lid on, no peeking. It is the most comforting thing in this book and it lands on the table in under two hours.

Comfort FoodOne PotSouthern
Prep
25 min
Cook
1 hr 20 min
Total
1 hr 45 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

The stew

Buttermilk dumplings

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Brown the chicken skin
    Pat the thighs dry and season with 1 1/2 tsp of the salt and the 1 tsp pepper. Heat the 1 tbsp oil in a 6 qt (5.7 L) Dutch oven over medium-high and lay the thighs in skin-side down, working in two batches so they never touch. Cook 6 to 7 minutes without moving them until the skin is deep golden and releases on its own. You are rendering fat and building fond, not cooking them through; flip for 2 minutes and move them to a plate.
  2. Pour off most of the fat
    Tip the pot and spoon out all but about 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the rendered chicken fat, saving it in case you need it later. Too much fat here will make the finished stew greasy and it will pool orange on the surface. The brown crust stuck to the bottom stays — that is your fond.
  3. Cook the vegetables and lift the fond
    Add the 4 tbsp butter, then the onion, carrots, celery, and remaining 1/2 tsp salt. Cook over medium for 8 to 10 minutes, scraping the bottom regularly as the vegetables release water. The pot bottom should go from crusted brown to clean, with all that color now in the vegetables. They should be soft and fragrant but not browned.
  4. Make the roux
    Sprinkle the 1/2 cup (60 g) flour over the vegetables and stir constantly for 2 minutes. It will look pasty and coat everything, which is correct — you are cooking out the raw flour taste so the stew does not taste like wallpaper paste. That much flour against 6 cups of broth is what gives you a gravy thick enough to hold the dumplings up on the surface instead of letting them sink and turn gluey. Keep it moving so nothing scorches on the bottom.
  5. Add the broth gradually
    Pour in the 6 cups (1.4 L) chicken broth about a cup at a time, whisking smooth after each addition before adding more. Adding it all at once is how you get lumps that never dissolve. Once it is all in, add the thyme sprigs and bay leaves and bring it to a gentle simmer, whisking as it thickens.
  6. Simmer the chicken through
    Nestle the thighs back in skin-side up along with any juices on the plate, lower the heat, and simmer partially covered for 25 minutes. Check the thickest thigh with an instant-read thermometer — it needs at least 165°F (74°C), and dark meat is even more tender at 175°F (79°C). The stew should barely bubble; a hard boil will toughen the meat.
  7. Shred the chicken
    Move the thighs to a board and let them cool 5 minutes. Pull off and discard the skin and bones, then shred the meat into bite-sized pieces and return it to the pot. You should have roughly 3 cups (about 1 lb / 450 g) of meat. Fish out the thyme stems and bay leaves now while you can still find them.
  8. Mix the dumpling dough
    Whisk the 2 cups flour, 1 tbsp baking powder, 1 tsp salt, 1/2 tsp baking soda, and parsley in a bowl. Pour the melted butter into the cold buttermilk — it will seize into little clumps, which is exactly what you want — then pour that over the dry ingredients and stir with a fork just until no dry flour remains, about 12 strokes. The dough should look shaggy and lumpy. Overmixing develops gluten and gives you rubber pucks instead of fluffy dumplings.
  9. Enrich the stew before dropping
    Stir the 1/2 cup (120 ml) heavy cream and the frozen peas into the pot and bring it back to a steady simmer over medium heat. The liquid needs to be actively bubbling so the dumplings start steaming the instant they land. Taste and salt now — you cannot season it once the dumplings are on.
  10. Drop the dumplings
    Scoop heaping tablespoons of dough, about 12 total, and drop them onto the surface of the simmering stew, leaving a little space between each. They should sit on top rather than sink; if they sink, your stew is too thin and you should let it reduce for 5 minutes first. Do not press them down.
  11. Lid on, no peeking
    Cover tightly, lower the heat to keep a gentle simmer, and cook for 15 minutes without lifting the lid once. The dumplings cook by trapped steam, and every peek drops the temperature under the lid and gives you a dense, gummy center instead of an airy one. A heavy lid that actually seals matters more here than the burner setting. Set a timer, put your hands in your pockets, and walk away.
  12. Check and serve
    Lift the lid — the dumplings should have nearly doubled, look dry and matte on top, and a toothpick pushed into the center should come out clean, around 200°F (93°C) inside. If the centers are still wet, cover and give them 3 more minutes. Scatter with parsley and serve immediately in wide bowls, spooning stew over each dumpling.
Know when it is done
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) at the thickest part of the thigh, though 175°F (79°C) makes dark meat more tender. Dumplings are done at about 200°F (93°C) in the center, when a toothpick comes out clean after 15 covered minutes.
Serve it with
A simple green salad with sharp vinaigrette to cut the richness, and a cold glass of unoaked Chardonnay or sweet tea.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆No buttermilk? Stir 1 tbsp (15 ml) lemon juice or white vinegar into 1 cup (240 ml) whole milk and let it sit 10 minutes. The acid is what reacts with the baking soda to make the dumplings rise.
  • ◆Mix the dumpling dough only when the stew is already simmering. Baking powder starts working the moment it hits liquid, and dough that sits on the counter loses its lift.
  • ◆Leftovers keep 3 days but the dumplings soak up liquid overnight. Store them separated from the stew if you can, and reheat gently covered with a splash of broth.
  • ◆Bone-in thighs give you more flavor and gelatin than breasts and are almost impossible to overcook. If you must use breasts, add them 10 minutes later and take them out the moment an instant-read thermometer reads 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part — that is the safe number for poultry, and one minute past it they go chalky.
  • ◆For a lighter, more Southern-style pot, skip the cream and add an extra cup (240 ml) of broth — the roux alone gives plenty of body.

New England Clam Chowder⏱ 1 hr 35 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Thick with potatoes and smoky bacon, built on the briny liquor from clams you steam open yourself. It tastes like a dock in Maine, and it is easier than it looks.

SeafoodCreamyClassic New England
Prep
25 min
Cook
55 min
Total
1 hr 35 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

The clams

The chowder

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Check and scrub the clams
    Scrub each clam under cold running water with a stiff brush to remove sand from the shell. Discard any clam that is cracked, or any open one that does not close when you tap it firmly on the counter — that clam is dead and unsafe. Live clams feel heavy and shut tight. Keep them in a bowl in the fridge, covered with a damp towel, never sealed in a plastic bag.
  2. Steam them open
    Bring the 1 cup (240 ml) water, 1/2 cup (120 ml) wine, and smashed garlic to a boil in a large pot, add the clams, cover, and steam over high heat for 5 to 8 minutes. Shake the pot once halfway. Pull each clam out with tongs the moment it gapes open — leaving them in longer turns them into rubber. Throw away any that stay shut after 10 minutes.
  3. Save the clam liquor carefully
    Let the steaming liquid settle for 5 minutes so grit sinks to the bottom, then pour it slowly through a fine mesh strainer lined with a paper towel or coffee filter, stopping before the last murky half inch. This liquor is the soul of the chowder and also the most likely source of sand in your teeth. You should have about 2 cups (480 ml); top up with bottled clam juice if you have less.
  4. Chop the clam meat
    Pull the meat from the shells and coarsely chop it into pieces about the size of a nickel, saving any juice that runs out and adding it to the strained liquor. You should end up with roughly 1 1/2 cups (about 8 oz / 225 g) of meat. Refrigerate it — it goes in at the very end, off the heat.
  5. Render the bacon
    Cook the bacon in a 6 qt (5.7 L) Dutch oven over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until crisp and the fat has fully rendered. Scoop the bacon onto a paper towel with a slotted spoon and leave about 3 tbsp (45 ml) of fat in the pot. Pour off any excess or the chowder will taste greasy.
  6. Sweat the aromatics
    Add the 2 tbsp butter, then the diced onion and celery, and cook over medium for 7 to 8 minutes until soft and translucent with no browning at all. Chowder should be ivory white, so you want the vegetables sweet and soft rather than caramelized. Scrape up any bacon fond as they release moisture.
  7. Make the roux
    Sprinkle the 1/3 cup (40 g) flour over the vegetables and stir constantly for 2 full minutes. It should smell faintly nutty like pie crust but stay pale blond. This cooks out the raw flour flavor while keeping the color light, and it is what gives chowder its spoon-coating body without turning it into wallpaper paste. That much flour is roughly matched to the bacon fat and butter already in the pot, which is what keeps the finished chowder thick rather than greasy.
  8. Add the liquor and potatoes
    Whisk in the strained clam liquor a splash at a time until smooth, then add the cubed potatoes, thyme sprigs, and bay leaves. Bring to a simmer and cook 12 to 15 minutes, until a knife slides into a potato cube with no resistance. Yukon Golds hold their shape while releasing enough starch to thicken; russets fall apart and turn the pot grainy.
  9. Add the dairy gently
    Lower the heat and stir in the 2 cups (480 ml) milk and 1 cup (240 ml) cream. Bring it up to 180 to 190°F (82 to 88°C) — steaming with the occasional small bubble at the edge, never a real boil. Boiling dairy in a salty acidic pot can curdle it into grains, and once it breaks there is no fixing it. Simmer gently for 5 minutes to marry.
  10. Add the clams last
    Turn off the heat, fish out the thyme stems and bay leaves, and stir in the chopped clams. They are already cooked, and the residual heat of the pot is more than enough to warm them in 2 minutes. Any longer over direct heat and they turn to erasers, which is the classic chowder mistake.
  11. Season and rest
    Add the 1/2 tsp pepper, then taste before adding any salt — clam liquor and bacon are both salty, so you may need only 1/2 tsp or none at all. Let the chowder sit off the heat for 10 to 15 minutes; it thickens noticeably and the flavors settle. Serve topped with the crisp bacon and chopped parsley, with oyster crackers on the side.
Know when it is done
Clams are cooked the instant their shells open, usually within 5-8 minutes of steaming — discard any that stay closed. Once the dairy goes in, hold the chowder at 180-190°F (82-88°C) and never let it boil.
Serve it with
Oyster crackers and a cold crisp lager, or a squeeze of lemon and a glass of unoaked white like Muscadet.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Short on time or landlocked? Use 3 cans (6.5 oz / 184 g each) of chopped clams plus 2 cups (480 ml) bottled clam juice. Drain the clams, use the juice as your liquor, and add the meat off the heat exactly as written.
  • ◆Chowder is better the next day, but reheat it over low heat, stirring, and never let it boil. Add a splash of milk to loosen it.
  • ◆For an even thicker old-school chowder, mash about a quarter of the cooked potatoes against the side of the pot before adding the dairy.
  • ◆Do not store live clams in water or a sealed bag — they suffocate. A bowl in the fridge under a damp towel keeps them alive for a day or two.
  • ◆The paper-towel-lined strainer for the clam liquor is not optional. One gritty spoonful will ruin an otherwise perfect pot.

Broccoli Cheddar Soup⏱ 50 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Thick, orange, and full of tender broccoli and sharp cheddar, done in under an hour in one pot. The trick is grating your own cheese and adding it off the heat so it never goes grainy.

WeeknightCheesyOne Pot
Prep
15 min
Cook
35 min
Total
50 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Break down the broccoli
    Cut the florets into small bite-sized pieces, no larger than 1/2 in (1 cm), so they cook evenly and fit on a spoon. Do not throw away the stalks — peel the tough outer layer off with a vegetable peeler and dice the sweet pale core, which tastes better than the florets. You should have about 6 cups of florets and 1 cup of diced stem.
  2. Sweat the onion
    Melt the 4 tbsp butter in a 4 to 5 qt (3.8 to 4.7 L) pot over medium heat and add the diced onion with a pinch of the salt. Cook 5 to 6 minutes until soft and translucent, stirring often, with no color at all. Browning here would muddy the pale gold color this soup is supposed to have. Add the garlic and cook 45 seconds more.
  3. Make a blond roux
    Sprinkle the 1/3 cup (40 g) flour over the onions and stir constantly for 2 minutes, then stir in the 1/2 tsp dry mustard, 1/4 tsp nutmeg, and 1/8 tsp cayenne. The mixture will clump into a paste and smell like toasting pie crust — that is the raw flour taste cooking off, and the dry spices need this same hot-fat contact or the mustard will taste raw and dusty in the finished bowl. Keep it moving and do not let it brown; a blond roux thickens more powerfully than a dark one and keeps the soup light in color. Forty grams of flour against five cups of liquid is what makes this thick enough to stand a spoon in.
  4. Whisk in the liquids
    Pour in the 2 cups (480 ml) broth in three additions, whisking each one completely smooth before adding the next. Then whisk in the 2 cups (480 ml) milk and 1 cup (240 ml) half-and-half. Adding all the liquid at once traps dry flour in lumps that never dissolve, so go slowly at the start when the paste is thickest.
  5. Simmer the base
    Bring the pot up to a gentle simmer over medium heat, stirring often and scraping the bottom so the milk does not scorch. It will thicken noticeably in 4 to 5 minutes and coat the back of a spoon. Watch it closely — dairy catches and burns on the bottom of a pot faster than water-based soups do.
  6. Cook the vegetables
    Add the broccoli florets, diced stems, grated carrot, and remaining salt. Simmer for 10 to 12 minutes, uncovered, until the broccoli is fully tender and a piece crushes easily against the side of the pot. The color will shift from bright to olive green, which is normal and means it is actually cooked. Keep the heat at a bare simmer, around 190°F (88°C).
  7. Blend part of it
    Use an immersion blender to pulse the soup 5 or 6 times right in the pot, or transfer 2 cups (480 ml) to a countertop blender, blend smooth, and stir it back. You want a thick base with plenty of recognizable broccoli pieces left, not a smooth green puree. If using a countertop blender, never fill it more than halfway with hot liquid and vent the lid with a folded towel.
  8. Add the cheese off the heat
    Turn the burner completely off and let the pot stop bubbling, about a minute. Add the grated cheddar and Gruyere in three handfuls, stirring until each is fully melted before the next goes in. Cheese proteins tighten and squeeze out fat above about 165°F (74°C), which is exactly how soup turns grainy and greasy. Patience here is the whole recipe.
  9. Season and serve
    Taste and add salt 1/4 tsp at a time until the cheddar snaps into focus — the mustard, nutmeg, and cayenne you bloomed into the roux will not read as themselves, but together they make the cheese taste twice as cheesy. If the soup has gone thicker than you like while the cheese melted, loosen it with a splash of warm broth rather than water. Serve immediately in warm bowls, ideally in a hollowed-out sourdough round or with crusty bread for dipping. This one does not sit well, so ladle it while everyone is already at the table.
Know when it is done
Simmer the vegetables at about 190°F (88°C) until tender, then take the pot fully off the heat before adding cheese — above 165°F (74°C) the cheese proteins tighten and the soup turns grainy.
Serve it with
A crusty sourdough bread bowl or a soft pretzel, with a cold pale ale or a crisp Riesling.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Grate cheese from a block. Bagged shredded cheddar is dusted with cellulose and potato starch to stop it clumping, and that coating makes soup gritty instead of silky.
  • ◆If your soup breaks and looks oily, pull it off the heat and whisk in 2 tbsp (30 ml) cold cream or a splash of cold milk. It often pulls back together.
  • ◆This does not freeze well — dairy and cheese separate on thawing. It keeps 3 days in the fridge and reheats fine over low heat with a splash of milk, stirred constantly.
  • ◆For a lighter version, use 3 cups (720 ml) broth and 2 cups (480 ml) whole milk with no half-and-half, and lean on the roux for body.
  • ◆A splash of the pasta-water trick works here too: if it gets too thick after sitting, thin with warm broth rather than water so you do not dilute the flavor.

Roasted Butternut Squash Soup⏱ 1 hr 25 min🍽 6 servingsEasy▾

Roasting the squash instead of boiling it concentrates the sugars and gives the soup a caramel depth you cannot fake. Silky, faintly sweet, and finished with sage and a spoonful of cream.

Fall CookingBlenderMake Ahead
Prep
15 min

Total
1 hr 25 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

To roast

The soup

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Halve the squash safely
    Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Trim a thin slice off the stem end so the squash sits flat, then stand it upright and cut down through it with a heavy chef knife, rocking the blade rather than forcing it. If it feels dangerous, microwave the whole squash for 3 minutes first to soften the skin. Scoop out the seeds and strings with a spoon.
  2. Season and roast cut-side down
    Rub the cut faces with the 2 tbsp olive oil and sprinkle with the 1 tsp salt and 1/2 tsp pepper, then set them cut-side down on a parchment-lined sheet pan. Wrap the garlic head in a small foil packet with a drizzle of oil and put it on the pan too. Cut-side down traps steam against the pan and gives you a deeply browned caramelized face rather than a dry surface.
  3. Roast until collapsing
    Roast for 45 to 55 minutes, until a knife slides through the thickest part with zero resistance and the cut edges are dark brown and syrupy. Do not pull it early — a squash that is merely soft tastes flat, while one that is truly caramelized tastes sweet and nutty. The garlic should be soft enough to squeeze out like paste.
  4. Start the aromatics
    About 15 minutes before the squash is done, melt the 3 tbsp butter in a 5 qt (4.7 L) pot over medium heat. Add the chopped onion, apple, and 1 1/2 tsp salt and cook 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the onion is soft and golden at the edges. The apple adds a gentle tartness that keeps the soup from tasting like baby food.
  5. Bloom the sage and spices
    Add the 8 sage leaves, the nutmeg, and the cayenne and cook for 60 to 90 seconds until the sage smells woodsy and the kitchen shifts. Fat-soluble aromatics need this brief contact with hot butter to release fully. The cayenne will not make the soup spicy; it just keeps the sweetness in check.
  6. Add the squash
    Scoop the roasted squash flesh out of the skins with a large spoon straight into the pot, scraping up the browned caramelized bits from the cut face too. Squeeze in the roasted garlic cloves from their papery skins. Discard the skins. You should have about 4 cups (roughly 2 lb / 900 g) of soft flesh.
  7. Simmer briefly
    Pour in the 4 cups (960 ml) broth, stir to break up the squash, and simmer for 10 minutes so the flavors come together. Everything in the pot is already cooked, so this is about marrying rather than softening — the apple and onion give up their sweetness into the broth and the roasted squash loosens enough to blend. Scrape the bottom every couple of minutes with a flat spoon, since a thick puree like this scorches far more easily than a thin soup. Four cups of broth to roughly four cups of squash gives a soup that is thick but still pourable.
  8. Blend until silky
    Blend with an immersion blender for a full 2 minutes, or in a countertop blender filled no more than halfway with the center cap removed and covered by a folded towel. Hot liquid expands violently in a sealed blender and can burn you badly. Blend longer than you think you need to; the difference between good and silky is about 90 extra seconds.
  9. Finish and balance
    Stir in the 1/2 cup (120 ml) cream, 1 tbsp maple syrup, and 2 tsp cider vinegar over low heat and warm through to about 180°F (82°C) without boiling. Taste carefully: it should be sweet, savory, and just barely tangy. If it tastes flat, it almost always needs salt or a little more vinegar rather than more sugar. Meanwhile, fry the remaining 6 sage leaves in the reserved 1 tbsp butter in a small skillet for about 20 seconds a side, until they stop sizzling and go crisp, then drain them on a paper towel and float them on top.
Know when it is done
Roast at 425°F (220°C) for 45-55 minutes, until a knife meets no resistance and the cut faces are deeply browned. Finish the soup below 190°F (88°C) after the cream goes in so it never boils.
Serve it with
A crusty baguette with salted butter, and a glass of off-dry Riesling or hard cider.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Buying pre-cubed squash saves 10 minutes but costs you flavor, since cubes dry out instead of caramelizing. If you use them, roast at 425°F (220°C) for 30 minutes and expect a lighter soup.
  • ◆This freezes better than almost any soup in the chapter. Freeze the blended base without the cream for 3 months, then thaw and stir in cream when reheating.
  • ◆Save the seeds. Rinse, dry, toss with oil and salt, and roast at 350°F (175°C) for 12 minutes for a crunchy garnish.
  • ◆For a vegan version, swap the butter for olive oil and the cream for full-fat coconut milk — the coconut and squash are a natural pair.
  • ◆If the soup is thicker than you want after blending, thin it with warm broth a 1/4 cup (60 ml) at a time. Water will dilute the flavor you spent an hour building.
