Minestrone with Beans and Greens⏱ 1 hr 45 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

A proper Italian vegetable soup built on a slow soffritto and a Parmesan rind, so it tastes savory and deep instead of like boiled vegetables. It uses whatever is in the crisper and still tastes intentional.

Vegetable ForwardOne PotItalian
Prep
25 min
Cook
1 hr 20 min
Total
1 hr 45 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Soffritto

The soup

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Cut the soffritto small and even
    Dice the onion, carrot, and celery to a uniform 1/4 in (6 mm) so they cook at the same rate and dissolve into the background of the soup. This takes ten minutes of knife work and it is the difference between minestrone and vegetable water. Keep the zucchini and green beans separate; they go in much later.
  2. Render the pancetta
    Heat the 1/4 cup (60 ml) olive oil in an 8 qt (7.6 L) pot over medium heat and cook the pancetta for 5 to 6 minutes until the fat renders and the edges crisp. If you are skipping the pancetta, just warm the oil. That rendered pork fat is one of two savory backbones in this pot, and the Parmesan rind is the other.
  3. Cook the soffritto slowly
    Add the onion, carrot, celery, and 1 tsp of the salt and cook over medium-low for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring every couple of minutes. They should turn soft, sweet, and pale gold — never browned or crunchy. Italians call this stage the base of everything, and rushing it in 5 minutes is why so much homemade minestrone tastes thin. Add the garlic and red pepper flakes for the last minute.
  4. Toast the tomato paste
    Push the vegetables aside, add the 2 tbsp tomato paste to the bare spot on the pot bottom, and fry it undisturbed for 90 seconds until it darkens from bright red to brick and smells sweet instead of tinny. Stir it through the soffritto so every piece is coated. This small step caramelizes the sugars in the paste and adds concentrated savoriness that raw paste simply cannot give you. It is also what keeps the finished broth a deep russet rather than a washed-out pink.
  5. Add and reduce the tomatoes
    Crush the canned tomatoes with your hands as they go into the pot, juice and all, and cook for 8 to 10 minutes until the liquid has thickened and the raw tin smell is gone. Hand-crushing gives you irregular pieces that hold their shape better than machine-crushed pulp. The mixture should look jammy before you add broth.
  6. Build the broth
    Pour in the 8 cups (1.9 L) broth and add the Parmesan rind, bay leaves, rosemary sprigs, and remaining 1 tsp salt. Bring to a simmer and cook uncovered for 15 minutes. The rind slowly softens and releases glutamates that give the broth a savory weight no amount of salt can replicate.
  7. Add the potatoes and beans
    Stir in the cubed potatoes and drained cannellini beans and simmer 12 minutes, until the potatoes are just tender at the center when pierced. Mash a few beans against the side of the pot with your spoon to release starch and lightly thicken the broth. Fish out the rosemary stems once the needles start to loosen.
  8. Add the quick vegetables
    Add the zucchini half moons and the cut green beans and simmer 6 to 8 minutes, just until crisp-tender and still bright green. These go in late on purpose — 40 minutes of simmering turns zucchini into gray mush and green beans into limp string, which is why so much homemade minestrone tastes tired. A knife tip should meet a little resistance when you pull them off. Taste the broth now and adjust the salt, remembering the pasta still has to go in and will soak some up.
  9. Cook the pasta
    Stir in the 1 cup (115 g) ditalini and cook for the time on the package, usually 8 to 9 minutes, until just al dente. That is deliberately a modest amount of pasta for 8 cups of broth — minestrone is a vegetable soup with pasta in it, not pasta in broth. If you plan on leftovers, boil the pasta separately in salted water instead and add it to each bowl, because pasta left in soup overnight swells into paste and drinks all the broth. Stir occasionally so it does not stick to the bottom.
  10. Wilt in the greens
    Add the 4 cups chopped kale or cabbage in handfuls, stirring each one down into the broth before the next goes in, and cook 4 to 5 minutes until tender but still deep green. Adding it all at once just mounds it above the liquid where it steams unevenly. Lacinato kale needs the full 5 minutes to lose its rawness; savoy cabbage wants about the same, while spinach would need only 60 seconds. Fish out the Parmesan rind and the bay leaves now, before they disappear into a bowl.
  11. Finish in the bowl
    Turn off the heat and stir in the 2 tsp red wine vinegar and the basil, then taste one final time for salt. Ladle into wide bowls, then finish each with grated Parmigiano and a real drizzle of good olive oil — that raw oil on top is traditional and it makes the whole bowl smell better. Serve with crusty bread.
Know when it is done
There is no internal temperature here — go by texture. The soffritto is ready when soft and translucent after 12-15 minutes, the potatoes when a knife meets no resistance, and the pasta at al dente. Keep the pot at a gentle simmer around 200°F (93°C).
Serve it with
A rustic Chianti or Sangiovese, with grilled bread rubbed with garlic and olive oil.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Save Parmesan rinds in a bag in the freezer. They cost nothing and they are the single easiest way to make a vegetable soup taste like it simmered all day.
  • ◆Minestrone is a use-it-up soup. Swap in any firm vegetable you have — fennel, celery root, butternut, peas — just add hard ones early and soft ones in the last 8 minutes.
  • ◆For a vegetarian pot, skip the pancetta, use vegetable broth, and add 1 tbsp (15 ml) soy sauce or a spoonful of miso for savory depth.
  • ◆It keeps 4 days in the fridge and gets better on day two, but only if the pasta was cooked separately. Otherwise it turns into a casserole.
  • ◆A spoonful of basil pesto stirred into each bowl at the table turns this into minestrone al pesto and is worth doing at least once.

Chicken Tortilla Soup⏱ 1 hr 25 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

The real Mexican version, where you char the tomatoes and toast the chiles, blend them, and fry the puree before adding broth. It takes about an hour and a half and tastes like nothing that comes from a jar of salsa.

WeeknightMexicanOne Pot
Prep
15 min
Cook
1 hr 10 min
Total
1 hr 25 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

The base

The soup

Tortilla strips and toppings

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Char the vegetables
    Set a dry cast iron skillet or comal over medium-high heat and lay in the whole tomatoes, the onion half, and the unpeeled garlic cloves. Turn them every few minutes for 10 to 12 minutes, until the tomatoes are blistered and blackened in patches and slumping, the onion is charred on both cut faces, and the garlic skins are browned. Those black spots are flavor, not mistakes — this dry charring is what gives the soup its smoky depth. Pull the garlic early at about 6 minutes so it does not turn bitter.
  2. Toast the chiles
    In the same dry skillet over medium heat, press the guajillos flat for 20 to 30 seconds per side until they puff and smell like dried fruit. Move them straight into a bowl of hot water to soak for 15 minutes. Watch them closely; scorched chile turns the whole pot acrid and there is no rescuing it.
  3. Blend the base
    Peel the garlic and put it in a blender with the charred tomatoes and onion, the drained soaked guajillos, the chipotle, the 1 tsp oregano, and 1 tsp of the salt. Blend on high for 90 seconds until completely smooth. Add 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the broth if the blender struggles to catch. The puree should be brick red and thick like a loose sauce.
  4. Fry the puree
    Heat the 3 tbsp oil in a 5 qt (4.7 L) pot over medium-high until it shimmers, then pour in the blended puree — it will spit, so stand back and use a splatter screen. Cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring often, until it darkens several shades, thickens to the consistency of tomato paste, and a spoon dragged across the bottom leaves a trail. This frying step is the heart of the recipe: it cooks off raw blender flavor and concentrates everything into a real sauce base.
  5. Add the broth
    Pour in the 6 cups (1.4 L) chicken broth, stirring to dissolve the fried base completely, and add the epazote or cilantro sprigs. Bring to a gentle simmer and cook for 10 minutes so the flavors join up. The broth should be a rich rusty red with a slick of chile oil on the surface.
  6. Poach the chicken
    Slide in the chicken thighs, lower the heat so the surface barely trembles, and poach for 15 to 18 minutes. Check the thickest piece with an instant-read thermometer — it must reach 165°F (74°C), and thighs stay tender even a bit beyond that. A hard boil would seize the meat and cloud your broth, so keep it gentle.
  7. Shred and return
    Lift the chicken thighs onto a board with tongs, let them rest 5 minutes, then pull them apart into bite-sized shreds with two forks. Resting first lets the muscle fibers relax and reabsorb their juices, so they end up in the soup instead of running out onto the cutting board. Return the meat and every drop of collected juice to the pot. Shredding rather than chopping also gives the broth more surface to cling to, so each spoonful tastes seasoned.
  8. Fry the tortilla strips
    Heat the 1/2 cup (120 ml) oil in a small skillet to 350°F (175°C) — a strip dropped in should bubble immediately and vigorously. Fry the tortilla strips in three batches for 60 to 90 seconds each, until stiff and just barely golden, then drain on paper towels and salt them right away while the oil is still wet. Crowding the pan drops the oil temperature and gives you greasy limp strips instead of crisp ones.
  9. Season the soup
    Remove the epazote sprig, stir in the 2 tbsp lime juice and the remaining 1/2 tsp of the salt, and taste. Add more salt 1/4 tsp at a time until the chile flavor comes forward — this soup takes more salt than people expect because the chiles and tomatoes are both mild. It should taste smoky, tangy, and just a little spicy.
  10. Build the bowls
    Put a generous handful of tortilla strips in the bottom of each warm bowl, then ladle the hot soup over them so they soften slightly but keep some crunch. Top with diced avocado, crumbled queso fresco, a drizzle of crema, and more strips. Serve with lime wedges and eat it right away, before the strips give up entirely.
Know when it is done
Chicken thighs must reach 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part, poached at a bare simmer around 190°F (88°C). Fry the tortilla strips in oil held at 350°F (175°C) so they crisp rather than absorb grease.
Serve it with
A cold Mexican lager with lime, or a tamarind agua fresca, and warm corn tortillas on the side.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Do not skip frying the blended puree. Pouring raw blended tomato straight into broth gives you thin, sour soup — the 8 minute fry is what makes it taste restaurant-made.
  • ◆Short on time, bake the tortilla strips instead: toss with 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil and bake at 400°F (205°C) for 10 to 12 minutes, tossing once.
  • ◆Make the fried base up to 5 days ahead and refrigerate it, or freeze it for 3 months. Then dinner is just broth, chicken, and toppings.
  • ◆Guajillos are mild and fruity, chipotle brings the smoke and heat. Add a second chipotle if you like it hot, or leave it out entirely and the soup still works.
  • ◆Leftovers keep 4 days, but store the tortilla strips and toppings separately at room temperature or they turn to mush.

Split Pea Soup with Ham Hock⏱ 2 hr 15 min🍽 6 servingsEasy▾

Cheap, humble, and quietly one of the best things you can make from a bag of dried peas and a smoked ham hock. It thickens itself, needs almost no attention, and feeds you for days.

BudgetMake AheadOne Pot
Prep
15 min
Cook
2 hr
Total
2 hr 15 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Sort and rinse the peas
    Spread the split peas on a sheet pan and pick out any small stones, shriveled peas, or bits of debris — bagged legumes genuinely do contain the occasional pebble and it will crack a tooth. Rinse them in a colander under cold water until the water runs clear. Unlike beans, split peas do not need soaking; they break down on their own in about 90 minutes.
  2. Build the aromatic base
    Melt the 2 tbsp butter with the 1 tbsp olive oil in a 6 qt (5.7 L) pot over medium heat, then add the onion, carrots, celery, and 1 tsp salt. Cook 8 to 10 minutes, stirring, until the onion is translucent and the vegetables are soft with a little gold at the edges. This is the flavor floor of the soup, and 5 minutes is not enough. Add the garlic and cook 1 minute more.
  3. Add the peas and hock
    Stir in the rinsed split peas and coat them in the fat for a minute, then add the ham hock, the 8 cups (1.9 L) water or broth, the bay leaves, and the thyme sprigs. Use water rather than broth if your hock is a good smoky one; it gives you plenty of flavor and lets the peas taste like themselves. Bring it up to a boil.
  4. Skim and settle into a simmer
    Once it boils, skim off the gray foam that rises with a shallow spoon and discard it. Lower the heat until the surface bubbles lazily, around 200°F (93°C), and set the lid slightly ajar. A hard boil scorches the peas on the bottom and makes the whole pot taste burnt, which is the classic split pea failure.
  5. Simmer and stir the bottom
    Cook for 75 to 90 minutes, stirring every 15 to 20 minutes and dragging your spoon flat across the bottom of the pot. Split peas sink and stick as they break down, so that scrape is not optional. Add hot water 1/2 cup (120 ml) at a time if the soup gets thicker than you want before the peas are done.
  6. Check the peas
    The soup is ready when the peas have completely lost their shape and dissolved into a thick, pale green puree with no gritty texture on your tongue. If they still feel firm at 90 minutes, your peas were old — keep simmering and check every 15 minutes, since stale legumes can take twice as long. Old peas are the only real risk in this recipe.
  7. Pull and shred the hock
    Lift the ham hock out with tongs onto a board and let it cool 10 minutes. Pull the meat off the bone, discard the skin, fat, and gristle, and chop the meat into bite-sized pieces — expect about 1 1/2 cups (8 oz / 225 g). The meat is fully cooked and pulls away easily once the collagen has broken down, which happens well past 195°F (91°C).
  8. Decide on the texture
    Remove the bay leaves and thyme stems. For a rustic soup, leave it as is; for a smoother one, blend about half with an immersion blender or pulse it a few times. If you use a countertop blender, fill it no more than halfway and vent the lid with a towel, because hot puree will blow the lid off a sealed jar.
  9. Return the meat and adjust
    Stir the chopped ham back in and warm it through over low heat for 5 minutes so the meat picks up the soup and the soup picks up the smoke. Split pea soup thickens dramatically as it sits, so thin it with hot water or broth, 1/2 cup (120 ml) at a time, until it flows off a spoon in a thick ribbon rather than plopping. Aim slightly looser than you actually want it in the bowl. Remember it will be noticeably thicker again by tomorrow, and thicker still the day after.
  10. Season and serve
    Add the 1 tsp black pepper and the 2 tsp cider vinegar, then taste before salting — smoked hocks vary wildly and some are salty enough that you need none at all. The vinegar cuts the starchy heaviness and makes the smoke taste sharper. Toss the 2 cups bread cubes in a skillet with the reserved 1 tbsp butter over medium heat for 4 to 5 minutes until golden, and scatter them over each bowl with a grind of extra pepper.
Know when it is done
There is no doneness temperature for the peas — they are ready when they have dissolved completely and feel smooth, not gritty, after 75-90 minutes at a bare simmer near 200°F (93°C). The smoked hock is already cooked and shreds easily once its collagen breaks down above 195°F (91°C).
Serve it with
Buttered rye toast or garlic croutons, with a cold pilsner or a cup of strong tea.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆The bone from a holiday ham is even better than a store-bought hock, and it is free. Freeze it after Easter or Christmas specifically for this pot.
  • ◆For a vegetarian version, skip the hock, use vegetable broth, and add 1 1/2 tsp smoked paprika plus 1 tbsp (15 ml) soy sauce to replace the smoke and savoriness.
  • ◆It thickens into something closer to spackle in the fridge. That is normal — reheat with 1/2 cup (120 ml) of water or broth per two servings, stirring over medium-low.
  • ◆Freezes for 3 months. Freeze in flat zip bags and thaw in a bowl of cold water in about 30 minutes.
  • ◆Never salt heavily at the start. The hock releases salt over 90 minutes, and a pot seasoned early can end up inedible by the time it is done.

Chicken and Andouille Gumbo⏱ 3 hr 45 min🍽 8 servingsAdvanced▾

It starts with forty-five minutes of stirring flour and oil until it turns the color of dark chocolate, and everything good about this dish comes from that. Serve it over rice and it will ruin every other gumbo for you.

Weekend ProjectCajunMake Ahead
Prep
30 min
Cook
3 hr
Total
3 hr 45 min
Serves
8 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Meat

The roux and trinity

The pot

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Prep absolutely everything first
    Dice all the vegetables, measure the flour and oil, warm the stock, and set every bowl within arm's reach of the stove before you turn on a burner. Once the roux starts you cannot leave it for even 60 seconds, and a roux that burns has to be thrown out and started over. This is the one recipe in the book where mise en place is genuinely non-negotiable.
  2. Season and brown the chicken
    Pat the thighs dry and season with the 2 tsp salt and 1 tsp pepper. Heat the 2 tbsp oil in a heavy 8 qt (7.6 L) Dutch oven over medium-high and brown the thighs skin-side down for 6 to 7 minutes without moving them, then 3 minutes on the second side. They will not be cooked through and that is fine. Move them to a plate.
  3. Brown the andouille
    Add the sliced andouille to the same pot and cook 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until the edges are browned and the pot has picked up more fond. Scoop the sausage out with a slotted spoon and set it with the chicken. Pour off all the accumulated fat and wipe the pot with a paper towel — the roux needs clean oil and an even, unmarked surface so you can read its color.
  4. Start the roux
    Add the 1 cup (240 ml) oil to the pot over medium heat until it shimmers, then whisk in the 1 cup (120 g) flour all at once until completely smooth with no dry pockets. Switch to a flat wooden spoon or heatproof spatula so you can scrape the corners. From this moment forward, stir constantly and never stop. Hot roux is called Cajun napalm for a reason; keep children and pets out of the kitchen and wear long sleeves.
  5. Work through the color stages
    Over 35 to 45 minutes at medium to medium-low heat, the roux moves through recognizable stages: blond and smelling like pancakes at 10 minutes, peanut butter at 20, copper penny at 30, and finally dark chocolate at 40. Keep the spoon moving across the entire bottom in a figure eight, never letting it rest. If you see black flecks or smell anything acrid and burnt, stop and start over — burnt roux poisons the entire pot and cannot be salvaged.
  6. Judge the finish
    You are aiming for the color of melted dark chocolate or an old copper penny, smelling deeply toasted and nutty. The darker it goes the more flavor it gives and the less it thickens, which is why classic gumbo is soupy rather than gravy-thick. If your kitchen is nerve-wracking, stop at copper — a slightly lighter roux still makes very good gumbo, and burnt is unfixable.
  7. Stop the roux with the trinity
    The instant the roux hits the color you want, dump in all the onion, bell pepper, and celery at once and stir hard. The cold vegetables drop the temperature immediately and halt the browning, which is the only reliable way to stop a roux from carrying past done. It will hiss and steam dramatically. Cook 8 to 10 minutes until the vegetables are soft and the mixture looks like dark, glossy paste.
  8. Add garlic and seasonings
    Stir in the minced garlic, 2 tsp thyme, 1 1/2 tsp smoked paprika, and 1 tsp cayenne and cook for 60 to 90 seconds until fragrant. Ground spices need this brief hot fat contact to open up. Cayenne is where the heat lives, so start with a teaspoon and add more at the end if you want it hotter.
  9. Whisk in the stock gradually
    Add the warm stock 1 cup (240 ml) at a time, whisking each addition fully smooth before the next goes in. Adding cold stock all at once seizes the roux into stubborn lumps that never dissolve. Once all 10 cups (2.4 L) are in, the pot should look like thin dark gravy. Add the bay leaves, Worcestershire, and hot sauce.
  10. Simmer and skim
    Return the browned sausage to the pot, bring to a simmer, then lower the heat so it barely bubbles and cook uncovered for 1 hour. Orange oil will rise to the surface — skim most of it off with a wide shallow spoon every 20 minutes. Some old-school cooks leave it, but skimming gives a cleaner, more balanced gumbo. Stir the bottom occasionally.
  11. Cook the chicken through
    Nestle the chicken thighs back in with their juices and simmer 30 minutes more, until an instant-read thermometer in the thickest thigh reads at least 165°F (74°C); dark meat is even better around 175°F (79°C). Lift them out, discard the skin and bones, shred the meat, and return it to the pot. The gumbo should now be the color of strong coffee with cream.
  12. Finish and serve over rice
    Taste and adjust with salt, more cayenne, or another dash of hot sauce — gumbo needs assertive seasoning to stand up to plain rice. Stir in most of the scallions and parsley and let it sit off the heat for 15 minutes. Serve by mounding a scoop of hot rice in the center of each bowl and ladling the gumbo around it, topped with the remaining scallions. Pass file powder and hot sauce at the table, but never boil the gumbo after file goes in or it turns stringy.
Know when it is done
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part of the thigh, with 175°F (79°C) giving more tender dark meat. The roux itself runs above 350°F (175°C) and will cause severe burns — treat it with real caution and never leave it unattended.
Serve it with
Cold Abita Amber or any crisp lager, with potato salad on the side the way they do it in south Louisiana.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Use a flat-edged wooden spoon or spatula, not a whisk, once the roux gets dark. A flat edge scrapes the pot bottom where scorching starts, and that is exactly where a whisk cannot reach.
  • ◆If you are nervous about stirring for 45 minutes, make an oven roux: whisk the oil and flour in a cast iron pot and bake at 350°F (175°C) for 1 1/2 to 2 hours, stirring every 25 minutes. It is nearly foolproof and frees your hands.
  • ◆Gumbo is definitively better on day two. Cool it, refrigerate overnight, lift off the fat cap, and reheat gently — the roux flavor rounds out and stops tasting sharp.
  • ◆Never add file powder to the pot while it is on the heat. Sprinkle it over individual bowls at the table, where it thickens and adds an earthy root beer note without going ropey.
  • ◆No andouille? Use kielbasa plus an extra 1/2 tsp smoked paprika and 1/4 tsp cayenne. It is not the same, but it is good.

Shoyu Ramen with Chicken Broth⏱ 5 hr 15 min🍽 4 servingsAdvanced▾

A clear, golden chicken and pork broth built over four hours, seasoned bowl by bowl with a soy tare you make yourself. It is a real project, and the first sip explains exactly why people bother.

Weekend ProjectJapaneseFrom Scratch
Prep
45 min
Cook
4 hr 30 min
Total
5 hr 15 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

The broth

Shoyu tare and aroma oil

Eggs and bowls

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Cold-soak the kombu and shiitake
    Put the 10 g kombu and the dried shiitake in a bowl with 3 cups (720 ml) of cold water and leave them in the fridge for at least 30 minutes, or overnight if you plan ahead. Cold extraction pulls glutamates out of kombu without the slimy, faintly fishy edge that boiling it produces. This dashi becomes part of your broth later, so save every drop.
  2. Parboil the bones
    Put all the chicken and pork bones in your largest stockpot, cover with cold water, and bring to a rolling boil over high heat. Boil hard for 10 minutes — a thick gray scum will foam up and look genuinely alarming. Drain everything into the sink and rinse each bone under cold running water, scrubbing off any clinging coagulated blood. Skipping this step is why homemade ramen broth often looks muddy and tastes like a barnyard.
  3. Scrub the pot too
    Wash the pot itself before the bones go back in, since scum sticks to the sides in a gray ring and will redissolve into your clean broth if you leave it there. Return the scrubbed bones and add the 16 cups (3.8 L) fresh cold water. Everything should be covered by about 2 in (5 cm); add water if it is not, because bones that poke above the surface dry out and contribute nothing. Starting over with cold water rather than hot also lets you catch any last foam as it rises.
  4. Bring it up slowly
    Set the pot over medium heat and let it come to a bare simmer over 30 minutes rather than blasting it. As it heats, skim any remaining foam from the surface with a fine mesh skimmer. For this clear chintan style broth you want a lazy bubble breaking every second or two, around 190°F (88°C) — a hard boil emulsifies the fat and turns the broth cloudy and greasy.
  5. Simmer for three hours
    Hold that bare simmer, uncovered or with the lid cracked, for 3 hours. Check every 30 minutes and top up with hot water if the bones become exposed. The broth will slowly turn pale gold and start to smell rich and clean, and it should feel slightly sticky between your fingertips from the gelatin.
  6. Add the aromatics late
    In the final 45 minutes, add the halved onion, sliced ginger, smashed garlic, and scallion whites, plus the soaked shiitake and their soaking liquid. Add the kombu only for the last 20 minutes and pull it before it goes slippery. Aromatics added at the start would simmer into bitterness over three hours, so they always go in late.
  7. Make the shoyu tare
    While the broth finishes, combine the 1 cup (240 ml) soy sauce, 1/3 cup (80 ml) mirin, 2 tbsp sake, 1 tbsp sugar, and the 5 g kombu in a small saucepan and warm it to just below a simmer, about 180°F (82°C), for 10 minutes. Turn off the heat, add the katsuobushi, and let it steep 15 minutes before straining. You should end up with about 1 1/4 cups (300 ml), which is exactly what you need: 1/2 cup (120 ml) for the eggs and roughly 3 tbsp (45 ml) per bowl. The tare is the seasoning of the entire bowl — the broth itself stays unsalted so you can dial each bowl exactly.
  8. Make the aroma oil
    Warm the 1/3 cup (80 ml) chicken fat or oil in a small pan over medium-low with the sliced scallion greens for 6 to 8 minutes, until the scallions are frizzled and the oil smells sweet and oniony. Strain out the solids. That layer of flavored fat floating on the finished bowl is what traps the aroma and keeps the soup blazing hot to the last spoonful.
  9. Cook the marinated eggs
    Lower room-temperature eggs into boiling water with a spoon and boil for exactly 6 minutes and 30 seconds for a jammy, barely-set yolk. Move them straight into ice water for 5 minutes, peel carefully, then submerge them in 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the tare thinned with 1/2 cup (120 ml) water for at least 2 hours or overnight. The ice bath stops the cooking cold; even 30 extra seconds gives you a chalky yolk.
  10. Strain and finish the broth
    Strain the broth through a fine mesh sieve into a clean pot, pressing gently on the solids, then strain again through a sieve lined with a paper towel if you want it crystal clear. You should have 8 to 10 cups (1.9 to 2.4 L). Skim the fat from the top and save it for aroma oil. Keep the broth hot, right around 195°F (91°C) — ramen must be served scaldingly hot or it dies in the bowl.
  11. Taste and set the salinity
    Test one bowl before committing: start with 2 to 3 tbsp (30 to 45 ml) of tare and 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of hot broth, then taste. It should be assertively savory, just this side of too salty, because the noodles are unsalted and will dilute it. Adjust up or down by the tablespoon and use that ratio for every bowl.
  12. Set up before the noodles
    Heat your serving bowls with hot tap water and dry them, then line up all the toppings — halved eggs, chashu, nori, sliced scallions. Ramen assembly takes 90 seconds and there is no time to hunt for anything. Bring a large pot of unsalted water to a rolling boil for the noodles.
  13. Boil the noodles and build
    Cook the fresh ramen noodles for 60 to 90 seconds, or exactly as the package says, then lift them out and shake them completely dry in the strainer. Put the tare and 1 tbsp (15 ml) aroma oil in the bottom of each hot bowl, pour in the hot broth, then lower in the drained noodles and lift them with chopsticks into a neat fold. Any water clinging to the noodles waters down the broth you spent four hours on. Top with the egg, chashu, nori tucked against the rim, and scallions, and eat immediately.
Know when it is done
Hold the broth at a bare simmer of 185-195°F (85-91°C) for the full 3 hours — boiling makes it cloudy — and serve it at 195°F (91°C). Marinated eggs need exactly 6 1/2 minutes in boiling water then an ice bath. If you are cooking the chashu pork belly yourself rather than buying it sliced, take it to 145°F (63°C) and rest it 3 minutes before slicing; any chicken you cook as a topping must reach 165°F (74°C).
Serve it with
Cold Japanese lager or barley tea, with gyoza on the side and chili oil at the table.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make the broth, tare, and aroma oil up to 4 days ahead, or freeze the broth for 3 months. Then a bowl of ramen is a 10 minute weeknight dinner.
  • ◆Chicken feet look strange but they are the single best source of gelatin, and they are what gives ramen broth its body. Ask the butcher counter — they are usually cheap.
  • ◆Never salt the broth itself. Every element of a ramen bowl is seasoned by the tare, which is how shops adjust each bowl and how you avoid an oversalted pot you cannot undo.
  • ◆Fresh ramen noodles from an Asian market are worth the trip. If you can only find dried, cook them a minute shy of the package time so they finish in the hot broth.
  • ◆If your broth comes out cloudy, the heat was too high. It will still taste good, but next time watch for the bubble that breaks only every second or two.

Garlic Mashed Potatoes⏱ 40 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Silky, buttery, and sweet with whole garlic cloves that simmered right alongside the potatoes. Once you mash them this way you will not go back to the boxed kind.

Comfort FoodHolidayMake Ahead
Prep
15 min
Cook
25 min
Total
40 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Potatoes

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Cut the potatoes evenly
    Peel the potatoes and cut them into chunks about 2 inches (5 cm) across, keeping the pieces as close to the same size as you can. Uneven pieces are the number one cause of gummy mash, because the small ones blow apart and turn waterlogged while you wait for the big ones. Drop the cut pieces straight into the pot so they do not sit out and oxidize.
  2. Start them in cold water
    Put the potatoes and the 8 whole garlic cloves in a large pot and cover with cold water by about 1 inch (2.5 cm). Starting cold lets the outside and the inside come up to temperature together, so the edges do not turn to mush before the centers cook. If you drop potatoes into already-boiling water you get a ragged, watery exterior every time.
  3. Salt the water properly
    Add 1 tablespoon (18 g) of kosher salt to the pot and stir. Potatoes are starchy and bland and they will only be seasoned all the way through if they cook in seasoned water — salting at the end never catches up. The water should taste noticeably salty, a little less than seawater.
  4. Simmer, do not boil hard
    Bring the pot to a boil over high heat, then drop it to medium-low so the water moves at a lazy simmer with just a few bubbles breaking the surface. Cook for 15 to 20 minutes, until the tip of a paring knife slides into a chunk and the piece falls off the blade with no resistance. A hard rolling boil knocks the potatoes against each other and washes starch into the water, which costs you creaminess.
  5. Warm the dairy, soften the butter
    While the potatoes cook, put the 1 cup (240 ml) milk and the 1/2 cup (120 ml) cream in a small saucepan over low heat until steaming but not simmering, about 5 minutes, then pull it off the burner. Leave the 8 tablespoons (113 g) of cut-up butter on the counter so it is soft but not melted — it goes in on its own, before the liquid. Cold dairy hitting hot potatoes seizes the starch and makes the mash stiff and pasty, while warm dairy gets absorbed instead. That is most of the difference between home mash and restaurant mash.
  6. Drain and dry them out
    Drain the potatoes and garlic in a colander, then tip them back into the empty hot pot and set it over low heat for 1 to 2 minutes. Shake the pot gently and you will see steam rising off the surface as the last of the water evaporates. Drier potatoes drink up more butter, and butter is the whole point.
  7. Rice them while hot
    Press the hot potatoes and the softened garlic cloves through a potato ricer or a food mill back into the pot. If you do not own one, use a hand masher and stop the second the lumps are gone. Never use a blender, food processor, or hand mixer on high — they rupture the starch cells and turn potatoes into wallpaper paste in about ten seconds.
  8. Butter first, then dairy
    Add all 8 tablespoons (113 g) of the softened butter to the hot riced potatoes and fold with a flexible spatula until it has completely disappeared. Only then add the warm milk and cream, in three additions, stirring gently after each one and stopping when the mash is as loose as you like it. Going fat-first coats the starch granules in butter so they cannot soak up the liquid and swell into glue — do it in the other order and you get wallpaper paste. Stop stirring as soon as everything is combined and glossy, because every extra stroke works more starch loose.
  9. Season and adjust
    Stir in 1 1/2 teaspoons kosher salt and the 1/4 teaspoon white pepper, then taste. Potatoes need more salt than you think, so add another 1/4 teaspoon at a time until the flavor snaps into focus rather than tasting flat. If the mash is thicker than you like, loosen it with warm milk 2 tablespoons (30 ml) at a time.
  10. Hold and serve warm
    Serve within 20 minutes, or keep the mash warm in a heatproof bowl set over a pot of barely simmering water with a lid on, stirring once every 15 minutes. Scatter the chives over the top just before it hits the table so they stay green. Mashed potatoes should be served hot, above 150°F (66°C), or the butter stiffens and the texture goes waxy.
Know when it is done
Potatoes are done when a knife meets no resistance, around 210°F (99°C) internal. Serve above 150°F (66°C) so the butter stays emulsified and the mash stays silky.
Serve it with
The natural partner to roast chicken, meatloaf, or any braise with gravy — pour a glass of unoaked Chardonnay or a soft red.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Yukon Golds are the sweet spot — waxy enough to stay creamy, starchy enough to fluff. Russets make a fluffier, drier mash; red potatoes turn gluey and are worth skipping here.
  • ◆Make ahead: mash up to 2 days early, cool, and refrigerate. Reheat in a covered baking dish at 350°F (175°C) for 30 minutes with an extra 1/4 cup (60 ml) of warm milk stirred in.
  • ◆For a deeper, sweeter garlic flavor, roast a whole head at 400°F (200°C) for 40 minutes and squeeze the cloves in at the end instead of boiling them.
  • ◆If the mash goes gluey, it cannot be fixed — but you can spread it in a buttered dish, top with cheese, and bake it into a potato casserole nobody will question.
  • ◆Leftovers make excellent potato cakes: mix in an egg, form patties, and pan-fry in butter over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes per side.

Extra Crispy Roast Potatoes⏱ 1 hr 20 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Parboiled, roughed up until the edges go fuzzy, then roasted in hot fat until they shatter. The outside is glass and the inside is cloud, and there are never enough of them.

HolidaySunday RoastCrowd Pleaser
Prep
15 min
Cook
1 hr 5 min
Total
1 hr 20 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Potatoes and parboil

For roasting

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Heat the oven and the fat
    Set a rack in the center of the oven and heat it to 450°F (230°C). Pour the 5 tablespoons (75 ml) of fat onto a heavy rimmed sheet pan and slide it into the oven while it preheats. Potatoes hitting an already-screaming-hot pan of fat start crisping instantly instead of slowly absorbing cold oil and going greasy.
  2. Cut for maximum surface
    Cut the potatoes into chunks roughly 2 inches (5 cm) across, aiming for pieces with several flat faces rather than smooth rounds. Every flat face is a future crispy plane, and every sharp corner is a future crunchy bit. Halve small potatoes and quarter large ones so they all cook at the same rate.
  3. Build the alkaline water
    Put the potatoes in a large pot with 3 quarts (2.8 L) of cold water, 2 tablespoons (36 g) kosher salt, and the 1/2 teaspoon baking soda. The baking soda makes the water alkaline, which breaks down pectin on the outside of each piece and creates the starchy slurry that turns into the crust. It is one half teaspoon and it is the entire trick.
  4. Parboil until the edges give
    Bring to a boil over high heat, then reduce to a strong simmer and cook for 10 minutes, until a knife slides into a chunk easily but the piece still holds its shape. Do not stir once they are tender or you will break them apart. If they are falling apart at 8 minutes, pull them immediately — different potatoes cook at different speeds.
  5. Drain and steam dry
    Drain the potatoes in a colander and let them sit for 2 full minutes, shaking once, until the steam stops pouring off and the surfaces look dull and dry. Surface water has to boil away before browning can start, so every second here is a second of crisping you buy back. Dry potatoes also stop the hot fat from spitting at you.
  6. Rough them up
    Tip the potatoes back into the empty pot, add the 1 teaspoon salt and the black pepper, and shake the pot hard 8 to 10 times with the lid on. The surfaces should go visibly fuzzy and coated in a pale starchy paste. That mashed-up exterior is what fries into the craggy shell — a smooth potato roasts smooth and disappointing.
  7. Get them into the hot fat
    Pull the sheet pan out carefully — the fat will be shimmering and may wisp slightly. Tip the potatoes on, then use tongs to turn each one so all sides are coated, and spread them out so no two pieces touch. Crowding traps steam and steamed potatoes never crisp, so use two pans if yours looks tight.
  8. Roast without touching
    Roast for 25 minutes without opening the door. The bottoms need uninterrupted contact with the hot pan to set a crust, and every peek drops the oven temperature by 25 to 50 degrees. You should hear a steady sizzle when you finally open it, not silence and not violent spitting.
  9. Flip and add aromatics
    Slide a thin metal spatula under each potato and flip it, scraping up any crust that wants to stick to the pan. Tuck the crushed garlic cloves and rosemary sprigs in among the potatoes now, not earlier — 45 minutes at 450°F (230°C) would turn them black and bitter. Return the pan to the oven.
  10. Finish to deep gold
    Roast another 20 to 30 minutes, flipping once more at the halfway point, until the potatoes are deep golden brown and sound hollow and hard when you tap them with tongs. Pale potatoes are undercooked potatoes — push them further than feels comfortable. The interior should read about 210°F (99°C) and be completely fluffy.
  11. Salt and serve immediately
    Transfer to a warm serving bowl, hit them with a pinch more salt while the surfaces are still hot enough to grab it, and scatter the parsley over. Serve within 10 minutes, because trapped steam softens the crust as they sit. Never cover the bowl with foil — that undoes an hour of work in three minutes.
Know when it is done
Roast at 450°F (230°C); the potatoes are done when the interior reads about 210°F (99°C) and the outside is deep brown and audibly hard when tapped.
Serve it with
Made for roast beef, a Sunday chicken, or a fried egg at midnight — with a cold beer.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Beef tallow or duck fat gives a deeper, savorier crust than olive oil and holds up better at 450°F (230°C). Save the fat from a roast in a jar in the fridge for exactly this.
  • ◆Make ahead: parboil, rough up, and refrigerate uncovered on a tray for up to 24 hours. The extra drying time in the fridge actually improves the crust.
  • ◆If the potatoes stick to the pan, they were flipped too early. Give them another 5 minutes and they will release themselves once the crust sets.
  • ◆Do not skip the baking soda but do not double it either — too much makes the potatoes taste faintly soapy and turns the exterior slimy.
  • ◆A nonstick or thin sheet pan will not do this. Use heavy aluminum or steel so the pan holds its heat when cold potatoes land on it.

Scalloped Potatoes with Gruyere⏱ 2 hr 15 min🍽 8 servingsAdvanced▾

Paper-thin potatoes simmered in garlicky cream, layered up, and baked until the top is bronzed and the middle is one tender, sliceable thing. It is the dish people ask you to bring.

HolidayMake AheadComfort Food
Prep
25 min

Total
2 hr 15 min
Serves
8 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Potatoes and cream

Assembly

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Heat the oven and butter the dish
    Set a rack in the middle of the oven and heat to 375°F (190°C). Rub a 9 x 13-inch (23 x 33 cm) baking dish generously with the softened butter, corners included. The butter is not just for sticking — it helps the edges of the potatoes brown and gives the finished gratin a cleaner release.
  2. Slice the potatoes thin
    Slice the peeled russets 1/8 inch (3 mm) thick, using a mandoline if you have one and the guard that came with it. Consistent thickness is the whole game: thick slices stay chalky in the middle while thin ones dissolve. If you are knife-slicing, cut a thin sliver off one side first so each potato sits flat and cannot roll.
  3. Do not rinse them
    Resist every instinct to rinse the slices in water. The surface starch is exactly what thickens the cream into a sauce that sets, and washing it away gives you a soupy gratin that runs across the plate. If you sliced ahead, hold them in a bowl and cover with a damp towel rather than water.
  4. Build the cream
    In a wide pot or deep skillet, combine the heavy cream, whole milk, minced garlic, thyme sprigs, bay leaves, 2 teaspoons salt, black pepper, and nutmeg. Bring to a bare simmer over medium heat, stirring occasionally, about 5 minutes. You are steeping flavor into the dairy — it should smell strongly of garlic and thyme before the potatoes go anywhere near it.
  5. Simmer the slices in the cream
    Slide the potato slices into the hot cream, separating any that are stuck together, and bring back to a gentle simmer. Cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring gently with a rubber spatula every couple of minutes so the bottom does not scorch. The cream will visibly thicken and coat the back of a spoon as starch leaches out, and the slices will bend without snapping.
  6. Fish out the woody bits
    Pull out the bay leaves and any bare thyme stems with tongs and discard them. Taste a slice of potato and a spoonful of the cream — it should taste slightly saltier than you want the finished dish to be, because the potatoes will keep absorbing seasoning in the oven. Adjust with another 1/4 teaspoon salt if it tastes flat.
  7. Layer half into the dish
    Spoon about half the potatoes into the buttered dish and use the back of a spoon to press them into a flat, even layer with no big air pockets. Pour over enough of the cream to just cover them. Flat layers are what let you cut clean squares later instead of serving spoonfuls of rubble.
  8. Cheese the middle
    Scatter half the Gruyere evenly over the first layer, right out to the edges. Cheese in the middle keeps the interior rich and gives you that pull when you lift a portion. Save the Parmigiano entirely for the top — it browns better than Gruyere and gives you the crackly lid.
  9. Finish the layers
    Add the remaining potatoes, press flat again, and pour over all the remaining cream — it should come up just below the top layer, not drown it. Top with the rest of the Gruyere and all the Parmigiano. Wipe any drips off the rim so they do not carbonize and smoke.
  10. Bake covered, then uncovered
    Cover the dish tightly with foil, set it on a rimmed sheet pan to catch bubble-overs, and bake for 40 minutes. Remove the foil and bake another 30 to 35 minutes, until the top is deeply browned in patches and the cream is bubbling slowly around the edges. Covered time cooks the potatoes through; uncovered time builds the crust.
  11. Test the center
    Push a paring knife straight down through the middle of the dish — it should meet no resistance at all, sliding through like soft butter. An instant-read thermometer in the center should show at least 200°F (93°C). If the knife catches, tent with foil and give it another 10 to 15 minutes.
  12. Rest before you cut
    Let the gratin sit on a rack for a full 20 minutes before serving. The cream is still liquid the moment it leaves the oven and needs that time to set into something sliceable. Scatter the chives over just before serving, and cut squares with a thin knife rather than scooping.
Know when it is done
Bake at 375°F (190°C) until the center reads 200°F (93°C) and a knife slides through with zero resistance. Rest 20 minutes so the cream sets.
Serve it with
Ham, prime rib, or a roast leg of lamb — and a glass of dry Riesling to cut the cream.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Russets have the most starch and give the best-setting sauce. Yukon Golds work and taste sweeter, but the result is a little looser — do not use waxy red potatoes at all.
  • ◆Make ahead: assemble completely, cover, and refrigerate up to 24 hours. Add 15 minutes to the covered bake and start from cold, not room temperature.
  • ◆Traditional scalloped potatoes have no cheese at all — leave both cheeses out and you have a classic potatoes dauphinoise, which is just as good with roast lamb.
  • ◆If the top browns before the center is tender, lay foil loosely over it. Browning is a surface event and can always be paused; undercooked potatoes cannot be rescued at the table.
  • ◆Leftovers reheat beautifully: cut a square, put it in a skillet with a teaspoon of butter over medium-low heat, and crisp both cut faces for 3 minutes each.

Steakhouse Creamed Spinach⏱ 35 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Thick, nutmeg-scented, and rich enough to eat with a spoon — the side dish that makes a steak dinner feel like an occasion. The secret is squeezing the spinach far drier than feels reasonable.

SteakhouseComfort FoodMake Ahead

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Spinach

Cream base

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Set up a blanch and a shock
    Bring 4 quarts (3.8 L) of water to a hard boil with 1 tablespoon (18 g) of salt, and fill a large bowl with ice and cold water next to the stove. Blanching then shocking locks in the bright green color instead of letting the spinach go army-drab. Have a colander in the sink ready to go, because this part moves fast.
  2. Blanch the spinach fast
    Push the spinach into the boiling water in two batches and cook each for just 30 to 45 seconds, pressing it under with tongs. It will collapse to a fraction of its volume almost immediately. Longer than a minute and you cook out both the color and the flavor, leaving you with nothing but the cream.
  3. Shock and drain
    Lift the spinach straight into the ice water and swish it around for 30 seconds until it is cold to the touch. Stopping the cooking cold is the difference between vivid green and dull olive. Drain it in the colander and press down with your palm to push out the first round of water.
  4. Squeeze it truly dry
    Gather the spinach in a clean kitchen towel, twist the ends in opposite directions, and wring hard over the sink. You should get out at least 1 cup (240 ml) of green water, and the ball left in the towel should be dense and about the size of a large orange. Every tablespoon of water you leave behind will thin the sauce into soup.
  5. Chop the ball
    Unwrap the squeezed spinach and chop it roughly, running your knife through the compressed mass 15 or 20 times. It will be tightly packed and want to stay in a puck, so pull it apart with your fingers as you go. Loose, chopped spinach folds into the sauce evenly instead of arriving in solid clumps.
  6. Sweat the aromatics
    Melt the 4 tablespoons (55 g) butter in a 10-inch (25 cm) skillet over medium heat, then add the shallot with a pinch of salt. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring, until it is soft and translucent but has taken on no color at all. Add the garlic and cook 45 seconds more, just until it smells sweet rather than raw.
  7. Cook out the flour
    Sprinkle the 1/4 cup (30 g) flour over the butter and whisk constantly for 90 seconds to 2 minutes. The paste will look sandy, then smooth, and will smell faintly like toasted pie crust. That smell means the raw flour taste is gone, which is the difference between a real bechamel and a chalky white sauce.
  8. Build the bechamel
    Pour in the 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of warm milk in a thin stream while whisking hard, adding about 1/2 cup (120 ml) at a time and letting each addition come together before the next. Adding it all at once makes lumps that no amount of whisking fully undoes. Once it is all in, stir in the 1/2 cup (120 ml) of heavy cream and bring to a gentle simmer. Two cups of liquid against 1/4 cup of flour is the ratio you want here — a thinner sauce will slide off the spinach and pool in the bowl.
  9. Thicken and season
    Simmer for 4 to 5 minutes, stirring often and scraping the corners of the pan, until the sauce coats the back of a spoon and holds a line when you drag a finger through it. Stir in the nutmeg, 1 teaspoon salt, and the black pepper. Make it slightly over-seasoned now, because 2 pounds of spinach is about to dilute it.
  10. Fold and finish
    Add the chopped spinach and stir until every strand is coated, then cook 2 to 3 minutes more to heat it through. Kill the heat and stir in the Parmigiano until it melts smoothly — off the heat so it does not break into greasy strings. Taste, add salt in 1/4 teaspoon increments, and serve hot in a warm bowl.
Know when it is done
No internal temperature to chase — the sauce is ready when it coats a spoon and holds a clean line under your finger. Serve hot, above 150°F (66°C).
Serve it with
Non-negotiable next to a ribeye, but just as good with roast chicken or spooned over a baked potato.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Frozen chopped spinach works genuinely well here and saves 15 minutes. Thaw it fully and squeeze it just as ruthlessly — 20 oz (570 g) frozen equals about 2 lb (900 g) fresh.
  • ◆Make ahead: the whole thing holds in the fridge for 3 days. Reheat gently over low heat with a splash of milk, stirring, because high heat will break the sauce.
  • ◆If your sauce is thin, it is almost always wet spinach, not a bad roux. Simmer uncovered for a few extra minutes and it will tighten back up.
  • ◆Grate the nutmeg fresh if you possibly can. Pre-ground nutmeg has lost most of its aroma, and nutmeg is the flavor that makes this taste like a steakhouse.
  • ◆For a bit of tang, swap 2 oz (55 g) of the Parmigiano for cream cheese stirred in off the heat.

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Sprouts

Balsamic glaze

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Get the oven properly hot
    Set a rack in the lower third of the oven and heat to 425°F (220°C), sliding a heavy rimmed sheet pan in to preheat with it. A hot pan sears the cut faces on contact instead of letting the sprouts slowly steam in their own moisture. The lower rack puts them closer to the heat source for better browning underneath.
  2. Trim and halve
    Cut a thin slice off the dry stem end of each sprout and pull off any yellowed or loose outer leaves. Halve each one straight through the stem so both halves stay held together. Halving is what gives you the flat face that browns — whole sprouts steam and stay bitter in the middle.
  3. Keep the stray leaves
    Collect all the leaves that fell off during trimming and add them to the bowl with the sprouts. They roast into crisp, dark green chips that are the best part of the pan. Anyone who tells you to throw them away has never eaten one.
  4. Toss with oil and salt
    Toss the halved sprouts and loose leaves with the 3 tablespoons (45 ml) olive oil, 1 teaspoon salt, and the pepper until every surface is lightly slicked. Dry patches will not brown, and puddles of oil will fry rather than roast. Use your hands so you can feel when the coating is even.
  5. Lay them cut side down
    Pull the hot pan out and quickly arrange the sprouts cut side down in a single layer, giving each one a little space. You should hear an immediate sizzle when they land. Taking two extra minutes to turn them all face-down is the single biggest thing you can do for the final result.
  6. Roast without stirring
    Roast for 18 minutes without touching or shaking the pan. That uninterrupted contact between the cut face and the hot metal is where the deep caramelization happens, and stirring at minute 10 resets the whole process. The kitchen should smell nutty and sweet, not sulfurous.
  7. Check and finish roasting
    Lift one sprout with tongs — the cut face should be deep mahogany brown with some near-black edges, and the sprout should give easily when squeezed. If it is still pale, give it 4 to 7 more minutes. Total roasting time runs 22 to 28 minutes depending on the size of your sprouts.
  8. Reduce the balsamic
    While the sprouts roast, simmer the balsamic vinegar and honey in a small saucepan over medium heat for 4 to 6 minutes, until it has reduced by about half and coats a spoon in a thin syrup. Watch it closely at the end — balsamic goes from glaze to tar in under a minute. Pull it off the heat and whisk in the butter and the red pepper flakes.
  9. Toss, shave, serve
    Tip the hot sprouts into a serving bowl, drizzle over the warm glaze, and toss just enough to coat — dressing them on the pan makes the crisp faces go soggy against the metal. Shave the Parmigiano over the top with a vegetable peeler. Serve right away, while the edges are still crunchy.
Know when it is done
Roast at 425°F (220°C). Done when the cut faces are deep brown to nearly black at the edges and a knife slips into the core with no resistance.
Serve it with
Great alongside pork chops, roast chicken, or a holiday ham — try a glass of Pinot Noir.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Buy sprouts of similar size, and if some are much bigger, quarter those instead of halving so everything finishes at the same moment.
  • ◆Make ahead: trim and halve up to 3 days early and keep them in a bag in the fridge. Do not oil them until roasting day.
  • ◆For a smoky version, cook 4 oz (115 g) chopped bacon on the pan for 10 minutes first, then roast the sprouts in the rendered fat and skip the olive oil.
  • ◆Bitterness means undercooked, not bad sprouts. Push them further into the brown than you think is right and the bitterness turns into sweetness.
  • ◆If you would rather skip reducing the balsamic, a good store-bought balsamic glaze drizzled over works fine — use about 3 tablespoons (45 ml).

▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Heat the oven high
    Set a rack in the upper third of the oven and heat to 425°F (220°C). Asparagus is mostly water and needs high, dry heat to brown before it collapses. A moderate oven at 350°F (175°C) will only ever steam it into something limp and gray-green.
  2. Snap or cut the ends
    Hold a spear near the bottom and bend it until it snaps — it breaks naturally right where the woody part ends, usually 1 to 2 inches (2.5 to 5 cm) up. Line up the rest of the bunch and cut them all at that same point with a knife. Woody ends stay stringy no matter how long you cook them.
  3. Dry the spears
    Rinse the asparagus and roll it in a clean kitchen towel until the spears are completely dry to the touch. Wet asparagus steams itself on the pan and never browns. This takes 30 seconds and changes the outcome more than any seasoning will.
  4. Dress on the pan
    Spread the spears on a rimmed sheet pan, drizzle with the 2 tablespoons (30 ml) olive oil, and roll them around with your hands until each one is glossy. Sprinkle over the 3/4 teaspoon salt and the pepper. Hold the garlic back for now — minced garlic burns and turns acrid in a 425°F (220°C) oven over a full 15 minutes.
  5. Give them room
    Arrange the spears in a single layer with a little space between them, all pointing the same direction so they are easy to turn later. Piled asparagus traps steam and comes out soft and drab. Use two pans rather than crowding one.
  6. Roast until just tender
    Roast for 8 to 10 minutes for medium spears, or 6 minutes for pencil-thin ones. They are ready when the color has gone bright, glossy green and a knife tip meets a little resistance at the thickest part. Overcooked asparagus goes limp and khaki and cannot be undone.
  7. Add garlic and cheese
    Pull the pan out, scatter the minced garlic and the 1/2 cup (50 g) Parmigiano over the spears, and dot the butter bits between them. Slide the pan back in for 3 to 5 minutes, until the cheese has melted into lacy golden patches and the garlic smells sweet. Watch it — the cheese goes from golden to bitter in about 60 seconds.
  8. Finish with lemon
    Transfer the spears to a warm platter, scraping every crispy cheese shard off the pan with a spatula, and squeeze over the 1 tablespoon (15 ml) lemon juice. Shower with the lemon zest. The acid at the very end wakes the whole thing up, and adding it before roasting would only dull the color.
Know when it is done
Roast at 425°F (220°C). Done when the spears are bright green, a knife tip meets slight resistance at the base, and the cheese is golden and lacy.
Serve it with
Perfect next to salmon, steak, or a spring roast lamb — pour a crisp Sauvignon Blanc.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Thickness matters more than the recipe: pencil-thin spears need 6 to 8 minutes total, thick ones need 12 to 14. Judge by the knife, not the clock.
  • ◆Store asparagus like flowers — standing in an inch of water in a jar in the fridge, loosely bagged. It stays crisp for 4 or 5 days instead of two.
  • ◆Grate the cheese yourself. Pre-shredded parmesan is coated with anti-caking starch and refuses to melt into that lacy crust.
  • ◆This works just as well on a hot grill: 4 to 6 minutes turning once, then toss with the garlic, cheese, and lemon off the heat.
  • ◆Leftovers are excellent chopped cold into a frittata or scattered over pasta the next day.

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Dry

Wet

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Preheat the oven and the skillet
    Set a rack in the center of the oven, put a 10-inch (25 cm) cast iron skillet on it, and heat the oven to 450°F (230°C). Let the skillet sit in there for a full 15 minutes after the oven beeps. A truly hot pan is what fries the outside of the batter into that crunchy shell the second it hits.
  2. Whisk the dry ingredients
    In a large bowl, whisk together the cornmeal, flour, sugar, baking powder, baking soda, and 1 1/4 teaspoons salt for 20 seconds. Whisking distributes the leaveners evenly, and a clump of baking soda tastes like metal and leaves a green streak. Make a well in the center.
  3. Melt and split the butter
    Melt all 6 tablespoons (85 g) of butter in a small saucepan or the microwave. Set 2 tablespoons (28 g) aside for the skillet and let the remaining 4 tablespoons (55 g) cool for 2 minutes. Pouring hot butter straight into eggs scrambles them, which is a mistake you only make once.
  4. Mix the wet ingredients
    In a second bowl, whisk the 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) buttermilk and the 2 eggs until uniformly pale yellow with no streaks of white, about 30 seconds. Whisk in the 4 tablespoons (55 g) of cooled melted butter. Room-temperature buttermilk matters here — cold buttermilk will resolidify the butter into little flecks. Do not be tempted to add more buttermilk: this much liquid against 210 g of cornmeal is what gives you a batter that domes instead of one that bakes into pudding.
  5. Combine with restraint
    Pour the wet into the dry and fold with a spatula just until no dry pockets remain, about 15 strokes. The batter should look slightly lumpy and pourable, like thick pancake batter. Overmixing develops gluten in the flour and gives you cornbread with a tight, rubbery crumb.
  6. Let it hydrate
    Let the batter stand for 5 minutes while the skillet finishes heating. The cornmeal absorbs liquid and softens in that time, which is the difference between a tender crumb and a gritty one. You will see the batter thicken noticeably.
  7. Butter the hot pan
    Pull the skillet out with a dry oven mitt, set it on the stovetop, and swirl in the reserved 2 tablespoons (28 g) of butter. It should foam and sizzle instantly and start smelling nutty within about 15 seconds. Tilt the pan so the butter climbs the sides — that is where the crispy rim comes from.
  8. Pour and level
    Pour all the batter into the center of the hot skillet in one go; it should hiss loudly and the edges should begin setting immediately. Give the pan a quick shake to level the surface rather than spreading it with a spatula. Get it back into the oven within 30 seconds so the pan does not lose heat.
  9. Bake until domed and golden
    Bake for 20 to 25 minutes, until the top is golden brown, the center is domed and springs back when you press it, and the edges have pulled slightly from the pan. A toothpick in the center should come out with a few dry crumbs and no wet batter. The internal temperature should read 200°F (93°C).
  10. Rest, then serve warm
    Let the cornbread rest in the skillet on a rack for 10 minutes so the crumb sets and the steam redistributes. Cut into 8 wedges right in the pan and serve warm with the honey and a pinch of flaky salt. Cornbread is best within an hour of baking — it stales faster than any other quick bread.
Know when it is done
Bake at 450°F (230°C) until the center reads 200°F (93°C) and springs back when pressed. Rest 10 minutes before cutting.
Serve it with
Chili, pulled pork, or a pot of collards — with a cold glass of buttermilk or a lager.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆No buttermilk? Stir 1 1/2 tablespoons (22 ml) of lemon juice or white vinegar into 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of whole milk and let it sit 10 minutes until it curdles.
  • ◆Southern-style is barely sweet; Northern-style is cakier. Drop the sugar to 1 teaspoon for a savory pan, or raise it to 1/3 cup (65 g) for a sweeter one.
  • ◆No cast iron? Use a 9-inch (23 cm) cake pan or a metal 8 x 8-inch (20 x 20 cm) pan, preheated the same way. Glass or ceramic will not give you the crust.
  • ◆Fold in 1 cup (170 g) of corn kernels, 4 oz (115 g) of grated sharp cheddar, or 2 minced jalapenos at the very end for a loaded version.
  • ◆Day-old cornbread makes the best stuffing and the best croutons — cube it, toast at 300°F (150°C) for 20 minutes, and keep it in a bag.

Soft Buttery Dinner Rolls⏱ 3 hr 5 min🍽 Makes 15 rollsAdvanced▾

Cloud-soft, pull-apart rolls with a shiny golden top and a slick of butter brushed on the second they leave the oven. Nothing you buy comes close to these.

BakingHolidayWeekend Project
Prep
30 min
Cook
20 min
Total
3 hr 5 min
Serves
Makes 15 rolls
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Dough

Finishing

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Warm the milk correctly
    Heat the milk to 105 to 110°F (40 to 43°C) — warm on your wrist like bathwater, never hot. Above about 130°F (54°C) you start killing the yeast, and below 90°F (32°C) it works so slowly your rise will take all afternoon. If you have a thermometer, this is a good moment to use it.
  2. Mix the dough base
    In the bowl of a stand mixer, whisk together the bread flour, yeast, sugar, and salt. Add the warm milk and the room-temperature egg, and mix on low with the dough hook for 2 minutes until a shaggy mass forms with no dry flour at the bottom. Let it rest 5 minutes — this autolyse hydrates the flour and makes the kneading much easier.
  3. Add the butter slowly
    With the mixer on medium-low, add the 6 tablespoons (85 g) of softened butter one tablespoon at a time, waiting until each piece disappears before adding the next. This takes about 5 minutes and looks alarming — the dough will break apart and slap around before it comes back together. Adding all the butter at once coats the flour and prevents gluten from ever forming.
  4. Knead to the windowpane
    Knead on medium for 8 to 10 minutes, until the dough is smooth, glossy, and pulls cleanly away from the sides while still sticking slightly at the bottom. Test it by stretching a walnut-sized piece between your fingers — it should thin to a translucent membrane before tearing. If it tears immediately, knead 3 more minutes and test again.
  5. First rise
    Oil a large bowl with the 1 teaspoon of neutral oil, turn the dough in it to coat, and cover with plastic wrap. Let it rise in a warm spot, around 75 to 78°F (24 to 26°C), for 60 to 90 minutes, until doubled. Judge by size, not the clock — press two fingers 1/2 inch (1 cm) into the dough and it is ready if the dent fills back only halfway.
  6. Divide by weight
    Punch the dough down gently and turn it onto a lightly floured counter. Weigh the whole mass — it should come to around 2 lb 1 oz (940 g) — then divide by 15 and cut equal pieces of about 2 1/4 oz (62 g) each. Equal weights mean equal baking times, and eyeballing it always leaves you with two burnt rolls and two doughy ones. Use the scale even if you never use it for anything else.
  7. Shape tight balls
    Flatten each piece, fold the edges into the center to make a rough ball, then flip it seam-side down and cup your palm over it, dragging it in small circles against the counter. The surface should tighten into a smooth, taut skin over about 10 seconds. That tension is what makes the roll rise up instead of spreading out.
  8. Arrange in the pan
    Butter a 9 x 13-inch (23 x 33 cm) baking pan and set the rolls in it in 3 rows of 5, leaving about 1/2 inch (1 cm) between them. They will grow into each other and give you soft pull-apart sides. If you want crustier rolls all round, space them further apart on a sheet pan instead.
  9. Second rise
    Cover loosely with plastic wrap or a damp towel and let rise 45 to 60 minutes at room temperature, until the rolls are puffy, touching each other, and look about 1 1/2 times their original size. Poke one gently — the dent should spring back slowly. Underproofed rolls burst open at the sides in the oven; overproofed ones collapse.
  10. Heat the oven and wash the tops
    Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C) about 20 minutes before the second rise finishes. Brush the tops gently with the egg wash using a soft pastry brush, going lightly so you do not deflate them. The egg is what gives you that deep mahogany shine instead of a pale, matte top.
  11. Bake until deeply golden
    Bake on the center rack for 18 to 22 minutes, rotating the pan halfway through, until the tops are a rich golden brown and the sides feel firm. The center of a middle roll should register 190°F (88°C) on an instant-read thermometer. If the tops brown before that, tent loosely with foil and keep going.
  12. Butter them hot
    The moment the pan comes out, brush the tops generously with the 3 tablespoons (42 g) of melted butter and sprinkle with the flaky salt. Hot rolls drink the butter straight in instead of letting it sit on top. Let them cool in the pan for 10 minutes before pulling them apart.
  13. Serve or store
    Serve warm, straight from the pan, with more butter on the table. They are at their absolute best within 4 hours of baking. Store leftovers in a zip-top bag at room temperature for 2 days and refresh them 5 minutes in a 300°F (150°C) oven.
Know when it is done
Milk for the yeast: 105-110°F (40-43°C). Bake at 375°F (190°C) until the center of a middle roll reads 190°F (88°C).
Serve it with
Any holiday table, any pot of soup — and honey butter alongside is never a mistake.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make ahead: after shaping, cover the pan and refrigerate overnight. In the morning let them sit at room temperature 60 to 90 minutes until puffy, then bake as written.
  • ◆Bread flour gives the chew and structure these need. All-purpose works but produces a softer, more cake-like roll that tears rather than pulls.
  • ◆If your kitchen is cold, proof the dough in the oven with only the light on — that pocket sits around 80°F (27°C), which is perfect.
  • ◆Freeze baked rolls for up to 2 months. Thaw at room temperature, then warm 8 minutes at 325°F (165°C) and brush with butter again.
  • ◆Active dry yeast works too — just dissolve it in the warm milk with a pinch of the sugar and wait 10 minutes for it to foam before mixing.

Caesar Salad with Real Dressing⏱ 40 min🍽 4 servingsAdvanced▾

A proper Caesar built from egg yolks, anchovies, and garlic, emulsified by hand until it clings to every leaf. Once you taste the real thing the bottled stuff stops existing.

ClassicDate NightFrom Scratch
Prep
25 min
Cook
15 min
Total
40 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Dressing

Croutons

Salad

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Toast the croutons
    Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Toss the torn bread with the 3 tablespoons (45 ml) olive oil and 1/2 teaspoon salt on a sheet pan and bake for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring once, until deep golden and crisp on the outside but still slightly chewy at the center. Rub the cut garlic clove over the hot croutons the second they come out — the heat pulls the garlic oil right in.
  2. Handle the raw yolks safely
    A classic Caesar uses raw egg yolk, so buy pasteurized eggs if you can find them. If you cannot, coddle whole eggs by lowering them into boiling water for exactly 60 seconds and then into ice water — that kills surface bacteria without setting the yolk. Anyone pregnant, elderly, or immunocompromised should use pasteurized eggs only, or 3 tablespoons (45 ml) of good mayonnaise in place of the yolks.
  3. Mash the anchovy paste
    On a cutting board, chop the 4 anchovy fillets with the grated garlic and 1/4 teaspoon of the kosher salt, then drag the flat of your knife across the pile 10 or 12 times until it turns into a smooth gray paste. The salt acts as an abrasive here, which is why the paste comes together faster than it would with the knife alone. Anchovies are not optional and they will not taste fishy — they dissolve into pure savory depth. Left in chunks, though, you get a nasty bite of raw fish in one forkful.
  4. Build the emulsion base
    In a medium bowl, whisk the egg yolks, anchovy-garlic paste, Dijon, lemon juice, and Worcestershire until completely smooth and pale, about 30 seconds. Set the bowl on a damp folded towel so it cannot spin while you whisk one-handed. Both the yolks and the mustard are emulsifiers, and this base is what will hold a full cup of oil.
  5. Add the oil drop by drop
    Start whisking constantly and add the neutral oil literally a few drops at a time for the first 2 tablespoons (30 ml). You will feel the mixture stiffen and turn glossy as the emulsion takes hold. This slow start is the entire difference between mayonnaise and a broken puddle of oil and egg.
  6. Speed up and finish the oil
    Once it has visibly thickened, pour the rest of the neutral oil in a thin, steady stream while whisking, then do the same with the olive oil. The dressing should end up thick enough to coat a spoon heavily and hold soft peaks. All the olive oil at once would make it bitter, which is why it goes in last and in a smaller amount.
  7. Rescue a broken dressing
    If it splits into a greasy, curdled mess — usually because the oil went in too fast at the start — do not throw it out, because every bit of that flavor is still in the bowl. Put the reserve egg yolk in a clean bowl with 1 teaspoon of warm water, whisk it smooth, then whisk the broken mixture into it a teaspoon at a time exactly the way you began. The fresh yolk gives the oil something to grab onto again. It comes back together every time, and nobody will ever know.
  8. Cheese and season
    Whisk in the 1 oz (30 g) of finely grated Parmigiano, the remaining 1/4 teaspoon kosher salt, and the 1/2 teaspoon black pepper. Taste on a lettuce leaf rather than a spoon, since a leaf tells you how it will actually eat. It should be aggressively sharp and salty — the romaine is going to mute it considerably. Anchovies and Parmigiano are both salty, so go a pinch at a time from here rather than a spoonful.
  9. Prep and dry the romaine
    Separate the leaves, wash them in cold water, and dry them thoroughly in a salad spinner or between towels. Water on the leaves is the number one reason Caesar salads turn watery and sad, because dressing slides off wet lettuce. Leave small inner leaves whole and tear the large outer ones into 3-inch (7.5 cm) pieces.
  10. Chill the leaves
    Put the dried leaves in a large bowl and refrigerate for at least 15 minutes, or up to 4 hours loosely covered. Cold, crisp romaine is what gives a Caesar its snap against the rich dressing. Room-temperature lettuce goes limp within a minute of being dressed.
  11. Dress with a light hand
    Add about two-thirds of the dressing to the cold leaves and toss with your hands, lifting from the bottom, until every leaf carries a thin sheen — not a puddle. Add more only if some leaves look dry. Over-dressed Caesar is heavy and slick; under-dressed can always be fixed at the table.
  12. Plate and finish
    Pile the leaves on chilled plates or a wide platter, tuck the croutons in among them rather than on top so they get a little dressing, and shave the 2 oz (55 g) of Parmigiano over with a vegetable peeler. Finish with the flaky salt and a few extra grinds of pepper. Serve immediately — a Caesar is a five-minute window.
Know when it is done
Use pasteurized eggs for raw yolks, or coddle whole eggs 60 seconds in boiling water. Keep the dressing and the salad below 40°F (4°C) until you serve.
Serve it with
A whole meal with grilled chicken or shrimp added, or the classic opener before steak — try a cold, dry Pinot Grigio.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make ahead: the dressing keeps 3 days covered in the fridge (2 days if using coddled rather than pasteurized eggs). It thickens when cold — whisk in a teaspoon of water to loosen it.
  • ◆A food processor or immersion blender makes this nearly foolproof: blend everything but the oil, then drizzle the oil in with the motor running.
  • ◆Day-old bread makes far better croutons than fresh. Fresh bread has too much moisture and steams into leathery cubes rather than crisping.
  • ◆Buy anchovies packed in oil in a glass jar rather than a flat tin — they are usually meatier, and the leftovers keep in the fridge for a month.
  • ◆For a grilled Caesar, halve the romaine hearts lengthwise, brush with oil, and grill cut side down over high heat for 90 seconds before dressing.

Village-Style Greek Salad⏱ 35 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

No lettuce, big chunks, and a slab of feta laid over the top the way they do it in Greece. It takes twenty minutes and tastes like a hot afternoon by the water.

No CookSummer20 Minutes
Prep
