35 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Salad

Dressing

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Buy the right tomatoes
    This salad has nowhere to hide, so use the ripest tomatoes you can find — heirlooms, vine tomatoes, or big beefsteaks in summer. They should smell like tomato at the stem end and give slightly when squeezed. Out of season, cherry tomatoes halved are far better than pale winter slicers.
  2. Never refrigerate the tomatoes
    Keep tomatoes on the counter until you cut them, not in the fridge. Below about 55°F (13°C) the compounds that make tomatoes taste like tomatoes break down permanently and the flesh goes mealy. This is the single easiest upgrade to any tomato dish.
  3. Cut in big chunks
    Cut the tomatoes into generous 1-inch (2.5 cm) wedges and the cucumber into half-moons about 1/2 inch (1 cm) thick. Greek village salad, horiatiki, is deliberately rustic — small dice turns everything to watery mush within minutes. Big pieces stay juicy and distinct.
  4. Salt the tomatoes and wait
    Put the tomato wedges in a colander set over a bowl, sprinkle with 1/2 teaspoon of the kosher salt, and let them sit 15 minutes. They will release a few tablespoons of intensely flavored juice, which seasons the tomatoes and stops the finished salad from flooding. Save that juice and whisk it into the dressing — it is free flavor.
  5. Tame the raw onion
    Slice the red onion as thin as you can manage, then soak the slices in a bowl of cold water for 10 minutes and drain well. This washes away the harsh sulfur compounds and leaves the sweetness and the crunch. Skip it and one aggressive onion slice can dominate the whole bowl.
  6. Whisk the dressing
    In a small bowl, whisk the olive oil, red wine vinegar, 1 teaspoon of the oregano, the black pepper, and any reserved tomato juice until it looks slightly cloudy and combined. The classic Greek ratio is about 4 parts oil to 1 part vinegar, which is gentler than a standard vinaigrette. Crush the dried oregano between your palms as you add it to wake up the oils.
  7. Combine the vegetables
    In a wide, shallow bowl, gently toss the drained tomatoes, cucumber, drained onion, pepper rings, and olives with the remaining 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt. Use a folding motion rather than stirring so you do not bruise the tomatoes. The olives go in with their pits, which is traditional — just warn whoever you are feeding.
  8. Dress and rest
    Pour the dressing over and toss gently to coat, then let the salad stand 5 minutes at room temperature. That short rest lets the vinegar and oil find their way into the cucumber and pepper. Room temperature is important — cold mutes olive oil and dulls tomato flavor.
  9. Lay the feta on top
    Set the whole 6 oz (170 g) block of feta on top of the salad rather than crumbling it in. Drizzle it with a little olive oil from the bowl, sprinkle over the remaining 1/2 teaspoon oregano and the flaky salt. Everyone breaks off pieces with their fork, which is the whole point — crumbled feta dissolves into the dressing and disappears.
Know when it is done
No cooking involved. Serve at cool room temperature, around 65°F (18°C) — colder than that and the olive oil turns waxy and the tomatoes taste like nothing.
Serve it with
Grilled lamb, chicken souvlaki, or just bread and a cold glass of Assyrtiko.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Buy feta in brine, not the dry pre-crumbled kind. Greek sheep's milk feta is creamy and tangy; the crumbled tubs are drier, saltier, and usually made from cow's milk.
  • ◆Serve with a piece of crusty bread and mop the bowl at the end. The oil and tomato juice left behind is considered the best part of the dish.
  • ◆Make ahead: chop everything except the tomatoes up to a day early. Cut and salt the tomatoes and dress the salad no more than 30 minutes before eating.
  • ◆Add 2 tablespoons (20 g) of capers, rinsed, or a handful of purslane if you find it — both are common in the Greek islands and both add a welcome sharpness.
  • ◆If your olive oil tastes flat, it is old. Good extra-virgin should taste peppery at the back of the throat, and in a four-ingredient dressing you will notice.

Crunchy, tangy, and creamy without ever turning into a puddle, because the cabbage gets salted first. This is the slaw that belongs on a pulled pork sandwich.

▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Cabbage

Dressing

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Shred the cabbage thin
    Cut each cabbage quarter into thin ribbons about 1/8 inch (3 mm) wide, working from the cut side down so the wedge stays stable. A sharp chef's knife gives better texture than a food processor, which bruises and shreds unevenly. Thin ribbons hold dressing; thick chunks just push it around the bowl.
  2. Salt and drain
    Toss the shredded green and red cabbage with the 1 tablespoon (18 g) kosher salt in a colander set over a bowl and let it sit for 30 minutes at room temperature. You will see a surprising amount of liquid collect underneath — often 1/2 cup (120 ml) or more. This is the entire secret to slaw that stays crisp instead of turning watery in an hour.
  3. Rinse the salt away
    Rinse the cabbage thoroughly under cold running water for 30 seconds, tossing with your hands so the salt washes off every ribbon. Skipping this leaves you with a slaw so salty it is inedible. The cabbage has already given up its water, and rinsing will not put it back.
  4. Dry it completely
    Spin the rinsed cabbage in a salad spinner in batches, or gather it in a clean towel and wring it out over the sink. It should feel barely damp, not wet. Any water left clinging will thin the dressing into something runny within twenty minutes.
  5. Grate the carrot
    Grate the peeled carrots on the large holes of a box grater and add them to the dried cabbage. Do not salt the carrots — they are much lower in water and salting turns them limp. The carrot is for sweetness and color as much as for crunch.
  6. Whisk the dressing
    In a medium bowl, whisk the mayonnaise, buttermilk, cider vinegar, lemon juice, sugar, Dijon, celery seed, black pepper, and 1/4 teaspoon salt until completely smooth. It should be thick enough to coat a spoon but pourable. The buttermilk is what keeps this from tasting like straight mayonnaise.
  7. Taste and balance
    Taste the dressing on its own and adjust before it goes anywhere near the cabbage. It should taste noticeably sharper and sweeter than you want the final slaw to be, since the vegetables will mute it. Add vinegar 1 teaspoon at a time for sharpness, sugar 1 teaspoon at a time for balance.
  8. Dress lightly at first
    Pour about three-quarters of the dressing over the cabbage and carrots and toss with tongs until every strand is coated. Add the rest only if it looks dry. You can always add more dressing, but you cannot take it back out.
  9. Chill to marry
    Cover and refrigerate for at least 1 hour before serving. The flavors need that time to settle together, and the cabbage softens just slightly into the perfect texture. Straight from the bowl it tastes disjointed, like raw cabbage next to mayonnaise.
  10. Refresh and serve cold
    Just before serving, toss the slaw again to redistribute the dressing that has settled to the bottom, and taste for salt one last time. Stir in the chopped chives now so they stay bright green. Serve cold, below 40°F (4°C), and keep the bowl on ice if it is sitting out at a cookout.
Know when it is done
No cooking. Serve and store cold, below 40°F (4°C); do not leave a mayonnaise dressing at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
Serve it with
Pulled pork, fried chicken, or a burger — and a cold cider or lemonade.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make ahead: this is better on day two and keeps 4 days in the fridge. The pre-salting is what lets it survive that long without weeping.
  • ◆For a vinegar slaw instead, skip the mayo and buttermilk and use 1/2 cup (120 ml) cider vinegar, 1/3 cup (80 ml) neutral oil, and 3 tablespoons (36 g) sugar.
  • ◆A bagged coleslaw mix works in a pinch, but still salt and drain it. Bagged cabbage is often wetter than a whole head, not drier.
  • ◆Celery seed is the flavor people cannot identify but always miss. It is worth buying a jar just for this and for potato salad.
  • ◆Food safety at a picnic: mayonnaise-based slaw should not sit above 40°F (4°C) for more than 2 hours, or 1 hour if it is above 90°F (32°C) outside.

Honey Roasted Carrots with Thyme⏱ 40 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Roasted until the edges caramelize, then tossed in a honey butter that turns them almost candy-sweet. Cheap, easy, and the first thing to disappear from the table.

WeeknightHolidayVegetarian
Prep
10 min
Cook
30 min
Total
40 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Carrots

Honey butter glaze

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Heat the oven high
    Set a rack in the upper third of the oven and heat to 425°F (220°C). Carrots are full of sugar and need real heat to caramelize rather than just soften. A lower oven gives you sweet steamed carrots, which are fine but forgettable.
  2. Cut on a bias
    Peel the carrots and cut them on a strong diagonal into pieces about 2 inches (5 cm) long, halving the fat ends lengthwise so every piece is roughly the same thickness. Angled cuts expose far more surface area than straight rounds, and surface area is where browning happens. Uniform thickness is what keeps the thin ends from burning.
  3. Dry and oil them
    Pat the cut carrots dry with a towel, then toss them in a bowl with the 2 tablespoons (30 ml) olive oil, 1 teaspoon salt, and the pepper. Every surface should look barely glossy. Wet carrots steam themselves and stay pale no matter how hot the oven is.
  4. Hold back the honey
    Do not add the honey yet. Sugar burns at roasting temperatures long before carrots are tender, and honey added at the start turns black and bitter in about 15 minutes. It goes on at the very end, when the carrots are already cooked through.
  5. Spread them out
    Arrange the carrots in a single layer on a rimmed sheet pan with space between the pieces, cut sides down where you can manage it. Crowding traps steam and the carrots will never brown. If your pan looks full, split them across two pans.
  6. Roast the first stretch
    Roast for 20 minutes without stirring. The undersides need continuous contact with the hot pan to develop those dark caramelized patches. You should smell something distinctly sweet by about minute 15.
  7. Flip and finish
    Turn the carrots with a spatula and roast another 8 to 12 minutes, until they are deeply browned in places and a knife slides into the thickest piece with only slight resistance. They should be tender but still hold their shape when you lift them. Total time runs 28 to 32 minutes depending on thickness.
  8. Make the honey butter
    While the carrots finish, melt the butter in a small saucepan over medium-low heat, then whisk in the honey, lemon juice, and thyme leaves. Let it bubble gently for about 60 seconds until slightly thickened and glossy. The lemon keeps the honey from being cloying and the thyme keeps it from tasting like dessert.
  9. Glaze and serve
    Tip the hot carrots into a warm serving bowl, pour the honey butter over, and toss until every piece shines. Scatter the toasted nuts and the flaky salt on top. Serve within 10 minutes — the glaze is at its best while it is still loose and warm.
Know when it is done
Roast at 425°F (220°C). Done when the edges are darkly caramelized and a knife meets only slight resistance in the thickest piece.
Serve it with
Roast chicken, pork loin, or a holiday ham — with a glass of off-dry Riesling.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Bagged baby carrots do not work well here. They are cut from larger carrots, hold extra water, and roast to a rubbery texture rather than caramelizing.
  • ◆Make ahead: peel and cut the carrots up to 3 days early and store them in water in the fridge. Drain and dry them thoroughly before roasting.
  • ◆Maple syrup works one-for-one in place of honey, and browns a little less aggressively if your oven runs hot.
  • ◆For a savory version, swap the honey butter for 2 tablespoons (30 ml) of olive oil, 1 teaspoon of cumin, and a squeeze of lime.
  • ◆If your carrots are old and bendy, soak them in ice water for 20 minutes first — they firm right back up and roast much better.

Green Beans Almondine⏱ 30 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Snappy blanched beans tossed in brown butter with toasted almonds and a hit of lemon. It is a fifty-year-old French restaurant classic and it still beats everything else on the table.

French ClassicHoliday30 Minutes
Prep
15 min
Cook
15 min
Total
30 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Beans

Brown butter almonds

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Set up the blanch and shock
    Bring 4 quarts (3.8 L) of water to a rolling boil with the 2 tablespoons (36 g) kosher salt, and fill a large bowl with ice and cold water right next to the stove. The water should taste like the sea — that is how the beans get seasoned all the way through. Having the ice bath ready before the beans go in is not optional, because you will need it within four minutes.
  2. Trim only the stem ends
    Line the beans up and cut off the tough stem ends in bunches, but leave the thin tapered tails on. Those tails are tender, they look beautiful on the plate, and trimming both ends is a habit worth breaking. Discard any beans that are limp or rusty at the ends.
  3. Blanch until snappy
    Drop the beans into the boiling water and cook for 3 to 4 minutes for standard green beans, or 2 minutes for thin haricots verts. Fish one out at 3 minutes and bite it — it should be bright green and squeaky with a little bite left, not soft. They will cook slightly more in the pan later, so pull them a touch early.
  4. Shock them cold
    Transfer the beans immediately into the ice water with a spider or tongs and swirl until they are cold all the way through, about 60 seconds. This stops the cooking on a dime and sets that vivid green color. Beans left to cool on their own keep cooking from residual heat and turn olive drab.
  5. Dry them thoroughly
    Drain the beans and spread them on a clean kitchen towel, then roll the towel up and pat them dry. Wet beans will hit the brown butter and spit violently, and the water will also loosen the sauce. At this point they can wait, refrigerated, for up to 2 days.
  6. Toast the almonds in butter
    Melt the 4 tablespoons (55 g) of butter in a 12-inch (30 cm) skillet over medium heat, then add the sliced almonds. Stir constantly for 3 to 4 minutes — the butter will foam, the foam will subside, and the almonds will turn golden. Never walk away from this; almonds go from perfect to burnt in about 30 seconds.
  7. Brown the butter
    Keep stirring as the milk solids at the bottom of the pan turn from pale to amber and the smell shifts from buttery to nutty and toasted, about 1 to 2 minutes more. Those browned milk solids are the entire flavor of the dish. If you see black flecks and smell anything acrid, start over — burnt butter cannot be saved.
  8. Add the aromatics
    Drop the heat to medium-low and add the sliced shallot and garlic. Cook for 90 seconds, stirring, until the shallot is soft and translucent and the garlic is fragrant but still pale. The lower heat stops the garlic from scorching in butter that is already very hot.
  9. Toss the beans through
    Add the dried beans along with the 3/4 teaspoon salt and the black pepper, and toss with tongs for 2 to 3 minutes until they are heated through and coated in butter and almonds. They should sizzle steadily, not smoke. Any longer and the beans go from snappy to soft.
  10. Finish with lemon
    Pull the pan off the heat and add the 2 tablespoons (30 ml) lemon juice and the zest, tossing to combine — it will sizzle and steam for a second. Off-heat acid keeps its brightness instead of cooking away. Taste, add salt in small pinches if needed, and serve straight from the pan while everything is hot.
Know when it is done
No internal temperature to hit. The beans are right when they are bright green and still snap slightly; the butter is right at amber with a nutty smell, around 250°F (120°C).
Serve it with
The classic partner to roast chicken, turkey, or a piece of sole — with a glass of white Burgundy.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make ahead: blanch, shock, and dry the beans up to 2 days early and keep them in a bag in the fridge. Then the whole dish is a 6-minute job at dinner.
  • ◆Haricots verts are thinner and more tender than standard green beans and are worth the extra dollar. Just cut the blanching time to 2 minutes.
  • ◆Buy sliced almonds, not slivered. Slivered almonds are too thick to toast evenly in a pan and stay hard against the tender beans.
  • ◆Use a stainless or light-colored skillet so you can actually see the butter change color. In a black cast iron pan you are browning butter blind.
  • ◆For a richer version, add 2 oz (55 g) of chopped bacon or pancetta at the start and use only 2 tablespoons (28 g) of butter.

Cauliflower Gratin with Mornay⏱ 1 hr 15 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Tender cauliflower under a proper Gruyere cheese sauce with a crunchy panko lid. It is macaroni and cheese in vegetable form, and nobody at the table will complain.

HolidayComfort FoodMake Ahead
Prep
25 min
Cook
40 min
Total
1 hr 15 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Cauliflower

Mornay sauce

Topping

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Heat the oven and prep the dish
    Set a rack in the upper-middle of the oven and heat to 375°F (190°C). Butter a 9 x 13-inch (23 x 33 cm) baking dish or a 3-quart (2.8 L) gratin dish with the softened butter. A wide, shallow dish gives you more browned top per serving, which is the point of a gratin.
  2. Cut even florets
    Break the cauliflower into florets about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) across, cutting through the stems rather than tearing so they stay intact. Trim the tough core but keep the tender inner stems — they are sweet and cook at the same rate as the florets. Even sizing means everything is tender at the same moment.
  3. Blanch the cauliflower
    Bring 4 quarts (3.8 L) of water to a boil with the 2 tablespoons (36 g) salt and cook the florets for 4 to 5 minutes, until a knife enters with slight resistance. You want them about 80 percent cooked, since they will finish in the oven. Raw cauliflower baked in sauce releases water and gives you a soupy gratin.
  4. Drain and dry very well
    Drain the florets in a colander and let them steam dry for a full 5 minutes, shaking once or twice, then blot the tops with a towel. Every drop of water still clinging will thin your sauce in the oven. This is the step people skip and then wonder why the gratin is watery.
  5. Start the roux
    Melt the 4 tablespoons (55 g) butter in a medium saucepan over medium heat until it foams. Whisk in the 1/4 cup (30 g) flour and cook, whisking constantly, for 90 seconds to 2 minutes. It will smell faintly like toast and turn a shade blonder — that is the raw flour taste cooking off.
  6. Build the bechamel
    Add the warm milk about 1/2 cup (120 ml) at a time, whisking hard until each addition is fully smooth before you add the next. Warm milk and gradual addition are the two things that prevent lumps. Once all the milk is in, the sauce should be smooth and pourable.
  7. Thicken and season
    Bring the sauce to a gentle simmer and cook 4 to 5 minutes, whisking often and scraping the corners, until it thickly coats a spoon. Whisk in the Dijon, nutmeg, 1 teaspoon salt, and the black pepper. Taste it — it should be assertive, because a pile of cauliflower is about to dilute it.
  8. Melt the cheese off the heat
    Pull the pan completely off the burner and let it sit 60 seconds, then add the Gruyere and half the Parmigiano in three handfuls, stirring until each melts. Cheese added over direct heat overheats, the proteins tighten, and the sauce turns grainy and greasy. Off the heat it stays glossy and smooth.
  9. Combine and fill the dish
    Fold the dried cauliflower into the sauce until every floret is coated, then transfer everything to the buttered dish and spread it into an even layer. Nudge the florets so they sit snugly rather than in a mound. Even depth means even baking.
  10. Make the crunchy topping
    Toss the panko with the 2 tablespoons (28 g) melted butter, the remaining Parmigiano, the parsley, and 1/4 teaspoon salt until the crumbs look evenly damp. Scatter it over the gratin in a thin, even layer. Buttered crumbs fry as they bake, which is what makes them crunch instead of going soggy.
  11. Bake until bubbling
    Bake for 25 to 30 minutes, until the sauce is bubbling slowly at the edges and the topping is golden brown. The center should register at least 165°F (74°C) on an instant-read thermometer. If the top is pale but the sauce is bubbling, run it under the broiler for 60 to 90 seconds, watching the whole time.
  12. Rest before serving
    Let the gratin sit on a rack for 10 minutes before you serve it. The sauce is thin straight out of the oven and needs that time to set enough to spoon cleanly. Serve hot, scooping down to the bottom so everyone gets both crust and sauce.
Know when it is done
Bake at 375°F (190°C) until the center reads at least 165°F (74°C) and the edges bubble. Rest 10 minutes so the sauce sets.
Serve it with
Roast beef, ham, or a big green salad if it is the main event — with a glass of dry Alsatian white.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Grate your own Gruyere. Pre-shredded cheese is dusted with cellulose to keep it from clumping, and that starch makes a Mornay sauce gritty.
  • ◆Make ahead: assemble everything except the panko topping up to 24 hours early and refrigerate. Add the topping just before baking and add 10 to 15 minutes from cold.
  • ◆Swap in broccoli, romanesco, or a mix — the blanching time stays about the same for florets of the same size.
  • ◆If the sauce breaks and goes greasy, whisk in 2 tablespoons (30 ml) of cold milk off the heat. It usually pulls back together.
  • ◆For a sharper gratin, replace 2 oz (55 g) of the Gruyere with aged white cheddar. Do not use mozzarella, which turns stringy and bland in a Mornay.

Crispy Buttery Garlic Bread⏱ 25 min🍽 6 servingsEasy▾

Crunchy on top, soft underneath, and loaded with enough garlic butter to soak through. Twenty-five minutes and it makes any pasta night feel like a restaurant.

25 min

6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Heat the oven
    Set a rack in the upper-middle of the oven and heat to 425°F (220°C). A hot oven crisps the cut surface quickly, before the interior of the loaf dries out and turns to toast all the way through. Have a rimmed sheet pan ready but do not preheat it.
  2. Split the loaf
    Cut the loaf in half horizontally with a serrated knife, using a long sawing motion rather than pressing down so you do not crush the crumb. You want two long halves with as much flat cut surface as possible. That flat face is where all the butter goes.
  3. Rub with raw garlic
    Rub the cut faces all over with the halved garlic clove, pressing firmly so the rough surface of the bread grates the clove away. This layers a fresh, sharp garlic note underneath the mellow roasted garlic in the butter. It takes 20 seconds and it is the trick most recipes leave out.
  4. Grate the garlic finely
    Grate the 6 garlic cloves on a microplane into a bowl so they turn into a wet paste rather than pieces. Chopped garlic sits in chunks that scorch and turn bitter under a hot oven, while paste dissolves evenly through the butter. If you only have a knife, mince finely and then mash with a pinch of salt.
  5. Make the garlic butter
    Mash the softened butter with the garlic paste, half the Parmigiano, half the parsley, the 3/4 teaspoon salt, black pepper, and the red pepper flakes using a fork until it is a uniform, spreadable paste. The butter must be genuinely soft, around 65°F (18°C) — cold butter will not blend and melted butter will just run off the bread.
  6. Spread it all the way out
    Spread the garlic butter over both cut faces, going right to the crusts and into every hole in the crumb. Use all of it; it looks like too much and it is exactly the right amount. Bare edges are the parts that come out dry and disappointing.
  7. Bake cut side up
    Put the halves cut side up on the sheet pan and bake for 10 to 12 minutes, until the butter has fully melted into the bread and the edges are turning golden. The kitchen should smell strongly of garlic by minute 8. The bottom crust will crisp against the hot pan at the same time.
  8. Broil for the finish
    Scatter the remaining Parmigiano over the tops and slide the pan under the broiler for 1 to 2 minutes, until the surface is spotted deep golden brown and the cheese is bubbling. Do not walk away for even 30 seconds — broilers go from perfect to charcoal faster than anything else in the kitchen. Pull it when you see the first dark spots.
  9. Cut and serve hot
    Scatter the remaining parsley over, move the halves to a cutting board, and cut into 2-inch (5 cm) wide pieces with a serrated knife. Serve immediately, piled in a napkin-lined basket so the steam can escape. Covering it tightly softens the crust you just spent 15 minutes building.
Know when it is done
Bake at 425°F (220°C) then broil 1-2 minutes. It is done when the surface is spotted deep golden brown and the butter has soaked fully into the crumb.
Serve it with
Spaghetti and meatballs, lasagna, or a bowl of tomato soup — with a glass of Chianti.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make ahead: the garlic butter keeps 2 weeks in the fridge or 3 months in the freezer. Roll it in parchment into a log and slice off what you need.
  • ◆You can assemble the buttered loaf, wrap it in foil, and freeze it. Bake from frozen at 425°F (220°C) for 20 minutes in the foil, then open it up and broil.
  • ◆For soft, pull-apart garlic bread instead, wrap the buttered loaf in foil and bake 15 minutes at 350°F (175°C) without broiling.
  • ◆Skip the pre-minced garlic in a jar. It is preserved in acid and tastes sour and metallic once it hits heat.
  • ◆A dense, chewy loaf like ciabatta or a bakery Italian holds up best. Soft supermarket sub rolls collapse into a greasy sponge.

Buttery Rice Pilaf with Orzo⏱ 50 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Toasted orzo and long-grain rice cooked in seasoned broth until every grain is separate and glossy. It is the boxed stuff you grew up on, except actually good.

WeeknightMake AheadSide Dish

6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Pilaf

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Rinse the rice
    Put the rice in a fine-mesh sieve and rinse under cold running water, stirring with your fingers, until the water runs mostly clear — about 60 to 90 seconds. Rinsing washes away loose surface starch, which is what makes rice clump and turn sticky. Shake the sieve well and let it drain while you start the aromatics.
  2. Sweat the onion
    Melt the 3 tablespoons (42 g) butter with the olive oil in a heavy 3-quart (2.8 L) saucepan over medium heat. Add the diced onion and a pinch of the salt and cook 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until soft and translucent with no browning. The oil raises the smoke point so the butter does not scorch while the onion sweats.
  3. Toast the orzo
    Add the orzo and stir constantly for 2 to 3 minutes, until the little grains turn a nutty golden brown, like the color of a toasted almond. This toasting is what gives pilaf its distinctive flavor and keeps the pasta from going gluey. Watch closely — the pieces at the edge of the pan color first.
  4. Toast the rice too
    Add the drained rice and the minced garlic and stir for another 90 seconds to 2 minutes, until the grains look chalky and opaque rather than translucent, and smell faintly popcorn-like. Coating each grain in fat helps them stay separate in the finished pilaf. The garlic goes in now because a full two-minute toast would burn it.
  5. Add the broth
    Pour in the 3 1/4 cups (780 ml) of broth all at once, add the bay leaf, the remaining salt, and the black pepper, and stir once to loosen anything stuck to the bottom. It will steam and hiss loudly. The ratio here is a little over 1 1/2 parts liquid to 1 part grain, which is what 1 1/2 cups of rice plus 1/2 cup of dry orzo actually need — cut the broth back and the orzo comes out chalky in the middle. Scraping the bottom now matters too, because a stuck patch of orzo will scorch during the simmer.
  6. Bring to a boil, then drop it
    Raise the heat and bring the pot to a full boil, then immediately reduce to the lowest setting that keeps a bare simmer going. Cover with a tight-fitting lid. If your lid is loose, lay a sheet of foil across the pot before putting the lid on, since escaping steam means undercooked rice.
  7. Simmer undisturbed
    Cook, covered, for 18 minutes without lifting the lid or stirring even once. Every peek releases the steam that is doing the cooking, and stirring rubs starch loose and turns the pilaf into risotto. Trust the timer and walk away.
  8. Rest off the heat
    Take the pot off the burner and let it stand, still covered, for 10 full minutes. The rice continues to steam and the moisture redistributes from the wetter grains at the bottom to the drier ones on top. Skipping this rest is why home-cooked rice is so often soggy underneath and firm on top.
  9. Fluff and enrich
    Remove the lid and the bay leaf, dot the cold tablespoon (14 g) of butter over the surface, and fluff with a fork, lifting and separating rather than stirring. The grains should fall apart individually and look glossy. If you see any liquid at the bottom, leave the pot uncovered over low heat for 2 minutes.
  10. Finish and serve
    Fold in the parsley, lemon zest, and the toasted almonds if you are using them, and taste for salt — broth-cooked rice usually needs another 1/4 teaspoon. Serve hot, in a warm bowl. Pilaf holds well covered for about 20 minutes if dinner runs late.
Know when it is done
Simmer covered on low for 18 minutes, then rest 10 minutes off the heat. Serve hot, above 140°F (60°C); cool and refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours.
Serve it with
Roast chicken, lamb kebabs, or anything with a pan sauce that needs somewhere to land.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Broken vermicelli works in place of orzo and is the more traditional choice. Snap it into 1/2-inch (1 cm) pieces and toast it exactly the same way.
  • ◆Make ahead: cook completely, cool, and refrigerate up to 4 days. Reheat covered with 2 tablespoons (30 ml) of water in the microwave or a low oven.
  • ◆Use low-sodium broth so you control the salt. Regular broth plus a teaspoon of salt will come out aggressively salty once it reduces into the rice.
  • ◆If the rice is still firm after resting, add 3 tablespoons (45 ml) of hot water, cover, and give it 5 more minutes on the lowest heat.
  • ◆For a richer pilaf, stir in 1/3 cup (50 g) of golden raisins with the broth and finish with toasted pine nuts instead of almonds.

Breakfast is mostly eggs, batter, and butter — three things that reward low heat and a little patience, and punish rushing more than almost anything else you cook.

Fluffy Buttermilk Pancakes⏱ 30 min🍽 Makes 12 four-inch pancakesEasy▾

Tall, tangy, cloud-soft pancakes from one bowl of dry and one bowl of wet. The whole trick is a lumpy batter and a griddle that is genuinely hot before the first scoop goes down.

Weekend30 MinutesKid Friendly
Prep
10 min
Cook
20 min
Total
30 min
Serves
Makes 12 four-inch pancakes
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Dry

Wet

For the griddle and table

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Heat the griddle first
    Set a large nonstick skillet, griddle, or cast-iron pan over medium heat and let it sit for a full 5 minutes before you mix anything. You are aiming for a surface around 375°F (190°C), and the test is simple: flick a few drops of water on it, and they should skitter and disappear in about 2 seconds. If they vanish instantly with a violent hiss, it is too hot; if they just sit there and slowly steam, keep waiting. A pan that is still warming up is the single most common reason first pancakes come out pale and flat.
  2. Whisk the dry ingredients
    In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, baking soda, and salt for a good 15 seconds until you see no streaks of white powder. Whisking the leaveners through the flour now means they are evenly spread, which is why every pancake rises the same amount instead of one puffing and the next staying flat. Spoon the flour into the measuring cup and level it with a knife rather than scooping — scooping packs in up to 20 percent extra flour and gives you dense, dry pancakes.
  3. Mix the wet ingredients
    In a second bowl, whisk the buttermilk, eggs, and vanilla until the mixture is one uniform pale color with no clear ropes of egg white left. Drizzle in the melted butter while whisking so it disperses into tiny droplets instead of seizing into hard yellow flecks. Adding the vanilla to the wet bowl rather than at the end means it distributes evenly through every pancake instead of perfuming one bite. If your buttermilk came straight from the fridge, the butter will firm up a little — that is fine and it will still work, but room-temperature buttermilk gives you a smoother batter.
  4. Combine, but barely
    Pour the wet into the dry and fold with a rubber spatula just until no dry pockets of flour remain, about 10 to 12 strokes. The batter should look lumpy and shaggy, and that is exactly right — those lumps are unmixed flour that will hydrate as it rests. Every extra stir develops gluten, and gluten is what turns a tender pancake into a rubbery one. If you can still see a few small lumps the size of peas, stop.
  5. Rest the batter 10 minutes
    Leave the bowl alone on the counter for 10 minutes while the griddle finishes heating. During this rest the flour absorbs liquid, the lumps dissolve on their own, and the baking soda starts reacting with the acidic buttermilk to build bubbles. You will actually see the surface puff slightly and go a little foamy. Do not stir it again after the rest, or you will knock the air right back out.
  6. Grease the pan lightly
    Drop about ½ teaspoon of butter on the hot surface, swirl it around, then wipe most of it away with a folded paper towel. You want a barely-there film, not a pool. Too much fat fries the outside of the pancake into a blotchy, uneven brown before the inside sets. Re-wipe with the same buttery towel between batches rather than adding fresh butter each time.
  7. Portion the batter
    Scoop a scant ¼ cup (60 ml) of batter per pancake and pour it from about 2 inches (5 cm) above the pan so it spreads into a neat circle on its own. Fit only 3 pancakes in a 12-inch skillet, leaving at least 2 inches (5 cm) between them so you have room to get a spatula under each one. Resist the urge to spread the batter with the back of the spoon — a thick pancake is a tall pancake.
  8. Wait for the bubble signal
    Cook undisturbed for 2 to 3 minutes. The pancake is ready to flip when bubbles rise and pop across the whole surface and the holes stay open instead of filling back in, and the edges look dry and matte rather than wet and shiny. Peek underneath with a thin spatula — you want an even golden brown, not dark spots. Flipping early gives you a raw seam through the middle.
  9. Flip once and only once
    Slide a thin spatula fully under the pancake and turn it over in one confident motion, close to the pan so it does not splat. Cook the second side for 1½ to 2 minutes; it will never brown as evenly as the first side, and that is normal. Do not press down on the pancake with the spatula — you are squeezing out the exact air you spent ten minutes building. The pancake is done when the sides feel springy and the center domes slightly.
  10. Hold them properly and serve
    Transfer finished pancakes to a wire rack set on a sheet pan in a 200°F (95°C) oven while you cook the rest, for up to 20 minutes. A rack lets steam escape from underneath so the bottoms stay dry; stacking them on a plate traps that steam and makes them soggy in about 90 seconds. Serve with softened salted butter and maple syrup you have warmed for 30 seconds in the microwave, because cold syrup instantly chills a hot pancake.
Know when it is done
Griddle surface about 375°F (190°C) — a water droplet should skitter and vanish in roughly 2 seconds. A finished pancake reads about 200°F (93°C) in the center and springs back when pressed.
Serve it with
Crisp bacon, hot black coffee, and cold orange juice — the salt and acid keep all that sweetness from getting heavy.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆No buttermilk? Stir 2 tbsp (30 ml) lemon juice or white vinegar into 2 cups (480 ml) whole milk and let it sit 10 minutes. It will not be as thick, so the pancakes spread a little more, but the acid still activates the baking soda.
  • ◆The first pancake is a test pancake in every kitchen on earth. Use it to calibrate your heat, then adjust the burner up or down half a notch before the real batch.
  • ◆For blueberry pancakes, do not stir the berries into the batter — the juice turns everything gray-green. Pour the batter, then scatter 6 to 8 fresh berries on top of each pancake before it sets.
  • ◆Make-ahead: whisk the dry ingredients into a jar up to a month in advance. In the morning it is a two-minute job. Fully cooked pancakes freeze flat on a sheet pan, then bag them and reheat in a toaster straight from frozen.
  • ◆If your pancakes are browning before they rise, the pan is too hot. Pull it off the burner for 60 seconds, lower the heat a notch, and start again.

Crisp Belgian Waffles⏱ 45 min🍽 Makes 6 Belgian wafflesMedium▾

Deep-pocketed waffles with a shattering crust and a custardy middle, thanks to a little cornstarch and whipped egg whites. They stay crisp on the plate instead of wilting after two minutes.

WeekendBrunchMake Ahead
Prep
15 min
Cook
30 min
Total
45 min
Serves
Makes 6 Belgian waffles
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Dry

Wet

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Preheat the iron completely
    Turn the waffle iron on to medium-high and give it a full 10 minutes before the first waffle, even if the ready light comes on sooner. Most indicator lights only track the bottom plate, and a lukewarm top plate is why waffles come out pale and floppy on one side. The iron is truly ready when a drop of water flicked on it evaporates in a couple of seconds with a sharp hiss.
  2. Whisk the dry ingredients
    In a large bowl, whisk the flour, cornstarch, sugar, baking powder, baking soda, and salt together for 15 seconds. The cornstarch is not filler — it has no gluten, so it dilutes the flour's protein and gives you a crust that stays crisp for 10 minutes instead of going soft the moment it hits a plate. Make sure no white lumps of baking powder survive, since one concentrated pocket tastes soapy.
  3. Separate the eggs carefully
    Crack each egg and let the white run into a clean, completely grease-free medium bowl, dropping the yolk into a second bowl. Any speck of yolk in the whites will keep them from whipping properly, so separate each egg over an empty cup first and transfer it once you know it is clean. Room-temperature whites whip taller and faster than cold ones, so pull the eggs out 15 minutes early if you can.
  4. Mix the yolk base
    Whisk the two yolks with the buttermilk and vanilla until smooth and uniform in color. Stream in the melted butter while whisking constantly so it emulsifies into fine droplets rather than pooling on top. If the butter is too hot it will cook the yolks into little threads, so let it cool for a couple of minutes off the heat — it should feel warm, not hot, on your wrist.
  5. Whip the whites to soft peaks
    Beat the egg whites with a hand mixer on medium-high for about 90 seconds, or by hand with a balloon whisk for 3 to 4 minutes, until they hold a peak that flops over gently when you lift the beater. Stop there — stiff, dry peaks break into clumps and will not fold in smoothly. These whites are what give a Belgian waffle its light, almost hollow interior.
  6. Combine wet and dry
    Pour the yolk mixture into the dry ingredients and stir with a rubber spatula just until the flour disappears, roughly 12 strokes. Lumps are fine and expected. Overworking the batter now builds gluten and gives you a chewy, bready waffle instead of a crisp one, so stop while it still looks a little rough.
  7. Fold in the whites
    Add about a third of the whipped whites and stir them in normally to loosen the thick batter. Then add the rest and fold gently: cut down through the middle with the spatula, sweep along the bottom of the bowl, and lift the batter over the top, rotating the bowl a quarter turn each time. Stop when you still see a few faint white streaks — fully erasing them means you have deflated the air you just whipped in.
  8. Grease and fill the iron
    Brush both plates with melted butter or oil, even on a nonstick iron, because the sugar in the batter loves to stick. Ladle about ¾ cup (180 ml) of batter into the center of a standard Belgian iron and spread it toward the edges with the back of the ladle, stopping about ½ inch (1 cm) short. It will expand and fill in on its own; overfilling means batter oozing out the sides and burning onto the hinge.
  9. Cook without peeking
    Close the lid and cook for 4 to 5 minutes without opening it. Opening the iron early tears the waffle in half, because the structure has not set yet. Your real cue is the steam: at first it will billow out the sides, and when it slows to a thin wisp the waffle is close. Open it then and look for a deep, even golden brown with dry-looking ridges.
  10. Rest on a rack, never a plate
    Move each waffle straight to a wire rack set over a sheet pan in a 200°F (95°C) oven while the rest cook. Stacking waffles traps steam and softens the crust you just worked to build; a rack lets air circulate on all sides so they actually get crisper as they sit. They will hold beautifully for up to 30 minutes this way.
  11. Serve hot with warm syrup
    Dust the waffles with powdered sugar through a small sieve and serve with maple syrup you have warmed for about 30 seconds. Belgian waffles are best within a minute or two of leaving the iron, so bring people to the table rather than trying to cook everything first. A pat of salted butter melting into the deep pockets is the whole point of those pockets.
Know when it is done
Cook on a medium-high iron for 4 to 5 minutes, until the steam slows to a wisp and the waffle is deep golden. The interior reads about 205°F (96°C) when fully set.
Serve it with
Strawberries macerated with a spoonful of sugar and a mound of lightly whipped cream, plus strong coffee.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆For overnight yeasted waffles with a deeper flavor, swap the baking powder for 1 tsp (3 g) instant yeast, mix everything except the egg whites the night before, and refrigerate. Fold in the whipped whites in the morning.
  • ◆Freeze leftovers flat on a sheet pan, then transfer to a bag. Reheat straight from frozen in a toaster on medium — they come back crisper than any microwave version.
  • ◆If waffles stick to the iron, it usually means you opened it too early or under-greased it. Let them cook 30 seconds longer next time and brush both plates, not just the bottom.
  • ◆Buttermilk substitute: 1¾ cups (420 ml) whole milk plus 1 tbsp plus 2 tsp (25 ml) lemon juice, rested 10 minutes. The texture is slightly less rich but the rise is the same.
  • ◆Savory version: skip the sugar and vanilla, fold in ½ cup (55 g) grated sharp cheddar and 2 tbsp chopped chives, then top with a fried egg.

Thick-Cut Brioche French Toast⏱ 30 min🍽 4 servingsEasy▾

Custardy all the way to the center with a lacy, caramelized crust — the version that tastes like a bread pudding you can eat with a fork. Thick, slightly stale brioche is the entire secret.

30 MinutesBrunchKid Friendly
Prep
10 min
Cook
20 min
Total
30 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the toast

Custard

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Start with dry bread
    Brioche that is a day or two old soaks up custard like a sponge; fresh, soft brioche turns to mush the second it hits the bowl. If your loaf is bakery-fresh, lay the slices on a sheet pan and dry them in a 275°F (135°C) oven for 10 minutes, flipping once. They should feel dry and slightly firm to the touch but not toasted or colored. Cut the slices a full 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick so there is enough interior to stay creamy.
  2. Whisk the custard properly
    In a wide, shallow dish, whisk the eggs alone for 30 seconds first, until they are completely uniform and no ropey strands of white remain. Then whisk in the milk, cream, sugar, vanilla, cinnamon, salt, and nutmeg until the sugar dissolves. Undissolved egg white is what causes those rubbery, omelette-like patches on the surface of finished French toast, so this first solo whisk matters more than it looks.
  3. Preheat the pan and the oven
    Set a large nonstick or cast-iron skillet over medium-low heat and heat the oven to 200°F (95°C) with a wire rack on a sheet pan inside. French toast wants gentler heat than pancakes — the custard needs time to set through a thick slice before the exterior burns. If the pan is over medium-high, the sugar in the brioche will be black before the middle is warm.
  4. Soak each slice
    Lay two slices in the custard and let them sit 20 to 30 seconds per side, pressing very gently with your fingertips to help the liquid move in. For very dry bread, go up to 45 seconds a side. Lift a slice and look at the edge — you want the custard to have penetrated about halfway in from each side, meeting in a thin pale line at the center. Let the excess drip off for 3 seconds before it goes in the pan.
  5. Butter the pan
    Add 1 tablespoon of butter and 1 teaspoon of oil to the hot skillet and swirl until the butter foams and the foam just begins to subside. The oil raises the smoke point so the milk solids in the butter brown instead of burning. If the butter browns and smells nutty within 10 seconds, the pan is too hot — pull it off the heat for a minute and lower the burner.
  6. Cook the first side
    Lay the soaked slices in the pan without crowding — two at a time in a 10-inch skillet, three in a 12-inch. Cook for 3 to 4 minutes without moving them, until the underside is a deep golden brown with darker lacy edges. If you peek at 2 minutes and it is still pale, nudge the heat up slightly; if it is already dark, drop it down.
  7. Flip and finish
    Turn each slice with a thin spatula and cook the second side for another 3 to 4 minutes. The toast should puff slightly in the middle as the custard sets — that gentle dome is your sign the eggs have cooked through. Press the center lightly with a finger; it should feel set and springy, not squishy and wet.
  8. Check the center temperature
    Slide an instant-read thermometer into the side of the thickest slice, aiming for the middle. You want 160°F (71°C), which is the temperature at which egg custard is both safely cooked and still creamy. If it reads low, move the slices to the 200°F (95°C) oven for 3 to 5 minutes rather than pushing them longer in the hot pan, which would just darken the crust.
  9. Wipe the pan between batches
    Between batches, wipe the skillet clean with a folded paper towel held in tongs and add fresh butter and oil. Burnt custard and milk solids left in the pan will make the next round taste bitter and look spotty. This takes 15 seconds and is the difference between the last batch matching the first and looking like an afterthought.
  10. Hold, dust, and serve
    Keep finished slices on the wire rack in the warm oven for up to 20 minutes — the rack keeps the bottoms from steaming soft. Just before serving, dust with powdered sugar through a fine sieve, pile on the berries, and pour over warm maple syrup. Warming the syrup for 30 seconds keeps it from chilling the toast on contact.
Know when it is done
Cook until the center of the thickest slice reads 160°F (71°C) — the point where egg custard is safely set but still creamy. Pan should be at medium-low, around 325°F (163°C).
Serve it with
Crisp bacon or breakfast sausage on the side, and a mimosa or a very strong latte to cut the sweetness.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make-ahead: whisk the custard the night before and refrigerate it, and cut the bread so it dries out overnight on the counter. Morning-of becomes a 20-minute job.
  • ◆Any enriched bread works — challah, Texas toast, panettone, even leftover croissants split in half. Avoid thin sandwich bread, which collapses before it can absorb anything.
  • ◆If the outside browns before the inside sets, your slices are thicker than the pan heat can handle. Finish them on a rack in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 5 to 7 minutes.
  • ◆For a boozy grown-up version, add 1 tbsp (15 ml) dark rum or bourbon and swap the cinnamon for ½ tsp orange zest.
  • ◆Leftovers reheat well: 8 minutes on a rack in a 350°F (175°C) oven brings the crust right back. The microwave turns them into steamed bread.

Eggs Benedict with Real Hollandaise⏱ 45 min🍽 4 servingsAdvanced▾

Poached eggs and warm ham on a toasted muffin under a blanket of buttery, lemony hollandaise you made yourself. It is the most impressive thing you can cook before noon, and it is mostly about timing.

Special OccasionBrunchDate Night
Prep
20 min
Cook
25 min
Total
45 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Hollandaise

Poached eggs

Assembly

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Set up before you cook
    Benedict has four moving parts that all need to be hot at the same moment, so lay everything out first: yolks separated, lemon juiced, butter melting, muffins split, ham sliced. Fill a wide saucepan or deep skillet with the water and set it over medium heat. Once you start the hollandaise you should not be hunting for a strainer. Give yourself 10 quiet minutes of setup and the last 10 minutes will feel easy.
  2. Melt the butter gently
    Melt the butter in a small saucepan over low heat or in the microwave in 20-second bursts until fully liquid but not sizzling — you want it around 120 to 130°F (49 to 54°C), warm enough to emulsify but not hot enough to scramble yolks. Let it stand a minute and, if you like a silkier sauce, pour off the clear golden fat and leave the milky solids behind. Keep it somewhere warm; cold butter will not emulsify.
  3. Build the sabayon
    Bring 1 inch (2.5 cm) of water to a bare simmer in a saucepan and set a heatproof bowl on top, making sure the bowl does not touch the water. Whisk the yolks, lemon juice, and cold water in the bowl constantly and vigorously for 3 to 4 minutes, scraping the sides, until the mixture roughly triples in volume and turns pale, thick, and glossy. It is ready when the whisk leaves a trail that holds for a second and the temperature reads 145 to 150°F (63 to 66°C). Above 160°F (71°C) the yolks scramble, so lift the bowl off the heat for a few seconds any time it feels too hot on your knuckles.
  4. Stream in the butter
    Off the heat, add the warm butter a few drops at a time while whisking hard, until you have added about 2 tablespoons and the sauce visibly thickens and looks like mayonnaise. Only then start pouring in a thin, steady stream, whisking the whole time. Rushing the first 2 tablespoons is the number-one reason hollandaise breaks — that early stage is where the emulsion actually forms.
  5. Season and hold the sauce
    Whisk in the salt, cayenne, and an extra squeeze of lemon to taste; it should taste bright and buttery, not flat. If it is thicker than heavy cream, whisk in a teaspoon of warm water at a time to loosen it. Hold the sauce in a warm spot — near the stove, or in a thermos rinsed with hot water — for up to 1 hour. Never put it over direct heat again, and never refrigerate it and try to bring it back.
  6. Rescue a broken sauce
    If the hollandaise goes greasy, thin, and curdled-looking, it has broken, and it is fixable in 60 seconds. Put 1 tablespoon of hot water in a clean bowl and whisk the broken sauce into it one tablespoon at a time, letting each addition come together before adding the next. If that fails, start with a fresh yolk in the clean bowl and whisk the broken sauce into it the same way.
  7. Set the poaching water
    Bring the water to 180 to 190°F (82 to 88°C), which looks like small bubbles rising lazily from the bottom but no rolling boil, then add the vinegar and salt. A boil will beat the whites into ragged shreds. The vinegar helps the whites set faster and tighter, and the small amount used here leaves no taste on the finished egg.
  8. Strain the eggs
    Crack each egg into a fine-mesh sieve set over a bowl and swirl gently for a few seconds. The loose, watery outer white drains away, leaving only the tight white that clings to the yolk — this one step is the difference between a neat oval egg and a wispy cloud. Tip each strained egg into its own small cup or ramekin so you can slide them into the water quickly.
  9. Poach the eggs
    Lower each cup right to the surface of the water and let the egg slip in, adding no more than 4 eggs at a time so the temperature does not crash. Cook for 3 minutes for a fully set white with a completely liquid yolk, or 3½ to 4 minutes for a jammy one. Lift one out with a slotted spoon and press the yolk gently with a fingertip: it should feel soft and yielding, like the pad of your palm. Rest each egg on a paper towel for a few seconds to drain.
  10. Toast the muffins and warm the ham
    Split the English muffins with a fork rather than a knife so you get those craggy nooks, then toast the halves until deep golden and butter them lightly. In a dry skillet over medium heat, warm the Canadian bacon for about 1 minute per side until the edges curl and it is heated through. Warm ham and hot muffins matter — a cold base will chill the whole plate in seconds.
  11. Assemble fast
    Put two muffin halves on each warm plate, top each with a slice of ham, then a drained poached egg. Work quickly and do not stop to admire anything — Benedict is a dish where 90 seconds of hesitation means lukewarm eggs. Warm the plates under hot tap water and dry them if you want a little extra insurance.
  12. Sauce and serve
    Spoon about 3 tablespoons of hollandaise over each egg, letting it flow down the sides rather than drowning the muffin. Finish with chopped chives and a good crack of black pepper. Serve immediately — this is not a dish that waits, and the runny yolk breaking into the sauce is the entire reward.
Know when it is done
Hollandaise sabayon: 145 to 150°F (63 to 66°C), never above 160°F (71°C) or the yolks scramble. Poaching water: 180 to 190°F (82 to 88°C), never boiling. Poached eggs: 3 minutes for set whites and a liquid yolk.
Serve it with
A cold mimosa or a dry sparkling wine, with roasted asparagus or simple dressed greens to cut the richness.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Poach the eggs up to a day ahead: cook them 2½ minutes, drop them straight into ice water, and refrigerate. Reheat for 60 seconds in 150°F (66°C) water right before serving. This is exactly what restaurants do.
  • ◆Runny yolks and warm hollandaise are not pasteurized. If you are pregnant, feeding a young child, or cooking for anyone immune-compromised, use pasteurized shell eggs — they poach and whisk exactly the same.
  • ◆Fresh eggs poach far better than old ones. Crack one on a plate first: if the white sits up tight around the yolk it is fresh; if it spreads out thin and watery, expect wisps.
  • ◆Blender hollandaise is a legitimate shortcut. Blend the yolks, lemon, and a pinch of salt for 20 seconds, then drizzle in 10 tbsp (140 g) hot melted butter with the motor running. It is slightly less airy but nearly foolproof.
  • ◆Eggs Florentine swaps the ham for a handful of wilted, well-squeezed spinach; Eggs Royale uses smoked salmon added after the egg so it does not cook.

Classic French Omelette⏱ 10 min🍽 1 servingAdvanced▾

Pale gold, silky, and rolled into a smooth cigar with a barely set center — no browning anywhere. It takes about two minutes to cook and a few tries to nail, and then you have it forever.

30 MinutesTechniqueOne Pan
Prep
5 min
Cook
5 min
Total
10 min
Serves
1 serving
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Beat the eggs thoroughly
    Crack the eggs into a bowl and beat them with a fork for a full 30 to 45 seconds, until the mixture is one uniform pale yellow with no visible ropes of white and only a light foam on top. A French omelette has no browning and no visible layers, so any unmixed white will show up as a rubbery streak. Keep the fork tines against the bottom of the bowl to avoid whipping in too much air.
  2. Salt the eggs now
    Whisk in the salt and let the eggs sit for 5 minutes if you have time. Salt begins to break down the egg proteins so they set into a more tender, less springy curd, and it dissolves fully instead of leaving salty spots. This is a small step that noticeably changes the texture. Strain the eggs through a fine sieve if you want the most refined result possible.
  3. Choose the right pan
    Use an 8-inch (20 cm) nonstick skillet with sloped sides — this size makes exactly the right thickness for three eggs. A larger pan spreads the eggs too thin and they overcook before you can roll them; a straight-sided pan makes the roll nearly impossible. Have a flexible silicone spatula and a warm plate within reach before you turn on the heat.
  4. Melt the butter over medium-low
    Add 1 tablespoon of butter to the pan over medium-low heat and swirl until it melts and foams. The moment the foam subsides is your window; if the butter turns tan and smells nutty, the pan is too hot for a French omelette. Pour it out, wipe the pan, and start again with fresh butter — brown butter means a browned omelette.
  5. Stir constantly for 20 to 30 seconds
    Pour in the eggs and immediately begin stirring in small circles with the flat of the spatula while shaking the pan back and forth with your other hand. You are making thousands of tiny curds suspended in loose egg, which is what gives the finished omelette its custardy texture. Keep everything moving and scrape the bottom constantly — anything that sits still for two seconds will set and toughen.
  6. Let the base set
    When the eggs look like very loose, glossy scrambled eggs — thickened but still wet — stop stirring. Spread the curds into an even layer with the spatula, then tilt and rotate the pan so any liquid egg runs into the gaps. Let it sit undisturbed for 10 to 20 seconds so a thin skin forms on the bottom and holds everything together. The top should still look shiny and slightly underdone.
  7. Add the filling
    Scatter the cheese and half the chives in a line across the third of the omelette nearest the handle. Keep the filling well clear of the edges so nothing leaks out when you roll. Less is more here — a heavy filling tears the delicate egg sheet and turns the roll into a scramble.
  8. Roll it up
    Tilt the pan away from you to about 45 degrees and use the spatula to fold the near edge of the omelette over the filling. Then tap the pan handle firmly with your fist or nudge with the spatula so the omelette rolls over on itself again, two or three turns, gathering at the far lip of the pan. Work quickly and confidently; hesitating gives the eggs time to overcook.
  9. Turn it onto the plate
    Hold a warm plate in your free hand, bring the far lip of the pan right up to it, and roll the omelette out seam-side down. If the shape is imperfect, drape a clean paper towel over it and gently nudge it into a neat torpedo — this is a real French kitchen trick, not cheating. The whole cooking process should have taken under two minutes.
  10. Butter, garnish, and eat
    Rub the remaining ½ tablespoon of soft butter over the top so it melts into a glossy sheen, then shower with the rest of the chives and a pinch of pepper. Serve it right now, while the center is still barely set and creamy. A French omelette waits for absolutely no one, and it will keep cooking on the plate for another 30 seconds.
Know when it is done
Medium-low heat: butter should foam but never brown. The omelette is done when the exterior is set and pale yellow and the center is still creamy — about 160°F (71°C) at the surface and softer than that inside. That barely-set center sits below the 160°F (71°C) USDA safe temperature for eggs, so use pasteurized shell eggs, or roll it 30 seconds later so the whole thing reaches 160°F (71°C), when serving anyone pregnant, very young, elderly, or immune-compromised.
Serve it with
A green salad with a sharp mustard vinaigrette and a torn baguette — the classic Parisian lunch plate.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆The most common mistake is heat that is too high. If the pan hisses when the eggs go in, it is too hot — you want a quiet, gentle sizzle at most.
  • ◆For an American-style diner omelette instead, use the same eggs but medium heat, let the base set fully without stirring, add fillings, and fold in half. Browning is welcome there.
  • ◆Room-temperature eggs cook more evenly than fridge-cold ones. Sit them in warm tap water for 5 minutes if you forgot to take them out.
  • ◆A dedicated nonstick pan reserved for eggs is worth the drawer space. Never use metal utensils in it and never put it in the dishwasher.
  • ◆Scale it up by cooking one omelette at a time, not by making a bigger one. Three eggs is the maximum a 20 cm pan handles gracefully.

Low and Slow Soft Scrambled Eggs⏱ 17 min including the 5 minute salt rest🍽 2 servingsEasy▾

Small, glossy curds that fall somewhere between eggs and custard. The only real ingredient is patience — eight minutes over low heat instead of two over high.

30 MinutesTechniqueOne Pan
Prep
3 min
Cook
9 min
Total
17 min including the 5 minute salt rest
Serves
2 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Beat the eggs until uniform
    Crack all six eggs into a bowl and beat them with a fork for 45 seconds, until the color is a completely even pale yellow with no streaks of white anywhere. This is the one place where more mixing is better — any white left unincorporated will cook into a firm, rubbery ribbon in an otherwise silky pan of eggs. Do not add milk or cream at this stage; it dilutes the eggs and makes them watery.
  2. Salt them early
    Whisk the salt into the beaten eggs and let them sit for at least 5 minutes, or up to 15 while you make coffee. Salt dissolves some of the egg proteins so they cannot bond as tightly, which produces a noticeably more tender curd and helps the eggs hold onto their moisture. Salting only at the end gives you slightly tougher eggs and salty patches.
  3. Start cold with the butter
    Put 1½ tablespoons of the cold butter in a 10-inch nonstick skillet and set it over low heat — genuinely low, the second-lowest mark on most stoves. Let it melt slowly without foaming aggressively or browning. If you can hear anything sizzle, the pan is already too hot for this method.
  4. Add the eggs to a cool pan
    Pour the eggs in while the butter is still melting. Starting with a cool pan means the eggs warm up gradually and set into small, soft curds instead of hitting hot metal and seizing into big rubbery sheets. Nothing should sizzle when the eggs go in. If it does, take the pan off the heat for a minute and let it cool down before continuing.
  5. Stir constantly and slowly
    Using a silicone spatula, stir the eggs in slow, continuous figure-eights, scraping the bottom and pushing along the sides of the pan the entire time. For the first 2 to 3 minutes it will look like nothing at all is happening — that is the process working, not failing. Do not walk away and do not turn up the heat out of impatience, which is what ruins this dish nine times out of ten.
  6. Watch the curds form
    Around the 4-minute mark the eggs will start to thicken and small soft curds will appear along the bottom of the pan. Keep stirring and keep scraping; the goal is many tiny curds suspended in a creamy sauce, not a few large ones. If it is thickening faster than you can stir, lift the pan off the burner for 20 seconds and keep stirring in the air, then return it.
  7. Pull them early
    Somewhere between 6 and 9 minutes total the eggs will look thickened, glossy, and still slightly loose — like very soft, small-curd cottage cheese with a little cream around it. That is the moment to take the pan off the heat, and it will feel about 30 seconds too early. Carryover heat in the pan keeps cooking them, so eggs that look perfect in the pan are overcooked on the plate.
  8. Finish off the heat
    Stir in the remaining ½ tablespoon of cold butter and the crème fraîche while the pan is off the burner. The cold fat drops the temperature immediately and stops the cooking, and the extra dairy adds a little tang and a glossy finish. Keep stirring for another 15 seconds until everything is smooth.
  9. Plate and serve immediately
    Spoon the eggs onto warm buttered toast, top with the chives and black pepper, and eat right away. These do not hold, reheat, or wait — within two minutes on a hot plate they tighten up and weep water. If you want fully set eggs for food-safety reasons, cook 60 to 90 seconds longer until they reach 160°F (71°C), accepting a firmer texture.
Know when it is done
Cook over low heat for 6 to 9 minutes and pull while glossy and slightly loose. For fully set eggs, cook to 160°F (71°C), the USDA safe temperature for egg dishes.
Serve it with
Thick buttered sourdough toast, sliced avocado, and hot black coffee.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆The single biggest upgrade to scrambled eggs is turning the heat down and setting a timer for 8 minutes. Almost nobody cooks them slowly enough the first time.
  • ◆For an even richer version, cook them in a double boiler over barely simmering water. It takes 12 to 15 minutes and it is nearly impossible to overcook them.
  • ◆Add-ins go in at the very end, off the heat: smoked salmon, grated cheddar, a spoonful of boursin. Adding cheese early makes the eggs seize and go grainy.
  • ◆Use a nonstick or well-seasoned pan and a silicone spatula. Stainless steel grips the eggs and you will lose half the curds to the pan bottom.
  • ◆Leftover soft scrambled eggs do not reheat. Make exactly what you will eat, figuring 2 to 3 eggs per person.

Shakshuka with Feta and Herbs⏱ 55 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Eggs poached right in a smoky, garlicky tomato-pepper sauce, served straight from the skillet with bread for scooping. One pan, pantry ingredients, and it feeds a table.

One PanVegetarianBrunch
Prep

▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Sauce

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Pick the right pan
    Use a 10- or 12-inch skillet with a lid — cast iron, carbon steel, or any heavy oven-safe pan. The sauce needs enough surface area to reduce and enough room for six eggs to sit in their own wells without touching. A pan that is too small piles the sauce deep and the eggs never set evenly.
  2. Soften the onion and pepper
    Heat the olive oil over medium heat until it shimmers, then add the onion, bell pepper, and ½ teaspoon of the salt. Cook, stirring every minute or so, for 10 to 12 minutes until both are genuinely soft and the onion edges are turning golden. This is not a step to rush — undercooked onion stays sharp and crunchy and you will taste it in the finished dish.
  3. Add the garlic and spices
    Stir in the sliced garlic, paprika, cumin, and cayenne and cook for 60 to 90 seconds, stirring constantly. The spices should smell warm and toasty almost immediately. Do not let them go past that point — ground spices burn in well under two minutes over medium heat, and burnt cumin tastes acrid all the way through the sauce.
  4. Cook out the tomato paste
    Push everything to one side, add the tomato paste to the bare spot, and let it fry in the oil for about 2 minutes, stirring, until it darkens from bright red to a deep brick color. This caramelizes the sugars and cooks off the tinny raw taste, adding real depth. Then stir it through the vegetables until everything is evenly coated.
  5. Add the tomatoes
    Pour in the canned tomatoes along with their juice, crushing each one in your fist over the pan so you get rough, rustic pieces rather than a smooth puree. Add the sugar and the remaining ½ teaspoon salt, and stir to combine. Whole peeled tomatoes crushed by hand give a far better texture than pre-crushed, which is often watery and over-processed.
  6. Simmer the sauce down
    Bring to a lively simmer, then reduce the heat to medium-low and cook uncovered for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring occasionally. You want it thick enough that a spatula dragged across the bottom leaves a trail that fills in slowly. A watery sauce will not hold the eggs in place and will flood the plate, so keep going until it mounds slightly on the spoon.
  7. Taste and adjust
    Taste the sauce now, before the eggs go in, because this is your last chance to fix it. It should be bold, slightly sweet, and a little smoky; add salt in ¼ teaspoon increments if it tastes flat, or another pinch of sugar if the tomatoes are aggressively acidic. Remember the feta adds salt at the end, so stop just short of perfect.
  8. Make wells for the eggs
    Use the back of a spoon to hollow out six evenly spaced wells in the sauce, pushing down to expose the pan bottom in each one. Crack each egg into a small cup first, then slide it into its well — cracking directly over a hot pan is how you end up with shell in the sauce and a broken yolk. Space them so the whites do not run together.
  9. Poach the eggs covered
    Season the eggs with the black pepper, cover the pan, and cook over medium-low heat for 6 to 9 minutes. Start checking at 6 minutes: you want the whites fully opaque and set and the yolks still soft and jammy. The steam trapped under the lid cooks the tops, so if the whites near the yolk are still clear, give it another minute or two with the lid back on.
  10. Finish and serve from the pan
    Scatter the crumbled feta and the roughly chopped cilantro or parsley over the top and let the pan sit for 2 minutes off the heat so the eggs firm up slightly. Add the herbs off the heat and at the last second — cilantro wilts to a dull khaki and loses its perfume within a minute over a hot pan. Serve straight from the skillet with warm bread or pita for scooping, giving each person an egg and plenty of sauce. Set the pan on a trivet in the middle of the table — this is a communal dish, not a plated one.
Know when it is done
Cover and poach the eggs 6 to 9 minutes over medium-low, until whites are fully opaque and yolks are jammy. For fully cooked eggs, continue to 160°F (71°C).
Serve it with
Warm pita or crusty sourdough for scooping, plus a cucumber and tomato salad dressed with lemon and olive oil.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make-ahead: the sauce keeps in the fridge for 5 days and freezes for 3 months. Reheat it in the skillet until bubbling, then add the eggs — a weeknight dinner in 10 minutes.
  • ◆For a green shakshuka, swap the tomatoes for 1 lb (450 g) wilted spinach and chard with 1 cup (240 ml) stock, and finish with lemon zest.
  • ◆If your whites are setting too slowly, the sauce was too thick and cool. Turn the heat up slightly and make sure the lid actually fits — trapped steam does most of the cooking.
  • ◆For a spicier version, add 1 seeded and minced jalapeño or 1 tsp harissa with the garlic. Shakshuka should have a gentle heat, not a burn.
  • ◆Whites set at 180°F (82°C) and yolks at 158°F (70°C). If you or your guests need fully cooked yolks, cook 3 to 4 minutes longer until they reach 160°F (71°C).

1 Ingredients

Batch

Potatoes

Filling

Assembly

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Roast the potatoes
    Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Toss the cubed potatoes with the 2 tablespoons of oil, kosher salt, smoked paprika, and pepper, then spread them in a single layer on a sheet pan with space between the pieces. Roast for 25 to 30 minutes, flipping once at the halfway mark, until deeply browned and crisp at the corners. Crowding the pan steams them into soft, pale cubes, so use two pans if you have to.
  2. Brown the sausage
    While the potatoes roast, cook the sausage in a 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat, breaking it into rough ½-inch pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook for 7 to 9 minutes until deeply browned and cooked through — ground pork must reach 160°F (71°C) for safety. Do not stir it constantly; letting it sit for a minute at a time builds the brown crust that carries the whole burrito.
  3. Drain but keep some fat
    Transfer the sausage to a paper-towel-lined plate and pour off all but about 1 tablespoon of the fat from the skillet. That remaining fat is loaded with flavor and will season the eggs. If your sausage was very lean, add a teaspoon of oil so the pan is not dry.
  4. Beat and salt the eggs
    Whisk the eggs with the fine sea salt for 45 seconds, until completely uniform with no streaks of white. Let them sit while you wipe out the pan. Well-beaten eggs make even, tender curds; poorly beaten eggs make rubbery white ribbons that are very obvious inside a burrito.
  5. Scramble the eggs softly
    Melt the butter in the skillet over low heat, add the eggs, and stir slowly and constantly with a silicone spatula for 4 to 6 minutes. Pull them off the heat while they are still glossy and slightly underdone — they will finish cooking from residual heat, and they get reheated again when you sear the burrito. Overcooked eggs in a burrito turn dry and squeaky.
  6. Warm the tortillas
    Heat each tortilla directly over a low gas flame for 15 seconds per side, or in a dry skillet over medium for 30 seconds per side, until soft and pliable with a few brown spots. A cold tortilla cracks the moment you fold it. If you are using an oven, wrap the stack in foil and warm at 350°F (175°C) for 8 minutes.
  7. Drain the wet ingredients
    Tip the salsa into a fine sieve and let it drain for a minute, pressing lightly. Excess liquid is the number-one cause of a burrito that falls apart or goes soggy in the fridge. The same goes for any watery pico de gallo or sour cream — go light, or leave them on the side for dipping.
  8. Build in the right order
    Lay a warm tortilla flat and pile the filling in a horizontal log just below the center, leaving 2 inches (5 cm) clear on each side. Go cheese first, then hot potatoes and sausage, then eggs, then salsa and avocado — putting cheese against the tortilla lets it melt into a glue that helps everything hold together. Use about a quarter of each component and resist overfilling; a burrito you cannot close is just a bowl.
  9. Roll it tight
    Fold the bottom edge up and over the filling, then use your fingers to tuck and pull it back toward you, compressing the filling into a tight cylinder. Fold both sides in over the ends, then roll the whole thing forward, keeping steady tension the whole way. A loose burrito unravels in the pan; a tight one holds its shape when you slice it.
  10. Sear the seam
    Wipe out the skillet, add the remaining 1 tablespoon of oil, and set it over medium heat. Lay each burrito seam-side down and press gently with a spatula for 2 minutes until golden and sealed, then roll it to brown the other sides, about 1 minute each. This step welds the seam shut and gives you a crisp, toasted exterior that makes an enormous difference.
  11. Rest, then cut and serve
    Let the burritos rest for 2 minutes so the cheese sets slightly and the filling stops shifting. Cut them in half on a sharp diagonal with a serrated knife, using a sawing motion instead of pressing straight down. Scatter cilantro over the top and serve with extra salsa and hot sauce.
Know when it is done
Ground pork sausage must reach 160°F (71°C). Roast potatoes at 425°F (220°C) until crisp, and pull the eggs while still glossy since they cook again during the sear.
Serve it with
Hot sauce, extra salsa, and cold horchata or a strong black coffee.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Freezer meal: wrap each cooled burrito tightly in foil, then in a freezer bag, for up to 3 months. Unwrap the foil, microwave from frozen for 2 to 3 minutes, then crisp it in a dry skillet for 2 minutes per side.
  • ◆Let every component cool to just-warm before rolling if you plan to freeze them. Steam trapped inside makes ice crystals and a soggy tortilla.
  • ◆Grate your own cheese. Pre-shredded cheese is coated in starch to keep it from clumping, and it melts into a grainy, greasy texture instead of a smooth one.
  • ◆Swap the sausage for 1 lb (450 g) crumbled Mexican chorizo (cook to 160°F / 71°C), sliced bacon, or a can of drained and rinsed black beans with an extra teaspoon of cumin.
  • ◆If your burritos keep splitting, you overfilled them or your tortillas were cold. This recipe makes about 8 cups of filling, so figure a generous 2 cups per 12-inch tortilla, and always warm them first — a 10-inch tortilla will not close around this much.
