Biscuits and Sausage Gravy⏱ 1 hr🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Tall, flaky buttermilk biscuits split open under a peppery, creamy sausage gravy. It is the most comforting plate in American breakfast cooking, and both halves are easier than they look.

Comfort FoodWeekendSouthern
Prep
25 min
Cook
35 min
Total
1 hr
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Buttermilk biscuits

Sausage gravy

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Get everything cold
    Put the butter in the freezer for 15 minutes and keep the buttermilk in the fridge until the second you need it. Cold butter is the whole architecture of a flaky biscuit: solid pieces of fat melt in the oven and release steam that pushes the dough into layers. Warm butter blends into the flour and gives you a dense, scone-like puck instead.
  2. Heat the oven hot
    Set a rack in the upper third of the oven and heat it to 450°F (230°C). Line a sheet pan with parchment. A very hot oven flashes the water in the butter into steam quickly, which is what makes biscuits shoot up rather than slump — a moderate oven melts the fat before the structure can set.
  3. Whisk the dry ingredients
    In a large bowl, whisk the flour, baking powder, baking soda, sugar, and salt together for 20 seconds. Both leaveners are here for a reason: baking soda reacts with the acidic buttermilk for immediate lift and browning, while baking powder gives a second push in the oven. Make sure there are no visible pockets of powder left.
  4. Grate in the butter
    Grate the frozen butter on the large holes of a box grater directly into the flour, tossing with your fingers every 20 seconds so the shreds stay separate. Alternatively, cut it in with a pastry cutter until the largest pieces are the size of peas. Work fast — if the butter starts to look shiny or feel soft, put the whole bowl in the freezer for 10 minutes.
  5. Add the buttermilk
    Pour in the 1¼ cups cold buttermilk all at once and stir with a fork just until a shaggy, sticky dough comes together and there are no dry patches at the bottom, about 15 seconds. It will look rough and unpromising, which is correct. Overmixing at this point develops gluten and turns a tender biscuit tough.
  6. Fold for layers
    Turn the dough onto a floured counter and pat it into a rough 1-inch-thick rectangle. Fold it in thirds like a letter, rotate 90 degrees, pat it out, and repeat three more times. Each fold laminates butter between sheets of dough, and this is what creates the pull-apart layers you can peel with your fingers. Keep a light hand and add flour only if it truly sticks.
  7. Cut without twisting
    Pat the dough to a final 1-inch (2.5 cm) thickness and cut rounds with a floured 2½-inch (6 cm) cutter, pressing straight down and lifting straight up. Twisting the cutter pinches the edges shut and the biscuit rises lopsided or not at all. Push scraps gently together and cut again — the second round will be slightly less tender, so make them yours.
  8. Bake them touching
    Arrange the biscuits on the parchment so their sides just touch, which forces them to climb upward instead of spreading outward. Brush the tops with the remaining tablespoon of buttermilk. Bake for 14 to 17 minutes, until the tops are deep golden and the interior reads 205 to 210°F (96 to 99°C) on an instant-read thermometer.
  9. Brown the sausage
    While the biscuits bake, cook the sausage in a 12-inch skillet over medium heat, breaking it into bite-size crumbles. Cook for 8 to 10 minutes until well browned and cooked through to 160°F (71°C). Do not drain the fat — you need about ¼ cup (60 ml) of drippings in the pan to make the roux, so add butter if your sausage was very lean.
  10. Make the roux
    Sprinkle the flour evenly over the sausage and stir constantly for 2 minutes, keeping the heat at medium. The mixture will look pasty and clumped around the meat, which is exactly right. This step cooks out the raw flour taste; skipping it leaves a chalky flavor that no amount of salt will hide. The ratio to remember is 4 tablespoons of fat and 4 tablespoons of flour to 2½ cups (600 ml) of milk — that lands on a gravy that coats a split biscuit instead of running off it or setting up like wallpaper paste.
  11. Add the milk slowly
    Pour in about ½ cup (120 ml) of the warm milk and stir hard until it is completely smooth and thick, then add the rest in two more additions, stirring between each. Adding all the milk at once is how you get lumps. Warm milk incorporates far more smoothly than cold, so give it 90 seconds in the microwave first.
  12. Simmer to thicken
    Bring the gravy to a gentle simmer and cook for 5 to 8 minutes, stirring often and scraping the bottom, until it coats the back of a spoon and a finger drawn through leaves a clean line. Stir in the pepper, salt, sage, and cayenne. It will thicken more as it cools, so pull it a touch looser than you want it.
  13. Taste and serve
    Taste and adjust — sausage gravy should be aggressively peppery, so do not be shy about adding another ½ teaspoon of black pepper. If it has gone too thick, whisk in warm milk 2 tablespoons at a time. Split the hot biscuits with a fork, lay them cut-side up on plates, and ladle the gravy generously over the top.
Know when it is done
Sausage must reach 160°F (71°C). Bake biscuits at 450°F (230°C) until the interior reads 205 to 210°F (96 to 99°C) and the tops are deep golden.
Serve it with
Fried eggs on the side, a few dashes of hot sauce, and coffee with cream.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make-ahead: cut the raw biscuits, freeze them solid on a sheet pan, then bag them. Bake straight from frozen at 450°F (230°C) for 18 to 20 minutes — no thawing, and they rise even better.
  • ◆No buttermilk? Use 1¼ cups (300 ml) whole milk plus 1 tbsp (15 ml) lemon juice, rested 10 minutes. Keep both leaveners in the recipe.
  • ◆The gravy thickens dramatically as it sits. Reheat it over low heat with a splash of milk and it comes right back — do not try to fix a cold, gluey pan with more heat alone.
  • ◆For flakier biscuits, chill the cut rounds for 10 minutes on the sheet pan before baking. Cold dough into a hot oven is always the best combination.
  • ◆Sausage matters. A good pork breakfast sausage with sage and black pepper carries this dish; a bland one leaves you salting a beige sauce.

Overnight Cinnamon Rolls⏱ 3 hr 45 min including rising🍽 Makes 12 rollsAdvanced▾

Soft, pull-apart enriched dough with a molten cinnamon-sugar swirl and tangy cream cheese frosting. Do the work the night before and wake up to the best smell in the house.

Weekend ProjectMake AheadBaking
Prep
40 min
Cook
28 min
Total
3 hr 45 min including rising
Serves
Makes 12 rolls
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Dough

Cinnamon filling

Cream cheese frosting

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Warm the milk correctly
    Heat the milk to 105 to 110°F (40 to 43°C) — warm on your wrist like bathwater, not hot. Above 130°F (54°C) you start killing the yeast, and cold milk simply slows everything to a crawl. Use a thermometer the first few times; guessing here is the most common reason enriched dough refuses to rise.
  2. Mix the dough
    In a stand mixer bowl fitted with the dough hook, combine the flour, instant yeast, sugar, and salt, then add the warm milk and eggs. Mix on low for 2 minutes until a shaggy dough forms and no dry flour remains at the bottom. Instant yeast can go straight in with the flour and does not need to be proofed separately.
  3. Add the butter slowly
    With the mixer on medium-low, add the 6 tablespoons of softened butter one tablespoon at a time, letting each piece disappear before adding the next, about 4 minutes total. The dough will look broken and greasy in the middle of this and then suddenly come back together — that is normal. Adding all the butter at once coats the flour and prevents gluten from developing at all.
  4. Knead until it passes the windowpane
    Knead on medium for 8 to 10 minutes, until the dough is smooth, elastic, and pulls cleanly away from the sides of the bowl while still sticking slightly at the bottom. Test it by stretching a walnut-sized piece between your fingers: it should thin out enough to see light through it before tearing. If it rips immediately, knead for another 2 minutes and test again.
  5. First rise
    Shape the dough into a ball, place it in a lightly oiled bowl, cover with plastic wrap, and let it rise in a warm spot for 60 to 90 minutes, until doubled in size. Poke it 1 inch (2.5 cm) deep with a floured finger — if the dent springs back slowly and only partway, it is ready. If it springs back immediately, give it another 15 minutes.
  6. Make the filling
    Stir the very soft butter, brown sugar, cinnamon, and salt together until it forms a spreadable paste, like thick frosting. Softened butter is critical: melted butter runs out of the roll and pools in the bottom of the pan, while cold butter tears the dough as you spread it. If yours is melted, chill it for 10 minutes and stir again.
  7. Roll out the dough
    Punch the dough down gently and roll it on a lightly floured counter into a rectangle about 16 by 12 inches (40 by 30 cm) and ¼ inch (6 mm) thick, with a long side facing you. Keep the corners square by pulling them out with your hands — round corners give you skinny end rolls. If the dough springs back and fights you, let it rest 5 minutes and try again.
  8. Spread and roll up
    Spread the filling over the dough with an offset spatula, going all the way to the edges except for a bare 1-inch (2.5 cm) strip along the far long edge. Roll the dough toward that bare strip, keeping it tight and even, then pinch the seam firmly to seal. A loose roll gives you a hollow center and a spiral that unwinds in the oven.
  9. Cut clean spirals
    Trim the ragged ends, then cut the log into 12 equal pieces about 1¼ inches (3 cm) wide, using either unflavored dental floss slid under the log and crossed over the top, or a very sharp serrated knife with a gentle sawing motion. A regular knife pressed down squashes the spiral flat. Mark the log lightly before cutting so all twelve come out the same size.
  10. Second rise or overnight chill
    Arrange the rolls cut-side up in a buttered 9 by 13-inch (23 by 33 cm) pan, leaving a little space between them. Either cover and let them rise at room temperature for 45 to 60 minutes until puffy and touching, or cover tightly and refrigerate overnight for up to 16 hours. If they went in the fridge, pull them out and let them sit at room temperature for 45 to 60 minutes before baking.
  11. Bake to temperature
    Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) and bake the rolls for 22 to 28 minutes, until the tops are golden and the center of the middle roll reads 190°F (88°C) on an instant-read thermometer. Temperature is far more reliable than color here, because the outer rolls brown well before the middle is done. If the tops darken too fast, tent the pan loosely with foil.
  12. Make the frosting
    While the rolls bake, beat the cream cheese and butter together until completely smooth with no lumps, about 2 minutes. Add the sifted powdered sugar, vanilla, and salt and beat for another minute, adding milk a teaspoon at a time until it is spreadable but not runny. Both fats must be genuinely at room temperature or the frosting will be lumpy no matter how long you beat it.
  13. Frost warm, not hot
    Let the rolls cool in the pan for 10 minutes before frosting. Frosting them straight from the oven melts everything into a thin glaze that soaks in and disappears; waiting until they are cold means the frosting sits on top in a stiff cap. Ten minutes gives you that half-melted layer that sinks into the crevices and still coats the tops.
  14. Serve and store
    Spread the frosting over the warm rolls and serve them straight from the pan while the centers are still soft and gooey. Leftovers keep covered at room temperature for 2 days or refrigerated for 5. Reheat individual rolls for 20 to 30 seconds in the microwave, which brings the crumb right back to soft.
Know when it is done
Milk for the yeast: 105 to 110°F (40 to 43°C). Bake at 350°F (175°C) until the center roll reads 190°F (88°C), which is the doneness point for enriched dough.
Serve it with
Strong black coffee or a cold glass of milk, and something salty like bacon to balance the sweetness.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Overnight is the point: assemble through the pan stage the night before, refrigerate, and pull the pan out 45 to 60 minutes before you want to bake. Cold dough rises more slowly but develops much better flavor.
  • ◆Weigh the flour if you can. A cup of flour can vary by 20 percent depending on how you scoop it, and enriched dough is unforgiving about that — 480 g is 480 g.
  • ◆No stand mixer? Knead by hand for 12 to 15 minutes on a lightly oiled counter using a slap-and-fold motion. It is sticky at first and comes together suddenly around minute eight.
  • ◆For a gooier bottom, pour ¼ cup (60 ml) of warm heavy cream over the risen rolls right before they go in the oven. It bakes into a caramel-like layer underneath.
  • ◆Unfrosted baked rolls freeze well for 2 months. Thaw at room temperature, warm at 300°F (150°C) for 10 minutes, then frost.

Thin French Crepes⏱ 1 hr 5 min including resting🍽 Makes 12 crepesMedium▾

Paper-thin, lacy, faintly sweet pancakes that go sweet or savory depending on the mood. The batter takes five minutes and one blender, and the rest is a rhythm you pick up by crepe three.

Make AheadBrunchFrench
Prep
10 min
Cook
25 min
Total
1 hr 5 min including resting
Serves
Makes 12 crepes
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Batter

For cooking and serving

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Blend the batter
    Put the milk, eggs, melted butter, sugar, salt, and vanilla in a blender, then add the flour on top and blend on high for 20 to 30 seconds until completely smooth. Adding the liquids first keeps the flour from packing against the blades and forming a paste. If you are working by hand, whisk the flour and sugar together, make a well, and gradually whisk in the liquids to avoid lumps.
  2. Rest the batter
    Cover and refrigerate the batter for at least 30 minutes, or up to 48 hours. This rest lets the flour fully hydrate and lets the gluten you just developed in the blender relax, which is what makes crepes tender and stretchy instead of rubbery. It also lets the bubbles settle out so you get smooth crepes rather than pockmarked ones. This step is not optional if you want the good texture.
  3. Check the consistency
    After resting, the batter should be the thickness of heavy cream and coat a spoon in a thin, translucent film. If it has thickened in the fridge, whisk in milk 1 tablespoon at a time until it flows freely off the whisk. Too-thick batter makes heavy, pancake-like crepes that will not swirl to the edges of the pan.
  4. Heat the pan properly
    Set an 8- or 10-inch nonstick skillet or crepe pan over medium heat for 3 to 4 minutes. It is hot enough when a drop of water dances and evaporates in about 2 seconds. Too cool and the crepe goes pale and soggy; too hot and it sets before you can spread it. Getting the heat right takes a couple of test crepes, and everyone sacrifices the first one.
  5. Grease very lightly
    Melt a small knob of butter in the pan, swirl to coat, then wipe out almost all of it with a folded paper towel. You want the barest film. A puddle of butter fries the underside into a blotchy, spotted crepe instead of an even golden one, and it makes the batter slide around instead of grabbing.
  6. Pour and swirl fast
    Lift the pan off the heat, pour in a scant ¼ cup (about 50 ml) of batter at the center, and immediately tilt and rotate your wrist so the batter runs out to the edges in a thin, even circle. That is the amount that just covers an 8-inch pan; this batch makes roughly 600 ml of batter, which is where the twelve crepes come from. You have roughly three seconds before it sets, so commit. If there is a hole, dribble a few drops of batter into it right away and swirl again.
  7. Cook the first side
    Return the pan to the heat and cook for 60 to 90 seconds, until the surface looks dry and matte, the edges lift and turn faintly golden, and the whole crepe slides freely when you shake the pan. Peek underneath: you want a lacy, mottled brown map, not a uniform tan. If it is still sticking anywhere, give it another 15 seconds.
  8. Flip with confidence
    Loosen the edge with a thin silicone spatula or your fingertips, lift the crepe, and flip it over in one motion. Cook the second side for just 20 to 30 seconds — it never browns as evenly and does not need to, since this side ends up on the inside. Overcooking the second side is what makes crepes stiff and brittle.
  9. Stack them as you go
    Slide each finished crepe onto a plate and stack them directly on top of each other, no parchment needed. They will not stick, and the trapped steam actually keeps them soft and pliable. Cover the stack loosely with a clean kitchen towel to keep them warm while you finish the batch.
  10. Adjust as you cook
    Watch the color of each crepe and adjust the burner in small steps. If crepes are browning in under a minute, drop the heat a notch; if they are still pale at 2 minutes, nudge it up. Re-wipe the pan with the buttery paper towel every second or third crepe, not every time.
  11. Fill and serve
    Spread about 2 teaspoons of the jam or Nutella, or a scatter of berries, over one quarter of each crepe, then fold in half and in half again to make a triangle, or roll it into a cigar. Go light — a crepe is meant to be a thin wrapper around a little filling, and overloading one is what makes it tear as you fold. Dust with powdered sugar and serve with a lemon wedge for squeezing — sugar and lemon on a plain crepe is the classic Breton street version and still the best one. Serve warm, two per person.
Know when it is done
Medium heat, around 350°F (175°C) — a water droplet should dance and evaporate in about 2 seconds. Cook the first side 60 to 90 seconds and the second only 20 to 30.
Serve it with
Sugar and lemon, or Nutella and sliced banana, with a bowl of café au lait.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make-ahead: the batter is better on day two, and cooked crepes keep stacked and wrapped in the fridge for 3 days or frozen for 2 months with parchment between every four.
  • ◆For savory galettes, drop the sugar and vanilla and replace ½ cup (65 g) of the flour with buckwheat flour. Fill with ham, Gruyère, and an egg cracked into the center.
  • ◆The first crepe always fails. That is not a mistake, it is how you learn whether the pan is at the right temperature.
  • ◆A ¼ cup measure or a small ladle gives consistent crepes. Eyeballing the pour is why one crepe is thick and the next has holes.
  • ◆If the crepes tear when you flip them, the batter is too thin or the first side is undercooked. Wait for the edges to lift and go golden before you commit.

Huevos Rancheros⏱ 45 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Fried eggs over crisped corn tortillas and refried beans, flooded with a smoky ranchero salsa. Rustic, filling, and built almost entirely from cans and eggs.

One PanSpicyBrunch
Prep
15 min
Cook
30 min
Total
45 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Ranchero salsa

Beans and tortillas

Eggs and garnish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Start the salsa
    Heat the 2 tablespoons of oil in a medium saucepan over medium heat until it shimmers, then add the onion and jalapeño with a pinch of the salt. Cook for 5 to 6 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the onion is soft and translucent and just starting to turn golden at the edges. Softening the aromatics properly is what separates a real ranchero sauce from warmed-up salsa from a jar.
  2. Bloom the spices
    Add the minced garlic, cumin, and oregano and stir constantly for 45 to 60 seconds until the kitchen smells strongly of toasted cumin. Crush the dried oregano between your palms as you add it to release its oils. Watch closely, because garlic goes from fragrant to bitter in well under a minute at this heat.
  3. Simmer the salsa down
    Pour in the tomatoes with all their juice and the remaining salt, and bring to a simmer. Cook uncovered for 12 to 15 minutes, stirring now and then and mashing the tomato pieces against the side of the pan with a spoon. You want it thick enough to sit on a tortilla without running off the plate. Taste and add salt in small increments until the flavor snaps into focus.
  4. Warm the beans
    In a small saucepan over low heat, warm the refried beans with the 2 tablespoons of water, stirring until they are smooth, hot, and spreadable, about 5 minutes. Canned refried beans are stiff straight from the tin and will tear the tortillas if you try to spread them cold. Keep them covered over the lowest heat so they do not dry out and crust over.
  5. Crisp the tortillas
    Heat the ¼ cup of oil in a small skillet over medium-high until it shimmers, around 350°F (175°C). Fry each tortilla for 20 to 30 seconds per side until it is lightly golden and just starting to firm up but still flexible enough to fold. This is the traditional step people skip, and it is what keeps the tortilla from turning into wet paper under the salsa. Drain them on paper towels and sprinkle them with about ¼ teaspoon of the salt while they are still glistening, since salt only sticks to a hot, oily surface.
  6. Set up the plates
    Warm four plates in a 200°F (95°C) oven for a few minutes while you fry the eggs. Lay two crisped tortillas slightly overlapping on each plate and spread each one with a few tablespoons of the warm beans. Building the base before the eggs are cooked means you can plate everything the moment they come out of the pan.
  7. Fry the eggs
    Melt the butter in a large nonstick skillet over medium heat until foaming, then crack in four eggs, spacing them apart. Season with about ¼ teaspoon of the remaining salt and cook for 2½ to 3 minutes, until the whites are fully set and opaque and the yolks are still liquid. For sunny-side up, cover the pan for the last 30 seconds so the steam sets the film over the yolk without flipping.
  8. Cook the second batch
    Slide the first four eggs onto the waiting tortillas, then repeat with the remaining butter and eggs. Wipe the pan if any browned bits are left behind, since they will stick to the next batch and taste burnt. Keep the finished plates in the warm oven for the two minutes this takes.
  9. Sauce the plates
    Spoon the hot ranchero salsa generously over and around the eggs, deliberately leaving the yolks exposed so they stay visible and do not get cooked further by the hot sauce. About ⅓ cup (80 ml) per plate is right. The salsa should be hot enough to steam when it hits the plate.
  10. Garnish and serve immediately
    Scatter the crumbled cotija, avocado slices, and cilantro over the top and tuck a lime wedge onto each plate. Serve right away with a knife and fork, and tell everyone to break the yolks into the salsa and beans — that is the whole idea. A squeeze of lime at the table brightens the entire plate.
Know when it is done
Fry eggs 2½ to 3 minutes for set whites and runny yolks; cook to 160°F (71°C) for fully set yolks. Tortilla frying oil should be about 350°F (175°C).
Serve it with
Cold Mexican lager or hibiscus agua fresca, with extra lime and a hot sauce you like.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make-ahead: the ranchero salsa keeps for 5 days in the fridge and freezes for 3 months. With salsa in the freezer this becomes a 15-minute breakfast.
  • ◆If you would rather not shallow-fry, brush the tortillas with oil and bake them at 400°F (200°C) for 6 to 8 minutes, flipping once. They will be crisper and less pliable but they hold up fine.
  • ◆Runny yolks are not pasteurized. Cook the eggs to 160°F (71°C) with a fully firm yolk if you are serving anyone pregnant, very young, or immune-compromised.
  • ◆Add chorizo for a heartier plate: brown 8 oz (225 g) of Mexican chorizo to 160°F (71°C) and scatter it over the beans before the eggs go on.
  • ◆Homemade refried beans are a real upgrade: fry a can of drained pinto beans in 2 tbsp lard or oil with half a diced onion, mash, and loosen with water.

Quiche Lorraine⏱ 3 hr 15 min including chilling and cooling🍽 8 servingsMedium▾

A crisp butter crust holding a barely set, silky custard shot through with bacon and Gruyère. Serve it warm or at room temperature and it works for breakfast, lunch, or a light dinner.

8 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Crust

Filling

Custard

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Make the pastry
    Pulse the flour and salt in a food processor to combine, add the cold butter cubes, and pulse 10 to 12 times until the largest pieces are the size of small peas. Those visible butter pieces are what make the crust flaky — if you process it to fine sand, you get a crumbly cookie crust instead. Working by hand with a pastry cutter or your fingertips works equally well if you move quickly.
  2. Add water sparingly
    Drizzle in 3 tablespoons of ice water and pulse just 5 or 6 times. Squeeze a handful of the mixture: if it holds together when pressed, it is done; if it crumbles apart, add the last tablespoon. Too much water makes the dough easy to roll now and tough and shrunken later, so err on the dry side.
  3. Chill the disk
    Tip the dough onto a sheet of plastic wrap, gather it into a disk about 5 inches (13 cm) across without kneading it, wrap tightly, and refrigerate for at least 1 hour or up to 2 days. Chilling hydrates the flour evenly and lets the gluten relax so the crust does not shrink down the sides of the pan in the oven. Cold dough also rolls out without the butter smearing.
  4. Roll and line the pan
    On a lightly floured counter, roll the dough into a 13-inch (33 cm) circle about ⅛ inch (3 mm) thick, rotating a quarter turn after every few passes so it does not stick. Drape it into a 9-inch (23 cm) pie plate or tart pan and ease it into the corners without stretching — stretched dough always shrinks back. Trim the overhang to ½ inch (1.5 cm), fold it under, and crimp. Freeze the lined shell for 20 minutes.
  5. Blind bake the shell
    Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C). Line the frozen shell with parchment or foil, fill it to the very top with pie weights or dried beans, and bake for 20 minutes. Then lift out the weights and parchment and bake another 8 to 10 minutes, until the bottom looks dry and pale gold. Skipping this step is exactly how you get the dreaded soggy bottom under a wet custard.
  6. Seal the crust
    As soon as the shell comes out, brush the inside all over with a little beaten egg from your four eggs and return it to the oven for 2 minutes. The egg cooks into a thin waterproof film that keeps the custard from soaking into the pastry. Then lower the oven to 325°F (165°C) and let it come down while you make the filling.
  7. Cook the bacon
    In a skillet over medium heat, cook the bacon for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the fat has rendered and the pieces are browned but still slightly chewy rather than shatteringly crisp. They will firm up further in the oven. Pour off all but 1 tablespoon of the fat.
  8. Soften the shallot
    Add the minced shallot to the reserved bacon fat and cook over medium-low for 2 to 3 minutes until soft and translucent but not browned. This is a small addition that rounds out the smoky bacon with a little sweetness. Transfer the bacon and shallot to a paper-towel-lined plate to drain, since extra grease will float to the top of the custard and pool.
  9. Whisk the custard
    Whisk the remaining eggs with the cream, milk, salt, pepper, and nutmeg for about 30 seconds, until smooth and uniform but not foamy. Whisking hard enough to make bubbles gives you a puffed, spongy quiche instead of a dense, silky one. For the most refined texture, pour the custard through a fine sieve to catch the chalazae — those white cords attached to the yolks.
  10. Layer the filling
    Scatter the drained bacon and shallot evenly over the bottom of the warm crust, then the grated Gruyère on top. Putting the solids in first means they stay distributed instead of floating up and forming a raft on the surface. Set the pie plate on a sheet pan on the oven rack before you pour, so you never have to carry a full quiche across the kitchen.
  11. Fill and bake
    Pour the custard over the filling, stopping about ¼ inch (6 mm) below the rim — you may have a little left over, and that is better than an overflow. Bake at 325°F (165°C) for 35 to 45 minutes. The low oven is what keeps the custard silky; a hot oven curdles the eggs and makes it weep water.
  12. Judge doneness carefully
    The quiche is done when the edges are set and puffed slightly, the center 2 inches (5 cm) still wobble like loose gelatin when you nudge the pan, and an instant-read thermometer inserted 1 inch (2.5 cm) from the center reads 170°F (77°C). That is comfortably above the 160°F (71°C) USDA safe temperature for egg dishes while still being creamy. A quiche baked until the middle is firm is a quiche that will be grainy when it cools.
  13. Cool before slicing
    Let the quiche rest on a wire rack for at least 30 minutes before cutting. The custard continues to set as it cools, and slicing it hot gives you a soupy wedge that collapses on the plate. It is genuinely best warm or at room temperature rather than piping hot, which is why it makes such a good make-ahead dish.
Know when it is done
Blind bake at 400°F (200°C), then bake the custard at 325°F (165°C) until the center reads 170°F (77°C) — safely above the 160°F (71°C) minimum for egg dishes but still creamy, with a slight wobble in the middle.
Serve it with
A sharply dressed green salad and a glass of dry white wine, or coffee if it is still morning.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make-ahead: bake the whole quiche a day early, refrigerate, and reheat at 325°F (165°C) for 20 minutes. The blind-baked shell can also be frozen for a month.
  • ◆Store-bought pie dough works perfectly well here — just blind bake and egg-wash it exactly the same way. The custard is where the quiche is won or lost.
  • ◆The classic ratio to remember is 1 large egg per ½ cup (120 ml) of dairy. Stray from it and you get either scrambled eggs in a crust or a filling that never sets.
  • ◆Gruyère is traditional, but Comté, Emmental, or a sharp white cheddar all work. Keep it to 4 oz (115 g) or the fat separates and the custard gets greasy.
  • ◆If your crust slumps down the sides during blind baking, the dough was not cold enough or the weights did not reach the top rim. Freeze the shell hard and fill the weights all the way up.

Hash Browns That Actually Crisp⏱ 33 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

A single golden, lacy potato cake with a shatter-crisp crust and a tender middle. Two rules do all the work: rinse the starch away, then squeeze the potatoes truly bone dry.

Diner ClassicOne PanVegetarian
Prep
15 min
Cook
18 min
Total
33 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Use russets, not waxy potatoes
    Russets are high in starch and low in moisture, which is exactly what fries into a crisp shell. Yukon Golds and red potatoes hold too much water and turn gummy and pale no matter how hot the pan is. Peel about 1½ lb (680 g), which shreds down to roughly 4 packed cups.
  2. Shred them coarsely
    Grate the potatoes on the large holes of a box grater or with the shredding disk of a food processor, aiming for long strands rather than short stubs. Longer shreds tangle together and hold the cake in one piece when you flip it. Work quickly, because raw grated potato starts oxidizing and turning pink-gray within a couple of minutes.
  3. Rinse away the starch
    Dump the shreds into a bowl of cold water and swish them hard with your hand for 30 seconds — the water will go cloudy white almost instantly. Drain and repeat until the water runs nearly clear, usually two or three changes. Surface starch is glue: leave it on and the shreds cement together into a dense, gummy pancake instead of separate crisp strands.
  4. Squeeze them bone dry
    Pile the drained potatoes into the center of a clean kitchen towel, gather the corners, and twist hard over the sink. You should get a genuinely surprising amount of water out — keep twisting until nothing more drips, then squeeze again. Water in the pan turns to steam, and steam boils potatoes instead of frying them. This one step is the difference between a hash brown and a sad potato patty.
  5. Season right before cooking
    Tip the dried shreds into a dry bowl and toss with the kosher salt and pepper using your fingers, separating any clumps. Do this at the last moment: salt pulls moisture straight back out of the potatoes, undoing all your squeezing if it sits for even ten minutes. The shreds should feel dry and fluffy in your hand.
  6. Heat the fat properly
    Add the butter and oil to a 10-inch cast-iron or nonstick skillet over medium heat and let it get fully hot, about 2 minutes, until the butter foam subsides and a shred dropped in sizzles steadily right away. The oil raises the smoke point so the butter can brown without burning. It should sizzle steadily, not smoke.
  7. Press into an even layer
    Add all the potatoes and spread them into an even layer about ½ inch (1.5 cm) thick, pressing down firmly with a spatula to compact the cake and force contact with the pan. Even thickness means even browning; a mound in the middle stays raw while the thin edges burn. Make sure the fat bubbles up around the edges.
  8. Do not touch it
    Cook undisturbed for 6 to 8 minutes. Every time you stir or lift the potatoes you break the crust that is forming and release steam back into the cake. Peek at the edge with a spatula only after 6 minutes — you are looking for a deep, even golden brown across the whole underside and edges that have pulled slightly away from the pan.
  9. Flip in one move
    Slide the cake onto a plate, invert the skillet over it, and flip the whole thing back into the pan — or if you are confident, use two spatulas and turn it in one go. Add another teaspoon of oil around the edge if the pan looks dry, letting it run underneath. Press the cake down again and cook the second side for 5 to 7 minutes.
  10. Drain, salt, and serve
    Slide the hash browns onto a wire rack or a paper towel for 30 seconds to shed any surface grease, then salt the top lightly while it is still hot, since salt clings best to a hot, slightly oily surface. Cut into wedges, scatter with chives, and serve immediately — hash browns start softening within about five minutes. If you must hold them, use a rack in a 200°F (95°C) oven, never a covered plate.
Know when it is done
Medium heat with fat around 350°F (175°C) — a shred should sizzle steadily on contact without smoking. Potatoes are cooked through at about 205°F (96°C), by which point the crust is deep golden.
Serve it with
Fried eggs, thick bacon, and hot sauce — the classic diner plate.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make-ahead trick: parboil whole peeled potatoes for 8 minutes, cool them completely in the fridge overnight, then grate. Partly cooked starch crisps even harder and the shreds will not oxidize.
  • ◆For individual hash brown patties, portion the shreds into 4 mounds in the pan and press each to ½ inch (1.5 cm). More edges means more crunch, and they are far easier to flip.
  • ◆If the potatoes turn pink or gray after grating, that is harmless oxidation. Cooking hides it entirely, and rinsing slows it down.
  • ◆Clarified butter or ghee is the ideal fat here — all the butter flavor with no milk solids to burn at high heat.
  • ◆Never crowd the pan or cook more than 1½ lb (680 g) at a time in a 10-inch skillet. Two batches beat one steamed, soggy mass every single time.

Diner Bacon Egg and Cheese⏱ 20 min🍽 2 sandwichesEasy▾

A toasted English muffin, crisp bacon, a folded egg, and cheese melted into every crevice. Fifteen minutes, one pan, and better than anything you can buy at a counter.

30 MinutesOne PanWeeknight
Prep
5 min
Cook
15 min
Total
20 min
Serves
2 sandwiches
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Start the bacon in a cold pan
    Lay the bacon in a cold 10-inch skillet and then turn the heat to medium. Starting cold lets the fat render out slowly and evenly, so the strips end up flat and uniformly crisp instead of curled and burnt at the edges. Cook for 8 to 10 minutes total, flipping every 2 minutes, until deep golden and as crisp as you like it.
  2. Drain and reserve the fat
    Transfer the bacon to a paper-towel-lined plate and pour off all but about 1 tablespoon of the fat, saving the rest in a jar for potatoes another day. That tablespoon left in the pan is what you will cook the eggs in, and it makes an enormous difference. Wipe out any burnt bits with a paper towel held in tongs.
  3. Toast the muffins
    Split the English muffins with a fork rather than a knife so you keep the craggy nooks that catch butter, then toast the halves until deep golden and crisp at the edges. Do this in a toaster or face-down in the bacon pan for about 90 seconds. A properly toasted muffin is structural — an untoasted one goes soggy under a hot egg in under a minute.
  4. Butter them immediately
    Spread the softened butter over the hot cut sides right away so it melts and soaks in. This also creates a light fat barrier that helps keep the bread from absorbing egg and grease. If you want a sauce, spread mayonnaise on the top half and add hot sauce at the very end.
  5. Beat and season the eggs
    Crack the eggs into a bowl and beat them with a fork for a full 30 seconds with the salt and pepper, until the mixture is completely uniform in color with no ropes of white left. Any unbeaten white cooks into a rubbery translucent ribbon that you will absolutely notice inside a sandwich. Beaten eggs cooked in a thin sheet fold neatly into a square that fits the muffin, which is the classic diner move — much easier to eat than a fried egg that slides out the side. Salting now rather than at the table also gives the salt a couple of minutes to dissolve, so you get even seasoning instead of sharp grains.
  6. Cook the eggs as a sheet
    Set the skillet with its tablespoon of bacon fat over medium-low heat and pour in the eggs. Let them sit undisturbed for 60 to 90 seconds, then use a spatula to pull the set edges toward the center, tilting the pan so the raw egg fills the gaps. Cook for another 60 seconds until the top is just barely set and no longer runny.
  7. Fold and melt the cheese
    Lay the cheese slices over half the egg sheet, then fold the bare half over the top and cut the folded egg into two squares roughly the size of your muffins. Turn off the heat and let the residual warmth melt the cheese for about 60 seconds. American cheese melts smoothest, but a sharp cheddar gives you far more flavor if you accept a slightly greasier melt.
  8. Check that the eggs are cooked through
    The folded egg should be fully set with no glossy liquid anywhere, which corresponds to 160°F (71°C) — the USDA safe temperature for beaten egg dishes. If any part still looks wet, cover the pan for 30 seconds off the heat rather than turning the burner back on. Overcooked eggs on a sandwich turn dry and squeaky.
  9. Build and press
    Put a cheese-wrapped egg square on each bottom muffin half, break the bacon strips in half and stack two pieces on top so they lie flat, add hot sauce if using, then crown it with the top half. Press the sandwich firmly with your palm for 5 seconds — that compression melds the layers so it eats like one thing instead of sliding apart. Wrap it in parchment or foil for 60 seconds if you want the full deli effect, then eat it hot.
Know when it is done
Cook the beaten egg until fully set with no liquid, which is 160°F (71°C), the USDA safe temperature for egg dishes. Bacon is done when deep golden and rendered, about 8 to 10 minutes over medium.
Serve it with
A big cup of black coffee and a handful of crispy hash browns.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Cook bacon for the week ahead: bake a whole pound on a rack at 400°F (200°C) for 18 to 20 minutes, then refrigerate. Two strips reheat in 20 seconds and this sandwich becomes a five-minute job.
  • ◆Sausage patty version: form 3 oz (85 g) of breakfast sausage into a thin patty wider than the muffin, since it shrinks, and cook to 160°F (71°C).
  • ◆For a round fried egg instead, cook it in a greased metal ring or a clean tuna can with both ends removed, covered, for about 3 minutes.
  • ◆Bagels and croissants both work, but English muffins are best because their flat, sturdy structure holds up without squeezing the filling out.
  • ◆Wrapping the finished sandwich in foil for a minute is not just for looks — the trapped steam softens the muffin's interior slightly and finishes melting the cheese.

Lemon Dutch Baby Pancake⏱ 45 min including the 20 minute skillet preheat🍽 2 to 3 servingsEasy▾

One blended batter poured into a screaming-hot skillet puffs into a dramatic, custardy pancake with crisp climbing walls. It looks like a project and takes ten minutes of actual work.

ShowstopperBrunchCast Iron
Prep
10 min
Cook
22 min
Total
45 min including the 20 minute skillet preheat
Serves
2 to 3 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Batter

For the pan and top

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Preheat the skillet in the oven
    Put a 10-inch cast-iron skillet on the middle rack and heat the oven to 425°F (220°C), leaving the pan inside for at least 20 minutes after it reaches temperature. A genuinely ripping-hot pan is the entire mechanism here: the batter hits it, the water in it flashes to steam, and the pancake climbs the walls. A merely warm pan gives you a flat, eggy disk.
  2. Bring everything to room temperature
    Take the eggs out ahead of time, or sit them in warm tap water for 5 minutes, and warm the milk to about 100°F (38°C) in the microwave. Cold batter hitting a hot pan cools it down and blunts the puff dramatically. This is the second-most-common reason a Dutch baby comes out disappointing, right after an underheated skillet.
  3. Blend the batter smooth
    Put the eggs, milk, sugar, vanilla, salt, and nutmeg in a blender and blend on high for 20 seconds, then add the flour and blend another 30 seconds until completely smooth and slightly foamy. All that whipping incorporates air, and air plus steam is what creates the rise. If you are whisking by hand, beat the eggs alone for a full minute first, then whisk in the liquids and finally the flour.
  4. Rest the batter briefly
    Let the batter sit at room temperature for 10 minutes while the oven finishes heating. This lets the flour hydrate so the pancake is tender rather than tough, and lets any large bubbles settle. Do not rest it in the fridge — the goal is a batter that is close to room temperature when it hits the pan.
  5. Melt the butter in the hot pan
    Pull the hot skillet out with a dry oven mitt, set it on the stovetop, and drop in the butter. Swirl it as it melts and foams, coating the bottom and swiping it up the sides with a brush or a folded paper towel held in tongs. Greasing the walls is what lets the batter climb; bare cast iron grips it and holds it down. Work fast so the pan does not lose heat.
  6. Pour and go straight back in
    Pour the batter into the center of the pan all at once — it should sizzle audibly as it hits — and immediately slide the skillet back into the oven. Every second the oven door is open costs you height. Do not stir or spread the batter in the pan; it will level itself.
  7. Do not open the oven
    Bake for 18 to 22 minutes without opening the door once. The pancake will billow up the sides in wild, uneven ridges and the center will stay comparatively flat, which is exactly right. Opening the door drops the oven temperature by 50°F (28°C) or more and the whole thing can collapse before the structure sets.
  8. Judge doneness by color
    It is done when the walls are tall, deeply golden brown, and dry-looking, and the pale center is set with no wet shine. The edges should feel crisp when tapped with a fingertip. If the middle still looks glossy and liquid at 18 minutes, give it another 3 to 4 minutes rather than pulling it early.
  9. Expect it to deflate
    The Dutch baby will start sinking within 30 seconds of leaving the oven, and that is not a failure — it is physics, and every Dutch baby does it. Carry it to the table immediately if you want anyone to see it at full height. What is left is a crisp-rimmed bowl with a custardy center, which is the actual good part.
  10. Dress and serve
    Dust generously with powdered sugar through a fine sieve, squeeze a whole lemon wedge over the top, and scatter with berries if you have them. The acid is essential, cutting through what is a genuinely rich, eggy pancake. Cut it into wedges and serve straight from the skillet — remember the handle stays dangerously hot for a long time, so drape a towel over it.
Know when it is done
Bake at 425°F (220°C) for 18 to 22 minutes, until the walls are deep golden and the center is set with no wet shine — about 200°F (93°C) in the custardy middle.
Serve it with
Fresh berries and cream, or crisp bacon and hot coffee if you want to balance the sweetness.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆The ratio is easy to remember and easy to scale: equal volumes of eggs, milk, and flour. Three eggs is about ½ cup, so ½ cup milk and ½ cup flour.
  • ◆No cast iron? Use any oven-safe heavy skillet, a metal cake pan, or a glass pie dish. Avoid nonstick above 400°F (200°C) since most coatings degrade at that heat.
  • ◆Savory version: skip the sugar and vanilla, add ¼ tsp black pepper and 2 tbsp grated Parmesan to the batter, and top the baked pancake with prosciutto and arugula.
  • ◆If it barely rose, the culprit is almost always an underheated pan or cold ingredients. Give the skillet a full 20 minutes at 425°F (220°C) and warm the milk.
  • ◆It does not keep. Dutch babies are a make-it-and-eat-it dish, so time it for when people are already at the table.

Garlic Herb Compound Butter⏱ 2 hr 20 min🍽 Makes about 1 cup (225 g), 16 slicesEasy▾

A log of butter whipped with garlic, parsley, thyme, and lemon that lives in your freezer and rescues weeknights. One cold coin melting over a hot steak does more than most sauces that take an hour.

Make AheadFreezer FriendlySteak Night
Prep
15 min
Cook
5 min
Total
2 hr 20 min
Serves
Makes about 1 cup (225 g), 16 slices
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the butter

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Soften the butter properly
    Leave the two sticks on the counter for 45 to 60 minutes until they reach about 65°F (18°C) — cool to the touch, but your finger presses in easily. If you microwave it and any part goes liquid, the butter's natural emulsion breaks and the finished log will be greasy and weep in the pan. In a hurry, cut the cold butter into ½-inch (1 cm) cubes and it will soften in about 20 minutes.
  2. Tame the raw garlic
    Warm the minced garlic with the 1 tsp olive oil in a small skillet over low heat for 60 to 90 seconds, just until it smells sweet and looks barely blond. You are not browning it — the moment garlic takes on real color it turns bitter, and bitter garlic sitting in cold butter only gets harsher over a week. Scrape it onto a plate and let it cool completely to room temperature before it goes near the butter.
  3. Chop the herbs bone dry
    Wash the parsley, chives, and thyme well ahead and dry them thoroughly in a salad spinner or between two towels. Water is the enemy here: wet herbs make the butter separate and cut the shelf life in half. Strip thyme leaves by pinching the stem near the top and pulling downward, then chop everything to about the size of a grain of rice so it distributes evenly instead of clumping.
  4. Whip the butter smooth
    Put the softened butter in a medium bowl and beat it with a sturdy spoon, a fork, or a hand mixer on medium for 60 to 90 seconds, until it looks pale and creamy like frosting. Whipping works a little air into it, which is what makes the finished butter spreadable straight from the fridge instead of a hard brick. A stand mixer with the paddle attachment does this in about a minute if you are doubling the batch.
  5. Fold in garlic and herbs
    Add the cooled garlic, parsley, chives, thyme, lemon zest, and lemon juice all at once and fold rather than beat, about 20 strokes with a rubber spatula. Over-mixing at this stage bruises the herbs and streaks the butter a dull grey-green instead of leaving clean flecks. The lemon juice sounds fussy but it is what lifts the whole thing — without a little acid, compound butter tastes flat and heavy on meat.
  6. Season and taste it
    Add the 1 tsp fine sea salt and ½ tsp black pepper and mix just until they disappear into the butter. Taste a small smear on a piece of bread rather than off the spoon, because straight butter always reads saltier than butter that has been spread. It should taste one notch saltier than you think you want, since it will be melting over unseasoned meat or vegetables.
  7. Roll it into a log
    Scrape the butter down the center of a 12-inch (30 cm) sheet of plastic wrap or parchment in a rough line. Fold the near edge over the top, then push a ruler or the edge of a sheet pan against the base of the roll to tighten it into a smooth cylinder about 1½ inches (4 cm) across. Twist both ends like a candy wrapper — the tighter the twist, the fewer air pockets, and air pockets are exactly where freezer burn starts.
  8. Chill until firm
    Refrigerate the log for at least 2 hours, until it is firm all the way through and reads about 38°F (3°C) at the center. Firm butter slices into clean coins that sit on top of a hot steak and melt slowly down the sides; soft butter slumps and turns straight into a greasy puddle. If you need it faster, 30 minutes in the freezer works, but set a timer so it doesn't freeze rock solid.
  9. Slice and use it
    Unwrap and cut ⅜-inch (1 cm) coins with a warm knife, wiping the blade between cuts for clean edges. Put one on a rested steak, a piece of grilled fish, or a split baked potato right before serving, or melt two coins into a pan of green beans with a splash of water for an instant sauce. It is also excellent pushed under chicken skin before roasting, where it bastes the breast from the inside as it renders — roast the bird until the thickest part of the thigh reads 165°F (74°C).
  10. Store it right
    Wrapped tightly, the log keeps 2 weeks in the fridge at or below 40°F (4°C) and 3 months in the freezer. Slice the log into coins before freezing and stack them with squares of parchment between, so you can pull one at a time without thawing the whole roll. Frozen coins go straight onto hot food with no thawing at all.
Know when it is done
No cooking temperature. Mix the butter at about 65°F (18°C) so it stays emulsified, and chill it to 38°F to 40°F (3°C to 4°C) before slicing.
Serve it with
Melts onto everything from a ribeye to roasted carrots to a torn hunk of sourdough; open whatever red is already in the house.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Double the batch and freeze one log. This is the fastest way there is to make a plain weeknight chicken breast taste like it came from a restaurant.
  • ◆No fresh herbs? Use 1 tbsp dried parsley and ½ tsp dried thyme, but bloom them in the warm oil along with the garlic so they rehydrate instead of staying gritty.
  • ◆If the butter looks curdled or separated after mixing, it simply got too warm. Chill the bowl for 10 minutes, then beat it again and it comes right back together.
  • ◆Salted butter works fine — just cut the added salt to ¼ tsp and taste before adding more.
  • ◆Swap in 2 tsp anchovy paste and skip the lemon for a savory steakhouse version, or 1 tbsp minced chipotle in adobo for something smoky on corn.

Red Wine Pan Sauce for Steak⏱ 25 min🍽 Makes about ½ cup (120 ml), enough for 2 steaksMedium▾

The five-minute sauce that turns the brown bits left in your steak pan into something glossy and deep. Once you can do this, you never look at an empty skillet the same way again.

30 MinutesDate NightCast Iron
Prep
10 min
Cook
15 min
Total
25 min
Serves
Makes about ½ cup (120 ml), enough for 2 steaks
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Rest the meat first
    Move the seared steaks to a cutting board or warm plate and tent them loosely with foil while you work — the sauce takes about the same 8 to 10 minutes the meat needs to rest anyway. Never wash the skillet. Those stuck-on brown patches, called fond, are concentrated browned protein and sugar, and they are the entire reason this sauce tastes like anything.
  2. Pour off the excess fat
    Tip the pan and spoon out all but about 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the fat, leaving every bit of the browned residue behind. Too much fat and the sauce will never emulsify — it will look like salad dressing that split. If the fond looks black rather than deep mahogany it burned during searing, so start the sauce in a clean pan with 1 tbsp butter instead, because burnt fond will make the whole thing bitter.
  3. Sweat the shallot
    Set the skillet over medium-low heat and add the minced shallot with a pinch of the salt. Cook, stirring, for 2 to 3 minutes until it is translucent and smells sweet — you want a quiet sizzle, not a crackle, and no color at all. Add the garlic and cook just 30 seconds more; garlic burns in a hot pan in under a minute and turns acrid.
  4. Deglaze with the wine
    Pour in the ¾ cup wine all at once and immediately start scraping the bottom with a wooden spoon or flat-edged spatula. Every brown speck should release and dissolve into the liquid within about 30 seconds — that dissolving is literally the flavor moving from the pan into the sauce. Use a wine you would actually drink; cooking wine is salted and will make the finished sauce taste tinny.
  5. Reduce the wine hard
    Raise the heat to medium-high and let the wine bubble until it has reduced by about two-thirds, roughly 3 to 4 minutes, until only ¼ cup (60 ml) of syrupy liquid remains. This step boils off the raw alcohol, which otherwise tastes harsh and thin. You will know it is close when the bubbles get bigger and lazier and the liquid just coats the bottom of the pan.
  6. Add stock and thyme
    Pour in the ¾ cup stock, add the thyme sprig, and let it simmer briskly until reduced by about two-thirds, another 4 to 5 minutes. You are looking for about ⅓ cup (80 ml) of liquid that leaves a clear trail when you drag a spoon across the pan bottom. Any juices that have pooled under the resting steaks go in now too — that is free flavor most people pour down the drain.
  7. Whisk in the Dijon
    Turn the heat to low and whisk in the 1 tsp Dijon mustard until it disappears. Beyond the flavor, mustard is a genuine emulsifier — its ground seed coats hold fat and water together, which makes the butter step that comes next far less likely to break. Pull the thyme sprig out now; leave it any longer and it goes medicinal.
  8. Mount the butter off heat
    Take the pan completely off the burner and wait 30 seconds so it drops below about 190°F (88°C). Add the cold butter one piece at a time, swirling the pan or whisking constantly and only adding the next piece once the last has melted — this should take about 90 seconds total. Cold butter melting slowly into warm liquid suspends the fat in tiny droplets, which is what makes the sauce glossy and thick instead of oily.
  9. Rescue a broken sauce
    If the sauce looks greasy and separated, it got too hot. Pour it into a small bowl, put 1 tbsp (15 ml) of cold stock or water in the empty pan off the heat, and whisk the broken sauce back in a spoonful at a time, letting each addition come together before the next. Ninety percent of the time it re-emulsifies within a minute.
  10. Season and finish
    Taste and add the remaining salt and the black pepper, then decide about acid: if the sauce tastes rich but a bit flat, 1 tsp of red wine vinegar or lemon juice will sharpen everything without reading as sour. Remember the sauce is going onto salted steak, so it should taste balanced on its own, not aggressive. Strain it through a fine sieve if you want it silky and restaurant-smooth, or leave the shallots in for a more rustic look.
  11. Serve immediately
    Spoon 2 to 3 tbsp over each sliced steak, or pool it on the plate and lay the meat on top so the crust stays crisp. This sauce does not hold well — reheating drives it back over temperature and breaks it — so plate it the moment it is done. If you absolutely must wait, keep it in a warm spot off the heat and whisk in a teaspoon of cold water right before serving.
Know when it is done
Finish the sauce off the burner, below 190°F (88°C). Butter whisked into liquid hotter than that will split into oily droplets instead of emulsifying. Pull the steaks that made the fond at 130°F (54°C) for medium-rare — carryover adds about 5°F (3°C) while they rest, finishing them near 135°F (57°C).
Serve it with
Made for a rested ribeye or strip steak with mashed potatoes; drink the rest of the bottle you deglazed with.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Have every ingredient measured and next to the stove before the steaks come out. The whole sauce happens in about 8 minutes and there is no time to go hunting for the Dijon.
  • ◆No wine in the house? Use ½ cup (120 ml) extra stock plus 2 tsp (10 ml) balsamic vinegar and reduce the same way.
  • ◆This exact method works for pork chops and chicken thighs — just swap in chicken stock and use white wine or dry vermouth. Cook pork chops to 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest, and chicken thighs all the way to 165°F (74°C).
  • ◆A splash of brandy or cognac (2 tbsp / 30 ml) added with the wine gives it a steakhouse depth. Add it off the heat first if you cook on gas.

Béarnaise Sauce with Tarragon⏱ 30 min🍽 Makes about ¾ cup (180 ml), serves 4Advanced▾

Hollandaise's sharper, more interesting cousin — egg yolks and butter carried by a tarragon and vinegar reduction. It is the single best thing that has ever happened to a steak.

Date NightClassic FrenchSteak Night
Prep
10 min
Cook
20 min
Total
30 min
Serves
Makes about ¾ cup (180 ml), serves 4
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the reduction

For the emulsion

In reserve, in case it breaks

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Build the reduction
    Combine the wine, vinegar, shallot, tarragon stems, and cracked peppercorns in a small saucepan over medium heat. Simmer until only about 2 tbsp (30 ml) of liquid remains, roughly 6 to 8 minutes — tilt the pan and you should see barely a puddle. This concentrated, acidic base is what separates béarnaise from hollandaise, and reducing it properly is why the finished sauce tastes layered rather than just buttery.
  2. Strain and cool it
    Pour the reduction through a fine-mesh sieve into a heatproof bowl, pressing the solids firmly with the back of a spoon to get every drop, then discard the stems and peppercorns. Let it cool for 3 to 4 minutes until it is warm rather than hot. Adding hot liquid straight to egg yolks starts cooking them before you have any control, and that is how you end up with sweet scrambled eggs.
  3. Set up a gentle bain-marie
    Bring 1 inch (2.5 cm) of water to a bare simmer in a saucepan that your mixing bowl can sit inside without touching the water — about 180°F (82°C), with small bubbles rising lazily. Direct contact with the water or a hard boil will take the bowl past 165°F (74°C) fast and scramble the yolks. Keep a bowl of ice water and a splash of cold water within arm's reach as your emergency brake.
  4. Melt and hold the butter
    Melt the 8 tbsp butter gently in a small pan and keep it somewhere warm, around 130°F (54°C) — warm enough to stay liquid, cool enough that you can hold a finger in it. Butter hotter than about 150°F (66°C) will curdle the yolks as you stream it in. For an extra-stable sauce, let the melted butter settle for 2 minutes and pour off the clear golden fat, leaving the milky solids behind.
  5. Whisk the yolks and water
    Add the 3 egg yolks and 1 tbsp cold water to the bowl with the cooled reduction and whisk them together off the heat until smooth and slightly frothy, about 20 seconds. The water is not filler — it gives the yolks room to expand and buffers them against overheating. Use a bowl with a rounded bottom so the whisk can reach everywhere; square corners are where sauces scramble first.
  6. Cook to the ribbon stage
    Set the bowl over the simmering water and whisk constantly and vigorously, scraping the sides every few seconds. In 3 to 5 minutes the yolks will triple in volume, lighten in color, and thicken enough that the whisk leaves visible trails and a ribbon of sauce falling back holds its shape for 2 seconds. Take the bowl off the heat the moment it reads 160°F (71°C) — that is both the safe temperature for eggs and the point of maximum thickness before they curdle.
  7. Stream in the butter
    Off the heat, or with the bowl only touching the steam intermittently, start adding the warm butter in a thin, steady thread while whisking without stopping. Go painfully slowly for the first 2 tbsp — those first drops are where the emulsion forms, and dumping butter in is the number one reason béarnaise breaks. Once about a third is in and the sauce visibly thickens, you can pour a little faster; the whole process should take 2 to 3 minutes.
  8. Adjust the consistency
    The finished sauce should be thick enough to coat a spoon and hold a soft peak-like mound, but still pourable. If it is stiff or pasty, whisk in warm water 1 tsp (5 ml) at a time until it loosens — this also makes the emulsion more stable, not less. If it is thin, put the bowl back over the steam for 20 to 30 seconds while whisking.
  9. Rescue a broken sauce
    If it goes greasy and grainy, do not throw it out. Put 1 tbsp (15 ml) of very hot water, or a fresh egg yolk with 1 tsp cold water, in a clean bowl and whisk the broken sauce into it a teaspoon at a time, letting each spoonful come together before the next. Broken from overheating usually needs cold water; broken from adding butter too fast usually needs a fresh yolk.
  10. Finish with the herbs
    Fold in the 2 tbsp chopped tarragon leaves, the chervil or parsley, the ½ tsp salt, and the cayenne. Add the herbs at the very end so they stay bright green and aromatic — cooked tarragon goes dull and tastes like licorice cough syrup. Taste, and only if it seems flat add the 1 tsp lemon juice; the reduction has already brought most of the acidity you need.
  11. Hold it safely
    Béarnaise lives in a narrow window: keep it between 130°F and 140°F (54°C and 60°C) in a thermos, or in a bowl set over water that has been taken off the heat, for up to 1 hour. Above 145°F (63°C) it scrambles, below 120°F (49°C) the butter starts to set and it turns grainy. Whisk it every 10 minutes or so and never reheat it directly over a burner.
  12. Serve it right away
    Spoon 2 to 3 tbsp over sliced steak, roasted asparagus, or a piece of poached fish just before it goes to the table. Warn anyone eating it that this sauce is genuinely rich — 3 tbsp per person is plenty. Leftovers cannot be reheated, but they are wonderful cold, spread on a steak sandwich the next day.
Know when it is done
Cook the yolk base to 160°F (71°C) so the eggs are safe, then keep the finished sauce between 130°F and 140°F (54°C and 60°C). Past 145°F (63°C) it scrambles. The steak underneath should be pulled at 130°F (54°C) for medium-rare, where carryover during the rest carries it to about 135°F (57°C).
Serve it with
The classic partner for a grilled strip steak and frites; a crisp Sancerre or a chalky Chablis cuts the butter beautifully.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Room-temperature yolks emulsify far more easily than cold ones. Set the eggs on the counter 30 minutes before you start, or sit them in warm tap water for 5 minutes.
  • ◆Make the reduction up to 3 days ahead and keep it strained in the fridge. That splits the recipe into a calm part and a fast part, which makes dinner much less stressful.
  • ◆If fresh tarragon is nowhere to be found, use 2 tsp dried in the reduction and 1 tsp stirred in at the end, but know the finished sauce will be noticeably softer in flavor.
  • ◆A wide bowl over a narrow pot gives you more surface area and more control than a deep bowl. Sauces break in the corners you cannot reach with a whisk.
  • ◆For choron sauce, whisk 2 tbsp (30 g) tomato paste into the finished béarnaise — it is the classic pairing for filet mignon.

Classic Hollandaise Sauce⏱ 25 min🍽 Makes about 1 cup (240 ml), serves 4Advanced▾

Warm lemon and butter held together by egg yolks — the mother sauce that makes eggs Benedict worth getting out of bed for. It sounds intimidating and takes about twelve minutes.

BrunchClassic French30 Minutes
Prep
10 min
Cook
15 min
Total
25 min
Serves
Makes about 1 cup (240 ml), serves 4
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Understand what you are building
    Hollandaise is an emulsion: egg yolk lecithin suspending melted butter in a small amount of water so it behaves like a cream instead of a puddle of grease. Everything that can go wrong comes down to temperature or speed — too hot and the yolks scramble, too fast with the butter and the emulsion never forms. Read the whole recipe once before you start, because there is no pausing halfway.
  2. Melt and hold the butter
    Melt the 10 tbsp butter in a small saucepan over low heat, then move it somewhere warm and let it sit 2 minutes. It should be about 130°F (54°C) — liquid, but you can dip a finger in without flinching. If you want a firmer, longer-lasting sauce, pour off the clear golden fat and leave the milky white solids in the pan, which is clarified butter and gives you a more stable emulsion.
  3. Rig a double boiler
    Bring 1 inch (2.5 cm) of water to a bare simmer in a saucepan, around 180°F (82°C), and find a metal or glass bowl that rests in the rim without its bottom touching the water. Steam, not contact heat, is what cooks the yolks gently enough to control. Turn the burner to its lowest setting once the water is simmering; a rolling boil will overshoot you in seconds.
  4. Whisk the yolk base
    Off the heat, whisk the 3 yolks, 1 tbsp cold water, and 1 tbsp lemon juice in the bowl for about 30 seconds until pale, smooth, and a little foamy. The water and lemon juice do real work here — they add the liquid phase that the butter will suspend in, and acid helps keep the proteins from clumping. Use a balloon whisk if you have one, since it incorporates far more air than a flat one.
  5. Cook to the ribbon stage
    Set the bowl over the simmering water and whisk hard and continuously for 3 to 5 minutes, scraping the sides constantly. The yolks will double or triple in volume, turn pale yellow, and thicken to the point where a drizzle falling from the whisk sits on the surface for 2 seconds before sinking. Pull the bowl off at 160°F (71°C) — that is safe for eggs and the very top of the thickening curve.
  6. Start the butter slowly
    With the bowl off the heat and sitting on a damp towel so it does not skate around, add the warm butter a few drops at a time while whisking without stopping. Spend a full 30 seconds on the first 2 tbsp — this is where the emulsion is born, and rushing it is why most hollandaise fails. You will feel the sauce grab and thicken; that is the signal you can go on.
  7. Stream in the rest
    Once about a third of the butter is in and the sauce clearly holds together, pour the remainder in a thin steady thread, still whisking. The whole butter addition should take 2 to 3 minutes. If you clarified the butter, stop when you reach the milky solids at the bottom of the pan — they add water and can loosen the sauce.
  8. Adjust to nappe consistency
    The finished sauce should coat the back of a spoon so that a finger drawn through leaves a clean line that does not run — chefs call this nappe. If it is too thick, whisk in warm water 1 tsp at a time; counterintuitively, a bit more water makes an emulsion more stable, not thinner in flavor. If it is loose, return it to the steam for 20 seconds while whisking.
  9. Rescue a broken sauce
    Greasy, separated, or grainy sauce is fixable. Put 1 tbsp (15 ml) of hot water in a clean bowl and whisk the broken sauce into it drop by drop, or start over with one fresh yolk whisked with 1 tsp cold water and dribble the broken sauce in. If it broke because it got too hot and there are visible cooked bits, strain it through a fine sieve first.
  10. Season at the end
    Whisk in the ½ tsp salt, the cayenne, and the white pepper, then taste. It should be bright and lemony enough to cut through butter — if it tastes heavy, add the extra teaspoon of lemon juice. Season last, because a reduced or thickened sauce concentrates whatever salt is already in it.
  11. Hold and serve
    Serve within 30 minutes, keeping the bowl in a warm spot between 130°F and 140°F (54°C and 60°C) — near the stove is usually about right. A thermos rinsed with hot water holds it perfectly for an hour. Never refrigerate and reheat hollandaise; the emulsion will not survive it, though the cold sauce is very good stirred into mashed potatoes.
Know when it is done
Bring the yolk base to 160°F (71°C) for egg safety, then hold the finished sauce at 130°F to 140°F (54°C to 60°C). It curdles above 145°F (63°C).
Serve it with
Poached eggs on English muffins, roasted asparagus, or steamed new potatoes; a mimosa or a dry Prosecco is traditional for good reason.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆If you are nervous, use a blender: buzz the yolks, lemon juice, and salt for 20 seconds, then stream in butter heated to 200°F (93°C) with the motor running. It is nearly foolproof, just slightly less silky.
  • ◆For eggs Benedict, make the hollandaise first and hold it warm. Poached eggs and toasted muffins wait far worse than the sauce does.
  • ◆Pasteurized eggs in the shell are widely available and worth buying if you are cooking for someone pregnant, elderly, or immune-compromised.
  • ◆One yolk will emulsify roughly 3 to 4 tbsp (45 to 55 g) of butter. That ratio is how you scale this recipe up or down without guessing.

Beurre Blanc for Fish⏱ 30 min🍽 Makes about 1 cup (240 ml), serves 4Advanced▾

A whole stick and a half of cold butter whisked into a shallot-and-wine reduction until it turns into pale, tangy silk. Nothing makes a plain piece of white fish look more expensive.

Classic FrenchDate Night30 Minutes
Prep
10 min
Cook
20 min
Total
30 min
Serves
Makes about 1 cup (240 ml), serves 4
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the reduction

To finish

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Cube the butter cold
    Cut the 12 tbsp butter into 12 roughly equal cubes and put them back in the refrigerator until the moment you need them. Cold butter is the whole trick: as each cube melts slowly, its own water and milk proteins disperse the fat into droplets instead of letting it pool. Butter that has softened on the counter melts too fast and gives you a greasy, separated sauce.
  2. Start the reduction
    Combine the wine, vinegar, shallot, peppercorns, and bay leaf in a small heavy-bottomed saucepan — stainless steel, not aluminum, which reacts with acid and can turn the sauce grey. Bring it to a simmer over medium heat and cook for 6 to 8 minutes. A heavy pan matters here because thin pans create hot spots that will break the emulsion later.
  3. Reduce to a glaze
    Keep going until only about 2 tbsp (30 ml) of syrupy liquid remains and the shallots look like a wet mound rather than sitting in a puddle. Tilt the pan and drag a spoon across the bottom — the liquid should be slow to fill the gap. This concentrated acid is what keeps a stick and a half of butter from tasting like nothing but fat.
  4. Add the cream insurance
    Pour in the 2 tbsp heavy cream and simmer 1 minute until it barely thickens. Traditional beurre blanc has no cream, but the milk proteins in cream are powerful emulsifiers and they roughly double how long your sauce will hold before splitting. If you skip it, whisk more attentively and serve faster.
  5. Drop the heat right down
    Turn the burner to its lowest setting, or better, pull the pan onto a cool burner for 30 seconds first. From here on the sauce must never simmer again — the target is 120°F to 135°F (49°C to 57°C), warm enough to melt butter and no warmer. If your stove runs hot even on low, set the pan on a folded towel or work over a bowl of barely warm water.
  6. Whisk in the first cubes
    Add 2 cubes of cold butter and whisk constantly until they are almost but not entirely melted, about 20 seconds. That last bit of unmelted butter is your temperature gauge: as long as you can still see solid butter, the sauce is not too hot. If the butter vanishes instantly, the pan is too hot — pull it off the heat for 30 seconds before continuing.
  7. Build the emulsion
    Keep adding butter 2 cubes at a time, whisking each addition until nearly melted before the next goes in — the whole process takes 4 to 6 minutes. The sauce will slowly turn pale, opaque, and thick enough to coat a spoon like heavy cream. Lift the pan on and off the heat as needed; a steady rhythm beats constant high heat every time.
  8. Watch for the danger signs
    If the sauce starts looking thin and shiny with oil pooling at the edge, it is about to break. Pull it off the heat immediately, drop in 1 more cold butter cube, and whisk hard for 15 seconds — that usually pulls it back. If it has already separated completely, see the rescue step below.
  9. Rescue a broken sauce
    Put 2 tbsp (30 ml) of heavy cream or 1 tbsp (15 ml) of cold water into a clean warm pan off the heat, then whisk the broken sauce into it a tablespoon at a time, waiting for each addition to come together. Working slowly is not optional — dump it in and you will just have a bigger broken sauce. A stick blender used on low for 10 seconds will also usually bring it back.
  10. Strain and season
    Pour the sauce through a fine-mesh sieve into a warm bowl, pressing gently on the shallots, then whisk in the ½ tsp salt and 1 tsp lemon juice. Straining is what makes it look like restaurant food — smooth, pale, and glossy with no bits. Taste it: it should be tangy first, buttery second, and not at all greasy.
  11. Hold it, briefly
    Beurre blanc holds for about 30 minutes in a bowl set over water that has been taken off the heat, or in a preheated thermos. It cannot be refrigerated and reheated. Fold in the chives just before serving and spoon 2 to 3 tbsp over each piece of fish, ideally under the fillet so the skin stays crisp.
Know when it is done
Hold the pan between 120°F and 135°F (49°C and 57°C) the entire time you add butter. Above 136°F (58°C) the emulsion breaks and the sauce turns to oil. The fish going under it is done at 145°F (63°C) in the thickest part, when it flakes with gentle pressure.
Serve it with
Spoon it under roasted halibut, cod, or scallops with steamed potatoes; pour the same crisp white you used in the reduction.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make the wine reduction hours ahead and leave it in the pan. The butter step is only 5 minutes, which means you can start it while the fish is in the oven.
  • ◆Serving with scallops or shrimp? Substitute 2 tbsp (30 ml) of their pan juices for part of the wine — the sauce picks up the sweetness of the shellfish.
  • ◆For beurre rouge, swap in red wine and red wine vinegar. It is stunning on salmon and duck breast.
  • ◆Do not salt the reduction. Reducing concentrates salt, and you can always correct at the end when you know exactly how much sauce you have.
  • ◆If your stove will not go low enough, build the whole sauce in a metal bowl set over a pan of hot-but-not-simmering water. Slower, but far harder to break.
