Nutty Brown Butter⏱ 12 min🍽 Makes about ¾ cup (170 ml)Easy▾

Butter cooked until the milk solids toast and the whole kitchen smells like hazelnuts. Five minutes of standing at the stove buys you a flavor you cannot get any other way.

15 MinutesOne PanMake Ahead
Prep
2 min
Cook
10 min
Total
12 min
Serves
Makes about ¾ cup (170 ml)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Pick a light-colored pan
    Use a stainless steel or light-enameled saucepan rather than nonstick or cast iron, because you need to see the color of the milk solids to know when to stop. A 2-quart (2 L) pan is about right for a cup of butter — too wide and it browns unevenly, too narrow and you cannot see the bottom. Have a heatproof bowl sitting next to the stove before you start.
  2. Cut the butter up
    Cut the butter into 1 tbsp pieces so it all melts at roughly the same rate. If half the butter is liquid while the other half is still a cold block, the melted portion starts browning early and you get scorched solids alongside pale ones. This 30-second step is the difference between even, nutty butter and a batch that tastes half burnt.
  3. Melt over medium heat
    Set the pan over medium heat and swirl occasionally as the butter melts, which takes about 2 minutes. Resist the urge to crank the heat — butter is roughly 16 percent water, and it has to boil that water off before it can brown, which is a process you want to happen steadily. It should bubble energetically but never spit violently.
  4. Boil off the water
    The butter will foam up loudly and sputter for 3 to 5 minutes as the water evaporates. This is the noisy phase and it is completely normal — the crackling sound is water escaping. When the noise quiets down and the foam subsides, you are close to the browning stage and you must stop doing anything else and watch the pan.
  5. Watch for the color change
    Once the sputtering stops, the milk solids at the bottom will go from pale to golden to a deep hazelnut brown in about 60 to 90 seconds. Swirl the pan constantly now and tilt it to look under the foam — the color lives on the bottom, not on the surface. The smell will change from buttery to distinctly nutty and toasted, which is your most reliable cue.
  6. Add the sage if using
    If you are making sage brown butter, drop the 8 sage leaves in during the last 30 seconds of browning. They will crackle and go crisp almost immediately, perfuming the butter and giving you something wonderful to crumble over the finished dish. Fish them out with a fork and set them on a paper towel if you want them to stay crisp.
  7. Stop the cooking immediately
    The moment the solids are the color of a copper penny — around 300°F (150°C) — pour the butter into your waiting heatproof bowl, scraping every brown speck out with a spatula. A hot pan keeps cooking off the burner and will take you from nutty to acrid in 20 seconds. If you are stuck without a bowl, adding the 1 tbsp cold water will halt it instantly, though it will spit.
  8. Season and finish
    Stir in the ¼ tsp flaky salt and, if you like, the 1 tsp lemon juice — the acid keeps rich brown butter from feeling one-note. Taste it on a spoon: it should be nutty and deep with no bitterness at the back of your throat. Bitter means it went too far, and unfortunately there is no fixing that.
  9. Use it everywhere
    Toss it with cooked ravioli or gnocchi and grated Parmigiano, spoon it over roasted squash or green beans, or pour it over pan-seared fish. In baking, use it in place of melted butter in cookies and blondies, but let it cool and add 1 tbsp (15 ml) water back per stick to replace what evaporated. It is also outstanding whisked into mashed potatoes.
  10. Store the extra
    Cooled brown butter keeps 2 weeks in a sealed jar in the fridge at or below 40°F (4°C) and 3 months in the freezer. It solidifies with the brown specks settled at the bottom, so stir it before using to redistribute all that toasted flavor. Warm it gently in a pan or for 15 seconds in the microwave — do not re-brown it.
Know when it is done
Butter browns between 250°F and 300°F (120°C and 150°C) once its water has boiled away. Pull it at 300°F (150°C), when the solids are hazelnut-colored and it smells toasted.
Serve it with
Best on cheese ravioli, roasted squash, or seared scallops; a glass of unoaked Chardonnay handles the richness.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Never walk away during the last two minutes. Brown butter goes from perfect to burnt faster than almost anything else in cooking.
  • ◆Salted butter browns just as well; simply skip the finishing salt and taste before adding any.
  • ◆For baking, weigh the butter before and after. You will lose about 15 percent to evaporation, and adding that weight back as cold water keeps cookies from turning out dry.
  • ◆Brown butter plus a squeeze of lemon and a handful of capers is a two-minute sauce for any white fish — it is essentially fish meunière.

Argentinian Chimichurri Sauce⏱ 50 min🍽 Makes about 1½ cups (350 ml)Easy▾

Chopped parsley, oregano, garlic, and vinegar loosened with good olive oil — the sharp green sauce Argentinians put on everything off the grill. It takes twenty minutes and no cooking at all.

No CookMake AheadGrilling
Prep
20 min
Cook
0 min
Total
50 min
Serves
Makes about 1½ cups (350 ml)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Chop, do not blend
    Real chimichurri is hand-chopped, and it genuinely matters. A food processor pulverizes the parsley cells and releases chlorophyll and bitter compounds, giving you a dull, khaki-colored paste that tastes like lawn clippings. Hand-chopping keeps the pieces distinct so the sauce stays bright green with visible texture.
  2. Prep the parsley properly
    Wash the parsley and dry it completely in a salad spinner or between towels — wet herbs dilute the sauce and make it spoil faster. Gather the leaves and tender upper stems into a tight bundle and chop them fine with a sharp knife, about 20 to 30 passes. A dull knife bruises rather than cuts, which is another route to that grey-green color you are trying to avoid.
  3. Soften the garlic and shallot
    Mince the 4 garlic cloves and the shallot as finely as you can, then put them in your mixing bowl with the 3 tbsp red wine vinegar and 1½ tsp kosher salt. Let them sit for 10 minutes before anything else goes in. The acid and salt chemically blunt the harsh sulfur bite of raw garlic and onion, which is why some chimichurris taste aggressive and this one will not.
  4. Bloom the pepper flakes
    Stir the 1 tsp red pepper flakes into the vinegar mixture along with the garlic. Chile heat and aroma are fat- and acid-soluble, so giving the flakes a few minutes in liquid draws the flavor out into the sauce instead of leaving it locked in dry specks. If you prefer real heat, use a fresh red chile, seeded and minced fine.
  5. Add the herbs
    Stir the chopped parsley and oregano into the bowl. If you are using dried oregano rather than fresh, add it now with the vinegar so it has time to rehydrate — dried oregano straight into oil stays gritty and tastes dusty. Fresh oregano is punchier than most people expect, so start with the 3 tbsp and add more only after tasting.
  6. Stir in the oil last
    Pour in the ¾ cup olive oil in a slow stream while stirring with a fork. Chimichurri is not an emulsion and it is supposed to separate a little — you are just coating the herbs, not building a dressing. Use a decent but not precious extra-virgin oil; the very grassy, peppery ones can fight with the parsley.
  7. Loosen with warm water
    Stir in the 2 tbsp warm water and the 1 tbsp lemon juice. The water sounds odd but it is traditional — it softens the raw edge of the vinegar and gives the sauce a looser, more spoonable consistency that runs into the cuts of a sliced steak. The finished texture should pour off a spoon in a heavy stream, not sit in a mound.
  8. Rest it 30 minutes
    Cover and leave the bowl at room temperature for at least 30 minutes, or up to 2 hours, before serving. The herbs need that time to release their oils into the olive oil and for all the sharp edges to knit together — freshly mixed chimichurri tastes like separate ingredients sitting in a bowl. Do not skip this; it is the difference between good and very good.
  9. Taste and correct
    After resting, taste it on a piece of bread or a bit of plain meat rather than off a spoon, since chimichurri tastes far more intense neat. Add the remaining ½ tsp black pepper, then adjust: flat means more salt, harsh means more oil or water, dull means a splash more vinegar. It should be assertive enough to stand up to a charred ribeye.
  10. Serve and store
    Spoon it generously over sliced grilled steak, chicken thighs, roasted potatoes, or a fried egg. Refrigerated in a jar with a film of oil on top, it keeps 5 days at or below 40°F (4°C), though the color dulls after day two. Always let it come back to room temperature before serving, because cold olive oil turns cloudy and tastes waxy.
Know when it is done
No cooking involved. Serve at room temperature, around 68°F (20°C) — straight from the fridge the olive oil is cloudy and the flavors read muted. Pull the steak it goes on at 130°F (54°C) for medium-rare and rest it 5 minutes; carryover finishes it at about 135°F (57°C).
Serve it with
Made for grilled skirt steak and charred bread; a big juicy Malbec is the traditional and correct answer.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Do not use a food processor. If you truly must, pulse only 4 or 5 times and expect a darker, less lively sauce.
  • ◆Chimichurri also works as a marinade — toss flank or skirt steak in half the batch for 2 to 4 hours in the fridge, then serve the untouched half at the table. Throw the used marinade out rather than spooning it over cooked meat, and grill the steak to a 130°F (54°C) pull for medium-rare.
  • ◆Freeze it in an ice cube tray, then bag the cubes. One cube dropped into a hot pan of vegetables or a bowl of soup is a small miracle in February.
  • ◆Cilantro-heavy versions exist, but the Argentinian original is parsley and oregano. If you swap in cilantro, add 1 tsp ground cumin to keep it balanced.

Catalan Romesco Sauce⏱ 1 hr 15 min🍽 Makes about 2½ cups (600 ml)Medium▾

Roasted peppers, toasted almonds, and fried bread blitzed with smoked paprika and sherry vinegar into a thick, smoky, faintly sweet sauce. It makes grilled vegetables and plain chicken taste like a holiday.

Make AheadVegetarianGrilling
Prep
20 min
Cook
25 min
Total
1 hr 15 min
Serves
Makes about 2½ cups (600 ml)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For roasting

For the sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Heat the oven hot
    Set an oven rack in the upper third and heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). You want real heat here — romesco depends on the peppers and tomatoes actually charring rather than gently steaming, because those blackened patches are where the smoky backbone comes from. Line a sheet pan with foil to save yourself the cleanup.
  2. Roast the vegetables
    Halve and seed the bell peppers, halve the tomatoes, and toss everything including the unpeeled garlic cloves with the 2 tbsp olive oil. Lay the peppers skin-side up and roast for 20 to 25 minutes, until the pepper skins are blistered and black in patches and the tomatoes have collapsed. Pull the garlic out at 15 minutes so it does not turn bitter.
  3. Steam and peel the peppers
    Move the hot peppers to a bowl and cover it tightly with a plate or plastic wrap for 10 minutes. The trapped steam separates the skin from the flesh so it slips off in sheets instead of coming away in frustrating scraps. Peel them, and peel the tomatoes and garlic too — skins left in will give the finished sauce a papery texture no amount of blending fixes.
  4. Soak the dried chiles
    While the peppers roast, tear open the ñora or ancho chiles, discard the stems and seeds, and cover them with 1 cup (240 ml) of just-boiled water for 15 minutes. Push them under with a spoon so they hydrate evenly. Once soft, scrape the flesh from the skins with a paring knife if you want the smoothest possible sauce, or use the whole soaked chile for a rustic version.
  5. Toast the nuts
    Toast the almonds and hazelnuts in a dry skillet over medium heat for 4 to 6 minutes, shaking often, until they smell fragrant and are lightly golden inside when you break one open. Toasting is not optional — raw nuts make a chalky, flat sauce, while toasted ones bring the roasted sweetness that defines romesco. Tip them onto a plate right away so they stop cooking.
  6. Fry the bread
    In the same skillet, add 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the extra-virgin olive oil and fry the torn bread over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes, turning, until it is golden and crisp all over. The bread is the thickener — it is what gives romesco its body without cream or eggs. It should be crunchy like a crouton, not merely warm and soft.
  7. Grind the dry ingredients first
    Put the toasted nuts and fried bread in a food processor and pulse 15 to 20 times until they look like coarse sand. Grinding the solids before anything wet goes in is what gets you an even texture — add liquid too early and you will be left with stubborn nut chunks. Scrape down the sides once during this.
  8. Add the roasted vegetables
    Add the peeled peppers, tomatoes, roasted garlic, soaked chile flesh, smoked paprika, cayenne, and 1½ tsp salt. Process for 30 to 45 seconds until it forms a thick, coarse paste. It should look rough and rustic at this stage, not smooth — the emulsifying happens next.
  9. Stream in the oil
    With the motor running, pour in the remaining olive oil in a thin steady stream over about 45 seconds. Going slowly lets the oil emulsify into the paste rather than sitting on top of it, which is the difference between a glossy sauce and an oily one. Then add the 2 tbsp sherry vinegar and pulse 3 or 4 times to combine.
  10. Correct the texture
    Romesco should be thick enough to mound on a spoon but loose enough to spread with the back of it — think hummus, not tomato sauce. If it is too thick, add the chile soaking liquid 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time. If it is too thin, pulse in another small piece of fried bread or a few more toasted almonds.
  11. Rest, then taste
    Let it sit for at least 30 minutes at room temperature before you judge the seasoning — the paprika and chile need time to bloom into the oil. Then taste and adjust: more salt if it is flat, more sherry vinegar if it tastes heavy, more cayenne if it is too polite. Romesco should be smoky, gently sweet, and tangy in roughly that order.
  12. Serve and store
    Serve it at room temperature, around 70°F (21°C), spooned over grilled spring onions, charred asparagus, roasted potatoes, seared fish cooked to 145°F (63°C), or a chicken breast cooked to 165°F (74°C). Stored in a jar with a thin layer of oil on top, it keeps 1 week in the fridge at or below 40°F (4°C) and 3 months in the freezer. The flavor is genuinely better on day two.
Know when it is done
Roast at 425°F (220°C) until the pepper skins blister and blacken in patches. Serve the finished sauce at room temperature, about 70°F (21°C), and store it below 40°F (4°C).
Serve it with
Wonderful with grilled vegetables, lamb chops, or seared shrimp; a chilled Spanish rosado or a dry fino sherry is the local move.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Two 12 oz (340 g) jars of drained roasted piquillo peppers will get you a very good romesco in half the time on a weeknight. Skip straight to the toasting step.
  • ◆Ñora chiles are traditional and worth ordering online, but ancho gives you a similar sweet, raisiny depth and is in most supermarkets.
  • ◆Leftover romesco is outstanding stirred into scrambled eggs, spread on a sandwich instead of mayo, or thinned with pasta water into a sauce for orecchiette.
  • ◆If you have a nut allergy in the house, replace the nuts with ¾ cup (45 g) more fried bread plus 2 tbsp (18 g) toasted sunflower seeds.
  • ◆Freeze it in a flat bag so you can snap off a portion; it thaws in about 20 minutes on the counter.

Pesto alla Genovese⏱ 25 min🍽 Makes about 1½ cups (350 ml), dresses 1 lb (450 g) pastaMedium▾

Basil, pine nuts, two cheeses, and good olive oil — no cooking, no shortcuts, and finished in twenty minutes. Done properly it stays a vivid green instead of the muddy stuff in jars.

No CookVegetarian30 Minutes
Prep
20 min
Cook
5 min
Total
25 min
Serves
Makes about 1½ cups (350 ml), dresses 1 lb (450 g) pasta
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the pesto

Optional, for color and for tossing

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Choose small basil leaves
    Look for small to medium leaves, ideally Genovese basil, and pull off any thick stems since they are fibrous and bitter. Large mature leaves carry more of the minty, aggressive compounds that make pesto taste harsh. Wash and dry the leaves completely — any water clinging to them will dilute the sauce and speed up the browning.
  2. Toast the pine nuts gently
    Toast the ⅓ cup pine nuts in a dry skillet over medium-low heat for 3 to 5 minutes, shaking the pan constantly, until they are pale gold and smell sweet. Pine nuts are extremely high in oil and burn in seconds, so never step away. Tip them onto a cold plate immediately and let them cool completely, because warm nuts will wilt the basil.
  3. Blanch for lasting green
    This step is optional but it is what keeps pesto emerald for days. Drop the basil into the salted boiling water for exactly 10 seconds, then lift it straight into the ice water, and squeeze it bone dry in a towel. The brief heat deactivates the enzyme that turns cut basil black, at the cost of a slight softening of the aroma.
  4. Chill your equipment
    Put the food processor bowl and blade, or your mortar, in the freezer for 10 minutes before you start. Heat is the enemy of pesto: friction from a spinning blade can push the mixture past 105°F (40°C), which oxidizes the basil and turns it a dull olive brown. A cold bowl buys you the extra thirty seconds you need.
  5. Start with garlic and salt
    Put the garlic cloves, pine nuts, and ¾ tsp coarse sea salt in the processor and pulse 10 to 12 times until you have a coarse, sandy paste. The salt crystals act as an abrasive that tears the garlic apart, which is exactly what a mortar and pestle does mechanically. Starting with the hard ingredients means you will not have to over-process later to break down a stray clove.
  6. Add the basil in pulses
    Add the basil leaves and pulse in short bursts — 1 second on, 1 second off, about 15 to 20 pulses — scraping down the sides twice. Never let the machine run continuously, because sustained blade contact bruises the leaves and releases bitterness. You are aiming for a rough green paste with visible flecks, not a smooth purée.
  7. Stream in the oil
    With the motor running in short pulses, add the ¾ cup olive oil in a thin stream over about 30 seconds. Use a mild, fruity extra-virgin oil rather than a peppery Tuscan one — a bitter oil plus bitter over-processed basil is how pesto goes wrong. Stop as soon as it comes together into a loose, glossy paste.
  8. Fold in the cheese by hand
    Scrape the pesto into a bowl and stir in the Parmigiano-Reggiano and Pecorino Romano with a spoon rather than the machine. Blending cheese makes it gummy and can make the sauce claggy; folding keeps the texture light. Grate the cheese as finely as you can on a Microplane so it melts smoothly into the oil.
  9. Taste and season
    Add the pinch of black pepper, then taste the pesto on a piece of bread or a plain boiled potato rather than straight off the spoon — neat pesto always reads sharper and saltier than it will once it is coating something starchy. Both cheeses are already salty, so you may need nothing more, but if it tastes flat add salt ⅛ tsp at a time and stir well between each addition. If it tastes harsh or faintly metallic, that is usually over-worked basil or too peppery an oil, and another tablespoon of mild olive oil will round it back out. You are aiming for basil first, cheese second, and garlic sitting quietly behind both.
  10. Sauce pasta off the heat
    If you are dressing pasta, never cook the pesto. Drain the pasta, reserving ¼ cup (60 ml) of the starchy water, then toss the hot pasta with the pesto and a splash of that water in a warm bowl off the burner. The residual heat is enough to release the aroma, while a hot pan would cook the basil and turn everything brown and grassy.
  11. Store it under oil
    Pack leftover pesto into a jar, smooth the top flat, and pour a ⅛-inch (3 mm) layer of olive oil over the surface to block air. It keeps 5 days in the fridge at or below 40°F (4°C). For longer storage, freeze it in an ice cube tray without the cheese and stir the cheese in after thawing, which keeps the texture much better.
Know when it is done
No cooking. Keep everything below 105°F (40°C) — the basil oxidizes and blackens above that, which is why cold equipment and short pulses matter.
Serve it with
Toss with trofie or linguine and a glass of Vermentino, or spoon it over a sliced tomato and mozzarella salad.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆A mortar and pestle genuinely makes better pesto — the crushing action releases oils instead of shredding cells. It takes about 12 minutes and is oddly relaxing.
  • ◆Pine nuts are expensive. Toasted walnuts or blanched almonds are traditional in parts of Liguria and work beautifully for a third of the price.
  • ◆The classic pasta for pesto is trofie or trenette, cooked with sliced potato and green beans in the same pot. Try it once and you will understand why.
  • ◆If your pesto turns brown, it is oxidation, not spoilage. It is still perfectly good to eat, and a squeeze of lemon juice will freshen the flavor.
  • ◆Thin leftover pesto with a little more olive oil and lemon juice for a fast dressing on sliced tomatoes, or on grilled chicken cooked to 165°F (74°C).

Fettuccine Alfredo Sauce⏱ 25 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

The real Roman version: butter, Parmigiano, and starchy pasta water beaten into a glossy cream with no actual cream in it. It is three ingredients and entirely about technique.

30 MinutesComfort FoodVegetarian
Prep
10 min
Cook
15 min
Total
25 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

For the sauce

For the pasta

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Know what you are making
    Authentic fettuccine Alfredo has no cream, no garlic, and no flour — it is an emulsion of butter, cheese, and starchy water, the same principle as cacio e pepe. That means it lives or dies on temperature and timing rather than on a list of ingredients. If you want the American cream version, that is in the tips, but try this one first.
  2. Grate the cheese finely
    Grate the full 6 oz Parmigiano-Reggiano on the smallest holes of a box grater or a Microplane so it looks like snow. Coarse shreds do not melt evenly and are the single most common cause of stringy, clumped Alfredo. Buy a wedge and grate it yourself — pre-grated cheese is coated with cellulose anti-caking powder that refuses to emulsify.
  3. Soften the butter
    Let the 12 tbsp butter sit at room temperature until it is soft enough to smear, about 65°F (18°C), then cut it into small pieces. Room-temperature butter incorporates far more readily than cold, and you are not melting it in a pan — it will melt from the heat of the pasta. High-fat European-style butter at 82 to 84 percent fat gives a noticeably richer, more stable sauce.
  4. Warm a wide serving bowl
    Fill a large wide bowl with hot tap water, let it stand while the pasta cooks, then dump the water right before you need it. Building the sauce in a cold bowl drops the temperature so fast the butter seizes and the cheese clumps. A warm bowl also holds the sauce at a workable temperature while you toss.
  5. Salt the water properly
    Bring the 3 quarts of water to a rolling boil and add the 2 tbsp kosher salt — it should taste like a mild broth. Use slightly less water than you might for other pasta so the cooking water ends up more concentrated in starch, which is what carries the emulsion. Do not add oil to the water; it coats the noodles and stops the sauce from clinging.
  6. Cook the pasta al dente
    Cook fresh fettuccine for 2 to 3 minutes, or dried for 1 to 2 minutes less than the package says. Bite a strand — you want a firm, slightly chalky core, because it will finish cooking in the sauce. Overcooked pasta releases too much starch and turns the finished dish gluey.
  7. Save the pasta water
    Before you drain anything, dip a heatproof measuring cup into the pot and pull out a full cup (240 ml) of that cloudy water. This is the most important ingredient in the recipe: the dissolved starch is what physically bridges the butter fat and the cheese proteins. Forgetting it is the most common way this dish fails, and there is no way to get it back.
  8. Build the butter base
    Drain the pasta and immediately pile it into the warm bowl with the butter pieces and ½ cup (120 ml) of the pasta water. Toss vigorously with tongs for about 30 seconds until every strand is coated and the butter has completely melted into a loose, milky sauce. Work fast; the pasta is your heat source and it is cooling by the second.
  9. Add the cheese off the heat
    Add the grated Parmigiano in three handfuls, tossing hard after each one and adding a splash more pasta water if it looks tight. Never do this over a burner — above about 175°F (79°C) the cheese proteins tighten, squeeze out their fat, and you get stringy clumps floating in oil. Off the heat, in a warm bowl, is the whole secret.
  10. Toss until it turns creamy
    Keep tossing and stirring for a full 60 to 90 seconds. The sauce goes through an ugly stage where it looks separated and watery, and then quite suddenly it comes together into something opaque, glossy, and clinging. That transformation is the emulsion forming, and it will not happen if you stop early.
  11. Fix a broken sauce
    If it stays greasy or clumps into strings, the mixture is too hot or too dry. Add 2 tbsp (30 ml) of hot pasta water and toss hard for 20 seconds, repeating once if needed. If instead it is thin and soupy, add another small handful of cheese and keep tossing — more starch and more protein both pull it back.
  12. Pepper and serve at once
    Grind the 1 tsp black pepper over the top, then taste and work in the ½ tsp fine sea salt — add it in two goes, because the salted pasta water and the Parmigiano have both been seasoning the dish while you tossed. Serve immediately in warmed bowls. Alfredo waits for nobody; within 5 minutes the emulsion tightens and it starts to congeal. Serve smaller portions than you think you need, because this is extremely rich food.
Know when it is done
Build the sauce off the heat, below 175°F (79°C). Parmigiano's proteins seize and squeeze out fat above that, which is exactly why Alfredo goes stringy.
Serve it with
Serve with a sharp green salad to cut the richness and a glass of crisp Frascati or Pinot Grigio.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆For the American cream version, simmer 1½ cups (350 ml) heavy cream with 4 tbsp (55 g) butter for 5 minutes, then whisk in 1½ cups (150 g) Parmigiano off the heat. It is far more forgiving and holds better.
  • ◆Use the pasta water generously. Most people are too timid with it, and a dry Alfredo is a broken Alfredo waiting to happen.
  • ◆Add grilled chicken cooked to 165°F (74°C), or sautéed shrimp, on top rather than stirring them in — extra liquid from the protein will thin the emulsion.
  • ◆Leftovers do not reheat well in the microwave. Warm them in a skillet over low heat with a splash of milk or water, stirring constantly.

Marinara Sauce from Scratch⏱ 1 hr🍽 Makes about 5 cups (1.2 L)Medium▾

Good canned tomatoes, a lot of garlic, olive oil, and about an hour of quiet simmering. Make a double batch on a Sunday and you have pizza, pasta, and meatball nights covered.

Make AheadFreezer FriendlyVegetarian
Prep
10 min
Cook
50 min
Total
1 hr
Serves
Makes about 5 cups (1.2 L)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Buy the right tomatoes
    Whole peeled tomatoes beat crushed or diced every time, because the diced varieties are treated with calcium chloride to help them hold their shape and they never break down properly. Look for the D.O.P. seal on San Marzano cans, or any brand whose ingredients are simply tomatoes and tomato juice — no citric acid, no basil, no salt. This one decision affects the finished sauce more than anything you do at the stove.
  2. Crush them by hand
    Pour the tomatoes and their juice into a large bowl and squeeze each one through your fingers until it is in rough, irregular pieces. Fish out and discard any hard white core near the stem end, which stays tough no matter how long you cook it. Hand-crushing gives you a rustic texture with real body; a blender whips in air and turns the sauce a pale orange.
  3. Warm the oil and garlic together
    Put the ⅓ cup olive oil and the sliced garlic in a cold 4- to 5-quart (4 to 5 L) heavy pot, then turn the heat to medium-low. Starting them cold together lets the garlic infuse the oil slowly over 3 to 4 minutes rather than scorching on contact with hot oil. Cook until the slices are pale gold at the edges and the kitchen smells sweet, then move quickly to the next step.
  4. Sweat the onion
    Add the diced onion and the ½ tsp red pepper flakes and cook for 6 to 8 minutes over medium-low, stirring occasionally, until the onion is soft and translucent with no color. You want a steady quiet sizzle. Browning the onion here would push the sauce toward a deeper, roasted flavor, which is lovely in a ragù but wrong for a bright marinara.
  5. Add the tomatoes
    Pour in the crushed tomatoes along with every drop of juice, then swirl about ½ cup (120 ml) of the water in each empty can to rinse out the last of the tomato and add that too — 1 cup (240 ml) between the two cans. Stir in the 1 tsp kosher salt and the dried oregano — dried herbs go in early so they have time to rehydrate and release their oils. Add the Parmigiano rind now if you are using one.
  6. Bring it to a lazy simmer
    Raise the heat until the sauce just begins to bubble, then immediately drop it to low. You are aiming for about 200°F (93°C) — a bubble breaking the surface every second or two, not a rolling boil. Boiling drives off the fresh, bright top notes and can scorch the sugars on the bottom of the pot.
  7. Simmer partly covered
    Set the lid on askew, leaving a gap of a couple of inches, and simmer for 40 to 45 minutes. The gap lets steam escape so the sauce reduces and concentrates, while the lid catches most of the spattering. Stir every 10 minutes, scraping the bottom corners of the pot where things stick first.
  8. Add the basil sprig
    Drop the whole basil sprig into the pot for the last 15 minutes of the simmer, stem and all, pushing it under the surface with a spoon so it steeps rather than scorches. A whole sprig perfumes the sauce and then comes out cleanly, while basil chopped and added early turns black and tastes like hay. Fish the sprig and the Parmigiano rind out before serving — the rind will have gone soft and gluey, which is exactly what it is supposed to do after 40 minutes of giving up its savoriness. If the rind has partly melted, chase the pieces down now rather than finding them on someone's plate.
  9. Judge the consistency
    The sauce is ready when a spoon dragged across the bottom leaves a channel that fills back in slowly, and when you can see olive oil pooling slightly at the edges — that separation means the water has cooked off. Expect to end up with about 5 cups (1.2 L). If it is still watery at 45 minutes, simmer uncovered another 10.
  10. Balance the acidity
    Taste it now. If it is sharp or metallic, stir in the ½ tsp sugar, or better, the 2 tbsp butter, which rounds off acid without making the sauce sweet. Add more salt in ¼ tsp increments until the tomato flavor snaps into focus — undersalted tomato sauce always tastes thin and sour.
  11. Finish with fresh basil
    Off the heat, tear the 10 basil leaves and stir them in, then let the sauce sit for 5 minutes before serving. Adding fresh basil at the very end preserves the sweet, perfumed aroma that cooking destroys. Taste one more time; residual heat can make salt read differently than it did at a full simmer.
  12. Store or freeze it
    Cool the sauce to room temperature within 2 hours, then refrigerate at or below 40°F (4°C) for up to 5 days or freeze for 6 months. Freeze it in 2-cup (475 ml) portions, which is the right amount for a pound of pasta for two people. Leave an inch of headroom in the container because it expands.
Know when it is done
Hold the pot at a lazy simmer, about 200°F (93°C), with a bubble breaking every second or two. Cool leftovers to below 40°F (4°C) within 2 hours.
Serve it with
Spaghetti with a shower of Parmigiano, or as the base for pizza and baked ziti; a simple Chianti is all it needs.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆This doubles perfectly in a big pot and only needs about 15 minutes more simmering. Sunday afternoon marinara pays you back all week.
  • ◆For arrabbiata, triple the red pepper flakes and skip the basil. For a quick vodka sauce, simmer 1 cup (240 ml) of this with ¼ cup (60 ml) vodka and ½ cup (120 ml) heavy cream for 10 minutes.
  • ◆If the sauce tastes flat no matter how much salt you add, it needs acid, not salt — 1 tsp (5 ml) of red wine vinegar usually wakes the whole pot up.
  • ◆Save your Parmigiano rinds in a bag in the freezer. Dropped into a simmering sauce or soup, they add a savory depth you cannot buy.
  • ◆Do not use a nonstick pot for long tomato simmers; a heavy stainless or enameled cast iron pot conducts more evenly and scorches far less.

Kansas City Barbecue Sauce⏱ 55 min🍽 Makes about 3 cups (700 ml)Medium▾

Thick, sweet, tangy, and dark with molasses — the sauce most people picture when they hear barbecue. Homemade takes forty-five mostly unattended minutes and buries anything in a bottle.

Make AheadGrillingHomemade Staple
Prep
10 min

55 min

Makes about 3 cups (700 ml)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Wet ingredients

Dry seasonings

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Measure everything first
    Line up all seventeen ingredients before you turn on the stove, because once the sauce starts simmering you will not want to be digging through the spice drawer. Put the dry spices — paprika, garlic powder, onion powder, chili powder, black pepper, cayenne, salt, and allspice — together in one small bowl, and keep the ½ cup brown sugar separate, since it only goes in later once there is enough liquid to dissolve it. Combining the spices ahead means no clumps of cayenne hiding in the finished sauce. This is a recipe where mise en place genuinely saves you.
  2. Bloom the tomato paste
    Melt the 1 tbsp butter in a 3-quart (3 L) heavy saucepan over medium heat, then add the 2 tbsp tomato paste and cook it, stirring, for 2 minutes until it darkens from bright red to brick and smells sweet rather than raw. Cooking tomato paste in fat caramelizes its sugars and removes the tinny flavor it has straight from the can. This one small step is what makes homemade sauce taste deeper than bottled.
  3. Toast the spices
    Add the bowl of dry spices — everything but the brown sugar, right down to the ½ tsp allspice — to the pot and stir constantly for 30 to 45 seconds until they are fragrant. Ground spices are full of volatile oils that only wake up in hot fat, and the difference between bloomed and unbloomed paprika is dramatic. Do not go past a minute or the paprika and chili powder will scorch and turn bitter.
  4. Add the liquids
    Pour in the ketchup, cider vinegar, molasses, water, Worcestershire, and yellow mustard, and whisk until completely smooth. Scrape the bottom of the pot as you go to lift the toasted spice paste into the sauce. Everything should look uniformly dark red-brown with no streaks of unmixed molasses.
  5. Dissolve the brown sugar
    Whisk in the ½ cup dark brown sugar until you cannot feel any grit against the bottom of the pot with the whisk. Undissolved sugar sinks and scorches, which will give the whole batch a burnt edge you cannot undo. Dark brown sugar rather than light matters here; the extra molasses is where Kansas City sauce gets its color and depth.
  6. Bring it to a bare simmer
    Raise the heat until you see the first bubbles, then drop it straight to low — you want about 195°F (91°C), with the surface blipping occasionally rather than actively bubbling. Sugar-heavy sauces catch and burn on the bottom faster than almost anything, so low and slow is not optional here. Set the lid on askew to catch spatters.
  7. Simmer and stir
    Cook for 35 to 45 minutes, stirring every 5 to 7 minutes and scraping the bottom corners with a flat-edged wooden spoon or silicone spatula. The sauce will darken noticeably and reduce by roughly a quarter. If it starts spitting like a volcano, the heat is too high — pull it off for a minute and turn the burner down.
  8. Test the thickness
    It is done when it coats the back of a spoon and a line drawn through it with your finger holds for a full 2 seconds without flooding back. Remember it thickens further as it cools, so stop slightly looser than your ideal. If it has gone too thick, whisk in water 1 tbsp (15 ml) at a time.
  9. Balance it to your taste
    Take it off the heat and taste with a clean spoon, letting it cool for a few seconds first so the heat does not mask the flavors. Too sweet wants another 1 tbsp (15 ml) of cider vinegar, too sharp wants another 1 tbsp brown sugar, and flat wants ¼ tsp more salt. This is your sauce now, so adjust it until you actually like it.
  10. Use it late on the grill
    Because of all that sugar, this sauce burns readily over direct heat. Brush it on ribs, chicken, or pulled pork only during the last 10 to 15 minutes of cooking, in two or three thin coats, letting each one set into a tacky glaze before adding the next. Keep a separate bowl of unused sauce for the table so nothing that touched raw meat comes back. Sauce is a finish, not a cooking method: chicken still has to reach 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part of the thigh, pork chops 145°F (63°C) plus a 3-minute rest, and pulled pork or ribs only give up around 203°F (95°C).
  11. Cool and store it
    Cool the sauce to room temperature, then pour it into clean jars and refrigerate at or below 40°F (4°C), where it keeps a full month thanks to all the vinegar and sugar. The flavor improves after 24 hours as the spices hydrate and settle. It also freezes for 6 months, though the texture is very slightly thinner after thawing.
Know when it is done
No doneness temperature for the sauce — hold it at a bare simmer, about 195°F (91°C), until a line drawn through it on a spoon holds for 2 seconds. Store it below 40°F (4°C). The meat under it still has to hit its own numbers: 165°F (74°C) for chicken, 145°F (63°C) plus a 3-minute rest for pork chops, about 203°F (95°C) for pulled pork and ribs.
Serve it with
Slathered on ribs, pulled pork, or grilled chicken thighs with slaw and a cold lager.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Making pulled pork or ribs? Save a cup of the sauce unheated and stir in 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the meat's own defatted drippings — it is a genuine upgrade.
  • ◆For a smokier sauce, swap the sweet paprika for smoked paprika, or add 1 tsp (5 ml) liquid smoke off the heat at the very end.
  • ◆This is also a burger glaze, a meatloaf topping, a dip for fries, and the base of a great sandwich sauce mixed 1-to-1 with mayonnaise.
  • ◆Molasses varies a lot by brand. Blackstrap is bitter and mineral-heavy — if it is all you have, use half the amount and add 2 tbsp (30 ml) honey.
  • ◆Bottle it in a swing-top jar with a handwritten label and it is a real gift.

Greek Tzatziki with Cucumber⏱ 1 hr 50 min🍽 Makes about 2½ cups (600 ml)Easy▾

Thick strained yogurt, squeezed cucumber, garlic, and dill — cool, sharp, and ready for anything grilled. The one non-negotiable step is getting the water out of the cucumber.

No CookMake AheadVegetarian
Prep
20 min
Cook
0 min
Total
1 hr 50 min
Serves
Makes about 2½ cups (600 ml)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Start with real Greek yogurt
    Use full-fat strained Greek yogurt, not regular yogurt and not a low-fat version. Regular yogurt has far too much whey and will turn soupy within an hour no matter how well you drain the cucumber, and low-fat yogurt tastes thin and sour once the garlic goes in. If all you can find is regular yogurt, strain it through cheesecloth in the fridge for 4 hours first.
  2. Grate the cucumber
    Trim the ends and grate the whole cucumber on the large holes of a box grater, skin and all — English cucumber skin is thin, tender, and adds flecks of green. Do not peel or seed it if you are using an English or Persian cucumber. If you only have a standard waxy field cucumber, peel it and scrape out the watery seed core with a spoon.
  3. Salt and drain it
    Toss the grated cucumber with the 1 tsp kosher salt in a colander set over a bowl and let it sit for 20 to 30 minutes. Salt draws water out of the cells by osmosis, and you will be genuinely surprised how much liquid collects underneath. This step is the entire difference between tzatziki and watery yogurt soup.
  4. Squeeze it bone dry
    Gather the drained cucumber in a clean kitchen towel or a few layers of cheesecloth and wring it hard over the sink. Keep twisting until almost nothing more comes out — expect to remove roughly ½ cup (120 ml) of liquid. The cucumber should look compressed and almost dry, and yes, this feels like too much, and yes, it is correct.
  5. Make garlic paste
    Grate the 3 garlic cloves on a Microplane, or mince them and then smear them against the cutting board with the side of your knife and a pinch of salt until they form a paste. Chunks of raw garlic in tzatziki are unpleasantly hot in the mouth and only get sharper overnight. A true paste distributes the flavor evenly through the yogurt.
  6. Mellow the garlic in acid
    Stir the garlic paste together with the 1 tbsp lemon juice and 1 tsp red wine vinegar in a small bowl and let it stand 5 minutes. The acid deactivates some of the allicin, which is the compound responsible for raw garlic's aggressive burn. Skip this and the sauce will be noticeably harsher on day two.
  7. Combine everything
    In a medium bowl, stir together the yogurt, squeezed cucumber, garlic-lemon mixture, olive oil, dill, mint if using, ¾ tsp fine sea salt, and white pepper. Fold gently with a spatula rather than beating it — vigorously whisked yogurt breaks down and turns runny. It should look thick enough to hold the mark of the spatula.
  8. Chill for at least an hour
    Cover and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, or up to overnight. The garlic, dill, and cucumber need time to move into the yogurt, and tzatziki eaten immediately tastes like three separate ingredients in a bowl. It also firms up as it chills, so judge the final texture cold, not warm.
  9. Taste and finish
    Taste it cold and adjust — it should be tangy, garlicky, and clearly salted, since it is meant to season whatever it lands on. Add salt ⅛ tsp at a time and another squeeze of lemon if it tastes rich rather than fresh. If it has loosened at all, stir in 2 tbsp (30 g) more yogurt.
  10. Serve it cold
    Spread it in a shallow bowl, drag the back of a spoon through it to make a swirl, and pour a little olive oil into the groove with a few dill fronds on top. Serve straight from the fridge at 38°F to 40°F (3°C to 4°C) with warm pita, grilled lamb, chicken souvlaki, or roasted potatoes. It keeps 4 days refrigerated, though the garlic strengthens each day.
Know when it is done
No cooking. Serve cold, 38°F to 40°F (3°C to 4°C) — warm tzatziki tastes flat and the raw garlic reads much harsher.
Serve it with
Warm pita and grilled lamb or chicken souvlaki; a cold Greek white like Assyrtiko or just an ice-cold beer.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make it a day ahead if you can. Tzatziki is genuinely better on day two, once the garlic has settled into the yogurt.
  • ◆Watery tzatziki is always a cucumber problem, never a yogurt problem. Squeeze harder than you think you should.
  • ◆For a Turkish cacik, thin the finished sauce with ¼ cup (60 ml) cold water and serve it as a chilled soup-like dip with extra mint.
  • ◆It doubles as a salad dressing thinned with a little water, and as a marinade for chicken thighs, which the yogurt's acid and enzymes tenderize beautifully — grill them to 165°F (74°C) and throw the used marinade away.

Thai Peanut Dipping Sauce⏱ 22 min🍽 Makes about 3 cups (700 ml)Medium▾

Coconut milk, red curry paste, and peanut butter simmered into something rich, salty, and just sweet enough. Twenty minutes, and it turns satay, noodles, or plain rice into dinner.

30 MinutesMake AheadOne Pan
Prep
10 min
Cook
12 min
Total
22 min
Serves
Makes about 3 cups (700 ml)
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Do not shake the coconut milk
    Open the can without shaking it and spoon the thick white cream off the top into a saucepan, setting the thinner liquid aside for later. That solid cream is nearly pure coconut fat, and you are going to fry the curry paste in it. This technique is called cracking the coconut cream and it is the step that separates a real Thai peanut sauce from a smoothie.
  2. Crack the coconut cream
    Heat the coconut cream in a 2-quart (2 L) saucepan over medium heat for 3 to 5 minutes, stirring occasionally. It will bubble, thicken, and then visibly separate as clear coconut oil pools at the edges — that is exactly what you want. If your coconut milk has stabilizers and refuses to split, just carry on; add 1 tbsp (15 ml) of neutral oil to compensate.
  3. Fry the curry paste
    Add the 2 tbsp red curry paste to the hot fat and fry it, mashing and stirring, for 2 to 3 minutes until it darkens a shade and smells intensely aromatic. Frying paste in fat rather than just stirring it into liquid unlocks the chile, lemongrass, and galangal oils that are otherwise locked in. The kitchen should smell like a Thai restaurant at this point.
  4. Add aromatics
    Stir in the grated garlic and the 1 tsp grated ginger and cook for just 30 seconds more, keeping everything moving with a wooden spoon. Grated this finely they cook almost instantly, and left any longer in fat this hot they scorch and turn acrid — a bitterness you cannot take back out of the sauce. What you want is for the raw, sharp edge to disappear and the smell to turn sweet and fragrant. If the pan looks dry or the paste starts catching, slide it off the burner for a few seconds rather than adding liquid.
  5. Whisk in the peanut butter
    Add the ⅔ cup peanut butter and whisk hard — it will seize into a stiff, alarming paste for a moment, which is completely normal. Keep whisking and add the reserved thin coconut liquid a little at a time, and it will loosen into a smooth sauce over about a minute. Natural peanut butter with no added sugar or hydrogenated oil gives a far cleaner flavor than the sweetened supermarket kind.
  6. Season the sauce
    Whisk in the fish sauce, palm sugar, and rice vinegar and stir until the sugar has fully dissolved, about 1 minute. Thai cooking balances salty, sweet, sour, and spicy, and this is the moment you set those four dials. Palm sugar has a caramel note that brown sugar approximates well, so use whichever you can find.
  7. Simmer gently
    Let the sauce bubble gently for 3 to 4 minutes at around 190°F (88°C), stirring frequently and scraping the bottom of the pan where the peanut butter likes to settle. A hard boil drives the peanut oil straight back out of the emulsion and leaves you with a grainy, greasy sauce, so keep it at a lazy blip — a bubble breaking the surface every second or two. In that time it will thicken noticeably and stop tasting like separate ingredients sitting in a pan. If it thickens in much less than 3 minutes your burner is too high, so slide the pan half off the heat.
  8. Thin to the right texture
    Whisk in warm water 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time until it reaches the consistency you want — pourable like heavy cream for tossing with noodles, thicker like a loose hummus for dipping satay. It will thicken considerably as it cools, so leave it a little looser than seems right. Expect to use ¼ to ½ cup of water in total.
  9. Finish with lime off the heat
    Take the pan off the burner and stir in the 2 tbsp fresh lime juice. Lime juice added while the sauce is still cooking loses its perfume and goes slightly bitter, so it always goes in at the end. Taste now: it should hit salty, sweet, and sour in quick succession with warmth from the curry paste behind it.
  10. Adjust and serve
    Correct the balance with what it needs — 1 tsp more fish sauce for salt, 1 tsp more sugar for sweetness, another squeeze of lime for brightness, or a pinch of chile flakes for heat. Pour it into a bowl and scatter the chopped roasted peanuts over the top for crunch. Serve warm or at room temperature with chicken satay, summer rolls, grilled pork, or cold noodles.
Know when it is done
No internal temperature applies. Keep the pan at a gentle simmer near 190°F (88°C) — a hard boil splits the peanut oil out and turns the sauce grainy. Chicken satay served alongside must reach 165°F (74°C), and grilled pork 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest.
Serve it with
Chicken satay, fresh summer rolls, or cold rice noodles; a cold Singha or a slightly sweet Riesling handles the heat.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆It thickens a lot in the fridge. Reheat gently with a splash of water or coconut milk, stirring, and it comes right back.
  • ◆Keeps 1 week refrigerated at or below 40°F (4°C) and freezes for 3 months. Make a double batch — it disappears fast.
  • ◆For a peanut allergy, swap in the same amount of sunflower seed butter or tahini. Tahini makes a noticeably more savory, less sweet sauce.
  • ◆Thinned with an extra ¼ cup (60 ml) of water and an extra tablespoon of lime, this becomes an excellent dressing for a crunchy cabbage and carrot salad.
  • ◆Curry pastes vary hugely in heat. Start with 1 tbsp if you are unsure, taste after the sauce comes together, and add more from there.

All-Purpose Steak and Beef Rub⏱ 20 min🍽 Makes about 1¼ cups (165 g), enough for 8 to 10 steaksEasy▾

Whole peppercorns and coriander toasted and cracked with salt, garlic, and paprika into a rub that makes any cut of beef taste like it was cooked by someone who knows what they are doing.

Make AheadGrillingHomemade Staple
Prep
10 min
Cook
5 min
Total
20 min
Serves
Makes about 1¼ cups (165 g), enough for 8 to 10 steaks
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Whole spices to toast

Ground seasonings

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Start with whole spices
    Pre-ground pepper loses most of its aromatic oils within a few weeks of grinding, which is why a jar of black pepper from the back of the cupboard tastes like dust. Whole peppercorns and coriander seeds toasted and cracked fresh are a genuinely different ingredient. This one change does more for the rub than any other.
  2. Toast them dry
    Put the peppercorns, coriander seeds, and cumin seeds if using in a dry skillet over medium heat and toast for 3 to 4 minutes, shaking the pan constantly. They are ready when the coriander turns a shade darker and the mixture smells warm and citrusy — you may hear a few seeds pop. Tip them onto a cold plate right away, because a hot pan keeps toasting them into bitterness.
  3. Cool before grinding
    Let the toasted spices cool completely, about 5 minutes. Warm spices are oily and will gum up a grinder or clump into a paste instead of cracking cleanly. Cooling also lets the flavors set; freshly toasted spices smell fantastic but taste flatter than they will in ten minutes.
  4. Crack, do not pulverize
    Pulse the cooled spices in a clean coffee grinder 5 or 6 times, or crush them in a mortar or under the bottom of a heavy pan. You want a coarse crack with pieces roughly the size of coarse sand, not a fine powder. Coarse cracked pepper forms a crust on a steak that you can actually see and feel; powder just dissolves and can burn.
  5. Combine with the dry seasonings
    Tip the cracked spices into a bowl with the kosher salt, garlic powder, onion powder, paprika, dried thyme, mustard powder, and cayenne. Whisk for a full 30 seconds so it is completely uniform — powders love to settle in layers. Crush the dried thyme between your palms as you add it to release its oils.
  6. Decide about the sugar
    Add the 2 tbsp brown sugar only if you are grilling or smoking, where it caramelizes into a beautiful crust over indirect heat. Leave it out for high-heat searing in a cast iron pan, because sugar starts to burn around 350°F (177°C) and a sear runs far hotter than that. Keeping two jars, one sweet and one not, is worth the five extra minutes.
  7. Know the salt ratio
    This rub is a little over a quarter salt by weight — about 45 g of salt in a 165 g batch — which means roughly 1½ tbsp of rub per pound (450 g) of meat lands you near the 0.7 percent salt that seasons beef properly. If you are salting a steak separately, use a version of this blend with the salt left out so you do not double up. Measuring by the meat's weight rather than by eye is the fastest way to stop under- or over-seasoning.
  8. Apply it properly
    Pat the steaks completely dry with paper towels, then sprinkle the rub from about 10 inches (25 cm) above so it falls evenly instead of landing in clumps. Press it in gently with your palm — do not rub aggressively, which just drags the seasoning into piles. Cover every surface including the fat cap and the edges.
  9. Let it dry brine
    Set the seasoned steaks on a rack over a sheet pan and refrigerate uncovered for at least 45 minutes, or up to 24 hours for thick cuts. The salt first pulls moisture to the surface, then that seasoned liquid is reabsorbed while the exterior dries out, which is precisely what you need for a hard sear. A steak seasoned and cooked immediately steams instead of browning.
  10. Store it in the dark
    Keep the rub in an airtight jar somewhere cool and dark, away from the stove where heat and steam degrade spices fastest. It stays vibrant for about 3 months and remains safe far longer, just gradually duller. Write the date on the lid, because everyone thinks they will remember and nobody does.
Know when it is done
The rub has no cooking temperature of its own. Use it on steaks and pull them off the heat early, because carryover keeps cooking them: 125°F (52°C) pull rests up to about 130°F to 135°F (54°C to 57°C) for medium-rare, and a 135°F (57°C) pull rests up to about 140°F to 145°F (60°C to 63°C) for medium. Ground beef gets no such latitude and must be cooked through to 160°F (71°C).
Serve it with
Built for ribeyes and strip steaks off a screaming cast iron pan or a hot grill, with a bold Cabernet.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆This is excellent on more than steak — try it on burgers, on a pork shoulder before a long roast, on roasted potatoes, and on thick-cut mushrooms.
  • ◆Salt brands are not interchangeable by volume. Morton kosher salt is nearly twice as dense as Diamond Crystal, so use about 3 tbsp of Morton where this recipe calls for ⅓ cup of Diamond Crystal — or simply weigh out 45 g of whichever one you own.
  • ◆For a Montreal-style version, double the coriander and add 1 tbsp (5 g) dried dill seed.
  • ◆Make a salt-free version of the same blend and keep it beside the salted one. It lets you season meat by weight with salt first and add flavor separately, which is how restaurants do it.

Pan Gravy from Roast Drippings⏱ 30 min🍽 Makes about 3 cups (700 ml), serves 8Medium▾

The gravy you make in the roasting pan while the bird rests, built on flour, fat, and everything stuck to the bottom. Nothing from a jar has ever come close.

Holiday30 MinutesOne Pan
Prep
10 min
Cook
20 min
Total
30 min
Serves
Makes about 3 cups (700 ml), serves 8
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Move the roast and rest it
    Lift the finished roast onto a board or platter and let it rest, loosely tented, while you make the gravy — 20 minutes for a chicken, 30 to 45 for a turkey. Confirm it hit its safe temperature before you start using the juices: 165°F (74°C) in the thickest part of a turkey or chicken thigh, 145°F (63°C) plus a 3-minute rest for pork. The rest and the gravy take almost exactly the same amount of time, which is not a coincidence.
  2. Separate the fat
    Pour everything in the roasting pan into a fat separator or a tall glass measuring cup and let it settle for 5 minutes. The clear fat rises to the top and the dark savory juices sink below it. Skim off 6 tbsp (90 ml) of the fat for your roux and save the juices — those juices are pure concentrated flavor and go into the gravy later.
  3. Deglaze the roasting pan
    Set the roasting pan across two burners over medium heat, pour in the ½ cup wine, and scrape hard with a flat wooden spatula. Every stuck brown patch should dissolve within about a minute of bubbling — that is the roasted flavor moving into your gravy. Let the wine keep bubbling until it has reduced by about half, another 2 minutes, so the finished gravy tastes of roast rather than raw alcohol. Pour this liquid in with the reserved pan juices and set it aside.
  4. Start the roux
    Put the 6 tbsp reserved fat in a 3-quart (3 L) saucepan over medium heat. If you came up short on fat, top it up with butter — you need the full 6 tbsp to match the flour, because a roux is equal parts fat and flour by volume, and 6 tbsp of each is what it takes to thicken 3 to 4 cups of liquid into gravy rather than soup. Wait until the fat shimmers before the flour goes in.
  5. Cook the flour out
    Whisk in the 6 tbsp flour all at once and cook, whisking constantly, for 2 to 3 minutes. The paste will foam, then smooth out, then start smelling nutty like toast rather than raw and pasty. For a darker, deeper gravy suited to beef, keep going another 2 minutes until it is the color of peanut butter, but watch it closely because roux burns quickly.
  6. Add liquid gradually
    Have your stock and pan juices hot, then add them to the roux about ½ cup (120 ml) at a time, whisking each addition until completely smooth before the next goes in. Adding hot liquid to hot roux slowly is the whole secret to lump-free gravy — dump it all in cold and the flour seizes into knots instantly. It will look alarmingly thick after the first addition; that is correct.
  7. Simmer and thicken
    Once all the liquid is in, add the thyme sprig and sage leaf and bring the gravy to a full simmer at about 200°F (93°C), whisking often. Let it bubble for 5 to 8 minutes; flour-thickened sauces do not reach their full thickening power until they actually boil. It will thicken visibly during this time.
  8. Adjust the consistency
    The gravy should coat the back of a spoon so that a finger drawn across leaves a clear path. If it is too thin, simmer a few more minutes or whisk in a slurry of 1 tsp cornstarch mixed with 1 tbsp (15 ml) cold water. If it is too thick, whisk in hot stock 2 tbsp (30 ml) at a time — remember it thickens further as it cools on the plate.
  9. Fix any lumps
    Lumps are not a disaster and they are never a reason to start over. Pour the gravy through a fine-mesh sieve into a clean pan, pressing the lumps against the mesh with the back of a ladle, or run a stick blender through it for about 10 seconds until it is smooth. Do this before you season, because straining always leaves a little volume behind in the sieve and you want to be salting the exact amount of gravy you will actually serve. Wipe out the first pan and pour the gravy back in if it is the only warm pan you have.
  10. Season carefully
    Pull out the herbs, then taste and add the ½ tsp salt and ½ tsp pepper. Go slowly on salt: pan drippings from a brined or heavily seasoned bird can already be very salty, and you cannot take it out. Add the 1 tsp soy sauce if the gravy looks pale or tastes thin — it deepens both color and savoriness without reading as soy.
  11. Brighten and gloss it
    Off the heat, stir in the 1 tsp lemon juice or cider vinegar and, if you like, whisk in the cold tablespoon of butter until it disappears. The acid cuts through all that fat and makes the gravy taste less heavy, while the butter gives it a glossy sheen. Both take ten seconds and both are genuinely worth doing.
  12. Hold it hot and serve
    Keep the gravy above 140°F (60°C) until serving, either over the lowest burner setting or in a warmed gravy boat, and whisk it if a skin forms. Any juices that pool under the resting roast go in at the last second. Leftover gravy keeps 3 days refrigerated below 40°F (4°C) and reheats well with a splash of stock.
Know when it is done
The roast itself must reach 165°F (74°C) in the thigh for poultry before its juices go into the gravy. Bring the finished gravy to a full simmer at 200°F (93°C) and hold it above 140°F (60°C) until served.
Serve it with
Poured over roast turkey or chicken with mashed potatoes and stuffing; a light Pinot Noir or a hard cider works with either.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Make a backup batch of gravy ahead of time using stock and butter instead of drippings, then whisk the real drippings into it at the last minute. It removes every bit of holiday panic.
  • ◆Roast a few chicken wings, an onion, and a carrot alongside the bird if you are worried about not having enough drippings. They render plenty of flavorful fat and fond.
  • ◆For gluten-free gravy, skip the roux entirely and thicken 3 cups of the deglazed liquid with a slurry of 3 tbsp (24 g) cornstarch in ¼ cup (60 ml) cold water, simmered 2 minutes.
  • ◆Giblet gravy: simmer the neck and giblets in the stock for 45 minutes while the bird roasts, then chop the meat fine and stir it in at the end.
  • ◆Always heat the stock before adding it. Cold liquid into hot roux is the single most common cause of lumpy gravy.

Everything here is a real classic with the weights written out, so nothing is left to guessing — bake the cookies on a Tuesday, save the cheesecake for a weekend when you have the afternoon.

Brown Butter Chocolate Chip Cookies⏱ 1 hr 55 min🍽 Makes 20 cookiesMedium▾

Browning the butter turns a good chocolate chip cookie into a toffee-scented one, with crisp edges and a middle that stays soft for days. The chill in the fridge is what makes them taste like a bakery instead of a mixing bowl.

Bakery StyleMake AheadWeeknight Baking
Prep
20 min
Cook
35 min
Total
1 hr 55 min
Serves
Makes 20 cookies
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Dry

Wet

Chocolate and finishing

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Brown the butter
    Melt the butter in a light-colored 10-inch (25 cm) skillet or saucepan over medium heat, swirling every 20 seconds or so. It will foam loudly, go quiet, and then the milk solids on the bottom will turn amber and smell like toasted hazelnuts — this takes 5 to 7 minutes total. A light pan matters because you have to see the color; in a black pan you will smell scorched butter before you see it. Pull it off the heat the second it smells nutty, since it goes from brown to burnt in about 30 seconds.
  2. Rehydrate and cool it
    Scrape every bit of butter and the toasty brown specks into a large mixing bowl, then stir in the 2 tbsp (30 ml) milk. Browning boils off roughly 2 tablespoons of water, and putting it back keeps the cookies chewy instead of greasy and flat. Let the butter sit for 15 minutes, until it is warm rather than hot — if it is over about 110°F (43°C) it will scramble the eggs later.
  3. Whisk the dry ingredients
    In a separate bowl, whisk the flour, baking soda, and kosher salt for a solid 15 seconds so the leavening is evenly spread. Measure the flour by spooning it into the cup and leveling it off, or better, weigh out 280 g. Scooping straight from the bag can pack in an extra 30 g of flour, which is the single most common reason homemade cookies come out dry and cakey.
  4. Beat in the sugars
    Add both sugars to the warm brown butter and whisk hard for a full minute until the mixture looks like wet, glossy sand. You are not creaming air into cold butter here, so the goal is simply to dissolve some of the sugar and build the chewy texture. The dark brown sugar carries molasses, which is what keeps these soft on day three.
  5. Add eggs and vanilla
    Whisk in the eggs one at a time along with the vanilla, beating 30 seconds after each until the batter turns smooth, thick, and noticeably lighter in color. Room-temperature eggs emulsify into the fat instead of seizing it, so if yours are cold, sit them in warm tap water for 5 minutes first. The batter should look like a glossy caramel ribbon when you lift the whisk.
  6. Fold in flour and chocolate
    Switch to a rubber spatula, add the dry ingredients all at once, and fold just until the last streak of flour disappears — about 20 strokes. Overmixing builds gluten and gives you tough, bready cookies. Fold in the chopped chocolate; using a chopped bar instead of chips gives you both big melting pools and fine shards that marble through the dough.
  7. Chill the dough
    Cover the bowl and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, or up to 72 hours for a deeper, more butterscotch flavor. Chilling firms the fat so the cookies spread slowly and stay thick, and it gives the flour time to fully hydrate. If you chill longer than 3 hours, let the dough sit at room temperature for 15 minutes before scooping or it will crack the scoop.
  8. Heat the oven and portion
    Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C) with a rack in the upper third and line two sheet pans with parchment. Scoop 3-tablespoon balls (about 55 g each) — the dough gives you about 20 — and place only 8 per pan, spaced 3 in (7.5 cm) apart, because these spread to nearly 3 1/2 in (9 cm) across. That means three batches, so keep the unscooped dough in the fridge between pans and let each pan cool before you reload it; warm pans melt the butter on contact and the cookies spread thin and greasy. Roll each ball tall rather than flat — a taller puck bakes up thicker with a softer center.
  9. Bake one pan at a time
    Bake a single sheet at a time for 10 to 12 minutes, rotating the pan front to back at the 7-minute mark. They are done when the edges are set and deep golden but the centers still look puffy, pale, and slightly underdone. Cookies carry over on the hot pan, so pulling them at the underdone stage is exactly what gives you a gooey middle. If you bake two pans at once, add 2 minutes and swap racks halfway.
  10. Bang, salt, and cool
    Right out of the oven, rap the pan flat on the counter once from a height of about 4 in (10 cm) to deflate the puffed centers into rippled ridges. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt immediately, while the surface is still molten enough to grab it. Let the cookies set on the pan for 5 minutes before moving them to a rack — straight off the oven they are too soft to lift without tearing.
  11. Store or freeze
    Keep baked cookies in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 4 days, with a slice of sandwich bread tossed in to keep them soft. Raw scooped dough balls freeze beautifully on a tray, then go into a zip bag for up to 3 months. Bake from frozen at the same 375°F (190°C), adding 2 to 3 minutes, so you can have two warm cookies on a weeknight without making a whole batch.
Know when it is done
Bake at 375°F (190°C); pull when the edges are set and golden and the centers still look soft and underdone, about 10 to 12 minutes. Butter should be cooled to under 110°F (43°C) before the eggs go in.
Serve it with
A cold glass of whole milk, or a scoop of vanilla ice cream pressed between two of them.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆If your butter browns and the specks look black rather than amber, start over — burnt milk solids turn the whole batch bitter and there is no fixing it.
  • ◆Weigh the flour if you have a scale. 280 g is exact; a scooped cup can be off by 20 percent, which is the difference between chewy and dry.
  • ◆For bakery-style cookies, press a few extra chocolate chunks onto the tops of the dough balls right before baking so the finished cookies look as good as they taste.
  • ◆Dough that has chilled 24 to 48 hours tastes measurably better — deeper toffee notes and a more even brown. Make it the night before you want cookies.
  • ◆Flat, greasy cookies almost always mean the butter was still hot when the eggs went in, or the dough was not chilled. Both are fixable next time; chill the remaining dough 30 extra minutes now.

Fudgy Chocolate Brownies⏱ 1 hr 45 min🍽 Makes 16 squaresEasy▾

Dense, glossy-topped, and genuinely fudgy — melted chocolate for richness, cocoa for depth, and just enough flour to hold it together. One bowl, one pan, thirty minutes in the oven.

One BowlCrowd PleaserUnder an Hour
Prep
15 min
Cook
30 min
Total
1 hr 45 min
Serves
Makes 16 squares
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Chocolate base

Batter

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Prepare the pan
    Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a rack in the center. Line a 9-in (23 cm) square metal pan with a parchment sling that overhangs two sides by 2 in (5 cm), then butter the exposed corners. This batter weighs a little over 2 lb (about 1 kg), which is too much for an 8-in pan — in a 9-in it settles to a proper 3/4-in (2 cm) slab that bakes through in half an hour. Metal conducts better than glass here; a glass pan will need about 5 extra minutes and tends to overbake the edges. The sling lets you lift the whole slab out for clean cutting instead of digging squares out with a spatula.
  2. Melt the chocolate and butter
    Put the butter and the 6 oz (170 g) chopped chocolate in a large heatproof bowl set over a saucepan with 1 in (2.5 cm) of barely simmering water, making sure the bowl does not touch the water. Stir with a spatula until smooth and glossy, about 4 minutes. You can also microwave in 30-second bursts at 50 percent power, stirring between each. Chocolate scorches easily, so pull it while a few small lumps remain and let the residual heat finish the job.
  3. Bloom the cocoa
    Off the heat, whisk the cocoa powder and espresso powder into the warm chocolate mixture until it is completely smooth. Hot fat dissolves cocoa's flavor compounds in a way cold mixing never does, which is why these taste so deeply chocolatey. The espresso powder is not there to taste like coffee — it sharpens the chocolate. Let the mixture cool for 5 minutes so it is warm, not hot.
  4. Whisk in the sugars
    Whisk both sugars into the warm chocolate and keep whisking for a full 60 seconds until the mixture looks grainy and thick, like wet sand. Dissolving a good part of the sugar in warm fat is what creates that thin, crackly, tissue-paper top everyone chases. It will look broken and unpromising at this stage — that is normal.
  5. Beat in the eggs
    Add the eggs one at a time, whisking vigorously for about 30 seconds after each, then whisk in the vanilla. By the third egg the batter should turn thick, satiny, and noticeably lighter — that shine is dissolved sugar coming to the surface. Do not skimp on the whisking here; it is the only aeration these brownies get.
  6. Fold in the flour
    Sprinkle the flour and fine sea salt over the batter and fold with a spatula just until no dry streaks remain, roughly 15 to 20 strokes. Stop the moment it comes together — extra mixing develops gluten and turns fudgy brownies rubbery. Fold in the 4 oz (115 g) chocolate chunks with two or three last passes.
  7. Spread and level
    Scrape the batter into the lined pan and spread it into the corners with an offset spatula, then tap the pan on the counter three times to release large air bubbles. The batter is thick and will not settle on its own, so level it deliberately or you will get a thin edge that overbakes. Sprinkle the flaky salt over the top.
  8. Bake until just set
    Bake for 28 to 32 minutes. The top should be dry, matte, and slightly puffed at the edges while the center still has the faintest wobble when you nudge the pan. A toothpick 2 in (5 cm) from the center should come out with thick, moist crumbs clinging to it — never clean. If you want an instant-read confirmation, the center reads about 200°F (93°C) for fudgy; 210°F (99°C) and up gives you cakey.
  9. Cool completely
    Set the pan on a wire rack and let it cool for at least 1 hour, ideally 2, before cutting. Warm brownies are structurally soup; the starch and fat need time to set or every square will tear. If you truly cannot wait, chill the pan in the freezer for 20 minutes to firm the center enough for one clean slice.
  10. Cut clean squares
    Lift the slab out by the parchment sling onto a cutting board. Cut a 4 by 4 grid with a long chef's knife, wiping the blade clean with a hot damp towel between every cut. Wiping matters more than technique — a smeared blade drags fudgy crumb across the next face and makes tidy squares look ragged.
  11. Store them right
    Keep the brownies in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 4 days; they get denser and fudgier on day two. Do not refrigerate them uncovered, since the fridge dries the cut faces out fast. For longer storage, wrap individual squares in plastic and freeze up to 3 months, then thaw at room temperature for 30 minutes.
Know when it is done
Bake at 350°F (175°C) for 28 to 32 minutes; the center should read about 200°F (93°C) for fudgy brownies, and a toothpick should show moist crumbs, never clean batter or a clean pick.
Serve it with
Vanilla ice cream and a cold glass of milk, or a small glass of tawny port if you are feeling grown-up.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Use a chocolate bar you would happily eat, not baking chips. Chips contain stabilizers that keep them from melting into the batter, and here the melt is the whole point.
  • ◆Underbaking by 2 minutes is always better than overbaking by 2. Brownies keep cooking in the hot pan after they come out.
  • ◆For clean bakery edges, chill the fully cooled slab for 30 minutes before cutting and use a hot, dry knife.
  • ◆Swap the flour for 3/4 cup (95 g) measure-for-measure gluten-free blend and they work nearly identically — the structure here comes from eggs and chocolate, not gluten.
  • ◆Make them ahead: baked and wrapped, they are better on day two than day one, so this is the dessert to make the night before company.
