Classic New York Cheesecake⏱ 12 hr 10 min🍽 12 servingsAdvanced▾

Tall, dense, and impossibly smooth, with a graham crust and a sour cream tang. It is a weekend project mostly because of the waiting, and the waiting is what makes it perfect.

Weekend ProjectMake AheadSpecial Occasion
Prep
30 min
Cook
1 hr 40 min
Total
12 hr 10 min
Serves
12 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Graham crust

Cheesecake filling

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Get everything to room temperature
    Set the cream cheese, eggs, sour cream, and heavy cream on the counter 2 hours before you start, or until the cream cheese dents easily under your thumb at about 68°F (20°C). Cold cream cheese will never beat smooth — it breaks into little lumps that no amount of mixing later can rescue, and those lumps are the number one cause of a grainy cheesecake. This single step matters more than any technique that follows.
  2. Build and bake the crust
    Heat the oven to 325°F (165°C). Stir the graham crumbs, sugar, and salt together, pour in the melted butter, and mix until it looks like damp sand that holds a squeeze. Press it firmly into the bottom and 1 in (2.5 cm) up the sides of a 9-in (23 cm) springform pan, using a flat-bottomed glass to compact it. Bake 10 minutes until fragrant and just set, then cool on a rack while you make the filling.
  3. Waterproof the pan
    Once the crust has cooled, wrap the outside of the springform in two wide sheets of heavy-duty foil, or better, set the whole pan inside a slightly larger cake pan or an oven bag. Springform seams leak, and a single drip of water bath turns your crust into wet sand. Take the extra minute to check that the foil comes all the way up the sides with no punctures.
  4. Beat the cream cheese smooth
    In a stand mixer with the paddle attachment (not the whisk), beat the cream cheese alone on medium-low for 3 minutes, stopping twice to scrape the bowl and the paddle. You are looking for completely smooth and slightly fluffy, with no visible lumps at all. Keep the speed low from here on out — every bubble you whip in now becomes a crack later, because air expands in the oven and then collapses.
  5. Add sugar, starch, and salt
    Whisk the sugar, cornstarch, and salt together, then add them to the cream cheese in three additions on low speed, scraping between each. Beat just until smooth and no longer, about 2 minutes total. The cornstarch is insurance — it makes the custard more forgiving of a few extra minutes in the oven and helps guarantee a sliceable, crack-free top.
  6. Add the dairy and flavor
    With the mixer still on low, add the sour cream, heavy cream, vanilla, lemon juice, and zest and mix until just combined, about 1 minute. Scrape the very bottom of the bowl with a spatula, where unmixed cream cheese loves to hide. The lemon is not there to taste lemony — it cuts the richness so the last bite is as good as the first.
  7. Add the eggs last, gently
    Add the eggs and the extra yolk one at a time on the lowest speed, mixing only 15 to 20 seconds after each, just until the yellow disappears. Eggs are the structure, and overbeaten eggs mean a soufflé that rises, cracks, and sinks. Finish by folding the batter three or four times by hand with a spatula; it should be silky and pourable, like heavy pancake batter.
  8. Set up the water bath
    Pour the filling over the cooled crust and smooth the top, then tap the pan gently on the counter a few times to bring bubbles up and pop them with a toothpick. Set the wrapped pan in a large roasting pan and pour boiling water into the outer pan until it comes 1 to 1 1/2 in (2.5 to 4 cm) up the sides. The water bath holds the oven's humidity high and the custard's temperature gentle, which is the real secret to a smooth, pale, uncracked top.
  9. Bake low and slow
    Bake at 325°F (165°C) for 80 to 95 minutes without opening the door for the first hour. It is done when the outer 2 in (5 cm) look set and matte and the center 3 in (7.5 cm) still jiggles as one soft unit when you nudge the pan — like set gelatin, not like liquid. An instant-read thermometer in the center should read 150°F (65°C); do not push past 155°F (68°C) or the proteins tighten and squeeze out water.
  10. Cool it in stages
    Turn the oven off, crack the door open about 4 in (10 cm) with a wooden spoon, and leave the cheesecake inside for 1 hour. Then lift it out of the water bath, run a thin knife around the very top edge to release it from the pan, and cool on a rack to room temperature, about 1 more hour. Cheesecakes crack when they cool fast and the shrinking edges pull against a stuck rim, so slow cooling plus a freed edge solves both problems at once.
  11. Chill overnight
    Cover the cooled cheesecake loosely with foil, tenting it so nothing touches the surface, and refrigerate at least 8 hours or overnight. This is not optional — the custard needs that time to fully set and the flavor to round out from tangy to rich. A cheesecake cut after 4 hours will be soft and slumped, and it will taste flatter.
  12. Unmold and slice
    Run a thin knife dipped in hot water around the sides, then release and lift off the springform ring. Slice with a long thin blade dipped in hot water and wiped dry between every single cut — this is what gives you those clean bakery faces. Let slices sit at room temperature 20 minutes before eating; straight from the fridge, the texture is firm and the flavor is muted.
Know when it is done
Bake at 325°F (165°C) until the center reads 150°F (65°C) on an instant-read thermometer and still jiggles as one soft unit; stop before 155°F (68°C) to avoid a grainy, weeping texture.
Serve it with
Fresh macerated strawberries and strong black coffee, or a glass of late-harvest Riesling.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Use block cream cheese only. Tub-style spreadable cheese has added water and gums, and the cheesecake will never set firm.
  • ◆If a crack appears anyway, it is still delicious — cover it with sour cream topping (1 cup / 240 g sour cream, 3 tbsp / 38 g sugar, 1 tsp vanilla, spread on and baked 8 minutes) or with fresh berries.
  • ◆It keeps 5 days covered in the fridge and freezes well: freeze uncovered until firm, then wrap in plastic and foil for up to 2 months and thaw overnight in the fridge.
  • ◆No roasting pan large enough? Set the springform on the middle rack and put a rimmed pan of boiling water on the rack below. You get most of the humidity benefit with none of the leak risk.
  • ◆Take everything out of the fridge before bed the night before if you plan to bake in the morning — an hour on the counter is often not enough for four blocks of cream cheese.

Tiramisu with Cooked Zabaglione⏱ 6 hr 50 min🍽 9 servingsMedium▾

Espresso-soaked ladyfingers under a mascarpone cream that is cooked over a water bath, so it is both safer and more stable than the raw-egg version. It needs a night in the fridge and no oven at all.

No BakeMake AheadDate Night
Prep
40 min
Cook
10 min
Total
6 hr 50 min
Serves
9 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Zabaglione base

Mascarpone cream

Assembly

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Set up a water bath
    Bring 1 1/2 in (4 cm) of water to a bare simmer in a medium saucepan, then find a metal or glass bowl that rests on the rim without its bottom touching the water. Steam, not contact with the water, is what cooks the yolks gently. If the bowl touches the water, the eggs on the bottom scramble before the rest ever warms up.
  2. Cook the zabaglione
    Whisk the yolks, sugar, Marsala, and salt in the bowl off the heat until smooth, then set it over the simmering water and whisk constantly for 8 to 10 minutes. It will go from thin and yellow to pale, thick, and foamy, roughly tripling in volume, and it should coat the back of a spoon. Cook until an instant-read thermometer reads 160°F (71°C), which pasteurizes the yolks and makes this safe for anyone. Never stop whisking, and keep the heat at a bare simmer.
  3. Cool the base
    Take the bowl off the heat and set it in a larger bowl of ice water, whisking occasionally for about 5 minutes until the zabaglione is barely warm, around 80°F (27°C). Folding warm custard into mascarpone will make it loose and soupy, and folding it into whipped cream will deflate everything. Rushing this step is the most common way tiramisu ends up runny.
  4. Loosen the mascarpone
    In a wide bowl, stir the mascarpone with a spatula for 30 seconds until it is creamy and smooth but not beaten. Mascarpone is high fat and it will curdle into grainy little clots if you whip it hard or if it is cold from the fridge, so keep it at cool room temperature and use a gentle hand. If it does look grainy, stir in 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the heavy cream to bring it back.
  5. Fold base into mascarpone
    Add about a third of the cooled zabaglione to the mascarpone and stir until smooth, then fold in the rest in two additions with a spatula. Working in stages keeps the mascarpone from seizing against a rush of liquid. The mixture should look like thick, glossy pudding with no yellow streaks.
  6. Whip the cream
    In a cold bowl, whip the heavy cream with the vanilla to firm peaks — the whisk should leave clear tracks and the peak should stand up with just a slight curl at the tip, about 2 to 3 minutes on medium-high. Stop before it looks grainy or buttery. Firm peaks, not stiff, give you a cream that folds in smoothly and still holds a clean layer.
  7. Fold and finish the cream
    Fold the whipped cream into the mascarpone mixture in three additions, cutting down through the middle with the spatula and sweeping up the side, rotating the bowl a quarter turn each stroke. Stop as soon as it is uniform; overfolding knocks out the air you just built. The finished cream should mound softly on the spatula and hold its shape.
  8. Mix the dipping coffee
    Stir the cooled espresso, rum, and 1 tbsp (13 g) sugar together in a shallow dish wide enough to lay a ladyfinger flat. The coffee must be at room temperature or cooler — hot coffee dissolves the biscuits instantly and turns the bottom layer into paste. Taste it; it should be strong enough to be almost bitter, since the cream is sweet.
  9. Dip fast, not long
    Dip each ladyfinger flat for about 1 second per side, then lift it out immediately. It should still feel firm in the middle when you set it down, because it will keep absorbing moisture from the cream for hours in the fridge. Soggy tiramisu is almost always over-dipping; count out loud if it helps. Line the bottom of a 9-in (23 cm) square dish — you want one that holds about 2 1/2 quarts (2.4 L), because this much cream will climb over the rim of a standard shallow 8-in pan — with a snug single layer, breaking pieces to fill gaps. That takes roughly 15 to 18 biscuits per layer.
  10. Layer it
    Spread half the mascarpone cream over the ladyfingers in an even layer, right to the edges, using an offset spatula. Dust it lightly with about 1 tbsp (5 g) of the cocoa through a fine sieve — a hidden middle cocoa layer adds a bittersweet edge in every bite. Add a second dipped layer of ladyfingers, then the rest of the cream, smoothed flat.
  11. Chill overnight
    Cover with plastic wrap without letting it touch the surface and refrigerate at least 6 hours, ideally 12 to 24. During that time the biscuits soften into cake and the cream firms into something sliceable — a tiramisu eaten after 2 hours is a different, much sloppier dessert. It holds well for 3 days.
  12. Dust and serve
    Just before serving, dust the top generously with the remaining cocoa through a fine sieve and add chocolate shavings if you like. Dust at the last minute, because cocoa applied hours early absorbs moisture and goes patchy and dull. Cut with a knife wiped clean between slices and serve cold, straight from the fridge.
Know when it is done
Cook the yolk base over a water bath to 160°F (71°C) to pasteurize the eggs; cool it to about 80°F (27°C) before folding, and chill the assembled tiramisu at 40°F (4°C) or below for at least 6 hours.
Serve it with
A small cup of espresso, or a glass of Vin Santo if you are making a night of it.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Use crisp, dry Savoiardi ladyfingers from the cookie aisle, not the soft cakey sponge ones. Soft ones collapse into mush the moment they hit coffee.
  • ◆To make it alcohol-free, skip the Marsala in the zabaglione and use 1/3 cup (80 ml) strong coffee instead, and leave the rum out of the dipping liquid.
  • ◆The cooked zabaglione is what makes this safe for anyone avoiding raw eggs, and it also makes the cream far more stable — it will not weep after a day like the classic raw version can.
  • ◆Make it in a glass dish so you can see the layers, and build it a full day ahead. This is the rare dessert that is measurably better on day two.
  • ◆If the cream ever looks curdled while folding, stop and whisk in 1 to 2 tbsp (15 to 30 ml) of cold cream by hand; the extra liquid usually pulls it back together.

Vanilla Creme Brulee⏱ 5 hr 25 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

A silky vanilla custard under a sheet of glass-hard caramel you get to crack with a spoon. Five ingredients, and the only real skill is knowing when to pull it from the oven.

Date NightMake AheadRestaurant Classic
Prep
15 min
Cook
40 min
Total
5 hr 25 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Custard

Caramel top

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Heat the oven and pan
    Heat the oven to 325°F (165°C) with a rack in the center and set six 6-oz (180 ml) shallow ramekins in a roasting pan large enough that they do not touch. Shallow, wide ramekins are traditional because they give you a higher ratio of caramel crust to custard and they cook faster and more evenly than deep ones. Put a kettle of water on to boil now so it is ready when you need it.
  2. Infuse the cream
    Put the cream, the scraped vanilla seeds, and the empty pod in a saucepan over medium heat and bring it to a bare simmer, about 180°F (82°C), when small bubbles ring the edge. Take it off the heat, cover, and let it steep for 15 minutes. Steeping pulls far more flavor out of the pod than dumping seeds into cold cream, and it is the difference between vaguely sweet and genuinely vanilla.
  3. Whisk the yolks
    In a medium bowl, whisk the yolks, sugar, and salt together for about 45 seconds, until the mixture lightens slightly and the sugar starts to dissolve. Do not whip it to a foam — air bubbles rise during baking and leave a pitted, bubbly surface that will not caramelize evenly. You want smooth and combined, nothing more.
  4. Temper the eggs
    Pour about 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the warm cream into the yolks in a thin stream while whisking constantly, then whisk in the rest of the cream in a slow, steady pour. Adding the hot liquid gradually raises the yolks' temperature without cooking them — dump it in all at once and you get sweet scrambled eggs. Discard the vanilla pod, or rinse and dry it to bury in a jar of sugar.
  5. Strain and rest
    Pour the custard through a fine-mesh sieve into a pitcher or large measuring cup with a spout, which catches any chalazae and stray cooked bits. Let it sit for 5 minutes, then skim off any foam from the surface with a spoon. Foam bakes into a rough skin, and the whole appeal of this dessert is a mirror-flat top.
  6. Fill and add water
    Divide the custard among the ramekins — you have about 950 ml of custard, so that is a generous 150 ml each, filling them to about 1/4 in (6 mm) below the rim. Set the roasting pan on the oven rack first, then pour boiling water into the pan until it reaches halfway up the sides of the ramekins. Filling the bath at the oven avoids sloshing water into the custards, and hot water gets the bath up to temperature immediately for even cooking.
  7. Bake until barely set
    Bake for 30 to 40 minutes. They are done when the outer inch is set but the center 1 1/2 in (4 cm) jiggles like loose gelatin when you tap the ramekin — not liquid, not firm. An instant-read thermometer in the center should read 170 to 175°F (77 to 79°C); above 180°F (82°C) the custard curdles and weeps. Start checking at 28 minutes, since shallow ramekins can be done surprisingly early.
  8. Cool and chill
    Lift the ramekins out of the water bath with tongs or a wide spatula and cool them on a rack for 30 minutes. Cover each with plastic wrap and refrigerate at least 4 hours or overnight; they need to be thoroughly cold, or the torch will melt the custard beneath the sugar instead of just crisping the top. They keep, uncaramelized, for 3 days.
  9. Dry the surface
    Right before serving, uncover the custards and blot the surface gently with a paper towel to remove any condensation. Wet sugar dissolves into syrup instead of melting into glass, and condensation is the reason so many home brulees end up with a sticky top rather than a crackly one.
  10. Torch the sugar
    Sprinkle 1 tbsp (about 12 g) sugar evenly over each custard, tilting to coat and tapping off any excess so the layer is thin and uniform. Hold a kitchen torch 3 to 4 in (8 to 10 cm) away and move it in small continuous circles until the sugar melts, bubbles, and turns deep amber, about 45 seconds per ramekin. Keep the flame moving — parking it in one place burns black spots that taste acrid. No torch? Run them 3 in (7.5 cm) under a blazing hot broiler for 2 to 4 minutes, watching every second.
  11. Rest 2 minutes and serve
    Let the caramelized tops sit for 2 minutes so the molten sugar hardens into a sheet. Serve within 20 minutes of torching, because the sugar starts pulling moisture from the custard and softening after that. The test of success is a distinct crack when the spoon goes in.
Know when it is done
Bake at 325°F (165°C) until the custard center reads 170 to 175°F (77 to 79°C) and jiggles like set gelatin; past 180°F (82°C) it curdles. Chill to below 40°F (4°C) before torching.
Serve it with
Fresh raspberries on the side and a small glass of Sauternes or a shot of espresso.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Turbinado sugar torches faster and more evenly than fine sugar because the larger crystals melt before they scorch, but plain granulated works if that is what you have.
  • ◆Save the egg whites in a jar in the fridge for up to 5 days or freeze them; eight whites make a fine batch of meringues or a couple of egg white omelets.
  • ◆Make the custards up to 3 days ahead and keep them covered in the fridge. Only torch right before serving — a caramel top will not survive an hour, let alone a night.
  • ◆If your custards come out with tiny holes throughout, the oven ran too hot or the bath water dropped below level. Check the water halfway through and top it up with more boiling water if needed.
  • ◆For a coffee version, steep 2 tbsp (10 g) whole coffee beans with the cream; for citrus, steep the peel of one orange in wide strips.

Molten Chocolate Lava Cakes⏱ 27 min🍽 4 servingsMedium▾

Twelve minutes in the oven and a warm chocolate center that pours out when you cut in. This is the dessert to make when someone unexpectedly stays for dinner.

30 MinutesDate NightMake Ahead
Prep
15 min
Cook
12 min
Total
27 min
Serves
4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Ramekins

Batter

To serve

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Heat the oven high
    Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) with a rack in the center and set a rimmed sheet pan on the counter. The high heat is what makes this work: the outside sets fast while the middle stays liquid. A moderate 350°F (175°C) oven would cook the cakes through evenly, which is exactly what you do not want here.
  2. Prep the ramekins carefully
    Brush four 6-oz (180 ml) ramekins with softened butter using upward strokes on the sides, then add a spoonful of cocoa to each, rotate to coat completely, and tap out the excess. Cocoa instead of flour keeps the outside dark and chocolatey rather than pale and dusty. Any bare patch is where the cake will stick and tear when you invert it, so be thorough right up to the rim.
  3. Melt chocolate and butter
    Melt the chocolate and butter together in a heatproof bowl set over 1 in (2.5 cm) of barely simmering water, stirring until glossy and smooth, about 4 minutes. Or microwave at 50 percent power in 30-second bursts, stirring after each. Let the mixture cool for 5 minutes until it is warm but not hot to a fingertip, so it will not cook the eggs.
  4. Beat the eggs and sugar
    In a separate bowl, beat the whole eggs, yolks, sugar, salt, and vanilla with a hand mixer on medium-high for 3 to 4 minutes, until the mixture is pale, thick, and falls in a ribbon that sits on the surface for a couple of seconds. That whipped volume is the only lift these cakes get — there is no baking powder. Underwhipped eggs give you a dense puck instead of a delicate shell.
  5. Combine gently
    Pour the warm chocolate down the side of the egg bowl and fold with a spatula in wide strokes until just a few streaks remain, then fold in the flour until it disappears. Stop mixing the moment it is uniform, around 20 strokes total. Every extra stroke deflates the eggs and firms the crumb, so a light hand is the whole trick.
  6. Fill and rest briefly
    Divide the batter evenly among the ramekins, filling each about three-quarters full — the batch makes roughly 2 cups (500 ml), so that is about 1/2 cup (125 ml), or 130 g, per ramekin. Do not fill them to the rim: these puff hard at 425°F (220°C) and a full ramekin will dome over the edge and then collapse. Tap them lightly on the counter to settle the batter and set them on the sheet pan. At this point you can cover and refrigerate for up to 24 hours; add 2 minutes to the bake time if they go into the oven cold.
  7. Bake 12 to 13 minutes
    Bake for 12 to 13 minutes. The tops should be puffed and dry with a thin crust, the outer 1 in (2.5 cm) firm to a light touch, and the center 1 in (2.5 cm) still visibly soft and wobbly when you jiggle the pan. If the whole top looks matte and set, you have a very good chocolate cake but no lava, so err on the early side and check at 11 minutes.
  8. Rest one minute exactly
    Move the ramekins to a rack and let them sit for exactly 60 seconds. That minute lets the outer shell firm up just enough to survive the flip, and any longer and residual heat starts setting the center you are trying to keep molten. Set a timer; this is the one step people improvise and regret.
  9. Invert onto plates
    Run a small offset spatula or paring knife around the inside edge of each ramekin, set a dessert plate upside down over the top, and flip the whole thing over in one confident motion using a towel to hold the hot ramekin. Give it a gentle shake, then lift the ramekin straight up. If a cake resists, tap the bottom of the ramekin firmly once and it will drop.
  10. Dust and serve immediately
    Dust with powdered sugar through a small sieve and add a scoop of vanilla ice cream beside each cake, never on top, so it does not melt the shell before it reaches the table. Serve right away — the molten window is about 5 minutes, after which residual heat sets the center. Warn whoever you are feeding that the inside is very hot.
Know when it is done
Bake at 425°F (220°C) for 12 to 13 minutes — edges set and firm, center still soft and jiggling. The molten middle is uncooked batter by design; use pasteurized eggs if serving anyone who should avoid undercooked eggs.
Serve it with
Vanilla ice cream alongside and a glass of ruby port or a cup of strong coffee.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆The center is intentionally underbaked batter. If you are serving someone pregnant, elderly, or immune-compromised, use pasteurized shell eggs, which behave identically here.
  • ◆Make the batter up to 24 hours ahead and keep the filled ramekins covered in the fridge — this is the ideal dinner-party dessert because the work is all done before guests arrive.
  • ◆No ramekins? A standard muffin tin works: butter and cocoa six cups, fill two-thirds, and bake 9 to 10 minutes at the same temperature.
  • ◆Use a chocolate bar you like the taste of, between 60 and 70 percent. Chips resist melting and anything over 75 percent makes a bitter, thin center.
  • ◆If your first cake comes out fully set, drop the bake to 11 minutes for the next batch. Ovens run differently and 60 seconds genuinely changes the result.

Lattice-Top Apple Pie⏱ 7 hr 15 min🍽 8 servingsAdvanced▾

An all-butter crust, two kinds of apple so the filling has both structure and sauce, and a woven top that looks like you have done this a hundred times. Plan a lazy afternoon for it.

Weekend ProjectHolidayFrom Scratch
Prep
45 min
Cook
1 hr 10 min
Total
7 hr 15 min
Serves
8 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

All-butter double crust

Apple filling

Finishing

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Cut the butter into flour
    Whisk the flour, sugar, and salt in a large bowl, add the cold butter cubes, and toss to coat. Using your fingertips or a pastry cutter, flatten each cube into a rough disc until the mixture looks like a mix of large flakes and pea-sized pieces. Those visible butter shards steam in the oven and blow the dough into flaky layers, so leaving them intact is the entire point — do not work it to a uniform sandy texture.
  2. Bring the dough together
    Stir the vinegar into 6 tbsp (90 ml) ice water, drizzle it over the flour a few tablespoons at a time, and toss with a fork after each addition. Add water only until the dough holds together when you squeeze a handful — usually 6 to 8 tbsp total, more on a dry day. The vinegar slightly slows gluten development, which keeps the crust tender. Overworked, wet dough bakes up tough and shrinks in the pan.
  3. Chill two discs
    Divide the dough into two portions, one slightly larger for the bottom, and press each into a flat 1-in (2.5 cm) thick disc. Wrap in plastic and refrigerate at least 1 hour or up to 3 days. Chilling lets the flour hydrate and, critically, re-firms the butter so it does not smear when you roll. Warm dough is the reason crusts come out greasy instead of flaky.
  4. Macerate the apples
    Toss the sliced apples with both sugars, the cinnamon, nutmeg, salt, and lemon juice in a large bowl and let them sit for 30 minutes. They will release 1/2 cup (120 ml) or more of liquid, which is exactly what you want out of them now rather than inside the pie later. Using two apple varieties means the Granny Smiths hold their shape while the Honeycrisps soften into sauce.
  5. Drain and thicken
    Drain the apples in a colander set over a bowl and reserve the juice. Boil that juice in a small saucepan over medium-high heat until it reduces to about 1/3 cup (80 ml) and turns syrupy, roughly 5 minutes, then let it cool for a few minutes. Whisk the cornstarch into the cooled syrup, pour it back over the apples, and toss. This is how you get concentrated apple flavor and a filling that slices instead of floods.
  6. Roll the bottom crust
    On a lightly floured counter, roll the larger disc into a 13-in (33 cm) circle about 1/8 in (3 mm) thick, rotating a quarter turn after every few passes and re-flouring underneath as needed. Drape it into a 9-in (23 cm) pie plate by folding it over the rolling pin, then ease it down into the corners without stretching it. Stretched dough springs back and shrinks down the sides during baking. Trim the overhang to 1 in (2.5 cm) and chill the shell.
  7. Cut the lattice strips
    Roll the second disc into a 12-in (30 cm) circle and cut it into ten strips about 1 1/4 in (3 cm) wide with a pizza wheel and a ruler. Slide the strips on a parchment-lined sheet into the fridge for 15 minutes. Cold strips are firm and easy to lift; warm ones stretch, tear, and stick to everything. Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) now with a rack in the lower third and a foil-lined sheet pan on it.
  8. Fill the pie
    Pile the apples into the chilled shell, mounding them slightly higher in the center and pressing them down firmly with your palm to eliminate air pockets. Big gaps collapse during baking and leave a hollow dome under the crust. Scatter the cubed butter over the top, which enriches the filling as it melts.
  9. Weave the lattice
    Lay five strips across the pie in one direction, evenly spaced. Fold back every other strip halfway, lay a strip perpendicular across the center, and unfold the strips over it; then fold back the alternate strips, lay the next perpendicular strip, and repeat outward in both directions. Trim the ends flush with the pie plate rim, press them into the bottom overhang, and fold the whole edge under and crimp. If the dough gets soft and sticky while weaving, slide the pie into the fridge for 10 minutes and pick up where you left off.
  10. Chill, wash, and sugar
    Freeze the assembled pie for 20 minutes — this is the step that keeps the lattice sharp and the edges from slumping. Brush the crust evenly with the egg-cream wash, getting into the crimped edge, then sprinkle the demerara sugar over everything. The wash gives you the deep mahogany shine and the coarse sugar adds crunch and sparkle.
  11. Bake hot, then moderate
    Bake on the preheated sheet pan at 425°F (220°C) for 25 minutes to set the crust and start the bottom browning, then reduce the oven to 375°F (190°C) and bake 35 to 45 minutes more. It is done when the crust is deep golden brown all over and the juices bubble thickly and slowly through the lattice at the center, not just at the edges. Thin, fast bubbles mean the starch has not cooked out yet. If the edges darken too fast, cover them with a foil ring.
  12. Cool at least 4 hours
    Set the pie on a wire rack and leave it alone for a minimum of 4 hours, ideally overnight. The cornstarch only finishes setting as the filling drops below about 150°F (65°C), so a warm pie will run all over the plate no matter how well you baked it. Air circulating under the rack also keeps the bottom crust from steaming itself soft.
Know when it is done
Bake at 425°F (220°C) for 25 minutes, then 375°F (190°C) for 35 to 45 minutes until the center juices bubble thickly; the filling should read about 195°F (91°C) so the cornstarch fully activates. Cool below 150°F (65°C), at least 4 hours, before slicing.
Serve it with
A scoop of vanilla ice cream or a wedge of sharp cheddar, with hot coffee.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Grate the butter on the large holes of a box grater straight from the freezer if you find hand-cutting fussy — it gives you even flakes fast and keeps everything cold.
  • ◆Blind-baking is not needed, but the preheated sheet pan is: direct bottom heat is what prevents the dreaded soggy bottom.
  • ◆Make the dough up to 3 days ahead in the fridge or 3 months ahead in the freezer. Thaw frozen discs overnight in the fridge before rolling.
  • ◆Never use only Granny Smiths. All-tart apples stay crunchy and one-note; the second sweeter variety is what makes the filling taste like pie.
  • ◆Leftover pie keeps 2 days loosely covered at room temperature. Reheat slices at 350°F (175°C) for 12 minutes to re-crisp the crust — the microwave makes it limp.

Key Lime Pie⏱ 4 hr 45 min🍽 8 servingsEasy▾

Tart, cool, and creamy on a toasted graham crust — four ingredients in the filling and fifteen minutes in the oven. It tastes like the best possible version of summer.

Make AheadSummerBeginner Friendly
Prep
20 min
Cook
25 min
Total
4 hr 45 min
Serves
8 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Graham crust

Lime filling

Whipped topping

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Make the crust
    Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Pulse the graham crackers in a food processor to fine crumbs, or seal them in a zip bag and crush with a rolling pin, then stir in the sugar and salt. Pour in the melted butter and mix until every crumb is damp and the mixture clumps when squeezed. If it feels dry and loose, add 1 more tbsp (14 g) melted butter — a dry crust falls apart the moment you cut it.
  2. Press it firmly
    Tip the crumbs into a 9-in (23 cm) pie plate and press them evenly across the bottom and up the sides, using the flat bottom of a measuring cup to compact them. Pay attention to the corner where the bottom meets the side, where crumbs pile up thick and then crumble. A tightly packed crust holds its shape under a heavy filling.
  3. Bake the crust
    Bake the crust for 10 minutes, until it smells toasty and looks slightly darker at the edges. This sets the butter and sugar into a solid shell and adds a real toasted flavor you do not get from a chilled-only crust. Set it on a rack while you make the filling; it does not need to cool completely.
  4. Whip zest into the yolks
    In a medium bowl, beat the egg yolks and lime zest with a hand mixer on medium-high for 3 to 4 minutes, until the yolks turn pale yellow and thicken visibly. Beating the zest with the yolks bruises the peel and releases its oils into the fat, which is where lime flavor actually lives. Bottled juice alone tastes flat; zest is what makes this taste like fresh limes.
  5. Add the condensed milk
    Pour in the sweetened condensed milk and beat on medium for 3 minutes until the mixture is thick, glossy, and pale. Do not substitute evaporated milk, which has no sugar and will not set. This is the whole structure of the pie, so give it the full time.
  6. Add the juice last
    With the mixer on low, pour in the lime juice and salt and beat just until combined, about 30 seconds. The acid immediately starts to thicken the condensed milk — you will feel the batter tighten. Add the juice at the end so the mixture does not set before you get it into the shell.
  7. Fill and bake
    Pour the filling into the warm crust and smooth the top with a spatula. Bake at 350°F (175°C) for 15 to 17 minutes, until the filling is set around the edges and the center 2 in (5 cm) jiggles slightly as one piece when you nudge the pan. The surface should look matte, not shiny, and it must not brown or crack. Baking also brings the yolks to a safe 160°F (71°C).
  8. Cool then chill
    Cool the pie on a rack to room temperature, about 1 hour, then refrigerate uncovered for at least 3 hours or overnight. It will look soft when it comes out of the oven and it firms up entirely in the fridge. Chilling it uncovered first prevents condensation from beading on the surface; cover it once cold.
  9. Whip the cream
    In a cold bowl, whip the heavy cream, powdered sugar, and vanilla on medium-high to firm peaks, 2 to 3 minutes — the peaks should stand with just a slight droop at the tip. Powdered sugar contains a little cornstarch, which stabilizes the cream so it holds for hours instead of weeping. Stop as soon as it holds; another 20 seconds turns it grainy.
  10. Top and serve cold
    Spread or pipe the whipped cream over the chilled pie and finish with a shower of lime zest. Slice with a knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry between cuts, and serve straight from the fridge — this pie is best cold and firm. It keeps, covered, for 3 days.
Know when it is done
Bake the filling at 350°F (175°C) for 15 to 17 minutes until it reaches 160°F (71°C) in the center, which sets the yolks safely; the center should still jiggle slightly as one piece. Chill to 40°F (4°C) before slicing.
Serve it with
Strong iced tea or a cold Mexican lager on a hot afternoon.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Bottled key lime juice is genuinely fine here and saves you juicing twenty tiny limes. What you cannot skip is fresh zest, and regular Persian limes zest beautifully.
  • ◆If you only have regular limes, use their juice — the pie will be slightly less floral but still excellent. Do not use lemon juice; the balance is different.
  • ◆Make the whole pie a day ahead and add the whipped cream within 2 hours of serving so it stays fluffy and clean-looking.
  • ◆For a firmer, more sliceable pie, chill overnight. Three hours is the minimum but the texture at eight hours is noticeably better.
  • ◆Do not skip baking the filling. The bake sets the eggs and brings them to a safe temperature — the no-bake versions rely on acid alone and are softer and less stable.

Brown Sugar Banana Bread⏱ 2 hr🍽 Makes 1 loaf, 10 slicesEasy▾

Moist, deeply banana-forward, with a crackly sugar top and a tender crumb from a little sour cream. It is the best possible use for the three sad bananas on your counter.

One BowlBeginner FriendlyFreezer Friendly

Serves
Makes 1 loaf, 10 slices
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Wet

Dry

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Heat the oven and prep the pan
    Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a rack in the lower third, which keeps the top from browning before the center cooks. Butter a 9x5-in (23x13 cm) loaf pan and line it with a parchment sling that hangs over the long sides. A metal pan browns better than glass; if you only have glass, drop the oven to 325°F (165°C) and add about 10 minutes.
  2. Use bananas that look ruined
    Your bananas should be at least half covered in brown or black spots and soft enough to mash with a fork with no effort. Underripe yellow bananas have starch that has not converted to sugar, and the loaf will taste bland and pasty. If yours are not there yet, roast them in their skins at 300°F (150°C) for 20 minutes until black and syrupy, then cool before using.
  3. Mash and mix the wet
    Mash the bananas in a large bowl with a fork until mostly smooth with a few small lumps left for texture. Whisk in the melted butter and brown sugar until glossy, then the eggs one at a time, then the sour cream and vanilla. Make sure the butter is cooled to warm rather than hot — hot butter cooks the eggs into little threads.
  4. Whisk the dry separately
    In another bowl, whisk the flour, baking soda, salt, and cinnamon for 15 seconds so the baking soda is evenly dispersed. Clumped soda leaves bitter metallic pockets and creates uneven rise. Measure the flour by spooning and leveling, or weigh 220 g — too much flour is the main cause of dry banana bread.
  5. Fold, do not beat
    Add the dry ingredients to the wet and fold with a rubber spatula just until the last streak of flour disappears, about 15 strokes. The batter will look thick and slightly lumpy, and that is correct. Overmixing develops gluten and gives you a tough loaf with a long tunnel down the middle. Fold in the nuts with two final strokes if using.
  6. Fill and top
    Scrape the batter into the prepared pan and smooth the top, then run the tip of a knife down the center lengthwise about 1/2 in (1 cm) deep. That shallow line encourages the loaf to split evenly along the middle instead of cracking randomly. Sprinkle the turbinado sugar over the whole surface for a crunchy lid.
  7. Bake and tent
    Bake for 55 to 65 minutes. At the 40-minute mark, check the color — if the top is already deep brown, lay a piece of foil loosely over it for the rest of the bake. Banana bread has a lot of sugar and browns well before the middle is cooked, so tenting is often necessary.
  8. Test for doneness properly
    The loaf is done when a skewer inserted into the center comes out with a few moist crumbs but no wet batter, and an instant-read thermometer reads 200 to 205°F (93 to 96°C). Do not judge by the top alone; a beautifully domed loaf can be raw in the middle. If the skewer is wet, give it another 5 minutes and test again.
  9. Cool in the pan, then out
    Cool the loaf in the pan on a wire rack for 15 minutes, then use the parchment sling to lift it out and cool it directly on the rack. Leaving it in the pan longer traps steam against the sides and makes them gummy. Cool at least 30 more minutes before slicing; hot banana bread tears and compresses under the knife.
  10. Slice and store
    Cut thick slices with a serrated knife using a gentle sawing motion. Store the loaf wrapped in foil or in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 4 days — it is honestly better on day two once the flavor settles. It also freezes well; wrap slices individually and toast them straight from frozen.
Know when it is done
Bake at 350°F (175°C) for 55 to 65 minutes until the center reads 200 to 205°F (93 to 96°C) and a skewer shows moist crumbs but no wet batter.
Serve it with
A thick slice toasted with salted butter and a hot cup of coffee.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Freeze overripe bananas in their skins as they turn. Thaw and squeeze them out when you have three, and the extra liquid they release only makes the loaf moister.
  • ◆Add 3/4 cup (130 g) chocolate chips with the nuts if you want it to feel like dessert rather than breakfast.
  • ◆Sour cream can be swapped for buttermilk, plain yogurt, or even 1/4 cup (60 ml) whole milk with 1/2 tsp lemon juice — you just want a little acid and fat for tenderness.
  • ◆Do not double the recipe into one pan; make two loaves. A deeper batter burns on the outside before the middle sets.
  • ◆For muffins, divide into 12 lined cups and bake at 375°F (190°C) for 18 to 22 minutes to the same internal 200°F (93°C).

Carrot Cake with Cream Cheese Frosting⏱ 3 hr 25 min🍽 12 servingsMedium▾

A moist, spiced two-layer cake made with oil so it stays tender for days, under a tangy cream cheese frosting that is not too sweet. This is the birthday cake people ask for again.

BirthdayLayer CakeMake Ahead

12 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Dry

Wet and add-ins

Cream cheese frosting

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Prep the pans
    Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a rack in the center. Grease two 9-in (23 cm) round cake pans, line the bottoms with parchment circles, and grease the parchment too. Carrot cake is moist and sticky, and a lined bottom is the difference between a clean release and half a layer left in the pan.
  2. Grate the carrots finely
    Peel the carrots and grate them on the small or medium holes of a box grater, or use the fine shredding disc of a food processor. Coarsely shredded carrot stays fibrous and stringy in the finished cake, while fine shreds melt into the crumb and release their moisture into the batter. You need 3 packed cups (330 g); do not use pre-shredded carrots from a bag, which are dry and woody.
  3. Whisk the dry ingredients
    In a medium bowl, whisk the flour, baking soda, baking powder, cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, and salt together for 20 seconds. Mixing the leaveners and spices thoroughly now means you can mix the batter minimally later. Any clump of baking soda that survives will taste soapy in someone's slice.
  4. Emulsify sugars, oil, and eggs
    In a large bowl, whisk both sugars with the oil for 30 seconds, then whisk in the eggs one at a time until the mixture is smooth, glossy, and slightly thickened, about 1 minute total. Add the vanilla and applesauce. Oil-based cakes need no creaming, which is why this comes together by hand — and oil stays liquid at fridge temperature, which is why the cake stays moist for days.
  5. Combine and fold in carrots
    Add the dry ingredients to the wet and fold with a spatula until just barely combined, with a few streaks of flour still visible. Add the carrots and 1 cup (100 g) pecans and fold 8 to 10 more strokes until everything is evenly distributed and no dry flour remains. Finishing the mixing with the add-ins means you never overwork the batter.
  6. Divide and bake
    Divide the batter evenly between the pans — this batch runs about 1,600 g, so roughly 800 g each if you weigh them — and smooth the tops. The pans will be a little over half full, which is exactly right for a cake that rises this gently. Bake for 30 to 35 minutes, until the cakes spring back when pressed lightly in the center and a toothpick comes out with a moist crumb or two. The internal temperature should read about 205°F (96°C). Rotate the pans front to back at 20 minutes for even color.
  7. Cool completely
    Cool the cakes in their pans on a rack for 15 minutes, then run a knife around the edge, turn them out, peel off the parchment, and cool completely on the rack, at least 1 hour. Frosting a warm cake with cream cheese frosting is a guaranteed slide-off — the butter melts and the whole thing slumps. You can speed this up with 30 minutes in the fridge.
  8. Beat the frosting base
    Beat the cream cheese and butter together with the paddle attachment on medium for 2 minutes, until completely smooth with no lumps, scraping down the bowl twice. Both should be at cool room temperature, around 65°F (18°C) — cold cream cheese gives you lumps and overly soft butter gives you soup. Block cream cheese only; the tub kind has too much water.
  9. Finish the frosting
    Add the sifted powdered sugar in three additions on low speed, then the vanilla and salt, and beat on medium for just 1 minute until fluffy. Do not overbeat cream cheese frosting — extended mixing breaks it down and it turns runny and soupy. If it is too soft to spread, chill it for 20 minutes and stir it smooth again.
  10. Level and fill
    If the layers domed, shave the tops flat with a long serrated knife. Set one layer on a plate or stand, anchoring it with a spoonful of frosting underneath, and spread about 1 cup (250 g) of frosting to the edges. Top with the second layer, bottom side up, so you get a perfectly flat top surface to work with.
  11. Frost the cake
    Spread a thin crumb coat over the top and sides and refrigerate for 20 minutes to lock the crumbs in place. Then apply the rest of the frosting in generous swoops with an offset spatula, finishing with a spiral pattern on top. Press the reserved 1/2 cup (50 g) chopped pecans around the bottom third of the sides, which hides any imperfections and looks intentional.
  12. Chill, then serve at room temp
    Refrigerate the frosted cake for at least 30 minutes to set the frosting, then let it stand at room temperature for 30 minutes before slicing. Cold cream cheese frosting is stiff and mutes the spices, while room-temperature cake is soft and fragrant. Slice with a hot dry knife, wiping between cuts.
Know when it is done
Bake at 350°F (175°C) for 30 to 35 minutes until the center reads about 205°F (96°C) and springs back to the touch. Keep the frosted cake refrigerated at 40°F (4°C) or below since the frosting is dairy-based.
Serve it with
Hot black tea or coffee — the bitterness balances the sweet frosting perfectly.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Cream cheese frosting must be refrigerated. Store the cake covered in the fridge for up to 5 days and pull slices out 30 minutes before serving.
  • ◆Bake the layers up to 2 days ahead; wrap the cooled cakes tightly in plastic and keep at room temperature, or freeze up to 2 months.
  • ◆If you like raisins, fold in 3/4 cup (110 g) with the carrots; soak them in hot water for 10 minutes and drain first so they stay plump. Either way, do toast the pecans — 8 minutes at 350°F (175°C) doubles their flavor and keeps them crunchy in a moist cake.
  • ◆For a sheet cake, bake in a 9x13-in (23x33 cm) pan at 350°F (175°C) for 38 to 45 minutes and frost right in the pan. Same batter, far less fuss.
  • ◆If the frosting turns loose, it is nearly always temperature. Chill the whole bowl for 20 minutes and stir gently by hand rather than adding more sugar.

A deeply dark, tender cake made with hot coffee and buttermilk, poured over with glossy ganache while it is still pourable. It is the cake that makes people go quiet for a second.

BirthdayLayer CakeCrowd Pleaser
Prep
25 min
Cook

Total
3 hr
Serves
12 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Dry

Wet

Ganache

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Prep the pans and oven
    Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a rack in the center. Grease two 9-in (23 cm) round pans, line the bottoms with parchment, and grease the parchment. This batter is very thin and very moist, so a parchment liner is not optional if you want the layers to release cleanly.
  2. Whisk the dry ingredients
    Sift or whisk the flour, cocoa, sugar, baking soda, baking powder, and salt together in a large bowl until uniform in color with no dark cocoa streaks, about 30 seconds. Cocoa clumps stubbornly and those clumps stay dry and bitter in the finished crumb. Dutch-process cocoa gives the darkest color and the smoothest flavor here.
  3. Add the wet ingredients
    Add the eggs, buttermilk, oil, and vanilla and beat on medium speed for 2 minutes, or whisk hard by hand for 2 minutes, until the batter is smooth and thick. Room-temperature dairy and eggs blend without seizing the oil. Scrape the bowl once halfway through to catch dry pockets at the bottom.
  4. Stir in the hot coffee
    With the mixer on low, pour in the hot coffee in a steady stream and mix just until combined, about 30 seconds. The batter will become alarmingly thin, like chocolate milk — that is exactly right and it produces a very moist crumb. Hot liquid blooms the cocoa for a deeper flavor, and no, the cake will not taste like coffee.
  5. Divide and bake
    Pour the batter evenly into the two pans, about 700 g each — the full batch weighs roughly 1,400 g, and a kitchen scale is the only reliable way to get two layers the same height when the batter is this loose. Bake for 30 to 35 minutes, until the tops spring back when lightly pressed and a toothpick in the center comes out with a few moist crumbs. The internal temperature should read 205 to 210°F (96 to 99°C). Do not open the oven before 25 minutes; this batter is thin and a rush of cold air can sink the middle.
  6. Cool completely
    Cool the layers in their pans on a rack for 15 minutes, then invert onto the rack, peel off the parchment, and cool completely, at least 1 hour. Because the crumb is so moist it is fragile while warm, so handle the layers with a flat plate or cake board underneath. Chilling the cooled layers for 20 minutes makes them much easier to frost.
  7. Chop the chocolate finely
    Chop the chocolate into pieces no bigger than a pea and pile them in a heatproof bowl. Even, small pieces melt at the same rate in the hot cream, which is the key to a smooth ganache. Big chunks leave you stirring and stirring, and the ganache cools too far before it is emulsified.
  8. Make the ganache
    Heat the cream in a small saucepan until it just begins to simmer at the edges, about 190°F (88°C), then pour it over the chocolate along with the corn syrup and salt. Let it sit undisturbed for 3 minutes so the heat penetrates the chocolate, then stir slowly from the center outward with a spatula until it comes together glossy and smooth. Stir in the softened butter last for extra shine. Stirring too early or too vigorously beats in air and dulls the finish.
  9. Let the ganache thicken
    Let the ganache stand at room temperature for 20 to 40 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it thickens to the consistency of soft pudding and holds a faint ribbon. Too warm and it runs straight off the cake; too cool and it drags the crumb. If it sets too firm, warm the bowl over a pan of hot water for 20 seconds and stir.
  10. Fill and stack
    Level the layers with a serrated knife if they domed. Set the first layer on a plate, spread about 3/4 cup (200 g) of thickened ganache over it right to the edge, and top with the second layer bottom side up. Press down gently and evenly so the layers sit level; a tilted cake only gets worse once you glaze it.
  11. Glaze the top and sides
    Pour the remaining ganache onto the center of the cake and nudge it outward with an offset spatula, letting it fall over the sides in thick curtains. Work quickly with as few passes as possible, since repeated spreading dulls the shine and picks up crumbs. A few deliberate swoops on top look better than a fussy attempt at perfectly smooth.
  12. Set and serve
    Let the cake stand at room temperature for 30 minutes so the ganache sets to a soft, sliceable shell — or refrigerate 15 minutes if your kitchen is warm. Slice with a long knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry between cuts. Serve at room temperature, where the crumb is softest and the chocolate flavor is fullest.
Know when it is done
Bake at 350°F (175°C) for 30 to 35 minutes until the center reads 205 to 210°F (96 to 99°C). Heat the cream for the ganache to about 190°F (88°C) — just simmering at the edges, never boiling.
Serve it with
Cold milk, or a glass of Cabernet if this is the end of a real dinner.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆No buttermilk? Stir 1 tbsp (15 ml) lemon juice or white vinegar into 1 cup (240 ml) whole milk and let it sit 10 minutes. The acid is what activates the baking soda, so do not substitute plain milk.
  • ◆Use hot water instead of coffee if you prefer, but coffee makes the chocolate taste more like chocolate — it is a flavor amplifier, not a flavor.
  • ◆Bake the layers up to 2 days ahead and wrap them tightly at room temperature, or freeze up to 2 months. Ganache can be made 3 days ahead and gently rewarmed.
  • ◆If the ganache breaks and looks oily, whisk in 1 tbsp (15 ml) warm cream at a time until it comes back together — it almost always does.
  • ◆For cupcakes, fill 24 lined cups two-thirds full and bake at 350°F (175°C) for 18 to 20 minutes, then dip the tops in thickened ganache.

Vanilla Bean Panna Cotta with Berries⏱ 4 hr 25 min🍽 6 servingsMedium▾

Barely set, wobbling, pure cream and vanilla with a bright berry sauce spooned over. Fifteen minutes of work and the fridge does everything else.

Make AheadNo BakeDinner Party
Prep
15 min
Cook
10 min
Total
4 hr 25 min
Serves
6 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Panna cotta

Berry sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Bloom the gelatin
    Sprinkle the gelatin evenly over the 3 tbsp (45 ml) cold water in a small bowl and let it sit undisturbed for 5 to 10 minutes. It will absorb the water and turn into a solid, wrinkled, applesauce-like mass — that is called blooming, and it is what lets the gelatin dissolve smoothly later. Sprinkle rather than dump, or you will get a dry lump in the middle that never hydrates.
  2. Warm the cream
    Combine the cream, milk, sugar, salt, vanilla seeds, and the empty pod in a saucepan over medium heat. Warm it, stirring to dissolve the sugar, until it reaches 175°F (80°C) — steam rising and small bubbles just forming around the rim. Do not let it boil; boiling changes the flavor of the cream and can weaken the gelatin's setting power.
  3. Melt in the gelatin
    Take the pan off the heat, add the bloomed gelatin, and whisk for 30 to 60 seconds until it has completely dissolved. Rub a little of the liquid between your fingers — if you feel any grains at all, keep whisking over low heat without boiling. Undissolved gelatin means a rubbery bottom layer and a soupy top.
  4. Steep and strain
    Cover the pan and let the mixture steep for 10 minutes to draw out more vanilla flavor, then remove the pod and pour everything through a fine-mesh sieve into a pitcher with a spout. Straining catches any stray gelatin bits and bits of pod. Stir gently for another minute so it cools slightly and the vanilla seeds stay suspended rather than sinking to the bottom.
  5. Portion into glasses
    Divide the mixture among six 6-oz (180 ml) glasses, ramekins, or small bowls — you have about 720 ml, so roughly 120 ml each, which fills them about two-thirds full. One packet of gelatin sets exactly this much liquid to a soft, spoonable wobble; stretch the same packet over more cream and you get a panna cotta that never quite firms up. If you plan to unmold them, lightly oil the ramekins first with a neutral oil on a paper towel. Serving in glasses is easier and looks lovely with the sauce on top, so there is no shame in skipping the unmolding.
  6. Chill until set
    Cool the glasses on the counter for 20 minutes, then cover loosely and refrigerate for at least 4 hours or overnight. Panna cotta sets slowly and gently; at 2 hours it will still be soupy in the center. It holds well in the fridge for 3 days, so this is a genuinely good make-ahead dessert.
  7. Make the berry sauce
    Toss half the strawberries with the sugar, lemon juice, and salt in a small saucepan and cook over medium heat for 5 to 7 minutes, until they break down and the liquid thickens slightly and coats a spoon. Take it off the heat and stir in the remaining raw berries so you get both a syrupy base and fresh, bright pieces. Cool completely before spooning it over the cold panna cotta.
  8. Check the set
    A properly set panna cotta wobbles noticeably when you shake the glass and holds the impression of a spoon without being firm or bouncy. If it is soupy after 6 hours, the gelatin was under-dissolved or the mixture boiled. If it is rubbery and springs back, there was too much gelatin — use 2 tsp next time.
  9. Unmold, if you like
    To unmold, dip a ramekin in hot tap water for 8 to 10 seconds, run a thin knife around the very edge, set an inverted plate on top, and flip. Give it one firm shake and it should drop with a soft sigh. If nothing happens after two attempts, dip it for another 5 seconds; too long in hot water and the outside melts to a puddle.
  10. Serve cold
    Spoon the cooled berry sauce over each panna cotta right before serving and finish with a few flakes of sea salt or a mint leaf. Serve cold, straight from the fridge, since it softens quickly at room temperature. Add the sauce at the last minute so the surface stays clean and the fruit stays bright.
Know when it is done
Warm the cream mixture to 175°F (80°C) — steaming with small bubbles at the edge — and never let it boil, or the gelatin weakens. Chill at 40°F (4°C) or below for at least 4 hours until it wobbles but holds a spoon mark.
Serve it with
A glass of Prosecco or a cup of espresso, with extra berries on the side.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆For a firmer panna cotta you can unmold confidently, increase the gelatin to 3 tsp (9 g). For a barely-there, spoonable texture served in glasses, 2 1/4 tsp (7 g) is right.
  • ◆Vanilla bean paste is the best value here — it gives you the visible seeds and true vanilla flavor without buying a whole pod.
  • ◆Infuse the cream with other flavors while it steeps: a wide strip of lemon peel, 2 tbsp (10 g) coffee beans, or a cinnamon stick all work beautifully.
  • ◆Make it up to 3 days ahead and keep it covered in the fridge. Add the sauce only when you serve.
  • ◆If you are avoiding gelatin, agar agar works but sets much firmer and needs to boil for 2 minutes — use 1 tsp (2 g) powdered agar for this quantity and expect a sliceable rather than wobbly texture.

Churros with Thick Chocolate Sauce⏱ 45 min🍽 Makes 16 churros, 4 servingsAdvanced▾

Crisp ridged sticks rolled in cinnamon sugar, with a chocolate sauce thick enough to stand a churro in. Fried right, they are crackly outside and hollow-light inside.

Deep FriedServe ImmediatelyWeekend Treat
Prep
20 min
Cook
25 min
Total
45 min
Serves
Makes 16 churros, 4 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Churro dough

Frying and coating

Chocolate sauce

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Set up before you start
    Fit a large piping bag with a large closed star tip (Ateco 848 or a Wilton 1M), stand it in a tall glass, and line a sheet pan with paper towels. Mix the coating sugar and cinnamon in a wide shallow dish. Frying moves fast and the dough is easiest to pipe while warm, so having everything in place before you turn on the heat genuinely matters here.
  2. Boil the liquid
    Combine the water, butter, sugar, and salt in a medium saucepan over medium-high heat and bring it to a full rolling boil, stirring until the butter has completely melted. Do not let it simmer for long before adding the flour, because evaporation changes the water-to-flour ratio and the dough will come out stiff. Everything should hit the boil together.
  3. Cook the paste
    Dump in all the flour at once and stir hard with a wooden spoon until it forms a shaggy ball, then keep cooking over medium heat for 2 minutes, mashing and turning the dough against the pan. It will smooth out, pull cleanly from the sides, and leave a thin film on the bottom of the pan. That film is your signal — you are drying the dough so it can absorb the eggs.
  4. Cool it before the eggs
    Transfer the dough to a mixing bowl and beat it with a paddle or wooden spoon for 2 minutes to release steam, until it is warm rather than hot, about 140°F (60°C). Adding eggs to scalding dough scrambles them and ruins the texture. The dough should no longer steam heavily when you stop stirring.
  5. Beat in the eggs
    Add the eggs one at a time, beating until each is fully absorbed before adding the next, then beat in the vanilla. The dough will look slick and separated after each egg and then come back together — keep going, this always happens. Finished dough should be thick, glossy, and fall from the spoon in a slow V-shaped ribbon.
  6. Make the chocolate sauce
    Whisk the cornstarch into 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the milk in a small bowl, then heat the remaining milk, cream, and sugar in a small saucepan until steaming. Whisk in the cornstarch slurry and simmer 1 minute until slightly thickened, then take it off the heat, add the chopped chocolate and salt, and let it sit 2 minutes before whisking smooth. Spanish chocolate a la taza is meant to be thick enough to coat a churro heavily — keep it warm over the lowest heat.
  7. Heat the oil precisely
    Pour all 8 cups (1.9 L) of oil into a heavy 4-quart (3.8 L) Dutch oven or deep pot about 9 in (23 cm) across, which gives you the 2 in (5 cm) depth a churro needs to float rather than sit on the bottom, and heat it over medium to 360°F (182°C) on a clip-on thermometer. Use a wider pot and you will need noticeably more oil to reach that depth. Temperature is everything here: below 340°F (171°C) the churros absorb oil and go greasy, and above 375°F (190°C) they brown before the inside cooks and can split violently. Never fill the pot more than halfway with oil.
  8. Fill the piping bag
    Scrape the warm dough into the prepared piping bag and twist the top closed, pushing the dough down to eliminate air pockets. Trapped air causes the churro to burst in hot oil and spit at you. Work while the dough is still warm, since it stiffens considerably as it cools.
  9. Pipe and fry in batches
    Pipe 6-in (15 cm) lengths directly over the oil, snipping the dough free with kitchen scissors, and fry only 4 at a time so the oil temperature does not crash. Fry for 2 to 3 minutes per side, turning once with tongs or a spider, until they are deep golden brown all over. Pale churros are raw inside; you want a genuinely dark gold. Check the oil temperature between batches and let it recover to 360°F (182°C).
  10. Drain and coat
    Lift the churros out to the paper towels for 20 seconds only, then roll them in the cinnamon sugar while they are still hot and slightly oily. Waiting even a minute means the sugar will not stick. Do not let them sit on the towels long enough to steam, or the ridges soften and you lose the crackle.
  11. Serve immediately
    Pile the churros on a plate and serve at once with the warm chocolate for dipping. Churros are at their absolute best within 10 minutes of frying and are noticeably worse after 30 — this is a dessert you make while everyone hovers in the kitchen. Reheat any leftovers at 400°F (200°C) for 4 minutes to bring back some crispness.
  12. Cool and store the oil safely
    Turn off the heat and let the oil cool completely in the pot, at least 2 hours, before doing anything with it. Strain it through a coffee filter or fine sieve into a sealed jar and reuse it two or three times for sweets. Never pour hot oil, and never pour any oil down the drain.
Know when it is done
Fry in oil held at 360°F (182°C) — below 340°F (171°C) they turn greasy and above 375°F (190°C) they burn outside while raw inside. Cook 2 to 3 minutes per side until deep golden all over.
Serve it with
Thick hot chocolate for dipping, or strong coffee with a splash of milk.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆The closed star tip is not decorative — those deep ridges create surface area that crisps, and a round tip gives you a doughnut stick instead of a churro.
  • ◆If your piping bag threatens to burst, use two bags doubled up or a sturdy canvas bag. This dough is thick and takes real hand strength to pipe.
  • ◆For a make-ahead version, pipe the churros onto a parchment-lined tray, freeze solid, then fry straight from frozen at 350°F (177°C) for about 4 minutes per side.
  • ◆Keep a lid nearby whenever you fry. If the oil ever smokes or catches, slide the lid on and turn off the heat — never use water.
  • ◆Churros that split open in the oil usually mean the oil was too hot or there were air pockets in the bag. Drop the temperature by 10 degrees and press the dough down firmly next batch.

No-Churn Vanilla Ice Cream⏱ 6 hr 15 min🍽 Makes about 1 1/2 quarts, 8 servingsEasy▾

Two ingredients, no machine, no custard to cook — just whipped cream folded into condensed milk and frozen. It scoops like real ice cream and takes fifteen minutes of work.

No MachineMake AheadSummer
Prep
15 min
Cook
6 hr freeze
Total
6 hr 15 min
Serves
Makes about 1 1/2 quarts, 8 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Ice cream base

Optional add-ins, pick one

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Chill your equipment
    Put a large metal mixing bowl and the beaters in the freezer for 15 minutes before you start, and keep the cream in the fridge until the second you need it. Cream whips faster, higher, and more stably when everything is cold, because the fat globules stay firm enough to trap air. Warm cream can take twice as long and never reaches the same volume.
  2. Mix the sweet base
    In a separate medium bowl, whisk the sweetened condensed milk with the vanilla, salt, and vodka if using until completely smooth. Doing this first means you are not stirring a thick sticky liquid into delicate whipped cream later. The salt matters more than it sounds — without it, this reads as flatly sweet.
  3. Whip the cream to stiff peaks
    Whip the cold cream in the chilled bowl on medium-high for 2 to 3 minutes, until it holds stiff peaks that stand straight up when you lift the beaters. Stiff rather than soft peaks are essential here, since the whipped air is the only thing standing between you and a block of frozen milk. Stop the moment it looks thick and matte; a few seconds more and it turns grainy and starts becoming butter.
  4. Lighten the base
    Scoop about a cup of the whipped cream into the condensed milk mixture and stir it in without any care for deflating it. This sacrificial cup loosens the dense base so the rest folds in with far fewer strokes. It is a small step that saves you a lot of lost volume.
  5. Fold the rest together
    Add the lightened base back to the whipped cream in two additions, folding with a spatula — cut down the center, sweep along the bottom, and lift over the top, rotating the bowl a quarter turn each time. Stop as soon as the color is uniform with no white or yellow streaks, about 20 folds. Stirring instead of folding knocks the air out and gives you a hard, icy result.
  6. Add your mix-ins
    Fold in solid add-ins like chocolate chips or crushed cookies with a few final strokes. For a swirl of jam or caramel, layer the base into the pan in thirds and dollop the sauce between layers, then drag a butter knife through it two or three times only. Over-swirling turns a beautiful ribbon into a muddy pink-brown blur.
  7. Transfer and cover
    Scrape the mixture into a 9x5-in (23x13 cm) metal loaf pan or a 1 1/2-quart (1.4 L) container and smooth the top. Press a piece of plastic wrap directly onto the surface before putting on a lid. Direct contact keeps air off the surface, and air is what forms those crunchy ice crystals on top of long-stored ice cream.
  8. Freeze until firm
    Freeze for at least 6 hours, ideally overnight, on a flat freezer shelf toward the back where the temperature is most stable, ideally 0°F (minus 18°C). It will look set at 3 hours but the center will still be soft and it will not scoop cleanly. A metal pan freezes faster and more evenly than glass or plastic.
  9. Temper before scooping
    Take the container out and let it sit on the counter for 5 minutes before serving. Ice cream scoops best around 10°F (minus 12°C), and straight from a cold freezer it can be hard enough to bend a spoon. Dip your scoop in hot water and shake off the drops between scoops for clean round balls.
  10. Store it well
    Keep it frozen for up to 2 weeks with the plastic pressed back onto the surface after each serving. The optional 2 tbsp (30 ml) of vodka lowers the freezing point just enough to keep it soft and scoopable in week two without any taste of alcohol. Beyond two weeks, freezer burn starts to win.
Know when it is done
No cooking required. Freeze at 0°F (minus 18°C) for at least 6 hours until firm, then let it sit 5 minutes at room temperature so it scoops at about 10°F (minus 12°C).
Serve it with
Warm brownies or a slice of peach cobbler, with hot fudge if you have it.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Do not substitute evaporated milk for sweetened condensed milk. They sound similar and are completely different products; evaporated milk has no sugar and will freeze rock hard.
  • ◆Coffee version: whisk 2 tbsp (10 g) instant espresso powder into the condensed milk. Chocolate version: whisk in 1/3 cup (28 g) cocoa powder and 2 tbsp (30 ml) hot water first to make a smooth paste.
  • ◆This is the ideal thing to make with kids or on a hot day when you do not want the oven on at all — no cooking of any kind.
  • ◆If your finished ice cream is icy rather than creamy, the cream was underwhipped or overfolded. Both mistakes remove the air that makes this work.
  • ◆A metal loaf pan chilled in the freezer beforehand shortens the freeze time by nearly an hour.

Peach Cobbler with Buttermilk Biscuits⏱ 1 hr 40 min🍽 8 servingsEasy▾

Jammy peaches bubbling under craggy buttermilk biscuits with crunchy sugar tops. It is the easiest good fruit dessert there is, and it is even better with ice cream melting into it.

SummerCrowd PleaserBeginner Friendly
Prep
20 min
Cook
50 min
Total
1 hr 40 min
Serves
8 servings
▶️ Watch it made📷 See real photos

1 Ingredients

Tap each one as you gather it.

Batch

Peach filling

Buttermilk biscuit topping

2 How to make it

Tap a step when it is done.

  1. Heat the oven and pick your dish
    Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C) with a rack in the center and set a foil-lined sheet pan on the rack below to catch drips. Use a 9x13-in (23x33 cm) baking dish or a 12-in (30 cm) cast iron skillet. Cobbler almost always bubbles over, and cleaning burnt sugar off the oven floor is a genuinely miserable job.
  2. Peel the peaches easily
    If the skins bother you, score a small X in the bottom of each peach, drop them into boiling water for 45 seconds, then straight into ice water — the skins will slip right off with your fingers. Ripe peaches should smell sweet at the stem and give slightly under gentle pressure. You can absolutely leave the skins on; they soften in the oven and add color.
  3. Toss the filling
    In a large bowl, toss the sliced peaches with both sugars, the cornstarch, lemon juice, cinnamon, salt, and vanilla until every slice is coated and no dry cornstarch remains. Let it sit for 10 minutes while you make the biscuits so the juices start to draw out and the starch hydrates. The lemon keeps the peaches tasting like fruit rather than just sweet.
  4. Whisk the biscuit dry mix
    In a separate bowl, whisk the flour, sugar, baking powder, and salt together for 15 seconds. Baking powder clumps in the box and an unmixed clump means one biscuit with a bitter yellow center. This mixture can be made ahead and kept in the fridge.
  5. Cut in cold butter
    Add the cold butter cubes and rub them into the flour with your fingertips or cut them in with a pastry blender until the largest pieces are the size of small peas. Work quickly and stop while you can still see distinct butter — those pieces steam in the oven and create the flaky layers. If your kitchen is warm, pop the bowl in the freezer for 10 minutes.
  6. Add the buttermilk
    Pour in the cold buttermilk and stir with a fork just until a shaggy, sticky dough forms with no dry patches, about 12 strokes. It should look rough and lumpy, not smooth — this is a drop biscuit dough, not a kneaded one. Overmixing gives you dense, tough biscuits instead of tender craggy ones.
  7. Fill the dish
    Pour the peaches and all their juices into the baking dish and spread them into an even layer. Do not drain the juice; the cornstarch needs that liquid to thicken into a glossy sauce. The dish will look very full, which is right, since the fruit collapses considerably as it bakes.
  8. Drop the biscuits
    Scoop the dough into 8 or 9 rough mounds of about 1/4 cup (60 g) each — the batch weighs roughly 520 g, so do not try to stretch it to a dozen — and drop them over the fruit, leaving gaps between them. Those gaps let steam escape so the fruit thickens instead of steaming the biscuit bottoms into paste. Sprinkle the turbinado sugar generously over every biscuit top.
  9. Bake until bubbling
    Bake for 40 to 50 minutes, until the biscuits are deep golden brown and the fruit is bubbling thickly around the edges and in the center. Fast, watery bubbling means the cornstarch has not activated yet, so keep going. The biscuits are done when their centers read 200 to 205°F (93 to 96°C), or when a skewer inserted into one comes out clean.
  10. Rest before serving
    Set the dish on a rack and let it rest for 20 to 30 minutes before serving. The filling thickens dramatically as it cools, and served straight from the oven it will be soupy and lava hot. Warm, not hot, is the sweet spot — serve it with cold vanilla ice cream so it melts into the juices.
Know when it is done
Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 40 to 50 minutes until the filling bubbles thickly and the biscuit centers read 200 to 205°F (93 to 96°C). Rest 20 to 30 minutes so the cornstarch sets.
Serve it with
A big scoop of vanilla ice cream, and sweet iced tea on the porch.

3 Chef tips

  • ◆Out of season, use 3 lb (1.4 kg) frozen sliced peaches straight from the freezer without thawing and add 1 extra tbsp (8 g) cornstarch plus 10 minutes of bake time.
  • ◆No buttermilk? Stir 2 tsp (10 ml) lemon juice into 3/4 cup (180 ml) milk and let it stand 10 minutes. The acid is what reacts with the baking powder for a tall, tender biscuit.
  • ◆Cobbler is best the day it is made but keeps 2 days covered in the fridge. Reheat at 350°F (175°C) for 15 minutes to bring the biscuit tops back to life.
  • ◆Underripe hard peaches will not soften enough in the oven. Ripen them on the counter in a paper bag for a day or two first.
  • ◆The same recipe works with blackberries, plums, or a mix of peaches and berries. Keep the total fruit at about 8 cups and adjust the sugar by how sweet the fruit tastes raw.
